en: The *Sphuṭanītikaraṇa* was composed by Bhāskarācārya at a single location; however, it was completed by Gaṇeśa Daivajña. This is the work of Śaṅkara. It represents the direction for the study of Indian astronomical calculation. The venerable Bhāskarācārya composed the treatise named *Siddhāntaśiromaṇi* in the year 1072 of the Śaka era. It possesses four chapters (*adhyāyas*). Among them, the first is the *Pāṭīgaṇita*, also known as the *Līlāvatī*.

The second is known as *Bījagaṇita* (Arithmetic of Seeds); the third is the *Grahagaṇita* (Calculation of Planets); and the fourth is celebrated as the *Golādhyāya* (Chapter on the Sphere). Through these four chapters, the teacher’s entire life was dedicated by those fortunate enough to be his disciples. The author of the commentary on this present work, titled *Gūḍhārthaprakāśinī*, is named Munīśvara, who is the son of Raṅganātha. His birth indeed took place in the year Śaka 1525.

His commentary on the *Līlāvatī*, titled the *Līlāvatī-vivṛti*, consisting of seven thousand verses, stands out as a work of great brilliance. He also possesses a commentary on *Aṅkagaṇita*. Furthermore, his independent treatise, the *Siddhāntasārvabhauma* (composed in Śaka 1572), is indeed extant among his two major works.

From the leaf that happens to come into view at the end of the *Marīci-ṭīkā*, it appears that the first half of the *Marīci-ṭīkā* was completed in the year Śaka 1557 and the second half in the year 1560. This commentary consists of twenty-five thousand verses; indeed, it shines as an exceedingly extensive work, overflowing with the words of the ancient masters. This Munīśvara, by the grace of Ārtikeśvara, [was known] by the name Viśvarūpa...

"I have acquired knowledge"—thus [he] himself stated in the *Marīci-ṭīkā*: "This Nārāyaṇa, a disciple of Eṣṇa, taught me this. Is it not so? Thus [it was said] by the Yavana ruler. That this Munīśvara was his patron is made clear from that very work! In the year 1549:

It is understood from the *Jyotiṣaratnamālā-ṭīkā* that his coronation as a sovereign (*sārvabhauma*) took place in the year [of the Śaka era], on a Monday during the auspicious muhūrta consisting of three ghaṭikās after sunrise, according to the established doctrine of the Siddhāntasārvabhauma. His contemporary rival was Amalākara, the author of the *Siddhāntatattvaviveka* (his date of birth is approximately Śaka 1530).

In the year 1582 Śaka, while residing in Gārāṇasī, he composed the *Siddhāntaharṣaṇa* according to the *Sūryasiddhānta*. Furthermore, this Lālabhaṭṭa harbored a great sense of pride toward Bhāskara Ācārya; consequently, he displayed much novelty and refuted [Bhāskara’s] errors.

It is not only this much; however, the *māñjika* method is also seen to be employed here and there (pp. 154–55). For those among the Indians who possessed the great ambition to bring about a uniformity between the methods of the *Gaṇaka* and the *Ācārya*, there was no occasion for doubt regarding the fact that what is stated in the present chapter on *Bhola*—namely, that the ray (*marīci*) exists in various kinds of jewels—is indeed so.

[2] 3. We desire to exert our pen in order to provide a comprehensive survey of the domain of astronomy and its various directions. It follows that certain ancient authors, being included within the lineage of teachers belonging to the school of Gaṇaka, were indeed in agreement with the fundamental *kalpa*. Therefore, their conception of the nature of *utkrānti* (the soul's departure) was certainly of a transcendent character. Consequently, this [conception] of mine does not conflict with the ancient method in every respect.

It came to pass by its very innate nature. Is the earth spherical and without support? According to the view that "the eclipse of the moon arises from the shadow of the earth," and so forth—even though these [views] are contrary to the Purāṇas, they have not become accepted by people nowadays. Alas! During this intermediate period, the Yavana dynasty flourished, and our own royal names [of the past] became lost.

From that time onwards, the continuous tradition of the study of astronomy and mathematics, which had been handed down from time immemorial, came to an end. Bharata’s *Jyotiṣa* remained at the stage of its initial composition and did not reach the point of further development. Although ancient texts survived in the form of manuscripts in the possession of some individuals, the subjects they taught did not appeal to the vision of people during that period of great difficulty.

The necessity of composing this work appeared particularly urgent to me; for it was the duty of a twice-born man to refute the attachment to restrictive rules (niyamasaṅga). At that time, the tradition of studying the Siddhāntas and the systematic method of reflection upon the subject of mathematics were still vibrant in certain families. In such a lineage, he had been devoted from his very youth to the practice of mathematics through the succession of teachers and the succession of gurus.

The tangible fruit of his practice was as follows: in a single generation (*yuga*), [his son] composed a commentary on *Piṅgalagaṇita*; the second [son] composed the *Vājasaneya-gaṇita*; and the third composed a commentary on the *Golādhyāya*. Following the order of their seniority, he himself also composed a commentary on the *Sūryasiddhānta* at that very time.

State the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). Regarding the observation of a foul odor when writing with *śaṇa* fibers, what authority is there for this? In this matter, the authors of the commentaries (*ṭīkākāra*) must necessarily have had some basis for their statement. On account of this reason, a difference of opinion arose among those who possess the commentaries. One whose heart is [versed in] logical proof, through both perception and scripture, has established that position; thus, the discussion regarding this has proceeded.

O Sage, in order to demonstrate the errors existing among the people, [the author] has composed the work *Siddhāntatattvaviveka*. By observing the wild dance of Kali, it can be inferred that in the seventeenth century, the Indians were submerged in ignorance regarding which Veda they belonged to.

Then, with the passing of time following the end of the Yavana kingdom, during the reign of the Maratha kings, the Indian system of astrology and mathematics was revived. To this end, the preeminent among astronomers composed works that were useful for the five limbs [of calculation]. This came within the range of my vision. To set forth his future life story here would be inappropriate; therefore, I shall observe silence on that matter, fearing prolixity.

Regarding the subjects of domestic duties, study and teaching, astrology, and mathematics—"Peśavāī"—these were taught until their completion; and teachers of these subjects existed at that time. From the commencement of British rule, various opinions arose among Indians as to whether the ancient tradition should be maintained or whether Western education should be adopted.

In this regard, it is certain that among those scholars who were present at the assembly, the illustrious Mr. Colebrooke was preeminent in maintaining that the *Jyotiṣa* [of the Veda] must be transmitted according to the traditional recitation of ancient India. Alas! However, by the extraordinary eloquence of the great scholar M. Mēkala in the council of fate, his view was completely refuted. Oh, what a pity! In effect, the position of Mēkala has become firmly established.

From that time forward, the Western tradition, which had no concern for the study of astrology, became firmly established as if by force. Nevertheless, there were scholars such as the illustrious "Re. Bajesha" residing in Ahmadabad, Paṇḍita Bāpūdeva Śāstrī dwelling in Vārāṇasī, and the venerable Paṇḍita Sudhākara Dvivedī, who remained entirely immersed in the study of astrology.

Among them, the illustrious Reḍḍibhaṭṭa and the followers of Kolbuṅga made their own conclusions public solely on the basis of their own authority. Regarding this, some scholars suspect that Indian knowledge concerning the *yati* was acquired from the Greeks; however, this is not true. For those fundamental principles had, in fact, arisen within the very depths of the minds of the Indians themselves.

The very same fundamental doctrines were elaborated upon by Indian scholars of sharp intellect through their own purity of insight, skill, and rigorous practice. It was not that these Indians adopted the tenets of the Greeks. This view of Mr. Bissu was not accepted by certain individuals such as Whitley Stokes, V. A. Smith, and others, nor by the Parsis; they held an entirely different opinion.

Consequently, in order to clarify the true meaning, some scholars, like blind men led by the blind, strove to support their own respective views; others began the publication of ancient commentaries, whereby the publication of texts accompanied by commentaries became prevalent. However, it was impossible to produce a work that included the original root text along with its commentary. What is the use of this mere publication of complete works?

At that time, in the Mahārāṣṭra country, there were scholars such as Lomanya Tilaka, Paṇḍita Śaṅkara Bālakṛṣṇa Dīkṣita, Paṇḍita Keru Nānā Chatre, Paṇḍita Veṅkaṭeśa Bāpūjī Ketakara, and Paṇḍita Vināyakaśāstrī Khānāpūrakara—who had mastered the secrets of all the astrological treatises—and they exerted great effort in that regard.

However, despite their competence, they were unable to fulfill the other commitments they had undertaken. For example, the highly distinguished Adhvaryu priests specializing in astronomy composed the jewel of a work titled *Bhāratīya-Jyotiḥśāstra-tattvasaṃgraha*.

In this work, there is a brief overview of various topics, including the determination of chronological sequence (*paurvāparya*) and other matters in those respective places, the threefold excellence and precision of the Indian astronomical system (*jyotirgaṇitapaddhati*), and a comparison with the Western-British astronomical system. Furthermore, the mathematical methods found in ancient texts have not been fully mastered by Paṇḍita Vīkṣita, as that was not his primary objective.

Some, due to their own contentious nature, their lack of specialized insight, or for some other reason, have established among the Indians a prejudice against the periodic study of the treatises on astronomical principles (*jyotiṣasiddhānta*). However, that is merely a blind assertion; for as the saying goes: "Only Mount Mandara, whose massive body is submerged in the depths of the ocean, knows the true depth of the sea. Thus, following such delusive words, they have not investigated this matter in its entirety.

Whether the five senses were made objects of enjoyment by Varavaraśrī, the author of the Siddhānta, through the suffix *kan* (as in *pañcaka*) like the limbs of an animal; or whether our own system is merely a partial adaptation of the Western systems, and to what extent there is a mixture or where there is disagreement; or again, which specific Greek words appear in our Siddhānta texts—such reflections have been conducted here with the perspective of a bird’s-eye view.

Therefore, I maintain that our own system of study—consisting of practice, hearing, reflection, and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*)—is necessary; for it is only by casting aside the Western perspective that the secret of Indian philosophical texts can be understood by an Indian, and certainly not by one trained merely in logic.

Venerable scholars, should any errors have escaped my notice during the occasion of this textual revision—whether due to the limited knowledge common to humans, insufficient access to a vast range of literature, visual impairment, negligence, the inadvertence of the lead-type setters, or any other causes—may all such mistakes be pointed out by those who are oceans of compassion; then, at the time of the second printing, they shall be carefully examined. Thus, with palms joined in reverence and with humble submission.

And having prayed again and again, "May we now desist from this employment of the pen," [I conclude]—peace! This is the command of the learned. On the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, in the year 1865, at Puṇyapattana. Balavanta Śarmā, born of the Āpaṭe family and son of Dattātreya, [writes]. Om. Salutations to Brahman, who is Tat-Sat. Herein lies the Golādhyāya (Chapter on the Sphere) from the Siddhānta-śiromaṇi composed by the venerable Bhāskarācārya, together with the Vāsanā-bhāṣya and the Marīci commentary.

In this *Govadhyāya*, whatever unprecedented and difficult *layas* (temporal rhythms) there are, I shall explain them briefly for the sake of easy understanding. For the *Golagrantha* is indeed very extensive; however, those unprecedented and difficult ones not mentioned by others, I explain those here in brief. Here, the word "yā yā" ending in the nominative case and the word "tāstā" ending in the accusative case should be explained by the intelligent [reader] accordingly.

In this regard, first of all, preceded by a salutation to his chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*), he says, "I shall speak the *Golādhyāya*": "Having prostrated before Him and Her—the Lord of the Earth (*Goloka*) who is stainless, and the Goddess of Speech (*Bhāratī*)—I shall speak for the awakening of the simple-minded. She is the Goddess of Speech (*Bhāratī*) who, through the grace of remembering whom, one quickly attains the goal to be accomplished; whose speech, adorned with various words and full of graceful charm, dances like a dancer upon the stage of the mouths of the learned. "I shall speak" means "I say. Who is the speaker? The author, Bhāskara. What is it that he speaks? [The *Golādhyāya*.]

The chapter on the *Goṅa* [is begun]. Of what nature is it? It is faultless (*nirdoṣa*). Of what nature is it for us? It is for the easy understanding of children; that is to say, it is not difficult. Having performed *praṇipāta*—having paid homage preceded by prostration—to whom? To him. Not only to him, but also to her. Who is he? And who is she? He says: from the remembrance of which deity the desired goal of men is quickly and powerfully accomplished—that, by implication, is the King of Vināyakas (*Vināyaka-rāja*).

Likewise, by the grace of that Goddess, the speech (*bhāratī*) of the accomplished ones—the wise—becomes like a dancing *bhāratī* (actress). For *bhāratī* refers to both speech and an actress. How is this speech and how is the actress? Her words are variegated, possessing a diverse arrangement of feet; she is well-adorned, marked with the seals of beautiful ornaments; and she is instantly accessible, endowed with the quality of sweetness. If one asks how she dances so excellently: [it is as follows].

The speech, consisting of prose and verse, which possesses the qualities of divine and most gentle words resembling a mass of trickling drops of nectar, and which causes wonder in the minds of the wise, appears as if it were dancing. What kind of *bhāratī* (speech)? On the stage of the mouth (*mukharanga*). The mouth itself is the stage (*raṅga*), meaning the place of dance. By whose grace such speech may exist in the mouths of the accomplished; she, by implication, is Sarasvatī. And having prostrated before her...

Since auspicious things at the beginning and weapons that produce a ringing sound are considered to bring success, the words *sic* (augment) and *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) have been placed at the beginning of this work. [Maṅgalādhyāya Maṭīkā]—I meditate upon the Lord who is the form of eternal bliss and knowledge, the great one capable of destroying the darkness of ignorance regarding all things, known as Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the omnipresent cause of all, for the sake of attaining all desired goals at all times. Now, in the latter half [of the verse], by the grace of the pair of lotus feet of my preceptor, Rāmakṛṣṇa, my paternal uncle...

It is being explained by the Lord of Sages (*munīśvara*) according to his wisdom for the satisfaction of those who rely upon computers. Now, following the injunction inferred from the conduct of the learned that one should perform an auspicious rite (*maṅgala*) at the beginning of a path—that is, at the start of a work—just as the first half was completed without obstacle, so too this second half should be commenced and brought to completion; with this desire, he has composed an auspicious salutation in the form of a prostration, which he intends to bind [to the beginning] for the instruction of his disciples, using the *śārdūlavikrīḍita* meter to ensure the attention of the students.

He makes a formal declaration: "Success. By the use of the pronouns *tam* (him) and *tām* (her), he refers to the God and the Goddess present in the mind, since pronouns denote that which is currently in the mind. The particle *ca* (and) is used for conjunction; thus, the meaning is "the two. *Alam* means "exceedingly," in the sense of until the cessation of all obstacles. And the realization of that [success] occurs upon the completion of the work intended to be begun. Having prostrated—having performed a salutation preceded by full prostration—he uses the past tense (*praṇipatya*) because the act of salutation precedes the action to be performed.

The word *pra* (forth) illuminates the exultation characterized by an excess of devotion (*bhakti*) and faith (*śraddhā*). Devotion is the knowledge [of the Lord] as the one to be worshipped; faith, however, is the certainty that the fruit [of practice] will necessarily come to pass as taught in the Vedas and other scriptures. The phrase "in the throat" refers to a book describing the terrestrial globe (*bhūgola*) and so forth, since that too is denoted by the term *gola*. Because of the verbal root *bruva* ("to speak"), there is an ellipsis of the object *mām* ("me"). Thus, the meaning is: "I shall speak this *Gola*."

One might object: "Is not your effort vain, since the description of the *golā* (the celestial sphere) is seen in the *Bhāgavata* Purāṇa and other texts? To this he says: "Pure" (*amalam*). This means it is free from defects. The point is that the description in the *Bhāgavata* and elsewhere has been disregarded because it contradicts direct observation and because it does not serve as a basis for planetary calculation (*graha-gaṇita*). One might further object: "Even so, since the description is found in the *Sūryasiddhānta* and other works in accordance with direct observation, is not this effort of yours still purposeless? To this he says: "For the understanding of children" (*bālabodham*).

The meaning is as follows: since the knowledge of calculation (*gaṇita*) and its application (*upapatti*), the understanding of the true state of the earth, planets, and asterisms, and the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) [arise] from this [work]; and furthermore, since that exposition is concise in the *Sūryasiddhānta* and other texts, comprehension does not arise for those who are ignorant due to its difficulty—therefore, for the sake of their understanding, I shall provide a clear and easy exposition of that very same subject matter. He explains what is held in the intellect with the word "established" (*siddham*): [it belongs] to that Supreme Lord.

The meaning is: of that which is taught by such scriptural passages as, "From this very Self, space was produced. "From remembrance" means from an internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) intent upon the aforementioned meditation. "Swiftly," without delay, one attains—that is, reaches—perfection, the state of being free from all sides, regarding the desired object of experience, the Puruṣa. This result, characterized by being the creator of the world and so forth, is illustrative; therefore, it should be understood that other great fruits, difficult for even a man to achieve, are also accomplished.

The word *siddhi* at the beginning serves the purpose of auspiciousness (*maṅgala*). He explains what resides in the intellect [of the author] with the words "by grace" (*prasādāt*). This means by the grace of that Goddess, namely Māyā, who is established by such scriptural passages as "the one unborn, red, white, and black. Likewise, from such an indescribable production and favor; *bhāratī* is the Goddess of Speech. She is "dancing," meaning performing a dance. Regarding the dance, since it requires a location, he says: "on the stage of the mouth" (*mukharaṅge*).

The very mouth of the accomplished ones—the wise—is the stage; she has gone there, being present. To explain how she dances, he provides an illustration: "Like the *Bhāratī* of Bhārata. This is the *Bhāratī* (the speech/dance style) of the dancer Bhārata. [Interjection: "Indeed! Just as there is praise for the excellence of the ball in the houses of fortunate men. Maṭhara’s Commentary (*Maṭhara-ṭīkā*): A certain female dancer (*nartakī*), standing at the front part of the stage (*raṅgasthānāgrimabhāgasthā*), performs a dance; such is the meaning.

The comprehension of similarity between the exemplum (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the subject of comparison (*dārṣṭāntika*) is achieved through the mention of common attributes, which he states as "possessing variegated words" (*citrapadā*). In the case of *Sarasvatī*, it refers to that in which there exist various kinds of words (*padāni*) consisting of nominal and verbal forms. In the case of the actress (*naṭī*), it refers to the arrangement of various limbs such as the feet, or alternatively, to the various words of the singers. This is a unique characteristic of dancing: "well-adorned" (*svalaṃkṛti*).

In the sense of Sarasvatī, it is "well-endowed" (*suṣṭhu-dūṣaṇarahita*), meaning it possesses qualities (*guṇa*) and figures of speech (*alaṃkāra*). Its verbal ornaments (*śabdālaṃkāra*) include alliteration (*anuprāsa*), rhyme (*yamaka*), and the various types of *citrapunaruktabhāsa*. It also contains the well-known poetic figures of sense (*arthālaṃkāra*) such as simile (*upamā*), metaphor (*rūpaka*), poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*), doubt (*saṃdeha*), concealment (*apahnuti*), paronomasia (*śleṣa*), suggested meaning (*samāsokti*), and illustration (*nidarśana*). Furthermore, this work is an aid for the discerning, serving as an ornament of gold for the actresses. It is characterized by grace and charm (*lālityalīlāvatī*).

In the sense of Sarasvatī, *lālityam* (gracefulness) is the state of being *lalita*. It is endowed with the qualities (*guṇas*) mentioned in the *Kāvyaprakāśa*: "Coalescence (*śleṣa*), clarity (*prasāda*), evenness (*samatā*), sweetness (*mādhurya*), delicacy (*sukumāratā*), explicitness of meaning (*arthavyakti*), loftiness (*audārya*), vigor (*ojas*), and splendor (*kānti*). Furthermore, it is free from the defects of words (*duṣṭapada*) as defined there: "A defective word is one that is harsh to the ear, corrupt in grammar, unidiomatic, non-expressive, having a suppressed meaning, having an inappropriate meaning, meaningless, non-denotative, ambiguous, obscure, vulgar, or having a figurative meaning, or it may be considered 'strained' (*kliṣṭa*)."

The "unclarified predicate" (*avimṛṣṭavidheyāṃśa*) and the "causing contradictory cognition" (*viruddhamatikṛt*) occur only within a compound; thus, by virtue of being free from those [faults], it possesses the quality of being well-heard (*saṃśravasva*). Its "play" (*līlā*) is its graceful movement (*vilāsa*). She in whom that shines forth is [the subject]. The movement of a river or a stone—such as going and so forth—is performed with a certain agility (*liṭṭaṅgatayā*). It is "graceful" (*kāntathā*); for the *Saṃgītaratnākara* states that grace (*lalita*) is known as the nature of the side-glances (*apāṅga*) of a woman of delicate limbs.

Furthermore, this qualifying term "in the form of a dancer" (nartanarūpa) is also indicative of the fruit [of the work], because Māyā is likewise the producer of the world; thus, it should be understood that other fruits also arise. Some say that here there is a salutation to Gaṇeśa and Sarasvatī, based on the fact that Śiva is the lord of obstacles and that the word *bhāratī* is accepted as signifying both speech and its meaning. That is not correct, because at the commencement of the description of the nature of the Lord—who is fashioned by the Māyā of the Supreme Lord—the salutation to those two alone is appropriate.

1 || Now, he states the reason for composing the *Golādhyāya*: "A mathematician who seeks excellence, if he lacks the demonstration (*upapatti*) of the calculation of the celestial bodies (*yusad*), does not attain preeminence in the assemblies of the learned, nor is he free from doubt himself. That pure sphere (*gola*) is perceived directly like a myrobalan fruit in the palm of the hand; therefore, this treatise on the sphere (*golaprabandha*) is composed here for the sake of understanding its demonstration. || 2 || End of verse 2.

Ma0ḍī0: [Objection: But surely the commencement of the description of the celestial sphere (*gol*) is useless because it serves no purpose. To this, he declares that the promised description of the sphere *is* indeed purposeful, by means of the *śārdūlavikrīḍita* meter, beginning with the words "madhya... (the mean...). Therefore, for that reason, in the first half of this Siddhānta text, the tenfold calculation—consisting of the mean, the true, and so forth, which was set forth for the mean positions of the planets—is the subject matter for the description of planetary computation (*grahagaṇita*).

For the sake of understanding the treatise, there is a method (vidhi)—that is, a procedure (prakāra) for the knowledge of the reasoning (upapatti) that establishes it; this refers either to the composition of the *Golādhyāya*—the textual body (*granthasandarbhārtha*) intended to impart knowledge of the nature of the celestial sphere (*gola*)—or to the construction of the sphere (*golabandhārtha*). This is because the construction of that [sphere] will be described later. For this very reason, since the description of the sphere was previously promised, the second promise regarding the construction of the sphere is appropriate.

Otherwise, there would be the consequence of the proposition being redundant. Through the force of the action "I am moving," the object "I" is implied. Thus, since the knowledge of the proof (*upapatti*) is the motivator, the definition of the sphere (*gola*) is not useless; this is the sense. Now, one might object: "Is it not for the sake of knowing the proof that the proof must be defined, and not the sphere? To this, he states the reason indicated [by the text]: "the sphere. That is the proof.

The spheres described in the *Gola* are pure and faultless; they are seen and known through direct perception (*pratyakṣapramāṇāt*) by mathematicians who understand the true nature of the spheres—this is the remainder [of the sense]. To explain how they are known through direct perception, he states it by way of an illustration: "like the hand, the temple, and the cloth."

Just as, having ascertained through visual perception an *āmalaka* fruit held in one’s hand, the knowledge arises that "there is an *āmalaka* in my hand," so too, having ascertained the nature of the celestial sphere (*gola*), the demonstration (*upapatti*)—which consists in the ease of observing the [astronomical] field therein—is established by the wise. The sense is that this demonstration possesses the nature of a logical proof (*upapatti-svarūpatva*) because it relies upon the essential nature of the mathematical objects (*gaṇita-padārtha*). Here, the illustration of the *āmalaka* fruit should be understood as being for the purpose of comprehending the nature of the celestial sphere.

[Objection: But surely, even the determination of the time that necessitates full comprehension (*upapatti*) is useless, since it would be an object of indifference due to the absence of a purpose for that purpose. To this, he says: "Without *upapatti*... The term *gaṇaka* means one who knows the calculation of the planets. Without *upapatti*—that is, apart from the knowledge of the reasoning for producing those [calculations]—one does not attain proficiency in learned assemblies. "Learned" (*prauḍha*) refers to those who are skilled in discerning the true meaning of words and their referents; in their gatherings (*samāja*), one does not attain proficiency, which is the skill in distinguishing between what is sound and what is unsound.

Furthermore, just as the status of being honored by the world (*lokamānyatva*) arises for an astrologer who performs calculations because he lacks the capacity to answer the questions of scholars—such as "How does such an eclipse occur?"—the very purpose of knowing the underlying rationale (*upapatti*) is precisely that status of being honored by the world which results from having the capacity to provide those answers. For if one possesses that status, discerning people will engage in bathing and giving at auspicious times, such as the *saṅkrānti*, on the authority of his words; otherwise, such engagement would be untenable.

The intended meaning is that it would result in the destruction of the Dharma. Now, one might object: "Even from the words of an ordinary astrologer who knows its derivation, the practice of that Dharma is possible, because the authority of his words is ascertained through the power of the correspondence between his predictions and the actual results of observations such as eclipses. To this, he says: "without doubt" (*niḥsaṃśaya*). One who is himself skilled in planetary calculation would not be "without doubt"—that is, one from whom doubt has departed—and thus would not possess certain knowledge in the absence of knowledge regarding its derivation.

And thus, regarding the knowledge of pure planetary calculation (*kevalagrahagaṇita*), there may arise a doubt or delusion as to which of the earlier texts is authoritative when discrepancies occur; this is because it is impossible for [the planets] to be positioned exactly as described in those texts. Since the performance of religious duties (*dharmānuṣṭhāna*) would otherwise be ruined, the possibility of determining the truth arises through the knowledge of their actual positions. Furthermore, due to the capacity of location and the instruction regarding that location, the performance of religious duties becomes possible—this is the underlying sense. Now, with two verses, he mocks the astrologer who is ignorant of the celestial sphere (*gola*) by praising the sphere, just as one might praise food: [The verses follow.]

Just as all flavors are tasteless without clarified butter, or as a kingdom deprived of its king does not shine, so too an assembly devoid of eloquent speakers lacks luster; likewise, an astrologer here who is ignorant of the *golā* (the celestial sphere) is like that. [This is the praise of the *golā*. An arrogant speaker of small intellect, having entered the assembly of the learned without knowledge of grammar, speaks with pride using clever, frowning brows and crooked speech; yet, being humiliated, he receives only ridicule—just so does an astrologer who is ignorant of the *golā*.

[This verse] is clear in its meaning. (3–4) Ma0 Ḍī0 [Commentary]: Now, one might object: "Since the performance of religious duties (*dharma-anuṣṭhāna*) is possible by relying on the local place through the power of the *muhūrta* and other calculations—which are in agreement with the teachers of the *Sūryasiddhānta*—the knowledge of the rationale (*upapatti-jñāna*) is useless, and therefore the description of the celestial sphere (*gola-nirūpaṇa*) is redundant. To this, he says "It is to be studied," using the *upajāti* meter.

In this regard, among those established in the Siddhāntas, an astrologer who knows the nature of the terrestrial globe and so forth, yet is ignorant of the celestial sphere (*gola*), does not shine in the world nor produce wonder; "likewise" (*tathā*) indicates the illustration for this, which he states as "food" (*bhojya*). Food that possesses all flavors—since "flavor" is illustrative of all qualities—is not manifest without clarified butter (*ghṛta*). Now, one might object: it is not proper to claim that clarified butter holds primacy among edible substances.

And because there is no determining factor (*vinigamakābhāvāt*) as to why food devoid of sweet flavor should be [the object of desire], he states another example out of this same sense of dissatisfaction: "The kingdom," and not "the arrow. [Objection: Surely, since a kingdom can become fraught with calamities without a ruler, the king's primacy in the kingdom is established; however, it is not so for a *gaṇin* (member of a monastic community), for whose primary quality is knowledge of the *gola* (the sphere/monastery). Since the practical application of commands and the like is possible through the aforementioned method, there is a disparity between the two examples. Out of this sense of dissatisfaction, he states another example: "The assembly" (*sabhā*).

"Devoid of a good speaker": it means lacking those scholars who speak with reasoning and words that are well-articulated; such is the assembly of scholars (*paṇḍitasabhā*). Just as a common assembly of scholars in the world, though captivating, becomes exceedingly captivating by virtue of being presided over by one who is supremely wise, so too is this [assembly].} (The word *iva* means "in accordance with reality. Thus, even a general assembly of scholars is charming, but it is most charming when it relies upon one who is pre-eminently wise.

Similarly, although those who possess only the calculations of planetary motion are also proficient in practical affairs, an astronomer who understands the celestial sphere (*golajña*) is superior to them due to his excellence in the knowledge of the underlying rationale (*upapatti*). Thus, the intention is that the exposition of the celestial sphere is not in vain, as it serves to establish this superiority. Now, one might object: "Even without regard for superiority, its exposition is indeed useless; otherwise, since superiority would be established through the knowledge of other objects of measurement, there would follow the necessity of expounding those as well. To this, he says in the *Śārdūlavikrīḍita* meter: "The horse... and so forth.

In an assembly of astronomers where there are no experts in the celestial sphere (*gola*), all the members of that assembly are considered experts in the celestial sphere by virtue of the title "astronomer" (*jyotirvid*), because the stars and other celestial bodies depend upon the celestial sphere. Otherwise, it would follow that everyone who possesses general knowledge of the stars would be an astronomer according to your own position. [This is concluded] through the elaborate statements of questions posed by highly skilled mathematicians.

The meaning is as follows: those who are skilled calculators and astronomers who know the true nature of the celestial sphere (*golaka*)—their inquiries constitute the prima facie arguments (*pūrvapakṣa*). The various statements related to those, expressed through diverse rhetorical devices (*nānāvidhabhaṅgi*), are full of derision. By them [the opponent] is "shamed" (*hīṇa*), that is, overcome, because he is unable to provide an answer. He is "good" (*san*) because shame does not arise for a wicked person due to his ignorance of his own faults. Thus, he incurs derision like a [failed] example. He states the example with the words "If... (*yadīti*).

One who is an expert in logic (*tarka*), grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), and other sciences; without grammar—that is, apart from grammar—only among the learned (the word "only" excludes others). Having entered the assembly with audacity, he prattled out of pride (*smaya*), speaking incoherent words preceded by the laughter of the scholars. Being of small intellect, he was incapable of concealing his own ignorance. Among the learned, there were clever youths (*baṭu*)—either children or disciples—who were proficient in grammar and other sciences.

The frowns on their brows and the sarcastic remarks they uttered—such as, "How can this man speak of pure *saṃskṛta* as an object of knowledge?"—were enough for even a child among scholars to perceive me as a fool and mock me through those words. Being ashamed that I am such a fool, [I thought: "A virtuous person is one who recognizes his own faults."

Thus, it serves as a source of ridicule for one who knows only the calculation of planetary positions (*kevalagrahagaṇitajña*), because his words lack authority due to being disregarded by all true astronomers (*sarvajyotirvit*) owing to his ignorance of the underlying rationale (*upapatti*). Alternatively, since he is excluded from the ranks of astronomers, the description of the celestial sphere (*gola*)—which necessarily requires knowledge of that rationale—is not intended for mere intellectual curiosity; therefore, it is not something that should be imparted [to him]. This is the intended meaning. Now, he describes the nature of the celestial sphere (*gola*): "The configuration and dimensions of the earth, the stars, and the planets are established solely through illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*)."

The *gola* is known as a specific type of field (*kṣetra-viśeṣa*); therefore, it is to be understood through what has been stated by means of *prāsa*s (parabolic trajectories). [Verse 5] Ma0 Ṭī0: Now, one might object: "Is it not proper that the definition of the nature of the *gola*, which serves as the basis for the knowledge of its derivation (*upapatti*), should be distinct from the exposition of the established doctrine (*siddhānta*)—just as grammar is the basis for all treatises? For the instruction on the categories of the established doctrine does not include the derivation; how then is its definition appropriate here?"

Therefore, it is logical that after the exposition of planetary calculation (*graha-gaṇita*), there follows the exposition of the two types of calculation (*dvidhā-gaṇita*); after that, the exposition of problems with their solutions (*sottara-praśna*); and following that, the description of the positions of the planets on the surface of the earth (*bhūmiṣṭha*) and so forth. Consequently, under the guise of establishing the determination of the celestial sphere (*gola-nirūpaṇa*), [the author] states in the *Indravajrā* meter the purpose of the established celestial sphere (*siddha-gola*)—which is based on the previously promised construction of the celestial sphere (*golabandha*)—by means of an example (*udāharaṇa*).

The "configuration" (*saṃsthāna*) refers to the arrangement and position of the terrestrial planets and the celestial bodies (stars and planets). Its "measure" (*māna*) means the determination of their nature and position through valid means of knowledge such as direct perception and reasoning. For the purpose of explaining and defining that, there is the "sphere" (*gola*). This is a sphere produced from bamboo, wood, cloth, and so forth, established by the method of constructing a sphere to be described; it is merely an illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*). By the use of the word "only" (*eva*), it is not the actual physical form. It was "remembered" or proclaimed by those of ancient times who knew the true nature of the essence of the throat of wisdom.

Likewise, for the sake of thoroughly understanding the configuration [of the heavens], it is not easily comprehensible without an illustration that defines the nature of the celestial sphere (*gola*); thus, an illustration has been established by means of the method for constructing the celestial sphere (*golabandhavidhi*). In this very context, there is the definition of the very subject matter of the Siddhānta—the knowledge of the positions of the Earth, the observer, and the planets—and not an additional definition, because such [additional] matters are included within this. To the question, "What is the proof for its being an illustration?", he says: "Because it is the subject of the field (*kṣetra*)."

In the description of the nature of the sphere (*gola*), those hundreds of fields (*kṣetra*) which belong to the various branches [of geometry] are here directly perceived within this circular sphere (*vṛttagola*) such as the meridian and so forth; for it is accepted that the specific fields of the sphere exist by virtue of their connection with horizontal, vertical, and downward lines, circles, and so on. The point is that the fact of not being the locus of the planetary orbs (*grahabimba*) does not disqualify it from serving as an illustration (*dṛṣṭāntatva*). Now, one might object: "Is it not more appropriate to describe that [the sphere] immediately after the description of the motion of the planets?"

It is not by way of an immediate succession separated by the investigation of the two types of *ṇita*; otherwise, following the order of the enumeration, after the chapter on the solution of problems (*praśnādhyāya*), there would be the investigation of the three types of *laya*. Therefore, he says: "This" (*eṣa*). Because it consists of specific fields (*kṣetra-viśeṣa*). This is the praise of the *śala*. [Maṇittha’s Commentary]—This sphere (*gola*) is accessible (*gamya*), that is, knowable, by means of this *pāṭīgaṇita* (arithmetic).

And thus, since the practical application of geometry (*kṣetravyavahāra*) cannot occur without knowledge of the sides, the base, and the hypotenuse related to a figure, its inclusion within *pāṭīgaṇita* (arithmetic) is justified; for such knowledge is impossible apart from arithmetic. Therefore, the underlying sense is that after the exposition of the two types of calculation—the manifest (*vyakta*) and the unmanifest (*avyakta*)—the exposition of *gaṇita* (geometry) is appropriate.

Because questions are infinite and because the determination of their validity depends on knowing their logical justification (*upapatti*), it would be inappropriate to present the *Prakṣādhyāya*—which indicates knowledge of answers to unasked questions—prior to the description of the celestial sphere (*gola*). This is because the questions and their answers are [discussed] later; thus, it should be understood that this [section] is for the purpose of establishing the "Statement of Questions on the Celestial Sphere" (*Golapraśnoddeśa*) which follows the previous [section]. 5.

Now he speaks in praise of calculation (gaṇita): "The fruit of the science of astronomy (jyotiḥśāstra) is called 'prediction' (ādeśa) by ancient calculators; surely this [prediction] is based on the true positions of the planets. Those [calculations] depend upon the celestial sphere (gola), yet the celestial sphere itself cannot be known without calculation. Therefore, how will one who does not know calculation understand the celestial sphere and so forth? ||6|| [This concludes verse 6.]

Ma0 Ṭī0—Now, one might object: "Since the determination of the planets was previously established by first describing the two types of calculation (gaṇita) and then the throat (gala), and since the knowledge of the objects situated in the throat alone gives rise to the calculation of the planets, and because planetary calculation depends on various methods such as addition (saṃkalana) and so forth—which would be untenable without arithmetic (pāṭīgaṇita)—how then can it be so? To this, he says "yotiḥ" in the Śārdūlavikrīḍita meter: "By ancient astronomers... [and so on].

The meaning is: because the ancient astronomers, such as Varāhamihira and others, have determined and ascertained through that science (astronomy) the purpose, utility, and prediction of the *jyotiḥśāstra*—which consists of the three branches of *saṃhitā*, *hōrā*, and *gaṇita*—namely, the declaration of present, past, and future auspicious and inauspicious events; this is what is being stated or accepted. Furthermore, as an ornament of speech, it is said: "This prediction (*ādeśa*) is certainly (*nūnam*) based on the strength of the *lagna*."

The meaning is that in the determination of birth [horoscopes] and so forth through practical applications, [the results] depend on the strength of the planetary positions within their respective diagrams (*kuṇḍalikā*). The strength of those various planetary positions in the diagrams depends upon the true planets (*spaṣṭagraha*). Since the section of the mathematical treatise concerning eclipses, heliacal risings, altitudes, and so forth, is directly dependent on the true planets, it is established that the subjects expounded in the science of astronomy—whether directly or indirectly—are dependent on the knowledge of the true planets. Therefore, in the Siddhānta, they are perceived as being situated within the celestial sphere (*gola*) by virtue of resting upon the visible celestial sphere (*hagola*).

The meaning is that the knowledge of the celestial sphere (*gola*) is dependent upon its formal description, since the attainment of understanding the sphere's configuration is established through this means. Without mathematics—that is, apart from the calculation of planetary positions—the sphere is not known. Furthermore, by the use of the word "also" (*api*), it is implied that the true positions of the planets and the methods for determining them (such as *grahaṇa*, or eclipses) are likewise not known. The point is that for the sake of understanding the sphere, the knowledge of the technical categories of planetary calculation as they are traditionally taught is essential, and that knowledge is to be accomplished through the exposition of those mathematical principles.

The sense is that, since knowledge of the celestial sphere (gola) is dependent upon knowledge of calculation (gaṇita), its description immediately following that is logical. Now, one might object: "Since the general understanding of the subject matter of that [calculation] is established through the very description of the celestial sphere, there is no need for knowledge of planetary calculation (grahagaṇita) within the description of the celestial sphere. To this, he provides the answer under the guise of a conclusion, beginning with the words "Therefore" (tasmāt).

Therefore, for the reason stated above, he who desires to study the *Golādhyāya* (the chapter on the celestial sphere) but does not know—that is, does not master—mathematics (*gaṇita*), how will he know the answers to questions regarding the celestial sphere? The meaning is that he will not know them. Thus, without knowledge of planetary mathematics (*grahagaṇita*), a correct understanding of the celestial sphere (*gola*) does not arise; at best, there would be only a semblance of such knowledge. This is the intention behind first establishing planetary mathematics and then proceeding with the description of the celestial sphere.

By this, the presentation of planetary calculation (*grahagaṇita*) after the chapter on the celestial sphere (*golādhyāya*) in the *Siddhāntasundara* is refuted. (6) Now, he states the qualification for hearing the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*): "Two kinds of calculation have been described: that involving manifest [arithmetic] and that involving the unmanifest [algebra]. One who is devoted to understanding these, and is most proficient in the science of grammar (*śabdaśāstra*), if such a person exists, is qualified to study this vast variety of Jyotiṣa; otherwise, he is merely a bearer of the name. (7) The meaning is clear. (7)

Now, with the verse beginning "Or else" (*atha vā*) and so forth, the author states the nature of the *Golādhyāya*—which he intends to expound—in the *Mālinī* meter for the sake of brevity: "Of two kinds" (*dvividha*). "Two-fold calculation" (*dvividhagaṇita*) means calculation stated in two ways; this is what is set forth in this treatise. He clarifies these two modes: "The manifest" (*vyakta*). The manifest is *pāṭīgaṇita* (arithmetic); the unmanifest is *bījagaṇita* (algebra). It is "joined" (*yukta*), meaning accompanied by, both *pāṭīgaṇita* and *bījagaṇita*.

And thus, after the exposition of planetary calculation (*graha-gaṇita*), having first explained arithmetic (*pāṭī-gaṇita*) because of its utility in the [astronomical] procedure (*prakriyā*), the author subsequently expounded algebra (*bīja-gaṇita*), which depends upon arithmetic and is useful for establishing the specific proofs within planetary calculation; this is the meaning. He states the aforementioned utility: "one whose focus is on the comprehension of that" (*tad-avagamananiṣṭha*). The meaning is: one who possesses the knowledge in which there is a firm conviction (*niṣṭhā*)—that is, certainty—regarding the comprehension (*avagamana*), i.e., the knowledge, of those two types of calculation.

Since he stands between those two, it is established that he alone is "one who possesses knowledge of the calculation of the planets. In the science of grammar (*śabdaśāstra*), he is "most proficient" (*paṭiṣṭhaḥ*); that is, exceedingly clever or skillful. The meaning is: one who knows the true principles (*tattva*) of the science of grammar. If such a person exists, then indeed that seeker of learning (*pipaṭhiṣu*) is qualified to study thoroughly and to understand the truth of this renowned science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*), which has many divisions, including the *gola* (spherics), the *yantra* (astronomical instruments), and the section consisting of the chapters on *praśna* (questions/foretelling).

One who lacks the nature described above is merely a bearer of the name [of a scholar]; though desiring to study that [grammar], he is not truly one who seeks knowledge of its reality. For such a person, even a single portion of this work is difficult to master—this is the meaning. (7) Now, he describes grammar: "He who knows the exposition of the Vedas knows the Veda itself; for what other scripture is there outside the assembly? Therefore, having first studied this, one becomes qualified to understand the various branches of the Veda. (8) Thus ends the eighth verse.

The Question Concerning the Nature of Indolence (Ālasvarūpapraśna). Ma0 27: Now, by means of the example beginning with "yadi," it was stated that grammar is useless without another science, but it was not stated that the science of astronomy (*jyotiḥśāstra*) is likewise [useless]. Here, because the Golādhyāya—which occupies the position of grammar—is accepted, the statement "it has been said in the science of words (*śabdaśāstra*)," which was previously mentioned, is repeated; therefore, he says "ya" as a refutation.

For this reason, this grammar is indicated as the first among the auxiliary sciences (vedāṅgas). Having studied it, the wise person becomes qualified for the hearing and recitation of other Vedic branches; for hearing has as its object the conjunction of the ear and the mind. By the word "wise" (*śrīmān*), which is a common expression, and by the two words "of the eye" (*akṣṇaḥ*) and "in recitation" (*paṭhane*), a great excellence is indicated.

And thus, since the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*) is also a distinct branch of knowledge, the previously stated point—that one who is qualified for grammar is likewise qualified to study this—is indeed correct; such is the intended meaning. Now, one might ask: "What is the purpose of that [grammar] in the study of another branch of knowledge? To this, he states the reason with the word "ya" (who). Because of which reason, he who desires to recite the Veda knows grammar thoroughly; he, desiring to recite, knows the Veda—the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*). By the use of the word "api" (also), the sense is that he knows it as something that has overcome even the most difficult points of its meaning. He knows it.

In other treatises, by comparison with that [grammar], what need is there to say that one knows them easily? Since grammar is the mouth of the Veda, through its mastery one attains an understanding of the Veda; thus, there is no difficulty in knowing the complete meaning of the Veda. The sense is that because the meanings of words are determined by it. This may be so; but from where does the knowledge of other supreme treatises arise? To this he says: "The abode. For (*hi*) certainly, it is the abode—the home—of Brahmi Sarasvati, who is the embodiment of all the sciences.

Grammar is the abode of Sarasvatī, because the nature of the scripture consists of words. Thus, the sense is that through the knowledge of grammar—which is the house where she resides—of Sarasvatī who is the embodiment of all scriptures, there arises knowledge of Sarasvatī in her form as the totality of all scriptures. || 8 ||

Now, for the purpose of introducing the *Golagrantha*, he speaks by way of an indirect address (*anyokti*): "O friend, if you have the inclination to hear, listen to this work of Bhāskara; it is neither too concise nor excessively verbose. It is accessible through play, beautifully composed, and delightful in its inquiry. Therefore, O learned one, it reveals the brilliance of those who recite it in the assembly of scholars. (9) [This is] clear. (9) Thus ends the chapter on the praise of the *Gola*.

Bhāskara’s Commentary (Bhāṣya-ṭīkā): Now, one might object that since there are already treatises on the sphere (Golādhyāya) composed by Lakṣmīpati and others, the present work on the sphere would be redundant; therefore, he says "golām" in the Mandākrāntā meter: "O wise one, if you have the intelligence to hear or study the *Gola*—the chapter on the celestial sphere—then [you will realize] that the commencement of this *Golādhyāya* is not in vain. By the word "you" (*tvayi*), it is indicated through the reasoning previously stated that the beginning of the *Golādhyāya* is not purposeless, for otherwise, the excellence of that [previous work] would be logically untenable.

In that case, listen to and study this *Golādhyāya* composed by Bhāskarācārya, the follower of Bhāskara. Since ancient texts exist, they say [this] here. To the question "How so?", he says: "That" (*sa*). Commentary on the *Mañjarī* (ma0 ṭī) regarding the *Golādhyāya*: Because for this reason, this treatise on the celestial sphere (*golagrantha*) composed by Bhāskarācārya reveals (*vyanakti*)—that is, makes manifest—the speech of the learned (*paṇḍitokti*) to those scholars in the assembly (*vidvasadasi*), the circles of pandits, who are reciting it.

The sense is this: when one recites this in an assembly of scholars, those present perceive that "this person is a scholar"; however, when one recites the *Golādhyāya* of Bhāskara, because such a statement is not found there, [the author implies] that what I have spoken—this "throat-knot" (*galagrantha*)—is not in vain. As for the question of how it manifests the words of the scholars, he provides a qualification of Bhāskara’s *Gola*: "the essence of the science" (*śāstratattvam*). This means it is the quintessence of all treatises on the celestial sphere (*gola*). He states two qualifying attributes that serve as the reason for this: "not... [and so forth]. It is not concise in the sense of having little investigation.

The meaning is that it is not excessively prolix, nor is it expanded pointlessly even though it is extensive. [Objection: "In that case, it will become difficult to understand. To this he says: "accessible through play" (*līlāgabhya*). The meaning is that this entire treatise is mastered through just a little instruction. Here he provides a qualifying epithet containing a reason: "delightful with well-fashioned words" (*sulalitapadaprakṣaramya*). Those works in which there exist very charming words (*sulalitāni padāni*) are "well-fashioned words"; and those questions (*praśnāḥ*) are "delightful" (*ramyaḥ*). Thus, it is delightful because of its beautiful questions.

And thus, because the five [verses] possess difficult meanings through their graceful words (*lalitapada*), the *Golādhyāya* is accessible through play (*līlāgamya*)—the sense being that even though the answers to those questions are composed in various meters, they are easy to grasp by understanding the intent of the questions through such paths. By the word "question" (*praśna*), it is indicated that the *Golapraśnādhyāya* has been stated here separately immediately following this. ||9||

Now, one might object: "Having set aside the chapter on the celestial sphere (*golādhyāya*) which was promised, something entirely different has been described here. To this, he says by way of a formal statement (*phakkikā*): "Thus, in the *Siddhāntaśiromaṇi*, [this is] the praise of the celestial sphere (*golapraśaṃsā*). The *Śiromaṇi* is a work by someone [Bhāskarācārya] that concludes with the chapter on planetary conjunctions (*pātādhikāra*). This present text, however, is a distinct chapter on the celestial sphere (*golādhyāya*). To prevent the confusion that these two are the same, he specifies "in the *Siddhāntaśiromaṇi*," because the intended categories of the Siddhānta have not yet been fully established at the end of the chapter on conjunctions.

The connection with the exposition of the chapter on the celestial sphere (golādhyāya) has been stated; since the sphere (gola) will be described later by this very work, there is no deficiency. In this work titled *Śiromaṇimarīci*, composed by the son of the illustrious Raṅganātha Gaṇaka, whose presence was served by a lineage of the most excellent astrologers, let the praise of the celestial sphere, esteemed by the circle of wise mathematicians, reach its conclusion. (19)

Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "Praise of the Sphere" (*Golapraśaṃsā*), in the *Marīci* commentary on the *Siddhāntaśiromaṇi*, composed by the astrologer Munīśvara, also known as Viśvarūpa, the son of the illustrious Raṅganātha Gaṇaka, the sovereign of all astronomers. Now, in two verses, [the author] describes the configuration of the spheres: "The sky-dweller moves in the sky which is adorned with the wheels of the sun and moon; by whom is the earth supported so that it does not fall downward? (1) What is its shape, and what is its measure? This is determined through the investigation of various scriptures. (2)

Tell me, what kind of support for the lord of the islands (the earth) has been established? (1-2) This earth, joined with the sky-dwellers and the celestial beings—by whom was it held so that, while existing in the sky all around, it does not fall downward? How is it situated in the sky? This has been understood: because it revolves within the circle of the stellar sphere (*bhacakra*). [The question concerns the nature of the spheres of the luminaries. 11. *Bī* means a collection; the circle of the stars itself is the *bhacakra*.

The meaning is that if the earth is accepted as having a succession of supporting elements (bhūtadhāra-paramparā), then the rotation of the dense stellar sphere (ghanabhacakra) situated upon its support would not be possible. Furthermore, what is the shape and what is the extent of that earth; and what is the condition of the continents (dvīpas) and the mountain ranges (kulaparvatas)—all these [questions] arise from the investigation of various scriptures. Thus, the meaning is that [the system] has surpassed the position of the Buddhist and Vaiśeṣika proponents. ||1||2||

Now, this *Prakṣādhyāya* (Chapter on Corrections), which consists of inquiries regarding the celestial sphere (*golaprakṣa*) in the form of questions on the justification (*upapatti*) of the arrangement of the sacrificial fires (*dhishnya*), the planets (*graha*), and the configuration of the sphere (*gola*), is intended to ensure the coherence between the preceding and subsequent portions of the text by relying on the knowledge of those justifications. Since the general understanding of the mathematical subjects was established in the previous chapter, a desire for their specific details necessarily arises; thus, it is understood that this very chapter has effectively become the "Chapter on Refutation" (*khaṇḍanādhyāya*) of the first half [of the work].

As long as no refutation is made before one who knows the true nature of these categories by a seeker desiring to know them, so long will their desire for the correct understanding of those respective truths persist. Since it is possible for disciples to attain knowledge of those truths through the teacher’s desire to explain them, this first chapter on inquiry is now being explained.

In this regard, in order to refute the configuration of the stellar sphere (bhacakra) as established in the preceding chapter on planetary calculation—which serves as the basis for that system—the author refutes the Earth’s lack of support by means of a question regarding its support, while simultaneously establishing the Earth’s sphericity through its position at the center of that sphere. He begins with the words "bhramat" [revolving]: "within the revolving wheel of the stellar sphere."

The wheel (*cakra*) refers to the collection of constellations (*nakṣatra*) beginning with Aśvinī; the support for that is the five-elemental substance in the form of a sphere (*golākāra*) which revolves. Within its neck (*gala*), at a location situated at a distance from the points of the sphere equal to half the diameter of its circumference, there is a central point in the intervening space. That is the center of the celestial sphere (*valakendra*). The earth situated there in the sky is surrounded on all sides by the celestial wanderers—the great lords such as the Moon, Mercury, Venus, the Sun, and so forth.

Just as the celestial sphere (gola) containing the constellations exists at an equal distance from all sides of the earth, so too do the planets move within the space contained therein at an equal distance from the earth; this is the meaning. This earth, which is our own support and is perceptible, by what substratum is it held? The meaning is that it remains eternally stable by virtue of being situated in a particular portion of space located in its center. [The questioner says: "Tell me that substratum by which this earth would not move downward from that particular portion of space situated in its lower center. This is the remainder of the sense.

This is the intended meaning: It has been stated in the treatises on astronomy (*jyotiḥśāstra*) that, following the passage beginning with "having created the circle of stars," the constellations, planets, and so forth revolve in the sky at equal distances all around the earth due to the impact of the *pravaha* wind, as otherwise the phenomena of rising and setting would be inexplicable; however, this is not tenable by reason. For if these were grasped [held] on all sides of the earth, it would be impossible for the earth to be situated in their center. Indeed, no object whatsoever is established in the sky without a support.

On the contrary, due to its weight, there would be only a falling toward the earth; consequently, O Śramaṇa, the rotation of the celestial spheres and so forth around the earth would be impossible. Furthermore, if the earth were supported by something just as that [support] is supported by space, then because that support resides in space, a fall would be possible; thus, another support would be required, and for that one as well, and so on, resulting in an infinite regress of supports clinging to a specific point in space, which makes such rotation impossible.

And thus, because this arrangement of the zodiacal circle is illogical, there follows the total abolition of all planetary calculations based upon it; for it has been stated that planetary calculation depends upon the motion of the planets. Furthermore, [the planets] would have to be supported by the earth or some other substratum to the east or west at every moment, as explained in the *Bhāṣya* on the *Adhyāya*; and because there would be an absence of an astronomical system with a fixed domain.

By the phrase "the wheel of wheels" (*cakracakra*), it is also indicated that even though the forms, positions, movements, and so forth of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) and planets (*graha*) are being described, the support for their continuous succession is established; thus, the objection that their motion would be obstructed because they move by piercing through the supporting planets and lunar mansions does not arise, as the stated impossibility is refuted. Therefore, under the guise of a specific question regarding the earth, he states—"What is the shape of the earth?"—thereby following up on the partial inconsistency in the calculation.

Let it be stated and considered: what is the shape of the earth? It must be investigated as follows: since the fact that the earth has the shape of a hollow sphere is established by direct perception, and because, if [the earth were flat], the simultaneous occurrence of sunrise and sunset in all locations would lead to the impossibility of differences in day-length due to longitudinal distance (deśāntara); and because, given the necessity of a difference in the local horizons (kṣitija-bheda) in order to account for such differences in day-length and longitudinal distance, this is perfectly consistent with the earth being spherical in shape.

The sense is that, in his view, since the sphericity of the earth is not established, there would be the great fault of contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣabādha*). Now, one might object: "Just as the lunar orb, which is a sphere and the basis for our perception of its horns, is nevertheless perceived by us as being circular, so too the terrestrial globe might be perceived as having the shape of a mirror due to some defect; thus, there is no fault. To this, he says: *kiyanmānā* (of what measure). [This means: "Of what measure—that is, what is the dimension—does the earth possess? Let it be determined how many *yojanas* the earth actually measures."

"From the investigation of various scriptures": this refers to the investigation of numerous scriptures, such as the Purāṇas, astronomical treatises (*jyotiṣa*), and commentaries, for the purpose of establishing their consistency (*ekavākyatva*) regarding the size of the earth and other matters. Accordingly, since there is a mutual disagreement among the various texts—including the *Sūryasiddhānta* and others composed by Āryabhaṭṭa, Brahmagupta, Lalla, Śrīpati, and Bhaṭṭotpala—as well as the Purāṇas, concerning the measurement of the earth, it is impossible even for Brahmā himself to bring about their consistency. Furthermore, because it is impossible to determine a single definitive measurement, there arises the undesirable consequence (*apatti*) of the total disappearance of calculation based on such measurements.

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that the circumference of the earth is precisely that which is determined by the calculation of the shadow (of a gnomon) when the sung [value] corresponds? Therefore, there is no loss of the calculation. To this, he says: "Of what sort?"—let it be determined: of what kind and in what manner is the earth, which is sealed—that is, pervaded—by these continents, principal mountain ranges, oceans, and mountains other than those such as Indrapada?

Likewise, if the earth were spherical in shape, it would be impossible for these objects such as lamps to remain there, because their upper portions would constitute the very surface [of the sphere], whereas elsewhere they would be situated obliquely or below, making stability impossible. However, if it were like the interior of a mirror, then while stability for all things would be possible, it would follow that the calculated distances to other regions and so forth would be abolished. Furthermore, the sense is that there is no evidence to establish the analogy that the lunar orb and the like are similar to the interior of a mirror. || 2 ||

Now, in two verses, he asks about the rationale for the correction of the planets: "From the established number of elapsed days, by means of the orbital revolutions and through proportion, whatever [mean] planet is obtained, how is it that it is not accurate? And how is it made clear in many ways? Is there longitudinal difference (deśāntara), or difference in rising (udayāntara)? Ah, is there difference in amplitude (bāhvantara), or diurnal arc (cara), or apsis (ucca), or node (pāta)—the slow and the fast? Tell me, Father, what is considered the [true] node? (3)

What is the center, what is born from the center, what is moving, or what is stationary? From what does its fruit arise, and by what is it joined or separated so that this clear result is produced? What is the nature and luster of the throat? (13) What is the correction for observation (*dṛkkarma*) at the time of rising and setting? O Sage, tell me all this clearly and flawlessly, if you truly know the stainless *gela*. (4)

Regarding this, explain clearly everything that was asked—such as "what is another place" or "what is the end of rising"—so that it may become pure for me, provided you understand the *Golādhyāya* composed by the great poet Balabhadra and others. The rest is clear. [Commentary on verse 34]: Now, since the entire collection of mathematical problems is rooted in the configuration of the stellar sphere (*bhacakra*), and because it is generally considered impossible to refute [the system] even through calculation, the author poses questions in the *Śārdūlavikrīḍita* meter, beginning with "saṃsiddha... (established).

The meaning is as follows: from the *ahargaṇa* (day-count) which is "perfectly established"—that is, proven to be faultless because it has been correctly calculated from the *yuga-gaṇa* (cycle-count); and from the *ahargaṇa* described by the statement beginning with "the solar revolution-number elapsed since the Kalpa," which is faultless because its validity is established through logical proof (*upapatti*). By means of the "revolution-numbers of the cycles" (*yugādibhagaṇaiḥ*)—meaning by the revolution-numbers associated with the [four] cycles mentioned for the planets, which consist of the complete revolutions through the twelve zodiac signs; and by the revolution-numbers of the Sun and others intended in the *Sūryasiddhānta*, as indicated by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*).

In this context, it should be understood that the inclusion of the word "yu" (you) was not made for the sake of the student’s intellectual development or as a mere habit of study. By means of proportion (*anupāta*), the measure (*pramāṇa*) and the desired quantity (*icchā*) exist at the beginning and the end as being of the same kind (*samānajātī*); however, the *pala* is of a different kind. According to the method of the three terms (*trairāśika*) as stated—namely, the procedure established by the rule beginning with "the planet multiplied by the circle of the wanderers" (*graha dyucaracakrahata*) and so forth—the non-clarity, the lack of precision, and the unreality of that planet arise. This is because the day-count (*ahargaṇa*), the number of revolutions (*bhagaṇa*), and the civil days (*kudina*) are real.

The meaning is that by the statement "how could the planet derived from that [calculation] not be the true one? From where is the mean [planet] known?", the section on the mean motion (madhyamādhikāra) is refuted. Now, one might argue that since the planet calculated through proportion does not correspond with what is observed in the sky, its status as the "mean" must be inferred from the results [of observation]; therefore, the section on mean motion is not useless. To this, he says: "How? (katham).

Now, even though the middle planet has been established in some way as being free from contradiction, why has the clarification of the true planets not been stated in a single uniform manner? Just as all the middle planets have been stated by means of a single consistent proportion, so too those true planets have not been stated by means of a single consistent proportion.

The sense is that if one assumes the bringing [of the planets] while they are established in different longitudes (bhinnabhikṣā), there is an absence of agreement (saṃvāda); therefore, since agreement occurs only occasionally, the section on the "clear" (spaṣṭa) is inappropriate. The intention is that it is for the sake of that [agreement]. Now, one might object: since agreement of the planets is necessarily produced by the aforementioned calculation of the "clear" (spaṣṭākriyā), the section explaining the "clear" calculation is not useless; to this he says: "What?"—meaning, why is the "longitude difference" (deśāntara), as stated in the section on the "mean" (madhya), necessary? That is to say, it is useless. "Aho! expresses astonishment.

Why was the "difference of rising" (*udayāntara*) for the planets—which is described in the *Sphuṭādhikāra*—assumed [by him]? Since it was not mentioned in the earlier treatise, that which he assumed by his own intellect is also incorrect. The very configuration of what was stated by the ancients has now become difficult to reconcile; how is it that he has added this superfluous "difference of rising" for the planets? This is a great point of contention. Furthermore, that which was called the "difference of amplitude" (*bāhvantara*), known as the "arm" (*bhuja*), as stated in the context of eclipses, is also useless.

Furthermore, the diurnal arc (*cara*) is useless. For instance, since the [mean] Sun’s longitude depends on the rising time and thus pertains to the time of its rising, the mean planet produced from it pertains to that same time; consequently, the true planet produced from that mean planet would also pertain to that same time. Therefore, the corrections for longitudinal difference (*deśāntara*), ascensional difference (*udayāntara*), and the diurnal arc (*cara*)—which are taught in the fifteenth chapter on the sphere (*golādhyāya*)—are inconsistent for the purpose of establishing a time pertaining to both places. This is because the Earth, being shaped like the interior of a mirror, has the same rising time everywhere.

Furthermore, there is no evidence that the *ahargaṇa* (accumulated days) corresponds to the time of sunrise at Laṅkā when it is spherical in shape; rather, let it be taken as corresponding to the time of local sunrise. Thus, even though the two chapters on Mean and True Motion (*madhyaspaṣṭādhikāra*) are complete in themselves, the sense is that a portion of the chapter on Mean and True Motion is redundant because of the introduction of corrections for longitudinal difference (*deśāntara*) and the equation of time (*bhujāntara*). Now, one might object that even so, it has not been proven that these two entire chapters are inconsistent; to this he says: "Moreover" (*kiṃca*). That which was established in the chapter on Mean Motion regarding the revolutions of the spheres (*bhagaṇa*) and so forth [is contradicted here].

This [point] is understood to be like a planet (*graha*): it is slow (*mṛdu*), at its apogee (*ucca*), and at its perigee (*mandocca*), and it is "unsteady" (*cañcala*). By the use of the word "and" (*ca*), the meaning is: "How can there be an apogee or a node (*śaśriocca*) in the sky? The word "and" (*cakāra*) serves to collect the questions. Thus, since the seven planets beginning with the Sun are seen in the sky, it is logical to describe their revolutions (*bhagaṇa*). However, because an apogee is not seen in the sky and lacks a measure (*māna*) therein, how can the description of their revolutions be consistent? Therefore, the section on the mean motion (*madhyamādhikāra*) is untenable.

The meaning is that the *spaṣṭādhikāra* (the chapter on true [mean] motion) is refuted precisely because it depends upon those [other chapters]. To refute by means of clear exposition those other chapters which were already rejected due to their dependence on the *prasaṅga-mahopajīvin* (the great dependent treatise), he poses the question: "What? O Father, what is this "pāta" (node) mentioned in the *madhyamādhikāra*—brought forth by means of the revolutions (*bhagaṇa*) and so forth—which exists in the sky? And thus, since the nature of the *pāta* is not perceived, there is a lack of evidence for the existence of the *pāta*.

Even regarding the arrow produced by the *pāta*, the mention of the shadow of the planet’s grasp (*graha*) in that section is entirely useless; thus, those sections have been discarded. It has been said: "One who knows only this much is easily propitiated, but one who possesses specialized knowledge is propitiated with even greater ease; yet even Brahmā cannot please that man who is arrogant due to a mere fragment of knowledge. Having stated this, such a fragmentary [work] should be disregarded by one who knows the truth. For one who desires the knowledge of reality, there should not be even a slight delay; therefore, the address "O Father" (*tāta*) is used.

The meaning is that whatever has been stated by the father, whether consistent or inconsistent, you should reconcile it all in its entirety with a focused mind. (3) Now, one might object: "Even if the true nature of the [mean] Sun and others is not seen, since the result in the form of the difference between the mean and the true planet depends upon them, there is no lack of consistency with the previous sections due to their inherent nature. To this, he says in the Śārdūlavikrīḍita meter: "Is the planet in a quadrant?"—meaning, what is the form of the difference from the planet in a quadrant?

The meaning is: what is the nature of the interval in the sky? And what is the nature of the *bhuja* (versed sine), the *koṭi* (complementary sine), and the resulting *jyā* (sine) produced from the center (*kendra*)? What is the nature of that result—the result produced by its *bhuja*—is it "moving" (*cala*), meaning the equation of center (*śīghra*), or "fixed" (*acala*), meaning the equation of apsis (*manda*)? The word "and" (*vā*) is used for conjunction. Furthermore, why has the difference between the mean and the true planet—the result in degrees—not been established in a uniform manner for Mars and the others, just as it is for the Sun and Moon?

The sense is that the *spaṣṭādhikāra* (the chapter on true [mean] motion) is untenable because there is no logical justification for how those two fragments are established through the assumption of distinct centers. Now, one might ask: "Let the difference be derived by whatever method possible. To this, he says: "From what? For at times the planet—the mean planet—minus that [difference], being subtracted by the correction (*phala*), becomes the true [planet]. From what cause? And at other times, by the word "and" (*ca*), the mean [planet] plus the correction, being added by the correction, from what cause does it become the true [planet]?

And thus, the slow motion (*mandaphala*) occurring in the quadrants beginning with Aries and Libra is positive; that same [motion] in the two other quadrants, which possess the nature of the throat (*galasvarūpa*), is threefold [in sign]. (15) Maṇidīpikā-commentary: Since there is no authority for an irregularity such as "positive or negative" (*dhanarṇam*), and because a uniform form is more appropriate, the sense is that the section on true [longitude] (*spaṣṭādhikāra*) is indeed incorrect. Now, one might object: "This is not at all contradictory, because their distinctness (*vejātya*) is established by the strength of the result through the attainment of observational consistency (*dṛksāmya*). To this, he says: "What? (*kimiti*).
