The wise, knowing that, [apply] the correction for parallax (*dṛkkarma*) in two ways—meaning in two forms: one dependent on the rising sun at the times of rising, and the other dependent on the setting sun at the times of setting—to the planet; they should thus correct it. What is meant by "only at the times of rising and setting"? It means that without the correction for parallax, the achievement of visual coincidence (*dṛksāmya*) is not possible. Otherwise, the very designation of "parallax" (*dṛkkarma*) would be contradicted.

Therefore, for the sake of establishing the true longitude (gṛhaspaṣṭatva), the correction for parallax (dṛkkarma) must also be applied, just like the results of the mansions and signs; thus, its inclusion is useful solely for the purpose of calculating the ascendants at rising and setting—this is the intended meaning. Consequently, he concludes that what you have stated in the first half [of your verse], regarding the calculation of planetary positions, is incorrect according to the method described: "All this," etc. "If" (cet) means "if."

O wise one, you know that which is stainless and faultless; therefore, tell me all that entire system of mathematics previously described by me, which is pure and beyond reproach. The sense is that because the first half [of the work] provides only a general understanding of the meanings of those terms, it fails to establish the true nature of those categories, and thus the entire system of mathematics is inconsistent. || 4 ||

Now, regarding the difference in the duration of day and night as determined by the three questions, he speaks in two verses: "O wise one, tell me: when the sun is in the northern hemisphere (Uttaragola), is the day great and the night small? Or, when it has moved to the southern direction (Dakṣiṇadiggata), is the day small and the night great? "Is the day and night of those dwelling in the land of the Yavanas equal to a year of the gods? And for the enemies of the gods (the Asuras), is it equal to a year of the Pitṛs? Likewise, what is the measure of a day for the serpents (Vahiṇa), which is equal to a thousand Yugas multiplied by a hundred? [Verse 5 and 6 are clear.]

Now, with the verse beginning "atha caraghaṭīsahitā rahitā" (then, [the day] joined with or devoid of the *caraghaṭī*s), the author refutes—by means of the *drutavilambita* meter—the established conclusion that in the northern hemisphere the day is greater and in the southern hemisphere it is smaller, as stated in the *Sphuṭādhikāra*: "O mathematician, O knower of calculation! When the sun is situated in the northern hemisphere, oh, what a wonder! It is said that the day is great; how then can the night be small?"

Because the earth is unchanging [in its nature], and because the places of sunrise and sunset are situated on the same meridian, and because day and night are equal at the junction of the celestial sphere (the equinox), how could there be an increase or decrease of day and night in the northern hemisphere? There is no cause for it. Why does the opposite not occur? This is a point of wonder. Likewise, O wise one who investigates the true nature of things, when the sun with precession (sāyana-sūrya) is situated in the southern hemisphere during its southward course, [how could this happen]? The word "nanu" indicates the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) or expresses doubt.

The day is short and the night is long; tell me, what is the cause of this? Furthermore, it is improper for the day and night to be equal according to the sequence of the northern and southern solstices (*golaka*), since they ought to be of a constant form. Therefore, it is said that the inequality of the day and night is inconsistent due to a lack of logical justification—this is the meaning of the verse. (Golādhyāya, Maṇiprabhā Commentary, Verse 5). Now, as an incidental topic, he establishes the days and nights of the gods, the ancestors, and Prajāpati, as stated in the section on the middle sphere (*madhyādhikāra*), using the *drutavilambita* meter: "Bhavati... etc.

Of the gods dwelling in heaven and of the Daityas who are enemies of the gods—the word "ca" (and) serves as a conjunction; thus, the meaning is [the cycle] of both gods and Daityas. A day and night (*dyuniśam* = *ahorātram*) measured by a solar year (*dyumaṇivarṣamitam* = *sauravarṣapramāṇam*) occurs; for what reason does it occur?

Just as in our own country a day and night (ahorātra) is measured by sixty *ghaṭīs*, so too for those two [the gods and the demons] a day and night is measured by a solar year (*sauravarṣa*). And how is it stated in the *Madhyādhikāra* by what reasoning that the day and night of the gods and demons is exactly that? Furthermore, why is it stated to be measured by sixty *ghaṭīs*? Likewise, regarding the ancestors (*pitṛs*), a day and night is measured by a lunar month (*cāndramāsa*). And this is what was stated by the phrase "this is the day and night of the ancestors" (*paitraṃ dhurātram*); from what reason is this so?

The day and night of Brahmā, the Creator, consists of two kalpas, which is a thousand yugas; a thousand yugas constitute a single day of the Creator, and that kalpa is likewise his day and night. But how has it been stated [in the verse] that "two kalpas" are his day and night? For there is no such reason. Now, he states the alternative view regarding the rising of the zodiacal signs: "Are the degrees of the circle of the ecliptic equal, while the zodiacal signs are indeed unequal? Do they rise together because of the sphere (gola), for they are not equal even in all their constituent parts? (7)

This is clear. || 7 || Ma0 Ṭī0—Now, with the *hutavilambita* meter, he refutes the previously stated [claims] regarding the great sine of a single sign (*rāśi*) and the right-ascensions (*nirakṣodaya*) as well as the oblique-ascensions (*veśodayāṃśa*), by stating: "The signs... The signs, beginning with Aries (*meṣa*), indeed attain their rising (*udaya*) in unequal and equal times respectively; this is certain (*khalu*). Why? From what [source]? Why is it not stated that the rising time for all signs beginning with Aries is equal? Why have they been calculated as dissimilar? The term "rising times" (*udayakālāḥ*) is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*).

It should also be considered why the times of rising and setting are not equal. One might object: "Since the measures of the zodiac signs are unequal, it is logical that their rising and setting durations are likewise unequal. To this, he states the qualification of the signs: "equal" (*samaḥ*). Each and every sign consists of thirty equal parts. For Taurus is not greater than Aries, nor Gemini greater than Taurus, by degrees; therefore, it is impossible for the times of their rising and setting to be mutually shorter or longer.

The meaning is as follows: why is it inconsistent that the times of sunrise and sunset for the sign named Meṣa (Aries) are not equal to those of the thirty parts named Vṛṣa (Taurus), as stated in the *Sphuṭādhikāra*? Since there is no evidence for their being equal, he says: "of the ecliptic" (*bhavalayasya*). The zodiac signs are indeed (*kila*)—meaning certainly—not exceeding twelve parts each, being equal to the twelfth part of the circle related to the night. This is the intended sense.

And thus, since the zodiacal sphere completes one revolution in sixty sidereal *ghaṭīs*, a twelfth part—five *ghaṭīs*—is the time for the rising and setting of a sign; this is logically consistent, whereas [the other view] is not equal to it. This is the intended meaning. Now, one might object that even at the same time, a specific portion of the zodiacal sphere possesses such power; therefore, he says: "But what? O knower of the sphere (*golavit*)! This is a question regarding the nature of the sphere.

Even though the true nature [of the sun] is known, why do the times of rising and setting not become uniform across all regions, despite being calculated by the limbs [of the sphere] in whatever manner possible? Why have dissimilar risings occurred in every country? The implication is: "Is it not because the earth is uniform [in its spherical nature]? || 7 ||

Now, he describes the determination of the shapes of the celestial latitude (dyujyā), terrestrial latitude (kujyā), and so forth, in verse: "O learned one, show the configuration of the fields in the sphere of the sky, such as the celestial latitude, the terrestrial latitude, and the equatorial circle. This is clear. Now, posing a question regarding the difference in time between the lunar and solar eclipses, he says in a half-verse: "If the eclipse of the Moon occurs at the end of the lunar day (tithi), why does that not happen for the Sun? Does the commencement of the Moon's eclipse take place in the east, while that of the Sun takes place in the west? (8)

"O best among the wise, what indeed is the obscuring object (ālambana) and what is the nature of the eclipse? What is its refinement on the lunar day (tithi) corresponding to the number five (bāṇa)? When that is established, from where and by what means does it arise? In this regard, the intention of the questioner is as follows: During a lunar eclipse, the shadow of the Earth (bhūbhā) acts as the eclipsing body. At the end of the full moon, because of the equality of the Earth and the Moon, their conjunction ought to occur. Similarly, during a solar eclipse, at the end of the Moon's phase as an obscuring body, there ought to be a conjunction due to their equality.

Therefore it was asked: "At the end of the lunar day (tithi), is there a parallax for the Moon, the lord of the stars, or not for the Sun? Alas! What indeed is this so-called "parallax" (gamaka-sambandha)? And what is its depression (nati)? Is its correction applied to the lunar day (tithi) or to the ghatis? By means of parallax, is the lunar day corrected, or the ghatis? Furthermore, another question: "Those two being established, from where, from where?"—meaning, from what cause, and from what [radius] of the Earth (pṛthivī) are those two, namely parallax and depression, calculated? The meaning is: they are calculated by means of half the diameter of the Earth.

Likewise, Indra is in the eastern direction; what about the Sun in the western direction? Tell me all such things. (8–9) Bhaṭṭotpala’s Commentary: Now, in the section concerning the calculation of the three lunar fortnights (*tripakṣa*), although [the previous verses] were almost exhausted, he speaks again in the *mandākrāntā* meter, refuting [the opponent's view], beginning with "yujyā": O Vibudha—O Knower of Rays—[tell me] the configuration of the figures (*kṣetrasaṃsthā*) of those geometrical objects related to the diagrams, which were described in the chapter on the Three Problems (*tripraśna*) as being derived from the products of the sine of latitude, the sine of co-latitude, and the sines of the ascensional difference and declination, starting with the shadow (*śaṅku*) divided by the first term.

Show [the sphere] in a terrestrial globe (golaka) constructed according to the method described in the upcoming section on the construction of the celestial sphere (golabandha); that is to say, demonstrate it in such a way that its position in the sky is indeed certain. Furthermore, explain it so that the nature of the primary celestial sphere (mukhyagola), including its geometric figures and other properties as stated in the *Tripraśna*, becomes clearly understood. The underlying intention is that what was previously presented was considered incorrect because it lacked a logical demonstration.

If the middle eclipse of the Moon, the lord of the stars, occurs at the end of the lunar day (ṛkṣānta) or at the end of the full moon (paurṇamāsī-anta), then that is the end of the new moon (amānta) for the Sun; this is the meaning. Why was "middle eclipse" not mentioned? For it has been stated: "The middle eclipse results in the cessation of the lunar phase (parva)."

In the eighteenth chapter of the second century [of the work], it is stated that the middle eclipse of the moon occurs at the end of the new moon (*amānta*), whereas the middle eclipse of the sun occurs at the time of full conjunction (*pūrṇayoga*). It would have been more appropriate to state this there; however, since the end of the lunar fortnight (*parvavirāma*) was established there as the clear and most precise time for the middle of the eclipse, how can it be said that the middle eclipse occurs at a time near the end of the new moon (*amānta*), whether before or after? Therefore, the sense is that because the middle time is logically untenable, the section on eclipses (*grahaṇādhikāra*) is considered improper.

Now, it may be argued that since there is no parallax (*lambana*) during a lunar eclipse, it is logical that the middle of the eclipse should occur precisely at the end of the immersion (*amanta*). In a solar eclipse, however, because of that [parallax], the middle of the eclipse occurs at a time other than the end of the immersion. Therefore, when there is an absence of parallax, the middle of the eclipse should indeed be at the end of the immersion; thus, there is no fault. To refute this with another objection, he says: "The Moon" (*indu*), etc. The first contact (*pragraha*) or touch of the Moon occurs in the east.

Is the touch (sparśa) of the Sun in the west? Likewise, one should also consider why the point of contact (malkṣa) of the Moon is in the east. Thus, since there is no distinction between the two in terms of being eclipsed, the calculation of the deflection at the point of contact (sparśa-makṣa-valana) is inappropriate due to the difference in direction; this is the intended meaning, because such a state does not exist [in reality]. Now, one might object: "Since the drawing of the diagram (parilekhana) serves no practical purpose, it is proper that the section on eclipses (grahaṇādhikāra) should end right here. To refute this previous objection, he establishes [the necessity] with the verse beginning with "lambakam."

"O best among the wise, what is this 'parallax' (*lambana*) which you yourself have refuted? Alas! Why is it that you have even mentioned it in the context of solar eclipses? Since there is no distinction in their both being types of eclipses, why should parallax not also apply to lunar eclipses? For parallax is certainly not improper in a lunar eclipse; indeed, its necessity in a solar eclipse has been demonstrated by you. Thus, the sense is one of regret, thinking: 'How is it that even something inconsistent with your own doctrine must now be reconciled through your own words?'"

He states that another refutation of the belief in the existence of a breast has occurred to him as well, beginning with the words "And what...": "What [is] *nati*? Of what nature is it? The word "and" (*ca*) is used in a cumulative sense. It means that at a lunar eclipse (*candragrahaṇa*), *nati* (the southward deflection) is not established; whereas at a solar eclipse (*sūryagraha*), its establishment is possible. How then is it appropriate for one who knows eclipses to speak thus? He states another refutation, beginning with "That" (*tat*): "On the lunar day (*tithau*) which is the new moon (*amānta*); on the occasion of the solar eclipse (*vāṇe*) when the moon is eclipsed by the sun—at these times respectively, by which young woman was their correction (*saṃskṛtiḥ*), namely the correction of those two, *lambana* and *nati*, declared?"

If the parallax (*lambana*) is to be corrected at the point of the [true] moon, then why is the correction for the latitude (*nati*) not also applied there? What prevents the correction for latitude from being combined with the correction for parallax at that very spot? The intended meaning is: why should there not be a combination of both in one place? Why should the correction for latitude and parallax not be applied sequentially to the [true] moon on the lunar day (*tithi*)? He states another objection: "Those two," etc. Those two—parallax and latitude—are further [removed] from the earth by one and a half [units], as it were. For what reason?

When the [lunar] parallax is established, the parallax is four *ghaṭikās*; and when the depression (*nati*) is calculated, the maximum depression is fifteen minutes of arc, and the Earth's diameter is half a *yojana* of motion. Thus, the calculation of the distance from the center of the Earth is derived from half the Earth's diameter. Furthermore, since this is common to both types of eclipses, it would necessarily apply even to a solar eclipse. The intention is that, by defining the parallax and depression, these three chapters on eclipses alone are sufficient.

9 | The Question Concerning the Nature of the Cowherd (Gopāla). 19 8. Now, Śṛṅga and Nemi describe the waning and waxing of the moon’s white [phase]: "Alas! This king of the twice-born (the moon), though naturally white, has become ill-behaved; from where does this come? Even though he has reached the state of the sun (the day-maker), it is as if due to excessive attachment to the faults arising from fatigue. Then, having returned once more to the refuge of that very one who possesses the body of the three Vedas (Viṣṇu), does the white [moon] indeed attain the state of being well-behaved and the renown of increasing luster? 10.

"O astrologer, this moon, the king of the twice-born, though he has attained good conduct (*suvṛtta*) and reached his full state on the full-moon day (*paurṇamāsī*), for what reason does he become ill-behaved (*kuvṛtta*) and assume a dark form? It is as if due to excessive attachment to the fault (*doṣa*) arising from wandering. Here, *doṣa* means 'night. Likewise, on the full-moon day, there is the contact (*saṅga*) of the entire moon; that which follows such contact is the destruction of its white luster."

By that other [association], it appears that one might become a "bad tree" (kuvṛkṣa), meaning one of censurable conduct. Just as the King of the Twice-born (the Moon), though possessing excellent conduct even while Brahmā, has fallen into a state of constant decline due to excessive attachment to the company of those who wander in delusion and possess a nature of broken vows; through such association with the base, he loses his pure luster. Thus, one would become of censurable conduct. Now, furthermore, there is a third...

Having reached the Sun-god in his subtle form (*tanu*), immediately thereafter, through the increase of his white splendor (*tejas*), he likewise attains virtuous conduct (*sadvṛttatā*) and perfect roundness (*suvartulatā*). This occurs solely by taking refuge in the threefold body (*trayītanu*) of that Blessed One. Just as it is stated in the *Smṛti*—that one who has committed a wicked deed (*kuvṛtta*) reaches the assembly of the three worlds (or the three-fold path) and, having been graced by Him, attains an increase of splendor and returns once more to virtuous conduct—the meaning here is the same. || 10 ||

Thus ends the second chapter, on the Questions regarding the Sphere (*golapraśnādhyāya*), in the *Mitākṣarā* commentary on the *Siddhāntaśiromaṇi*, within the section on the Sphere (*golādhyāya*). Now, [the author] introduces the chapter on the Rising of the Lunar Crescent (*candrakalonnatyadhikāra*) with a verse in the *Śārdūlavikrīḍita* meter, beginning with "kukalasya": "This is directly perceived: the king of the twice-born, the Moon—oh, how wonderful!—has attained the state of perfect circularity (*sadvṛttatva*), having reached fullness through his complete orb. [Note: The commentary explains that the Moon is the "king of the twice-born" (*dvijarāja*), and expresses wonder (*aho*) at its beauty. It has attained the nature of being perfectly round (*vartulatva*), which is the essence of a true circle (*maṇḍala*), and has thus been transformed into a complete orb.]

The word "api" (even/also) serves as an ornament of the light of the boon-bestower. Why does Vṛtra possess such a wretchedly shaped orb—a state resulting from the decline and diminution of that splendor and brilliance belonging to the lunar disc during the bright fortnight? At the end of the full moon, the moon has a perfectly full orb; thereafter comes the dark fortnight. Why then does the moon become one with its own orb no longer full?

In that regard as well, the state of being a full orb does not occur. Whether it is when the orb is incomplete, or even when it is being filled, it would not be a full orb. Therefore, the possibility of a full orb having a fragmented orb [within it] is utterly contradictory; it is a point of wonder. Therein, he imagines the waning of the white light as being "as if from contact with the fault" (*doṣa*). "Fault" (*doṣa*) refers to the night; "contact" (*saṅga*) means the arrival of the moon in the sign of Cancer (*karkaṭa*), which is the sixth sign. From that, there is no internal union.

On any day of the bright fortnight other than the full moon day, there is no conjunction of the moon with the entire night; however, on that [full moon] day, there is a conjunction of the moon throughout the entire night. Therefore, although it is impossible for this [conjunction] to be the actual cause, the word *eva* (indeed) here indicates a poetic conceit (*utprekṣā*), suggesting that it is imagined to be the cause. The sense is that if it were the actual cause, the question [of why the moon does not rise fully at other times] would be logically untenable.

[Objection: Since the cause of the excessive attachment to defects is indeed its prior occurrence, why then is there no poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) regarding the full moon’s orb acting as a *laghu* (light/short syllable)? [Response: To specify the particularity of this excessive attachment to defects, he says: "because it arises from delusion" (*bhramabhavāt*). This means: because it has arisen from the moon’s rotation toward the west.

And thus, since the moon rises at the time of sunset on that day, it is understood that if one were to travel facing toward the west (the direction of the moon), there would necessarily be a connection with the entire night; therefore, the excessive conjunction [of the moon] alone is considered the cause. The sense is that because the full orb of the moon remains visible for only a moment at its end, it cannot be accepted as the cause. Immediately thereafter, this moon, having reached the body of the sun and resorted to the new-moon phase (*darśanta*), follows that from the commencement of the dark fortnight (*bahulapakṣa*).

"By resorting to that sun" means by its abiding therein; the particle *eva* (only) excludes dependence on any other planet. If the reading is *iva*, it implies a poetic conceit (*utprekṣā*). It should be understood that this is because dependence on the sun is logical, whereas [dependence on] anything else is not a cause for it. "Of the white light" means gradually, in the sequence of the lunar days (*tithi*) of the month; that is to say, in the same measure as the increase of the bright fortnight from the beginning of the dark fortnight. The particle *eva* serves to exclude any measure other than that.

By means of increase and decrease. Furthermore, after the breaking of the circle (maṇḍalabhaṅga), why does it attain the state of being a perfect circle (*saṃpūrṇamaṇḍalatā*) within another month at the end of the full moon? Likewise, why should it not remain exactly as it was after the breaking of the circle; from what would a perfect circle arise again? Thus, qualities such as forbearance (*kṣamā*) do not come into being. The sense is that this section on the "Horns" (*śṛṅgaveranītyadhikāra*) is thus shattered by its lack of systematic consistency (*avyavasthitatā*).

Thus, since the conjunctions of planets, the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*), the conjunctions of planets, the *pāta*, and eclipses are established as being "fragmented" (*khaṇḍita*) by virtue of their dependence on fragmented objects, even an ignorant person knows this; therefore, for the sake of prominence, we have not provided a refutation (*khaṇḍana*) of them here. It should be understood that this is because there is no existence of additional solid objects (*kaṭhinapadārtha*) therein. Now, the second meaning of this verse: This certain king of Brahmins (*vijarāja*), a member of the priestly class, is "established in good conduct" (*sad-vṛttatva-gata*), meaning he is devoted to virtuous behavior. The word "even" (*api*) is used to indicate an apparent contradiction (*virodhābhāsa*).

Perhaps, due to the mind being occupied with thousands of other objects, there arose a delusion consisting of restless distraction; from that, a fault in the form of the transgression (*pratyavāya*) born from the non-performance of obligatory duties (*nityakarman*) might arise. By the destruction of the exceedingly pure and bright Brahminical luster through such intense attachment, one becomes "of evil intent" (*kubuddhi*), meaning one whose covering is contemptible—how, indeed, has such a censurable state arisen? This is a marvel!

Immediately thereafter, he [the sage] shattered that body composed of the three Vedas; having approached and obtained the best of the learned, who was a practitioner of the Vedic meaning, he did so by means of the grace and refuge of that one whose nature is the Veda and who is capable of bestowing supreme favor upon the learned. The word "eva" (only) serves to exclude any other form of grace. Through the gradual growth of that pure Brahmarṣi, it became such that it remained indestructible throughout his entire life. This is the meaning of the word "ebha."

Furthermore, what wonder is there that he attains virtuous conduct and devotion to the practice of wandering? The sense is that this is because of his favor toward the learned. || 10 || [End of] *Bhuvanakośa* || 2.1 || In the *Madhṭīe*: Thus, having explained the refutation (*khaṇḍana*), Kākeki speaks—thus ends the section on the inquiry into the spheres (*golapraśna*). The word "gola" is used to prevent the confusion that the questions already presented have been fully explained; however, the mathematical problems (*gaṇitapraśna*) along with their solutions are stated at the end of the work.

The sense is that these [verses], consisting of inquiries regarding the nature of objects situated on the celestial globe (*golasthita*), were described for the sake of providing a thematic connection (*saṃgati*), even though they were not explicitly introduced [in the table of contents]. || 10 || In this work titled *Śiromaṇimarīci*, composed by the son of the illustrious mathematician Raṅganātha—whose feet are served by a continuous lineage of the most eminent astrologers—the first section, consisting of the inquiry concerning the celestial globe (*golapṛcchā*), has indeed reached its conclusion. || 2 ||

Thus ends the chapter on Astronomical Problems (Praśnādhyāya) in the *Marīci*, a commentary on the *Siddhāntaśiromaṇi*, composed by Gaṇaka Munīśvara—also known as Viśvarūpa, the son of the illustrious Gaṇaka Raṅganātha, the sovereign of all astronomers. Thus the twentieth chapter is completed. 20.

Now, desiring to state the proof for the configuration of the earth—the answer to the first question—the author first mentally prostrates before the Supreme Brahman, the primordial source of all principles such as the earth and so forth, and the sole seed for the generation of the entire universe. From that [Brahman], through the agitation of Prakṛti and Puruṣa, there arose the Great Principle (Mahat); from its womb came the syllable *Oṃ*; and from that union, ether, fire, water, and earth were produced.

May that primordial Supreme Brahman, the ultimate Reality, be ever victorious—He from whose belly the universe emerged, and from whose roar the earth stood firm; He from whom, through the agitation of Puruṣa and Prakṛti, the Mahat-tattva arose, and from the Mahat, the Garbha (the cosmic embryo), and from that, the Ahaṃkāra, and so forth. Herein, this is what is intended: [He is victorious] by existing in a state of absolute preeminence. What is that? The Supreme Brahman. Of what nature is that primordial Reality? It is that from which, through the two—the agitated Puruṣa and [Prakṛti]—the Mahat came into being; from the Mahat, the Garbha; from that, the Ahaṃkāra, and so on. This is what is stated here.

That which has been described in the Sāṃkhya and other medical treatises, as well as in the Śrutis and Purāṇas regarding the initial creation, is stated here. In that regard, "Prakṛti" is known by such terms as the Unmanifest (avyakta), the Undifferentiated (avyākṛta), the Equilibrium of the Guṇas (guṇasāmya), and the Cause (kāraṇa); these are synonyms for the primordial source. Within that Prakṛti exists the Lord, the all-pervading Puruṣa. The qualities (guṇas)—Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas—exist in perfect equilibrium; therefore, it is called the Equilibrium of the Guṇas.

Likewise, at the beginning of the dissolution of primordial nature (*prakṛti*), there exists Time (*kāla*), which is the cause of destruction and preservation. When that Blessed Lord Vāsudeva, known as Parabala, desires to create, then a portion (*aṃśa*) called Saṃkarṣaṇa issues forth from Him and produces agitation in Primordial Nature and the Spirit (*puruṣa*), who are situated in proximity to one another. From those two, thus agitated, the Great One (*mahat*) arises. Indeed, the Great One is a moment of intellect (*buddhi*); that is called both the principle of the Great One (*mahattattva*) and the principle of intellect (*buddhitattva*).

That which is the Great Principle (*mahat-tattva*) is a portion (*aṃśa*) of the Blessed Lord named Pradyumna. From that Great Principle, as it undergoes transformation, there arose the ego (*ahaṃkāra*), which is named Aniruddha. These—the forms of Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha—are specifically well-known in the Vaiṣṇava scriptures as distinct manifestations (*mūrti-bheda*). That ego became threefold under the influence of the qualities (*guṇa*): that which was characterized by *sattva* is the *vaikārika*; that which was characterized by *rajas* is the *taijasa*.

That which is *tāmasa* is the *bhūtādi*. As it is stated in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa: "The *vaikārika*, the *taijasa*, and the *tāmasa* known as *bhūtādi*—this threefold *ahaṃkāra* was born from the Great One (*mahat*). Therein, that *ahaṃkāra* which is *tāmasa* is the *bhūtādi*. From it, the five great elements (*pañcamahābhūtāni*) came into being. What are those elements? They are space, air, fire, water, and earth. Space is *ākāśa*; air is *vāyu*; the crested one is *agni*; water is *udaka*; and the broad one is *pṛthvī*. These elements arose preceded by their respective qualities.

Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are the primary qualities (*mukhya-guṇa*) of ether and the other elements. Among these, from egoity (*ahaṃkāra*) arises the subtle element of sound (*śabda-tanmātra*). The state of a quality existing in an extremely subtle form is denoted by the term *tanmātra*. From the subtle element of sound comes ether; from ether, the subtle element of touch; from that, air; from air, the subtle element of form; from that, fire; from fire, the subtle element of taste; from that, water; from water, the subtle element of smell; and from that, earth. Thus, ether and the subsequent elements came to possess one additional quality each.

Furthermore, regarding the organs for the apprehension of those qualities such as sound and the rest: here, the ear, eye, tongue, and nose constitute the four organs of perception (*buddhīndriya*). Speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals are the five organs of action (*karmendriya*). Then there is the mind (*manas*), which partakes of the nature of both. Indeed, the apprehension of qualities cannot be performed by the organs independently; therefore, their presiding deities are [as follows]: for the organ of hearing, the quarters (*diś*); for the skin, the wind (*vāyu*).

The Sun is the presiding deity of the eyes; Varuṇa, of the tongue; the Aśvins, of the two nostrils; likewise, Agni, of speech; Indra, of the two arms; Viṣṇu, of the anus; Mitra, of the rectum; Prajāpati, of the generative organ; and the Moon, of the mind. These are the presiding deities of the senses. Among them, those which are the senses arise from the *taijasa* (fiery) *ahaṃkāra*; those which are the gods arise from the *vaikārika* (pure/sattvic) *ahaṃkāra*. As it is stated in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*: "From the *taijasa* [ahaṃkāra] arise the five sense organs, and from the *vaikārika* arise the ten gods."

"Eleventh is the mind; these are remembered as the deities of transformation (vaikārika). Then, from that contraction, the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) arose. Thus, from the collection of the produced principles (tattvas), prior to the dissolution of primordial nature (prākṛtika-pralaya), there came into being the cosmic egg in the form of a bubble, which subdues all inert matter. Within its interior was the earth in the shape of a lotus. Therein, Mount Meru was shaped like the pericarp, and upon it rested the four-faced one born from the lotus (Brahmā). From him, the entire universe—including gods, humans, and demons—came into existence.

Since, from the primordial Supreme Brahman, through the agitation of *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*, a succession of *ahaṃkāra*s was produced, and from that emerged the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), within which the multitude of beings on earth arose; thus, this entire universe came into being from the Creator (Dvirañci). This occurs perpetually and without interruption. At the conclusion of that [cycle], there is another Brahman, whose purpose is the dissolution of the senses and their objects. Therefore, may that primordial state of yours be victorious! [May] the inquiry regarding the earth and the sky [be successful].

Chapter 23: The Chapter on the Treasury of the World (Bhuvanakosa), consisting of questions and answers regarding the configuration of the Earth, is now explained. Therein, desiring to state the nature of the Earth’s stability and so forth—which serves as the answer to the question concerning the Earth—in order to establish the configuration of the desired stellar sphere (bhacakra) as understood from the preceding statement beginning with "sapūrvī bhacakram," [the author] first presents the fundamental process of creation by means of reasoning, in order to dispel the doubt as to how the occurrence of creation came about.

Under the guise of composing an auspicious opening by means of a series of appropriate questions and answers, he says in the *mandākrāntā* meter: "From which... (*yasmād iti*). That reality—which is "inexpressible" (*anirvacanīya*) according to the Vedic scripture, "From which words turn back, together with the mind, having failed to reach it"—is "victorious," meaning it exists in a state of supreme excellence. By this, an act of salutation (*namaskāra*) is implied. [An objection: But if it is inexpressible, how can it possess supreme excellence precisely because of its falsity? To this, he replies: "That reality" (*tattvam iti*). It is "substantial" (*vastubhūta*) according to the scriptural text, "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*).

The sense is that, because of this, the falsity of the elaborations (prapañca) in the Vedānta doctrine is not [the case], and its own superiority is self-evident. To provide the specific qualification that serves as the reason for this understanding, he says: "Brahman. Because it is vast (bṛhat), it is unlimited and all-pervasive; this is the meaning, according to the scripture: "Oṃ, that is Brahman. The sense is that the world-phenomenon (prapañca) lacks such a nature. He states the authority for its existence: "Āśrama."

The meaning is that its existence is established through inference based on the mark of the effect (*kāryaliṅgakānumāna*), namely, by virtue of its persisting through the time prior to the world's origination, acting as the instrumental cause for that [world]; and also from scripture, such as: "From which indeed these beings are born," and "Having created it, He entered into it. [Objection: But in the Vedānta system, is this not established by the existence of Māyā? To this he says: "Śaśvat" (eternal). The meaning is "not subject to destruction. The sense is that because Māyā is perishable, it is not established [in the ultimate sense], and thus the Lord (Īśvara) is established.

[Objection: But in this way, since the eternal *prakṛti* is established in the Sāṃkhya system, its [the Supreme’s] establishment does not follow; therefore, he says: “The Supreme” (*paramam*). It means "excellent. For the Śruti declares: "That is Truth, that is the Self; Thou art That; It is Consciousness, Bliss, and Power. The sense is that in the Supreme Lord, who consists of Being, Consciousness, and Bliss by virtue of being omniscient, there is no *prakṛti*-like insentience. [Objection: But even though it is insentient, according to the doctrine of the sage Kapila, *prakṛti* clearly extends its fruitful activity in the vicinity of the Self.

Just as insentient iron moves of its own accord in the presence of a magnet, and just as the activity of insentient milk proceeds for the sake of the increase of curds, so too does the activity of *pradhāna* proceed for the sake of the liberation of the *puruṣa*. By stating that "the activity of this [pradhāna] is for the sake of the *puruṣa*," it is established that even though *prakṛti*—which is the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) consisting of *jaḍa* (insentience)—is itself insentient, it possesses the agency of creating the world solely through the proximity of the *jīva*. Thus, the meaning is that there is no difference between the material cause and the agent even in the case of the Supreme State (*paramapada*). May that Supreme Brahman be eternally victorious!

Therefore, since the proof of *prakṛti* is established through the word "this" (*yam*), and because the proof of the *negdharā* [the non-creator] follows from that, he states its proof by means of the established doctrine of creation based on the prior acceptance of the Pātañjala system—beginning with the words "yasmāt. The meaning is "for which reason. "By the agitated *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*" means by those two in a state of agitation. "Agitation" (*kṣubdhatva*) refers to the state of being ready for immediate manifestation.

The two who are agitated are *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*. In the Sāṃkhya treatise, *pradhāna*—also known as the *avyakta* (the unmanifest) and the equilibrium of the *guṇas*—is well-known as the cause of the universe. Its agitation (*kṣobha*), however, consists of the movement of the *guṇas*. *Puruṣa* is the Lord (*īśvara*), according to the Vedic scripture: "He indeed is this *puruṣa*. And from that arises the desire to create (*sisṛkṣā*). The meaning is: "from those two, *prakṛti* and *virāj*, when they have become agitated. The qualification "agitated" is used to exclude the state of non-creation. [From them arises] the *mahat* (the Great One).

The Great Principle (*mahat*), characterized by intellect (*buddhi*)—which is synonymous with *sva* and *apara*—came into being. By the will of the Lord, through faith, the Great Principle was emitted from *prakṛti*. This is because, in that system, it is accepted [as being] like a sphere (as stated in the *Golādhyāya*, verse 2). Within the womb—the "womb" here indicating the interior of the agitated Great Principle—the Ego (*ahaṃkāra*) came into being; the meaning is that it became manifest within the Great Principle due to its magnitude.

This threefold *ahaṃkāra*—namely, the *vaikārika*, the *taijasa*, and the *bhūtādi* which is *tāmasa*—was born from the *mahat* (the Great Principle) due to the predominance of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* respectively; this is as stated in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa. From that *tāmasa-ahaṃkāra*, the subtle elements (*tanmātras*) arose: ether, air, fire, water, and earth, each preceded by its own specific quality. For this very reason, the *tāmasa-ahaṃkāra* is called *bhūtādi* (the origin of the elements). Thus, from the *tāmasa-ahaṃkāra* comes the subtle element of sound (*śabda-tanmātra*), and from that, ether (*ākāśa*).

From this [tamas] comes the subtle element of touch; from this, air; from this, the subtle element of form; from this, fire; from this, the subtle element of taste; from this, water; from this, the subtle element of smell; and from this, earth. Sound is the quality of ether (*ākāśa*); sound and touch are the qualities of air; sound, touch, and form are the qualities of fire; sound, touch, form, and taste are the qualities of water; and sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are the qualities of earth—thus these five great elements (*mahābhūta*) possess an increasing number of qualities and are produced from the *tāmasa* ego (*ahaṃkāra*).

A *tanmātra* is a constituent part that, being endowed with a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*), initiates the formation of an element (*bhūta*). An element, however, consists of a collection of *tanmātras*. According to the stated sequence: "From this very Self, space (*ākāśa*) was produced; from space, air; from air, fire; from fire, water; from water, earth. From these [elements] arise the five organs of perception (*buddhīndriya*): hearing, touch, sight, taste, and smell, which grasp the qualities of sound and so forth. The five organs of action (*karmendriya*) are: speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals.

The eleven organs—consisting of the ten senses and the mind (*manas*)—are produced from the *taijasa* (fiery) *ahaṃkāra*. Since the senses are insentient, they cannot independently perceive qualities; therefore, their presiding deities are, respectively, the gods of Space, Wind, Sun, Varuṇa, Brahmā, Indra, Viṣṇu, Mitra, Ka, and the Moon. As stated in the Vaiṣṇava [Purāṇa]: "They say the senses are *taijasa*, while the ten [deities] are *vaikārika*; here, the eleventh, the mind, is also considered a *vaikārika* deity. The *vaikārika* [aspect] arises from the *sāttvika* *ahaṃkāra*.

Thus, there are seven principles that are both primordial material causes (*prakṛti*) and evolutes (*vikṛti*): namely, primordial nature (*prakṛti*), the Great One (*mahat*), the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), and the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*). There are sixteen that are merely evolutes (*vikāra*): the eleven organs and the five gross elements. And there is the one *puruṣa*. Rooted in primordial nature, the seven beginning with the Great One are both causes and effects; the group of sixteen is only an effect; and the *puruṣa* is neither cause nor effect. These are the twenty-five principles well-known in the Sāṃkhya system.

If it is asked, "How is it that the Teacher speaks of this extraordinary matter as consisting of eleven organs? we say no; for it is appropriate [to speak thus] merely because of their utility in determining the positions within the stellar sphere (*bhacakra*). Furthermore, there is no absolute necessity for the organs themselves [in this context]. From the *saṃhati*—meaning from the blending, the becoming one, and the aggregation—and by virtue of the word "ca" (and), the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) arose from the five great elements (*pañcamahābhūta*). Therein, the vessel is composed of the five elements and is shaped like a sphere (*golākāra*).

And thus, by connecting the phrase "because" (*yasmāt*) with the word "egg" (*aṇḍa*), the meaning is that since the cosmic egg arose as described above, there is no obstacle whatsoever to the establishment of God (*īśvara*). Furthermore, because the cosmic egg exists as a transformation (*pariṇāma*) of primordial matter (*prakṛti*), it follows from the principle of the "possibility of the substratum" (*sambhavādhikaraṇa*)—which is synonymous with being the material cause—that primordial matter, being insentient, is incapable of producing the cosmic egg without a conscious agent who is its self.

The sense is that He alone, like a potter who is the maker of a jar, manifests [the world]; this is the intention. Furthermore, the doctrine of the sage Kapila is to be disregarded because agency is never observed in that which is insentient; otherwise, even without the activity of a clod of clay, there would be the production of a jar through its mere proximity. Thus ends the inquiry regarding the cosmic egg (bhuvanakośa). Maṇidīpikā: Because it would result in the production of a jar [without a cause].

Since it has been established through the aforementioned examples that *prakṛti* is either the substratum of consciousness or distinct from it, how could *prakṛti* possibly possess agency in the absence of the presence of the *jīva*? This is because the *jīvātman*s are conscious. Nor is *prakṛti* dependent upon consciousness, for the *jīvātman*s are not insentient. For this very reason—that the *jīvātman*s are not agents—the term "puruṣa" does not refer to the *jīvātman*.

In the Sāṃkhya system, although the term *puruṣa* refers to the individual soul (*jīvātman*), it is established by the force of scripture that the *puruṣa* understood here—indicated by the dual number—is indeed the Lord (*īśvara*). Even though, in their view, the Lord is accepted as merely the controller and as being extraneous (*taṭastha*), and since they do not admit a causal material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*), it is *prakṛti* alone that possesses the status of the material cause of the world.

The Lord cannot be its material cause (*upādāna*), because, being changeless (*nirvikāra*) and untransformable (*apariṇāmin*), He lacks the nature of a material cause; for even if something were transformable, how could that which is insentient (*acetana*) be the transformation of that which is sentient? Thus, the status of being a material cause indicated by the dual number [in the term *pradhāneśvarau*] is not appropriate for the Lord. Furthermore, since we have designated *prakṛti* as the material cause, those two [the Lord and *prakṛti*] are mentioned as general causes; therefore, it is entirely consistent that they are described through their relationship as the material cause and the controller, respectively, according to their respective natures. Or else:

Material cause (*upādāna*) is of two kinds: that which undergoes transformation (*pariṇamamāna*) and that which is illusory appearance (*vivartamāna*). Among these, that which undergoes modification is subject to change, such as clay with respect to a jar. On the other hand, illusory appearance is devoid of actual modification, such as pure silver [appearing] in relation to mother-of-pearl. In this regard, according to the Vedānta doctrine, there is no contradiction in maintaining that although God does not possess a material cause in the sense of undergoing transformation, He is nevertheless the material cause in the sense of being the locus of illusory appearance. Thus it is established.

However, according to the followers of the Bhavavīta school, [the author] specifies the Supreme Brahman—the cause of the universe whose nature is Being-Consciousness-Bliss—as to how it is so; thus he says, "From whom" (*yataḥ*). From that Supreme Brahman, the Great Principle (*mahat*) arose through the agitation of *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*, and so forth. *Prakṛti* is well-known. *Puruṣa* is the individual soul (*jīva*). These two were agitated by the will of the Lord, whose essential nature is Consciousness and Bliss. And the fruit of this [agitation] is the manifestation of the world. These two are the beginningless and endless powers of the Lord.

Because that [Pradhāna] is beginningless, they say that both Prakṛti and Puruṣa are indeed beginningless. However, the Paurāṇikas [state]: "The Great Lord, having quickly entered both Prakṛti and Puruṣa, agitated them by means of his supreme Yoga. Thus, from the ancient Pradhāna and Puruṣa, he brought about agitation."

"A great *vajra* appeared, [born] from the action of the Pradhāna and Puruṣa"—thus they speak of the Puruṣa as being distinct from Brahman, who knows the nature of speech. This contradicts the Sāṃkhya system. Furthermore, Brahman is treated as being distinct from Īśvara, as in the Vedānta school; by what means, then, could there be no contradiction between them? Nor can this verse be explained according to the Vaiśeṣika doctrine, because it would contradict the process of creation, since [the *vajra*] would be included within the *mahat* and *ahaṃkāra*. Enough of this confusion caused by the diversity of philosophical systems. Now, what is the authority for the *kaṇṭhasvasva*?

Since the proof [of the existence] of the Creator has not yet been established, he says: "From Viriñci. From Brahmā, the universe—consisting of Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ—came into being. Thus, because the entire universe is perceptible, at the time of perceiving any part of the universe, the universal form (viśvarūpa) is inferred; and from that, its creator, Brahmā, is also inferred. In the same way, let this cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) also be inferred, on the grounds that it is a single part of the universe. This is the intended meaning.

Now, one might ask: what is the proof that the universe is but a single part of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*)? To this, the author provides a qualifying epithet for Brahmā that indicates the manner in which impurity arises: *arha-yat*. The "belly" (*jaṭhara*)—meaning the interior or the central embryonic bulb—of that cosmic egg-globe (*brahmāṇḍagola*), wherein the earth resides as its very center; and the surface (*pṛṣṭha*) of that earth, which serves as the support for all things.

In that regard, the meaning is that Maheśvara composed such a chapter as "The Purpose of the World's Abiding" (Niśvāsa-sthitārtha), [namely] the eighth chapter. And likewise, for the sake of the creation of the universe, the Supreme Lord fashioned Bala, who is His own portion; the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) itself is of the nature of the transformation of *prakṛti*, which is the generator of His body. When the primordial state has expanded, it is designated as the "Field-born" (*kṣetraja*).

The intention is that this is not without authority, for it is well-known in the Purāṇas and other texts that the Lord Hiraṇyagarbha, Brahmā—who was born from the golden egg—is the creator of the universe, and that the universe is situated upon the earth itself, while the earth is situated within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa). Now he describes the nature of the earth: This globe of the earth, composed of earth, air, water, ether, and fire, is surrounded by the circular orbits of the Moon, Mercury, Venus, Jupiter, the Sun, and the stars. || 2 ||

Supported by nothing else, he moves solely by his own power; the entire universe—including the *asuras*, humans, *ādityas*, and *daityas*—remains eternally and invariably established upon his back on all sides. He is covered everywhere by mountains, groves, villages, and clusters of shrines, like a cluster of *kadamba* flowers by the spreading filaments of its blossoms.

This terrestrial globe, composed of the five elements—consisting of earth, air, water, fire, and ether—is spherical in shape and has a circular foundation. It is indeed surrounded by the single-wheeled chariot of the moon, which possesses a circular orbit; supported by its own power alone, it stands fixed and certain in the sky. And upon its surface rests the world, inhabited by gods with their offspring, demons, humans, and Ādityas, as well as the Vidyādharas and Asuras; together with them, it stands encompassed on all sides.

The remainder is clear in meaning. [2.3] Now, he provides the answer to the two questions—"What is it? and "What is at the end of the vowel *a*"—in the *Sragdharā* meter, beginning with the words "Of the earth" (*bhūmeḥ*). This is the substratum. The "mass of the earth" (*bhūmeḥ piṇḍaḥ*) refers to the unification of its own parts through solidity. It exists here, in this cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), in the vicinity of the wind, in the central portion of the space delimited by the cosmic egg; the meaning is that it exists in the form of a unified mass at its own center. But is this not untenable? Because of its extreme density... [text fragment].

Because this would contradict [the established doctrine], he says: "consisting of earth, air, water, ether, and fire. "Earth" refers to *mṛt* (clay); its parts are complete and have attained a state of unity. Of air, water, ether, and fire, each possesses a portion equal to one-fourth of a complete part of earth; this lump (*piṇḍa*) consists of these and is of the nature of their unification. Thus, although a lump cannot exist through the parts of earth alone without those other forms, the state of being a lump is not untenable as the unification of the earth-parts occurs in conjunction with portions of the elements such as water and so forth.

The point is that for this very reason, even though other regions exist, because the terrestrial regions are so numerous, there is the conventional usage "the Earth-egg" (pṛthivī-aṇḍa). Now, one might object: since non-conscious matter is stable, the space delimited by that egg remains below; however, if it is said that its location is in the space within the interior of the Brahmāṇḍa, that is not tenable. To this he says: "fixed" (niyatām).

Because, by the sequence of time, while remaining at the center of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), he is capable of establishing the non-perception of the poison of consciousness situated lower and lower in space; such is the splendor of the Bhuvanakosa—this is the meaning. (34) [Bhaṭṭāraka-Ṭīkā].

Now, one might ask: "How is it known that this body (*piṇḍa*) exists as the very embryo within the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*)? To this, he provides the answer by way of describing the arrangement of the *ābhacakra* (the wheel of light) which dispels the doubt that this body could not possibly possess such manifold forms, while simultaneously explaining the nature of that body: "The conch," and so forth. Then, at the beginning of creation, Brahmā fashioned the mind (*manas*) in the form of the ego (*ahaṃkāra*). From the mind was born the Moon, and from his eyes, the Sun, the treasury of splendors.

From the Sun and the Moon arose Anaraṇya, Bhāskara, Indu, and then Tvaṅrakā and the others; from Tejas, Bhūmi, Āpas, and Vāyu, five [beings] were born in succession. Then, dividing himself twelvefold, he created the circle of the zodiac (rāśimaṇḍala), and further, the form of the constellations (nakṣatra) consisting of twenty-seven parts. Thereafter, he fashioned the entire universe of moving and non-moving beings, beginning with the gods; this is established by the cosmogony described in the Sūryasiddhānta.

The celestial spheres (ākāśagolāḥ) associated with the paths suitable for the revolution of the Moon, Mercury, Venus, the Sun, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, and the asterisms (nakṣatra), are like the surfaces of the orbits (kakṣāvṛtta). This mass (piṇḍa)—meaning this [Earth]—is joined with, covered by, and pervaded on all sides at equal intervals by them; it is circular (vṛtta), that is to say, spherical (vartula) like a ball. Due to the co-occurrence with the term *kakṣā*, the spheres are situated in ascending order according to the sequence mentioned; and from the fact that what was previously mentioned is followed by what is subsequently mentioned, their state of being enveloped is obtained.

And thus, at the equinox, according to the rule that the day and so forth are seen immediately after sunrise and likewise not seen immediately after sunset, the sphere [of the stars] must reside in the central part of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa). The point is that there is no evidence for assuming that the spheres of the stars and so forth maintain an equal distance from the circumference of the cosmic egg.

If the planets and stars were situated within a single celestial sphere (*golā*), then in the absence of light, their conjunction at one place would be impossible due to the movement of those two [planets] with extremely vast discs, which would result in the destruction of the spheres; therefore, they occupy separate spheres. Among them, the stellar sphere (*nakṣatrabhrākāśagola*) consists of the five elements and is blue, while the middle sphere consists of space (*ākāśa*). For this very reason, there is the perception that "the sky is blue. Here, the stars were established by Brahmā according to his own will.

If the stellar sphere (*nakṣatragola*) were composed of empty space alone, it would be impossible for its tenfold divisions—the zodiacal signs (*rāśi*)—to move; consequently, as the planets situated beneath them would rotate westward due to the force of the [celestial] wind, they would necessarily complete the transit through all twelve signs, which would result in the loss of their own respective zodiacal positions. Nor can it be argued that the movement of the signs—which are essentially identical to the regions of space occupied by the asterism Revatī—is established simply by the movement of Revatī itself, even though the signs are indeed of the nature of spatial points.

Because the nature of the spatial divisions (*ākāśapradeśa*) is not continuous, there is an absence of continuity in the zodiacal signs (*rāśi*). For this very reason, although the twelve divisions of the domain consisting of the five elements (the zodiac) are fixed, motion is possible for them due to the *pravaha* wind. Consequently, there is no occurrence of a planet’s separation from the sign it occupies. Since the planet also moves solely by means of the *pravaha* wind, even when there is a vertical interval between above and below, there is no east-west displacement; thus, its position is accepted as being on the same meridian line.

For this very reason, since it is possible for the terrestrial globe to move hither and thither due to the impact of the wind, the hypothesis of the two poles—North and South—is logically established to prevent that movement and ensure stability in its own location. However, it should be understood that since the planets revolve within their respective celestial spheres (ākāśagola), there is no contradiction in not postulating material globes for them. Now, one might object: the terrestrial globe, situated in the center of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), requires a support; otherwise, its stationary state would be untenable.

Even a support requires another support for its own stability; thus, because of this succession of supports, the revolution of the planets and stars would be untenable. Therefore, the meaning is that there is no other material support. To this, the Elemental Being (Bhūta) says: "No. [Commentary on verse 38]: It is impossible to deny that the Lord, who exists as the support of the universe, is also the support of the terrestrial globe situated within that universe; otherwise, it would result in the undesirable conclusion that the world is without a support.

Now, one might object: "In this way, you have established the existence of the terrestrial globe (bhūgola) without any support. To this he says: "By its own power" (*svaśaktyaiva*). The meaning is that the terrestrial globe exists there by its own inherent power—that is, by an indefinable power capable of effecting its supportless stationing. The sense is that, just as a magnet possesses the power of attraction, so too does this [globe] possess the power of supportless stationing.

By the phrase "the terrestrial globe is situated within the cage of the host of stars composed of the five great elements (pañcamahābhūta), like a ball of iron within its own mold," it is stated that the earth is spherical. Through the power of the host of stars, the fact that the earth resides in space is accepted by Vārāha; however, the word "eva" (only) is used here to exclude the views of some who accept two worlds, as well as the doctrines of Paraśakti and Guru-kalpa. It should be understood that the view of Śivaśaktipāda is the lighter [or simpler] one. Now, an objection may be raised: since this [earth] is not perceived as being a sphere due to its being supported by the earth itself, how can it be said to be spherical?

Since the earth situated within the celestial sphere (*bhagola*) is established by direct perception as having a physical foundation, he says: "of this" (*asya*). On the surface of the terrestrial globe (*bhūgola*) contained within the celestial sphere, the entire world consisting of *bhūr*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svaḥ* is eternally situated. On its surface, the regions of the worlds (*lokabhūmayaḥ*) were divided by Brahmā according to their divisions. The meaning is that the interior of the terrestrial globe is not fit for habitation. By the word "and" (*ca*), it should be understood that the oceans, rivers, islands, and so forth are also included here.

To the question, "Why is this offered to Brahmā?", he states the specific qualification: "together with the Danujas," and so forth. *Danujas* are the Dānavas; *manujas* are humans; *ādaiityas* are the gods; and *daityas* are the sons of Diti. The distinction between Daityas and Dānavas is well known in the Purāṇas and other texts due to the difference between the lineages of Danu and Diti. The meaning is that [Brahmā] is present together with these.

The sense is that the division of the universe has been fashioned as a place of residence unmixed with the beings created by himself—such as humans, Daityas, and others. Now, one might object: since the upper portion of the earth is its very nature (*svarūpa*), how can there be such a structural arrangement [of inhabitants] there, given the fear of falling elsewhere due to the impossibility of such a state? To this he says: "on all sides" (*samantāt*). Thus, it is precisely on the upper portion of the terrestrial globe (*bhūgola*) that this arrangement exists.

Nor, however, does it mean that they are arranged on the surface of the sphere according to their respective positions; such is the sense. Now, one might ask: since a horizontal or downward position is extremely unstable, there is a possibility of falling at some later time—how, then, can they remain? To this he says "constantly" (śaśvat). They remain perpetually; the sense is that even at a later time, the possibility of falling has already been refuted further on.

And thus, according to the Vedic scripture stating "the earth is the supporter of the universe," it is the terrestrial globe situated within the stellar sphere (bhagola) alone that serves as its own support. As for the non-perception of its spherical shape, this will be established later on the basis of other instruments of knowledge; therefore, there is no possibility of the revolution of the stellar sphere (bhacakra) due to the existence of two separate earths. The sense is that the terrestrial globe within the stellar sphere is not distinct from the earth that serves as its support. Regarding the word *sarvataḥ*: the terrestrial globe established in the preceding verse is *sarvataḥ*, meaning on all sides, everywhere, and completely.

Mountains, groves, and gardens; villages are well known, as are cities; and a *caitya* is a Buddhist sanctuary. It is filled and pervaded by the collection of these things. Indeed, sentient entities—even through their own dissolutions—are somehow capable of maintaining stability within the sphere (*gola*) everywhere in the cosmic egg (*bhuvanakośa*), whereas insentient objects are not. *Bhāṣya-ṭīkā* (Commentary): [It is] capable of maintaining stability, not an insentient object.

To dispel the doubt as to how mountains, trees, and so forth exist in horizontal, upward, and downward positions without one displacing another, he provides an illustration beginning with "kadamba": "The cluster of filaments in a *kadamba* flower is pervaded on all sides. Just as the filaments are situated below, horizontally, and all around within the bud of a *kadamba* flower, so too are these mountains and other things situated in horizontal, upward, and downward directions; thus, there is no room for such doubt. This is the intended meaning. (3)

Now, refuting the succession of supports for the earth as recited in the Purāṇas, he says: "If Sūta is the supporter of the earth, then another must support him, and yet another that one; thus there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) here. If others are to be postulated due to [Sūta's] own incapacity, then why not postulate [the earth itself] as the support? Is the earth not the very form of the Eight-formed Lord (*aṣṭamūrti*)? (4) [This is] clear. Maṭīkā: But surely, it is improper to claim that the terrestrial globe has no supporter, because this is contradicted by direct perception (*pratyakṣabādha*).

For that which possesses weight must necessarily fall downward in the absence of a support; furthermore, because power (*śakti*) is not apprehended through the means of perception (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*). For this very reason, Śeṣa is well known as the supporter of the earth, as evidenced by the words of the best of sages, such as "The earth was supported by the head of the foremost of serpents," as well as by the statements of Kaśyapa and others, and by the consensus of those who follow the Purāṇas.

Anticipating the objection—"In that case, how is it logical to say that [the sky] remains fixed in the atmosphere by its own nature alone, without another substratum?"—the author refutes this in the *Śālīnī* meter, beginning with the word "mūrta" (embodied). [The sky] is "embodied" (*mūrta*) for the purpose of preventing the fear of falling from the earth—the ground which is the universal substratum. An "embodied" entity is defined by the characteristic of having a substrate (*adhikaraṇa*) whose dimension is delimited by spatial extension (*iyattā*).

If you say that there exists some primordial earth (*śrīrādimana*) which is the supporter (*dhāraka*), then immediately after that, what would be the supporter of that earth, distinct from its own nature as a supported entity? Otherwise, it would be impossible for the earth to remain suspended in space. Therefore, another supporter, distinct from the support of the earth, must be postulated for it; by the force of the word "also" (*api*), yet another must likewise be imagined. In this manner, [the regress continues].

If you accept the position that there is a succession of supporting substrates (*dhāraka-paramparā*), an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) follows. For if such a series were to continue indefinitely, there would be the great defect of an infinite regress. Now, if you say that to avoid this defect, there is another—namely, that the final substrate, which is accepted by the wise as being like the earth, is the Lord’s own power (*svaśakti*), whose nature is compassion (*karuṇā*) and consists in abiding in the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*)—then why is it not likewise postulated for Śeṣa, who is the final substrate? And how so? [Because he too is the ultimate support.]

By the maxim of the lamp on the threshold (*dehalīdīpanyāya*), since it is simpler to postulate a power for the boar (*varāha*) residing in the letter *na* than to postulate a residual power [for the earth], the letter *ṣa* itself would be its own power; this would result in the futility of the tortoise and the boar as the support and the supported (*ādhārādhārayoḥ*). [Objection: This is indeed acceptable (*iṣṭāpatti*), because the purpose of the Purāṇic descriptions of supports is to prevent the earth from being without a support, and thus they intend to determine the support of the earth. [Reply: To this, he says: "What? (*kimiti*).

If it is argued that the remaining [ether] possesses the capacity to abide in the intermediate space (antarikṣa), then why is that same capacity for abiding in the intermediate space not attributed to the earth? Because of extreme parsimony (atilāghava). [Objection: Let the capacity of the earth to abide in the intermediate space be postulated. [Reply: No, because there is no rule that capacity must be cognizable through direct perception (pratyakṣa); thus, the meaning is that your argument is unestablished. And so, the earth has no support. Ma. Ṭī.: [The meaning is: Let the capacity [of the earth] to abide in the intermediate space be postulated. However, there is no necessity that a capacity must be understood through direct perception; therefore, the point you have stated is unproven. Thus, the earth has no substratum (ādhāra).

The meaning is as follows: by the authority of the scripture, "He supported this earth and that [heaven]," and because the Lord is the support of the universe, it is accepted that the earth has the formless Lord as its support and that it has no other support; however, the intention is that this is equivalent to being without any support at all. Now, one might object: while it is reasonable to postulate the power of remaining in the intermediate space for Śeṣa and others because they are portions of the Lord, such a postulation of power is unreasonable for the earth since it lacks that status. To this, he says: "of the eight-formed one" (aṣṭamūrteḥ).

By the use of the word "ca" (and), that earth is the form—the body—of Maheśvara, who consists of eight forms: earth, water, fire, air, ether, sun, moon, and the sacrificer. Thus, the intention is that since the earth is a form of the Lord, it is entirely logical to conceive of its capacity for abiding within the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*). By this, the Yavana doctrine—that the terrestrial globe sinks into the water—is refuted; for as it is said, "the dissolution of clay would occur in water," and therefore the stability of the earth in the waters is not tenable.

Now, as for the statement "contained within a vessel," how could that not also apply to the earth? For if the earth is situated in water, then tell me, upon what is that water established? If the earth-sphere were to rest upon water, why would it not likewise rest in the sky? This follows from the words of Laṭṭha, from the universal perception that "this water is upon the earth," and from the continuous relationship of container and contained between the earth and the water. (4)

Now, avoiding the objection that this [gravity] might be an inherent power of the earth, he says: Just as heat is in fire and coldness in the moon, or hardness in stone; just as the wind is mobile and the earth is immobile by nature—alas, the powers of things are indeed diverse! (5) And the earth possesses a power of attraction; by which, through its own power, it draws toward itself whatever is heavy and situated above. It appears as if falling, even though it falls equally on all sides upon level ground in the sky. (6) The previous verse is easy to understand.

By the statement "and the earth has the power of supporting," the possibility of the earth falling downward, as well as the fear of things situated horizontally or below it falling downward, is refuted. Bhaṭṭoji Dīkṣita: Now, one might object: since the earth is included within the eight forms of Maheśa, if one postulates for the earth the power of remaining in the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), then one should likewise postulate for water and other elements the power of remaining in the intermediate space. To this, he says "yathā" (just as) in the *vaṃśastha* meter: "Just as the sun and fire have heat"—that is, the state of being the substratum of hot touch; the word "vā" is used in the sense of "or," indicating another illustrative example.

The moon is the substratum of cold touch; water is the substratum of fluidity; stone (pāṣāṇa) is hardness; and the wind is motion. Likewise, by its very nature—that is, by its own essential form—the earth is immovable and stable. Now, one might ask: "From what cause do these possess such qualities by their very nature? To this, he says: "Because... That is to say, because the *vastu-śaktayaḥ*—the powers inherent in things, which consist of the capacity of objects to produce their own effects—are such that they exist by their very essence. The word "vata" expresses lamentation.

There are various and manifold [qualities]. By this, [the objection] that [the earth] must possess the nature of being non-fluid, moving, and possessing a non-cold touch, and so forth, is refuted; for conceptual construction (kalpanā) is supported by empirical examples (dṛṣṭānta). Thus, the sense is that while the power of movement and so forth is directly perceived in air and other elements, the power of immobility in the earth is inferred. Let this be so; however, when one accepts the entry of those who have entered your fold (your followers), then whether it be called a "power" (śakti) or a "nature" (svabhāva), it is merely a designation for the reality as it appears through the light of the cosmic egg (bhuvanakośa).

31. It should be understood that in our view, the impossibility of the earth falling toward the region below will be established later. Regarding this, the astronomers who follow the Purāṇas ask: as for the stability of the earth that has been stated, is it due to some additional power (*atiśaya-śakti*) or its own inherent nature (*svabhāva*)?

In that regard, is that [potency] also inherent (*sahajā*) or adventitious (*āgantukā*)? It cannot be the former; for in an entity consisting of an effect-substance (*kārya-dravya*), there is an invariable rule that inherent potency is preceded by a potency residing in the constituent parts (*avayava-niṣṭha-śakti*) which serve as the inherent causes (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*) of the qualities of the effect, such as color, which are produced from the color and other qualities residing in the cause. For example, the burning power (*dāhakatā*)—which is the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for fire’s causality toward a blister—is produced solely by a potency residing in the parts of its cause. If it were so in this case as well, then the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) would be unavoidable even in the case of a large lump of clay, since it too would possess such a potency.

Furthermore, in the theory of *śakti* (potency), such a restriction is accepted because of the existence of that very kind of potency. It is not anything else; for if one were to admit that this [potency] is something produced by other factors—just as the potency produced by sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and threshing (*avaghāta*) exists in rice grains in passages such as "he sprinkles the rice grains" and "he threshes the rice grains"—then it would follow that one has entered into our own position. However, regarding the second alternative, which accepts its non-existence, [the opponent argues] that its stability is established by the force of the etymological derivation: "one's own state is its nature" (*svasya bhāvaḥ svabhāvaḥ*).

In that case, the very nature of the earth itself would not be sufficient for its being a single body; even during an earthquake, there would be no such movement [of the whole], because the nature of a thing never perishes. Now, it might be argued: "We do not say that the mere nature of the earth is the cause for the effect consisting in the absence of movement; rather, it is that nature when accompanied by auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*) and characterized by the absence of obstructors (*pratibandhakābhāva*) that acts as such."

If it is argued that, since we observe the alteration of the nature of things in the present case, some kind of obstructing factor must be postulated at that time, we say no. Is such a factor capable or incapable [of being perceived]? It cannot be the former, because there is no perception of it, and because you yourself have stated this after due deliberation. Nor can it be the latter; for since it is unestablished, it cannot logically function as an obstruction, as an obstructing factor is understood as the counter-positive of an existing state that serves as the cause.

Furthermore, let it be granted that the will of God, which is capable of inference, acts as an obstacle to stability by producing earthquakes. However, since His will is eternal, if it were to obstruct stability, there would be movement at all times; moreover, because an eternal entity cannot be the counter-positive of a non-existence, it is impossible for it to function as an obstructing factor.

Now, one might argue: "Even if there is no such will of the Lord, nevertheless, the unfavorable *adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit/demerit) of the living beings existing at that time must certainly act as an obstacle. If this is so, then the downward movement of the earth toward lower and lower levels is indeed established. For, by that, the mathematical calculation would be undermined. To explain:

during the period of an earthquake lasting one, two, or three days, because the auxiliary cause in the form of the relationship between the stability [of the earth] and its obstructer is not firm, the effect consisting of its remaining in the atmosphere does not arise; rather, it is determined that the extremely heavy earth simply moves downward.

Furthermore, during that period, as numerous earthquakes occurred one after another, the earth sank down by thousands of *yojanas* due to its own weight and excessive velocity, as if from a great force; consequently, the calculation of planetary positions based on observational data was interrupted. Moreover, because the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) is the uncommon cause [of such events], even though the visible [earth] rose up like a mountain, it did not return to its original state, as established by authorities such as the *Pratīlataka*. This is because the luster of jewels is perceived only when there is no obstruction.

Furthermore, since it is possible for memory to serve as a means of perception (*dṛṣṭakaraṇa*), it is improper to postulate [an unseen cause] when a perceived one is available. Moreover, even in another object, there would be no perception of its stable nature (*sthiratva*), because it would be qualified by a single [momentary] self-nature (*svabhāva*). If you argue that this is because such a self-nature is impossible, then is this due to the lack of a cause, or the presence of a contrary cause? In the *Golādhyāya*, Maṇirāma’s commentary states: "Not the first."

Because it is unique [to that specific entity] and resides only in that particular substance—just as a seed, being unique, cannot possibly reside in its own sprout by producing it—the aforementioned consequence of permanence does not apply to the stability of the subject. Nor is there any other [reason], for even if burning capacity and the like, which are unique to fire, could possibly reside in another substance possessing the same general properties, they are nonetheless restricted to residing in their own constituent parts; otherwise, the same would follow even for a jar and so forth.

For there is a rule that whatever establishes its own nature (*svabhāvatva*) in that which is delimited by a certain property must necessarily reside in all things belonging to that same class. For example, "burning capacity" established in what is delimited by "fireness" resides in many individual instances of fire, but not in jars and the like. Similarly here, since it would be of a different genus (*vijātīya*), that [nature] would not exist in earth; thus, it is inconsistent for stability to be the inherent nature (*svabhāva*) of earth. In reality, however, immobility is simply the absence of motion. This is because the cognition "this is stable" occurs precisely with respect to that which possesses the absence of such motion.
