And this being so, since there is the possibility that the stability of the mind is entirely of the nature of non-existence; if it is argued, "But surely the non-existence of non-existence is observed to be existence," we say no. Let that be as it may. In the present context, however, because movement is of the nature of action (*karma*), it possesses the character of existence; therefore, its absence is impossible for you [to maintain]. Furthermore, that [absence] occurs in some cases by means of a substratum, in some cases through the conjunction with another perceived object, and in some cases through one's own volition in the conscious self.

Therefore, in the case at hand, it is precisely by means of the substratum of the remaining [factors] that the absence of rotation itself attains the state of stability. Regarding an object in which motion has been produced through the obstruction of rotation, that substratum and so forth merely maintain the prior non-existence of motion. As for the term *tattvam* (the essence), it refers to the fact that in an object of that same kind, there is indeed that [stability]. Now, one might object: "Why not consider both [rotation and stability] as corporeal, given that they possess the nature of a body? To this we say: no.

Since they are incarnations of the Lord and possess supreme power, it is accepted that there exists a single, manifoldly conceived effort capable of producing their stationing in the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*) therein—an effort which brings about the state of immobility characterized by the absence of motion.

Even in the case of birds flying in the depths of the sky and so forth, [the capacity for such action] is restricted by the fact that this body serves as the substratum for the earth and other stable objects contained within it, due to its possession of a certain power of exertion capable of supporting those objects in the atmosphere—just as in the case of Puruṣa and others who possess mastery over all branches of knowledge through long practice. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the total destruction of the common experience of people in the aforementioned instances. For this very reason, in my view, the possibility of the exhaustion of the serpent-king’s head from being weighed down by the burden of the earth is established.

This is because an earthquake and so forth can be accounted for simply by the trembling of the hoods of the serpent kings who support the earth, as the power of such movements to cause the earth to shake is well known from many instances. Nor should it be argued that, since the bodies of Śeṣa and the other supporting serpents are extremely massive, they would obstruct the rotation of the sky, making such rotation impossible; for [the capacity for movement is not precluded by size].

Because those [seven cities] are situated within the netherworld (pātāla), they are internal; and since the planets move by circumambulating them while remaining in a position below them, they lack the power to obstruct the movement of the planets due to their being situated transversely in relation to them. Now, if it is argued that even though the earth is not distinct from these [cities] due to their being internal, and even if the authority of the Purāṇas is understood to be established otherwise, the acceptance of that [distinction] appears to be motivated merely by a desire for novelty—this is not so.

Since the earth is insentient, it is impossible for it to remain suspended in the space within the cosmic egg; therefore, the Supreme Lord, having entered the terrestrial globe in the form of the Kūrma incarnation, remains in the space within the cosmic egg—this is because it is accepted that the earth is supported by [the Tortoise] Adharaṇī. Now, if it is asked how the terms "stable" and "moving" are applied to the earth in the *Tadbrahmāṇḍa* and other texts, the answer is that these are metaphorical designations applied to the earth with respect to its supporting action. (5) [This is as stated in the *Bhuvanakosa*: "The earth is stable and moving."

33. Maṭī: Furthermore, the reason for the equal practice of both [virtues] lies in their being inherent. Thus it is said: "How could a quality be accidental in that which is stable? Therefore, a quality is indeed innate. Just as heat is the natural property of fire and fluidity of water—both being eternal and uncreated—so too is this [virtue] appropriate. The ancients have declared that the eyes and other [senses] are the guardians; how then could one who is within the cage of the body, though possessing the six senses, not be bound by the Veda? (Note: The provided text contains fragments of philosophical argumentation regarding the inherent nature of qualities (*guṇa*) and the authority of the Vedas.)

If the earth possesses the quality of supporting the weight of the world, why does it not likewise possess the power of burning like fire? Similarly, even though the tortoise supports the serpent-demons, the vulture remains capable of striking; thus, one of limited strength is such. Why then does he, in the form of the tortoise, not support the earth and its mountains at every moment? He destroys the stability that has been acquired through the practice of his own nature.

Furthermore, immediately after [the verse], by the statement beginning with "That earth is not so" (*na mahī tayā*), the power of attraction (*ākṛṣṭi-śakti*) was refuted; otherwise, there would be no logical connection between the preceding verse and the verse beginning with "The power of attraction," which would result in it being nothing more than a final incoherent rambling. Nor should it be said that the verse beginning with "The power of attraction" is intended as a salutation (*namasya*) in the *Śiromaṇi*, for you yourself have rejected its intended meaning by stating, "If it were so, the power of attraction would not exist. Thus, it is established that this is not the case.

The removal of the delusion of the world through the destruction of greed is seen in that very [text] by one’s own experience, or else it is the recitation of the *Dṛṣṭāntapañcaka*. It is the indicator of the truth, worthy of respect, and the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). Indeed, this alone is the great heart.

5. To avoid the absence of an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*), [the author] states that there is no perception of the earth as a mass (*rāśi*) and so forth; for how could the earth, which has the nature of being immovable (*acala-svabhāva*), abandon its state of being a solid mass (*ghana*)? 6.15. Then, having established the lightness of the jar, it moves along the three paths (*pathatraya-vara*). 35. By the falling of the chariot, the six parts (*ṣaṭ-khaṇḍa*) fall down with a great force (*abhimata-aśaṅka*). How does the answer arise? 6.16. It is said: "The power of the enemy" (*āri-śakti*). The earth is the broad ground; it is the power of the unseen (*adṛṣṭi-śakti*).

"Not false" (*akūṭam*): Just as power (*śakti*) exists in that [earth], so too [is it] equal for me. It does not mean that the earth lacks the capacity to serve as the locus (*adhikaraṇatvam*) for the downward movement of things; rather, the meaning is that it possesses such a capacity. Now, one might ask: what is the true nature (*saddharma*) of this [power]? To this he says: "By that. By that earth, through its own power, by means of its nature of attraction—[it holds] that which is situated in the sky and that which is below. It is the substance common to the parts of water and earth, serving as the locus for heaviness.

That region of the earth which faces the direction of the wind is seen by the drawing [of the cloud] toward its face. As it moves toward its own region, it is drawn forward; the object cast down from that ground falls. This falling, impelled by the force of the descent, appears as the scattering of the terrestrial elements. Just as a moving being plunging into the sky performs a drawing-in [of its limbs], so too is this similar to the case of the arrow. Thus, by the well-known drawing-in of the terrestrial surface, there occurs the scattering of the water-drops.

It is also indicated that the power of attraction residing in the sky belonging to the Earth acts as an attractor from its own station; thus, there is no possibility of the downward fall of the worlds situated below. Furthermore, the power inherent in the Earth is natural, for even the weight of the earth itself does not cause it to descend, just as a magnet attracts unmoving iron.

Because the earth possesses the nature of being a stable attractor, and because its stability is established by the fact that objects do not fall despite the pull of gravity, its constituent parts must likewise possess stability as their substrate. Furthermore, the perception of falling is indeed non-erroneous, just like the perception of "darkness" (which is actually the absence of light). In this context, instability consists in the presence of internal voids containing one's own parts, such as the hollows within a mango fruit.

Therefore, when an earthquake occurs in a portion of a region inhabited by those who follow the worldly view (*lokadṛṣṭi*) and is thus subject to fault, there is no loss of the firmness of one's refuge. For it cannot be argued that there is a movement of the entire interior of the earth therein, by which the destruction of the refuge would result from its shaking; because in that case, only a part of the world is admitted [to be shaken], and because even an earthquake that is occurring is perceived as being limited to a specific location.

By this, the objection that "since the earth does not descend, there would follow a mathematical contradiction regarding its connection with the subterranean regions" is refuted. For this very reason, the earth is designated as "stable" and "immovable. There is no evidence for this being merely figurative. Indeed, the word "stable" (sthira) does not denote a tortoise; if it did, the earth could be so designated by virtue of its connection with it. By this, those arguments which are offered to establish the earth's inherent stability are also shown to be untenable.

Because stability (*sthairya*) consists in being substantial (*bhāvātmaka*). It has been stated that the six [qualities] are not possible in earth, because even if they were present, their existence as such would be untenable; and furthermore, because stability is impossible in water and the other elements. Now, if it is argued that although the capacity for producing a chariot exists in earth, that capacity is actually a defect (*dūṣaṇa*), and thus the power of stability is also mobile (*cara*)—we say no. This is because we accept the existence of that very power even in a part of the earth.

Nor can it be argued that this movement of the earth is caused by the attraction of terrestrial particles situated in space; for such an assumption is not tenable. This is because the stability of the earth is already established, and if the earth were subject to motion, it would be impossible for the earth—whose mass is calculated based on its connection with the earth—to lack a center of gravity. Furthermore, it is impossible for the earth to be attracted [by external forces], as we observe that when two persons of unequal strength engage in a mutual tug-of-war, it is the stronger one who draws the weaker toward him. Thus, by analogy, the earth cannot be drawn away from itself.

When two large bodies, such as the earth and a mountain, are situated facing one another, there occurs a mutual attraction between them due to their proximity; however, because the earth's power of attraction is greater, the mountain remains situated at a distance from it rather than being drawn toward it. Here, some [object] that is situated does not prove the existence of the earth’s power of attraction, for this would involve deviation, non-inclusiveness, and contradiction.

For instance, wherever an attractor such as a man is seen to attract something else, in every such case, the initial contact with the attractor belongs to that which is lighter; as, for example, in the act of pulling a stone with two betel nuts strung on a thread. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of contradicting the common experience of all people. This is because, in the play of children, the contact with the string is observed by everyone to belong to the betel nut itself rather than to the surface of the stone.

This earth, though possessing such power, might first attract smoke rather than a heavy object; yet the opposite is observed everywhere. Therefore, how can this be explained by the claim that it acts according to the rules of logic? Furthermore, since the power of attraction is not established, the earth’s power of stability is likewise limitless; thus, even for Brahman, it would be impossible to refute the existence of a support by asking how the earth could remain in the atmosphere without one. As it is said in that very text: "The earth possesses the power of attraction."

The suspicion that "the unclarified butter, being heavy, would surely fall downward" as it is seen to do so, must not be entertained by us; for in the case of substances, their qualities—characterized by specific capacities—vary according to differences in location. For instance: cool moonstones melt in the sun, yet pure water flows from sun-stones; diamonds float upon waters, while magnets attract iron even when it is far away.

The mountain becomes higher and the ocean water [seems] lower; indeed, such is the region characterized by its wonderful qualities. For differences in speech, customs, and capacities are observed even within a single land due to regional distinctions. How much more so, then, in other regions? Therefore, it is established in his own treatise that "stability" (*sthairya*) and "power" (*śakti*) belong to those things, meaning that by virtue of the excellence of their respective inherent capacities, there is an absence of falling for the objects found in those various regions; thus, stability and power are established through their effect.

They say that the assumption of infinite powers [in all objects] is a flaw in the theory of the authoritative [logicians], because it cannot otherwise be accounted for. [To this we reply: No, because we accept that attraction is threefold—divided by upward, downward, and horizontal directions—and because, even if your stated rule were true regarding horizontal and downward attraction, we observe that in the case of two objects, one heavy and one light, situated at the same place, the first contact with the attractor belongs to the heavy object and subsequently to the light one. Furthermore, there is no subverting evidence against the possibility of the earth possessing the power of upward attraction.

Because it is impossible for the earth itself to possess the power to draw [water] downward from all sides below; otherwise, rain would never occur in the regions of the subterranean depths or on the horizontal surface. Furthermore, if the crops and other things dependent upon that [rain] were not produced, how could those situated below remain alive? Moreover, since upward flaming alone is the natural property of fire, its capacity to produce cooking (pāka) in the subterranean or horizontal regions would not exist. Thus, in either case, there would be a doubt regarding life there; yet such is not the case.

It might be argued that since the Earth is situated at the very lowest point, below all others, and since people dwelling in the lower regions would fall right there, there is no harm in it remaining in that position; thus, the postulation of a supporting power (*dhṛti-śakti*) is useless. To this we reply: No, for that postulation is not made merely for the sake of avoiding such a calamity; rather, it is postulated as the cause for preserving the Earth's power of stability. What is the use of this long and eloquent argument? [The answer is: Because of this [power], the Earth, though heavy and stable, is supported.

He is called "Deva" because he supports all that stands upon the earth; he has descended not for the sake of obstructing the earth. In this regard, by the mere lifting of his four feet while standing with majesty, he has illustrated the burden-bearing capacity of the earth. Since the world was drawn toward [him] by the unseen power of the Lord, such is the sense. Thus, according to the intention of you, the son of Bhava (Śiva), who were inscribed by him, you have now come here, drawn by the power of attraction, along with your limbs and hands.

Now, one might object that when an object is pulled upward, it is impossible for it to move to another location by turning back after its contact with the earth; however, such movement is possible upon falling due to the impact [of the ground]. To avoid the undesirable consequence of denying the experience of falling—and thus the necessity of postulating two distinct powers (śakti)—the author states "on level ground" (*same*). This spherical earth is level because of its [spherical] nature.

Let it fall everywhere, from its own base up to the very edge of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), into the equal and uniform void (*kha*)—that is, into the atmosphere (*bhūtalādhyāya*) or the intermediate space (*manthala*)—neither in a moving nor a stationary place; such is the meaning. Thus, the postulation of two powers is stated to resolve the earth’s lack of support by accepting the space as one's own agreed-upon locus.

In reality, however, because the earth-sphere is situated within the interior of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), the space within the cosmic egg is equal on all sides of the earth-sphere; thus, even though it is devoid of a physical support, since there is no determining factor as to which specific path in the sky it should fall, simultaneous falling in all directions is impossible. Furthermore, because there is no "lower" region relative to the earth-sphere—since it is at the zenith with respect to every location—falling is not possible, for the same reason applies to every point.

For nothing situated below requires a support that could oppose its falling, nor does it fall toward the lower region; thus, there is no fault arising from the postulation of such a power. As stated by Laghu-Aryabhaṭa—"Where would [the earth] go? Upward, or sideways, since its motion is obstructed by its entirety?"—and as stated in the *Sūryasiddhānta*—"The terrestrial globe stands in the sky in the center, supported on all sides by the supreme power of Brahmā, which is of the nature of sustenance. This is the intended meaning. 6.

Now he states the arguments of the Buddhists and others: From observing the revolution of the cage of the stars, there arises the perception that the earth is devoid of support and is falling. Since the sky is not seen as a support, the Buddhists therefore say that the earth is moving downward through space. Two suns and two moons, and likewise two zodiacal circles (bhagaṇas) separated by one sign (ekāntara), rise together; since the inhabitants of the sky (the Buddhists) have spoken thus, I shall therefore state the reasoning against them. (8)

As the earth rotates on its own axis, those [Buddhists] formed the conviction that the earth is without support. Likewise, no heavy object whatsoever is seen situated in space; therefore, the Buddhists say that the earth moves. Just as a person standing on a boat does not perceive the boat as moving, so too a person standing on the earth does not perceive it. Furthermore, there are two suns, two moons, and fifty-four constellations.

Mount Meru is like a pillar due to its motion; the two [suns] rise by virtue of the movement of the Meru-particles within the single-interval corner-chariot—thus the Jains have declared. (8) Now, in order to refute the contradictory Buddhist doctrine, [the author] first establishes that doctrine using the Upajāti meter, beginning with "bha": "The perception of the earth revolving all around the sphere inhabited by the constellations and planets occurs without any support"—such is our conviction and experience.

Otherwise, the established phenomenon of sunrise and sunset would be inexplicable. A "heavy" object is a substance that possesses the quality of gravity (*gurutva*). Nothing insentient situated in space has ever been observed [to remain stationary]. This is also established by experience, as indicated by the word "and" (*ca*) in the verse. Therefore, due to the exhaustion of [the support of] experience, the earth—the terrestrial world—though placed within the empty space of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), sinks downward into space every moment; yet the person on the ground does not perceive it, just as one standing on a boat does not perceive its own movement.

Thus, the heretics (pāṣaṇḍins) who do not accept the Vedas as authoritative [criticize] the Buddhists; they treat [the system] as a limb [of their own doctrine]. || 7 || Question on the Structure of the World. 37. Commentary: Just as in the case of imagining a support, the impossibility of the earth's rotation does not arise; for it is well-known from the Purāṇas and other sources that the earth's rotation consists in its circumambulation of Mount Meru. Indeed, the rotation of the stellar sphere (bhapañjara) is not caused by the earth.

Since the earth has no support, it would otherwise wander everywhere due to its weight; therefore, providing a justification for that [support] and intending to refute it, he makes his formal proposition (*pratijñā*) in the *Upajāti* meter with the words "Two... and so forth. "Two" refers to the sun and moon—two suns and two moons. "Bha" refers to the lunar mansions (*nakṣatras*), and "ma" refers to the planets beginning with Mars (*Bhauma*). This [group] is twofold. The word "ca" (*svaḥ*) signifies conjunction. These two are thus of a dual nature. "Separated by one" means that there is an interval of one day and night (*ahorātra*) between them.

"At the time of rising, they shall attain visibility; that is, they reach the state of being visible. On whichever day a particular [planet] such as the Sun rises, on the second day another [planet] such as the Sun rises; on the third day the first, and on the fourth day the second. The meaning is that this occurs again and again in this manner. "In this way" refers to the method described above. "The first among the Digambaras": those for whom there is no *ambara* (clothing) or *avana* (protection) are *digambara*. Among the Buddhists, the *Digambara* is the primary division; thus, it refers to a pure Buddhist.

Since he knows his own work well, he states the nature of the *golava* (the celestial sphere) by means of the verse beginning with "sujjā" (*sujjā...*)—namely, "Oṃ, this... Now, the meaning is as follows: the rotation of the cage of stars (*bhapañjara*) around Mount Meru on its slopes is established; the fixed position of the constellations and their relationship [to that rotation] are thus proven. Therefore, the rotation of the stellar cage and the downward movement of the earth, which serves as the support for all the gods and the world, have been correctly explained.

However, regarding the object, because its upper, lower, rear, and front two parts are perceived through direct observation, it is stated that those parts are equal on all sides—being a regular quadrilateral with equal ears (diagonals). Therein, when the Sun revolves around its own orbit while the wheel rotates completely around the upper, lower, rear, and front four parts, that day of its observation occurs in connection with the other three parts during that revolution.

Because the observation of that [motion] is not seen, and because the experience of a day being multiplied by thirty would contradict the experience of a night, the stellar sphere (*bhacakra*) was conceived for the sake of preserving that [experience] as consisting of twenty-four signs (*rāśi*) and fifty-four constellations (*nakṣatra*). Therein, on the half-circumference, there are twelve signs and twenty-seven constellations in sequence. On the full circumference, this is the order of the days and constellations beginning with the *Dāsrās* (Aśvinī).

The interval between the two constellations Takṣaka and Sekasa is half the stellar sphere (*bhacakrārdha*). Thus, as in the case of the movement of planets, half the stellar sphere is traversed; and because the sun also rises at half the stellar sphere, the constellations remain situated there in two ways. Therefore, they are established as such.

Regarding the refutation of the [opponent's] view: [The opponent claims that] when the day-measure is equal to the night-measure at the time of the sun's setting, another sunrise occurs precisely at that same moment; thus, they argue that the practice of designating "day" based on a subsequent sunrise while the previous sunrise is still occurring contradicts experience. This [argument] is unestablished upon examining their position, because [the earth] has a curvature such that Mount Meru is surrounded on all sides by the earth.

Accepting the rotation of the celestial sphere (bhapañjara) and, according to their view, the square shape of Meru, they maintain that the doubling of the sun and other luminaries is logical in order to prevent the impossibility of experiencing day and night as in the case of Cūla; such is their intention. Regarding this, the Jains assert that there is a stable state for that which would otherwise fall downward in the infinite sky. Furthermore, they describe it according to the words of Śrīpati: "Meru is twice [the size] in its base, resembling a four-armed pillar."

Therefore, there is no contradiction in the statement "because of observing the revolution of the stellar sphere" (Golādhyāya, Bhāṣya-ṭīkā 38) regarding the exposition of the views of the former [school]. Nor should it be said that these two views are distinct because they belong to different Buddhist sects; for even if the exposition of the first view were appropriate in the context of the earth's stability, the exposition of the second view would result in a lack of coherence, and furthermore, its coherence is established by its being stated later in the *Madhyagativāsanā* as belonging to that very school.

[Objection: "Surely, since this [space] falls away entirely from the Buddhist doctrine—which is established through both reasoning and experience—as being 'empty,' your own position is untenable because it contradicts experience. To this, he says: "I say. Therefore, because of that contradiction with experience, I shall immediately state a refutation against those Buddhists that is consistent with reason. The sense is: their doctrine is untenable due to its contradiction with experience, whereas our own doctrine, as explained above, has already been stated to be non-contradictory to experience. || 8 ||

Now he states the refutation of their argument: "How can the notion that 'the earth indeed moves downward through space' be in vain? For even though one sees a heavy object, such as an arrow, cast into the sky, it returns to the earth. (9) If the earth were moving downward, then an object like the moon cast upward would never return to the earth, because both would be moving in the same direction—downward. Furthermore, if it is argued that the earth has a slow motion while the arrow and other objects have a rapid one, that too is not correct; for a heavier object falls more quickly. The earth is extremely heavy, whereas the arrow and such objects are very light.

"O Buddhist, even though you have seen the earth, how can this notion of yours—that it goes downward—be so futile? Maṇikaṇṭha: Now, wishing to state his own position, he first refutes with an Anuṣṭubh verse the Buddhist doctrine previously presented regarding the earth's descent into the nether regions, beginning with "The earth is space. O Buddhist, you who accept direct perception: that object which is situated in space (kha), that is to say, in the sky... (the particle *tu* indicates that very thing).

Having seen [an object] going to and coming from the ground, your previously stated notion—that it "goes down" or "descends" into the space below the earth—is vain and useless; how has it arisen as something intended to be refuted? By the word "api" (even/also), it is implied that even when a heavy object is thrown upward, your assumption regarding its reaching the earth—based on the certainty of its contact with the earth—is contradicted by the perceptual evidence (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*) of its falling back down. Thus, in comparison to the lightness of its flight, [the notion of downward motion is untenable].

Your statement—that the earth descends rapidly because of the perceptually established experience of the teacher’s rapid fall—is untenable. Otherwise, since the earth is extremely heavy, it would follow that objects thrown upward with great force would fall slowly due to their relative lightness compared to the earth, and that heavy objects thrown upward would never fall back to the ground. Nor can it be argued that this fault is avoided by postulating an attractive power inherent in the earth that accounts for its stability. This must be stated [as a refutation].

If the earth were to descend into the space within the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) from its initial position, then the day would decrease and the night would increase as it moved further and further downward. But this is not an acceptable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*), because it would result in the day and night becoming excessively long. Furthermore, since the distance of the celestial sphere (*bhacakra*) above [the earth] is known to be fixed in *yojanas*, if the earth were to descend, it would fall below the celestial sphere; consequently, sunrise and sunset would become impossible, and because the sun would always be visible, the absence of night would follow.

Nor should it be argued that one must accept an infinity of orbital dimensions for the celestial sphere and so forth; for that would entail the destruction of the entire field of observation, including the astronomical calculations based on fixed measurements. If it is argued that—since no heavy object situated in space is observed to fall—the earth within the celestial sphere is not a distinct entity separate from the celestial sphere or the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa-gola*), and thus there is nothing contradictory even in the claim that it moves along with them for hundreds of millions of kalpas—this is not so.

Because the assumption of motion for all things is simpler than the assumption of their being stationary; because it contradicts perception that heavy and light objects fall at the same rate; and because the movement of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) has never been heard of anywhere. By this, the view that "the earth moves" is refuted—whether on the grounds that the observation of objects thrown upward falling back to the ground would otherwise be inexplicable, or by the non-perception of the stationariness of insentient things situated in space, leading to the assumption of their motion; for no upward movement of insentient objects is observed.

Because it would result in the celestial sphere (bhacakra) coming into proximity with the region situated upon the thighs; and because, due to the consequence of the celestial sphere moving far away, there would be a perpetual non-perception of the sun, leading to the world being overwhelmed by darkness. Furthermore, the motion of all objects has already been refuted previously by the reasoning stated above. Therefore, since falling would be impossible—given its location beneath Meru and its status as the support of all things—the previously stated view that the celestial sphere is fixed in the space at the center of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) is more logical; this is the intended meaning. || 9 ||

Now he states the refutation of the Jaina logic: "What fault of yours is to be counted, you who have rendered the six qualities useless by observing the daily revolution of the Dhruva-fish among the lunar mansions? (10) When the sun is situated in the Bharaṇī mansion, then at that time the Dhruva-fish is positioned crosswise; its mouth-star is in the west and its tail-star is in the east. At that time, the sun is on the line of the mouth-star—this is the meaning.

Now, at the end of the night, the "mouth-star" (mukhatārā) moves toward the east, while the "tail-star" (pucchatārā) moves toward the west. Consequently, the rising of the sun is observed precisely along the thread of the mouth-star; therefore, the claim that there are two suns is untenable. Hence it is said: "What, what is this single defect of yours that is to be counted, by which—despite seeing the constant revolution of this [pole star]—you do not acknowledge the defect regarding the sun and the moon? (10)

Now, under the guise of refuting the alleged defects of the planets beginning with the Sun, [the author] establishes in the *anuṣṭubh* meter that the Earth has the shape of a ball as previously stated by himself—beginning with the words "What [is it]? O Digambara, how can your "defect"—that is, your ignorance—be counted? The number of your ignorances is impossible to calculate. The sense is: since you are a Digambara (naked one), you are like a dog (*śvapaca*); therefore, we must observe that all virtues reside in you. Thus, your so-called "defects" are in fact virtues.

[Objection: "What I have stated is established by direct perception; therefore, how can there be ignorance in me? To this, he says: "Deficiency" (*vaiguṇyam*). You have certainly perceived it through the means of direct perception. Having seen the revolving of that certain constellation—which, situated in the northern direction, appears in the form of a fish due to its many preceding and succeeding positions on the surface of the earth—you have ascertained it through direct perception.

The meaning of the word "api" (also/even) is that even the act of not seeing [the stars] is superior. The sense is that you have rendered the deficiency of the moon and other [luminaries] in vain. How could your imagined deficiency be accepted as a matter of direct perception, given that it contradicts the experience of the pole star (*dhruvatārā*) situated there? For neither of those two has been seen by any eye such that what you say would be logical; this is the intended meaning. Furthermore, in the line of the tail of the four [stars] of the pole star, the constellation Bharaṇī exists.

When the sun situated there sets, then at the beginning of the night, or at a time subsequent to that, the tail-star (pucchatārā) is facing westward while the head-star (mukhatārā) is toward the east. Then, at the end of the night, or at a time prior to that, the tail-star revolves and the head-star is toward the east; by this direct revolution, the tail-star is toward the west. Thus, because the line of the tail-star of the sun is seen to be severed during both its rising and setting, there is only one sun, not two.

The same applies to others as well. Otherwise, even according to your own view, since you accept that the fish revolve and that the *śnacakrasa* (the circle of the stars) is complete, it would follow that at the end of the second night—given its connection with the time of day and night—the tail-star could possibly be situated in the eastern direction; thus, its being situated in the eastern direction at the end of the first night would be untenable. For this very reason, the variant reading "ahan" (day) in place of "api" (even/also) found in some manuscripts is well-founded.

For there are not four poles on the celestial sphere (bhacakra) by which the conjunction of the two solstices (saradhrughaṭṭa) could be established; since the north-south axis exists as a single entity within the sphere, it is impossible for two northern poles to be situated there. Therefore, the sense is: how at all is it appropriate for the "Naked One" (Digambara) to state this, given that it contradicts the evidence of direct perception?

And thus, since it would follow that day and night are always equal everywhere, and since those two [unequal durations] would be impossible if they were identical, it is established by this line of reasoning that the previously mentioned ball-like shape of the earth is well-founded; for if the earth were a flat square with equal sides on all sides, there would be no perception of night anywhere, as the day-measure would be tripled [in duration], and because the observation of varying day and night measures in different places every day would otherwise be inexplicable. || 10 ||

Now, refuting the flatness of the earth, he says: "If the blessed Earth were flat, resembling the surface of a mirror, why would the Sun, though situated far above the ground and laboring [in his course], not be seen by men as if by the immortals? (11) "If the Golden Mountain (Meru), the progenitor of night, were inside that [flat earth], why is it not seen? Furthermore, since Meru rises in the north, how is it that the Sun rises in the southern region? (12)

In the Purāṇas, the earth is described as being like the ocean of the terrible rasa (the ocean of blood). O timid one! In its center, surrounded by Jambūdvīpa, which is inhabited by people, there is an ocean of salt water equal in measure to that [continent]. Beyond that is another continent; beyond that ocean is another continent. Each successive continent is double the size of the preceding one, and each ocean is double the size of the preceding continent. Certainly, in the middle of the seventh continent, Puṣkaradvīpa, there is a mountain named Mānasottara, shaped like a bow.

The wheel of the sun’s chariot revolves at a distance of one hundred thousand *yojanas* above his head on the day of the equinox; it revolves to the north when he is in the northern hemisphere (*uttaragola*) and to the south when he is in the southern hemisphere (*dakṣiṇagola*). Now, liberation is described: if the sun, having traveled far above him, were equal [in size] to the moon, why is he not seen by us, as he is constantly seen by the gods? If the sun is hidden by Meru, why is that Meru itself not seen?

If the rising of the sun were to occur as it emerges from Meru, then the rising of the sun would necessarily have to be to the north of the east, since Meru is situated to the north. But how is it that [the sun] is seen rising on the southern side? Therefore, the meaning is that this is not logically tenable on a level earth. [This concludes the section] on the "splendor of the universe" (bhuvanakośa). [Maṇibhadra’s Commentary]: Now, one might object: "The circular shape of the earth is established because otherwise the differences in the lengths of day and night for each day and each location could not be accounted for."

Or this island, which is as broad as a million *yojanas* within the interior of the calyx of a blue-lotus bud, perfectly circular like a lotus leaf, upon which there are nine regions each nine thousand *yojanas* in extent, well-divided by eight mountain ranges called the Mayadās; in the center of these is the region named Ilāvṛta, the innermost region, in whose navel stands Mount Meru, the king of the principal mountain ranges, made entirely of gold, equal in diameter and height to the island, serving as the pericarp of the blue-lotus.

To the extent that there is a difference from the mental sphere (*mānasatara*), to that same extent the earth is said by others to be like the surface of a mirror; this is the arrangement of the *Bhāgavata*. Furthermore, since the difference in the duration of day and night has been established by that very [text], one might object that its globular shape (*golākāratva*) contradicts direct perception. Anticipating this, he refutes it in the *Drutavilambita* meter with the words "If... (*yadīti*). "Dharā" means the earth. "Resembling the interior of a mirror" means resembling the surface of a mirror. "The Blessed One, the Sustainer of the Universe (*viśvaṃbharā*), is so described by some."

By some it is said to be like the back of a tortoise; by others, that its form is not that of a lotus, according to the scriptural tradition. Now, if one accepts the view that the earth is situated in the center of the celestial sphere (golaka), then because the sphere would be obstructed by the earth itself—which is fixed at the center of the circumference—the revolution of the planets would be impossible. To this, [the author] says: "The belly is supported by the earth. Here, "going" (*ga*) refers to the Lord. "Bhām" refers to the stars; by implication, it also includes the planets.

Because the sun (bhaga) revolves daily from left to right [around it], Meru is called Bhaga. According to that view, since the revolution of the stellar sphere is accepted as occurring around Meru, she who possesses that [Meru] is "Bhagavatī"; the meaning is that she possesses the pillar-like mountain (meḍha-parvata). Furthermore, according to that system, the earth is not disk-shaped; for in that view, the revolution of the stellar sphere beneath the earth is not accepted, which would otherwise render such a revolution untenable.

However, the sense is that there is no contradiction, because the mechanism of its revolution—by which it circles clockwise around the center of the earth's surface together with its mountains—is indeed by means of a circular path (*valaya*). Now, for that purpose, the intended meaning stated in the *Bhāgavata Purāṇa* is expressed: this earth is perfectly round, having the shape of a wheel.

Therein, from the center of the earth, extending outwards by a radius of five thousand *yojanas*, there is a circle; up to that limit, the terrestrial mandala is the continent of Jambūdvīpa, which is one hundred thousand *yojanas* in extent. In its center stands Mount Meru, rising eighty-four thousand *yojanas* above the earth. At its base, it is sixteen thousand *yojanas* in width, and it is of the same measure at the surface of the earth as well; at its summit, it is thirty-two thousand *yojanas* in width, thus having the form of a lotus pericarp (*karṇikā*).

Then, with three hundred and fifty thousand [yojanas], there is Plakṣadvīpa, which extends all around the salt ocean. Then, as before, with five hundred and fifty thousand [yojanas] is the ocean of sugarcane juice; with nine hundred and sixty thousand [yojanas] is Śālmalidvīpa; with one million three hundred and fifty thousand [yojanas] is the ocean of honey; with twenty-one hundred and eighty thousand [yojanas] is the ocean of milk; with five hundred and forty-two thousand [yojanas] is Kuśadvīpa; and with sixty thousand [yojanas] is the ocean of clarified butter.

Śākadvīpa is [measured] by ninety-three and a half lakhs [of yojanas]. The ocean of clarified butter (ghṛtoda) is [surrounded] by six times the [measure of] the [preceding] island. Puṣkaradvīpa is [measured] by ten thousand times the [measure of] Śrāddhaka. The ocean of sweet water (svādūdaka) is [surrounded] by twice the [measure of] that [island]. There, in the center of Puṣkaradvīpa, stands Mount Mānasottara, extending for ten thousand yojanas in both length and breadth. This very mountain is the boundary of the field; it is the great mountain of fear. *Maṭīkā on the Golādhyāya*: It is renowned as the Varṣaparvata (the mountain of the regions).

The mountain known as Mānasottara is indeed circular in shape, situated in the center. It rises fifty thousand *yojanas* above [the earth], and it is likewise broad by that same measure; for it is said to be "perfectly circular on all sides," thus they say its breadth and height are each fifty thousand *yojanas*. Along the diameter equal to the center of Jambudvīpa, the circumference of the earth is thirty-nine hundred thousand *yojanas*. At its base, the planets and stars are bound by two wind-ropes attached to the axle-pole of the yoke.

There, on the day of the equinox (viṣuvadina), the wheel of the Sun’s chariot revolves upon the earth at a distance of one hundred thousand yojanas from the ground in the sky, along the line passing through the center of Mount Mānasottara, held fast by the wind; in the northern hemisphere it is above that [mountain], and in the southern hemisphere it is below. The wheel of the Sun’s chariot is situated there, slightly less than the circle of the zodiac, inferred by the circle of the lunar mansions (nakṣatracakra), circular in shape, and tilted obliquely.

Thus, at a distance of two hundred thousand *yojanas* from the earth, the Moon is perceived above the rays of the Sun; possessing sixteen digits (*kalā*), it revolves, spreading out great festivals for the gods with its waxing digits during the bright fortnight and great feasts for the ancestors with its waning digits during the dark fortnight.

Above that [Meru], at a distance of five hundred thousand *yojanas* to the north and south, there are twenty-eight constellations, including Abhijit, ordained by the Lord Kālāyana, which revolve clockwise around Meru. At a distance of seven hundred thousand *yojanas*, Venus moves in front of and behind the Sun with equal speeds, both slow and fast. Mercury is at a distance of nine hundred thousand *yojanas*; Mars at eleven hundred thousand; Jupiter at thirteen hundred thousand; and Saturn at fifteen hundred thousand *yojanas*.

To the north, at a distance of twenty-six lakhs [of yojanas], they teach that the seven sages (Saptarṣis) reside; and nine crores, fifty-one lakhs, and eighty-four thousand yojanas is the circumference of the Mānasottara mountain. Therein, in the four directions starting from the east, the cities of Devadhānī, Nimlocanī, Vibhāvarī, and Alakā belong respectively to Indra, Yama, Varuṇa, and Kubera. Here, when it is midday for them, the sun rises to the left of that region at a distance of four hundred yojanas from the Mānasa mountain, and sets to the right.

Midnight occurs in the region directly opposite that [region]. Thus, whatever [phenomena] such as sunrise occur in regions on the Mānasottara and other mountains, they likewise occur in regions situated along the north-south line relative to those. By this very fact, the statement that Mount Meru stands to the north of all the continents (*dvīpa*) and sub-continents (*varṣa*) becomes consistent; for there is no rule that the directions such as east must remain fixed in one place for all locations. By this, the view that Mount Meru must be accepted as having a spherical shape because the meaning of the scriptural passage "situated in all directions" would otherwise be untenable, is refuted.

On the contrary, because there is no identity between the eastern and western positions, and because Meru would lack a fixed location, it would follow that upon entering below, Meru itself would end up to the south. For those situated on Meru, the sun always shines directly at the midpoint of the day; by its constant movement to the south, it causes [the shadow] to move.

This very [sun], by means of its slow, fast, and moderate motions known as the northern course (*udagayana*), the southern course (*dakṣiṇāyana*), and the equinox (*vaiṣuvata*), and by ascending, descending, and remaining level at their respective positions, brings about days and nights that are long, short, or equal, beginning with Capricorn (*makara*) and so forth. Thus, during the northern and southern courses, the days and nights increase respectively. Now, regarding the subject at hand: if one accepts this Purāṇic doctrine, the spherical nature of the earth (*golākāratva*) favored by us is not precluded; such is the meaning.

*Taraṇiḥ* means the sun. By *naraiḥ*, *bhūgaiḥ*, and *arayaiḥ*—that is, by those such as ourselves [who dwell on earth], and by the immortals (*amaraiḥ*) who reside upon the summit of Meru—[the sun] is not seen; rather, it is seen [by them]. And thus, just as there is constant sight of the sun for those situated on Meru, so too is this [world] for us. The sense is that since we do not perceive it in that manner, the existence of the sun is untenable. 53 10īe-dādīna [corrupt/fragmentary]. The meaning is that because of the impossibility of perceiving it in that way, its existence is logically inconsistent.

Now, one might object: since sunrise and sunset are perceived on the surface of the earth as being in contact with the ground, it would be impossible for the day and night known through them to be perceptible [as distinct from the ground]. To this, he says: "Of the earth" (*kṣiteḥ*). [The sun] revolves above the earth, moving upward while being carried by the *pravaha* wind. Thus, according to that system, because the revolution of the sun around the earth is not admitted, there would be no downward motion; consequently, the curvature of the earth (its "bending") would be untenable, leading to the undesirable conclusion that sunrise and sunset themselves could not occur at all. This is the intended meaning.

Now, it might be argued that for those residing on the northern slopes of Mount Meru, since there is no intervening obstacle, they would always see the sun; consequently, the impossibility of purification [due to the absence of night] would follow. However, for those situated on the surface of the earth, even though Meru revolves around them, other mountains can intervene, and thus the appearance and disappearance of the sun—resulting from its emergence and concealment—are possible, which accounts for the occurrence of day and night. It should not be said that, due to the vastness of the earth's circumference, the sun cannot be seen [by everyone at once].

Because he has accepted the error that [the sun] resides in a distant place, he says "gone far away" (*dūragata*) to refute it. According to the method described, situated on the same meridian as Mount Mānasottara, it moves to the north-west of Meru. The meaning is that even though it is not visible due to being exceedingly far away, its visibility is not contradictory because it consists of light.

The point is this: since the sun is situated above Mount Meru, there is no possibility of mountains and such obstructing its visibility, as they lack height relative to that limit. As for the objection that if [the sun] were reflected within the interior of a mirror, sunrise and sunset would occur simultaneously everywhere—so that, just as for the gods, why should there not be a day lasting up to six months for humans; and just as for humans, why should there not be a day lasting only six *ghaṭikās* for the gods?—that is not correct.

According to the statement of the Blessed One that for those residing there the sun always shines at midday, there is no night in their view, as it consists of the non-perception of the sun. Furthermore, the presentation of day and night according to the sequence of the northern and southern solstices is merely conventional; moreover, in their system, sunrise and sunset do not occur at the same time anywhere. As for the second alternative, since a divine day is imperceptible, even if one were to accept the undesired consequence (iṣṭāpatti), the subsequent [argument] would be impossible. || 11 ||

Now, one might object: even if there is no visibility from mountains and the like up to that extent, the equal height [of the mountain] is not the cause for the absence of obstruction; otherwise, shadows would not arise. To this we reply: just as a person standing within the shadow of a tree perceives the non-perception of the sun, so too, for people such as ourselves who are within the shadow of Meru, there is no contradiction in the occurrence of night. For this very reason, in the northern hemisphere (*uttaragola*), because the sun is at a greater altitude, it is seen for a long duration and not seen for a short duration due to the greater distance above Meru.

The day and night are reversed [in the southern regions] because the sun is near Mount Meru; due to its proximity to Meru, it is not seen for a long time, and thus the nights are long while the days are short. On the equinox day (*viṣuvaddin*), however, they are equal. This has already been correctly established above according to the Purāṇic view that the sun is at a distance of one hundred thousand *yojanas* from the earth. For those situated on Meru, however, there is an absence of night because they are never within the shadow of Meru.

One might suspect that because there is an absence of shadow on the inner surface of the golden ground of Meru, there is never night there, just as there is never day. Anticipating this objection, [the author] refutes it by means of a verse whose composition is delayed for the sake of the vow (*vrata*): "If... It should be understood that here, the word *nanu*, which indicates the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), connects first with the latter half of the verse. The term *kanakāloka* (golden light) refers to the golden ground of Meru, which produces the aforementioned [absence of shadow] in the manner described. The particle *iti* signifies the conclusion of the prima facie position; its purpose is to make known that this is the answer to the aforementioned position. This is found in the *Maṇiprabhā-ṭīkā* on the *Golādhyāya*, verse 44.6.

It should be understood that the word *atha* located in the second half of the verse serves the purpose of indicating immediate succession to the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*). The phrase "the answer is stated" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. He states the answer itself with the words "But... (*kiṃ tu*). The sense is this: why is Mount Meru not seen situated between those two—the sun and the earth—despite being placed there by an intervening space? Since whatever acts as an obstacle to the perception of something must necessarily prevent its perception, it would follow that Meru is visible; therefore, Meru cannot be the obstacle to the sight of the sun. Now, if it is argued that it is not seen because it is too far away...

If it is argued that this is because the earth and so forth are not perceived, and because they lack a source [of light], [we reply: there would be the undesirable consequence of perceiving them due to the reflection of the sun’s rays upon their golden and jeweled nature. If it is argued that they are obstructed, [we reply: the non-existence of other mountains and such, measured by Mount Meru, is already established by the Purāṇas; otherwise, one would have to conclude that the very obstruction of Mount Meru causes the night. Furthermore, that [obstruction] cannot be defined.

Now, if it is argued that there is invisibility during the day due to the predominance of sunlight and at night due to the intensity of darkness, [we reply: no, because at both sunrise and sunset, the mountain is perceived as rising up and not as being level with the ground; furthermore, at those times, it would follow that Meru itself would be visible. If it is further argued that although it is of great magnitude, it is not seen by observers, then its status as an obstructer of the sun's light is untenable, since it revolves around the cave [of the earth] and is situated high above the object [the sun]. If it is then argued that the invisibility is caused by multiple factors, [we reply:]...

How is it that the northern direction is not perceived as being covered by dense darkness, as if by a mass of clouds? This is because darkness originates from that very source, and because the fixed stars do not become visible until they reach the horizon. Now, one might argue that since the stars are situated at an immense distance relative to the sun, no obstruction can exist between them; therefore, their light should not result in the presence of dense darkness in the northern quarter.

Furthermore, since the terrestrial horizon is perceived as the base of Mount Meru, there is no contradiction whatsoever in accepting that Meru produces the night; moreover, this is not contradicted by the Purāṇas and other texts. Anticipating this objection, he states another reason, beginning with "udag" (northern). "Aṃśumān" refers to the Sun. How could it rise in the southern part—that is, in the region intended for the Southern Fire (*dakṣiṇāgni*)—within the southern hemisphere? The sense is that, given the direct observation in the southern hemisphere, the rising and setting [of the sun] in the southern part would be logically untenable.

Now, one might object: "In the northern hemisphere (uttaragola), in the southern hemisphere (dakṣiṇagola), in the southern region, in the assembly of stars, and in the east and west—is this not untenable? Otherwise, the [concept of] the sphere (gola) would be untenable. To this, he says: "To the north" (udak). This is the mountain Maru, well-known for being the cause of the production of night. "To the north" means situated to the north of its own location; the meaning is that because of this, there is no such inconsistency.

Thus, because Mount Meru stands at the center like a belly and acts as an obstruction, sunrise and sunset always occur only to the north, due to the beginning and completion of the respective obstructions. Since the sun moves in the southern part of the body [of the world-sphere], its rising and setting there are impossible. For it does not move toward those various directions by virtue of the mountain Meru, which would otherwise make such a thing possible; the sense is that this is impossible because Meru is immovable. And thus, the sun revolves above Mount Mānasa in the very shape of that mountain.

Since it is situated to the south of its own location, there would always be daylight there; consequently, at the point of twenty-four finger-breadths from the tip of the shadow, the presence of a shadow—perceived directly by one standing in the middle of the sky according to one's own six-finger measurement—would never arise.

The author of the *Bhuvanakosa* refutes the Puranic view with a multitude of objections, such as: the impossibility of the sun's rising from the north and remaining in the eastern direction; the impossibility of the observed differences in day-length for locations situated along the southern meridian; and the fact that, according to that school, the positions of sunrise and sunset would be fixed [rather than variable]. Thus, by the principle of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), the fact that the earth is actually spherical is established through the necessity of accounting for observations otherwise inexplicable.

And because the sun and other planets revolve around the earth, it is observed that one hemisphere of the terrestrial globe is visible while the other is not; thus, since the very region of the earth acts as an obstruction whenever the sun is seen at every step, the resulting difference in day and night at every revolution is empirically evident. Therefore, it should be understood that there is nothing whatsoever in this astronomical system that is logically inconsistent. || 12 ||

Now, dispelling the doubt regarding direct visual perception (of the earth's curvature), he says: "Since the circumference [of the earth] is equal [to its diameter] a hundredfold, and the earth is exceedingly vast, while the human being upon its surface is very small, it appears to him as level when he observes it. (13) Sixth [verse]. Now, he states the justification for the measure of the earth's circumference mentioned above: "If this distance between two cities were to the north, then what would it be in terms of degrees of latitude? (14)

The stated measure of the circumference is determined by means of the proportion of degrees. As the location of one's own place moves further south from the non-axial (nirakṣa) region, the equatorial circle becomes increasingly depressed relative to the celestial poles. The degrees of latitude (akṣāṃśa) are the interval between those two. These are calculated through proportion based on the *yojanas* of distance from the non-axial region. Therefore, having known the degrees of latitude in a certain city, the remainder [is found] when moving northward from that city to another city.

Then, by means of their intervening degrees and the intervening yojanas between the cities, there is a rule of three (anupāta): "If the intervening yojanas are seen for the intervening degrees, then what [distance] is obtained for 360 degrees of a circle?"

The result is the circumference of the earth in *yojanas*. [Verse 14] [Objection: Since a person moving high above at many *yojanas* does not perceive the earth as a part of a sphere anywhere on the ground, and since it is perceived everywhere as having the shape of a mirror (flat), the perception of its globular form (*golākāratva*) is untenable; therefore, how can this be established through direct perception? [Response: This is answered by the following verse. Because of that reason, for a person situated upon its surface—that is, standing on the surface of the terrestrial globe—wherever he may be situated below, [the earth appears globular].

That [image] is the entire earth-form, complete and full. It appears as if in a mirror; that is to say, because of the absence of its own substantial form, the cognition arises that "this is a reflection in a mirror. To explain the reason indicated by the word "even" (*sama*), he says: "Because... For this reason, [the image] would be like a straight staff, occupying a space equal to a hundredth part of the circumference of the circle, and not slanting.

When mustard seeds and the like are placed on the upper surface of a ball, even if they are positioned upon only a hundredth part of its circumference, they do not fall. From this, it is understood that even within this very object, such as the myrobalan fruit, there exists some portion that is level; for otherwise, such a state of stability would be impossible. Since an unstable [surface] is dependent on a downward slope, an object placed upon it would necessarily fall. Therefore, the "hundredth part" is used as an illustration for that which is level.

Furthermore, if the circumference were dependent on the diameter, then even a very subtle portion of the circumference, though situated within a part of the diameter, would not appear as such; yet that [portion] is necessarily visible. According to the statement of Śākalya, "That which is seen is indeed the part to be measured," it consists of ninety-six parts. This too is the first [section], 1080, in the chapter on the Sphere (Golādhyāya), verse 46.

Having understood that [the value] is "gross" because it does not arise from the realization of the subtler light of the *jyā* (sine), and considering it equal to two *aśvis*, the venerable Bhaṭṭa obtained [the result]; then, stating that even more subtle parts are to be subtracted until one reaches equality with the circumference, he declared that a part exceeding ten hundred is equal. In that regard, the Teacher (Ācārya) accepted for the sake of brevity a hundredth part as the midpoint between the parts agreed upon by the ancients and those by Puruṣa.

And thus, even though it is spherical in shape, because its parts appear equal [in curvature], there is no contradiction in perceiving it as circular; this is the sense. Now, one might object: "In that case, a ball (*kanduka*) would also have to be perceived as circular due to its uniformity. To this he says: "The earth" (*pṛthvī*). This refers to the ground. It is "exceedingly vast" (*nitarāṃ pṛthvī*); the meaning is that it is large, measuring slightly less than five thousand [yojanas]. The word "and" (*ca*) is used in the sense of accumulation. Therefore, because the ball has a form that is compressed in its parts, it does not produce a perception of that [circular] shape.

The meaning is that because the earth-globe possesses flatness in a portion measuring slightly less than five hundred *yojanas*, it appears in that [flat] form. Now, one might object: "In the case of a clay ball shaped like a large sphere, although a portion is perceived as flat, even when it is seen as flat, there is no cognition of it as a spherical part because its greater portion is not seen; likewise, even if a portion of fifty *yojanas* on the earth-globe is seen as flat, why would it not also be perceived as a spherical part when its greater portion is seen?"

To show that such a perception cannot occur, he says: "tanīyān" (minuter). This means that a human being (*nara*) is *tanīyān*, that is, exceedingly light or minute. And thus, since humans possess only a limited measure of form and magnitude, they lack the capacity to perceive even a portion of the earth's surface as a level plane within their field of vision; consequently, there is no perception of the earth as a complete, level whole, let alone a perception exceeding that. For this very reason, the perception of the earth as having the shape of a sphere (*golākāra*) does not arise.

By the phrase "of one situated on its back," it is indicated that because those at a higher elevation see a greater portion of the earth's surface than those standing on the ground, the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa) or Brahmā possesses the perception of the earth as being spherical (golākāra). Thus, it is stated in the *Sūryasiddhānta*: "Due to their small stature, people see this earth from all sides from their own positions; though it is circular, they perceive the earth as having the shape of a wheel. And so, the sense is that the perception of it as a circular disc does not contradict its being spherical.

Now, in response to the question "Of what magnitude [is it]?", the circumference of the earth (*kuparidhi*) is stated in terms of *yojanas*. Although this was stated in the very section on the middle sphere (*madhyamadhikāra*), it is consistent even if it contradicts the *Purāṇas*, because it is established through logical proof; thus he says in the *Upajāti* meter: "The distance between cities... and so forth, [measured] by the degrees of latitude and longitude.

The measurement of four thousand *yojanas* is intended as the distance between two cities situated on the north-south meridian line—cities whose latitudes will be described later as being one hundred and eighty degrees apart. This distance is determined by the degrees of difference in latitude (*akṣāṃśa*) serving as the standard unit of measure. In this context, "north" refers to the interval between the cities; it signifies the numerical value of the *yojana* distance in the form of the north-south separation. By specifying "north," the author establishes the rule that from a location with fewer degrees of latitude, a location with more degrees of latitude must necessarily be to the north. Thus, the direction is fixed.

It should be understood that the difference in the form of the slanting hypotenuse (*tiryak-kaṇa*) between the two cities connected by that same degree of longitude must not be taken [as the base]. If it were so, it would be perceived as the result. Then, by what [means]—by the degrees of the circle or by the desired signs of the zodiac—is how much measure obtained? This is the question regarding the skill of the world, formulated through the method of proportion (*anupāta*). 44. *Bhāṣya-ṭīkā*: It is called "proportion" (*anupāta*) because it is applied (*anu-pātyate*).

The meaning is that the result of the connection with the measure (pramāṇa) is produced by means of the relationship of desire. The phrase "in the section on the true" (sadbodhikā) means by that [section]. "Of the circumference" (paridheḥ) refers to the circumference of the celestial sphere (bhagola). "As previously stated" (niruktam) means as described in the previously mentioned "Section on the Mean" (madhyamādhikāra). It is logical that the measure consists of *yojanas*. The meaning is "not otherwise. And thus, because the Earth is globular, its circumference from south to north is equal everywhere; this is due to the Earth being situated within the wheel of the stars (bhacakra).

By means of a thread equal to the circumference of the ecliptic passing through the two cities situated on the same meridian, and by means of a thread equal to the number of *yojanas* known to lie between those two cities, there is a connection between the two points located on the terrestrial globe (bhagola) situated on that same meridian as those respective cities. Since the degrees of latitude (*palāṃśa*) are known from this, knowledge of the earth's circumference is indeed possible; for, since the terrestrial globe is occupied by the ecliptic and the degrees of the circle are equal in circumference everywhere, the knowledge of the earth's circumference arises through that connection.

The knowledge of that [longitude] is obtained through the method already stated for determining the longitudinal difference between two stars. This is because, except for the interval between the eastern and western points (the meridian), there is an absence of stars or other luminaries that can indicate positions on the same celestial circle (bhagola) at those specific locations; thus, knowing the longitude by means of such an interval is difficult to achieve. Although this explanation might be considered inappropriate due to the coarseness of the proportional calculation of degrees, there is no fault here, as the intent is merely to state that this method is established by the reasoning of one's own school (*svamata*) in comparison to the views of others, and because it is supported by other authorities. || 14 ||

Now, O King, confirming that very point: since the equinoctial shadow (*abanti*) is determined by calculation as being one-sixteenth of the latitude, the difference between [the true and calculated positions] multiplied by sixteen would be the *gamana* (precession). Why then was it stated to be so much greater? For by this [calculated] circumference, the rising of the horns, the conjunctions of planets, eclipses, and the like are indeed made possible. By that [same] fortune, the earth is known through the authority of its measure, joined with positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative exclusion (*vyatireka*). This is clear. 16.

The extent of the salt-water ocean situated between Sītodā and Meru, arising from sweet water, is measured at five hundred and thirty-five thousand yojanas (5,350,000). Then, including Mānasa and Uttara, the extent of the land is one million five hundred and seventy-five thousand yojanas (1,575,000), multiplied by the number of the subsequent mountains. Furthermore, the extent all around at the front is likewise; then, extending further all around, the earth is eighty-three million six hundred thousand yojanas (83,600,000) wide, reaching as far as the Lokāloka mountain.

Thus, the extent of the ground from Meru to the Lāḷa mountains is twelve and a half crores [125,000,000] yojanas. Likewise, from the center of Meru to the edge of the inner portion is also twelve and a half crores; thus, up to the Lokāloka mountain, the circumference of the earth is thirty-five crores [350,000,000]. Because it is a semi-circle on both sides, the diameter—the measurement of the circular ground from the Lokāloka mountain to the edge—is fifty-six crores [560,000,000].

[The opponent argues: "It is stated [in the Purāṇas] that it is fifty *koṭis* wide; however, this is incorrect because of the previously mentioned calculation based on the circumference being equal to the diameter. Since the Lokāloka mountain extends for fifteen *koṭis* all around the world, the entire circumference of the terrestrial sphere up to the edge of the Lokāloka mountain is fifty *koṭis*; therefore, it is said in the Purāṇa that it is 'extensive' (*vistīrṇa*). Some say: "Beyond that, there are fifty-three eyes (*akṣi*) in each direction. Then someone says: "Beyond that..."

In the *Golādhyāya*, Maṇidīpikā commentary (v. 48): "O fair-faced one, the earth is ten *koṭis* [of yojanas]. Since this is stated immediately after [the description of] Jambūdvīpa, it refers to a certain earth in both cases. Therefore, according to the *Śaiva-tantra*, in one case there is a golden earth (*suvarṇabhūmi*) five *koṭis* wide, beyond which is the Lokāloka mountain, and beyond that is the rest. Thus, in another [system], the extent up to the Lokaparvata is fifty-five thousand yojanas (550,000). Consequently, for the sake of determining the center of the earth, the earth extends for ten *koṭis* [from the edge]. In a circle with a diameter of sixteen hundred [yojanas], the circumference is five hundred and twenty-eight [yojanas].

Since it is stated in the *Sūryasiddhānta* that the diameter is sixteen crores [of yojanas], they accept the circumference to be five crores. How then is the measurement of the stellar sphere (*bha-parimāṇa*) as stated by you—though logically consistent—consistent with this? Therefore, preceded by the presentation of another previously mentioned argument, he refutes what is stated in the Purāṇas using an *upajāti* verse, beginning with "nirakṣa": because of which reason, from the place devoid of latitude (*nirakṣa-deśa*), namely Avantī (Ujjayinī).

The meaning is: situated on the meridian line other than the south, near the sun, which is like the absence of the pole-star (akṣa) characterized by constant elevation (dhruvonnati). When, according to the method of the essence of the equalized [calculation], it is twenty; he who possesses the poles (akṣa) is like the ten-faced one (daśamukha), namely Rāvaṇa; his region is Laṅkā. In the sixteenth part of the earth—that is, in the sixteenth portion of the circumference of the terrestrial sphere—it occurs through calculation, that is, by means of the investigation of the mathematics understood through the previously mentioned method. It would be so.

And thus, for the sake of the previously mentioned proportion, it was inferred by observing the degrees of latitude (*akṣāṃśa*) in the southern and northern cities that, due to a decrease in certain places situated on one's own meridian line, there exists a state of zero degrees of latitude.

Moreover, since the entire circle of the celestial sphere (bhagola) consists of three hundred and sixty degrees, and according to the reasoning previously stated, the latitude at Ujjayinī is twenty-two and a half degrees; and because the obliquity of the ecliptic (krānti) is approximately twenty-four degrees, [the point of intersection] falls at the sixteenth part of the terrestrial circumference from Avantī. Furthermore, because there is no southern meridian line extending from Laṅkā to other non-equatorial regions, the implication is that the [result] remains unsettled at the sixteenth part of the circumference relative to those points. From this reason, that interval [is established].

The distance between those two, Dvārakā and Ujjayinī, is a measure of the number of intermediate *yojanas* established by common worldly consensus, or established by counting the intervening regions. The circumference of the earth would be sixteen times that [distance], because that interval consists of degrees of latitude measured along the meridian.

By this [verse], it is stated that: "In whatever region there are certain degrees of latitude (akṣāṃśa) and degrees of obliquity (vaśvakāṃśa), and whatever the resulting value may be—in that region with its circumference, compared to a point on the equator situated to the south—the number of yojanas known to lie between them, when multiplied by that result, shall be the circumference of the earth. By these words, the very circumference as stated by us is established; thus, through the repetition of the phrase "by this," [it refers to] our own accepted circumference of the earth. It has been said: "The measurement of the earth’s circumference mentioned in the Purāṇas is many times five hundred [yojanas]. What is it? [It is the following:]

How is this established? It means it is illogical; for the sense is that since our own accepted [calculation] of the circumference is established by reasoning (*yukti*), the magnitude stated in the Purāṇas—which is based solely on scriptural authority (*āgama*)—must be disregarded. By this, the interpretation that "the earth has immeasurable *yojanas*" is refuted. For if the earth were surrounded by an immeasurable number of *yojanas*, how could it be protected? Indeed, [if it were so], the sun would not set over the region of Laṅkā while still being sixteen parts of the circumference away from Avantī, as is observed.

As for the argument that because the word *koṭi* is accepted as having multiple meanings, it denotes "hundreds" in the present context—thus meaning "extended over five hundred [yojanas]" and so forth, which is not contradictory—that is incorrect. For it would result in an inconsistency with the measurements of the continents and oceans stated in the Purāṇas. (15) Now, one might argue: since the measurement of the earth's circumference is established by the rule "from the middle of the mountain to the two cities on the opposite side," and since there is no contradiction regarding the various measurements of the circumference, the circumference of the earth mentioned in the Purāṇas is also appropriate even if it measures five hundred [yojanas].

The question regarding the measurement of the universe concerns the *yojanas* according to one's own accepted system and the *yojanas* according to the systems of others. [This is so] because there is a diversity in the distinction between *yojanas* due to the difference in the circumference of the earth and other spheres, as stated in verse 49: "Measured by their respective circumferences divided by the circumference of the earth. Therefore, by the previously mentioned reasoning—beginning with "eight *yava* grains and *udara*s make an *aṅgula*"—those intervening *yojanas* which have been calculated are, when multiplied by the rough factor (*rūkṣa*), the intervening *yojanas* according to that [other] system.

Since the circumference of the earth, measuring fifty million *yojanas*, is established for them by the reasoning already stated, the justification is equal even in their view; therefore, I say in the *Vasantatilaka* meter: "By the pure [calculation]," etc. For that reason, even the aforementioned measurement of the earth is correct. This is because the statement that the earth's circumference is "seven times nine oceans" (630) in *yojana* count is an experience of the true measure of the earth’s circumference. This is demonstrated through the method of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).

The former teachers (*pūrvācāryāḥ*)—meaning they said—[asserted] that in the absence of the measure stated by us regarding the circumference of the earth's orbit, there is an absence of being a valid experience (*yathārthānubhavatva*), [this being established] through the accompaniment of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). Now, one might ask: "Even if our stated measure is accepted, how can validity be asserted on the basis of the negative concomitance that 'there is an absence of being a valid experience'?"; therefore, he provides a qualification for the negative concomitance, saying: "connected with positive concomitance" (*anvayayukta*).

The meaning is that, in the apprehension of the means of valid cognition as stated by us, the nature of being a true experience [is established] by means of negative concomitance (vyatireka-sahacāra) assisted by positive concomitance (anvaya-sahacāra).
