Thus, the sense is that there is no possibility at all of the doubt that "in the apprehension of the means of valid cognition as stated by us, [the definition] has the nature of a true experience" [could be established] through positive pervasion (anvaya-vyāpti).

To prevent the doubt that "the status of being a valid experience (*yathārthānubhavatva*) exists in a definition even in the absence of the means of knowledge stated by me," the word "by way of negative concomitance" (*vyatirekeṇa*) was used. Thus, through both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka-sahacāra*), it is established that the status of being a valid experience belongs to the definition as stated by me. [Objection: But those very positive and negative concomitances are not yet established. How, then, is validity understood through them? [Response: To state the reason indicated by the word "therefore" (*tena*), he says: "Because of the rise of the Śūdra. For (*hi*)—that is, because of this reason—[the concomitances are established].

By this aforementioned circumference—the circumference of the terrestrial globe—that which is perceptible, such as the elevation of Mount Śṛṅgavera and so forth; the conjunction of two planets and the conjunction of two constellations from the point of planetary conjunction; the rising and setting of constellations and planets produced by their constant proximity to the sun; and by the word "shadow" (chāyā), the shadow of the sun, as well as the shadows suitable for the conjunctions of the moon and Venus—or alternatively, the tail of a comet—and for this very reason, by the word "and so forth" (ādi), the shadow of the arm (bhuja-chāyā) and its related applications are included.

Or, the prediction of results indicated by the arrangement of the established and clearly determined planets is consistent; that is, it accords with observation. Thus, from the established planets corrected by the longitudinal difference (*deśāntara*) produced by the circumference (*paridhi*) as stated by us, [the positions] become perceptible. And the solar eclipse, through the parallax (*lambana*) generated by the radius of the circumference as stated by us, is proven to follow the logical connection (*anvaya*). This is the intended meaning. Now, one might object: "Even so, since the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is not established, there is the risk of invalidity. To this he says: "No," [meaning] not by another.

The measurements of Bhṛṅga, Loka, and others accord with the circumference accepted by those who agree with our stated Purāṇas, rather than with the circumference you favor. Thus, the sense is that since agreement occurs when our stated measurement is present, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is also established. By this very fact, it is indicated that the other measurements of circumference lack authority, because both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) are unestablished for them.

And thus, the measurement stated in the Purāṇas regarding the circumference of the earth is consistent with your statement; this is the sense in which that measurement has been adopted because it serves as the basis for planetary calculation (*prahagaṇita*). In reality, however, by reducing the Jambūdvīpa—which you maintain to be one hundred thousand *yojanas* in extent—to our own accepted single *yojana*, the universal experience of the Jambūdvīpa as being well-known to consist of many *yojanas* would be rendered a mere handful of water poured away in vain.

[The text states: "The Himālaya, Meru, and others [are situated] with little effort in the Milk Ocean," etc. (Gai. 10). [Commentary: Furthermore, because it would follow that your statement contradicts the *paridhi* (circumference) mentioned in the Purāṇas, the refutation stated in the verse beginning with "the part of the meaning" (*arthāṃśapada*) is intended for the purpose of rejecting the [view] that grasps the surface as being below; such is the truth. Now, he describes the arrangement of cities on the terrestrial globe: "In the center of this [globe] is Yamakoṭi, and in the east and west are Romakapattana and [Siddhapura]. (Gai. 11)

Below it is Siddhapura; Sumeru is in the north, and the submarine fire (Vaḍavānala) is in the south. Those who know the sphere say that these places are separated by the distance of one-quarter of a globe. On Mount Meru dwell the hosts of gods and Siddhas, while in the submarine fire reside all the hells together with the Daityas. Whosoever stands upon the earth situated below, and another stands above it, each considers the other to be at the bottom; thus those situated in the four directions perceive one another as if they were horizontal.

With their heads downward, situated within the plowshare like men on the shore of the ocean, they remain there undisturbed, positioned sideways and below, just as we are here. (20) [This is easy to understand. (1718) (19) (20) Maṇibhadra’s Commentary: This might be so.

Regarding the phrase "from the region of no latitude" (*nirakṣadeśāt*), one might ask: how is the location of Laṅkā understood? For there, the [celestial] latitudes do not arise because they are absent there. To this, the following response is given under the guise of describing the arrangement of the vessel’s position, which serves as the answer to the doubt concerning the necessity of the existence of six parts—namely, the center, east, west, and the four cardinal directions—for any physical object: "In the center of the earth-globe" (*kumadhye*) means at the central part of the terrestrial sphere. Although the "center" on the surface of a sphere may be anywhere, [here it refers to the specific point].

It is incorrect to say that [the equator] is at the center of the earth; nevertheless, for the sake of practical usage, because the portion of the axis situated below the Bhagaṇa (zodiac) is incapable of being assigned to the circumference of the earth, it is imagined by Brahmā that the equator lies precisely at the center of the earth's surface. From this Laṅkā, in the eastern direction, is the city named Yamakoṭi; the word "and" (ca) implies that it is from the very location of Laṅkā. In the western direction is the city named Romaka.

Then, from the point of entry below Ṭhaḍkāda, there is the calculation of the latitudes for the central points of the locations of Laṅkā; otherwise, the conjunction of the upper and lower regions would be untenable. [Next is] Siddhapura. "Then" (atha) means immediately after. To the north (saumya) of the cities situated in the eastern and western lines previously mentioned, in the northern direction, is Mount Sumeru, the mountain of gold. By the use of the word "and" (ca), it is meant that in the southern direction, opposite the four cities situated on the aforementioned east-west line, lies the abode of Vāyu (the Wind-god).

And likewise, the intention [of the author] is that, as will be explained later in the section establishing the nature of the degrees of latitude (*akṣāṃśa*), it is shown that there is an absence of such elevation at places situated on the east-west line from Laṅkā; however, this is not the case for places situated on the north-south line passing through Nirakṣa (the equator). Now, an objection: "If the east-west line from the region of Laṅkā extends as far as Siddhapura, how much distance is there between the entry point and the exit point of the path of the sun's rays? Likewise, what is the distance for the north-south line from the place of the Rākṣasas (*rakṣasthāna*)? [The answer follows: It is exactly the same.

[The commentary on verse 11 begins: Regarding the radiance of the cosmic egg (bhuvanakośaprabha): [Question]—At what distance from the location of Laṅkā is the abode of Meru and the submarine fire (vaḍavānala)? [Answer]—In response to that, because the four cities beginning with Vaśaśiraḥ are situated along the east-west line from the city of Laṅkā and are accessible to humans, they are indicated as being like the realm of the Rākṣasas; and since the remaining two, Meru and the submarine fire, are inaccessible to humans, their abodes are established [there]. This is the resolution of the doubt.

Copajāti says: "The cities of Kuṣṭha, etc. refers to the ancient teachers who were well-versed in the nature of the terrestrial globe (*bhūgola*). Those aforementioned places of great number, situated in sequence—namely Indradyumna, Koṭisiddhapura, Romaka, Kūrma, Uru, Vaḍavānala, and Mañjā—are mutually separated by intervals equal to one-fourth of the circumference of the terrestrial globe; that is to say, they are situated at a distance from one another equal to a fourth part of the earth's circumference. They are separated by the distance of one-quarter of the earth's perimeter. This is the meaning.

They say that because the four cities established on the east-west and north-south meridians have already been described [in the previous section], and because their specific location on the terrestrial globe has not been mentioned here, they must be situated at intervals equal to one-fourth of the earth's circumference—according to the maxim "that which is not otherwise accounted for must be equal"—and thus they are established as such. Furthermore, they cite the *Sūryasiddhānta*, which states: "The Meru mountain stands at the center of the space between the signs beginning with Taurus (Vṛṣa), and it is there, indeed, that the gods reside. Thus they maintain.

And likewise, the locations of Yamakoṭi, Romaka, Vaḍavānala, and Setu are known respectively as being situated on the eastern, western, southern, and northern sides of Laṅkā; the sense is that they exist within these intervals. By this, it is stated that the distance between any two rival cities mentioned here, which are separated by [the central point], is half the circumference (paridhyardha). For example, as between Meru and Vaḍavānala, or between Laṅkā and Siddhapura, or between Yamakoṭi and Romaka.

On my [side] are the gods, Indra and others, as well as the Siddhas and the great seers (*maharṣi*) devoted to the practice of yoga; these constitute the two groups combined. Here, the plural number signifies an infinite multitude of armies. They dwell, that is, they preside over this place, which is the location of the submarine fire (*vaḍavānala*). All [these places] are hells (*naraka*); specifically, this is the hell of endless stones. Furthermore, below this is the *Tāmisra* hell, one of the twenty-eight hells well-known from the Purāṇas, where the sinful beings are consumed along with the Daityas—the Daityas being included among those to be destroyed. These are for the purpose of [their] offspring.

The word "ca" (and) implies that they dwell there. Because the submarine fire (*vaḍavānala*) is extremely scorching, it is logical that all those who have committed sins should reside beneath it, since through contact with it, they too become capable of extreme burning. Therefore, the sense is that for the Daityas—who have tasted the nectar of the lotus-feet of the Supreme Lord—it is fitting that their dwelling be in that very place. And so it is said in the *Sūryasiddhānta*: "A mountain made of Jāmbūnada gold, containing a multitude of various jewels..."

Mount Meru extends out from the center of the earth on both sides; above it reside the gods led by Indra and the great sages, while below it dwell the Asuras, who hate one another and depend upon each other. || 18 ||

Now, one might object: "In this way, since a city situated at a distance equal to a quarter of the earth's circumference from Laṅkā would be directly overhead for its inhabitants, it would be visible to them; likewise, Siddhapura, situated directly beneath Laṅkā, would also be possible [to see]. To address this, he clarifies the intention of what was previously stated—namely, that "the sky is the limit"—by means of two Upajāti verses, beginning with "yaḥ. "Yaḥ" means a living being (*jantu*). "Yatra" means in whichever part of the surface of the terrestrial globe (*bhūgola*) he stands or dwells. "Sa jīvaḥ" means that living soul. "Anīmaḥ" means the earth. "Kham" refers to the sky. [The verse continues: "Whatever portion of the earth's surface a person occupies, the sky above that very spot is his zenith; thus, the sky is indeed the limit. This explains that because the sky extends infinitely, there is no fixed point where another world could be situated directly above or below a given location on earth, thereby resolving the objection.

He considers himself situated on that very spot. [The word] *asyāḥ* refers to this earth. [The particle] *api* is used in the sense of "also. He considers himself to be upon the surface of the terrestrial globe (*bhūgola*). The word *ca* (and) implies a conjunction. Therefore, because it has been established in various ways previously that the earth is beneath everyone everywhere on the surface of the terrestrial globe—based on the common perception that "the earth is below us and we are above it"—it must be understood that the terrestrial globe is below [us] in every part and surrounds [us]. Since those situated at the bottom have no further region below them, there is an absence of falling.

19 || [Objection: Since the cities such as Laṅkā are situated transversely relative to that [central meridian], the people inhabiting them must necessarily be perceived as "transverse" (tiryak) and thus subject to falling; therefore, he says: "Below" (adhaḥ). The meaning is that for one situated on the earth's surface, there is no established "transverse" direction independent of the delimitation of all parts [of the body] as being "below. Those [people] residing in places such as Laṅkā are positioned at a distance equal to a fourth part of the earth's circumference; they are "mutually" (mithaḥ), that is, with respect to one another, "transverse" (tiryak), meaning horizontally displaced.

"Move about one another. By the word "as if" (iva), they declare that in reality such movement does not exist. And so, just as there is a fear of the fall of men residing in other regions [of the sky] because the Laṅkā region is situated obliquely relative to them, likewise, since the Laṅkā region is also seen to be oblique relative to other regions, the falling of the *kaṅka* birds residing there is likewise unavoidable. Thus, because a fall for all the worlds is logically untenable, the conclusion is that there is indeed no falling; this is the refutation. Now, one might object: "Those situated below must necessarily fall. To this, he says: "With their heads downward" (*adhaḥśirasphaḥ*).

They speak with their faces downward. [Objection: But if they have their heads below, there would be no falling down. [Response: Those situated on the opposite side of the earth's circumference, separated by half the earth's perimeter, speak of one another as having their heads downward; thus, for you, this results in a contradiction. Therefore, like shadow-people, their falling is prevented by that very [circumference]. Like shadow-people—that is, like people reflected in a mirror—on the shore of the sea, with water from a pond or river at their throats, just as the reflection of a person appears, so too does it happen here.

The meaning is that because there is no lower portion of the earth, downwardness is impossible, and thus there is an absence of falling. Now, one might ask: "Even so, how do the people living in those places conduct their affairs, being troubled by the fear of falling? Anticipating this question, he provides the answer under the guise of a conclusion: "unperturbed" (*anākula*). Those people residing there—whether situated horizontally or below—remain unperturbed and undisturbed in that region; and by the word "and" (*ca*), it is implied that they also carry out their worldly activities (*vyavaharanti*).

The sense is that the apprehension of falling has been dispelled. What is the proof for this? Therefore, he states the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) through an analogy: "We," and so forth. The meaning is: "Just as we remain here on this portion of earth occupied by us, without fear of falling, so it is with them. That is to say, since even the region occupied by us must necessarily be situated horizontally or below some other point, just as we have no apprehension of falling, so too they have none.

Otherwise, our own existence would be impossible; for those living upon the earth, in the absence of a region established by themselves, there could be no state of being below, nor could there be a state of being horizontal or downward on the terrestrial globe, since one’s own location would be untenable. There is no harm in [the earth] not being stationary, because falling toward another direction—whether downward or horizontal—is impossible. Thus, the notion of "downward" or "horizontal" on the terrestrial globe is merely a mental construction based on an arbitrarily chosen reference point, and not a reality in itself. This is the intended meaning. || 20 ||

Now he states the location of the mountains and oceans: "They say that Jambudvīpa, situated on the earth, extends as far as the salt ocean; in this context, to the south of the six islands, lie the abodes of the oceans of salt water, milk, and so forth. [Verse 23]. This concludes the inquiry into the structure of the world. First is the salt-water ocean, then the ocean of milk, from which nectar, the moon, and Śrī were born.

Where Vāsudeva dwells, whose lotus-like feet are honored by the gods beginning with Brahmā, and who is the abode of all; [therein lies] the base of clarified butter, sugarcane juice, wine, and sweet water, which reaches down to the submarine fire within the sweet waters. These netherworlds (pātāla-lokas) are the cavities of the earth. Within them dwell the hooded serpents along with hosts of asuras, illuminated by the rays from the jewels on their hoods.

And there, the Siddhas, possessing bodies as beautiful as lovely women and shining with the luster of brilliant gold, bestow [their gifts]. (24) Then, there is the Śāka, Śālmalī, Kauśa, and Kautha islands; and Gomedaka and Puṣkara. They declare that between each pair of oceans, there is one island. (25) Maedī0: Now, in response to the question "Of what kind is the island? and so forth, he describes the general division of the terrestrial globe in the Śālinī meter, beginning with the words "Of the earth" (bhūmeḥ).

The most eminent teachers who promulgated the science of astronomy, such as Sūrya and others, have declared—that is, they speak with authority—that Jambudvīpa occupies half of the terrestrial globe, situated on one side of the shore of the salt ocean (kṣārasindhu). By this, it is indicated that Jambudvīpa is established by the Purāṇas as being circular in shape, situated in the middle of the girdle of the salt ocean; likewise, here, from the hemisphere of the globe, it is shown to be encircled by the girdle of the salt ocean. This refers to the other—that is, the second—half of the terrestrial globe.

To the south of Jambudvīpa, situated on the shore of the salt ocean, there exists the location of the six islands and the oceans beginning with the Ocean of Milk; the meaning is that their arrangement is contained within it without overlapping. Thus, it is established that the seven islands and the oceans such as the Salt Ocean exist within the complete terrestrial globe, but do not exist in any region of the terrestrial globe beyond that.

Objection: Since it is not established that the region at the junction of the salt ocean and Jambudvīpa constitutes the center of the earth, the previously stated fact of Laṅkā being at the center of the earth is untenable; for that [center] does not exist on the terrestrial meridian (bhūparidhivṛtta) which forms the junction of the two hemispheres of the terrestrial globe as described. Otherwise, the existence of the Setubandha would be impossible. Nor should it be argued that since the center of the globe can occur anywhere, the two centers of the earth are merely conceptual constructs (kalpanāsat) existing both in Laṅkā situated on the far shore of the salt ocean and at the aforementioned junction. Response: This is not so. For the following reasons: [The text continues with the refutation.]

For this would entail the absurd consequence of denying that Laṅkā is situated at one-fourth of the earth's circumference from the center, which is well-established by ancient tradition as the center of Jambūdvīpa. Nor should it be argued that because of the phrase "of the salt ocean," the entire salt sea is contained within Jambūdvīpa; thus, since Laṅkā exists on the southern shore of the salt ocean where Jambūdvīpa begins, its location at the center is justified, and the existence of the Setubandha (Bridge) is thereby established. This cannot be said, because the presence of the salt ocean on the southern hemisphere is untenable.

[Objection: It may be argued that it is inappropriate for the salt ocean (lavaṇasamudra), which is well-known in the Purāṇas as being distinct from Jambudvīpa, to be considered part of Jambudvīpa. [Response: This is not so. Since Laṅkā is situated at the commencement of Jambudvīpa on the northern shore of the salt ocean, it is logically consistent for it to be the center of the earth. Nor is there any inconsistency regarding the construction of the bridge (setubandha).

Since it is well known in the *Bhāgavata Purāṇa* that the eight subcontinents (*upadvīpa*) of Jambudvīpa were fashioned by the sons of Sagara while they were digging the earth in search of the horse, and since [Laṅkā] is established as being within Jambudvīpa because the flow of the salt ocean reached there through digging in the northern part of Laṅkā—thereby making the construction of the bridge (*setubandha*) logical—it is evident that Laṅkā is a subcontinent due to its connection with the ocean on all sides. By this, [it is shown that] in portions equal to those surrounding the center of Meru, [the divisions of] the ocean [are established].

In the directions starting from the east, there are mountains created by the gods; thus, according to the *Sūryasiddhānta*, the four cities beginning with Aṣṭakapada are situated within the salt ocean, which is established in the midst of the ocean of curds (*dadhimadhya*). This is consistent with what was stated by Āryabhaṭṭa. Some, based on this very statement, say: "Within the circle of the earth's circumference (*jyāpiṇḍa*), there is the Parigha mountain, followed in sequence by the Salt Ocean (*lavaṇārṇava*). Situated like a girdle (*mekhalā*), it divides the realms of the gods and the asuras. Its width is one hundred and thirty *yojanas*."

In the middle of that, at equal intervals, are the four city-gates and archways of heaven; these four cities—Yamakoti, Laṅkā, Romāseddhapura, and Brahmasiddhāntapura—are fashioned by the gods. Regarding the four cities beginning with Laṅkā situated on the trees encircling the middle of the salt ocean, some say that they are located in the northern and southern halves of the terrestrial globe, specifically within Jambudvīpa and the six continents together with the six and a half oceans; however, they claim this is untenable. That is not so.

This is because the status of being an ocean-dweller (*samudradvīpa*) is not accepted [for Laṅkā], as otherwise that status would apply everywhere; and because, by way of illustration, the statement regarding Brahmā’s word refers to the location of salt [beneath the earth]. Furthermore, the phrase "in its midst" also serves to indicate that [Laṅkā] is situated within the salt ocean, which is reached by digging down. Thus, in the *Bhūvṛttapāda* [of the *Varṣabhedatantra*], the rhyme of the preceding verse is clearly heard: "O auspicious one, in the land of Yavabhadravarṣa there is a city with golden walls and arches; likewise, in the southern land of Bhāratavarṣa, there is the great city of Laṅkā."

In the western region called Ketumāla, the city named Romaka is celebrated; in Kuru-varṣa, it is known as Udāsiddhapurī, according to the Sūryasiddhānta. Although our stated reasoning establishes that they possess the status of being "varṣas" (regions) because they are situated on the same meridian, the restriction that they are located within Jambūdvīpa—specifically on the half of the salt ocean bordering the northern Kurus—is intended to exclude those [cities] situated across the ocean.

Precisely because of this absence of a complete salt ocean, the Teacher (Ācārya), disregarding the expression "of the salt oceans" (*kṣārāmbudhīnām*), should have stated "of the salt, milk, and other oceans" (*kṣārakṣīrādyambudhīnām*). This is because it has been stated that the flow of the three salt oceans is like the *jamjhuḍū* [a type of river], and because the inclusion of many [oceans] such as the *urvī* and others is well-known. This is also clear in the *Vṛddhavasiṣṭhasiddhānta*: "From the middle of the earth's circle, to the south, there shall be the Golden Ocean (*suvarṇārṇava*)."

Then the oceans of milk, of *darbha* grass, of clarified butter, of sugarcane juice, of wine (*madya*), and of sweet water (*svādunīra*) arose in succession. Their circumferences increase in order, and they flow respectively. On the northern shore of the salt-water ocean, there are four mountain ranges created by the gods, O best of the twice-born, situated at the center of the earth within that region known as the "Supervisor" (*adhyakṣa*), which marks the division between the gods and the asuras. These are adorned with golden ramparts and eastern gateways.

Great-souled Siddhas, free from all suffering, dwell there. Herein lies the source of light for the entire treasury of beings and worlds. (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 5.1.55) Commentary (Bhāvārthadīpikā): On the eastern side of the circle of Yavadvīpa, Bāṇa [is situated] with the twelve suns of Aṅga. Beyond that, O twice-born one, stands Yamakoṭi, crowded with throngs of human beings. It has been stated that the land of Jambudvīpa extends as far as the salt ocean to the north; however, in the other [direction], the southern part, there are islands beginning with Śaka. Therefore...

The salt ocean lies to the south of those situated on the three axes, while to its north is the Jambū [ocean]; its greatness is clearly stated by Laca—enough of this. Now, desiring to describe the oceans beginning with the salt ocean in sequence for the sake of specifically knowing the arrangement of the islands and oceans, he first speaks of the two oceans in the Mālinī meter, beginning with "Lavaṇa": At the outset, at the commencement of the oceans' placement upon the terrestrial globe, there is first the salt ocean; immediately following that is the milk ocean.

The particle *ca* indicates the location of the region within the interval; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of their identity. He states the proof for its existence with the word "Amṛtam" (the Nectar). From that ocean, the nectar well-known as the food of the gods [was produced]. "Adhṛtarāśmiḥ" refers to the Moon. "Śrī" refers to Lakṣmī. It "became" (*babhūva*). Likewise, by the force of the particle *ca*, the Vaiśravaṇa direction and so forth are included, as stated in the Purāṇa.

It is well known that various substances were extracted from the churning of the Ocean of Milk by the gods using Mount Mandara; therefore, since the moon is perceived in its midst and serves as its evidence, the existence of the Ocean of Milk is established through inference—this is the intended meaning. He states its existence through another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) with the word "in which" (*yatra*): in which ocean Vāsudeva, whose nature is the Supreme Brahman, dwells; and thus, according to the Purāṇas, because that ocean is the abode of the Supreme Lord.

Since [the existence of] the ocean is well-established, scripture (*āgama*) alone is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). The sense is that the *Purāṇas* and other texts are rooted in the Veda. Now, one might object: "Given that he is a human being, and his son likewise, what could be the eternal greatness of the ocean as their dwelling place, such that no doubt would arise regarding its existence? For it is by qualifying him with 'supreme lordship' (*parameśvaratva*) that [the author] establishes this. Thus, he says: "He whose dwelling is in the whole" (*sakalavasas*). This means he whose abode (*vasati-sthāna*) is in the entire world (*jagat*), consisting of both the stationary and the moving.

The meaning is that He alone is the all-pervading Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*). Now, even if that is so, how is it understood that this son of Śuddhadeva is indeed the Supreme Lord? To this, he says: "Mahita" (worshipped). By the gods beginning with Indra—who are worshipped by the learned and who are the foremost among the deities—He is praised as the one whose form is the protector of the world. Thus, He is the first and sole deity.

And the meaning is: "he who possesses [these qualities]. Beyond this, there is no lack of evidence for the existence of the Supreme Lord, who is established as the goal of the Vedas, who is the protector of the virtuous gods, who assumes the form of humans, and who destroys the ancient sins of the gods. The point is that there is no absence of proof regarding the existence of the Supreme Lord. It should not be argued that because He is a being (*bhūta*), His manifestation as the source of the Vedas and so forth is untenable.

Because the body of Your divine play (*līlāvigraha*) is purified by Your lip, it is therefore possible for it to exist in ten different ways through its very attire. By this alone, one should reflect that there is no futility in my composing this garland of verses nor in the reading of another; for [it serves] to destroy dullness. (22) Alternatively, following the sequence of the *Vasiṣṭha* (or *Śiṣṭa*) tradition, he states another specific distinction in the *Indravajrā* meter, beginning with "dama": immediately after that. Each of these is to be connected with the distant location.

By the word "and" (ca), [the author] indicates in the Golādhyāya that there are six oceans—[namely, Ma, 7, 8, 0, Samudraḥ]. By the word "last" (antya), it is indicated that after the ocean of sweet water (Svādūdaka), there is no other ocean. Thus, on the terrestrial globe, the group of oceans beginning with the salt ocean (Lavaṇa) forms a circular band in the southern portion; at the edge is the ocean of sweet water in the shape of an umbrella. This is the meaning: that there are seven oceans.

Now, one might object: "In this way, the presence of the *vaḍavānala* (submarine fire) at the southern extremity of the terrestrial globe facing Mount Meru would be contradicted by the presence of the ocean. To this, he says: "Between the salt water and the sweet water. This aforementioned well-known *vaḍavāgni* is situated in the middle of the *svādūdaka* (sweet-water) ocean. Thus, even though there is a contradiction between salt water and [ordinary] water, the existence of the specific entity called *vaḍavā* within the water is not contradictory; for this very reason, its nature as *vaḍavā* is established by its location within the water—this is the intended meaning.

[Objection: But if this is so, since the arrangement of all the continents and so forth on the earth's surface and the location of the netherworlds (pātālaloka) have not been mentioned, does it not follow that those two are denied? For in the Purāṇas, the existence of seven netherworlds beneath the earth is well-known; and according to that view, space is established as being immeasurable everywhere—above, across, and below the terrestrial globe. To this, he says: "The netherworlds. Those very cavities within the earth, which are hollow and constitute the coverings of the earth's interior, are themselves the seven netherworlds through their internal subdivisions.

The meaning is that it is not a false accusation to say that there exist within the earth, below the surface of the ground, subterranean regions in the shape of spheres—namely Atala, Vitala, Nitala, Gabhastimat, Mahītala, Sutala, and Pātāla. Now, one might object: "It is incorrect to speak of 'Pātālaloka' (the world of Pātāla), because there is no support for the abode of a world in such a location. Indeed, a region cannot possess the status of being a 'world' unless there is movement [of beings] within it. To this, he says "cadhadviti" (holding... in the Vasantatilakā meter: "In these regions of Pātāla... [and so forth].

The serpents headed by Vāsuki, along with the hosts of Asuras—the Daityas and Dānavas—dwell together with their exalted assemblies; that is to say, the serpents and Daityas occupy [these places]. According to the tradition of the Purāṇas, they reside one below the other as is appropriate. Here, by the words "with these" (*ācaya*) and "they dwell in these" (*eteṣu vasanti*), it is meant that in these subterranean hells and heavens, the Daityas and sons of Danu possess even greater sensual enjoyments, sovereignty, and bliss than in heaven itself, such as those found in Suptasṛbhavana, Uñchanaḍa, and other such realms.

The Lord’s authority is indicated by the fact that householders—possessing wives, children, prosperity, friends, and attendants, and ever-joyful and devoted—dwell with unimpeded physical pleasures even beyond the power of lords. Thus, the previously stated [view] that "the nights are short" is logical; this is the intended meaning. Now, one might object: since the sun revolves all around the terrestrial globe, there would be an absence of the characteristic [of day]; and during the time of darkness, when the sun's rays do not reach the netherworld (pātāla), how can the worldly activities of the people dwelling there proceed?

Regarding the existence of the world and its inhabitants, he says "cañcat" and so forth. The meaning is as follows: those whose light—that is, their illumination—is struck by the mass of rays (*kiraṇa*) from the jewels of the *phaṭikamaṇi* (crystal-like gems) that shine intensely; thus, they do not obstruct worldly transactions. This is because it is stated in the *Bhāgavata*: "There, the crest-jewels of the foremost great serpents dispel all darkness. This is the intended sense.

Now, as an incidental discussion, he states that this very place is the secret playground for the Siddhas residing on the summit of Meru with the words *vṛddhyanti* (they increase). In that region of Pātāla, the word *ca* (and) serves to exclude any other connection: by day, due to the intense radiance of Mount Meru, all people can see [the Siddhas], and thus a desire for sexual union arises in the Siddhas. This is the splendor of the *Bhuvanakośa*. (Verse 57, 080)—At that time, they are unable to sport there; however, according to the Purāṇic view, because it is their own domain, it should be understood that this state exists "always."

The *siddhas* are the yogins dwelling on the summit of Meru. By the use of the word "and" (*ca*), [it is implied] the gods (*devas*)—those celestial (*divya*) young women (*ramaṇyas*) born in heaven (*divi*, i.e., *svarge*). Since Meru itself is established as heaven, they are the beloved ones belonging to Meru; those who possess lovely bodies (*ramaṇīyadehas*)—that is, whose forms are charming and delicate—with them [the yogins] play and sport (*dīvyanti krīḍanti*). This is because they have no fear regarding their movement through other worlds that are exceedingly luminous. Now, one might ask: from where does the loveliness of the body derive? To this, he states a qualification of the body: "shining" (*lasat*).

And that gold, shining like fire—that very gold—shines and glitters with such splendor; the meaning is that it possesses the luster of such gold. (24) Now, one might object: "It is not appropriate to first describe the location of the six islands, which were initially introduced by the verse beginning 'In the midst of which [is] the lamp-vessel,' etc., before stating the location of the oceans. To this, he replies in the Upajāti meter: ("Kāñcaneti...")

In this context, they say that on the southern half of the terrestrial globe, there is one island (*dvīpa*) for each of the two oceans; by means of this repetition (*vīpsā*), there is one island between each ocean, thus resulting in six islands from the intervals of the seven oceans. Otherwise, it should be understood that the interval between two oceans separated by another ocean would be too slight.

And thus, since it is impossible to describe the arrangement of the continents without first describing the arrangement of the oceans, the arrangement of the oceans is stated first; this is the underlying sense. He states their names: "Śaka" and so forth. The island situated between the salt-water ocean (Lavaṇoda) and the milk-ocean (Kṣīroda), shaped like a ring, is Jambūdvīpa. Immediately after that, the space between the milk-ocean and the curd-ocean (Dadhyoda) is Śākadvīpa. After that, the space between the curd-ocean and the ghee-ocean (Ghṛtoda) is Kauśadvīpa. The space between the ghee-ocean and the sugarcane-juice ocean (Ikṣurasoda) is Kardamadvīpa. The word "ca" (and) is used for the sake of indicating the sequence.

The region between the oceans of sugarcane juice and wine is known as Gomedaka; the region between the oceans of delicious wine and water is Puṣkaradvīpa. By the use of the word "and" (ca), it is indicated that even though there is no contradiction with what is stated in the Purāṇas, there is no harm in adopting different opinions regarding specific details such as the shape of the earth. In the midst of the oceans of curd and milk, Kuśa and Dadhimaṇḍa [are situated], and likewise Krauñca between the two. Śālmaladvīpa is located between the oceans of sugarcane juice and clarified butter (*sneha*); this is stated by Laghvāryabhaṭṭa. [The oceans consist of] salt, milk, curd, clarified butter, sugarcane juice, honey, and fresh water.

It is surrounded by seven inner islands (antar-dvīpas), namely Śāka, Śālmala, Sāṭha, Kauñca, Gomedaka, Puṣkara, and [the seventh]. This [listing] from the *Laghu-vaśiṣṭha* should be regarded as merely illustrative. As for the measurement of the oceans and islands: "The circles, measured according to the [preceding] abodes, should be rotated by six times their own values; thus, from the ocean of sweet water (Svādūdaka) upwards, the portions [of the islands] are formed by their respective multipliers."

From that [Jambūdvīpa], the measurement of the ocean of salt water (lavaṇodadhi) is by all [the previous] measures; then, in the island named Puṣkara, the ocean of honey (madhvambudhi) is by thirty-two parts of four hundred and four (404); the ocean of sugarcane juice (ikṣvambhonidhi) should be sixty-four parts of forty-six (46); the ocean of wine (sādhunidhi) is joined with fifty-seven and a half parts (57½); the ocean of clarified butter (ghṛtāmbudhi) is sixty-two parts of six and a half (62½); and the ocean of milk (kṣīrārṇava) is measured by fifty-seven and a half degrees (57½).

The five islands beginning with Kuśadvīpa [are situated] at the petals [of the lotus diagram] by means of the numbers 5, 725, and 77. The limit for Śālmali-dvīpa is 71, which is the moon multiplied by its own parts (71). Beyond that, Śaka-dvīpa is by means of the numbers 86, 10, and 30. Pūrṇaka-dvīpa is established by the number 90. In the lower portion, there is the emergence of the earth; it is circular and marked by five degrees. One should write this at the beginning of the chapter on the Sphere (Golādhyāya), verse 80.

First, by the statement "the abode of the Daityas is situated within the ocean," the region of Romaka is to be meditated upon. Now, according to the arrangement of mountains in the center of Jambūdvīpa, he describes the nine divisions: "From the land of Laṅkā, Mount Dhema is to the north; from that, Hemakūṭa; and from that, another is Niṣadha. These are known to extend as far as the ocean. Likewise, to the north of Siddhapura, there are Śṛṅgavān, Śveta, and Nīla. The wise here declare these to be the Varṣas (regions), with the Droṇis (valleys) situated between them. (26)

This is Bhāratavarṣa; beyond it is Hiraṇmaya-varṣa, then Kimpuruṣa-varṣa, and after that Harivarṣa. Know that from Siddhapura lies Kuru, and from there, O wise one, Hiraṇmaya. To the east of Mālyavat and Yamaka-dvipa-pattana is indeed Gandhamādana; and between the Nīla and Niṣadha mountains lies Ilāvṛta, which is as broad as the ocean. That peak situated between Mālyavat and the sea they call Bhadraturaga.

Those who know the divisions of the earth see Ketumāla situated in the midst of a mass of fragrant mountains and waters. It shone, completely surrounded by the Niṣadha, Nīla, Sugandha, Kusumālya, and Ilāvṛta mountains; its ground was variegated with beautiful gold and filled with the nests of flocks of celestial birds at play. Here, the northern half of the terrestrial sphere is Jambudvīpa. The junction of this [continent] and the salt ocean is the region of the equator (the nirakṣadeśa).

In that regard, it is said that there are four cities—Ṭaṅga, Romaka, Siddhapura, and Yamakoṭi—separated by vast intervals of land. To the north of these cities lies Mount Meru, and the other [mountains] are to its south. To the north of Meru is the mountain named Himavat, which extends across the distance between the eastern and western oceans. To the north of that is Hemakūṭa, which likewise reaches to the edge of the ocean. Similarly, to the north of that is Niṣadha. Between them lie the regions known as the Varṣas (climatic zones).

Therein, first is Bhadrāśva; following that is Kimpuruṣavarṣa; and after that is Harivarṣa. Likewise, to the north of Siddhapura is the mountain named Śṛṅgavān; beyond that is Śvetagiri; and beyond that is Nīlagiri. These too extend as far as the Sindhu river. Between them are the regions (varṣas); among them, first is Kuruvarṣa; next is Hiraṇmaya; and after that is Ramyaka. Now, to the north of Yaśaskoti is the mountain named Mālyavat.

But that [mountain] Niṣadha possesses the strength of an elephant in rut. Between it and the ocean lies the region of Bhadrāśva. Thus, to the north of Romaka is Gandhamādana; between it and the ocean lies Ketumāla. Thus, the ninth division, surrounded by Niṣadha, Mālyavat, Gandhamādana, and Airāvata, is named Uttarakuru; it is the land of heaven (*svargabhūmi*). Therefore, there are the dwellings of the gods. This is the eighth [chapter]. 2028||21||10|| Question on the Structure of the World.

59. Ma. Ṭī.—Now, in order to provide an answer to the subordinate question of Kulīndaitya and wishing to state the divisions of the years based on the purification of the *jaṃbu* [continent], he first describes the six regions (*varṣas*) consisting of the divisions of the land in the *mandākrāntā* meter, beginning with "Laṅkā": After describing the locations of the islands, there is the Himagiri (Himalaya) mountain facing Meru in the northern direction from the location of Laṅkā. On the other side of this Himalaya, facing Meru, is Hemakūṭa, another second mountain.

Therefore, on the northern side of Mount Remakūṭa, facing Meru, there is another third mountain, Niṣadha. The word "and" (ca) indicates the region between them; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the three mountains being one. Since the particle "iti" indicates the conclusion [of the topic], it is established that there is no other mountain situated similarly facing Devabhūmi. Now, one might ask: do these mountains exist in space? To this he says: "They... (ta iti).

These mountains—named Himālaya, Chaya, Hemakūṭa, and Niṣadha—are divine, extending as far as the ocean; that is to say, their length reaches up to the shores of the salt ocean on both sides. This is what is meant: the terrestrial globe consists of two parts, each formed by a segment of the circumference passing through Meru, Yamakoṭi, and Romaka, divided by a line drawn through the middle.

There, these three mountains—Laṅkāsaṃdhi, Śaṅkha, and Phala—are the central peaks of Laṅkā, situated on the shore of the salt ocean at the edge of the land where the earth is split open; they are shaped like the curved tips of a bow. One should draw the ocean upwards from the region of Laṅkā for one hundred and fifty *yojanas* using the same proportions. That half-circle should be understood as the land known as Bhārata-varṣa, located between the slopes of the Himālaya and the sea.

Furthermore, by adding six and five [units] along with the female [digits], there is half a *vṛtta* (circle) equal to the Golden Mountain (*Hemakaṭādri*). The intermediate region between these two is called Kiṃnara. Again, by adding one and a half along with the assembly [of digits], and taking half of that, it is equal to the Niṣadha Mountain; the intermediate region between them is the Harivarṣa—thus it is stated by Romaka. Now, he describes the location of the Śakala mountains on another part of Jambudvīpa, beginning with "evam" (thus).

The meaning is "the city of Siddhapura," which is renowned for being situated on half of the *aṭṭaṅka* (peak) of Siddhapura. On its northern side, in the order facing toward Meru, there is a mountain called Śṛṅgavat, consisting of white and blue [peaks]. The word "api" (also/even) is placed separately due to metrical constraints. Thus, it extends as far as the Sindhu river. These [mountains] have the shape of a circle whose apex touches the northern shore of the salt ocean, located on the land-portion produced by three desired semi-diameters from the center of Siddhapura. The measurement of the degrees of their semi-diameters is equal to that of the Himālaya and other [mountains].

Thus, having established the location of Meru, one should divide it into three circular segments by means of these portions; these locations are called Śṛṅga, Śveta, and Nīla, as stated by Romaka. Now, he states the purpose of the arrangement of the mountains with the words "the regions" (varṣāṇi). "Of these"—meaning of the aforementioned salt ocean and mountains—"in the intervals," that is, in the intermediate spaces between two [mountains], there are the "valleys" (droṇis), which are the terrestrial regions situated in the middle as intervening spaces.

The term "regions of the Droṇī" was stated for the sake of designating and knowing the intermediate spaces that serve as the basis for conventional usage. The wise—those such as Vyāsa who know the true nature of the earth's surface—have declared here, regarding each of the two divisions belonging to Jambūdvīpa, their respective *varṣas* (regions). Thus, the land between the ocean and the Himālaya is one *varṣa*; the space between the Himālaya and the Hemakūṭa is the second.

The space between Hemakūṭa and Niṣadha is the third [region], thus making three regions (varṣas) in the portion belonging to the *gaulala* [division]. In the other portion, there is one region consisting of the land between the ocean and Śṛṅgavat; the space between Śṛṅgavat and Śukla is the second; and the space between Śukla and Nīla is the third—thus making three regions. In this way, there are six [regions] in total.

By this, it is indicated that the land situated between the Nīla and Niṣadha mountains, which has the shape of a crescent moon within the mountain range, does not constitute a single *varṣa* (region) with Meru at its center. By the word "Budha" (the wise), the authority of the Purāṇas is indicated; for when the earth is made level by Mount Meru being placed at its center, the Jambudvīpa, which is of the shape of a mirror according to the Purāṇas, arises. (26) Now, he states their names in the *Dadhaka* meter, beginning with "Bhāratavarṣam."

This first [region] is established by us and is directly perceived; for it is certain, meaning that it is established by the authority of the Purāṇas. It is called Bhārata and is increasing. To the north of this Bhārata-varṣa is the third, which is Kiṃnara-varṣa. Thus, to the north of Kiṃnara-varṣa is the third, which is Dhārtī-varṣa. In this way, three regions have been described within the portion of Jambūdvīpa presided over by Śaṅkha. Likewise, it is exactly the same from Siddhapura.

The meaning is that [the first] is the region situated to the north of the ocean of Abhaṭṭa connected with Siddhapura. This was the first mentioned on the portion of Jambūdvīpa presided over by Caṅka. Know—that is, understand—that [the second] is in the region named Kuru. From that Kuru-varṣa, know that the second and third regions, situated respectively to the north and further north, are the regions named Hiraṇmaya and Ramya. 27.

[Objection: "Is it not the case that in the Purāṇa, Jambūdvīpa is said to consist of nine divisions (*vardha*), whereas here you have stated that it consists of six regions (*varṣa*)? Since there is thus a contradiction, how can the authority of the Purāṇa be maintained here? To this, he replies with a *rathoddhatā* verse, beginning with "Mālyavān": From the city of Yamakoṭi—by the word "and" (*ca*), it is implied on the northern side—there is the Mālyavat mountain. [The word] "rogakān" [is used]; the "and" (*ca*) is for the purpose of conjunction. On the northern side is the Gandhamādana mountain. "Kila" indicates traditional report; the meaning is that it is accepted as authoritative by means of the scriptures (*āgama*).

Indeed, by the logic of the previously mentioned method, since that would be simpler, why was it not stated that each of these two mountains—Lahka and Siddhapura—is separated from the eastern mountain [Meru] by a distance of one hundred thousand yojanas? Since they were mentioned separately, he says "mala" etc. These two have Mount Malaya as their limit on the side of the Dharma continent and Mount Nila as their limit on the side of Videha. Here, because the word "mountain" (*śaila*) situated in the middle is connected to both, they are such that they have the Niṣadha and Nīla mountains respectively as their limits.

Due to the word "ca" (and), there is no sequential connection between the two; rather, each one [is connected] with both. First, regarding the effort: in the body, by means of the parts [of the letters], there are the Moon, Logic, and the quarters [of the compass]; within the cloth, there are indeed the lines called the Mountains. From their natural positions, that which is known as Māruta (Wind) would belong to the other, and that called Gandha (Fragrance) would likewise apply to these.

The distribution is by means of two sets of degrees. From the shore of the ocean adjacent to Romaka, facing Mount Meru, at an interval of fifty-nine and three-quarter degrees (59 3/4°) between the Niṣadha and Nīla mountains lies the Mālyavat mountain. Likewise, from the shore of the ocean adjacent to Romaka, facing Meru, at that same interval of degrees, at a distance equal to the space between the Niṣadha and Nīla regions, lies the Gandhamādana mountain; this is the meaning. Thus, the intention is that there is no separate description of the shape and nature of these mountains, as they have already been stated previously.

[Objection: But how is the authority of the Purāṇa established here by means of the two mountains? For it is not from those two that the establishment of a continent (varga) distinct from the six [already mentioned] follows, such that there would be a question regarding the "sheath of the worlds" (bhuvana-kośa) consisting of seven. To this, the author says: "The intermediate space" (antarālam). This refers to the interval between these two, Mālyavat and Gandhamādana. Is it not a portion of the earth, situated in the middle of Meru, known as Ilāvṛta? And thus, through the establishment of a continent distinct from the six, the authority [of the Purāṇa] is indeed established; this is the intended meaning. || 28 ||

Now, one might ask: even so, how can its authority be established here by means of proving [the existence of] nine regions? To this, he says in the *Rathoddhatā* meter: "And Mālyavat... The wise—the experts in Purāṇas and geographers—declare that the region situated between the Mālyavat mountain and a portion of the Salt Ocean (Lavaṇasamudra), located at the junction of those two fragments and forming the interval between the Nīla and Niṣadha mountains, is the region of Bhadrāśva. The word "tu" (and) [indicates this].

Because the name [Gandhamādana] is taken as a part of the word *gandhaśabda*, it refers to Gandhamādana; that is the mountain. Between the two oceans—the Ocean of Salt (*lavaṇasamudra*) and the Ocean of Water (*jaladhi*)—there exists a land-fragment situated at the junction of two halves, which has the form of the space between the two mountains [Himālaya and Śrīparvata]. "Those who know the *ilākalā* (the science of the earth's divisions) and are experts in the subtle reasoning concerning the terrestrial globe declared this region to be the *varṣa* named Ketumāla. Thus, by the presentation here of the nine *varṣas* as intended in the Purāṇas, the authority of the Purāṇas is established by its own nature; such is the meaning.

29 || Now, it might be argued that the presentation of Ilāvṛta as being situated between the Mālyavat and Gandhamādana mountains is incorrect, because it also exists within the space between those two mountains and the Niṣadha mountain. To clarify this, he explains Ilāvṛta in the *Vilambita* meter: "Niṣadha... and so on. *Niṣadha* and *Nīla* are well-known [mountains]. *Sugandha* is *Gandhamādana*.

The region of Ilāvṛta, which has a surrounding enclosure formed by four mountains named Mālyavat situated in the four directions, shone exceedingly—meaning it was most beautiful. Although the action is occurring in the present, the use of the past tense (the root *bhā*) is appropriate because of its connection to a past time.

Likewise, if it were stated that Ilāvṛta is situated between the Niṣadha and Hemakūṭa mountains alone, then it would follow that Bhadrāśva and Ketumāla are also situated within Ilāvṛta; to prevent this, it is necessary to state that Ilāvṛta is situated between Gandhamādana and Mālyavat as well. Therefore, for the sake of brevity, it is proper to state that Ilāvṛta is situated between those two [Gandhamādana and Mālyavat] alone, since its establishment is achieved by that very statement. This is clear. The sense is that Ilāvṛta is established as being bounded by four mountains. Now, one might ask: "What is the beauty of Ilāvṛta in being enclosed? To this, he says: "Amara... (referring to the verse beginning with *amara*).

It is filled—that is, pervaded—by the nests, meaning the dwellings, of the immortal gods for the sake of their private sport. Thus, the sense is that while the splendor of Ilāvṛta shines forth from the mass of light emanating from houses constructed of various jewels, gold, and other materials, its beauty is inherent to it of its own accord. Now, one might ask: "Why were such houses built there by the gods, and why were they not built elsewhere? To this, he says: "Rucira... (beautiful...).

It was covered with *śamī* trees, a region of the earth adorned with that beautiful, shining gold. Furthermore, since it is impossible for houses to be made of gold in any other continent, and because it is possible for them to possess even greater splendor by being constructed from a collection of various jewels, and because they provide seclusion due to being enclosed, the implication is that the houses were built here alone. || 30 ||

Now he describes the configuration of Mount Meru: "In this world, Mount Meru is indeed situated in the center, composed of liquid gold, and is the abode of the thirty gods; those who know the Purāṇas have described it as the pericarp of the lotus that is the birthplace of Brahmā. (31) "The supporting mountains are indeed Mandara, Sugandha, Vipula, and Supārśva; and upon them stand, respectively, the banner-trees known as Kadamba, Jambu, Vaṭa, and Pippala. (32)

From the juice of the *jambū* fruit and the *āmalaka* tree, the river Jambū flowed forth; that juice, having become solidified, turned into gold. Because of this, the hosts of gods and *siddhas*, who were devoted to drinking the nectar of immortality, constantly polished it, and thus it became known as *jāmbūnada*. Likewise, there is the wonderful Caitraratha forest, which delights the Apsarases, and the Vaibhrāja forest, which is renowned for its splendor and provides steadfastness and other virtues to the gods. Furthermore, there are these lakes in due order: Aruṇa, Mānasa, Mahāhrada, and Śvetajala.

In the lakes, the gods, languid from the fatigue of sporting with their consorts and longing for water-sports, take their delight. (35) On Mount Meru are three peaks made of gold; upon them are the cities of the enemies of the cities of Murāri and Purāri. Beneath those [three peaks] are the cities of Śatakratu, Jvalana, Antaka, and the eight cities of Rakṣas, Ambu, Vāyu, Anila, Śaśin, and Īśa. (36) In the center of that very enclosure stands Mount Meru, made of gold, shaped like a pericarp; it is the abode of the gods. Upon its summit are three peaks.

Upon those peaks are the cities of Murāri, Balarāma, and Purāri (Śiva). Beneath the peaks, on all sides, are the cities of the world-protectors, Indra and the others. Now, the supporting mountains of Meru are the Aśvakarṇa mountains. In whichever direction Yamakoṭi is located, starting from that direction, there are Mandara, Sugandha, Viśāla, and Supārśva in the various quarters. On Mandara is the Kadamba tree as the banner-tree, the Caitraratha forest, and the Aruṇoda lake. On the summit of the Sugandha mountain is the Jambu tree as the banner-tree.

By which this [continent] is called Jambūdvīpa; [there is] the Nandana grove, the Mānasa lake; on the peak of Vipuṭaśaila is the banner-tree, the banyan tree (vaṭa), the Dhṛti grove, and the Mahāhṛda lake; on the peak of Supārśva is the banner-tree, the Pippala tree, the Vaibhrāja grove, and the Vetoda lake. The rest is easy to understand. ||3132 || 33 || 34 || 35 || 36 ||

Ma0-60: [Objection: Since the gods dwell in heaven (*svar*), it is not heard that they reside on the earth; how, then, can their houses be possible here? To this, he says "iha" in the *Drutavilambita* meter: "Here"—that is, in the region of Ilāvṛta—"kila," meaning certainly; "hi," because Mount Meru is situated at the central center. Therefore, the sense is that the residence of the gods on the earth is not contradictory. [Objection: What is the proof for its location in Ilāvṛta? To this, he says: "consisting of gold and jewels."

Likewise, the inference of a highly symmetrical (*aticaturasra*) and compact conjunction based on its being covered by clouds and its golden nature is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). The intended meaning is that "the fit [is established] for the fit. Now, one might ask: even so, since Meru is stationary, how is the stationing of the gods established? To this he says: "The abode of the thirty" (*tridaśālaya*). Those who always possess the third stage (*daśā*), namely youth, are the *tridaśas*. According to the lexicon *Bhuvanakośabhāṣya*, "the thirty" (*tridaśa*) refers to the wise ones, the gods. They are the gods; their abode (*ālaya*) is in the form of a mountain (*giri*).

And thus, by way of establishing their residence on Meru, the sense is that for those who have gone to the wrong destination (*icchāgati*), there is no "hellish" state. Furthermore, even in that case, it is not contradictory for them to be considered inhabitants of heaven (*svarvāsin*); for even though they reside there, the *Bhāgavata Purāṇa* states that only the land of Bhārata is the field of karma, while the other six lands are terrestrial "heavenly stations" (*svargapada*) designated as places for the enjoyment of the remaining merit of those who dwell in heaven. Now, regarding their residence among the gods...

Even in the absence of a subverting proof (*bādhaka*), since one observes connections that are impossible, unfit, or improper, the inference establishing its existence there—apart from the Purāṇas—is not established; therefore, its existence there is without proof. With this intention, [the author], intending to show that the Purāṇas alone are the authority here, composes a description of Mount Meru as told in the Purāṇas, which is an object of his own indifference, beginning with the word "hiṇa. Those who know the Purāṇas are Vyāsa and others. "Amum" refers to Mount Meru. "The pericarp of the lotus that is the birth-place of Hiṇa": from which the birth or origin of Hiṇa (Brahmā) arises.

That is the lotus from Viṣṇu’s navel; that is its form. It is the lotus of the earth; the meaning is that she is born from it, or belongs to it. That which is well-known as the pericarp—situated within the interior of the lotus, yellow in color, and surrounded by filaments—is here [referred to] as "born of Brahmā" (*duhiṇajanmā*) for the purpose of describing, up to the limit of Brahmā’s dwelling on the summit of Meru. Thus, the term is applied by force of poetic convention.

And likewise, just as Brahmā resides upon the lotus from Viṣṇu’s navel at the time of creation, so too at the time of manifestation is Brahmā established upon the pericarp of the Earth-lotus; thus it is described by way of its being the pericarp (*karṇikā*). By the use of the word "and" (*ca*), [it is implied that] Kuraṅga, Kurara, Kusumbha, Vaikaṅkata, Trikūṭa, Śiśira, Pataṅgarucaka, Niṣadha, Asita, Vāsaka, Pāla, Śaṅkha, Vaiḍūryaja, Adhihaṃsa, Ṛṣabha, Nāgaka, Haṃsakara, Nārada, and others surround Mount Meru like filaments, just as they are situated around the pericarp.

"By nature" means that, according to the *Bhāgavata*, it has filaments and a pericarp; thus they described it. (31) Now, one might object: "Since the base of Meru’s pericarp-like form and its bark are crushed by the weight [of the world], would it not have collapsed? To this, he states another specific feature with the word "Viṣkambha": "Khalu" means certainly. "Of this" refers to Meru. "Viṣkambha mountains" are the supporting mountains; the ellipsis is that they exist in the four directions.

To answer the question "Which are they?", he says: "Bhāndara," and so forth. In the eastern direction is Bhāndara, the Sugandha mountain, distinct from the previously mentioned Gandhamādana mountain; in the south is Vipula; and in the north is Supārśva. Now, regarding these mountains, he describes the banner-trees (*dhvajavṛkṣa*) that serve as indicators of their mutual distinction: "On them," etc. On these foundational mountains, there are banner-trees—namely, those called Kadamba, Jambū, Vaṭa, and Pippala—situated according to the sequence associated with Mandara and the others.

The word "and" (*ca*) implies that there are others as well, such as Āsra and so forth. Thus it is stated in the *Vyāsasiddhānta*: "The Viṣkambha mountains, extending for ten thousand yojanas and rising high, are situated: Mandara by name to the east, Gandhamādana to the south, Vipula on the western side, and Supārśva located in the north. Upon these are the Kadamba, Jambū, Vaṭa, and Pippala; these trees, eleven hundred [yojanas] in height, serve as the banners of the mountains. It might be argued as follows:

Why is Ilāvṛta alone a land of gold? To answer this, [the author] states in the Golādhyāya (verse 64) using the Vasantatilaka meter: "The great, well-ripened fruits of the massive Jambū tree—[from] their pure, clear, flowing juice that falls down, the river Jambūnadī arose by becoming one with it. [The earth] became gold. The meaning is: the soil belonging to the land of Ilāvṛta-varṣa, being joined with the juice—that is, joined with the juice of the river—became gold.
To the question, "How is this known?", he says: "Jāmbūnada. For it is because of its expansion that it is called *suvarṇa* (gold); this is well-known in the treatise named *Jāmbūnada*.

And thus, by the etymology "jāmbūnada" [meaning "born from the Jambū river"], since it is possible for those jambū fruits of immense size to fall here and there everywhere in that very place, the ground produced from that substance—which exists all around it—is golden, like a pool of liquid essence; therefore, it is logical that it was previously described as having a beautiful, variegated earth of gold. Consequently, because this tree excels all others, the sense is that this continent is named after it.

For this very reason, he says "from this" (*ataḥ*) to explain that the gods drink that juice. The meaning is: because of contact with that juice, gold—which is a transformation of clay—is known; [thus] the host of *suras* and *siddhas* [drinks it]. "Eternally" (*śaśvat*) means constantly. They drink that pure juice of the *jambū* fruit. Now, one might ask: since nectar (*amṛta*) alone is the supreme and wholesome food for them, why do they drink this? To this he replies: "those who have turned their backs on drinking nectar."

The meaning is that, thinking "by drinking this juice our bodies become gold itself," they develop conviction; considering it superior even to nectar (*amṛta*) in its flavor, they become devoid of desire for drinking nectar. And so it is stated in the *Vyāsasiddhānta*: "O Great Sage, that [river] is the cause of the name 'Jambūdvīpa. Indeed, the fruits of that Jambū tree are the size of great elephants; falling upon the mountain in their entirety on the sixth day, they shatter completely."

From their essence, a river there known as the Jambūnadī indeed flows; it is also drunk by the inhabitants here. Among those beings whose minds are healthy from drinking that [juice], there arises neither hunger nor foul odor, nor old age, nor the decay of the senses. Having reached the bank, the juice of the *jambu* fruit, dried by the pleasant wind, becomes the gold known as *jāmbūnada*, the ornament of the perfected ones (*siddhas*). (33)

Now, regarding the forests situated within the trees, he speaks of the forests using the *upajāti* meter, beginning with "ghabhām": On those *ādhāra-parvatas*, there is a forest well-known from the collection of *purāṇas* and understood by all; it is a garden (*udyāna*). Indeed, it exists as a refuge for various trees in sequence. Among them, on Mount Mandara, there is the inexhaustible grove named Caitraratha. On the *ādhāra-parvata* called Gandhamādana, located in the southern region, there is the Nandana, the delight of the immortals (*asura*).

It is called "Apsaronandana" because it delights the celestial nymphs (*apsaras*) through secret amorous pastimes, glances, and the like; the meaning is that there is a grove (*udyāna*) by that name. By the use of the word "and" (*ca*), the sense is that there are also various other groves. It is a forest situated on the slopes of the vast mountain. Now, one might ask: "Are there not four divine gardens?"

Regarding the statement by the Blessed One that [the groves] are Nandana, Caitraratha, Vaibhrājaka, and Sarvatobhadra, and that this dense [grove] presided over by Him is called Sarvatobhadra, one might ask how it is designated as "Dhṛti" (Support). To this he says: "Yat" (That which...). If Nandana, known as Sarvatobhadra, provides support (*dhṛti*) for the gods, then likewise, when this [grove] is destroyed, there arises for the gods—who are intent on flight and terrified by the calamities caused by the Daityas—a question regarding the very existence of the worlds.

35. [Commentary on Bhāṣya-ṭīkā]: By the etymological derivation "that in which there is *bhadram* (welfare/auspiciousness)," the name *Dhṛti* is understood; the sense is that because I abide there with that [name], it was called by me *Dhṛti*. At Supārśva is the one named Vaibhrāja. It is radiant (*bhrājiṣṇu*), shining with various cries produced by many birds such as peacocks, swans, parrots, mainas, and cuckoos. This is because it is stated [in the scriptures] that Caitraratha, Nandanaka, Dhṛti, and Vaibhrāja are the forests in sequence. || 34 ||

Indeed, the forests and the lakes do not shine without the *sarasa* tree; thus he says by way of the *vaṃśastha* meter: "In these forests, there are lakes and ponds," meaning that within these groves there exist, in the order previously mentioned, ponds such as Aruṇa and the rest. By the use of the word "and" (*ca*), the sense is that other [ponds] also exist. As proof for their existence, he cites the Purāṇa as authority, stating "in the lakes" (*saraḥsu*), because they serve as places for the Lord’s water-sports.

"O God, they sport in the aforementioned lakes," meaning they are performing water-sports. To the question "Why do they perform water-sports?", he says: "Eager for water-play. This means their hearts are intent upon various kinds of water-sports, such as splashing one another with drops of water and immersing themselves in the water; they desire these things. To the question "Whence comes this desire?", he says: "Exhausted by the fatigue of sporting with Rāma."

"Rāmāḥ" refers to one's own wives; "with them" means together with those women. "Ramaṇa" refers to dalliance, play, sexual union, and so forth. One becomes "lazy" (ālasya) due to that—that is, incapable of engaging in other activities. The removal of that [laziness] occurs through water-sports, and thus a desire for such arises. Furthermore, the *Bhāgavata* is the authority here for the sense that those in the assembly of the immortals—leaders of the hosts of celestial nymphs whose greatness is sung by the groups of subordinate deities—indeed sport there. || 35 ||

Now, for the sake of further clarification regarding what was previously stated—that the hosts of *Suras* and *Siddhas* reside on Meru—the *Vasantatilakā* verse elucidates this common description in detail, beginning with "sadratna": The first peak is composed of excellent jewels and gold, fashioned from fine gems and gold. By the use of the word "and" (*ca*), it is implied that there are other peaks as well; for this very reason, it is called "Ratnasānu" (the Jewel-Peak). Upon those peaks are the cities of the enemies of Mura (Viṣṇu) and the enemies of Ripu (Śiva).

On one peak is the city named Vaikuṇṭha belonging to Viṣṇu; on the second peak is the city named Śātakumbha belonging to Brahmā; and on the third peak is the city known as Śivaloka. Beneath those cities of the liberated, on Mount Meru and in the eight directions surrounding it, there are eight cities. He states their names beginning with "Śatamasa": in the eastern quarter is Indra’s city, Amarāvatī; in the south-eastern quarter is the city of Vahni (Agni) named Tejovatī.

In the south-eastern quarter is Saṃyaminī, the city of Yama. In the south-western quarter are the dark-complexioned women of the Rākṣasa. In the southern and western quarters is Śraddhavatī, belonging to Varuṇa. In the north-western quarter is Gandhavatī, belonging to Vāyu. In the northern quarter is Mahadayā, belonging to Śaśin—that is, Soma or Kubera; this is well-known in the Vedas through the term *samapada*. In the north-eastern quarter is Yaśovatī, the city of Īśa, a specific manifestation of Maheśvara.

The summarized meaning is that there are cities of the eight guardians of the quarters (dikpālas) beneath that [Meru], each in its own direction. The meaning is that the Siddhas reside in the middle portion of the peak. In that chapter on the Sphere (Golādhyāya), he states another particularity: "The Viṣṇupadī, having fallen from the foot of Viṣṇu upon Meru, divides into four streams here; having reached the lakes situated on the summits of the supporting mountains (viṣkambhācala), it arrives through the sky. The Sītā flows to Bhadrāśva, and the Sālakanandā to the land of Bhārata. (37) [38]

Cakṣus went to Ketumāla, and she known as Bhadrā went to the Northern Kurus. (38) She who is heard of, desired, seen, touched, plunged into, drunk, spoken of, remembered, or praised—she purifies even sinful men in many ways. (39) When she moves, the entire multitude of bonds is shattered; when she goes, the host of [demons] leaps away. When her shore is reached by a man, the messenger of Death being conquered, he goes from hell to the world of the gods. (40)

Even as he begins the effort, thinking, "I am going to the Gaṅgā," the servants of Yama do not bind his ancestors who reside in hell. Then, as he proceeds along the path, those ancestors leap for joy, thinking, "Our son is going to the Gaṅgā; therefore, through the destruction of our evil karma, we shall attain an upward rebirth. They approach him with delight. Then, when he has reached the bank and his own son stands upon the edge of the Gaṅgā, they abandon their bodies through blows such as fist-strikes and go to the world of the gods.

The meaning is: "What other [rivers] are there compared to such a Gaṅgā, the Mandākinī? The rest is clear. ||3738||39||40|| Ma 780—Now, as an incidental topic, [the author speaks] of those bees who were formerly intoxicated by the powerful nectar of the Lord’s lotus feet, which had come to mind through remembrance.

In order to fulfill his own purpose through the renown of his birth, scholarship, and eloquence, and for the sake of performing auspicious rites (*maṅgalācaraṇa*) to ward off obstacles that might hinder the completion and widespread circulation of this work, the author first speaks with affection of the Gaṅgā on the foundational mountains, saying: "Viṣṇupadī. Viṣṇupadī refers to the Gaṅgā, which belongs to Viṣṇu—the one who dwells in Vaikuṇṭha, situated upon the four-faced [Brahmā]—and whose "pada" (foot) is his lotus-like foot. [She flows] from Viṣṇu’s foot.

From the foot of Viṣṇu, who is clad in yellow garments, [the river] fell in the form of a stream upon the summit of Mount Meru, in the midst of the celestial sphere. From that Mount Meru, she divided herself fourfold, manifesting her own self as four distinct streams, since it is possible for a flow of water to exist in multiple forms across various levels. Having come through the ether via a flash of lightning, she joined and merged with the lakes of Maṅgala, Ruṇā, and others situated on the upper regions of the supporting mountains.

As for the claim that the sky is the "footstep of Viṣṇu" (viṣṇupada) and that the Mandākinī is situated there in that sky—this is not so; for it is inconsistent with the context of the preceding and following passages. Furthermore, one who, without cause, denies the reality associated with the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara) is liable to be disregarded by all people. Now, as if to establish the splendor of Jambūdvīpa, [the author] describes how she has come from all sides to Jambūdvīpa by way of her movement: "She flows. She is the Gaṅgā, whose majesty is proclaimed in the Purāṇas and other scriptures.

[The river] named Sītā, flowing from the eastern side of Meru in the form of a stream, purifies the region of Ilāvṛta situated on the eastern part of Meru and proceeds toward the Varṣa of Bhadrāśva; having reached that path, it flows through the piercing of mountains and so forth, and enters the Salt Ocean (Lavaṇasamudra). The Gaṅgā, flowing from the southern side of Meru, is called Alakanandā due to its confluence with the waters of Lake Mānasa.

The Bhārata-varṣa meets the ocean by way of our own Bhārata-varṣa; the word "and" (ca) implies that it floods the regions of Ilāvṛta, Harivarṣa, and Kiṃnaravarṣa situated in the southern portion. The Gaṅgā, flowing through the western portion, reaches the ocean by way of the Mahāhrada known as Cakṣus, which is connected to Ketumāla; the word "and" (ca) implies the region of Ilāvṛta situated in the eastern portion. By that path, she has gone to the sea.

The river named Bhadrā, which consists of a portion of the Aśmaka region in the northern flow and is joined with white water, flows from the vicinity of Meru toward the northern regions known as the Kurus; the meaning is that she has gone to the ocean. By the plural "Kurūs," it is meant that she follows the path through the northern regions of Uttarakuru, Hiraṇmaya-kuru, and so forth. (38) Now, he describes her majesty, which was indicated by the word "she" (sā), beginning with "yā": "yā" refers to that Gaṅgā who is the nectar of the lotus-feet of Viṣṇu, and who has been heard of [as such] in the scriptures.

Desired: made the object of longing. This applies individually to each [verb]. Seen: gazed upon with reverence by both eyes. Touched: made the object of contact by a portion of the body. Immersed: made the object of churning water with all the limbs of the body. Drunk: made the object of the sense of taste through the drinking of water. Swallowed: drawn in by the palate and the lips. Remembered: made the object of meditation.

Praised—that is, made the object of descriptions of her various essential forms—in many ways and manifoldly; she purifies—meaning she makes exceedingly pure by means of the removal of sin—in people who are sinners, that is, those human beings who have committed great sins (mahāpātaka) or minor sins (upapātaka). By the use of the word "api" (even), the meaning is that she purifies even those sinful humans who are ineligible for ordinary expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*). Once purity has been established, union with the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara-sāyujya*) follows as a matter of course. What wonder, then, regarding those of virtuous deeds?

Here, it is indicated that, according to the sequence of the *ākāṅkṣā* (expectancy) and *yukti* (logical connection), what was stated previously serves as the basis for what follows; for example, the desire to hear arises after hearing, and the desire to see arises after that, and so forth. Now, by means of *śleṣa* (paronomasia), there is a further erotic meaning: she who is the beloved, whose face surpasses the full autumnal moon—the object of comparison—and who is exceedingly beautiful in many ways, [is sought] by sinful men who are full of passion and desirous of love.

It purifies; that is to say, it quickly dispels the suffering produced by the fire of separation from her. (39) Now, he describes another supreme greatness in the *dodhakā* meter, beginning with "yām" (her). Regarding "nare": among men. "Yām": when one makes the resolve, "I shall go," toward Gaṅgā—that is, when one begins the undertaking—then "tatpitṛsaṃghaḥ": the assembly of the ancestors of that man who has made the resolve. The term "assembly" (*saṃgha*) is used to include his own father, grandfather, great-grandfather, and so forth, as well as his mother, grandmother, and other female ancestors, and his father-in-law and others.

"O friend of the downtrodden! He by whom all the downtrodden have been crushed—by him the nooses bound by the messengers of Yama for his ancestors are severed. By this opening verse (64), it is indicated that sin results from binding them again after they have been liberated. When one proceeds along the path of the Ganges, the assembly of one's ancestors leaps for joy; because our evil deeds have been severed, they go from here to the world of the gods (*sura*). [Note: The text contains several scribal errors and archaic phrasing. The translation provided above interprets the core meaning based on the context of *gaṅgāmāhātmya* literature, where bathing in the Ganges releases ancestors from hell. The phrase "mārgasaṃlale" is interpreted as "on the path [of the Ganges]," and "sur" is taken as the destination, the celestial realm.]

Thinking that the world is his refuge and support, he rejoices. By this, it is indicated that there is even greater sin in turning back from the path, for they will once again experience that suffering.
