Having reached the bank—having reached the banks of the Gaṅgā—in such a noble family, one who has conquered and humiliated the messengers of Antaka (Yama) by means of the power of the Gaṅgā through blows with the fists and so forth; such a host of ancestors goes toward the surface of the earth from the depths of hell, the world of the nether regions.

It is also indicated that the fruit resulting from bathing and other such acts is indescribable. Now, he describes the nine divisions and seven principal mountain ranges within Bhārata as well: "The divisions [of Bhārata] are indeed Aindra, Kaśeru, Tāmraparṇa, Gabhastimat, Ilāvṛta, and that called Kuṅkumārika; then Nāga, Saumya, Vāruṇa, and another division known as Gāndharva—these are within the land of Bhārata. (41)

The establishment of the castes (*varṇa*) occurs only here in the land called Kumārikā; in all other remaining regions, people of mixed origin reside. Māhendra, Śukla, Malaya, Jambūmārga, Pāripātra, Sahya, and Vindhya—these are the seven mountains known as the Kulācalas (Principal Ranges) located here. [42] This is clear. [41, 42] *Bhāṣāṭīkā*: Now, he describes the nine divisions (*khaṇḍas*) of Bhāratavarṣa with the *Vasantatilaka* meter, beginning with "Aindram. "Here" means within our own governed Bhāratavarṣa, specifically in the region situated between the northern shore of the salt ocean and the Himālaya mountains.

Indeed; certainly. According to the sequence thus stated, there are transverse regions extending from the northern region facing Yamakoṭi up to the western part of the Himālayas facing Romaka. Among these, the first is the Aindra region; the second is the Kaśeru region; the third is the Tāmraparṇa region; immediately after that, the fourth is the Gabhastimat region; and by the use of the word "ca" (and), the fifth, Kumārikā region, follows immediately after this.

By the word "and" (ca), he indicates that there is a sixth division beyond Mālyavat, namely Nagakhaṇḍa. Immediately following is the seventh division, Saumya. After that is the eighth, Varuṇa. In the final region, the ninth division is named Gandharva. By this, it is indicated that there is no tenth division. Thus it is stated in the *Vyāsasiddhānta*: "Listen to the nine divisions of this continent of Bhārata: Indradvīpa, Kaśeru, Tāmraparṇa, Gabhastimān, Nāgadvīpa, Saumya, and Gandharva."

"But this ninth among them is the island surrounded by the ocean"—this is the question regarding the *vāruṇa* [region] within the *bhuvanakośa*. Regarding the objection: "Since the sequence *gandharva*, *vāruṇa*, and *aindra* is seen in this statement, how is the order stated by the Teacher (*ācārya*) consistent?"—it should not be said so. For it is stated by Vṛddhavasiṣṭha: "The regions known as *aindra*, *kairasa*, *tāmraparṇī*, *gabhastimat*, *kumārikā*, *nāga*, *saumya*, *varuṇa*, and *gandharva*—these nine are to be known, O Bhārata."

Here, because the eastward and westward flows of the ocean from the land of Laṅkā take the form of south and north respectively, the Kumārikā-khaṇḍa touches the oceans in the directions starting from the east; therefore, it is called an island (*dvīpa*). The others are also islands because they touch the ocean on their southern sides. Because Varuṇa is the lord of the western direction, [the western region] is called Varuṇamanta. In this region named Bhārata, between the junction of the Himālaya mountains and the salt ocean, there are thirteen and a half [yojanas].

One part should be given at the ocean-mark; there, three more marks should be made. On the mountain, one part (1/7) should be assigned. In the middle, one should place a line-mark; from this point, two segments are likewise established. Again, having made a mark at the twenty-ninth position on the line reaching Laṅkā, [one proceeds] with seven and forty-seven (47) parts. From that mountain, the final mark should thus be made by means of the two conjunctions.

The work should be performed with the mountain [7] and the portions of the earth [16]; by those two, the section should be divided by the cord itself. Thus, there are sections numbering four [4], and further, at the mark, it should be extended toward that mountain. With the portions [9] numbering six and a half [26], likewise afterwards, two separate [sections] from the three [3]. For the purpose of maintaining the cord, there shall be exactly three intermediate sections; thus, the number of marks therein shall be as follows.

One should mark their names preceded by these [words]: *sa-bhya-kṛttikā-dīni* (the asterisms beginning with Kṛttikā). In the center is the fruit of the maiden (*kumārī-śaphalam*); likewise, that which is called Aindra is in the east; the leaf of the foot of Agni is in the direction of fire (southeast); Gabhasti is situated in the south; Vāruṇa is in the west, and the leaf of the Gandharva of the Rakṣas is in the west.

One should draw the leaf of Nārada in the northwest (vāyavya) direction, which is very gentle (saumyasaumya), and likewise the Kaśeru in the northeast (aiśa); this is stated by Roma as yielding auspicious and inauspicious results for the purpose of determining the *aṃśas*, but it should not be thought of as being situated in a real, physical wheel (*vicakra*). This arrangement is merely for the sake of visualization. (41) Now, he describes the world-habitats (*lokavasati*), the nine divisions (*navakhaṇḍa*), the makers (*kāraka*), and the kulaparvatas in the Vasantatilakā meter, beginning with the word "varṇāti": "In this Bharatavarṣa, in that fifth middle division which is Kumārikākhaṇḍa... [and so on].

The particle *eva* serves to exclude other possible associations (*anyayogavyavaccheda*). The "establishment" (*vyavasthiti*) refers to the fixed order of the castes (*varṇas*), namely the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras. Regarding the "remaining" [regions], that is, in the regions of Aṃvārita and Khaṇḍa, all other people such as the Caṇḍālas and so forth dwell, being distinct from the established order of the castes. By the use of the word "and" (*ca*), it is indicated that there are certain Yavanas and others in the region of Kumārikā-khaṇḍa. Here in Bhāratavarṣa, there are seven principal mountain ranges (*kulācalas*): five beginning with Mahendra, and [two others].

In that regard, there is one mountain called Kakṣaka and one called Pāriyātra; the sixth is the Sahya mountain. Together with the seventh, the Vindhya, they are enumerated as such. As stated in the Vyāsasiddhānta: "Mahendra, Malaya, Sahya, Śuktimat, Kakṣaparvata, Vindhya, and Pāriyātra—these seven are the principal mountain ranges (kulaparvatas) here. Also: "Māhendra, Śukti, Malaya, Kakṣaka, and Pāriyātraka..."

Furthermore, according to the established doctrine of Vṛddhavasiṣṭha, "The Vindhya mountain here is the southern slope, and there are seven principal mountain ranges. It should be understood that by means of the Vindhya-Kumari-khaṇḍa alone, the lines forming the divisions do not extend as far as the two currents flowing into the ocean.

In this chapter on the sphere (*golādhyāya*), the description of rivers, mountains, and other regions, as well as the arrangement of the worlds in other continents and the arrangement of the six islands (*dvīpa*) and so forth, has not been stated by the Ācārya due to fear of prolixity and because they are not relevant to the present subject; these are to be understood from the Purāṇas and similar sources. Now, he describes the arrangement of the worlds: "In the terrestrial world (*bhūlaka*), there is the equatorial region (*vyakṣadaśā*); beyond that is this northern part of the earth (*bhuvaḥ*), and then the heavenly world (*svaḥ*) and Mount Meru."

This great splendor in the sky is attainable through merits by people who have performed very great austerities, truthfulness, and other virtues. (43) What has been stated here is all based upon the Purāṇas. Now he describes the arrangement of the directions: When there is sunrise at Saṅkapura, it is midday at Yamakoṭipuri; at that same time, it is sunset at Siddhapura below, and midnight at Romaka. (44)

Where the sun rises is indeed the East, and where it sets is the West; from that point [the equator], Meru is established as being situated above all others, like a fish. (45) Ma0bī0: Now, under the guise of describing the seven worlds, he provides a conclusion in the Śālinī meter, beginning with "bhūśca" (and the earth). From the equatorial region (nirakṣa-deśa), starting from the northern shore of the salt ocean up to the south—on the "earth-tortoise" (bhūgodha)—from that [point].

Beginning from the northern shore of the ocean, forest, and desert located at the line of no latitude (the equator), this [region] is the northern land-mass. This terrestrial world consisting of Jambūdvīpa is Bhuvarloka. Meru is Svarloka. The word "ca" (and) serves to exclude the notion of Svarloka as established in other Purāṇas; for since the Purāṇas state that Meru is the abode of the gods, there is no evidence for postulating anything else besides it. Bhuvarloka is situated in the southern cup-like cavity known as water, while Bhūrloka is situated in Jambūdvīpa to the north of the line of no latitude.

And because it is stated in the *Laghu-Vasiṣṭha-siddhānta* that "Svaloka shall indeed be Meru itself. He describes the remaining worlds with the word "in the sky" (*khe*). In the sky—that is, in the ether—above the sphere of the stars (*nakṣatragola*) is Maharloka, which is spherical in shape. Above Maharloka is Janoloka; above that is Tapoloka; and above that is Satya (Satyaloka). By the term "Satya," it is indicated that there are no further worlds above it. He states their progressive excellence according to their order with the word "lakṣa": by means of their own respective merits and religious duties (*puṇya-dharma*).

"By horses that are not small, but increasingly greater; by humans, [the goal] is to be attained. The meaning is that for humans, there shall be an attainment of higher and higher levels. Thus, the sevenfold world-system (sapta-pātāla-loka), beginning with Bhūrloka and so forth, is complete. The sense is that the fourteen worlds have been concluded according to the stated method. Now, an objection: since it was stated that "Yamakoti is at its center," and because Meru is situated to the north of Laṅkā, the question arises regarding the measurement of the universe (bhuvana-kośa).

By the passage beginning with "The Śādvala mountain is to the north," the arrangement of the three mountains facing Mount Meru is established; and by the passage beginning with "To the east of this, the Bhārata and other three regions," the arrangement of the three regions facing Mount Meru is correctly described. However, even so, the arrangement of the three regions facing Mount Meru remains unproven by the statement: "To the west, the Śṛṅgavān, Śveta, and Nīla mountains extend from the ocean."

Because Sidera is situated below Laṅkā, the inhabitants of that place face those of the land of Laṅkā; consequently, left and right are reversed for them, which makes it possible for Meru and Vaḍavāgni to be located respectively in the east, south, north, and west. This is because the directions such as east are determined to exist in a clockwise (savya) sequence. Thus, there would be the consequence of denying the well-known fact that Ilāvṛta lies at the center of Meru.

In the same way, for one situated in a city such as Laṅkā—which is located at the equator—the Lord resides in Siddhapura. This is because that [city] is also an equatorial location. Indeed, the Purāṇas do not proclaim a difference between the earth (Bhūloka) and the atmospheric region (Bhuvarloka). Nor should it be argued that there is no harm to the stated position because of a reversal of east and west in Siddhapura.

Since the rising and setting of the sun are observed everywhere at the same time, otherwise there would be a reversal of east and west as well as a reversal of south and north; thus, because both [theories] would be untenable, he says "Laṅkā" in the Upajāti meter: "At the time when the sun, as indicated by the planets and stars, reaches the meridian on the terrestrial portion delimited by the region of Laṅkā—at that very time. The particle *eva* (only/very) excludes connection with any other time and applies to each [term].

It is midday at the center of the earth's interior as delimited by the region of Yaśas. At that very same time, below Laṅkā and above [the equator], there is the time of sunset at the portion of the earth's interior situated in the lower part, namely Siddhapura. By the inclusion of the term "time" (kāla), it is shown that it is one and the same time which, due to the difference in limiting adjuncts (upādhi) according to those respective locations, receives various designations such as sunrise, midday, and so forth—this is the meaning of the *phuṭasu* [verse]. At that very same time...

Midnight occurs at the center of the earth's interior as delimited by the region of Romaka; this is by way of illustration for Laṅkā and for those regions situated on the line of the clear circumference (the equator) that are separated by a fourth part [of the circle]. Between these, at the point where the rising and setting portions are divided, midnight occurs at the center of the earth's interior as delimited by the two regions separated by a fourth part situated on the opposite side. It should be understood that what was stated—that "midday occurs at the center of the earth's interior as delimited by the region situated above that"—is likewise to be applied here.

The reasoning here is as follows: since the two fixed poles of the dual sphere revolve now around the terrestrial globe like a flowing river, and because the half-sphere situated above the sky is visible from a city at the center of the earth, the visible mountains lie at the junction of the two hemispheres. By accepting that the tree of the earth's circumference constitutes the horizon (*kṣitija*) of the globe, it follows—according to what was stated previously—that at every location there is indeed a horizon. Thus, sunrise and sunset are simply the beginning and end of the time during which the orbs of the planets and stars, situated in the celestial space along the same meridian line, enter and exit the rotation.

This is the horizon-circle (*takṣitijavṛtta*). When two points, one eastern and one western, are separated by a fourth part [of the circle], the *lala* [line] passes through them; thus, the disk situated on the line of equal altitude becomes situated on the north-south meridian. Consequently, it is easily understood that this corresponds respectively to midday and midnight, and so forth. By this very [explanation], the fulfillment of the stated matter—namely, that the horizon behind the aforementioned place is elevated by a distance of half the Earth's diameter—is established through direct perception.

One might argue that the earth’s sphericity is established through the principle of "otherwise-unaccountability" (*anyathānupapatti*), since it is understood by the Teacher himself that the earth must be spherical because it moves [in such a way]. However, this is not tenable; for if the earth’s sphericity were already established, then its movement would be understood according to the method stated [by him], and conversely, if its movement were understood, the earth’s sphericity would be established—thus there is a circular argument (*parasparāśraya*). Nor should it be said that because the aforementioned observation is established through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) in the eighth chapter on the sphere (*gola-adhyāya*), there is no risk of circular reasoning in the inference of the terrestrial globe based on that direction. *Note: The text contains a fragmentary reference to a commentary (Ma080) within the *Gola-adhyāya*.*

Since it is not established that the simultaneous observation of those respective phenomena by human beings is impossible—given that such observations do occur—how can there be a valid inference based on an unestablished reason (*asiddhahetu*)? Thus, it is stated in the *Siddhāntasundara*: "A celestial body situated above the city of Laṅkā is to the south of Sumeru, while from one located at Yamakoṭi it is to the west; from one at Romaka it is to the east, and from one at the submarine fire (*vaḍavānala*) it is to the north. Therefore, O wise one, the earth must indeed be spherical."

For why did Pṛthūdaka propose the argument that [the world] has the form of a ball of earth in the realm of Yama? Because it is not established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); therefore, those of dull intellect do not accept it as authoritative. Regarding this, the commentators on that [text] state: "If those who rely on conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) would not accept what was thus stated, then how could even the followers of the Purāṇas (*paurāṇika*) rely upon the conventional usage of six months as a day and night for the gods?"

Since for the gods residing in the northern portion of the equatorial plane of Laṅkā, the beginning of night occurs at that very same time [as the end of day for those on the opposite side], therefore, the horizon (kṣitija) of those [deities] is conceived as being precisely the meridian (nāḍīvṛtta). Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the impossibility of this very convention; for such a convention is common to both [the terrestrial and celestial spheres].

Likewise, that very same point of non-existence (nairātmya), which is the equatorial circle (*sama-maṇḍala*), is located ninety degrees away from the eastern *svastika* and above Mount Meru from the southern quarter. And so it has been said: because the fundamental convention is supported by the force of the subverting argument (*bādhaka*) consisting in the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the cessation of the universally accepted worldly conventions of days, nights, and so forth, its status as a valid reason (*saddhetutva*) is indeed appropriate; otherwise, they say, inference would be destroyed. That is not so.

According to the view of the Paurāṇikas, since the terms "day" and "night" are technical designations based on the visibility or invisibility of the sun, there is no contradiction in their usage; therefore, enough with this irrelevant dispute.

And thus, while there is an appearance of identity between sunrise and sunset at all locations, in reality they are distinct for every neighboring region; because there is no identity between the east and west at all locations, and because in Siddhapura situated below, the directions are understood through a reversal of east and west according to their own sequence, there is no contradiction whatsoever in what was stated regarding the non-difference of its south and north—this is the intended meaning. (44) Now, even if sunrise and sunset were to occur at the same time everywhere, let there be identity between the east and west.

Otherwise, since there is no spatial distinction between those two [the sun and the zenith] even at a single location due to their temporal occurrence, it would follow that every day there would be a difference in their respective positions as "east" and "west. Indeed, in no place whatsoever is there a perception of anyone that "this is the east and that is the other," for such a convention would otherwise be impossible to establish. Therefore, he says in the *Upajāti* meter: "Where... Where, in which region, the sun has risen—that is, at the end of the night, having become visible—there, in that very place, according to tradition (*kila*), lies the eastern direction.

"Eastern" (*prācī*) is explained by the term "eastern" (*prāc*), as previously stated. That direction in which a certain region reaches the state of being established [as the horizon] at the end of the day is the western direction (*aparā*). Thus, because the points of sunrise and sunset differ according to each location, a distinction between east and west is necessarily established: where the place of Laṅkā is the site of sunrise, that is the east; and where it is the site of sunset, that is the west. Where [the sun rises], there is the east; where it sets, there is the west.

Because it is sunset for those situated at Lanka, that direction is the west; and because it is sunrise for those situated at Siddhapura, that direction is the east. Thus, due to the reversal of the east and west of Siddhapura, the stated meaning is established as correct. This concludes the inquiry regarding the structure of the world (*bhuvanakośa*). [Verse 73, Maṭha 88] Nor should it be argued that there is the undesirable consequence of the east and west being indeterminate from day to day.

The intention is as follows: for the sake of common knowledge regarding which part is eastward and which part is westward on the horizon, there is a general statement characterized by the locations of sunrise and sunset; otherwise, it would be impossible to distinguish between east and west. However, subtle knowledge has already been stated in the section on the three latitudes (*triprakṣādhikāra*). Now, if there is a transposition of east and west, there must necessarily be a transposition of south and north.

Since the right and left sides of a person facing east are the reverse of the right and left sides of a person facing west, the same defect remains; therefore, he says: "from that, two fish arise. From those two positions, east and west, two fish are produced. By the word "and" (ca), the south and north are established from elsewhere.

And likewise, because of the rule that right and left correspond to south and north from the east, it follows that on Mount Siddhapura as well, right and left correspond to south and north; this is the intended meaning. Consequently, there is no fault. How so? He concludes by way of summary: "Thus it is struck. Therefore, since it is well-established (*prasiddham*)—that is, proven with excellence—that Mount Meru stands to the north of all the aforementioned regions, as is established for all people in the Purāṇas, there is nothing contradictory in this matter.

And thus, just as there is a division of directions such as east and so forth for the location of Laṅkā, exactly the same division of directions such as east and so forth applies to me [the observer] situated in Siddhapura and other places. At every point along the circumference of both [hemispheres], at a distance of one-fourth [of the radius], the locations of Meru and Vaḍavānala are established at the zenith and nadir respectively, facing south and north; therefore, the reversal of left and right is not a real thing, but is merely a form of delusion arising from the rotation of the lower hemisphere. For this very reason, the Pole Star (Dhruva) is situated above the summit of Meru.

The meaning is that it is established that [the pole star] is the North Pole (*uttaradhruva*). Now he states the specific distinction: "Just as those cities that are in the fourth part from the equator do not exist in the west of that [equator], so too in every case, wherever [a city] is from the equator, there it cannot be in the west. Therefore, other than in the region of the non-equatorial [pole], the west is situated in various ways. (46–47)

Having fixed the northern direction as being directly facing the desired location of Meru, and having made the south-facing direction toward the equator (nirakṣa) motionless, the east-west line should be established from those two points. In this way, when the marks for the north and south are established, the east-west line subsequently does not fall upon the previous line; this means that the east-west line has shifted due to the deviation (cara) of the north. The rest is easy to understand. || 46 || 47 ||

Ma0ḍī0—[Objection: Now, if Meru were situated at the zenith for all [places], then for all other regions, the division of directions into south and north would be untenable for those situated there, and thus the previously stated [doctrine] would be contradicted. Therefore, wishing to state the answer to that, he first states a supporting example in the Upajāti meter, beginning with "yathā" (just as). The meaning is: just as Yamakoṭi is located four quadrants of the earth's circumference to the east of Laṅkā, so it is here.

In the chapter on the sphere (Golādhyāya), Ma0ḍī0 states: From Ujjayinī, Yamakoṭi lies in the eastern direction at a distance of one-fourth of the terrestrial circumference (*bhūparidhi*). By the use of the restrictive particle *eva*, it is meant that there is no other [city] in that same eastern direction at a distance differing by more or less than one-fourth of the terrestrial circumference; that is to say, there is no other Yamakoṭi in that direction. Then, from the city of Yamakoṭi—[the word] *ca* (and) is used here to consider the opposite direction, namely, in which direction Avantī lies relative to Yamakoṭi—it would not be in the western direction.

[Objection: "In that case, does it not follow that there is no Yamakoṭi in the western direction? To this he says: "Laṅkā. The meaning is: "from that Yamakoṭi. Laṅkā is situated at one-fourth of a *kucaturtha* (one-quarter of a *krośa*) from the western direction. By the use of the particle *eva* ("only"), it is indicated that there is no specific non-axial region (*nirakṣadeśa*) other than Laṅkā in the western direction, [neither less nor more].

And thus, the meaning of the verse is that Lankā and Ujjayinī could not both exist as being separated by one-fourth of the earth's circumference to the east of Yamakoṭi and one-fourth of the earth's circumference to the west of Yamakoṭi respectively; rather, there would be only one Lankā situated between the south and the north.

The intended meaning is as follows: the line of the earth's circumference touched at the zero-latitude point such as Lankā is likewise [the line] for Ujjayinī, by imagining a line from the center of the earth; those eastern and western points of Ujjayinī lie along the path of that circumference-line on the terrestrial globe, because that circumference conforms to a circle.

And thus, on the terrestrial meridian circle from Laṅkā—which follows the east-west circle—at a distance of one-fourth [of the circumference], there are the locations of Yamakoṭi and Romaka; at those respective eastern and western points, the terrestrial meridian circle situated along the north-south line from Laṅkā and following the east-west direction is equal to that [circumference] and measures six [units]. Therefore, from both Laṅkā and Ujjayinī, at a distance of one-fourth of their own respective meridian circles, there are Yamakoṭi and Romaka in the east and west.

In Yamakoṭi and Romakā, the circle of the terrestrial meridian (bhūgolaparidhivṛtta) follows the previously established [meridian], and likewise the circle of the terrestrial meridian at Ukā is exactly the same; therefore, by those two, Laṅkā is neither in the west nor in the east of Ujjayinī, because the terrestrial meridian situated at Ujjayinī is known to be identical to that circle. (46) Now, by means of an illustration, he confirms the basis for the calculation of diurnal motion (cara) with an Upajāti verse—beginning with "tathā": "In that manner," meaning by way of the illustration. The particle *eva* serves to exclude any deviation from the method of the illustration.

In all entries related to the terrestrial globe (*bhūgola*): for indeed, because of that reason; from whichever place—whatever place exists in the east—from that point of the eastern direction, there would not be a limiting place in the west. It has also been stated that whatever place is in the west from a certain place, that place would not exist in the east when counting in reverse order. By implication, this refers to the great circle on the terrestrial globe that follows the east-west line at the center of the desired location.

In whichever regions [the shadow] is fixed, those regions—within the east-west line of the desired location—are to be understood as being situated in the east or west according to their respective divisions of the eastern and western halves. From those [points], the configuration of the desired location is determined by a circle parallel to the earth’s circumference; the purpose is that the desired location from those points shall not be situated in the western or eastern directions. Now, one might object: this is not a fixed rule.

Since there is no specific location on earth that is devoid of latitude—whether in the east or in the west—it necessarily exists either to the west or to the east [of any given point]. Because the term "latitude" (akṣa) denotes a single entity, this rule applies to all places other than that [point of zero latitude]. Thus, he concludes with the words "from the latitude-less region" (nirakṣadeśāt). This refers to the subject matter concerning the location of the latitude-less region. The inquiry regarding the "Cosmic Egg" (Bhuvanakośa) concerns the east and west directions as established in various ways through calculation.

55. "Meṇeī-vicitrā" means those two possess a wonderful, marvelous configuration (*saṃsthā*). The word "ca" (and) serves to exclude [the possibility of] a conjunction between the south and the north; thus, whatever place is the southern or northern [point], the place to its east is "northeastern" or "southeastern. This applies to both the meridian and the equatorial regions. For this very reason, it is a source of wonder. One should understand that while the common worldly perception—that from a given location, the place to the east is "eastern" and the place to the west is "western"—follows the clear, small circumference (the horizon) following the meridian circle.

According to the aforementioned method, by imagining a circle of latitude at a distance of one-fourth of the Meru from all equatorial regions (nirakṣadeśa) to the north, that very circle of circumference can indeed exist facing toward every equatorial region; and it is possible for such a circle situated on the north-south axis to be established at that one-fourth interval. Thus, the directions are established upon Meru through the principles of the celestial sphere (golayukti).

For this very reason, for those situated on Mount Meru, because they see the sun rising from the east, it is said that the sun rises there toward the east; however, the knowledge of "east" and "west" is impossible [in that absolute sense]. Nor should it be argued that "east" and "west" refer to the directions where its rising and setting occur at the end of night and day respectively.

Since the sun’s connection with the equinoctial circle occurs daily at different locations according to its divine measure, and because it is impossible for all parts [of the horizon] to be simultaneously delimited, no direction whatsoever—such as "east" or "west"—can be consistently maintained for the world; therefore, no such consideration need be made there. This is because of the statement by Śrīpati: "For first he attains visibility, and here he is in the east; since he is then in that [western] place, how can that same point be the west? Thus it is said.

By this explanation of the word "eastern" (*prācī*)—namely, that "the Sun moves toward the east"—it is established through the force of the traditional scriptures handed down by Brahmā, Soma, and Sūrya, that because the Self-existent One (Svayambhū) stationed himself in the middle of Janaloka and positioned the circle of stars in the sky directly to the east of all else, it is understood that visibility occurs precisely there; therefore, for those [beings], the "east" is that very location characterized by that [visibility].

Therefore, the claim that the eastern and western points for those [planets] are precisely where the celestial equator (kṣitija) and the meridian (meru-samavṛtta) intersect—and that these two [intersections] occur only at Siddhapura and Laṅkā respectively, such that the directions east and west of the gods are located right there—is refuted as being the hidden intent [of the author].

At the beginning of the Kalpa, regarding the terrestrial horizon of Laṅkā, since there is no definitive criterion for the orientation of the equator other than the direction already stated for the solar position at the Laṅkā-horizon, it would follow that for those residing in Sindhupura, the east would be located exactly at the zenith; furthermore, for those residing in Romaka, the west would erroneously appear as the east. However, because the prime meridian—which serves as the basis for planetary calculation—is accepted as being connected to the country of Laṅkā, one assumes that the terrestrial horizon of Meru, which is the crown of the equatorial region, constitutes the equator itself.

Thus, for us, that very place which lies on the line of the eastern and western extremities is the location of Meru. Since the locations of Laṅkā and Siddhapura lie in the middle of the celestial equator, while the southern and northern points lie on the terrestrial horizon of Meru, the conceptualization of the directions at Meru is logically consistent; therefore, it was correctly stated previously that "Bhadrāśva extends to the northern Kurus. For this very reason: "The Sītā river, traveling through the atmosphere, goes from that mountain to the eastern mountain; and from there, across the eastern region of Bhadrāśva, it reaches the ocean."

In the same way, O great sage, the Alakanandā flows toward the south and reaches Bhārata; having divided itself into seven streams, it enters the ocean. Then, having passed all the western mountains, it goes to the region named Ketumāla in the west and enters the sea. Likewise, O high-minded one, the Bhadrā passes beyond the Udaragiri mountain and the Northern Kurus, and from there enters the northern ocean.

Thus, the nature of the directions relative to Meru as established by Vyāsa’s definitive conclusion is consistent with the *Bhāgavata Purāṇa* and free from contradiction. As for the previous explanatory statement beginning with "where I have risen," that refers—by way of its connection to the location—to the limit of the sixty degrees of latitude within the region of Ācārya, as indicated by the passage beginning "where Lambakhalavājinaka. Therefore, there is no flaw; this is the intended meaning. (47)

Now he describes the arrangement of the revolution of the celestial sphere: In a place devoid of latitude (the equator), a person sees the two poles situated upon the terrestrial circle, one to the south and one to the north. The sky, supported by them, revolves like a wheel, with its axis passing through the head and the feet. (3.98) Just as a person moves toward the northern direction, so does the terrestrial circle appear to move [toward the south] due to the motion of the sky.

One observes that the North Pole (Udag-dhruva) rises above the horizon; the degrees of latitude (palāṃśas) between [the observer's position] and the zenith of the earth are equal in number to the yojanas. These degrees, when multiplied by the number of yojanas in the circumference of the earth, become the degrees [of the celestial sphere]. Conversely, from the degrees on the earth or in the celestial orbit, the yojanas are obtained by inversion. By the statement "As a person moves toward the north," the rule of proportion (anupāta) is indicated: if one degree of the circle is obtained for the yojanas of the earth's circumference, then what is obtained for the yojanas of the distance traveled? The result is the degrees of latitude (akṣāṃśas).

If the circumference of the earth is multiplied by the degrees of the circle (360), what is the result? The quotient shall be the *yojanas* of the distance between the equatorial region (*nirakṣadeśa*) and one's own location. The rest is clear. Thus, from the equatorial region, Mount Meru is indeed at one-fourth of the earth; there, the latitude is ninety degrees (90°). Ma.-Ṭī.: Now, he states the nature of the equatorial regions that have been mentioned by means of the Vaṃśastha meter, beginning with the words "nirakṣadeśa" (the equatorial region).

In this region of the earth, the north and south poles are situated upon the stellar sphere and adjacent to the terrestrial circle. At the point on the earth's surface where the terrestrial globe is both visible and invisible, intersecting at the center of the earth, lies the terrestrial meridian—the circle of the earth's circumference. By means of a line drawn through that point, the celestial sphere is metaphorically described as being a circle of the same shape.

In that regard, the two poles (dhruva) situated at the center of the earth within the terrestrial plane (kṣitija) are located in the sphere of the stars (bhagola); therefore, they are fixed with respect to the equatorial region (nirakṣadeśa), meaning they are stabilized by the southern and northern poles. As for that which is in space—it moves like a water-wheel (jalayantra), such as the well-known wooden mechanism used for drawing water from a well for the purpose of sprinkling gardens and so forth, provided with a pure framework and a circular structure; in that same manner, it revolves incessantly.

A non-resident of Madra (amadracarī), situated upon the celestial sphere while revolving facing westward, perceives [the celestial equator] above his own head. By the word "own" (nija), it is meant that he is a dweller in a region connected to the pole (dhruva) attached to the horizon. Above his head, he sees that circle which passes through the center of the terrestrial globe and lies between the two poles; the meaning is that it appears in the form of a great circle of the sky extending from east to west.

And likewise, since the poles are situated on the axis, by metaphorical extension (upacāra) that location is also called the "axis. Just as in the case of a specific region, the absence of the north-south direction at the center of the earth's equatorial plane (kṣitija) is what defines that place; such a place is denoted by the term "latitude" (nirakṣa). Thus, in whatever region the celestial sphere (bhagola) and the terrestrial sphere (bhūgola) are separated by equal intervals, and the circle of the horizon (athavṛtta) follows the east-west line—this is the inquiry regarding the structure of the universe (bhuvanakośa).

Ma0 Ṭī0: The meaning is that Laṅkā is well-known as being situated on the equatorial line (nirakṣapaddhati), characterized by these two features: its status as a place without latitude (nirakṣadeśatva) and its position upon the east-west meridian. || 48 || Now, he establishes the existence of latitude in places other than the equatorial region using the Vaṃśastha meter—beginning with "ug": "As a person goes from the equatorial region toward the northern direction, to whatever extent [he goes], to that same extent... [and so on]. "Uttarottaram" means further and further north. "Khat" [is an abbreviation for *kha* = zero].

The meaning is: from a point in space situated above the terrestrial globe (bhagola) along a line parallel to the well-established level ground. One perceives the equatorial circle (akṣamaṇḍala)—which is a great circle passing through the two poles of the terrestrial globe—as inclined, being bent toward the southern direction. The meaning is that one perceives the rotation of the sphere established by the stars as having its center at the midpoint between one's own head and the earth's surface. Now, one might ask: "Even if that location is not distinct from a non-axial (equatorial) region, how can it be considered 'with an axis' (sākṣa)? To this, he says: "In the northern hemisphere" (udagdhruvam).

The meaning is: from the terrestrial horizon (*kṣitija*) located at the center of the earth and delimited by its own region—that is, from the position of the earth's surface such as that of the demon Vṛtra—one sees the North Pole elevated, situated at its highest point. Just as one travels toward the southern direction from a non-axial location (*nirakṣadeśa*), so too does one see the South Pole elevated above the horizon; the implication is that one sees the stellar sphere depressed to the north. Furthermore, because the earth’s [equatorial] plane does not coincide with the terrestrial horizon, it is a location with latitude (*sākṣatva*), being distinct from a non-axial location.

But surely, since the pole star (dhruva) occupies the position of the axis (akṣa), it would instead follow that the equatorial region (nirakṣadeśa) possesses an axis; for in any other location, even if one pole is not seen while the other is seen, it is appropriate to consider that place as equatorial. Therefore, the demonstration of being at the equator based on the elevation of the pole star is inconsistent; to this he says: "between those two" (tadantare).

Between those two points—located on the meridian and the prime vertical of the celestial sphere (bhagola) and separated by the equatorial interval—and the point on the central circle of the celestial sphere marked by one's own zenith, or between the points on the local horizon circle: within that interval, on the southern declination circle (yāmyacaravṛtta), there exist the degrees of latitude (palāṃśakāḥ). Thus, since these degrees of latitude are designated as "degrees of co-latitude" (akṣāṃśa), and because they possess the nature of the complement of the [latitude] angles, it is logically established that they constitute the co-latitude; this is the intended meaning.

Now, if it is argued that "the knowledge of its parts" occurs upon seeing its elevation, how then can there be an answer regarding the distant *bhagola* by means of that qualification? To this he replies: "arising from the latitudinal degrees (*akṣāṃśa*) produced from those *yojanas*. This means: the latitudinal degrees produced from those *yojanas* which constitute the distance between one's own location and the equatorial region (*nirakṣadeśa*) along the southern or northern direction.

Thus, by the phrase "tathā vadagdiśām," it is intended to demonstrate that just as there is an interval between the equatorial region (nirakṣadeśa) and one’s own location, so too is the observation of the altitude of the celestial pole (dhruvonnati). Therefore, the meaning is that the degrees of latitude (akṣāṃśāḥ) are indeed the reduction [of distance] in yojanas of the interval between the equator and one’s own location; hence, the knowledge of those [degrees] is not impossible once the knowledge of yojanas is attained. Now, one might ask: "If the knowledge of yojanas is required, how can there be knowledge of those degrees? To this, [the author] states in verse: "yojaneti," [explaining that] yojanas and degrees are mutually related through a rhythmic connection (gīti).

The number of *yojana*s situated between one's own location and the location of the North Pole (*svanirakṣadeśa*), multiplied by three hundred and sixty, is divided by the circumference of the earth previously mentioned—since the earth's *yojana*s are known to exist on the earth itself—thereby resulting in a portion of *yojana*s corresponding to a specific part of the earth's circumference related to that location on the earth.

[Objection: Since the degrees of latitude produced on the earth's surface are indeed on the earth itself, how can they be considered "degrees of the [celestial] axis" (akṣāṃśa), given that by the aforementioned method they are restricted to being situated in the sky? To this, he says: "In the orbit" (kakṣāyām). The portion related to the connection with the earth is within the sphere (gola) presided over by the orbit. On the celestial sphere, there are two known points connected to two locations on the earth by means of two threads passing through their own latitudes; the interval between those two points, which consists of the difference in longitude (rāntara) in the north-south direction, is the "degree" (aṃśa). The word "or" (vā) indicates an alternative.

The meaning is that they exist in both places. The idea is as follows: since all the orbits (*kakṣā*) of the celestial dwellers are, according to the method stated in the *Madhyamādhikāra*, measured by a number of degrees equal to the number of degrees in the orbits of my [the Earth's] own parts—due to the assumption that the orbits are composed of a number of degrees equal to the number of degrees in the ten parts—the existence of the tenth part is not contradictory in either case.

Nor should it be argued that there is a mutual dependence (anyonyāśraya) because the previous statement requires knowledge of the degrees of latitude (akṣāṃśa), whereas this present one requires the circumference (paridhi). This is because, by piercing [the earth] with instruments and the like previously, the degrees of latitude are accepted as the degrees of declination (natāṃśa) of the sun at midday. By this, since the word "own" (sva) is employed in the phrase "its own circumference," if the yojanas on the earth are taken, then that is the terrestrial circumference (bhūparidhi).

Others, however, hold that because of the previously mentioned objection, the statement that "the area of the circular field multiplied by the circumference becomes the surface area" is a reasonable intended meaning, as it is established by logical proof and is not improper.

To dispel the doubt of the dull-witted as to why the result is incorrect due to an impurity in the underlying intent (tātparya), he concludes the refutation by stating, "Because it is defective" (duṣṭatvāt). The meaning is that this calculation, which pertains to the determination of the surface area of the earth while situated on the surface of Laṅkā, is defective—that is, improper—because the surface area of the terrestrial globe produced on the earth's surface, such as the value stated as "one hundred and five" (nagāśilīmukhe) and so forth, is seen to be incorrect; for that result has been produced by an inconsistent method. || 57 ||

Now, otherwise, the circumference of the sphere is to be conceived as measured by the sum of the sines, just as the lines from the top and bottom [of the fruit] are situated within an *āmalaka* fruit. (58) Just as the segments are seen there, one should conceive the segments upon the stalk according to the measure of the previously mentioned circumference, using lines drawn vertically and horizontally. (59) In that case, the area of a single segment is established through its parts: the sum of all sines, diminished by half the radius, divided by half the radius. (60)

Thus, that surface area of the segment would be equal to the product of the diameter and the circumference; therefore, the surface area of the sphere's surface is considered to be the product of the circumference and the diameter. Here, for any desired number of divisions, however many those divisions may be, their count multiplied by four [gives the number of lines]. From that, on the sphere, the circumference is established. For example, on the surface of a sphere divided into eight parts, it is determined by lines intersecting at right angles.

In this manner, the sub-fields (*vaprakas*) are seen to be determined according to the desired number on the back of a cow; by drawing lines from the head to the tail, one should calculate the area of the field for a single year. For example: here, the length is twenty-four *arpas* (six *hastas*). Therefore, a cow’s back is assumed to measure six *hastas*. By means of vertical and horizontal lines per *hasta*, that many sub-fields (*vaprakas*) are made. Therein, having placed an interval of one *hasta* between each pair of sub-fields, twenty-four sections are formed, equal in number to the bow-strings (*jyās*).

[The sines] are calculated. Then, the individual *jīvas* (sines), divided by the radius (*trijyā*), are the measures of the [intermediate] positions. The initial line is one cubit (*hasta*) in length; however, due to the influence of the sine, they are slightly shorter. Therein, the result is obtained as exactly one cubit. The product of the sine and the cosine is half the sum of the squares. These are combined with the results of the mandaphala calculation. That is the result for the auxiliary circle. When doubled, it becomes the result for one quadrant. This is established here for the sake of practical application.

"The sum of all [sides] minus half the base," and so forth. One of the values given as "arrows and eyes" (29) and so on is 542;33. This, diminished by three-fourths, becomes 525;4. Divided by six, this results in a field-area equal to the diameter, namely 30;33. For, by these very [calculations], the diameter of the circle is indeed 30;33.

The area above the surface is called the *paridhirūpaka* (the form of the circumference), while the result on the back of the cow is called the *goḍapṛṣṭhaphala* (the fruit of the cow’s back). Thus it has been stated: "In a field such as that of a threshing-floor (*asmyāṭī*), the product of the circumference multiplied by the height is the area; when multiplied by four, it becomes like a ball formed all around at the top. Furthermore, the fruit on the back of the cow is likewise the volume known as *ghanagaṇita* (solid calculation); it is the area multiplied by the diameter and divided by six, which results in the fixed volume.

The solid volume (ghana-phala) shall be one-sixth of the surface area multiplied by the diameter. Herein is the demonstration: Let as many cubical prisms as there are units of surface area be conceived as having sides equal to the radius and depths equal to the radius; these are to be arranged within the sphere. The meeting point of the needles occurs at the center of the sphere. Thus, the sum of the volumes of the needles results in the solid volume; this is established.

Furthermore, Āryabhaṭa, having been confused regarding the area of the circle, proposed the opinion of others—that the solid volume (ghana-phala) would be the area of the circle multiplied by itself—stating: "The square of the circumference multiplied by the diameter is the surface area. [58, 59, 60, 61] Ma0 Commentary: Now, although it has been established by the previously stated reasoning that the surface area of the globe's surface is necessarily less than five times the area of the circular base, why was it stated that it is four times? For, since both the multiplier and the divisor are reduced by a factor of four, it would follow that the surface area, which consists of the product of the circumference and the diameter, is correct.

It may be that, by means of the fourfold [method], one should determine the circumference of the sphere according to one's own preference through reasoning; for this is the question concerning the skill of release regarding the sphere. As many chord-segments as have been conceived, their number—multiplied by four—is to be taken as the circumference of that sphere. This is because it is established that the chords, being attached to the ends of the circumference, serve as the measure of the arcual portion of the circumference between the two chord-ends.

In the fourth part of Vaiśākha, by means of that measuring instrument, [the circumference] is multiplied by the months known as *jyotis* (luminaries) in the circle of multiplication; it is joined with the supreme authority derived from the many-fold chords (*jyā*). Because it is impossible to produce the rear-result (*pṛṣṭhaphala*) without this basis, it is said that "it is to be performed" since there is no possibility of a difference in the circumference's measurement without that. Immediately after that: "As before. Just as previously, by means of the lines at the mouth and the base of the *āmalaka* fruit, the mark for the portion of the mouth-tip is [established]; the "base" (*budhya*) is the sign of the tree.

The lines existing as the boundaries between those two [halves], established on both sides by their own nature, are seen as the embankments (*vapraka*) in the sections (*khaṇḍani*). Their measure is defined by the formula "the chord of three times the radius" (*trijyā*) applied to that circumference; the meaning is that they have that magnitude.

By means of lines drawn upward, downward, and obliquely, one should conceive of the upper portion of this region; from that, at a distance of one and a half circumferences, the lower portion is conceived. Taking that as a limit, one should construct ramparts with parallel lines drawn at intervals equal to half the circumference. Therein, for the purpose of understanding the surface area of the sphere's exterior, the area of the field is calculated by assuming equal segments, such that in a single rampart it is doubled by the segments.

In this manner, by calculating the areas of each segment according to the method described for the practice of *pāṭīgaṇita* (plane geometry), the sum of those areas—multiplied by the sine of the sum of all the latitudes (*jīvā*) and divided by half the radius of the celestial sphere (*trijyārdha*) minus that same sine—is established through effort as being achieved with precision. That result would be the area of the field, equal to the diameter of the sky-traversing [sphere], corresponding to the circumference of four times the sine-measure in a single forest-like [orb]. This is the intended meaning.

On a sphere whose circumference is equal to the equator, circles of the form of latitudinal parallels are drawn by means of the entry of imaginary lines from north to south, each separated by the distance corresponding to the previously determined measure of the circumference, multiplied by a count beginning with one up to the maximum [number of] chords (*jyā*). On the entire sphere, these are equal in measure to single and double chords respectively; on the hemisphere, they are measured on both sides by the chords.

Among those, the first sines (jīvās) starting from the initial arc and ending with the full diameter (vyāsa) are situated respectively within the Vyāsa-sine-resultant circle (*vyāsasūtra-phalavṛtta*), which is shaped like a rampart (*vaprākāra*), and within the circles shaped like a terrace (*talatalākāra*). For these [sines], there are triangular fields (*kṣetra*) formed by the base being that sine, the middle point being the center, and the height being the segment of that circle. Among them, the first field is a triangle, while the others are various quadrilaterals.

The arms of these [figures] are the circumference of the sphere at the edge of the rampart (*vaprānta*). This is because they are elevated by one unit and because there is no interval between the moles (*maṣaka*). The perpendiculars (*lamba*) are situated in one place. In the case of the first figure joined with a circle, there is an absence of a face due to the upward orientation of the arms from the [first] field. However, the ground is a portion of the internal circumference held in the shape of the first circle; it is the region situated at the edge of the tree in the shape of the second circle from the position of the rampart. In the previous field, this is the face. Thus it proceeds successively for each subsequent one.

In the question of the sages, [the radius] is constrained by one part of the circumference that causes dissolution; for it is not greater than the diameter of the triple-radius (trijyā). Therefore, since the diameter of the triple-radius is "one unit" (*ekamita*) as the earth, according to the rule "when the diameter is half the triple-radius, the earth is one unit," the earth is indeed less than one measure. And thus: "The first and subsequent sines divided by the triple-radius are established as the earth-measures within the figures."

Now, the area of the triangle is clearly the product of the base and half the height. First, in the first sector of the circle, the area of the figure is the first sine multiplied by the radius (trijyā). In the second sector... [the area is] greater than the product of the base and half the height.

By the statement "the Golādhyāya multiplied by Mañju-nighna [is] the sum of the squares of the sines," the area of the first figure is the half of one of the two sines (first or second) divided by the radius (*trijyā*). Because the halves of the sums are equal, the sum of the halves of the first and second sines divided by the radius results as the area of the second figure. The sum of the areas of the first and second figures is the area of the two segmental figures. In that case, there is a division by the divisor for both.

The sum of the first and second half-chords (*jyārdha*) is equal to twice the first half-chord; thus, it is established that when the first half-chord is added to the sum of the first and second half-chords, the result is twice the first half-chord. Divided by the radius (*trijyā*), this is the area of the two sectors. Similarly, in the subsequent sectors starting from the third, when the sum of the second and third half-chords divided by the radius is added to the previous chord-sum, it is established that the next half-chord added to the prior chord-sum, divided by the radius, is the result.

And so, since in the case of a quadrilateral (vapraka) the base of the final sector has the nature of the radius (trijyā), it is established that for the sake of the radius, one should add the previous sine and then divide by three. Here, the dividend results as the sum of all the sines multiplied by the radius. This product divided by the radius is indeed the area of one sector; the area of the other sector is the same. Therefore, doubling this gives the area of the entire square (ekavarga).

In that case, by subtracting the [sine] value from the whole, the result is established as: "the sum of all [sines] in one quadrant, diminished by half the radius, divided by half the radius. Nor should it be argued that, since the arc-segment has the shape of a triangle, the area of the segment must logically be the measure obtained by the method stated for the sine-measure (the perpendicular) according to the direction mentioned—that is, the measure itself being the area of the segment. This is because, given that the perpendicular and the base are each equal to a quarter of the circumference of the hemisphere, they cannot form a triangle due to their horizontal orientation; for it is accepted that the base and the perpendicular are not at right angles.

Nor should it be argued that, even in the case of a fragmented field (*khaṇḍakṣetra*), the area is not established because the long arms, the ground, and the faces are oblique due to being portions of the circumference at the neck; for it appears as equal by virtue of its being a fragment. Precisely for this reason, the more numerous the fragments, the more subtle the area becomes through the observation of equality in the area of the field. Therefore, the calculation of the area here according to the method involving quarters is inappropriate.

Thus, the teacher’s objection—that there is an absence of straightness because the two arms (*bhuja*) are portions of a circumference—is refuted; for even the perpendiculars (*lamba*) and the segments of the base (*bhūmi*) are of the same genus as portions of the circumference, thereby establishing the validity of the figure. Furthermore, due to their connection with the circumference, the arms and the perpendiculars possess equal status as sides. In a triangle, the sum of the areas resulting from the two similar right-angled triangles on either side of the perpendicular constitutes the total area.

Since the area of a long quadrilateral is equal to half the area of a right-angled quadrilateral of the same base, it is evident that half the product of the base and the perpendicular—which constitutes the area of the right-angled triangle—is the area of the right-angled triangle. Thus, because the two segments (abādhās) are respectively the base and the perpendicular of that right-angled triangle, the sum of the areas of the two triangles formed by the product of the base and the segments is the total area of the quadrilateral.

Since the perpendicular is the height (*bhūmi*) of the triangle, it is logical that half the perpendicular multiplied by the respective base gives the area of the figure. In an oblique quadrilateral, within the equal perpendicular triangle, there is an isosceles right-angled triangle on both sides; in that [triangle], the two sides of the isosceles triangle are the perpendicular and the base, and the hypotenuse is the diagonal. The segment of the base between the perpendicular and the side is the other base. Thus, the area of the figure is the product of the base-segment and half the perpendicular; likewise for the other side.

The area of the two resulting quadrilaterals is equal to the product of the sum [of the sides] when the two multiplied [sides] are added together. Because the two land-sections are equal, their sum, multiplied by the perpendicular (lamba), is the area of the central region. This is the question regarding the structure of the universe (bhuvanakośa). Maṭṭī: Since the perpendicular and the base are the hypotenuse and the side [respectively], their product is the area of the field; that [result] should be added there.

However, even though the knowledge of the entire ground is complete, because of the lack of knowledge regarding the application of the segments of the ground, the calculation of the area of the two similar triangles is achieved; therefore, since the face-ground is measured by that, the face-ground multiplied by the perpendicular (lamba) is the area of the two similar triangles.

Here, by means of two sections, [it is shown that] the product of the base and the multiplier (bhūmiguṇa) plus half the multiplier (lambardha), added to the product of the multiplier and the height (lambamukhaghāta), results in the sum of the base-multiplied-by-half-the-height and the height-multiplied-by-half-the-base; for even when there is addition or subtraction of the two multiplied quantities, they remain equal due to the reduction of the excess. Thus, the area of the field (kṣetraphala) is correctly obtained by adding the product of the height and the base (mukhabhūmyaiyyārtha) to the product of the height and the multiplier; enough with this digression.

And likewise, when the radius is diminished by one-sixth of the total circumference, the semi-diameter multiplied by the circumference obtained from a fourfold sine becomes the fine diameter. As in the present case—the sum of the twenty-four sines (jīvās) of the fine parts as determined by the origin of the sine, added to the parts of the sine and the eighty-six parts, equals 54,251; 38; 24. This, minus half the radius (3,438), results in 52,532; 38; 24.

In this circle, where the circumference is equal to the radius of the celestial sphere (cakrakalā), the diameter is twice the sine of ninety degrees (*ghūkṛtrijyā*), which is 6,879. If that is the case, what would the diameter be for a circumference of ninety-six, which is four times the measure of the sine of the *vapra*? By means of this proportion, the subtle diameter with its fractional parts is determined as 30; 332; 36. This is equal to the product of half the radius and the sine of ninety degrees. It is stated that the sum of the twenty-four sines is 54,233, which is measured by the "Veda-arrows" (454). Divided by the radius, this yields 12,514. This is the gross diameter: 30; 32; 44.

If you ask how it is that this is approximately equal to the product of three half-chords (*trijyārdha*), listen: although in this case there are many chords, and in the sum of all those chords minus half the radius (*tribhajyārdha*) the form of three times the product of the sine of the [maximum] angle and half the radius is not seen through reasoning, nevertheless, when one assumes three chords here, the form of three times the product of the sine of that [angle] and half the radius is established by reasoning in the sum of all chords minus half the radius; therefore, even in other cases, its assumption is established by inference supported by favorable logic.

For instance: half the sine of thirty degrees is the square root of this [value] from the square of the radius (*trijyā*) of the corresponding arc. The sine of thirteen times the fifteenth part of the radius divided by sixty-seven is [another value]. The sine of the radius multiplied by seven is yet another. When these are added together and the result is diminished by half the radius, it becomes the sum of the second and third sines. In that case, since the second sine consists of thirteen times the radius divided by twenty-four parts, it should be added to the second sine through the method of equal denominators (*samaccheda-vidhi*) using the common measure of the radius.

Its nature is as follows: the sine of three signs multiplied by twenty-eight and increased by its fifteenth part; when this is halved, multiplied by fifty-six, and divided by fifteen, its nature is established.

In this very context, by applying the inverse method to the rule "multiplied by twenty-four and divided by seven" (from the *Tanuṇa* section, where the dividend is 56 and the divisor is 15), one arrives at the following: the divisor for the circumference, which consists of eighty-four and twenty-two as its parts, is reduced by a factor of one and a half; thus, by taking the divisor position as being increased by six and five respectively, and by including the increment of one, the dividend and divisor ultimately resolve into the values 56 and 15.

The quotient obtained by dividing the sum of all sines minus the sine of the arc by half the radius is the diameter, which takes the form of the product of a single sine and the circumference. Therefore, since the product of the sine equal to the diameter and the circumference is equal to the number of degrees in the circle (360), then by the proportion: "If the result equal to the sine is obtained for [a circle with] a circumference equal to the number of degrees, what will it be for circles with circumferences equal to the number of degrees?", the product of the circumference and the diameter divided by the number of degrees is clearly established as the uncontradicted *pṛṣṭhaphala* (surface area). In the chapter on Spherics (*Golādhyāya*), verse 780 states: "The result equal to the sine... Thus, by the rule of three (*anupāta*): if the result equal to the sine is obtained for [a circle with] a circumference equal to the number of degrees, then what will it be for circles with circumferences equal to the number of degrees? By this proportion, the product of the circumference and the diameter divided by the number of degrees is the clear and consistent *pṛṣṭhaphala*.

It should be understood that, since the area of the circle is established by this very logic, the circumference was stated without hesitation in the *Paṭī* as four times the previously mentioned back-area (pṛṣṭhaphala), for the purpose of establishing that [circumference]. || 61 || Now he describes the expansion and dissolution of the earth: The increase of the earth on all sides shall be one *yojana* at the time of the *Bhava-bhūta-pūrva* [manvantara]; at the time of the *Bāla* [pralaya], there is destruction due to an increase of only one *yojana*, and at the time of the *Prākṛtika* [pralaya], there is the destruction of the entire earth. || 62 ||

That which perishes day by day along with all beings is called the daily dissolution (*dainaṃdina-pralaya*). At the end of Brahmā’s day, all beings enter into that *āla* dissolution, where they are dissolved. (63) Because at the end of the power (*bala*) [of the cycle], all things return to their primordial nature (*prakṛti*), the lords of the wise call it the "natural" (*prākṛtika*) dissolution. Having merged there, they are again separated from the modifications of nature (*prakṛti-vikāra*) within the interior of the sheath of karma. (64) Those whose entire merit and sin have been consumed by the fire of knowledge, having fixed their minds upon Hari, the Supreme Lord—

As for the yogin, dissolution (*laya*) is fourfold: that which pertains to Yama, the non-returning, the final, and [the daily]. (65) Here, "dissolution" means the destruction of the elements (*bhūta*). That occurs every day at present; it is called the daily (*dainandina*) dissolution. That which is the withdrawal of the three worlds at the end of a thousand cycles of four ages, at the conclusion of a day of Brahmā, is called the "great" (*bāla*) dissolution. In that state, the worlds—whose merit and demerit have been exhausted—enter the body of Brahmā through his mouth. Therein, the *tralaṇas* [attain liberation].

The Kṣatriyas [emerge] from the thighs; the Vaiśyas from the two thighs; and the Śūdras from the two feet. Then, at the end of that night, as the Brāhmaṇa contemplates dissolution, the Kṣatriyas and the others emerge from those very places—the mouth and so forth—because their respective actions (karma) were more predominant. During that period of dissolution, there is no destruction of the earth beyond its expansion of one *yojana*. Now, when the Brāhmaṇa reaches the end of his lifespan, that dissolution is called the Great Dissolution (*mahāpralaya*). In that state, the Brāhmaṇa remains within the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*).

Then [the elements dissolve] into the five gross elements: earth into water, water into fire, fire into air, air into ether, ether into the ego-principle (*ahaṃkāra*), the ego-principle into the great principle (*mahattattva*), and the great principle into primordial nature (*prakṛti*). Thus, all beings, with their merit and demerit undiminished, enter into dissolution. When the Blessed One, desiring to create, agitates primordial nature and the individual soul (*puruṣa*), then those elements emerge spontaneously from within the womb of karma.

As Parāśara stated in the *Śrī Viṣṇupurāṇa* regarding the cause of the world’s origin: "Since the potencies for creation, which constitute the causal principle of *pradhāna*, [proceed] from Him... The "potencies for creation" are their respective karmas; these alone are the primary cause of creation, while all others are instrumental causes. This has been declared by the venerable Jaimini in the *Bhuvanakośa-praśna*: "In this regard, [the question is]... [The text continues with the citation].

[Verse 61] Karma is not exhausted even in hundreds of millions of *kalpas* unless it has been experienced; likewise, for those who have not attained self-realization (*asmanām*), there is no experiencing of the fruits of karma without the body, and so forth. In this context, the meaning is that there is the destruction of the entire earth. Similarly, yogis whose various sins have been burnt by the fire of knowledge, having concentrated their minds upon the objects [of meditation] and having made that mind firmly composed, they depart—that is, they cast off the body. They go to the state of non-return (*anivṛtim*). That is the ultimate liberation (*ātyantikam śreyaḥ*). [Verses 62, 63, 64]

65. Ma. Ṭī.: Now, since the increase of the terrestrial globe is heard of [in the scriptures] from Brahmā onwards, the surface area of the terrestrial globe at the end of that day has been stated by Laṭa. To explain: the circumference of the earth (bhūvyāsa) stated by Laṭa is 1050 yojanas. The increase in yojanas for this [globe] at the end of that day is measured as 29,097 (saptaka-abhra-navāśva). For this purpose, the circumference of the earth at the end of a day of Brahmā is 30,147 (sat-indra-triṃśat-bhita).

When this [number] is divided by twenty-two, the circumference (paridhi) is obtained as slightly less than that stated by the rule "by the mountains" (sailaiḥ); it is taken with its fractional parts as 947; 47; 1; 30. The product resulting from the multiplication of these two is correctly established as 2,856,338,557. Thus, even in the opinion of Laṭṭa, since the product is accepted as the result without being explicitly asked for, the fact that his intention was not fully understood indicates that Bhāskara’s criticism reveals your own lack of knowledge.

To the objection that "the fault does not cause pain because one is detached from the bonds of existence," he says "vṛddhiḥ" (increase) in the *Indravajrā* meter: "In the day of the wandering Brahmā, on the surface of the earth—that is, upon the entire surface of the terrestrial globe—there would be an increase (*vṛddhi*) of one *yojana* [per day] due to the falling of grass, trees, living beings, mountains, stones, and so forth, brought down by the earth. Thus, at the beginning of a *kalpa*, the initial circumference of the earth would be two *yojanas* greater."

The sense is this: although it is stated that "on the day of Hiraṇyagarbha, the earth (Kāśyapī) increases by a hundred thousand *yojanas* on all sides," such an increase of that magnitude is not well-known; therefore, your [previous] statement is incorrect. Now, one might ask: "Even so, why have you not stated the surface area of the earth based on the initial circumference, which is greater than twice the diameter (*yojana*)? To this, he says: "In the dissolution (*laya*) related to Brahmā. This means when the dissolution has begun.

The meaning is that since the destruction of the earth occurs gradually as it increases by one *yojana* at a time, and likewise, because there is no stability in the increase of the earth, such a state of the globe exists at the end of the kalpa; furthermore, for us, there is no purpose in the result of that [calculation], and thus it is not accepted. Now, as an incidental discussion, he states the time of the destruction of the entire earth with the words "prākṛtika" (natural). At the time of dissolution connected to primordial nature (*prakṛti*), there is the destruction of the complete earth. || 62 ||

But surely, that which is artificial and made of clay meets its destruction at the end of the Creator’s night; thus, everything from Mount Meru onwards perishes upon the dissolution of the Creator. By this statement using the present tense (*laṭ*), it is established that there is a contradiction with the doctrine that all the earth perishes at the dissolution of Brahmā, whereas [according to some] there is a destruction of the increase by one *yojana* at the end of each day of Brahmā. Therefore, wishing to describe the fourfold dissolution (*laya*) in order, he first describes the first dissolution with an *upajāti* verse, beginning with "In the day" (*dine*).

92. [Śaulādhyāya] – 1981. Regarding that dissolution (*pralaya*) wherein living beings are destroyed day by day, every single day; wherein the elements (*bhūta*) and living beings (*prāṇin*) here abandon their mastery (*svāmya*); they call that [dissolution] "daily" (*dainandina*), according to the internal classification, as is certain (*hi*). The remaining words [of the verse] are: "the former teachers" (*pūrvācāryāḥ*). At the end of the period of many days, that destruction of beings (*bhūtavināśa*) which occurs, they call that "pertaining to Brahmā" (*brāhma*), according to its internal classification.

Now, one might object: since Brahmā perishes at the end of that day, how can there be a dissolution (*laya*) of living beings into him? To this, he says: "The beings" (*bhūtāni*). Because, for that reason, the beings—meaning living creatures—go to, or enter, the body of Brahmā (*brahmatanu*). Thus, even though there is no destruction of Brahmā himself, there is a dissolution of the beings within his body; hence it is called the "dissolution into Brahmā" (*brahmalaya*). At the end of that day: starting from that time until its conclusion, there is a gradual destruction through an increase of [the cosmic egg] by a *yojana* each day; thus, there is no contradiction. || 63 ||

Now, the third dissolution (*laya*) and its specific distinction are described by means of an *upajāti* verse: "The Brahma-dissolution" (*brāhma*). At the end of the hundred years of Brahmā’s life, upon the destruction of Brahmā, all beings go to—that is, they enter—the *prakṛti* (primordial nature) for this reason. The meaning is that they become merged (*līna*) within *prakṛti*. As the Blessed One has said: "O son of Kuntī, at the end of a *kalpa*, all beings go to my own *prakṛti*; again, at the beginning of a *kalpa*, I emit them forth."

For this reason, the best among the sons of Kuntī have described such a dissolution—distinguished by its intermediate divisions—as being "pertaining to primordial nature" (*prākṛtika*), that is, connected with *prakṛti*; thus, what was stated in the preceding verse should be investigated. As for the sequence of dissolution therein: here, along with all beings, the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) dissolves into the cosmic egg; that [egg], composed of the five elements, dissolves there: earth into water, water into fire, fire into air, air into ether, ether into the ego-principle (*ahaṃkāra*), the ego-principle into the Great Principle (*mahattattva*), and the Great Principle into its own source, primordial nature (*prakṛti*).

Now, one might ask: since the individual souls (*jīvas*) are in a state of non-distinction following the dissolution (*pralaya*), how is the possibility of a new creation established? To this, he says: "Not so" (*na iti*). Therefore, after the dissolution, when a disturbance arises in the modification of *prakṛti* due to the Lord’s desire to create, the elements that were dissolved are indeed [reproduced]. This is because, even upon the dissolution of those elements, the collection of previously acquired good and bad karma exists for each soul in the form of a "package" (*saṃpuṭa*), as it constitutes their respective aggregate. For the sake of experiencing those various karmas, they are brought forth individually—that is, they are created again.

Thus, at the dissolution of Brahmā, the worlds—whose merit and demerit remain undiminished—enter the body of Brahmā according to the order prescribed in the Vedas: the Brāhmaṇas into his mouth, the Kṣatriyas into his two arms, the Vaiśyas into his two thighs, and the Śūdras into his two feet. Then, during the intermediate period, as Brahmā contemplates creation, the Brāhmaṇas and the other classes emerge spontaneously from the locations of his mouth and so forth, due to their internal connection with the vessels of karma.

Likewise, even during the daily dissolution (*dainaṃdinapralaya*), living beings who reside in whatever world they occupy by the power of their own karma are born again on earth through the force of other karmas once that karma is exhausted. As it is said, "When merit is spent, they enter the world of mortals," there is no contradiction regarding their re-creation.

This is because of the statement in the *Viṣṇu Purāṇa*: "Since the powers of being created (*sṛjya-śaktayaḥ*) have become the primary agents," the meaning of which is that those very powers of being created—namely, their past actions (*karmāṇi*)—are the principal cause in creation, while all others are merely instrumental causes. Furthermore, this is supported by the Lord’s own words: "Taking hold of My own nature (*prakṛti*), I send forth again and again this entire multitude of beings, which is powerless under the sway of nature. Thus, it is by the power of *prakṛti*—that is, the force of past actions—that the universe is manifested.

Bhaṭṭoji: "By reason" means by the power of its own nature (*svabhāva*).
