The meaning is that [karma] does not perish; for it has been said: "Karma that has not been experienced does not perish even in hundreds of millions of eons; whatever karma, whether auspicious or inauspicious, has been performed must necessarily be experienced. This is the intended sense. (64) Now, with a *upajāti* verse, he concludes the fourth section, the pair of verses called "Liberation" (*mukti*), beginning with "The expansion of the scripture" (*śāstrāsphīti*). Because of which reason, for the practitioner (*yāgin*)—one who is devoted to the practice of yoga as taught in the Yoga scriptures—...

Having withdrawn the mind from the objects of the senses and having fixed it upon Hari, the Supreme Lord—having brought about its dissolution—they abandon uncertainty regarding the Divine and attain non-rebirth through oneness with the Supreme Lord. For this reason, they say that the dissolution of the yogi is an ultimate dissolution (*atyantika-pralaya*) distinguished by an intermediate state, as was stated in the previous verse; this should be understood here as well. [Objection: But surely, because actions (*karman*) are infinite, their cessation is not possible.

Because those [karmas] can only be destroyed by experience and cannot be blocked from arising again, he says "by knowledge" (jñāna). Knowledge is the knowledge of the Self (ātmajñāna); those by whom all—both merits and sins—are burnt, that is, reduced to ashes, by that fire which is that [knowledge], are so described. Just as, O Arjuna, a well-kindled fire reduces fuel to ashes, so does the fire of knowledge reduce all actions to ashes. (Gītā 4.37)

The statement, "The fire of knowledge reduces all actions to ashes," means that through devotion to the Lord and through knowledge, there is indeed the possibility of non-destruction (anirdhṛti)—that is, the destruction—of all actions other than those already commenced (*prārabdha*), even in the absence of their being experienced. This is because of the Lord's own declaration: "Taking hold of My own nature (*prakṛti*), I project again and again this entire multitude of beings, which is powerless under the sway of nature. The sense is that since the body and its functions arise solely from the influence of nature—which is caused by past actions (*sāñcīna-karman*)—there is no logical inconsistency in the cessation of such effects [once the cause is exhausted].

And so it was said by the Blessed One in this [text]: "Having restrained all the gates of the senses and having fixed the mind within the heart, holding the vital breath in the head, established in the yoga of concentration; uttering the single-syllabled Brahman 'Om' and remembering Me, he who departs, casting off the body, attains the supreme goal. Having reached Me, those great-souled ones do not undergo rebirth—which is a transient abode of suffering—having attained the highest perfection."

"The Unmanifest is called the Indestructible; they call That the supreme goal, attaining which they do not return—that is My supreme abode. The word "ca" (and) indicates something other than what has been mentioned, signifying that there is no [other] dissolution. Furthermore, the Great Dissolution (*mahāpralaya*) is the liberation of all living beings. However, that [Great Dissolution] never occurs for us, as it has already been refuted in another scripture by such statements as "this world... and so forth; this is indicated under the guise of the conclusion with the words "iti" (thus). "Iti" means in the manner stated. Destruction (*tayaḥ*)—the perishing of living beings—is fourfold, consisting of four types.

The destruction of the unconscious (acetana), however, is of only one kind. Regarding those who do not oppose the Sun (Bhāskara)—[as stated] by Vyāsa: "Mountains, arrows, swords, serpents, fire, earth, water, fish, elephants, and horses"—the circumference is 1050, and [the results are] 3298 and 4048. The surface area (pṛṣṭhaphala) is said to be measured by the product of the parts of the wheel and the number nine, but not otherwise. To explain: "mountains" (naga) refers to mountains; "arrows" (śilīmukha) refers to shafts; "sword" (karavāla) means iron (vaṅga); and "that upon which one does not fall" is the mountain-arrow (nagaśilīmukha).

"Parvataśatru" means Indra. "Bāṇabhūḥ" refers to one who was born from Bāṇa; he is both that [Indra] and a moving being (*jaṅgama*), namely the specific living entity Svāmikārtikeya. His "flame" (*jvalana*) is his mouth, as it is well known that fire resides in the mouth of a deity. To convey that Svāmikārtikeya is a deity, the word "flame," which denotes fire, is applied metaphorically (*lakṣaṇayā*) to his mouth. Because he is famously known to have six faces, there is a number six, just as in the expression "six fires" (*ṣaḍ-vahni*). (Golādhyāya, with commentary, verse 95). It is a fact.

The term *iṣu* refers to the wind (*vāyu*) because it "goes by means of smoke" (*idhuvannacchati*). From that [wind] is born the cloud (*megha*), for according to the statement of Kālidāsa, "a cloud is indeed a conjunction of smoke, light, water, and wind," the wind constitutes the predominant portion within the composition of the five great elements (*pañcamahābhūta*). By the word *meṣa*, the number seventeen is well-known. When the two Aśvins are multiplied by that [number], they become thirty-four; this includes the four [signs] beginning with Mṛga and Jāvin (Mṛgaśiras, Ārdrā, Punarvasu, and Puṣya) from the middle group of six signs (*madhyaṣaṭka*).

Therefore, they say that the passage beginning with "Thus, [the world] is defective like the surface of a ball" and ending with "the fourteen Daityas" is useless; but that is not so. For the meanings of the words are inconsistent, and because there is the fault of being long-winded, like the story of the snake and the basket. Now he describes the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*): "The earth, the mountains, the gods, the Dānavas, and humans, as well as the circles of the celestial bodies moving in the sky—all this, arranged in the order of the worlds one above the other, is within the belly of the vessel of the cosmic egg. (66) This is clear. (66)

Now, he restates the measure of the solar egg (brahmāṇḍa) mentioned by another, even though it was previously described, as it arises in this context: "Those who know the science of light (jyotiḥśāstra) declare that the circumference of the sky is these [number of] yojanas: 187,129,692,000,000,000,000."

Regarding the rim of the shell of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍakaṭāha*), some physicians call it the "Jathu" [the lower part of the abdomen], while other learned experts of the Purāṇas call it the "invisible-visible mountain. Those who know the entire sphere (*gola*) as pure as an *āmalaka* fruit held in the palm of the hand have declared that this is the circumference of the sky whose darkness is destroyed by the rays of the sun. Whether this cosmic egg be measured or not, in one *kalpa*, the sun traverses *yojanas*.

Whatever measure was previously stated here by our predecessors as being called "kakṣā," that is the opinion held by us. The meaning is that because it lacks a valid basis for measurement and because there is no practical purpose for it, the measurement of the *brahmāṇḍa* (the cosmic egg) has not been described by us. Thus ends the chapter on the "Description of the World" (*bhuvanakośa*) in the *Śrī Golabhāṣya*. [Commentary: Now, under the guise of concluding the previously mentioned arrangement of the earth and other spheres, he speaks regarding the *brahmāṇḍa* in the *vasantatilaka* meter, beginning with the words "kṣudhaḥ... etc. That... [text fragment].

This has been established: all things beginning with the earth exist within the belly of the vessel that is the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), meaning inside the sphere characterized as the cosmic egg. In response to the question "What is that?", he says: "The earth, mountains, gods, Dānavas, humans, etc. This refers to the earth, the mountains (parvatas), the thirty-three gods, the Dānavas, humans, and those who have been mentioned as "immobile" (*agā*) by virtue of the word "etc. (*ādi*), as well as the circular orbits of the planets (*viṣṇya*) and the celestial bodies moving in the sky (*gaganecara*).

The sequence of connection is as follows: the sphere (gola) is the support of the constellations; the orbits (kakṣā) are the successive upward positions of the planets; and the ether (ākāśa) is [the support] above them. This is that which possesses the splendor of the cosmic egg (bhuvanakośa). [In the commentary on verse 75, line 80: "In succession" (samuccaye); "above, above" means above the arrangement of the constellations. The meaning is: "as far as all that has been described by the verse beginning with 'The syllable Om, the state of Lak, the void, the great, the Janas, then the Tapoloka, Satyaloka, and others...'"—all that is meant here. 66.

Now, as an incidental matter, for the sake of knowing the measurement of the circumference of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍagola*), he restates here in the *śārdūlavikrīḍita* meter that which constitutes the beginning of the chapter on orbits (*kakṣādhyāya*) within the Middle Section (*madhyādhikāra*): "By [the number] multiplied by ten million," and so forth. The essential meaning is that this is the measurement of the circumference of the cosmic egg as accepted by the astronomers. (67) Now, since there is a doubt as to whether this circumference of the cosmic egg is external or internal, he states the certainty through the previously mentioned verse: "With the hands... and so forth.

This has been explained previously [verse 68]. Now, he restates his own view regarding the measurement of the Brahmāṇḍa (the cosmic egg), intended to clarify the calculation according to his own system, using the Bhramaravajrā meter—beginning with "brahmāṇḍam. The meaning has already been established previously [verse 69]. Now, he concludes the section on the questions and answers concerning the earth with a single verse, stating: "Thus, in the Golādhyāya, the Bhuvanakośa [ends]. This refers to the Golādhyāya, which is the latter half of the Siddhāntaśiromaṇi.

The treasury, that is, the collection, of the fourteen worlds consisting of the earth and other elements has been described by way of their configuration; this is the meaning. In this work composed by the son of the mathematician Raṅganātha—who is to be served by a lineage of virtues and the excellence of the Vaiyāsaki [Vyāsa]—this section on the configuration of the earth and other worlds, joined with the rays of the *Śiromaṇi*, concludes here. || 1 ||

Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, the *Bhuvanakośādhyāya* (The Chapter on the Structure of the World), in the *Siddhāntaśiromaṇimarīci*, composed by the venerable Raṅganātha Gaṇaka, the sovereign of all astronomers, who is also known by the name Munīśvara. Now, above the earth, there are seven layers of wind (*vāyuskandha*). [They are]: *Abhahīna*, *Bhuva-vāyu*, *Āvaha*, *Pravaha*—which is the first here—then *Udvaha*, and that which is named *Saṃvaha*.

Another wind, even more auspicious than that, is the *parivaha*; from this [root] comes the well-known wind called *pravaha*. || 1 || Ten *yojanas* beyond the earth, O mountain-dweller, lies the ocean; above that is the *pravaha* wind, which moves eternally. Its position is situated in the middle. || 2 || Because it is joined with the spheres of the stars and the celestial bodies, this cage of the constellations (*bhapañjara*), together with the circle of the sky-goers, is made to revolve by the force of the *pravaha* wind. || 3 ||

[This concludes] the commentary on verse 123b. Now, regarding the question of how the lack of precision (*asphuṭatā*) arises for that which is obtained through proportion (*anupāta*) by means of the revolutions (*bhagaṇa*) of the planets and so forth, the *madhyatithi* [chapter], which follows the *madhya* [chapter], is being explained. Therein, with the intent of describing the causes of the motion of the fundamental planets, the author first states the divisions of wind (*vāyu*) in the *Vasantatilaka* meter, beginning with "The wind of the earth" (*bhūvāyu*). Here, within the interior of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*).

These seven winds are known to be spherical in shape; this is the meaning of what is stated in the Purāṇas. To the question "What are these?", their sequence is given as "Vāyu" and so forth. Among them, the first is the *mayugola* (the sphere of wind), which has the form of the central terrestrial globe. Because of its connection with the earth, there is first a sphere of wind surrounding the earth; this is the meaning. Now, since wind is mobile, how does that wind blow? To this he says: "Āvaha. It blows (*vahati*) all around (*ā*), hence it is *āvaha*.

The meaning is that its circulation faces all directions and its movement is not fixed. This is because of the statement by others: "It is celebrated as the *pravaha* wind. By this, the claim that the *āvaha* wind resides twelve *yojanas* from the earth—that it is like water here and is the cause of contraction—and that the *pañcāṅgati* wind is therefore called *āvaha*, which describes the arising of the wind, is refuted. For that reason, since its position is above the *yuga* (the distance of four *yojanas*), there is a second [wind] in the form of the *pravaha* sphere (*golārūpa*) due to that expansion.

Following that, from the *pravaha* wind, five *dūrvas* (intervals) further on—this is the meaning—is the *udvaha* wind, which has the form of *ai* and *au*. The fourth is the wind-sphere named *saṃvaha*; by the word "and" (*ca*), the meaning is that it is above the *vahavāyu*. From there, by the word "also" (*api*), the meaning is "above" (*ūrdhvam*). Another, the fifth wind-sphere, is named *suvaha*. By this [explanation], the *suvaha* is not included among the seven winds due to ignorance, for fear of the impossibility [of having more than seven].

Therefore, the statement "udvaha, saṃvaha, parivaha, parāvaha, pūrvavaha, aparavaha, uttaravaha, and parāvaha" should be disregarded. Among these, following *bahu*, there is one preceded by *pari*. The meaning is that the sixth wind-system, named *parivaha*, consists of that which has the word *pari* preceding it and the word *vaha* following it. The seventh is the *babhru-yugola*, the *parāvaha*. It is situated above the *ujjahā* winds; by this, it is indicated that there is no wind-system above it.

Āvaha, Pravaha, Udvaha, Saṃvaha, Svādi-vaha, Parivaha, and Parāvaha—these are considered here to be the seven successive branches (skandhas) of the wind that sustains the universe; some call this the Āvaha wind, as stated by Śrīpati. (1) Now, for the purpose of knowing the initial position of the second wind, [the author describes] the extent of the first wind-sphere from the earth, and the nature of the movement of the second wind-sphere supported by it, in the Upajāti meter, beginning with the words "From the earth" (bhūmeḥ).

From the surface of the earth-globe, extending outwards on all sides for twelve *yojanas*, there is the terrestrial wind (*bhūvāyu*). This means that the [atmospheric] limit extends up to that point. By this, it is indicated that the outer circumference of the wind-sphere is separated from the center of the earth by a diameter consisting of twelve *yojanas* (half the diameter of the earth). The orbit of the terrestrial wind around the earth is stated to be five hundred and thirty-three *yojanas*.

The virtuous declare that its diameter is the oceans, mountains, and the sky; this is stated in the *Lakṣokti*. Furthermore, it is stated by Ladhvaryabhaṭa: "In all directions, within the earth-wind (*bhūvāyu*), there are sixty million [yojanas]. Here, in the earth-wind, there are clouds (*ambuda*), lightning (*vidyut*), and—by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*)—rainbows, celestial cities (*gāndharvanagara*), hail, and other such phenomena.

The extinguished firebrand, gold, the bow of Indra (the rainbow), lightning, and so forth, as well as earth, wind, sky-cities, halos, and other such phenomena associated with the [four] Śrīs, are observed; these are summarized here. Within the ocean of pure water stands the Vāḍava fire; submerged by the weight of the waters, it rises up in the form of columns of smoke that drift everywhere in the sky until they reach the wind. Heated by the rays of the sun, those sparks become lightnings; by this it is shown that [the fire] arises from the sweet-water [ocean], which is the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of the central region.

A succession of water-laden clouds consists of a combination of smoke, light, water, and air, and these are insentient. Their non-arrival every day is due to the absence of velocity induced by the will of such a Lord (Īśvara) and other factors; their arrival occurs when that [will] is present. If it is asked, "What is the determining factor here?", the answer is no, because the will of such a Lord acts as the regulator. As for thunder, it arises from the contact of fire with water, while the tossing of smoke here and there is caused by the wind.

Due to the force of the action (*karman*) born from the conjunction of those two, [the rain] falls suddenly from the sky. Regarding this, Karka says: "From the earth, through the accumulation of fierce winds, dust is raised; when the circle of clouds is freed from impurity, the coalescence of water droplets occurs here through their mixing. These fall as stones and then flow again upon the ground. Suddenly, the lightning-fire (*vaidyuta-tejas*), mixed with particles of earth," [descends].

A whirlwind is a mass of dust bound together by opposing winds—one favorable and one adverse—that have fallen upon it; for generally, these particles of dust do not spread during the rainy season. That [whirlwind] is inferred to be of three kinds: the earthy, which is consumed by the ground; the fiery, which arises from fires originating there; and that which is produced by the waters of pits and lakes situated on the earth. There is also the occurrence of lightning and thunder. As for the rainbow: it is the various colors of the sun struck by the wind.

"Those rays which appear in the shape of a bow are called Indra’s bow," so said the teacher Varāhamihira. "The intensely powerful rays of the sun and moon, formed into circles by the wind, appearing in various colors and shapes against a sky with thin clouds, are called a halo (*pariveṣa*). Thus ends the section on the halo.

O Goddess, those whose course is vast, which you traverse with your wind, remain far beyond all the sky-dwellers; they do not abide in fixed paths, yet they dwell beneath the moon, supported by it. Like the moon, they consist of water and shine like the sun; they are situated at the junction of the *āvaha* and *pravaha* winds. It is well known that when the eastern wind attains a state of stillness, these stars fall here and there by the power of their own motion.

At the end of the rains, the waters are dried up by the wind and become sparse; then, with only a slight residue of dust remaining, they fall upon the surface of the earth. By those particles in the form of dust, the earth is covered, O Niyoḍrama. Those particles, however, are again dried up by the sun's heat and, scattered by the wind, dissolve into the firmament. This is the description of the dissolution of dust, which causes the destruction of the milk of the cows and buffaloes that sustain that dust.

The twilight glow, arising from the dust and smoke rising up and settling in the sky at the ends of the quarters, shines with a reddish hue through the rays of the sun. By that [glow], which reveals even objects with sparse parts, the visible world appears as if it were not yet turned red, like a mass of hair. That twilight color is to be understood as occurring both at the beginning of the day and at its end.

It is well known in all other treatises that on the night of the full moon (*rākā*), at the beginning of the night, there is likewise the "moon-beam" (*indukara*); therefore, it should be understood that no further inquiry into this matter is necessary here. Now, these clouds and so forth, having indeterminate movements, are possible within the *pravaha* wind. Consequently, they cannot exist even in the *apūrva* wind, because it is impossible for planets and constellations to be obscured by clouds there. Thus, it is rightly stated that they reside in the atmospheric wind (*bhūvāyu*), and [the text says] "above that."

The second [wind] is the *pravaha*; therefore, situated between those two, that *pravaha* wind-sphere moves perpetually and incessantly toward the west, traveling in a westerly direction. He states that it does not have an irregular motion by saying "of that" (*tasya*). Its "middle position" (*madhyasaṃsthā*) means its central station. (Verse 13.48, Golādhyāya, Āryabhaṭīya)—the meaning is that it is situated with a velocity neither less nor more. By the word "but" (*tu*), it is implied that other winds have irregular motions.

It has been indicated that [the stars] move facing an indefinite direction. Now, he establishes the constant revolution of the fundamental stellar sphere (*bhacakra*), which is the subject at hand, by means of an *upajāti* verse—beginning with "nakṣatra"—and so forth. "From this" means from the existence of this cause, namely, the *pravaha* wind. "By that" refers to the *pravaha* wind, which possesses a fixed motion directed toward the west.

This is the visible stellar cage! A cage for the support of the planets and constellations, composed of the five elements, spherical in shape, consisting of the central ether, blue in color, and fashioned by Brahmā; it is gathered together and rotates incessantly and unceasingly, with each part serving as its own substratum. Because it is enveloped by its own space, its substratum—the Pravaha wind—also remains unimpaired even while situated within this atmospheric region.

[Objection: Granted that the stellar sphere (*bhapañjara*) may revolve due to the impact of that [wind], how is the revolution of the planets, which is established by direct perception, to be accounted for? To this he says: "joined with the wheel of the sky-goers" (*khecaracakrayukta*). The "sky-goers" (*khecarāḥ*) are the planets; their *cī* is a collection, namely the seven planets; it is joined with these. Thus, it is not the case that only the stellar sphere revolves due to the impact of the Pravaha wind; rather, the planets also revolve in accordance with it—this is the sense. [Objection: But how can the planets [revolve] along with the stellar sphere?

Because there is no connection [between them], the rotation of the stellar sphere (bhapañjara) is an error on their part; how could that be? Furthermore, since the stars and their cage (pañjara) are distinct, it is illogical for the stars to rotate when the cage rotates. Therefore, he says: "by the sky-goers [occupying] the stellar orbits" (nakṣatrakakṣākhacaraiḥ). For what reason is this stellar sphere accompanied by the stars, the orbits, and the sky-goers arranged in ascending order? The word *kakṣā* is used here as a conventional term (rūḍha). It is joined with, or associated with, those [three].

And thus, although there is a distinction between the stellar sphere (*bhagraha*) and the planetary sphere (*grahanakṣatrapañjara*) by virtue of their being the container (*ādhāra*) and the contained (*ādheya*), it is well known that when the container moves, the contained also moves; therefore, there is no flaw in the motion of the stars, for otherwise the status of the "stellar sphere" would be untenable. The point is that since the gnomon (*śaṅku*), the *viṣuva*, and the *saṃgraha* are situated in space within the stellar sphere, a relationship exists between them and the stellar sphere by way of their being supported by their own substratum; consequently, the revolution of the planets by means of the *pravaha* wind located within the stellar sphere is also logically established.

In this context, by the power of the cage (pañjara), the stars have been established here and there within the enclosure of the physical form that serves as their substratum by Brahmā; otherwise, the impossibility of their being consumed [by the fire] would follow. Therefore, since the stars do not actually reside within the cage itself, they do not possess the quality of "wandering" (*khacaratva*). It should be understood that the absence of such a supporting stream for the planets is due to their specific nature. However, some maintain that the conceptualization of the cage as the substratum of the stars is merely for the sake of measurement.

Since it is joined with the winds, the planets, the asterisms, and the celestial spheres, it is therefore said that the stellar sphere (bhapañjara) revolves in the sky along with the Prabhāṇila wind; the meaning is that the planets, being situated beneath the asterisms, revolve by their own motions through the Prabhāṇila wind alone. This is not so, for it is observed that grass, leaves, garments, and the like move through the atmosphere due to the support provided by the wind generated by them.

Because [if one were to interpret it otherwise], there would be the consequence of redundancy with the first half of the initial verse beginning with "having created Bhadraka," which describes the placement of the stellar sphere (*bhacakra*) in the wind; and because there would be the consequence of the first half of the subsequent verse—“and likewise the pole-star at its end”—becoming meaningless.

Furthermore, O Venerable Sir, since you accept that even for the luminous spheres (*tejogola*) of the stars there is a supporting substratum (*upaṣṭambhakatva*) consisting of a portion of the Earth, the simultaneous revolution by means of the wind would be untenable due to the establishment of relative heaviness and lightness resulting from the observation of varying degrees of brilliance among them. Moreover, if the stars were supported by material forms, the doctrine of mean motion (*madhyagativāsanā*) [would be contradicted]. Ma0 Ṭī0: By means of the wind, there is a revolution of the support; this is because the simultaneous revolution of the stars situated upon it—whose orbs possess unequal degrees of heaviness and lightness—is thereby established.

Nor should it be argued that the planets (*graha*) must likewise be conceived as having material form (*mūrta*). For this is untenable because the upward and downward motion of the planets—which is established by perception through the observation of their small-sized orbs—is otherwise inexplicable. Furthermore, the movement of the orbs would not be established by the motion of the [material] spheres themselves. Moreover, since the spheres consist of the five gross elements (*pañcamahābhūta*), it would follow that the planets and lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) would never be visible. Finally, postulating such a distinct entity is cumbersome (*gaurava*), for all conceptual construction must be rooted in what is observed.

By this [explanation], it is shown that above the seven planets there is the stellar sphere (*bhacakra*), and above that is the space designated as the zodiacal signs (*rāśi*). That [stellar sphere] revolves once around the axis of the constellations due to its fixed westward motion. By that very revolution, the space of the stellar sphere—along with the spaces occupied by Saturn and the others, which are endowed with life, possess parts, and are interconnected—revolves toward the west. However, the spaces of Saturn and the others move toward the east by their own power.

O you whose pure consciousness is like a stainless jewel, when possessed by elements such as *bhūta* and so forth, the stars and planets situated in their respective spaces are perceived exactly as they are by those on the surface of the earth. Just as a lamp situated inside a gem-encrusted vessel is seen by those at a distance exactly as it is, so too these specific living beings (*jīva-viśeṣa*), who are self-abiding, shaped like the forehead, endowed with special powers, and—like the earth—unsupported, are designated by the word "Self" (*ātman*).

Just as a gem or similar object is supported by the spaces [within its structure], even though it has emerged from them, it is carried here and there; thus, the movement of the planets situated therein is metaphorically designated by people as the "movement of space. The Yavana doctrine—that these spaces are joined together like the sheaths of a plantain flower—is refuted. This may be so.

To account for the rising and setting of the stars and planets, it would involve the conceptual complexity of postulating a "driving wind" (*pravaha-vāyu*) with a fixed motion directed toward the western quarter; however, for the sake of the aforementioned explanation, it is simpler to assume that the celestial sphere itself possesses a fixed eastward motion, consisting of revolutions completed in sixty sidereal ghaṭīs, while the stellar cage (*bhapañjara*) remains stationary. And as for the perception of contradiction: just as a person standing on a ship does not perceive the stationary shore as moving due to the ship's slow motion, so too there is no such error here.

Some say that the sphere of the stars, though moving with the motion of the earth's revolution, appears as if it were perfectly stable; however, this is refuted in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*. If the earth were rotating, how could birds reach their own nests? How could arrows released into the sky fall in the direction opposite to that of the earth's rotation? If the earth rotates toward the east, the clouds would move toward the west! Furthermore, if it were moving slowly, how could its revolution be completed in a single day?

By this playful argument: Just as birds wearing the sky as their garment do not fail to reach their nests because of the earth's rotation; furthermore, alas, even the clouds would not be such profuse rain-givers due to the long journey to the eastern region; and moreover, by the friction produced by the momentum of the terrestrial globe, comets and other celestial bodies would also be driven toward the western direction.

Even the peaks of the mountain-like palaces fall down; therefore, the multitude of stars whirls, while the Earth remains as immovable as a mountain—this was stated by the venerable Patañjali, thereby refuting that [opposing] position. Furthermore, the *Sūryasiddhānta* states: "The circle of the stars is fixed to the Earth and impelled by the Pravaha winds; it revolves incessantly, and upon it, the orbits of the planets follow in their respective order. (3)

Now, confirming by means of an illustration the eastward motion of the planets, even though it was not previously observed, he says: "Therefore, because the planet moves upon the zodiacal sphere with a swift eastward motion due to its own westward motion, it does not appear [to move eastward], just as a worm moving on a potter's wheel appears to go backward. (4)

11.4 [Golādhyāya]—Bhānu Daivajña: Now, since the observation of planets situated in Aśvinī at one time appearing later in Bharaṇī and so forth would otherwise be inexplicable, the previously stated eastward motion of the planets—as in the verse beginning "the stellar sphere moves toward the west"—is inconsistent because it contradicts direct perception. Therefore, he refutes that [view] with a verse in the Upajāti meter: "The planets (kheṭāḥ), by means of the swift westward motion of that stellar sphere (bhaṣañjara) due to the Pravaha wind... [This refers to their motion resulting from that westward velocity.]

The stellar sphere (*bhacakra*) is perceived as moving westward by means of a revolution of the wheel associated with sixty *nakṣatra-yojanas*. However, although the stars are actually moving eastward with a very slight velocity—measured in *kṣāyojana* units—generated by the westward-moving *pravaha* wind, they do not appear to move eastward across the eastern half of the ecliptic (*krāntivṛtta*). This is because their eastward motion is extremely diminished when compared to the specific circumference of the stellar cage (*bhapañjara*) that constitutes the ecliptic. Thus, while they are indeed traveling eastward, they do not manifest that motion.

The meaning is that the perception of the planets (*graha*) as having an eastward motion does not occur through direct observation (*pratyakṣataḥ*) by people. This is because if the westward and eastward motions were equal, the movement of the planets would be impossible to perceive. However, if the eastward motion were greater, it would follow that the eastward motion is directly perceived while the westward motion remains unperceived; therefore, since there is no lesser [westward] motion, the eastward motion is not seen through direct observation—this is the intended sense.

It has been indicated that for the asterisms (*nakṣatra*), there is no prior motion (*pūrvagati*) to be observed, as is the case with the planets. Now, if it is asked: "While the westward motion of the planets is caused by the Pravaha wind, what is the cause of their eastward motion?"—the answer is no. This is because, whereas in the phrase "by its other motion" (*tasyāparīghragatyā*) the connection to another factor is explicitly stated, in the phrase "by its own eastward motion" (*svapūrvagatyā*) no such connection to another is mentioned; thus, the eastward motion of the planets exists inherently. Furthermore, it is not the case that the asterisms and planets move toward the west solely by their own power.

It should not be argued that [the stars move] in the east due to the *pravaha* wind, because of the assumption that it moves toward the east; for if the *pravaha* wind were present even at the location of the stellar sphere (*bhapañjara*), it would follow that the constellations (*nakṣatra*) would also be observed to have an eastward motion. Furthermore, the postulation of a wind is necessary for the purpose of maintaining the stellar sphere within the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*). Moreover, there is unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*) in postulating two winds: one for the support and another for the dependent motion.

Furthermore, because it would result in the planets having the same prior motion as their abandonment [of fixed positions], and because of the statement in the *Laghu-Vasiṣṭha-siddhānta* that "the western wind is the driver," [the following applies]. Although it has been stated that—since the planets reside in their respective spaces within the celestial sphere (gola) according to the sequence of their orbits beneath the stellar cage (bhapañjara), and thus their eastward motion is possible in the intermediate space—they move with a light eastward motion upon the dhacakra, this is inconsistent; nevertheless, in their own respective orbital spheres (kajhagola), they are in the eastern space.

Even as the planets move, the answer to the question of how far they have traveled consists in the knowledge of their velocity; this is possible through their respective orbits. Since the position of a planet on the celestial sphere (bhapañjara) is determined by a line drawn from its original position, and its new position is determined by a line drawn from its current displaced position, the distance between these two points along a segment of the ecliptic makes the knowledge of their motion possible. Because of their connection with the pravaha wind, the planets remain aligned along this same line; for this very reason, the orbital path (kakṣāvṛtta) is logically established.

It has been stated that [the motion] follows the form of the ecliptic; this is logical. Now, one might object: "In reality, the planets move eastward by their own power; therefore, because of that eastward movement, they ought to be visible at every moment. Yet, they are seen only after a certain interval to the west. To this, he says: "Like the rotation of a potter's wheel, it is a movement to the left (*vāmaga*). The word *iva* indicates an illustration.

Just as a potter, the maker of jars, has established for himself a wheel with its center fixed on a pivot, situated in the air, which produces the jar; when that wheel undergoes rotation produced by the movement of the staff, and moves toward a certain direction—that is its internal latent impression (*vāsanā*). Then, small creatures such as ants, which are subtle in form, do not perceive those moving along the circumference of the wheel’s rim in a direction opposite to it, due to their own activity.

It does not appear that they move by their own activity; rather, they appear to move as if following the rotation of a wheel. Similarly, although they move toward the eastern direction by their own power, due to the force of the *pravaha* wind, they appear to move toward the western direction alone—this is the meaning. If it is asked what the proof for this is, [the answer is: no [other proof is required].

On a potter’s wheel, at the point where a worm was located prior to its rotation, once that spot is struck with a stick and the rotation ceases, the sight of the worm does not occur at that very same spot; rather, it occurs at some distance in the direction opposite to the rotation, as established by the means of direct perception (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*). Now, one might object: "Is there not a conceptual burden (*gaurava*) in postulating a prior motion for the planets?"

Due to parsimony (*lāghava*), it is sufficient to account for the fact that a planet situated in Aśvinī appears to be in Bharaṇī and so forth simply by means of the observed revolution of the planets toward the western direction caused by the *pravaha* wind. To explain: since the stellar sphere (*bhapañjara*) is rotated by the *pravaha* wind in sixty *nākṣatra* ghaṭīs, the Sun’s orb—which is heavy and situated below it—cannot be moved by that [wind] along with the stellar sphere; therefore, Saturn experiences a lagging behind its position in the stellar sphere by sixty *nākṣatra* ghaṭīs toward the east.

Below that, in order, beginning with Jupiter and Mars and ending with the Moon, they become increasingly heavy; thus, their support from the preceding [sphere] increases further and further due to the action of the Pravaha wind. For this very reason, the constellations have a westward motion. Among them, the constellations are extremely swift, while those situated below them—Saturn and the others—are progressively slower in their motion. As it is said in the Siddhāntasundara: "In the sphere of the stars, the celestial body moves toward the western direction due to the force of the Pravaha wind."

It is said that the planets beginning with Mercury (Budha), Venus (Śukra), Mars (Bhauma), the Sun (Sūrya), Jupiter (Guru), and Saturn (Śani) are indeed intercepted from the east by their heaviness (*gurutva*). However, it cannot be argued that, because the size of the disks increases progressively for Mercury, Moon, Venus, Mars, Sun, Jupiter, and Saturn, there would consequently follow an increase in heaviness, and thus a corresponding progressive increase in parallax (*avalambana*) toward the east; for the parallax of the Moon's eclipse is not such as to allow for this [argument]. This is because, in accordance with the stated sequence, even though the disks are larger, their heaviness is accepted as following the order of their orbits (*kakṣā*).

Now, this [objection] is untenable: "The sun is a sphere of fire; the planets and stars are spheres of water"—by this scriptural statement, since there are greater portions of earth and water in the larger orbs, there would be an excess of weight. Consequently, because only earth and water possess gravity while the sun lacks it, the phenomenon of parallax (avalambana) would be impossible. If this is argued, we say no, because with the exception of the moon, the other planets and stars are accepted as being composed of fire. As for the moon, however, its nature as consisting of water is admitted because otherwise the curvature of its horns (śṛṅgonnati) could not be explained.

[Objection: "Alas! If this is so, then previously the impossibility of the Sun's support was established, whereas now the impossibility of support for all [planets] except the Moon is established; thus, the correct position has been supported. [Reply: No. Even though the terrestrial regions are composed of fire (*taijasa*), their status as supporting bases (*upaṣṭambhaka*) can be postulated, thereby establishing their gravity (*gurutva*). Now, how is it logical that the motion of the planets is obstructed by gravity?

If it is argued that—since Mercury is vastly larger than the lunar disc, and given the possibility of its greater density relative to it—the intervening space-measures (*kalās*) between the Moon and [Mercury] must indeed be greater than those between the Moon and [the other planets]—because you yourself accept that in all cases, including the luminous spheres of the planets and stars, the supporting substance is composed of earth; this is true.

In all cases, one must follow the effect; therefore, in the case of the deity [the moon], one follows the cause. Thus, in the lunar orb, because both water and earth are present, the heaviness is as it were greater due to the collection of two supporting substances, since it is supported by being the locus of heaviness. And in the case of lightning and so forth, because they are not the substratum of heaviness, they are drawn back toward oneself by the weight of the supporting earthly atoms alone—which, compared to the former, is lighter—just as a clod of earth and a tuft of grass are suspended from clouds.

In some cases, since you yourself accept a supporting factor (*upaṣṭambhaka*), it cannot be prevented by anyone that I likewise postulate such a thing elsewhere on the basis of its belonging to that same class. Furthermore, the diameter of the lunar disc is four hundred and eighty [yojanas], whereas that of the sun is six thousand and twenty-two and a half.

Therefore, it should not be argued that because the supporting matter for the orbs of the Sun and others is more abundant than the supporting matter for the orb of the Moon—which is extensive—it is impossible for the Sun and so forth to be smaller than the Moon. For in those cases, the supporting matter is accepted as being sparse, like a tuft of cotton. This same principle applies equally to Mars and the other planets. On this point, some say:

Because they are born from the most excellent dharma, because they possess a luminous nature (*taijasa*), and because they are not born from a womb, they lack both childhood and old age; thus, all those residing in the world of the Sun (*arkaloka*) possess an identical temperature. Furthermore, since the supporting medium there is also uniform, there is no downward support due to equal gravity alone. Nor is this contradicted by perception, for even in its absence, that [perception] is accounted for by its own specific function. Now, how is there equality of taste among these fruits?

If it is argued that "in those cases, this [change] is indeed a change in dimension (*parimāṇa-anyathātva*), because of the teaching [of such a change] and because of perception," we say no. For, following the expansion of light associated with those [objects], there is the possibility of a variation—either less or more—in the orbs of living beings that imitate the intensity of the light from gems and the like, which are of equal dimension; thus, the teaching was given with reference to the orbs themselves. As for perception, they say it is merely an illusion due to the defect of intervention (*vyavadhāna*); but that is not so.

Since, even though there is no difference in the degree of mutual separation between Arundhatī and Vasiṣṭha when they are seated in the same place, or among the individual stars of the Aśvinī and other constellations, we perceive differences in their smallness and largeness, it is impossible to assert that those dwelling in the same location possess bodies of equal size. Others, however, maintain that the solar orb, which is the subject of dispute, is devoid of a supporting substrate because it is not the locus of qualities [such as touch], like a lamp.

"That which is not thus is not thus, as for example gold"—this is the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) of the pervasion (*vyāpti*). The reason (*hetu*) is "because of being the locus of color and touch that are suppressed" (*abhibhūta-rūpa-sparśa-adhikaraṇatvāt*). The word "etc. (*ādi*) includes "moon-likeness" (*candravatva*), which serves to exclude deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in cases such as hailstones (*karakā*); otherwise, since un-suppressed color and touch exist there, and because it lacks the absence of a supporting medium (*upaṣṭambhaka-śūnyatva*), there would be the consequence of deviation. That is not correct, because the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*). Furthermore, the reason as formulated—including the property of fluidity (*dravatva*)—is absent from both the subject (*pakṣa*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) in the *Hetu-dṛṣṭānta-dīpa*.

It should not be argued that there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of the reason under discussion due to its absence in hailstones (*karaka*), because even though fluidity (*dravatva*) is counteracted by coldness (*śīta*) therein, it is not suppressed. For suppression does not mean a non-perception caused by a momentary direct perception of a similar thing; rather, similarity consists precisely in the continued existence of the similar thing. Nor is this [similarity] defined by a genus (*jāti*) pervaded by the perceptibility of the quality-ness (*guṇatva*); rather, it is simply by way of being a quality (*guṇatva*). And since that [quality-ness] remains intact in fluidity as well, there is no deviation.

As for the claim that there is a deficiency in the corroborative instance (*dṛṣṭānta*) regarding lamps and the like, because their color is overwhelmed by redness and dimness—that is not so. For in those cases, we accept a color delimited by the genus of luminosity (*bhāsvaratva*). Indeed, if it were overwhelmed, it would not illuminate objects such as jars. Therefore, the argument that "it is not the color itself that is overwhelmed, but rather its whiteness" is refuted, as there is no evidence for this. Thus, since the heaviness [of the earth] is not established due to the absence of a supporting substrate, how can one deny its prior motion?

Nor should it be argued that because there is no suppression of color (*rūpa*) in the case of the sun and so forth, there must be a latent impression (*vāsanā*) of its being perceived as having a middle course; for if there were a suppression of touch (*sparśa*), how could one establish the absence of a supporting substrate (*upaṣṭambhaka-śūnyatva*) therein? It should not be said that the touch of the sun is also not perceived because it is itself unoverpowered and because of the absence of the relation of inherence in what is conjoined (*saṃyukta-samavāya*). Nor should it be asked why the touch of those rays is not perceived, just as the touch of the sun’s rays is perceived.

They say that it is like the touch of the luster of a gem because it is not perceived immediately; however, this is to be considered. For, since the solar disc is not supported [by a substrate], its perception as a corporeal object is untenable, just as in the case of a mirror. Furthermore, because it is not densely compacted, it is untenable for its specific qualities to be perceived instantaneously, as is the case with light from a gem or sunlight. Moreover, due to the absence of dense support, it is untenable for it to persist for a long time when struck by a powerful wind. Finally, it is because it is a form of light devoid of contact with other forms, touches, and so forth, like a flash of lightning.

And likewise, because they are supported [by the wind], it is improper for the stellar sphere (*bhacakra*) to move with its own power prior to the support generated at the time of revolution, due to the gravity resulting from such support. Nor should it be argued that, because of the varying degrees of heaviness and lightness among the constellations (*nakṣatra*), there would be no possibility of their revolving at unequal times, which would contradict the perceptible fact that the duration of one revolution of the constellations is measured as sixty *ghaṭī*s of the sidereal day.

Because the celestial sphere rotates due to the impelling wind (pravaha-vāyu), it follows that the time of revolution for all the asterisms and planets—whether heavy or light—is equal. Now, since the celestial sphere rotates about the two poles, and the asterisms and planets rotate in accordance with that, there would result a vertical alignment (avalambana) of the planets situated in clouds and so forth at the beginning of the Kalpa upon the equatorial circle (viṣuvavṛtta) along a straight path opposite to the direction of their [apparent] rotation; however, there is no such vertical alignment upon the ecliptic (krāntivṛtta) or other circles, as they are slanted.

If it is argued that this is logical because it is established by direct perception, we say no; for even though the planets are not supported by the equatorial circle (*viṣuvadvṛtta*), it is possible for that region [of the ecliptic] to be occupied due to the attraction toward themselves of the degrees of declination and latitude on the ecliptic circle (*krāntivṛtta*). This assumption is equally applicable even under the theory that the planets possess an eastward motion; otherwise, they would have to occupy their positions directly to the east on the equatorial circle itself.

For this very reason—[it has been said by the ancients]: "The eastward motion of the planets prior to their own [individual] operation; their north-south, downward-upward, and westward motions; and those which have gone due to the revolutions of the celestial sphere (golābhrama)—the causes for these have been stated. Their westward motion is by the power of the Pravaha wind, while that upward and downward motion is produced by the eccentric circles (nīcocca-vṛtta). But the north-south motion is due to the ecliptic and the solstitial colure (viṣuva-maṇḍala); thus the sixfold motion of the planets has been described here. By this, the six types of motion were stated by the ancients.

In the view of Manu, however, there is extreme brevity because the matter is carried out solely through the fivefold dependent motion (*paratantra-pañcavidha-gati*). By this, the objection that "the daily occurrence of the same form for the dragging of the heavy [earth] would result from the non-difference of gravity" is refuted; for the support by the planets is dissimilar due to the varying degrees of attraction. This might be so: that a single planet alone revolves in its orbit, while the earth moves along with it every day—this is what constitutes the contradiction.

It is not logical for any single soul to possess weapons that enable multiple modes of movement according to different directions. Furthermore, does it employ these specific modes of movement through a distinction in time (samaya) and so forth, or by means of a single temporal unit? Not the first; because if one were to perform various movements at different times, it would follow that each preceding mode of movement must be interrupted by the mere taking of food, and thus rendered unachievable. For a fixed object cannot be understood through such a sequence. Nor is the second [alternative] tenable.

O learned one, if [the soul] were to occupy multiple directions simultaneously, the body of the embodied being would be shattered, or it would result in the absurdity of it being motionless. If it is argued that there is a simultaneous pulling together from both sides, we say no; for in the case of a person possessing contradictory movements in opposite directions, [it would be impossible]. Chapter 144, Verse 60—by means of a single exit in the form of the self, and by virtue of having that as its sole substratum, the specific piece of wood [would be subject to] the limitation of each individual entry downward.

In this case, there would be either a state of being fixed upon a single substratum or a mutual destruction, due to the presence of two persons pulling in opposite directions with equal causes and a single point of support; otherwise, it would be impossible for the burning to occur through the division of locations and the varying strength of the pulling persons, as they would simply pull one [object] away.

Furthermore, it is observed through direct perception that when an arrow is discharged toward a target situated in a desired direction, its path is altered by a single simultaneous impact from a desert wind or similar cause, causing it to deviate toward another direction relative to the target. In the present case, however, if the planets were to move in opposite directions due to causes such as *pāta* (apsis) or *prema* (perihelion), there would be the fault of their having identical causes and identical substrata. Nor should it be argued that in these instances, only the motion resulting from the stronger cause would prevail.

Because of the relationship between the support and the supported (ādhārādheya-bhāva) between the wind and the great forms, there is no abandonment of their respective movements, according to the analogy of the boat and the water. Indeed, a boat being pulled by those standing on it does not abandon its following along the shore and instead move toward the middle of the river; rather, depending on the relative strength of the power to pull both, there is movement in two directions. For otherwise, if it were pulled in another direction, the [original] name would become impossible.

But [one might object]: "Since going in both directions simultaneously is impossible, what is the recourse in the theory of the sixfold planetary motion if one accepts that the planets move as previously stated? If you say this, we reply: No, for even in the case of men and others crossing a river, such a thing is observed by the eye. Furthermore, in that instance, there is merely a difference between the two banks of the stream; there is no contradiction as in the present case. Therefore, let it be accepted there. But in the present case, where there is well-known enmity, what is the example? If you say this, we reply: No.

In that very case, because it is well known that insects and the like falling into a stream move without being obstructed by the current, the point already stated is understood even by children through the simultaneous casting of an insect, poison, or a probe into the flow. Now, if you argue that even there one may infer a sequence based on the movement of two [objects] in opposite directions by means of the non-difference of extremely subtle moments, we say no; for in the relationship of container and contained, there is no occurrence of two [objects] situated in opposite directions.

Even though the supported conforms to the sluggishness of the support due to the force of that support, there is no obstruction to its other movements; for in examples such as the cart and the ant, the spider and the spider-web insect, the boat and the water-insect, or the current and the aquatic worm—wherever all causes of motion are present—it is observed that they do not delay in producing their respective effects. Furthermore, the inference of sequential order is refuted by a counter-reasoning (*pratikūlatarka*) consisting in the undesirable consequence that it would have to be accomplished through the same mathematical calculation [previously mentioned].

If it is argued that [the daily motion] is merely understood through calculation as being produced by the successive sequence of individual moments, we say no. For if that were the case, then due to the displacement occurring in each individual moment, it would follow that half of the daily motion would be traversed every day. Nor should it be said that the daily motion itself is likewise conceptualized in accordance with those [moments], for that consequence would apply even to your examples of the ox-cart, the ant, the man, and the elephant. To explain:

Space (*ākāśa*) extends for ten *hasta*s, a *vitasti*, and so forth; likewise, an ant situated on a blade of grass or a piece of cloth traverses a cart by its own movement in a certain number of *pala*s, and yet, when pulled by a driver or the like, it traverses that same distance again from the front by moving in the opposite direction of the driver's force. Thus, while there exists the relationship of container and contained (*ādhāra-ādheya-bhāva*), the motion of the container conforms to the motion [of the contained], even though a different motion [is produced] in the case of the latter.

In this case as well, if one follows the sequence of moments, then due to the delay of each individual moment, the time taken to traverse a stationary cart would result in traversing only half the distance; or, by the previous logic, it would result in traversing double the entire distance. And that is impossible in every respect, because such an observation has never occurred at any time or place. Thus, by this example, through the reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) of proving what is already established or the like, the intermediate mental impression (*vāsanā*) is refuted, because the inference based on it is contradicted.

Since it is equal to that very [case] at the gate of Prahlāda, one should conclude that traveling in multiple directions simultaneously is indeed possible, because it is perceived as such. Now, an objection: travel toward the south and north, or toward the low and high points, is untenable within the limitation of a single moment, involving movement in two mixed directions; otherwise, for one traveling toward Ayodhyā who is simultaneously pulled elsewhere, it would follow that he reaches the location of the Goddess on the Vindhya mountains at the same time.

If it is argued that this is not untenable because—in a place where birds are simultaneously ascending and descending trees—the cessation of their movement toward the east and so forth, as well as the eastward movement of an arrow being propelled from the north, are indeed perceived through the varying degrees of attractive force resulting from the support provided by the wind, we say no.

If it is argued that this [presumption] also functions only by way of apprehending another explanatory factor (*upapādaka*)—since it is established through the presumption (*arthāpatti*) based on the inference of forbearance (*kṣamā*) according to subtle moments, and because it occurs only when one perceives a fact that cannot otherwise be accounted for, as otherwise the perceived meaning would remain unestablished—then that is true. However, when there is an inconsistency (*anupapatti*), one must follow the other [the presumption]. In the present case, however, that very inconsistency does not exist. To explain:

For instance, although it is well known that pigeons and other birds, appearing before and behind trees and ponds with the desire to obtain fruit and water respectively, move up and down according to their whim by means of both paths simultaneously—traveling to both places at one and the same time—this is nonetheless contradicted by the undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭaprasaṅga*) previously established and forcefully argued against you. This consequence applies to you, whose mind is agitated by the delusion of imperceptible simultaneous moments, and who refuses to accept this [simultaneous movement]. To illustrate: [The verse continues: "O Lord, if a single person were to see two women simultaneously—one beautiful and one ugly—then tell me, O Protector, which of the two would he desire? (1.20) If a single person were to see two women at once, one beautiful and one ugly, then tell me, O Protector, which of the two would he desire? For if he were to desire both simultaneously, then tell me, O Protector, what kind of man that would be! (1.21) If he were to desire both simultaneously, then tell me, O Protector, what kind of man that would be! For if he were to desire neither of them, then tell me, O Protector, what kind of man that would be! (1.22) If he were to desire neither of them, then tell me, O Protector, what kind of man that would be! For if he were to desire both of them in turn, then tell me, O Protector, what kind of man that would be! (1.23) If he were to desire both of them in turn, then tell me, O Protector, what kind of man that would be! For if he were to desire one after the other, then tell me, O Protector, what kind of man that would be! (1.24) If he were to desire one after the other, then tell me, O Protector, what kind of man that would be! For if he were to desire both of them at once, then tell me, O Protector, what kind of man that would be! (1.25) If he were to desire both of them at once, then tell me, O Protector, what kind of man that would be! For if he were to desire both of them sequentially, then tell me, O Protector, what kind of man that would be! (1.26) If he were to desire both of them sequentially, then tell me, O Protector, what kind of man that would be! For if he were to desire both of them together, then tell me, O Protector, what kind of man that would be! (1.27) If he were to desire both of them together, then tell me, O Protector, what kind of man that would be! For if he were to desire both of them individually, then tell me, O Protector, what kind of man that would be! (1.28) If he were to desire both of them individually, then tell me, O Protector, what kind of man that would be! For if he were to desire both of them alternately, then tell me, O Protector, what kind of man that would be!
