Having determined the distance between the lake shore and the water’s edge by means of a cord or similar device, and having calculated that distance with the hands and other measures, one should, according to that measurement, prepare a wooden support of the required length. At the time of immersion there, if the ten *kūpala*s of water are traversed precisely at the moment of exceeding [the mark], then even when it is situated solely in an east-west direction, there would be no transgression. This is because, in the former case, due to the delay of a single *lakṣaṇa*, a transgression is possible only after a period of sitting equal to half the duration of its enjoyment.

In this way, for both the upward-moving and downward-moving [arrows] as well: even though the arrow possesses equal intervals due to its arrival at the same level of the earth at the time of crossing the other target-points situated within the range of the discharger’s isolation (*kaivalya*), there would be no crossing of other target-points before its own fall. This is because, as in the previous case, a delay of one moment for each [interval] applied through leveling is untenable due to the lack of parsimony (*lāghava*). Therefore, it is logical that the grasping [of the target] occurs with a motion toward multiple directions. This might be so.

However, because the celestial sphere (*bhapañjara*) is corporeal and significantly heavier than the planetary orbs due to its immense size, one might ask: how can it be established—as previously demonstrated—that light objects are supported by the *pravaha* wind during the period of sixty *nākṣatra* ghaṭīs? This is not a valid objection; for the celestial sphere, situated within the entire stellar assembly, revolves during the sixty *nākṣatra* ghaṭīs due to the intense force of the winds from both the exterior and interior of the stellar sphere.

If it is argued that at that very time, even though the planetary orbs are light, their rotation is observed through direct perception to vary according to the relative heaviness or lightness of the orb due to the impact of the velocity of the wind moving within them; and thus, the statement that the planets are seen at the end of the stellar sphere (bhacakra) moving with a light eastward motion is not consistent with reason—[then the following is said].

Regarding this, according to the *Siddhāntasundarī-ṭīkā*: although gravity is possible for the planets—which possess fiery bodies—due to their association with a supporting portion of earth, they do not descend from their previous positions. This is because, in those planets which rest upon air, their motion is necessarily concomitant with that descent; thus, by virtue of their nature being restricted by their substratum, that descent is obstructed. To explain:

In the case of persons seated in a cart that is not moving with effort (niṣprayatna), or those mounted on a boat, or insects and the like situated on a potter’s wheel—even though they follow the movement of their own bodies, they do not perceive it in the opposite direction; for even in these cases, the determining factor is precisely the state of having a support that possesses a uniform velocity.

Now, let it be granted that there is a dense conjunction in cases such as a cart-wheel; likewise, as in the case of the doctrine of the admission of [atoms] being joined at their bases, there may be an adherence through following the movement of two elephants in close proximity. However, this is impossible in the case of rarefied parts, such as wind and dust, and so forth. For instance, it is observed that in water, sand, or thin sticks, and in grass, palm leaves, or foliage moved by the wind, there is a state of possessing slow or rapid motion precisely according to the weight [of the objects], occurring at the very same time.

And so, why should such a postulation not also be applied to the case at hand? If it is argued that "postulation follows what is observed," we say no. For although in water there is an obstruction by other water due to contact with the ground above and below at every point—even within a finger's breadth—and in air there is an impossibility of equal velocity at every moment because of the impact of its own voids, as in the case of trees, mountains, and the like rising up against one another; nevertheless, in the case of a steady stream or where there is no excessive velocity, even light and heavy objects [pass through] the air, as in a whirlwind (*vātyā*) and the like.

This is because the equality of the object's motion is known by everyone through its contrary slowing down; for in both cases, an increase in speed and an equality of speed are observed. However, even if there were an absolute equality of speed, it would be impossible to prevent the transformation of speed in a flowing stream of water and the like, due to the impact of other water particles, internal friction, and so forth, occurring even in moments that are imperceptible as gross or subtle.

For this very reason, in cases such as the rising tide of the ocean, when the water completely fills the shore and for a moment a uniformity of velocity is perceived across all parts, even objects like conch shells or sticks are observed in the world to move without interruption until the point where the result of their motion is equalized. Now, one might object: "The equality of velocity is established in the case of wind and water; how is it understood in the present instance? For [the motion of the planets] is contrary to the movement of the examples cited, such as the rotation of a potter's wheel. This is not so.

In the case of water in a flowing stream, having cast all the light and heavy objects—whether situated on the banks or within the water—at one and the same time and in one single location, perceive them all directly as they emerge. In this illustration, it is not that the velocity is equal for all objects at every point around the center due to differences in their orbits; rather, it is so. Thus...

Even in the case at hand, if it is argued that "then, for the moon and other [planets], there would be distinct revolutions of ascent (ūrdhvaparyaya) following their revolutions in higher orbits (kakṣā), as per their respective orbital paths, and these would be determined in accordance with the illustrative examples," we say: no.

A whirlwind is the cause of the destruction of men, trees, staffs, and so forth; it arises from the differentiation of the placement and non-placement of winds, producing greater or lesser velocities through the distinction between successive stages. In the present context, however, this [whirlwind] is not [the cause], because the movement of all things occurs simultaneously with a wind that possesses equal velocity everywhere, driven by the natural and rapid motion of the Lord’s will. Now, even this equality of velocity is denied by the Raurava [scripture].

If it is argued that, just as in the case of the aforementioned relationship and so forth, this [wind] also functions as the motivator (*prayojaka*), that is true; however, its status as a motivator is recognized only when it is presented merely as the leading agent (*nāyaka*). This is because its role as a cause of delay is understood even when it has entered into a relationship of container and contained (*dhārādheya-bhāva*). For this very reason, in a situation such as the flow of water across the ocean, since the wind is presented solely through hearing of its leadership, when there is sometimes the commencement of looking toward another direction, there arises—due to the influence of desire and by means of a mental impression (*vāsanā*) formed from iron-like constraints—a sense of movement in the interval.

In the case of stabilizing a boat (*taristhirīkaraṇa*), there is no capacity [to prevent motion] merely through the obstruction of velocity (*begamatibandha*). Here, in instances of the relationship between locus and located (*ādhārādheyabhāva*), such as a whirlpool and Arundhatī, or Vasiṣṭha and others, it is observed that even when two things are unequal, they move together as equals; therefore, the inability to obstruct velocity is precisely what constitutes the incapacity [of the support]. Furthermore, in cases where a body becomes a locus, such as a stream of water, the stabilization of a boat by throwing a plow (*halaprakṣepa*) does not occur through the mediation of obstructing its velocity.

Because it is impossible for that [reflection] to be restricted by the relationship of container and contained (*ādhārādheyabhāva*). Now, one might object: "In such a case, when fire produced by bellows or other means is present nearby, what is the status of sand, wet cloth, or leaves, which are objects of reflection that are either delayed or not delayed? We reply: No; even there, it is appropriate that the fire acts merely as a leader (*nāyaka*) in determining the speed or delay [of the reflection]. Furthermore, if you argue, "But in those cases there is indeed the state of being a container (*ādhāratva*); how can it be 'merely that'?", we say: No, because that is unproven. For instance, the state of being container and contained exists simply through the inherent fitness (*svarūpayogyatā*) of the things themselves.

Lightness (*lāghava*) is not the determinant factor; rather, it is the capacity to obstruct [the downward fall] that constitutes the nature of being supported. For even though a specific piece of wood may be a hundred times heavier than a particular stone, its status as something supported (*ādheya*) does not disappear. If it is argued that, in such cases, being supported is restricted by heaviness (*gaurava*) alone, we say no. The cause there is simply the relation with a suitable object (*yogyavastu-sambandha*), and not heaviness. Otherwise, even an extremely heavy object would be unable to rest upon the surface of the earth.

And likewise, in a place such as a broken surface, the falling [of an object] is obstructed for even a moment by the air itself—which is necessarily present—by virtue of its velocity and duration; yet, the status of being supported (*ādheyatva*) belongs to that [object] despite its possessing a nature capable of falling. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) that even a stone, which possesses gravity, would have the status of being supported by water or the like when it possesses velocity. In such cases, the cognition of a substratum (*ādhāra*) must be explained through two factors: the property of having a tendency to fall and the obstruction [of that fall]. Furthermore, the formal argument (*prayoga*) is merely illustrative.

Therefore, it is not tenable that the entire stellar sphere (bhapañjara), which is capable of being supported by the wind, should be held by the force of its own momentum alone. As for the claim: "May the relationship of support and supported endure as long as the moon and stars; who, proud of the strength of his heart, would harm me?"—that must be considered. For if the wind were the support of the solar orb (go-bimba), and if one accepts its prior motion, then, like a bamboo pole moving forward at the front of a procession, the solar orb could not possibly revolve independently without being carried along with it. Thus, its stability is untenable.

Furthermore, because the horse of the *avalambana* wind is not observed to have a sound, what is it? Moreover, since there is a lack of evidence for the *pravaha* wind being the support for the multitude of stars beginning with Bhadra, its status as a primary mover (*nāyaka*) is also untenable; thus, the support for the celestial spheres is Brahman alone. Furthermore, in the *pravaha* wind, it would be impossible for the orbits (*kakṣā*) possessing equal velocity to revolve at the same time across all parts [of the sphere], for instance: [The argument continues: For example... (text fragment)

If the velocity of the portions of air situated within Saturn is equal to the velocity of the portions of air situated within the Moon, then there would be a contradiction regarding the nature of the air-portions within the Moon's belly. For, during the time of its revolution, because the air-portions situated on the same meridian as Saturn revolve at a great speed along Saturn’s path, it would be impossible for the air-portions within the Moon to complete a full revolution of Saturn’s diameter.

Therefore, because the parts of the Pravaḥa wind revolve at equal times within their own respective groups, their velocity is indeed unequal; however, for those situated in the same orbit, it is equal. For this very reason, in some cases, there is an equal movement of heavy and light objects in water, yet not by an equal velocity, but rather by a sequence of slower and faster speeds. Where there is movement of heavy and light objects in one place, the movement of the light object occurs without dependence on its own power, solely due to the support of the heavy one.

Therefore, it is impossible to establish a supporting cause (*ālambana*) for your position; this is the general direction of the argument. In reality, if the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) other than the moon and the solar orbs were composed of fire (*taijasa*), then due to their increasing weight according to their order in lower orbits, the consequence would be that they would fall down. Furthermore, although the sensation of heat is not perceived from bodies other than the sun because of the intervention [of other matter], there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of perceiving the sensation of heat at night due to the massing together of the fiery light of all the lunar mansions and solar orbs.

Since the discs of Jupiter, Saturn, and the others are much larger than that of the Sun, it is possible for them to possess a greater intensity of illumination even at night; thus, to avoid the consequence of their becoming "days" (i.e., appearing as bright as day), it is logical that the ancients accepted these other bodies to be composed of water. Furthermore, since the acceptance of the Moon as a watery sphere is necessary for explaining the phenomenon of its libration (śṛṅgonnati), there is no obstacle to accepting the same—namely, the nature of a watery sphere—for the other five planets and the lunar mansions (nakṣatras) by the same principle.

Since water consists of widely spaced particles, its aggregation into a solid mass is impossible; therefore, it cannot exist as a spherical globe of water. Consequently, it must be stated that terrestrial regions provide the necessary support for it. Furthermore, it has already been explained at length that their luminosity arises from the reflection of the sun's rays. Nor should it be argued that, by this process, Venus receives a greater degree of illumination than Mars and the other planets.

Because it is very close to the Earth and far from the Moon, Mars has a large orb; consequently, its light and radiance can occur with greater or lesser intensity as desired. As for Mercury, because its orb is smaller than that of the Moon and it is situated at a great distance, only a small amount of light is observed. Now, one might object: since Venus, Mars, and the others have larger orbs relative to the lunar orb, they would necessarily possess greater weight; thus, they would all fall even more so than the lunar orb due to gravity.

If, however, they are composed of light (*taijasa*), their support is to be understood according to what is appropriate, based on the observation of their prior movement. Nor should it be argued that there is no possibility of support because the weight would be equal—since all portions of earth and water that serve as supports for the solar disc would occupy the same amount of space within the image—as this would imply that the images must be of equal size when measured in *yojanas*.

And it should not be argued that, although the discs of the mirrors possess equal weight, a smaller volume is possible due to their constituent parts being closely packed or sparse; for this is impossible because the orbs of the planets are spherical. This is true.

The sphere of the stellar sphere (bhapañjara-gola), having become exceedingly heavy, revolves in the same amount of time through the internal hundred-naveled wind by means of the circulating air (pravaha-vāyu); at that very same time, Saturn and the other planets, possessing diminished weights according to their order of lower orbits, revolve solely due to the impact of the respective portions of the winds situated in their own locations, and so forth, because of the occurrence of deflection (lambana). This is because of the decrease in the velocity of the wind according to the order of the lower orbits and because of the smallness of the portions of the winds.

Nor should it be argued that, in view of the terrestrial [earth], the solar orb situated below it must necessarily cause an eclipse because of its great size; for, being composed of light (*taijasa*), even though it is large, the supporting portions of the earth are smaller than the water and earth portions existing on the terrestrial disk, and thus the shadow is small in accordance with those [supporting parts]. Furthermore, if it is argued that even so, because Mercury has a small disk and the lunar disk situated below it is larger than it, an eclipse cannot be prevented, we say no.

Even in the case of a small image, because there is a greater quantity of portions of earth and water that are more firmly conjoined, one determines an excess of weight compared to a large image produced by a smaller proportion of thinly distributed parts. Thus, for example, a small iron sphere possesses more weight than a large ball of clay. And the non-perception [of this weight] occurs because, in relation to the moon, its spherical image is half the size, it is separated by more than three times the distance, and it possesses a luminosity consisting of reflected solar rays (jyotsnā). Therefore, this is the doctrine regarding the motion of the center.

2" Meṃ0 80–In this way, at times during the period of the planet's strength (*balakāla*), its appearance becomes possible due to its proximity. [Budha says: "I am Budha, the son of the dull-witted Candra; I am appointed by Brahmā to a position above him. I feel ashamed to come within the range of vision in this world. Therefore, I shall not grant my sight. Others say that the occasional granting of sight is a form of punishment for the sin of having accepted such an office, intended to make known his own power.

And thus, in the hypothesis that the planets have a support, since they would otherwise fall toward the equatorial path (viṣuvadvṛtta) in a direction opposite to the direction of their revolution and rotation, it is necessary to postulate a southward upward force (yāmyoccarādiśakti) to prevent such a fall. Therefore, for the sake of parsimony (lāghava), it is more reasonable to postulate an inherent power (svaśakti) directed eastward. This is because, according to the arguments already stated, the planets revolve together with the wind, and thus no external support is established.

Nor should it be argued that since the planets move by their own power along the path of the equator (*viṣuvavṛtta*), why are they not seen [to deviate from it]? For even in this case, the assumption of a north-south motion would involve greater complexity (*gaurava*) when compared to the hypothesis of [the celestial sphere's] inclination. This is because, at the beginning of the Kalpa, Brahmā established the planets on their respective paths along a line coinciding with the point of intersection of the equator and the ecliptic (*krāntivṛtta*) within the stellar frame (*bhapañjara*); thus, one must assume that the planets move either along the ecliptic or according to their [specific] deviation (*vikṣepa*) along the original path. Consequently, there is no evidence for the planets moving along the equatorial path.

Furthermore, two successive and contradictory motions are impossible. This is because, once the conjunction with the previous location has ceased following the process of action and disjunction, a subsequent conjunction with a new location can only occur through a curved path; for the subsequent location is specifically the instrument [of that motion]. As for the upward and downward motion, it is established by the planets' own power as being solely a prior movement along a different path imagined as the celestial track associated with the ecliptic and other spheres. Thus, the truth is that there is only one natural motion, while the westward motion is due to the Pravaha wind.

If it is argued: "In that case, since the planets extend for hundreds of *yojanas* and so forth, and consist respectively of water, fire, and air, they are insentient; thus, even if their movement is possible as dependent on another [force], how can their own activity—movement prior to [any external] impulse—be possible? This contradicts the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). To this, the former teachers reply: Their sentience is established by the fact that they possess bodies made of light (*taijasa*), as proven by scriptural passages intended to establish the yellow, red, and other colors of the sun and other planets. For effort (*prayatna*) is logically consistent [with this], since it is of the nature of pleasure and is an attribute belonging exclusively to sentient beings.

Nor should it be argued that the accomplishment of those who possess consciousness in the form of mandalas is impossible because they lack such [gross] bodies; for there is no evidence for anything beyond that [consciousness], and [such a claim] would involve excessive complexity (gaurava). [Objection: Granted that they possess consciousness, how can their body be a replica of the [divine] image (bimba), and how can its extent be thousands of *yojanas* and so forth? This cannot be, because such a thing is never observed in any [ordinary] body. [Reply: This is not so. For the matter is explained by accepting the presence of another light (*tejas*) conjoined with it. To explain:

Just as light in contact with a gem or similar object assumes a form that follows the spreading circular shape [of the gem], or as the light-form associated with a lamp casts a halo around the lamp from all sides; in the very same way, the supreme light (mahas) conjoined with the bodies of the planets and other celestial bodies spreads incessantly from those respective bodies, having attained a form that conforms to their images. Precisely because it is thus spread out, and because it is obstructed by its own smoothness and its state of being veiled, its constituent parts and so forth do not appear distinctly.

However, it is only spheres of light that are perceived; in the case of a mango tree and the like that are being used, there is a collection of branches. And thus, to whatever extent a planet possesses excellence—such as the greatness, abundance, and so forth of its light resulting from its conjunction—the more extensive is its radiance in all directions.

Therefore, according to each respective context, the extent of its diameter in *yojanas* is understood to be equal to the number of *yojanas* between its eastern and western limits, or its northern and southern limits, or those arising from the intermediate directions (vidiś), measured from one end to the other; it is perceived as being like a ball. As for the Moon, however, its globe consists of water, and thereupon dwells the divine Moon, the Lord of Herbs, who stands as the presiding deity and the controller, like a helmsman.

Now, if it is asked how there can be the perception of the eight kinds of globular forms as having the shape of a mirror's surface, we reply: it is either due to the defect of obstruction (*vyavadhāna-doṣa*), or it is merely an illusion (*bhrama*). Just as in the case of a mountain or similar object which is obstructed—wherein, despite its actual largeness, there is a perception of shortness; and despite the disparity in its proportions, there is a perception of uniformity—so too is the appearance in the present case.

And by the command of Brahmā, they, driven by the wind in the atmosphere, having dedicated their own bodies for the benefit of the world, sink with effort from the east and are carried back by the wind from the west. "There is no one who can withstand my brilliance, nor do I have a moment to explain"—through such a clarification of the meaning expressed in the *Sūryasiddhānta*, there arises the realization of the aforementioned point regarding the dispute over the light associated with the body and the soul.

But we do not accept this hypothesis; for how could the moon’s revolution around the earth be accounted for without a cause? Furthermore, its being situated at a distance of four hundred and eighty yojanas has been stated by those very [opponents] to be impossible due to its being merely a sphere of water and its lack of suitability for specific observation. Moreover, because it is insentient, effort and the like are absent.

Furthermore, in those cases where—due to the context of war, or because their teacher is a propitiated deity who has become pleased with them, and so forth—they attain another world, there would follow the consequence that these [scriptures] lack authority; for as long as the moment of the kalpa lasts, there is no absence of wandering [in saṃsāra], and by virtue of being subject to affliction, even though they are deities, there is an absence of enjoyment in heaven. Therefore, the light, water, and earth-form images are the dwelling places for these embodied conscious beings, but the images are not of the nature of those [beings].

[Objection: "If this is so, then for all the planetary spheres (*grahamaṇḍala*), motion toward the east would be impossible due to their being heated by the sun; however, according to the view of the ancients, it is possible only for the motion of the moon. [Response: No. For those very spheres, favored by the Grandfather (Brahmā), move by the application of their own inherent power, without displacing their own insentient physical forms (*bimba*) which serve as their abodes—just as ships on the ocean are moved by helmsmen. [Objection: Even if that were so, motion to other worlds would still be impossible.

If it is argued that otherwise, at that time, the methods for the release [of the planet] through non-movement of the orbs (*bimba*)—such as the *vairāśika* calculation and so forth—and the means of attaining speed would be untenable, because mathematical calculation has no fixed object, we say: no, for we do not accept a rule of constant proximity. Even regarding those presiding over the orbs (*bimba*), it has been stated that they may preside according to their will, like a king who governs a village or a district. Furthermore, others hold that in a state of non-proximity, there is the authority of another command.

In reality, however, just as in the world certain insentient objects move due to the power of gems, mantras, and so forth—as if they were being set in motion—so too the movement of the lunar and solar orbs occurs solely through the power of their presiding deities; or rather, such movement is established by the force of the command, "You should go eastward," since the words of such persons are equivalent to mantras. Nor should it be argued that, in this manner, the stars themselves would not be moved eastward like the sun by the deities who preside over the stellar orbs.

Because there is no injunction from Brahmā; or rather, just as upward flaming is the nature of fire and horizontal blowing is the nature of wind, so too, by being drawn by the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), their connection with those respective zodiacal regions occurs through a prior motion. Their sitting in the middle is the very seat. (Bhāṣya-ṭīkā)—Because when the light of the solar disc arises in connection with that zodiacal sign, the possibility of obtaining happiness or its opposite among the worlds occurs.

If it is argued that the difference between the two orbs (the orb of the planet and the solar orb) is what is meant by "minus" (*ūna*), we say no. For in the Śruti passage, "This person who is seen within the sun... golden-hued, with a golden beard and golden hair," the intended meaning of the sentence is simply the connection of the Person with the solar disc denoted by the word *āditya*. Since the solar disc and the Person stand in the relation of locus and occupant, their difference is clearly understood.

Furthermore, in such scriptural passages as, "That which is this orb that shines, and the person who is in this orb," the difference between the orb and the person is indeed directly understood. The same conceptualization applies to the moon and other bodies, either through analogy or by the aforementioned reasoning; for this very reason, the description in the *Jātakaśāstra* of [the sun] as having the form and nature of a great person is consistent. Therefore, [the sun] revolves within the celestial sphere (bhapañjara) which is bound by the flow of the wind moving toward the western direction.

"Even though the planets revolve in the *saṃkhacara* (the stellar sphere), they proceed toward the eastern direction by their motion," according to the statement of the elder Vasiṣṭha. Therefore, it is not at all inconsistent to say that the planets move in the zodiacal circle with the stars as the east; enough of this elaboration. Now, desiring to explain the rationale for mean motion (*madhyagativāsanā*), [the author] first states the true solar civil day (*sphuṭasāvanadina*) preceded by the definition of a solar day: "Indeed, when the star and the sun rise simultaneously before the eye, the sun rises again after sixty *ghaṭīs*."

Then, from the product of the Sun’s [longitude] and its daily motion, divided by eighteen hundred (1800), one obtains years; these, when added to the years already arrived, constitute the Sun’s duration in sixty *nāḍikās*. This is the true solar day (*churātra*), derived from its motion, and it is variable. A solar day is always seen to consist of sixty *ghaṭīs*; when added to the breaths (*asus*) equal to its motion, it becomes the mean [day] of the Sun. In that year, the calculation for the auspicious [period] is thus reduced by one.

When the sun rises exactly at the same time as any particular lunar mansion (nakṣatra), and at the moment of sunrise no lunar mansion is observed [to be on the horizon], but rather only the conjunction is mentioned—why then is the word "kiṭa" used? Therefore, after that time, the sixty lunar mansions rise again; immediately after that, the sun rises. And by what amount of time? Thus it is stated: "The sun has clearly moved its previous position by a certain amount of time."

If eighteen hundred [degrees] of zodiacal signs rise by their own rising-ascensions (*svodayāsu*), then by how many [ascensional differences] do those [signs] with their true motions rise? Thus, after being divided by the ascensional differences (*lubdhāsu*), there is the subsequent rising of the Sun. For this very reason, it is not sidereal; sixty *ghaṭikās* increased by those obtained ascensional differences constitute the Sun’s true solar (*sāvana*) day-and-night. And that day-and-night is variable (*cala*). It increases every day. Every day, due to the addition of motion, there is an increase of one *kalā*, one *liptā*, and so on.

When sixty *yamunā*-ghaṭīs are equal to a mean solar revolution (*madhyama-bhukti*), that is called a mean civil day (*sāvana-dhūrātra*). This is because at the end of the year, however many true civil days there are, the mean ones must necessarily be the same. This is due to the equality between the decrease of the motions and the increase of the [mean] risings. Therefore, how is it that the Lord [Brahmā] and others have stated: "The civil day of the Lord is joined with the moments of the revolutions of the sun"? This would be so in the *Gaulādhyāya*.

If the sun moves along the equatorial circle (viṣuvanmaṇḍala) from the east, then one degree of the equator rises in a certain number of breaths (asus); in that case, it would be appropriate to say that [the rising occurs] in breaths equal to the degrees of the sun's motion. That, however, is not correct. The sun moves along the ecliptic (krāntivṛtta). Therein, eighteen hundred (1800) minutes of the sign Aries (meṣarāśi) are traversed in sixteen hundred and seventy (1670) breaths. For the other signs, the breaths may appropriately be calculated through proportion (anupāta) based on the minutes of their respective motions.

This being so, the true (sphuṭa) night becomes clearly evident. Therefore, that which was stated by them is indeed the mean (madhyama). Thus, within the course of a year, as many true civil days (sāvana) as there are, so many shall be the mean ones. "The revolutions of the asterisms (bhabhrama) minus one" means that the number of civil days is equal to the number of asterism-revolutions produced minus one. This is because the Sun, moving eastward, has completed one revolution; therefore, it is logically established that its number of risings is [the revolutions] minus one. || 5 || 6 ||

7 || Ma08e—Now, an objection is raised: "There is no evidence for the existence of the planets' prior motion day by day; rather, their presence in Bharaṇī and so forth from their position in Aśvinī and so forth occurs simply through their rising into the sky. Therefore, in order to dispel the doubt as to why the *ahargaṇa* (the accumulated number of days) is established as "perfectly realized" (*saṃsiddha*) at the very outset when answering the question beginning with "by means of the perfected revolutions of the Moon, etc.," and in order to establish the nature of that perfected [calculation], he states the proof of its validity through direct perception using the *upajāti* meter, beginning with the words "samām" (of the year).

"O Nakṣatraka, simultaneously at one and the same time, [the sun] rises together with the stars; however, on the surface of the earth, it rises immediately thereafter. 'Udita' means having attained a state established by the appearance of conjunction with the terrestrial horizon. Although the simultaneous observation of the sun and the stars is impossible due to the movement of the planets, it is indicated that such a certainty exists for the maiden. Furthermore, immediately after that, 'by the Āryā-ghaṭīs' means by sixty ghaṭīs of the nakṣatras."

"I see only that very constellation risen; however, at that time, the sun has not yet risen. The sense is this: if the sun were not moving eastward, then at the time of the next rising of that [constellation], the constellation preceding the sunrise would again appear; thus, the eastward motion of the stars is directly perceived. Now, one might ask: "At what point, after the second rising of the constellation, does the sunrise occur again? To this, he says: "The sun... [and so forth].

Then, the time interval between the rising of the second lunar mansion and the rising of the sun is derived from the product of the sun’s own rising [longitude] and its motion. From the sun as corrected for precession (*sāyana*), the time in *nāḍīs* and *pala*s for the rising of the asterism occupied by that sun in one's own locality is obtained; this is the meaning of the result produced by multiplying those two and dividing by one thousand eight hundred. By the word "and" (*ca*), it is meant that [the sun] has risen when measured by those *nāḍīs*. This is the underlying principle: at the time of the rising of the second lunar mansion, the sun’s own rising is delayed due to its prior movement.

Supported by that rising [longitude], at whatever time the Sun reaches the horizon due to the impact of the Pravaha wind, at that very time, the rising of the Sun occurs after a number of *nāḍīs* equal to the true daily motion of the Sun—pertaining to the interval between the two sunrises on the eastern mountain—minus the true motion of the Sun during that interval. And the calculation of the true longitude is performed by the proportion: "If one zodiac sign in minutes yields the *udayāsava*s (ascensional equivalents), then how many are yielded by the true motion in minutes? Thus, when the Moon's longitudinal distance from the rising point of the day corresponds to the rising of a particular lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), there is conjunction with that lunar mansion.

...medhyaṅgatasana | 113. Even though there is an increase in its [the Sun's] rising value, there is no increase in the life-force (āsu) of the world situated on the meridian-line, because it remains at the tip of the arrow; rather, it is due to those [life-forces] being near that [meridian]. This is because of the movement of the distinct great orb. And its non-release is stated for the sake of utility in the calculation of the day-count (ahargaṇa), since the stated day-count is solar (saura) and lacks the Savana [measure]. || 5 || Now, with this introduction, he states the solar Savana measure in the Pramāṇikā metre: "The accumulated lives joined together," etc.

Sixty *ghaṭikās* are obtained from the product of its own [longitude] and its daily motion (*bhukti*). This, added to the *asus* arrived at through the previously mentioned multiplication, shall be the true solar day (*ghrātra*) of the Sun, which is the calculation for the duration of the clear day. By the particle "tu" (but), it is indicated that the lunar day (*aharātra*) cannot be determined by the aforementioned method due to the lack of logical justification; thus, it was not mentioned.

Now, one might ask: "Is not the solar day fixed at sixty *ghaṭikās* according to the *sāvana* measure? Therefore, how can this calculated measure be considered non-fixed? To this he says: "That" (*tat*). That solar day-measure understood through the aforementioned method is "moving," meaning it is dissimilar from day to day. Thus, the sense is that this calculated measure is not fixed; therefore, it is impossible to establish that measure as a constant. One might further ask: "Why is it moving? Since it appears to be fixed by adding the elapsed *prāṇas*, he states the reason for its movement: "Because of rising, etc. (*udayād iti*).

The meaning is that because the times of the rising of the zodiacal signs (*rāśyudaya*) are not fixed, the *gaty-asava* (seconds of arc derived from motion) produced by them are also different; thus, when these are added together, there would be no fixed measure. Now, one might object: "Even so, it is appropriate to state that the measure is threefold at the non-axial (*nirakṣa*) location, but sixfold at the axial (*sākṣa*) location—this measure is indeed fixed. To this, he says: "From the elapsed portion of the day" (*thubhuktitaḥ*). Because the daily motion is distinct every day, the measure produced by it is also distinct every day, and is therefore not fixed in the manner described.

By the use of the word "ca" (and), it is indicated that even on a single day, there is a lack of uniformity in measurement due to differences in location. Thus, because the motion resulting from their own rising is of a different nature, the time produced by it is distinct; consequently, the measure of the *yoga* (conjunction) between them is established as being different. This is the intended meaning. Now, one might object: "The measure of a day and night as sixty *ghaṭīs* is merely a conventional construct; therefore, it is incorrect to base [the calculation] upon that. To this, he provides a reply and, in the course of the discussion, states another specific point in the *Indravajrā* meter, beginning with "ṣaṣṭhyā" (by sixty).

The Noble One has established that a lunar day (*nakṣatradina*) consists of sixty *ghaṭīs* every single day, based on the revolution of the stellar sphere (*bhapañjara*) measured by sixty *nākṣatra-ghaṭīs* within the interval between the divisions of the constellations. By this, it is indicated that a "lunar day" measured by the forward motion of the constellations according to the measurement of the constellations as previously described would not be possible.

For this very reason, since even the sixty *ghaṭīs* of those who seek to know the motion [of a planet] are dependent on the rising [of the sun], when added to that, the *sāvana* day—consisting of the interval of time between two sunrises—calculated by means of the *nakṣatra-patrikā*, will indeed become greater than sixty *ghaṭīs*; this is the intended meaning. Now, it might be argued that the statement "the *sāvana* day is equal to the moments (subh) equivalent to the minutes of arc of the constant solar motion" is incorrect and inconsistent with the established tradition (*laḍhā*).

Nor should it be said that the Sun’s revolution occurs solely along the path of the equinoctial circle—which is contrary to the directions intended for the rotation of the celestial flow—and therefore the calculation of *kalāsūnas* there is improper; for it has already been established previously that the Sun does not revolve by itself along the equinoctial path. To this, he says: "That" (*tat*). That day, measured in sixty *nakṣatra-ghaṭīs*, when added to the *asūs* equal to the degrees of its motion, shall be the mean solar [day].

Thus, the intention is that it is logical for the *sāvana* [day] associated with the *laya* (the fifteenth chapter, verse 69) to be accepted as the mean [measure]. Although the mean [longitude] stated for Laṅkā and other places is not the true mean, because it lacks the proper connection arising from the mean motion; and although the minutes of arc of the mean motion are obtained through the mean motion according to the aforementioned method, they are nevertheless disregarded due to the absence of uniformity in what arises from the mean motion.

Since the status of being "middle" (madhyama) is accepted precisely because of its single form, the middle nature of what has been stated is logical. Nor should it be argued that such a statement of measurement is improper—both in comparison to a clear measurement and in comparison to such indefinite middle measurements—due to its lack of utility; for the *ahargaṇa* (daily accumulation of days), which is to be accomplished through proportion (*anupāta*), does not have an indefinite scope, and because the measurement of that [year] is accepted as the basis upon which the *ahargaṇa* depends. Now, he states that the knowledge of the number of civil days (*sāvana*) in a year is established by the aforementioned measurement, beginning with the words "In this way" (*evam*).

When this has been stated by him who has understood the underlying logic: "Of the sun (kharāṃśu), that number is the number of civil days (sāvana-dina); in solar years (abda), it is less by one from the number of solar days associated with the solar year due to the revolution of the zodiacal signs (bhabhrama). The meaning is that it becomes diminished by one.

And likewise, if the former planet had no prior motion, then as many *bha*-days as there are for the simultaneous daily rising of the asterism and the sun would be the solar *sāvana* days at the desired time; however, because of the existence of that prior motion, simultaneous rising is impossible. Therefore, by means of the prior motion, as many *bha*-days as there are during the period of one revolution of the circle are the solar *sāvana* days, since a single revolution of the circle does not occur within that interval. Thus...

By the previous calculation, what was stated regarding the solar year as the time for the revolution of the zodiac (*cakrabhoga*) is indeed correct. Thus, because the increase or decrease of the *asus* of the true motion from the *asus* equal to the mean motion during the time of the revolution of the zodiac for these two—[the Sun] and [the Moon]—is respectively equal to that of the day-revolution (*ahacakrabhoga*), it should be understood that at the time of the revolution of the zodiac, the mean and the true *sāvana* days are equal. Now, he states the number of lunar days (*tithi*) within a year: "In a year of Kuniya, the lunar days are five times nine, three times fifteen, and one and a half times twenty-two."

A twelfth part of this solar year is declared to be a solar month consisting of thirty civil days (sāvana). In one solar year, there are three hundred and sixty-five (365) civil days, fifteen (15) nāḍīs, thirty (30) palas, and twenty-two and a half (22.30) vipalas. The proof for these values has already been stated in the Madhyagativibhāṣya. It is logical that a twelfth part of this solar year constitutes a solar month.

The *sāvana* month, however, is indeed [the measure] of *sāvana* days. (8) Ma0ḍī0: Now, having stated that the number of solar *sāvana* days in a solar year is of the form *x* (an integer), and since it was impossible to determine the number of months by that very form, he sets down that number; and in connection with that, he states the number for the solar month and the nature of the *sāvana* month in the Indravajrā meter, beginning with "paścāt... (afterwards...).

In a solar year (*sauravarṣa*), three hundred and sixty-five days, fifteen *ghaṭīs*, thirty *palas*, and twenty-two *vipalas*—when subtracted from the solar day-count—become the *bhaṭṭikā-pavipat-bhasma* (the destructive reduction of the solar day-measure). The derivation of this is stated in the *Madhyādhikāra*. [Regarding the calculation of elapsed time: It should not be said that this opinion regarding the determination of the [solar] day is indefinite; for its fixed nature is understood through the previously mentioned number of *kalpa*-solar and civil days (*sāvanadinasaṃkhyā*) when applied to a single year.

He states the definition of the solar month—consisting of thirty days, seven ghaṭīs, thirty-one palas, fifty-two vipalas, and thirty-seven tithis—as the basis for the solar year, in order to facilitate the calculation of the intercalary month (*adhimāsa*) which is about to be described: "Of this" (*asya*). The solar month is said to be the twelfth part of the total number of *sāvana* days belonging to a solar year; that is, thirty days, seven ghaṭīs, thirty-one palas, fifty-two vipalas, and thirty-seven tithis (30 | 7 | 31 | 52 | 37). Now, as an incidental matter, he states the number of days in a *sāvana* month for the purpose of understanding the calculations to be described later: "Thirty days" (*triṃśaddina*). The measure of a *sāvana* month is its own form, consisting of thirty days.

By the use of the particle *eva*, there is an exclusion of the solar and civil months previously mentioned. (8) Now he states the lunar month: "The time by which the moon returns again to conjunction with the sun in the zodiacal circle—that is the lunar month; its days are 29,31,50 *kudinās*. (9) At the end of the new moon (*darśānta*), the moon is indeed in conjunction with the sun. Thereafter, both move toward the east.

Of these two, the Moon, due to its swifter motion, moves ahead every day by the difference between their velocities. As it proceeds in this manner, when it has moved ahead by an interval equal to one *catraka*-kalā (1,609 units), it then attains conjunction with the Sun. The time between these two is fifteen *ambubhāsa* (water-measures); its magnitude is calculated through proportion.

Having first correctly determined the mean motions of the moon and sun along with their fractional parts, if one calculates the *kudina* (terrestrial day) by means of the divisor of motion in this manner, then by the proportion "how many [days] correspond to an interval equal to the circle (360 degrees)?", the *kudinas* for the lunar month are calculated as 29 days, 31 ghaṭīs, and 50 palas, which is established as 29;31,50. || 9 ||

Ma0ḍī0—Now, in order to establish both [the lunar month and the solar month], [the author] states the nature and measure of the lunar month (*candramāsa*) and its derivation from the sun (*sūryasādhana*) by means of the verse beginning with *kālena*. By the interval between the motions of the moon and the sun, moving through the stellar sphere (*bhacakra*) at a rate of twelve degrees (*rāśyaṃśa*) per day faster than the sun, after a certain period of time, it "returns to the sun" (*sūryaṃ prati*)—that is, it joins with it for a second time. By this, the two points in time when the conjunction of the two occurs are indicated as the limits. That period of time is the lunar month (*candramāsa*).

The meaning is that the lunar [month], defined by the interval between two conjunctions (darśānta) of the sun and moon, consists of a complete revolution of the zodiac. He states the mean number of solar civil days for that [lunar month] as "aṅkayamā" (179). The measure—that is, the numerical value—of the *kudina*s (civil days) of that lunar month, according to the solar civil reckoning, is thirty-nine days, thirty-one *ghaṭikās*, and fifty *palas*. Herein lies the demonstration.

By the statement "traversing through the opening of the path," it is indicated by means of this alternative method of motion that one solar *savana* day [is traversed]; then, the proportion (*anupāta*)—"if [this is so] by the degrees and minutes traversed, what [is it] by [the remaining] degrees and minutes? is indeed implied. Here, because there is no remainder in any part, no single portion of the parts has been omitted. || 9 || [End of Chapter 16 of the Golādhyāya]. Now, regarding the intercalary months and deficient months: [they are determined] by the lunar days obtained from the solar [days] through the lunar [cycle], and by the solar [days] obtained from the lunar [cycle] through the solar [cycle], [resulting in] thirty-two and sixteen [units respectively]. || 32 || 16 ||

By this [proportion], an intercalary month (*adhimāsa*) occurs for the moon within a *kalpa* through calculation by proportion (*anupāta*). (10) The lunar month is shorter than the solar month; therefore, they [the lunar months] are greater in number. Those months which exist as the difference between the solar and lunar [months] in a *kalpa* are declared to be the intercalary months (*adhimāsa*). (11) Regarding this, the second verse is explained first.

Because the lunar month is shorter than the solar month, the number of lunar months in a Kalpa exceeds the number of solar months due to that cause. Just as in the measurement of grain, a measure of six *sevika*-handfuls is greater than a measure of eight *sevika*-handfuls, so too, O King, it is said by the arrows (*pañca*, i.e., five). That number of intercalary months which exceed the solar months in a Kalpa has been thus calculated by them.

In this regard, it is stated how many solar days constitute one intercalary month (*adhimāsa*): "By the solar [days] and the lunar [days]," and so forth. When the lunar-sidereal days are subtracted from the solar-sidereal days, the remainder in the place of days is full; below that, there are fifty-four *ghaṭīs*, twenty-seven *vighaṭīs* (sixtieths), and thirty-two-and-a-half *prativighaṭīs* (one-hundred-and-twentieths), namely: 0; 54; 27; 312; 52; 30. This is the difference between the solar and lunar [periods] in one solar month, known as *kudināni*.

At the end of one *darśa* following the beginning of the *yuga*, the solar month (*sūryamāsa*) is complete; immediately thereafter, after fifty-four *ghaṭikās* and a fraction, the *saṃkrānti* of Taurus (*vṛṣabha*) occurs within the lunar month (*candramāsa*), and therein the solar month is complete. Then, at the end of another *darśa* month, there is the conclusion of another lunar month. After two such [lunar] months, by those same *ghaṭikās* doubled, the *saṃkrānti* of Gemini (*mithuna*) occurs. In this manner, the *saṃkrāntis* of Cancer and the subsequent signs occur at intervals of tripled and quadrupled [those same *ghaṭikās*].

In this way, the *saṃkrānti* proceeds further and further ahead. When it reaches the end of the [lunar] year (*parvānta*), then the solar months are one less than the elapsed lunar months. When the *saṃkrānti* passes beyond the end of the [solar] year and proceeds ahead, then by proportion (*anupāta*), as many solar months as there are, so many [elapsed lunar months] constitute one intercalary month (*adhimāsa*). Regarding that, the proportion is as follows: if by this interval between solar and lunar days, namely 54; 27; 31; 52; 39, one solar month is obtained, then [by that same ratio], the lunar [months]...

How many are the *kudina*s (terrestrial days) contained within the *bhārata* [period], namely 29; 31; 59? The result is the solar measure: 32; 15; 31; 28; 47. Now, if by the *adhimāsa*s (intercalary months) of a *yuga* one obtains the solar months of a *yuga*, then what is obtained by one? The result is precisely the *adhanta* (the end of the *adhimāsa*); thus the solar months are obtained. For by so many solar months, the [lunar] year becomes increased (*adhika*). Therefore, the *adhimāsa* possesses the nature of a lunar month (*cāndra*). It is easy to understand that even in a *kalpa*, the [values] are to be calculated through proportion (*anupāta*). || 10 || 11 ||

It has been indicated by Tukurāja that an intercalary month (*adhimāsa*) occurs when the *sāvana* days are fewer [than the lunar days]. The justification for this is as follows: the *sāvana* measure of one lunar month is greater than the *sāvana* measure of the other [the solar month] within that interval. Thus, it results that when a *sāvana* period equal to a lunar month occurs within the second lunar month immediately following the completion of the first lunar month, then one solar month is considered "complete."

Thus, since one solar month corresponds to an excess of this many lunar days, by the proportion "if [this] excess equals the calculation for a lunar month, then what [excess] corresponds to a lunar month? one should calculate the solar months. Where these solar months are connected with a lunar month plus one, those solar months become lunar months plus one by this method of counting; thus, there is an additional month compared to the solar reckoning.

In this context as well, it should be understood that because there is no absolute completeness (niḥśeṣatva) regarding any single component, the phrase "rich with blossoms" (*dalāḍhyaiḥ*) was stated without excluding other components. Now, one might object: "Even if, according to the reasoning already stated, an intercalary month (*adhimāsa*) occurs every so many solar months, how can the number of intercalary months in a Kalpa be accepted, given that the calculation of the *ahargaṇa* (the accumulated count of days) depends upon that [number]? To this, he says: "In a Kalpa... (*kalpe*).

Therefore, according to the method stated above, since the solar months and the intercalary months—which are the results derived from the known measures—are fewer [than the lunar months], then by the rule of proportion (*anupāta*), one may determine the number of intercalary months in a Kalpa: "If by the solar years of a *puṅgīva* (a specific large number) and the solar months associated with the occurrence of a single intercalary month, one intercalary lunar month occurs, then by how many solar months [associated with the current period] will how many [intercalary months] occur? || 10 || [Objection: Since the solar month is greater than the civil (*sāvana*) month, as seen from the calculation of the lunar month, how is it that you have stated [the contrary] regarding the exceeding of the solar?

Regarding the response to the question "Why are there intercalary months (adhimāsa)? given by Mandāśaka in the *Śālinī* meter: "Because of the solar [months]... This means that because the lunar *sāvana* month—which consists of the moon's motion—is smaller than the solar *sāvana* month, those lunar months that exceed the number of solar months by the difference between the two counts are the intercalary months; they have been included within that total.

The meaning is that the remainder between the two is established as being lunar (cāndra). || 11 || Now he states the justification for the *avama* (omitted days): "By the *sāvana* [days] lessened by the suspected [remainder], 0;28,10, divided by thirty, the resulting days with their parts—namely, sixty-three, fifty-four, and thirty-three (*rudrāṃśa*, *adhirasa*)—constitute the *kṣayāha* (omitted day); thus, the *sāvana* [day] is obtained here in a *yuga* through proportion. || 12 || In a *yuga*, the difference between the lunar days and the *sāvana* days constitutes those omitted days (*avamāni*).

Therefore, in one lunar month, the difference between the lunar and solar days (*kudina*) is taken as that which is named *kuḍi*. Therein, the day is 118 complete units; in the chapter on time-measurement, it is 10 *ghaṭikās* and 0;28,19 *pānīyapalas*. This is the fractional part of a *kudina*, known as an *avama*, within one lunar month consisting of thirty days. If by this [fraction] thirty lunar days are seen, then how many are obtained by one complete *avama*? By means of the rule of three (*trairāśika*), the result is 63;54 parts of eleven.

33. There is a *reka* (deficit) on the day of death (*kṣayāha*), and that is *sāvana*. This is the conceptualization of the desire to establish the nature of the unbroken form; thus, even in the calculation of the proportionate reduction (*avamānupāta*). Bhāṣya-ṭīkā: Now, he states the proof of the *avama* (intercalary/deficit day) in the *Upajāti* meter, beginning with "śaśākca" (and the moon...). The *sāvana* month, subtracted from the lunar *sāvana* month, should be divided by thirty using this middle value of 28;10. The resulting quotient in days is 4;59 (four days and fifty-nine *ghaṭīs*), which is the *sāvana* [measure] for the Moon. It is said that the *sāvana* [day] is the nature of sixty-four minus one-eleventh part. The deficit (*kṣaya*) of a single *sāvana* day would thus occur.

And thus, since the solar month (*sāvana-māsa*) is greater than the lunar month (*cāndra-māsa*), when the lunar month is completed, the solar month is not yet complete; therefore, that interval within the lunar month is a deficient solar [time]. Consequently, if thirty lunar days (*tithis*) constitute a lunar month, then by the rule of proportion (*anupāta*)—asking "how many [days] are there for one deficient solar unit?"—the lunar days are found to be 64 minus one-ninth (i.e., 63 8/9), with a very small difference.

The intended meaning is that since these solar days (*sāvana-divasa*) are then deficient [by one], one solar day is designated as an *avama* (omission). By the word "tu" (but), it is indicated that according to the true measure (*spaṣṭa-māna*), at that time, one *avama* occurs with those [solar] days. Now, one might ask: even if there is knowledge of the occurrence of one *avama* after slightly less than sixty-four lunar days (*cāndra-dina*), how can the number of *avamas* in a *kalpa*—which is the basis for the calculation of eclipses—be determined? To this he says, "ataḥ" (therefore). This means: because the result of the measure is one *avama* occurring after slightly less than sixty-four lunar days. [This applies] in a *yuga* or a *mahāyuga*.

By the word "also" (ca), it is implied that even in a hundred kalpas, the number of *candra* days associated with the falling together [of the sun and moon] is equal to the number of *candra* days in one *kalpa*. From this, the knowledge of the *avama* (omitted lunar days) is obtained through proportion: "If for *kalpa*-yuga *candra* days, there are these *avamas*, then for the *candra* days of the specific period, what will they be? Now, having stated that the intercalary month (*adhimāsa*) is a *candra* day and the *avama* is a *sāvana* day, he states the distinction between those *avamas* and intercalary months which were brought forward by the method of *viṭhoma* in order to calculate the elapsed time from the beginning of the *kalpa* using the *ahargaṇa*: "If those intercalary months are calculated from solar days, then they are *aindava* (lunar)."

If the solar [days] are calculated from the lunar [days], then those are the solar [periods] and the remainder is its period (daśā). If the lunar [days] are calculated from the solar [days], then those are the lunar [periods] and the remainder is its period likewise. Just as in the calculation of the day-count (ahargaṇa), when intercalary months are brought forward to calculate the lunar [days] from the solar [days], those are lunar and the remainder is lunar; if, however, solar [days] are calculated from the lunar [days], then those are solar and the remainder is also solar.

In this way, when the *avama* (omitted) days are subtracted from the solar days in order to calculate the lunar days, then those [solar] days become the means [for calculation]. If one wishes to convert the solar days into lunar days, then they become lunar; that is to say, they take on the status of being the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*). By the rule beginning with "divided by the desired number of days" (*abhimataṅgaṇāśvamairhṛtāt*), he has calculated the accumulated days (*ahargaṇa*). When that which was previously brought forward is thus reduced by the solar *avama* days, those [remaining days] are the lunar days.

The intercalary months calculated from the lunar days are solar; their remainder is for the purpose of that [solar] period. Whether the intercalary month is considered lunar or solar, the remainder of the intercalary month would be exactly the same. However, in one case the divisor is solar days, while in the other it is lunar days. Likewise, the remainder of the omitted days (avama-śeṣa) is also identical; in one case the divisor is lunar days, and in the other it is civil days (kudina). Having assumed the nature of the desired quantity for both the intercalary and omitted remainders, the intelligent have performed the calculations for the lunar days.

In that regard, those who are dull-witted wander about, deliberating upon the latent impressions (vāsanā). [Commentary: Now, since the lunar months are greater than the solar ones, their difference constitutes the intercalary months (adhimāsa); likewise, because the lunar months are fewer than the solar ones by that same interval, there must be a corresponding number of deficient solar months (nyūnasauramāsa). Why, then, is the mention of intercalary months stated as a fixed rule? To this, he says in an Anuṣṭubh verse: "From the solar... and so forth.

Those [solar days] which take the form of the difference between solar and lunar [days] are the intercalary months (*adhimāsa*). For the purpose of obtaining lunar days from those solar days, the intercalary months are calculated; then, the lunar days obtained from the quotient of the intercalary months are for the sake of computing the *ahargana*. Furthermore, for the sake of determining the lunar days corresponding to the desired solar days, the lunar days—calculated by proportion (*anupāta*) using the days of the interval between the end of the intercalary month and the current day—are indeed those very lunar days that constitute the difference between them.

The intercalary months (*adhimāsa*) whose nature is that difference [between solar and lunar] are calculated from the lunar [days] for the purpose of determining the solar [year]. When those obtained intercalary months are solar, they become solar months themselves—having the nature of that difference—calculated from the desired lunar days by means of the inverse rule, for the sake of not calculating from the *ahargaṇa*. Furthermore, since the *ahargaṇa* is necessary, the lunar intercalary months whose nature is that difference were stated in the previous treatise for the purpose of calculating it.

Since there is no absolute necessity for the calculation of the solar [month] (*saura*), and because that which is other than it (the lunar month) is disregarded due to its designation as "deficient" (*nyūna*), it is universally recognized as an intercalary month (*adhimāsa*). The sense is that when such a requirement arises, its designation is established by virtue of being solar. It should be understood that since both intercalary months and deficient solar months consist of the difference between the solar and lunar [periods], their addition and subtraction are appropriate here for the two [types of months].

Now, one might ask: "Even though intercalary months (*adhimāsa*) are of the same nature as the [mean] things to be proven (*sādhya*), how is their remainder to be known as either lunar or solar? In response to this doubt, he says: "That remainder" (*taccheṣam*). The meaning is that the remainder of the intercalary months becomes solar or lunar depending on the number of intercalary months obtained by multiplying that [remainder] by ten. Thus, it means it becomes solar or lunar; since the remainder of the intercalary months is dependent upon the intercalary months themselves, what is there to wonder at? This is the intended sense. || 13 ||

But surely, according to the very method already stated, since the *sāvana* days are fewer than the lunar days within that interval, it was said that "the *avama* [days] are the difference between them. Likewise, since the lunar days are greater than the *sāvana* days within that interval, why was it not said that "the additional lunar days are the difference"? To this, he replies with an *anuṣṭubh* verse beginning with "lāvāni": "If (*cet*) the *avama* days were calculated for the sake of knowing the *sāvana* days, then those [calculated] *sāvana* days would be deficient when used in the calculation of the *ahargaṇa*, because the *sāvana* days are fewer. The word *avama* signifies 'deficient' (*ūna*)."

The *ahargaṇa* (the sum of days) is established by subtracting the [mean] lunar days from the [mean] solar days; the purpose of this is that these [mean lunar days] are derived from the same source as those [mean solar days]. In the chapter on the *Gola*, it is stated that because the mean lunar days are subordinate to the interval between them, and because the *ahargaṇa* has great utility, only the *avamānas* (omitted lunar days) were mentioned for the sake of calculating that interval. Since there is no great utility for calculating the reverse, the previous authorities disregarded the name "mean lunar day" (*cāndradina*) for that interval.

The sense is that when such a requirement [for subtraction] arises, the designation of that [remainder] as an *avama* (omission) is established by its very nature as being less than a full unit of time. Here too, it should be understood that since the *avamānas* consist of additional lunar days (*cāndra-dina*), and because they are of the nature of the difference between lunar and solar days (*sāvana*), it is logical to combine them with other similar quantities. Now, one might object: "While it is appropriate for the *adhiśeṣa* (the remainder of omitted months) to be treated like an intercalary month (*adhimāsa*), it is improper for the *avamaśeṣa* (the remainder of omitted days) to be treated similarly; for the *avama* is of a nature contrary to the *adhimāsa*."

But if it were otherwise, the status of that [remainder] as a part would be destroyed; therefore, he says: "of its remainder" (*taccheṣām*). This refers to the remainder of the *avamā* (omitted lunar days), because of the adherence to the *sāvana* and *cāndra* [reckonings]. Thus, the meaning is that, like the *sāvana*, it does not possess the designator of the aforementioned name. Since the remainder of the *avamā* is a part of the *avamā*, and since there is no state of being an obstacle for that which exists in a form contrary to the *adhimāsa* (intercalary month), it is indeed logical that the parts possess a nature different from the whole; otherwise, the status of being a part would be untenable—this is the intended sense. || 14 ||

Now, regarding the specific point in this chapter on the calculation of the *ahargaṇa*: why are the solar months increased by the lunar months beginning with Caitra? Why are the remainders of intercalary months (*adhikamāsa*) and omitted days (*avama*) discarded, since the proportion involves fractional parts? He provides the answer to this question in these two verses: "A month equal to the moon [in duration] indeed exceeds ten [days]; however, the solar month has its limit at the *saṃkrānti* (solar ingress). Therefore, the remainder of the intercalary month always remains prior to the completion of the *saṃkrānti* degrees. (16)

The solar days are obtained by adding together the number of days from the new moon (darśānta) up to the current lunar date (tithi), measured in solar units. Since those days include an excess arising from the *adhiśeṣa* (the remainder of the intercalary period), that remainder of the intercalary month is subtracted from this total. The remainder of the *avama* (omitted day) always remains between the end of the lunar date (*tithyanta*) and the solar sunrise. By means of that [remainder], the lunar day (*tithi*) becomes one whose time of occurrence is at sunrise; otherwise, it would be at the end of the lunar date. The new moon (*amāvāsyā*) occurs according to the mean measure of the month; the end of the lunar month coincides with the end of that [new moon].

In whichever *viṣuva* (equinox) the transition of the *madhyamārkasya* (mean sun) occurs, at that time of transition, the solar months end. Likewise, in the interval between the ends of the solar and lunar months, those lunar days (*tithis*) along with their fractional parts that remain are the *adhikamāsa-śeṣa-tithis* (lunar days remaining from the intercalary month). An intercalary month (*adhikamāsa*) is the difference between the solar and lunar [measurements].

The elapsed [solar] days multiplied by twelve become the solar months. To these, the solar months corresponding to the elapsed lunar months since the beginning of the year are added; these become the "transit-multiples" (*saṃkramya-vadhāḥ*). To these, thirty times the elapsed [solar] days are added, which are equal to the elapsed solar days themselves. Consequently, they become increased by the difference between the solar and lunar [days]; this difference constitutes the days remaining from the intercalary month (*adhimāsa-śeṣa-dināni*), because it is the interval between the solar and lunar [reckonings]. Therefore, the days remaining from the intercalary month must be subtracted from those [totals].

Furthermore, in the calculation of intercalary months (*adhimāsa*), it must be stated that by means of the remainder of the intercalary months and the days of the deficient months (*avama*) multiplied by sixty, the solar days (*saurāha*) should be established as the divisor. Thus, in this case, the days of the deficient months—namely, one hundred and twenty-five (*125*)—are to be added. Among these, the deficient months are subtracted first. For this reason, the remainder of the intercalary months has been discarded. Now, the reason for discarding the remainder of the deficient months is stated: immediately after the [expired] years, however many *nāḍīs* (ghaṭikās) there are of the remainder of the deficient months until the sunrise, [that is the measure].

Since the difference between the lunar and solar days constitutes the *avamāna* (omitted lunar days), if the remainder of the *avamas* is not discarded, and if the lunar days are diminished by the *avama*-remainder minutes multiplied by eight, then the day-count (*ahargaṇa*) becomes based on the solar day. Furthermore, the limit of sunrise must be calculated: the day-count increased by the *avama*-remainder minutes becomes the limit of sunrise. Therefore, when the *avama*-remainder is discarded, the limit of sunrise occurs naturally. [115|13 617|18]

Mīna—Now, desiring to establish the determination of the *ahargaṇa* (the accumulated count of days) by first ascertaining the nature of the intercalary month (*adhimāsa*) and the omitted lunar day (*kṣayāha*), which serve as the basis for calculating the *ahargaṇa*, and wishing to demonstrate that first, [the author] addresses the objection of the students regarding the refutation of the great calculation of the *pūrvāñcala* school with an *upajāti* verse, beginning with "ahargaṇasya": "O calculator! regarding the calculation of the *ahargaṇa* as it has been correctly accepted and stated..."

The number of solar years (*arkasamāgaṇa*) occurring in the *kalpa* mentioned in the context of bringing about the true [mean] positions of the planets—which was set forth in the three verses beginning with "Of the year (*ahna*), of the knowledge of the year (*ahnajñāna*), of that which has become beneficial..."—is produced by the formula "the number of years in the stated *kalpa*, multiplied by twelve (*raviguṇa*). [This is] by means of the lunar months elapsed since the beginning of Caitra. Why are they joined? They are not fit to be added by the lunar months starting from Caitra, because of the phrase "joined with the elapsed months. This is because of their distinct nature (*vijayatvāt*).

The meaning is that yoga occurs among them when they are of equal genus (*samānajāti*), as has been stated. One should understand that in this way, the true nature of the *tithis* situated within the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*) and so forth is established by that very [statement]. Now, one might object: "Since the lunar months such as Caitra are understood through the necessity of otherwise explaining the solar months, why are they not joined with their own specific natures? To this, the answer is: "Because of the absence of a defect. Why? Because of the presence of an intercalary month (*adhimāsa*).

These [corrections] are established from solar days for the sake of achieving true sidereal time (*abhivārṣika-siddhi*) and likewise for the sake of achieving civil time (*sāvana-siddhi*), having subtracted one and nine [respectively]. In their respective cases: by these two, in order, [the corrections are applied] to the days and so forth, and the *ghaṭī*s and so forth.
