426. The meaning of "īṃdhī" is that which is within the interior (*antardena*). Now, [if one objects] that it is not possible for there to be a grasping (*grahaṇa*) or a seeking (*adhyaiṣa*) of the essence of the self (*ātman*)—which is free from the fear of servitude (*adhidāsa-bhaya*) and is characterized by the power of the *lakṣa*—then there is no capacity for such a thing. Thus, "atha etad" [is used]. From this, the act of "adhivamana" (overcoming) is well-known as being performed through that means; its fruit is seen to be entirely without remainder.

According to the method stated above for the subtraction of the qualities (guṇahāra), since the divisor is established by that [method], the division of the results of the new and full moons is performed by the conjunction of the signs (rāśi). For otherwise, there would be no quality (guṇa) by which those two could be determined. Thus, the well-known calculation of *dadhi* (curds) becomes consistent. By this very abandonment, the question also becomes consistent. The justification is that the twelve-fold [cycle] is not otherwise possible; otherwise, even in the half [period], there would be the fault of grasping an incomplete portion.

133. [Commentary by Bhaṭṭotpala]: Now, it might be argued that since the solar day-count (*ahargaṇa*) is based on the solar civil day (*sāvana*), and because its starting point is the sunrise, its lack of fractional parts (*niravayavatva*) must be established; otherwise, its validity would be untenable, and thus one should abandon the fractions. However, this is not so. By accepting the fractional parts established through logical proof (*upapatti*), the day-count is indeed shown to possess fractions, and there is no flaw in postulating a starting point distinct from sunrise. Therefore, the sense is that the aforementioned day-count is inherently incomplete (*asasiddhatva*). || 15 ||

Now, the intercalary month (*adhimāsa*), which serves as the basis for what follows, is described by way of its six-fold nature in the *Upajāti* meter: "By the words *avaśa-dhabhiḥ*. For [the lunar month] is certainly delimited by the new moon (*darśa*); that is, it is the lunar month whose boundaries are the two conjunctions with the teeth [of the sun]. The solar month is that which has the *saṃkrānti* (sun's passage into a zodiac sign) as its limit. By the word "but" (*tu*), it is indicated that this [lunar month] must be understood through mean calculation for the purpose of establishing the completed state of the accumulated days (*ahargaṇa*), because its completion is not achieved through true (apparent) measurement.

Therefore, because the difference between the solar and lunar [measures]—which constitutes the *rava*—is stated as twenty-five, there is always a remainder for an intercalary month (*adhimāsa*) prior to the time of the sun's entry into a zodiacal sign (*saṃkrānti*) at the end of a new moon (*darśānta*). The particle "eva" (only) serves to exclude any other connection. By this very fact, the status of the month containing a *saṃkrānti* as an intercalary one is established. Thus, when the time of the *saṃkrānti* is separated from the time calculated according to the standard of the Middle Country (*madhyadeśīya*) by an interval of lunar days (*tithi*), that [day] is treated as the mean value in the calculation of the day-count (*ahargaṇa*) and so forth.

It is indicated that at the desired time for the month, [the interval] up to the end of the day of the desired moon is equal to the difference in solar days; clearly, that [interval] between the two true [points], namely the new-moon and the solstice, is not useful here. Now, regarding the calculation of the *ahargaṇa*, the author sets forth the arrangement using an *upajāti* verse concerning the addition of the lunar months, the remainder of the previous correction, and the motion: "By the teeth... and so on. The solar days are joined with as many solar days as are measured by the lunar tithis beginning with the teeth.

The meaning is that [the solar months] are added to the solar months elapsed since the beginning of the Kalpa. Furthermore, since the years are solar, the solar months elapsed since the beginning of the Kalpa—multiplied by twelve for the years and increased by the intercalary months (adhika-māsa) up to the mean entry of Aries—are to be added to the current solar months at the start of the desired month for the sake of knowing that [mean position]. Then, to those [months], the number of days corresponding to the elapsed solar days from the beginning of the Kalpa up to the desired time should be added, having been multiplied by thirty. Thus, the elapsed solar days from the beginning of the Kalpa to the desired time are obtained.

It is impossible for these [mean solar days] to occur as they are stated. Since the mean solar days from the beginning of the year do not coincide with the desired time, the Teacher has added to the mean solar days elapsed at the start of the year only those solar months that correspond to the lunar months elapsed up to half a synodic month (ardha-cāndra-māsa), and so forth. Then, to those [days] increased by thirty, the solar days corresponding to the current lunar month and its specific day are added; this is the meaning of the latter half of the verse.

The meaning is that, just as a person who has committed a crime is dragged by the hair by a Candala, so too is this [intercalary month] treated. Now, he explains the rejection of the remainder of the intercalary month with the words "yataḥ" (since): because those desired solar days [of the month], when increased by the days of the [preceding] year, exceed the lunar days.

According to the stated method, for those whose solar [longitude] is equal to that of their own lord, and for those whose solar [longitude] is derived from the true longitude of the Sun, and for those whose solar [longitude] is derived from the head and the rest, if the solar days are produced by the calculation of the desired [period] through the *ṭaṅkaṅphi-sauvicā*, the meaning is that they are joined with the solar day-count. This is the underlying principle (*vāsana*) regarding the calculation of the months and the completion of the lunar year, following the path of the previous calculation to avoid that [error]. In this [calculation], the remainder of the division is discarded as days and so forth.

It was not taken for the sake of establishing the *ahargaṇa* (the sum of days). Just as solar months were added [to the calculation], the fractional part of the *adhiśeṣa*—namely, the remainder of the intercalary month (*adhika-māsa*)—was not added to the solar days. This is because that fraction previously existed as an *adhi* (intercalary element), and otherwise, since it would be greater than the lunar days (*iṣu-cāndra*), it would result in a lack of correspondence with reality; such is the meaning.

Nor can it be argued that there is no reason to discard [the calculated intercalary month] because the remainder derived from the calculation of the intercalary months based on non-real solar days is not equal to the remainder included within the calculated solar period—since the difference between the two remainders was previously established as being unnecessary. This objection is inconsistent, because that [difference] is established precisely by the very calculation of the intercalary months from the non-real solar days. || 17 ||

[Objection: But if, in this way, the *avamāni* (omissions) established for the beginning of the Kalpas and so forth are devoid of substance because the actual number of omissions is not understood, how can they be used for the purpose of establishing the end of the day (*sāyanasiddhi*)? For they have been made deficient by subtracting the remainder of the omissions from the great lunar cycle (*mahīṣṭacāndra*). To this, he gives the answer in the *upajāti* meter: "At the end of the lunar day" (*tithyante*), etc. Between the mean end of the lunar day (*tithyanta*) and the mean sunrise (*madhyamasūryodaya*)—which are the basis for calculating the *ahargana* (the accumulated count of days)—there exists an interval. "Always before sunrise from the end of the *tukārāci* (the final moment of the day), this [calculation] is invariably and entirely so; the particle *eva* (only) excludes any other application. Likewise, for the sake of establishing the *ahargaṇa*, the remainder of the omitted days (*avamāṃśa-śeṣa*) was previously subtracted; thereafter, for the sake of establishing the time-measure starting from sunrise, that same remainder of omitted days should be added. Thus, at the time of subtracting the omitted days, the remainder of omitted days was not subtracted for the sake of brevity—this is the intended meaning. In this way, the method for calculating the *ahargaṇa* stated above is proven to be correct. Now, he states the correction known as the "difference of rising" (*udayāntara*) for the mean solar day: "The *ahargaṇa* is divided by the mean solar day, because the true solar day is not equal [to the mean]."

The retrograde [periods] arising from that, increased or decreased by the result produced by the operation known as the difference between the ascendants (udayāntara), would be the [retrograde periods] at Laṅkā; however, they are not so [calculated], for it is understood that there is a difference, and that [difference] is moving and small. This day-count (ahargaṇa) which has been computed is indeed by means of the mean solar day (madhyama-sāvana). Why? Because the process of calculation for the true [mean motion] is difficult. The meaning is that the true [value] does not come forth by such a proportion (anupāta).

From the beginning of the current solar year until the present solar year, the mean civil day (madhyama-sāvana) is indeed equal to that very same clear civil day (sphuṭa-sāvana). However, because the solar year begins with zero [mean longitude], the mean civil day is not equal to the clear one. Therefore, the planets derived from that [mean calculation] must be increased or decreased by the correction known as *udayāntara* (the difference between true and mean sunrise); otherwise, they will not correspond to the true sunrise at Laṅkā. As for what has been stated by others—that the mean [longitude] corresponds to the sunrise of the Sun at Laṅkā—that is incorrect. || 19 ||

Now he states the calculation for the difference between two risings: "The elapsed *asus* at midday that were not mentioned [previously] for the non-axial latitude (*nirakṣa*), and those which are equal to the minutes of arc of the midday sun—whatever the difference between those two is, that shall be the interval between the true and mean planetary masses, diminished by the motion. Divided by the *ghrātri* (twenty-four) *asus*, it is in minutes; if the elapsed *asus* are fewer, the planets are subtracted. Otherwise, if they are with their own rising-times (*nijodaya*), then what was previously prescribed applies to the elapsed minutes. (20–21)

Thus, the *carakarma* (equation of time) is performed; this is the *carakarma* of the planets known as the "interior of the heart" (*hṛdayāntara*). [The procedure is as follows: By means of the sun with its precessional degrees (*sāyanāṃśa*), one determines the signs traversed starting from Aries. Taking the corresponding right-ascensions (*nirakṣodayāsava*)—such as 1670 and so forth—one sums them. From that total, the elapsed portion is subtracted. The remainder represents the elapsed degrees; these are multiplied by the rising-seconds (*udayāsava*) of that sign and divided by thirty (*triṃśat*). The rising-seconds of the [preceding] signs should also be added there.

In this manner, the elapsed *asus* (breaths) for the mean planet shall be determined. From the end of the day (*bhadinānta*) until that many *asus* have passed in the current day, at that moment the mean planet rises in the *ṭaṅkā*. For at that time, the planet is to be calculated. Now, those [mean planets] established by the *Bahūgaṇa* in the Siddhānta are positioned from the end of the day at the time of the mean planet's rising; therefore, the difference between the calculation of those *asus* and the actual [time] causes the sunrise to be displaced. That displacement from the sunrise is called the *karma* (correction).

Divide those intermediate breaths by the breaths of the day and night calculated for the sun with its [current] latitude (21,659); the resulting minutes of arc are the correction (*kāya*). If the breaths are fewer than the minutes of arc, it is negative; otherwise, it is positive. However, if this operation is performed after first determining the degrees traversed and remaining by means of the local risings (*udaya*), then the correction for the diurnal semi-arc (*cara-karma*) will also have been applied to the planets at their rising.

If, however, this operation were performed using the *asus* of the rising of the signs calculated from the true Sun, then all three—the longitudinal difference (*dyujyantara*), the difference in declination (*bhuja-antara*), and the diurnal semi-circle (*carakhaṇḍa*)—would be equal. Why, then, was this operation called *dyujyantara* not performed by us? To this he says: because that difference is variable and small; at the ends of the four quarters of the year there is an absence of difference, while in between them, the difference increases and decreases. (20–22)

Ma0ḍī0—Now, by means of the rationale of the *ahargaṇa* (the accumulated days), he states the correction for the difference in the times of sunrise (*udayāntara*) through four verses in the *Upajāti* meter, beginning with "The *ahargaṇa*": "The *ahargaṇa* is by the mean solar day; that is to say, by the mean [day] measured by sixty *nākṣatra* ghaṭīs, which is equal to the number of *sūryodaya* ghaṭīs produced by the mean motion of the Sun according to the assumed fixed measure. Thus it is correctly stated: "When the mean sun is near the horizon, [the planet is] mean. Now, one might ask: how then do the planets come to be at the time of the mean solar meridian transit? To this he says: "Saduraseṭa" (562). These are the planets produced by the proportion of the elapsed days.

They are increased by the *udayāntara* correction—consisting of one-sixtieth of a degree (*kalā*)—generated according to the rules stated in the *Sphuṭādhikāra*, following their respective motions. The intention is that they disregarded this difference—which is perceived through direct observation—neither because it was impossible to deny it by following its own course, nor because it was unproven; rather, it must be understood that they overlooked it. Now, one might object: "It is not right to disregard a difference that is directly perceived. To this he says: "Because" (*yataḥ*). For this reason, the subsequent result called "the interval of rising" (*udayāntara*), produced by the interval of rising at midday, is thus appropriately named. The sense is that these [results] have been disregarded because they are uncertain. Now, one might ask: "If this is so, how is it that clear and other such actions were mentioned by them? To this he says: "without a reward" (*arūpakam*). The meaning is that the fruit arising from the interval between those [actions] is extremely small; therefore, it was disregarded. The conjunction *ca* is used for accumulation. Thus, the sense is that while it is appropriate to state what is certain, abundant, and necessary to avoid, as well as what is certain and small, this [result] has been disregarded because its form is uncertain. However, I have not [mentioned it] because it is improper to speak of a result that is merely a conceptual construct (*vastubhūta*); this is how it should be understood.

[Objection: But surely, since the difference in rising times (*udayāntara*) is so minute, it does not even exist; for, as I have stated regarding the day-count (*ahargaṇa*) at the beginning of the Kalpa, there is a coming and going of many days produced by that interval. [Response: Therefore, he demonstrates that the difference in rising times is indeed of that nature [i.e., real] by saying, "subtracted from the mean sun."

Even there, since that [correction] is established by the very difference between the two middle true longitudes produced when the mean motions are equal, the *asus*—which are equal to the *kalās* of the mean Sun—are calculated from the solar year until the desired time by means of the proportion derived from the mean motion of the Sun; these [asus] correspond to the number associated with the *ahargaṇa*.

By the aforementioned method, according to the difference in the rising times of each sign at midday, there are certain numbers of *asava*s that are determined by the mean measure and connected to the *ahargana* (the count of elapsed days). And (*ca*) denotes conjunction. The difference between those two, whatever its number may be, is precisely the difference between the non-evident mean and the evident mean; it is the difference between the two *aharganas* obtained through the stated proportion based on the non-fixed mean measure, and not otherwise. If this [correction] were not to be applied to the group of elapsed days (*ahargaṇa*), then the calculation of the planets according to the method we have described would be correct; however, since the correction for the difference between true and mean [planets] is stated in the *Sphuṭādhikāra* (Chapter on True Planets), he says: "multiplied by the motion" (*gatighnam*). That difference is multiplied by its own respective mean daily motion in minutes of arc, and divided by the divisor derived from the mean motion; the resulting days are subtracted from or added to the [mean planet] as appropriate, whereby they become the true [planets] in minutes of arc. Otherwise, it is the reverse.

Regarding the opposite of what was stated [in verse 11]: 12. Since the *asus* (breaths) are greater than the eight *kalās*, the *prahās* (corrections) are obtained by means of the *tuka* (the remainder), the *labdha* (quotient), and the *kalās*, etc.; this is the meaning. They are "joined" (*yuktāḥ*), because that time has been subtracted; such is the sense. And thus, without the subtraction of the sun, its correction cannot be applied to the *ahargaṇa* (day-count). Furthermore, because of the labor involved in calculation and so forth from a *ahargaṇa* containing fractional parts, and for the sake of brevity, the motion is given as an additive to the planet; this is the underlying idea.

[Objection: But in this way, compared to what was stated previously, there would indeed be greater complexity regarding the correction (*saṃskāra*). To this, he says: "by their own risings" (*nijodayaiḥ*). If the first part of the day (*savana*)—meaning the day-and-night period (*ahorātrasava*), as indicated by the word "first"—is joined with the breaths of the rising of the [planets] in their own respective places, then the operation called "difference of rising" (*udayāntara*) is performed; that is, the correction for motion (*cara-saṃskāra*), which is a friend to the correction for motion, is applied. The meaning is that it is done in such a way that the days become corrected. And thus:

If the difference between two [solar] positions is calculated using the ascensions (udaya) of the equatorial points (*nirakṣa*), then indeed there is complexity; however, by using the ascensions of one's own location (*svadeśodaya*), that same result is achieved through the correction for the difference in oblique ascensions (*bhinnacara-saṃskāra*) and the correction for the difference in local ascensions (*karabhodayāntara-saṃskāra*). Thus, there is no room for complexity [in this latter method]. This simplicity in comparison has been demonstrated in the *Sphuṭādhikāra* (Chapter on True Motion). || 22 || Now, he describes the nature of longitudinal difference (*deśāntara*): "Those [mean planets] which are at the time of the Lanka-ascension become [the mean planets] at the local sunrise through the longitudinal difference (*deśāntara*)."

The longitudinal difference (deśāntara) is east-west, and likewise the latitudinal difference (anyayāmyottara); these are said to be known as "motion" (cara). Those planets that have arisen at sunrise in one location through the operation of longitudinal difference shall become those arisen at sunrise in one's own city through the operation of longitudinal difference. And that longitudinal difference is of two kinds: one is east-west, and the other is north-south; it is said to be designated as "motion."

In this regard, first: that line which goes from the easternmost to the westernmost point, touching regions such as Kurukṣetra while passing over Śrīnagarī and Ujjayinī and reaching Mount Meru, is declared by the wise to be the central meridian (madhyarekhā) of the earth. Since the sunrise occurs first in the eastern region and later in other regions relative to the rising of the meridian, therefore the resulting correction for the planets—arising from the interval between them—is applied as a subtraction or addition [respectively]. A line extending to Meru, passing through Ujjayinī, Kurukṣetra, and other regions, is called the "central meridian" (madhyarekhā).

When the sun rises at the prime meridian, it is already sunset in the eastern region; conversely, after the time of sunrise at the meridian, it is sunrise in the western region. The time interval between these two is known through proportion from the clear circumference (the earth's equatorial circumference) and the intervening yojanas. If sixty ghaṭīs are obtained for the yojanas of the clear circumference, then by the rule of three (trairāśika), what is obtained for the yojanas of the interval between the meridian and one's own city? Thus, the longitudinal correction (deśāntara-ghaṭī) is determined.

Then, having brought the nadīs (ghaṭīs) by means of mean motion, there is a proportion based on them: "If sixty ghaṭīs yield the planet's motion in kalās, then what is obtained by the ghaṭīs of longitudinal difference? Alternatively, the proportion is made using yojanas alone: "If the motion is obtained by means of yojanas of the true circumference, then what is obtained by the yojanas of longitudinal difference? The result is in kalās; they are positive because the rising occurs there first, and negative because the setting occurs there later, since the sun and others set there immediately after the meridian line. Thus it is established. || 24 ||

[Madhyagatavāmasana 1 134 Ma0 802]—By means of the correction for longitudinal difference (*deśāntara-saṃskāra*), the planets become [corrected] at the time of sunrise at Laṅkā. Then, how do they become [corrected] at the time of sunrise at one's own location? To this, he says "by this" (*anena*). Those planets which have been produced at the time of the sun's rising at Laṅkā by means of this correction for the maximum longitudinal difference (*saraphala-saṃskāra*), those same planets become [further corrected] at the time of the sun's rising at one's own city by means of the correction for longitudinal difference.

[Objection: But surely, since the correction for longitudinal difference (*deśāntaraphala*) is not perceived in Rekhapura, how can there be [a difference] there at sunrise? For there, the sunrise is not distinct from the rising of the *līkārya* even on days other than the equinox, such that no fault would arise. Therefore, the longitudinal difference is divided: "The longitudinal difference" (*deśāntaram iti*). One well-known longitudinal difference is designated as "eastern" or "western. The other is the second, which is "southern" or "northern. Thus, regarding the longitudinal difference; he removes the objection concerning its lack of renown with the word "that" (*tad iti*).

First, the longitudinal difference (deśāntara) associated with the north-south direction is called *cara* (motion), because it varies according to the difference in time; for this very reason, due to its instability, it is termed *cara*. The longitudinal difference associated with the east-west direction is termed *deśāntara* (place-difference), because of its stability. Both are designated as "longitudinal differences" (*deśāntara*) because they relate to spatial positions.

And thus, although there is no longitudinal difference (deśāntara) between the well-known eastern and western locations on the meridian line, because a longitudinal difference in the form of the maximum southern declination (yāmyacara) is established, it follows that [the phenomena] occur at sunrise by means of that very [difference]; this is the intended meaning. For this very reason, in a location to the east or west of Laṅkā that is on the equator (nirakṣa), they occur at the time of sunrise precisely due to the east-west longitudinal difference; however, in one's own location relative to the meridian line, they occur due to both longitudinal differences. This is because, as stated correctly, a distinction among the sines (visinām) is established in locations to the east, west, south, or north of Laṅkā, owing to the difference in the latitudes of the people (puṃsāṃ meḍhalakatvāt). Now... 23. Following the previous instruction, the author indicates that the determination of the longitudinal difference (*rekhādeśa*) is connected to the determination of the local place (*ṛṭṭekha*), and suggests the middle chapter on the description of the meridian line with half a verse. In connection with that, he states the proof for its calculation in the first half of a *śārdūlavikrīḍita* verse, beginning with "yad" (since), the meaning of which has already been explained previously. For—since, in a location situated to the east of one's own meridian line, the sunrise occurs first from the sunrise at the meridian line.

Because [the sun] sets immediately after its rising at Rekhā in the region situated to the west of Rekhāpurā; for that reason, the distance in *yojanas* between one's own meridian line (*svarekhā*) and one's own location—which exists within that interval—is found on the clear *parighasūtra*. From that, by means of proportion (*anupāta*), [one calculates] the *yojanas* situated between those points and one's own place.

The motion of a planet multiplied by the true circumference of the earth and divided [by sixty] results in a value; this is the correction known as *deśāntara* (longitude difference), which is to be added to or subtracted from the planets according to whether it is east or west. It should be understood that for those who use the equatorial meridian (*laṅkā*), since the longitudinal status is established through the correction of *cara* (ascensional difference), there is no fault in first explaining the nature of the *deśāntara* correction even for those using the prime meridian (*rekhā-kadaya*). || 24 ||

Now, regarding the determination of the true circumference of the terrestrial globe, [the author], distressed by the lack of clarity, says: "One should calculate one's own location from the Malaya mountain in all directions; for the true circumference of the earth is such that when multiplied by seven and divided by the radius of the celestial sphere (trijyā), it results in the desired value. (35) The number of *yojanas* between one's city and the center of Meru are equal to the degrees of latitude. Therefore, the *yojanas* of distance between one's city and the equator are the degrees of latitude.

The meaning is that from the parts, the *yojanas* were separately projected from Viṣṇupadī. By those vertical lines (*lamba-rajas*) and people, [the space] was filled with mountains and trees through their conjunction.

In the Bhaṭadīpikā: the terrestrial circumference (bhūparidhi) is clearly [stated]. Now, the calculation thereof: having assumed a diameter equal to three times the desired mean circumference, the half-diameter at one's own city—namely, the lambajyā (sine of the colatitude)—should be the half of the true (sphuṭa) circumference. Hence, there is a rule of three (trairāśika) with that.

If the mean circumference is taken as the radius of the trigonometric circle (trijyā), then what would it be when measured by the lambajyā? The result is the true circumference; thus it is established. Thus ends the exposition on the mean motion in the Golādhyāya. [Verse 87] — Now, the calculation of the correction for difference of longitude (deśāntara-phala) depends upon the true terrestrial circumference.

In this regard, since the earth is spherical (*bhūgola*), the circumference of the earth is equal everywhere; therefore, the true circumference of the earth is appropriate [to be calculated]. Thus, preceded by an exposition of its nature, he states the justification for its calculation in an *upajāti* verse beginning with "svadeśa": "One's own place" (*svadeśa*) refers to Meru. By the line passing through the center of Meru, there is a point on the surface of the earth; the meaning is that by the *yojanas* of the interval between those two—the point on the earth's surface connected to the center of Mount Meru and the point on the surface of the terrestrial globe—[the circumference is determined].

By calculating that center from all sides, the circle that is formed around it on the surface of the terrestrial globe (Bhūgola) by those *yojanas*—[how is this possible] since there is an absence of knowledge regarding those *yojanas*? To this he says: "produced from the degrees of colatitude" (*lambāṃśaja*). Just as *yojanas* are derived from degrees in reverse order according to the statement [of the rule], so too, by the degrees of difference between the equator and one's own location, the *yojanas* corresponding to the degrees of colatitude—which are ninety minus the degrees of latitude—become those *yojanas*. For this reason, that is the true circumference of the earth (*bhūparidhi*).

For this reason, since the equatorial circumference related to the poleless region (the equator) has been stated to be equal to the quotient obtained by dividing the previously mentioned *parama-spaṣṭa-parājya* (maximum true declination-cord) by the *lambajyā* (sine of colatitude), then by the proportion "if [this] is the terrestrial circumference at the poleless region, what is it at one's own location with the local *lambajyā*?", the terrestrial circumference is multiplied by the *lambajyā*. This multiplication by the *lambajyā* was performed for the purpose of establishing the true circumference according to the previously stated rule: "The terrestrial circumference divided by the *trijyā* (radius of the celestial sphere). || 25 ||

Regarding the question posed by Melibhūta—“How can there be an uncorrected [longitude] for that planet which is obtained through proportion?”—the author provides the answer in two successive statements: “Thus, by the method of mean motion... and “Here, it is stated according to the method of mean measure. The sense is that since the mean [longitude] is the basis for the true [longitude], it is appropriate to state the method of correction (*spaṣṭīkaraṇa*) based on the clear [mean] values.

Thus ends the second chapter, on the determination of the mean positions of the planets, within the *Marīci* commentary on the *Siddhāntaśiromaṇi*, composed by Gaṇeśa, whose feet are served by the eminent assembly of astrologers, and who is the son of Śrī Raṅganātha. And just as it is impossible to know the nature of a cloth without knowing the nature of the threads, so too it is impossible to know the nature of the sphere without knowing the nature of the sine (jyā); thus, the intent is that the derivation of the sine is stated first.

1} Now, he first states the configuration of the living being’s field (jīvākṣetra): The sine of three signs (90°) is desired as the *dhṛti* (the radius). The sine of the [desired] arc is the *bhuja* (sine), and its co-sine is the *koṭi*. The square root of the difference between their squares is the *doḥkoṭyaṃśalā* (the sine of the sum of the arc and its complement). These two sines of the successive arcs (*kramajye*) are separately subtracted from three signs (270°); they are the sines of the successive arcs of the complement and the sine of the arc. Indeed, between the sine and the arc, there is the sine of the arrow (the versed sine). The sine of the arc of five signs (150°) is the square root of half the square of the sine of three signs. From that, the sine of the arc of four signs (120°) is the same as the co-sine.

For the purpose of the sine table, the sine of ninety degrees (90°) is sixty (60), and its cosine is twenty (20). The square root of the sum of the successive and reverse sines is the sine of forty-five degrees (45°). The square root of half the product of the sine of ninety degrees and the reverse sine of that same angle is the sine of thirty degrees (30°). From that, one should likewise calculate the sines of fifteen degrees (15°) and seven and a half degrees (7.5°) using their respective cosines and the square roots of their products. In this manner, the wise should determine the desired sines for angles numbered as three, six, twelve, twenty-four, and so forth.

"Or, having calculated the sines for the desired planets on a circle of radius equal to the trijyā marked with zodiacal divisions. Here, the phrase "on a circle of radius equal to the trijyā marked with zodiacal divisions" is explained as a partial commentary on the latter half of the *nayavṛtta*.

The sine of three signs (trijyā) is assumed as the radius. On level ground in an assembly hall, one should describe a circle using a cord equal to that radius, marking the directions and marking it with degrees of the zodiac. Therein, each quarter of the circle consists of ninety degrees. Then, having divided each quarter into as many parts as there are half-sines (jyārdha) to be constructed, marks should be made at those points. For example:

Where twenty-four *jīvas* (sines) are to be established, there are twenty-four [points]. This is likewise for the second and fourth parts. Then, a thread extending from a directional mark to above two marks on both sides takes the form of a *jyā* (chord). In this way, there are twenty-four *jyās*. Their halves are the *jyārdhas* (semi-chords). Having measured their lengths with finger-breadths (*aṅgulis*), they are applied during the journey. Now, the explanation begins from the beginning: that which is desired as the triple-sine (*trijyā*) is the hypotenuse (*karṇa*). The wise call it *kavi*.

That which is the sine of the arc is the *bhuja* (side), and the difference between those two—the hypotenuse and the side—is the *koṭi* (perpendicular); this means the cosine-sine (*koṭijyā*). In that case, those which are the *bhuja-jyā* and *koṭi-jyā* are to be understood as being among the sines of the degrees of the *bhuja* and *koṭi*. To whatever extent the *bhuja-jyā* is subtracted from the radius (*trijyā`), to that same extent the versed sine (*utkramajyā*) of the degrees of the *koṭi* remains. Likewise, the radius diminished by the *koṭi-jyā* would be the versed sine of the degrees of the *bhuja*. Now, he shows the location of the versed sine (*utkramajyā*).

In that regard, the line drawn over the two marks on the previously drawn arc is called the *jyā* (sine). The portion of the circle situated between those two marks is called the *dhanuḥ* (arc). The arrow-shaped interval between the center of the arc and the center of the *jyā* is called the *koṭijyā*. [This] relates to the tip of the radius at the three signs (90 degrees). Thus, having explained the field of calculation in a general manner, now follows the determination of the *jyās* through the specified mathematical procedure.

The square root of half the square of the versed sine of three signs (90 degrees) shall be the sine of forty-five degrees. As long as its co-sine is calculated, it remains exactly that same value; for in that case, the degrees of the complement are also forty-five. Here is the proof: the radius (trijyā) is the hypotenuse and the sine of the [given] angle is the side; the square root of their difference shall be the side of an equilateral quadrilateral within the circle. That itself is the sine of ninety degrees; half of that is the first [sine].

Therefore, a fourth part of this square is *cha-sa*. At that very moment, it is half the square of the radius (*trijyā*); hence its square root is the sine of fifteen degrees. Now, the sine of thirty degrees would be equal to the radius (*trijyā*). Its co-sine (*koṭijyā*) would be the sine of sixty degrees. Here, the error is as follows: it is well known even in established calculation that half the chord of an equilateral hexagon inscribed within a circle would be this [radius]. Therefore, for the sake of the radius, the sine of thirty degrees is the hypotenuse.

Therefore, the *ukrama-jyā* (versed sine) is as stated previously: the *trijyā* (radius) diminished by the sine of sixty degrees is the *ukrama-jyā* of the sign; that is the form of the *koṭi* (adjacent side). The *krabhā* (sine of the arc) is the form of the *bhuja* (opposite side). The string fixed between those two is the *karṇa* (hypotenuse). That indeed is the form of the sine of the [sixty] degrees. Hence, its half is the half-sine of fifteen degrees; thus it is established. In this way, the proof for all cases up to the twelvefold moon-sine (*dvādaśa-śaśiñjinī*) should be understood. This is the *vāsanā* (explanatory principle) regarding the generation of the sines. Now, with the best of teachers, he states the sine of the twenty-fourth part.

"From the square of the radius diminished by the square of the sine of the argument," and so forth. The justification for this is stated here according to the method of algebraic computation (*bīja-prakāra*), using initial syllables as markers. In that context, the cosine of the argument is the *koṭijyā* (sine of the complement) of the radius. Its square is this: *u*¹ + *atri-bhā*² + *tri-va*¹. By this, the square of the radius multiplied by the square of the sine of the argument becomes: *uva*¹ + *atribhā*². This is the square of the sine of the argument added to the square of the sine of the complement. Its fourth part is: *unibhā*¹. The square root of this is *pra*. *Tra*. (Note: The variables used are likely abbreviations: *u* for *ujyā* [sine of the argument], *tri* for *trijyā* [radius], and *bhā* for *bhājyā* [sine of the complement].)

Therefore it has been said: "multiplied by the sine of the arc," and so forth. In this way, from that [sine], its complement is obtained; likewise, from the cosine as well, one may derive as many desired segments as required. For example: where there are twenty-four segments, the sine of the sign (rāśi) is the eighth segment (8); the cosine is the sixteenth (16); and the sine of the portion consisting of five and four (95°) is the twelfth (12). From these three segments, twenty-four segments are produced according to the method described.

From the eighth [sign], the fourth [part] is the sine (jyā) of the arc of the shadow (tadartha), which is 4; the sine of the angle of depression (vakoṭijyā) is 20. Likewise, the second from the fourth is 2, and the twenty-second is 22. From the third [sign], the first is 1, and the twenty-third is 23. Thus, from the eighth [sign], the tenth, fourteenth, fifth, nineteenth, seventh, seventeenth, eleventh, and thirteenth are 10, 14, 5, 19, 7, 17, 11, and 13 respectively. Now, from the twelfth [sign], the sixth, eighteenth, third, twenty-first, ninth, and fifteenth are 6, 18, 3, 21, 9, and 15.

The trijyā (radius) is twenty-four units [24]. Therefore, we shall explain the remaining derivation of the sines (jyā) further on. Bhāṣya-Ṭīkā: Therein, he describes the base of the sine (jyopajīvya), the *jātyayana*, and the specific difference (*viśeṣāntara*) in the *Śālinī* meter, beginning with "iṣṭa" (desired). According to the passage starting with "at the tip of the half-sine, the celestial body stands upon the sacrificial altar outside the central thread," etc., since the arc of two [sides] is here accepted as being halved, the half-sine (*ardhajyā*)—which is the radius (*vyāsārdha*)—is situated upon the side-arc that takes the form of a quarter of a tree (a quadrant).

That same [line], which is true for three signs at the fourth part of Vṛtra (the zodiacal sign Aries), is the trijyā when the middle syllable is elided. That is the desired measure from the center up to the circumference. In accordance with that, the line extending from the central meridian to a specific point on the desired circumference is the bhuja, taking the form of half a jyā (sine). The trijyā is the hypotenuse (karṇa).

From the other middle-sine up to its limit, the half-sine is the *koṭijyā* (sine of the complement). An equal [line] from the center to the base of the previous middle-sine is the *koṭi* (perpendicular), being the square root of the difference between the squares of the hypotenuse and the side. Because this was established previously, the first half [of the verse] is easy to understand. As for the second half, since it is stated in the *Sphuṭādhikāra* that "the sines of the respective [angles] of the side and the perpendicular, or the co-sines of those same [angles], when subtracted from the radius (*trijyā*), are the co-sines and sides," the meaning of the latter half is clear. In that context, the word *pṛthak* (separately) signifies the sense of "successively" (*krama*).

It should be understood that this [verse] serves as a proof for the non-disappearance of the *kaṇḍu* and the sequence of sines (*jyā*). Now, in order to understand the derivation of the latter half of the preceding verse, the author describes the nature of the versed sine (*utkramajyā*) and states the knowledge of the half-sine (*ardhajyā*) in the *Indravajrā* meter, beginning with "In the middle of the sine and the arc" (*jyācāpamadhye*). In the chapter on Spherics (*Gaulādhyāya*), a full chord (*sampūrṇajyā*) is a line joining two points of equal curvature on both sides of the central diameter. The corresponding portion of its circumference is the full arc (*sampūrṇacāpa*).

Between these two, within the interval, those portions situated inside the middle line (madhyasūtra) that take the form of lines are the *utkramajyā* (versed sine). Indeed, by the word "khalu" (indeed), the proof of the nature of the *utkramajyā* is easily understood. For example: the *bhujajyā* (sine of the arc) starting from the previous middle line is equal to the distance from the root of the *koṭijyā* (cosine) up to the other middle line starting from the east or north. The *utkramajyā* is the radius (half the diameter) diminished by that [distance].

In this manner, by means of another middle chord, the koti-jya is exactly equal to that; on the previous middle chord, up to the root of the bhuja-jya, the trijyā diminished by that [bhuja-jya] is the bhuja-ukta-majyā. Now, regarding the derivation of the sines for forty-five degrees, he says: "Of the square of the trijyā... The square root of half the square of the trijyā is the jīva (sine) of forty-five degrees.

Immediately following that, by the previously stated rule that "this sine of the arm (bhujajyā) has the radius (trijyā) as its hypotenuse," and by the rule "the square root of the difference of their squares," the sine of the perpendicular (koṭijyā) of this [arc] is equal to the measure of the sine of the arm; such is the meaning. The word "api" (also/even) serves to exclude the restriction that the sine of the arm and the sine of the perpendicular must be equal. Therefore, the proof here is well-known. To explain: when a circle is drawn with two median lines at an arc less than forty-five degrees, because the sine of the arm and the sine of the perpendicular are equal, even though they are known, their knowledge is easily obtained from the knowledge of the hypotenuse measured by the radius (trijyā).

Since the hypotenuse is the square root of the sum of the squares of the base and the perpendicular, the sum of the squares of the base and the perpendicular must equal the square of the hypotenuse. In this case, because the base and the perpendicular are equal, it follows that in the square of the given hypotenuse, the square of the sine of the base (or the sine of the perpendicular) is twice as large. Therefore, half of the square of the hypotenuse is the square of the sine of the base; its square root is the sine of the base, which is equal to the sine of the perpendicular. Thus, in accordance with a trijyā (radius) of 3438 (the number of elephants, elephants, Vedas, and fires), the square of the trijyā is 11,819,854, and its square root is 3,438.

Its subtle root is forty-five parts: the sine (jyā) is 2431; 1; 59. This is the twelfth among the twenty-four sines mentioned in the *Sphuṭādhikāra*. Now, he states—by means of an *upajāti* verse—the knowledge of the sine of the "head-quarters" (mūrdhāśā) degrees, which are the relationship between the known and unknown sines of one and two signs: "Half of the trijyā," etc. *Trijyābha* is the sine of thirty degrees. The cosine (koṭijīvā) of thirty degrees, according to the previously stated method, would be that of sixty-eight degrees.

For example, half of the trijyā (3438) is the sine of one sign (1719), which is the eighth [sine] in the present context. Its square is 2,954,961. Subtracted from the square of the trijyā (8,864,883), the remainder is 5,909,922. The square root of this is the sine of two signs (dviśijyā), which is the sixteenth [sine]: 2977; 23; 43. Regarding the "sine of the co-latitude" (jhamotkramajyā): for those degrees whose sequential sine (kramajyā) is known, the inverse sine (utkramajyā) of those same degrees—consisting of the trijyā minus the cosine (koṭi)—is to be understood according to the aforementioned method. Then, from the sum of the squares of those two sequential sines, the square root is halved.

The meaning is that the lord of the degrees related to the forward and reverse sine (jyā) sequences is their forward sine; for example, the forward sine of forty-five degrees is 2431. The cosine (koṭijyā) of those same degrees is equal to this. The reverse sine (utkramajyā) of those degrees is the radius (trijyā) diminished by that [cosine], which is 1007. From the square roots of these two squares—5908922 and 51014049—the derivation of the sine from the square root of 6933971 is according to the ancient method (ārṣa). The sine of twenty-two and a half degrees is 131540;19. (Ghaṭī = 60 minutes).

For example, the sine of one sign (ekarāśijyā) is 1719, and the inverse sine of two signs subtracted from the radius (dvirāśiyonatrijyā), which is the sine of the arc of one sign, is 461. The squares of these two are 2954961 and 212521. The square root of their product (2954961 × 212521 = 627482) is halved, yielding 889; 53, which is the fourth sine (caturthī jyā) of fifteen degrees. The proof for this is as follows: A circle with a diameter equal to the radius (trijyā) should be constructed, representing twelve signs. On its circumference, another circle is drawn with a diameter less than that. From the point where this second circle intersects the first, another circle is drawn with a diameter equal to the radius of the first.

Again, from the intersection with the eastern *paridhi* (circumference), by means of half that diameter, a circle is drawn; thus, six sectors are formed within the previous circle. Among these, the chord equal to the radius (*trijyā*) is the full sine (*sampūrṇajyā*) of two signs (*rāśi*), appearing as the hypotenuse (*bhuja*) of the right triangle; half of that is the half-sine (*ardhajyā*) of one sign. In the hexagon, those who know the sphere say that the chord called the "heart" is equal to the arms [of the triangle], because Śrīpati stated: "In a circle, the sine of a sixth part of the circumference is obtained equal to half the diameter."

The sine of that [angle] is the *virāśi* (180°) minus the *koṭi-jyā*. The *koṭi* is the northward sine; the *bhuja* is the sine up to the end of the northward [sine]. The square root of the sum of their squares is the *karṇa* (hypotenuse). Its degrees are not complete; by taking half of that, one reaches the middle of the degrees of its half. Thus, the statement "half the *bhujya*" and so forth is established. Now, stating the calculation of the sines of those degrees and their lords by means of another method for the sake of brevity, he says in the *Indravajrā* meter: "The trijyā is the reverse sine... and so on.

The square root of the product of the radius (*trijyā*) and the versed sine (*utkramajyā*) of a certain number of degrees is the versed sine of half those degrees; this is one method. Alternatively, there is another way: for example, the versed sine of forty-five degrees is 1007. Multiplied by the radius (3438), it becomes 3462066. Its square root is 1831.033, which is the [versed] sine of twenty-two and a half degrees, namely 1315.19. Similarly, the versed sine of one degree is 461. Multiplied by the radius (3438), it becomes 1584918. Its square root is 792.459, which is the sine of fifteen degrees, namely 890.12.

But the six types of living beings (ṣaḍjīva) are not established in this way, nor is there anything else; therefore, he explains the knowledge of that [sine] precisely by the method already stated, beginning with "of that" (tasyāḥ). From the perspective of the living beings, again according to the aforementioned manner, [one calculates] the sine (jyā) of the portions of its petals. From those, the sine of the lords of the portions related to them; and from those, the sine of their own lords, and so on repeatedly until the desired sine is achieved. From the complement (koṭi)—that is, from the portion of the complement—the sine is obtained by means of the circle (cakra). From the sine of the complementary portion, by the aforementioned method, one obtains the sine of the lords of the complementary portions.

Furthermore, the meaning is that by taking the sine (jyā) of those [angles] as their lords again and again, the desired result is established with ease. This is what is being said: the sine of the arc of fifteen degrees is the twentieth part of the sine of seventy-five degrees. The sine of fifteen degrees subtracted from the radius (trijyā) is the versed sine (utkramajyā) of fifteen degrees. From that, by the rule "the square root of the product of the radius and the versed sine," the second sine—that of seven and a half degrees—is obtained.

Thus, the sine of its complement (koṭijyā) for 82.5 degrees is the twenty-second [sine] in the present context; the versed sine (utkramajyā) for 7.5 degrees is the second in the present context. By the aforementioned method, the sine of 3.75 degrees is the first in the present context; its complement-sine for 80.25 degrees is the twenty-third in the present context; and the sine of the remainder from the radius (trijyā) is the first versed sine in the present context.

Then, according to the aforementioned method, from the thirty-sixty-four and a half *malādhyāyas* [degrees], by means of seventy-nine *kalās*, two parts are established. From that as well, according to the aforementioned method, there is the sine (*jyā*) and so forth of fifty-six and a quarter *kalās*. The versed sine (*utkramajyā*) of seventy-five degrees is the triguonometric sine (*trijyā*) diminished by the sequence of fifteen parts. By the aforementioned method, the sine of thirty-seven and a half degrees from that is the tenth; its co-sine (*koṭijyā*) is the fourteenth, which is the sine of fifty-two and a half degrees.

Subtracting that from the trijyā (radius) gives the *utkramajyā* (versed sine) of 71¼ degrees; subtracting that from the trijyā gives the *utkramajyā* of 37½ degrees in the fifth order. According to the stated method, the *jyā* of 18¾ degrees is the fifth [sine]. Its co-sine (*koṭijyā*) is the ninety-first *jyā*. By the stated method, the *jyā* of the degrees less than that is not useful in the present context. Thus, the *jyās* for those respective degrees should be calculated according to the requirements. Subtracting the *kramajyā* from the trijyā gives the fourteenth *utkramajyā*.

According to the method stated above, the seventh [sine] among those named up to the twenty-sixth part is the co-sine (koṭijyā) of forty-three and three-quarter degrees; it is the seventeenth [sine] of sixty-three and three-quarter degrees. Furthermore, the inverse sines (vyutkramajyā) are less than the sequential sines (kramajyā). From these two, the sine of those degrees is not required. The twenty-second sequential sine is the trijyā (radius) diminished by the second operation. According to the aforementioned method, its eleventh [sine] is that of forty-nine and three-quarter degrees. The sine of eleven degrees less than the radius (trijyā) is the versed sine (utkramajyā) of thirteen degrees; the sine of thirteen degrees less than the radius is the versed sine of eleven degrees. From these two, the sine of the remaining portion (adheśakajyā) is obtained by subtracting the sine of six degrees. The cosine (koṭijyā) of eight degrees is the sine of six and a half degrees; the sine of six degrees less than the radius is the versed sine of eighteen degrees; the sine of eighteen degrees less than the radius is the versed sine of six degrees. From these two, following the aforementioned method, the third and ninth sines of one and a quarter degrees and thirty-four and a quarter degrees respectively are their cosines.

In this same manner, the twenty-first and fifteenth [sines] are derived. Likewise, the sines for the names Athu, Śana, Abha, Ṣṭi, and Jyā are also to be established according to the method stated above. And as in the present case, the co-sine (koṭijyā) of the sine of twenty-two and a half degrees is 3176;24. Subtracting this from the radius (trijyā), the resulting inverse sine (utkramajyā) is 261;36. Multiplying this by the radius gives 898808; taking its square root and halving it yields the third sine, 67034. In this way, the others are to be calculated accordingly. Here, the inclusion or exclusion of a fraction exceeding one unit depends solely on following the tradition (mālā).

It should be understood that in some cases, the mention of "one" (in the term *ekagrahaṇa*) refers to a base that is half-deficient, precisely because of conformity with that [preceding rule]. Here is the proof: The square of the sine of the complement (*koṭijyā*) is given by the formula: *ū1 tri1* (where *ū* stands for *utkramajyā* and *tri* for *trijyā*). Since the negative and positive terms of equal magnitude cancel each other out, the essential nature of the sum of the products of the *utkramajyās* is: "The product of the *utkramajyā* and the radius, multiplied by two. Thus, the proof is established.

By the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*), "the square root of this" (*asya mūladalam*) should be understood as the square root of this very quantity. Since the square root of that quantity is the fourth part of its square, one should multiply by the desired [number] and divide by four; thus, the sines of the arc (*ukramajyā*) are obtained. Because there are four divisors for the product of the radius (*trijyā*) doubled, the reduction of the dividend and divisor by a common factor results in the established formula: the square root of half the product of the radius and the sine of the arc.

In this way, by means of establishing the origin of the sine (jyā) from its meaning, all living beings (*jīva*) would likewise originate as having that same form; therefore, [the author] states the following justification for its purpose: "Not indeed... By a wise mathematician, the desired sines (jīvā) of the desired degrees should be established—that is, they should be accomplished. In that interval, it is indicated that the sine (jyā) is not established by the method previously stated; rather, the sine is to be calculated there through proportion (anupāta) using the preceding and succeeding sines. With reference to that [the sine of 90°], there is a reliance on the sines of 20° and 18°. This is because the sine of 90° serves as the basis for calculation. Thus, since it is impossible to know the sines of the desired nine parts of 180°, and because the method of proportion would be inapplicable here, he states the knowledge of the subtle sine by another method: "Or else, in a circle made with the radius equal to the triple-sine (trijyā). In a circle drawn with a radius measured by the triple-sine, marked with the degrees of the twelve signs (360°), the desired sines are to be taken after having been counted and marked.

This is what is meant: on a level plane, one should draw a desired circle with a radius equal to the trijyā (the sine of 90°) and marked with degrees and other divisions. In the center of that circle, a vertical line and a horizontal line should be drawn. From the points where these lines meet the circumference, marks should be made at equal intervals on both sides.
