Therefore, the internal form between the two points—the upper point of the chord and the other point—is situated at the distance equal to the radius intercepted between the point of intersection of the line and the circumference and that other point; this is the half-chord (ardhajyā) of the degrees. Having calculated it by means of that very measure which is the radius (trijyā), this [half-chord] itself becomes the precise sine (sūkṣmajyā) of the desired degrees according to one's own will. || 6 ||

Now, the rising of the luminaries (Jyotpāta). Having risen along the path of the stars, from which it moves according to its nature, Bhāskara describes that [phenomenon] in various ways for the delight of skilled astronomers. A circle should be drawn with a diameter of desired finger-breadths, marked with the cardinal directions and the numbers one through nine. The number of deities obtained by dividing [the circumference] by nine is the first sine; the arc corresponding to that is this very [circle]. Having placed the arcs of the subsequent [sines]—which end in two, three, and so on—on both sides of the eight [divisions], [the calculation proceeds].

That [result] should be understood as being like a rope on the earth for one who lacks faith; and all [other] things are likewise [to be treated]. (3) Alternatively, I shall state those very same half-chords (*jyārdha*) clearly through calculation: the square of the radius (*trijyā`) minus the square of the hypotenuse (*karṇa*), its square root is indeed the sine of the complement (*koṭijīvā*). (4) The radius divided by the sum of the sine and the sine of the complement is the respective sine of the complement and the sine of the arc (*bhujokramajyā*) for the remaining portions. That arrow (*bāṇa*) which lies here between the chord and the arc is indeed the versed sine (*utkramajyā*); this should be understood by the wise in this manner. (5)

From the half of the radius (trijyā) of sixty degrees, the sine and the cosine of that arc are obtained. The square root of half the square of the radius is the sine of five hundred and forty degrees (540°). [The sine] of thirty-six degrees is derived from the square root of the product of the square of the radius and five, diminished by the square root of the product of the square of the radius and twenty-five, and then divided by eight. Alternatively, the sine of thirty-six degrees is the difference between the radius (trijyā) and 5,878; or it may be found by subtracting 10,000 from the square of the radius. Its cosine is the square root of the difference between the square of the radius and the square of the sine of thirty-six degrees.

The square root of the product of the radius (trijyā) and the sine of fifteen degrees (iṣu), diminished by the radius and divided by four, is thus the true sine of eighteen degrees. The square root of the sum of the squares of the successive and regressive sines, when halved, shall be the sine of its half-portion; or else, the square root of the half of the product of the radius and the regressive sine shall be the sine of that half-portion. From that [sine], again, the sine of its complemental portion, and likewise from the complemental sine, the sine of its complemental portion—thus the method for calculating other sines has been stated by the ancients. Now I shall describe a method more distinguished than this.

11–12. When the square of the radius (*trijyā*) is diminished by or added to the product of the radius and the sine of the arc (*bhujajyā*), the square roots of those two results are the sines of the halves of that [arc]. Having likewise assumed the complement and the arc as the sides (*bhuja*), [the same applies]. 13. The square root of the sum of the squares of the difference between the desired sine and the sine of the arc is the sine of the difference of the two arcs; or in various other ways, it is the sine of the half of the difference of the two arcs. [The sine] is equal to the square root of the half of the square of the difference between the sines of the side and the complement.

I shall now describe the method for finding the sine of the difference between the hypotenuse and the arms [of a right triangle] even without taking the square root. The sine of the difference between the hypotenuse and the arms, divided by the sine of one-third of a quadrant (i.e., the sine of 60°), is equal to the difference between the sines of the resulting angles. Or, some portions of the sine of the interval between the arm and the hypotenuse may be found here in this manner. The sine of the arm diminished by 6569, multiplied by ten, and divided by 573, yields the sine of the hypotenuse. The sum of these two values shall be the sine of the larger angle; the difference shall be the previous sine.

In this manner, the first sine (jyā) shall be sixty; from there, each subsequent one [is derived]. When the radius (vyāsārdha) is equal to eight times four (32), there will be ninety transverse sines. The cosine-sine (koṭijīvī) multiplied by one hundred and divided by five hundred and twenty-nine (529) is the first sine of the arc (dojya). That [first sine] diminished by its own four-hundred-and-sixty-seventh part (467/467) is equal to their sum. The sine of that [resulting] arc is the difference between those two, which is the previous sine. Thus, the first sine is [calculated as] one hundred and thirty-seven minus twenty-two-four-fifty-one (224.51). This is the first sine.

Or, by means of a continuous series of operations, one may likewise determine twenty-four sines (vimaurvikā) [for the desired arcs]. The lengths of two desired arcs, when multiplied by each other's cosine-sine (koṭijyaka) and divided by the radius (trijyā), shall yield the sine of their sum; this is the sine of the sum of the two arcs. The sine of their difference shall be equal to the difference between those two [products]. This method for the calculation of other sines is correctly explained as the "sine-formation" (jyābhāvanā). One is the formation of the sum, and the other is the formation of the difference; this is the rule for determining the sine of every single degree of the arc-parts of the given sines.

The chord which is obtained through proportion is transformed into the desired half-chord; this should be done repeatedly using the [resulting] hypotenuse and the side. When the state of stability is reached, the desired value will be clear. Here, I shall set forth the rough method for calculating the chord; that has not been explained by me previously. Thus ends the origin of the chord. The science of astronomy was previously stated in brief and is easy to understand. Now, however, I shall explain it there with its specific details. Therefore, I shall elaborate upon it here.

In this regard, the five verses beginning with "tatrādau cayana-pada-vī" and so forth are easy to understand. Here, for the sake of knowing the sines (*jyā*) through calculation, he states the various methods for establishing the four fundamental sines. Indeed, that method is based on algebra (*bījagaṇita*). The half-sine of the [first] arc is the sine of the [first] quantity, and so forth. By the half of the radius (*trijyā*), which is 1719, the sine of thirty degrees is obtained. The cosine (*koṭijyā*) of that is the square root of sixty times sixty. The square root of half the square of the radius is the sine of forty-five degrees.

Now, the sine of thirty degrees is obtained by subtracting the square root of five times the square of the radius from the square of the radius, and dividing the remainder by eight. Alternatively, the sine of thirty degrees is the square root of 5878 subtracted from the radius, divided by ten thousand. This is the simplification of calculation. The sine of forty-five degrees is half the cosine-sine (koṭijyā). Likewise, the sine of twenty-two and a half degrees is the square root of five times the square of the radius, diminished by the radius, and divided by four. This is the method.

From that, by taking seventy-two parts of the *koṭijyā* (sine of the complement), [the result] is as stated in the forty-third chapter [of the *Bhāsvatī*]. Otherwise, he says "the *kramajyā* of the hypotenuse," and so forth. The *trijyā* (radius) diminished by the *koṭijyā* shall be the *upajyā* (versed sine) of the base-angle (*bhuja*). The *trijyā* diminished by the *kramajyā* of the two bases shall be the *kramajyā* of the *koṭi*. The square root of the sum of the squares of the *kramajyā* of the base and the *kramajyā* [itself] shall be the *jyā* of half the degrees of the base. Alternatively, the square root of the difference between the *trijyā* and the square of the [base] shall be the *jyā* of its half; thus there is lightness in the calculation.

In this manner, from the sine of elevation (*utpattrajyā*), its corresponding cosine (*koṭijyā*) is obtained; from that, further other [sines] equal to those [previous] values are to be derived. And in the same way, other cosines are derived. For example: where there is a fourteen-fold [sine], the half-sine of the radius (*trijyārdha*) is the eighth [part], 8; its cosine is the sixteenth, 16. The sine of five [parts] (*śaraveddaśajyā*) is the twelfth, 12. Then, by the method of taking half-parts from the eighth, the fourth [part] is 4; its cosine is the twentieth, 20.

Thus, from the fourth [to] the second (2) and the twenty-second (22); from the second, the half (1) and the twenty-third (23); from the twentieth, the tenth (10) and the fourteenth (14); from the tenth, the fifth (5) and the nineteenth (19); from the thirty-second, the eleventh (11) and the thirteenth (13); from the fourteenth, the seventh (7) and the seventeenth (17); then from the twelfth, the sixth (6) and the eighteenth (18); from the sixth, the third (3) and the twenty-first (21); and from the horse (7), the ninth (9) and the fifteenth (15).

"The sine of twenty-four degrees is the radius" (trijyā). Thus, indeed, the calculation of the inverse sine (ayajyā) has been stated by these [authorities]. Now, he states a novel method even without the use of the inverse sine: "Multiplied by the sine of the arc... and so forth. The product of the radius and the sine of the arc, when diminished by one from the square of the radius in one case, and added to it in the other, is then halved. At their two ends: in the first, the arc diminished by the arc of fifteen degrees; in the second, the half-arc of the arc of fifteen degrees. This is another method as well. It is as follows:

The side [of the square] is sixteen (16). The fourteenth (14) and the twentieth (20), and the twenty-seventh (27). From the fourth to the tenth (10), and the fourteenth (14). Thus for all [the cases]. He states another method: "The difference between the two sines," and so forth. Whatever is the difference between the two desired sines, and whatever is the path of the perpendicular (koṭi)—the square root of those [two] is the sine of half the difference between the two firm arms. Other examples are as follows: suppose one is indeed the fourth (4) and the other is the eighth (8) to be given.

From the second [sine] by means of the two [first and second], the third is established; from the second and fourth, the first, and so forth. Likewise, the square root of the difference of the squares of the sine and cosine (doḥkoṭijyā) shall be the sine of half the interval between the sine and the cosine. For example, let the sine be 8 and the cosine be 16; from these, the fourth [sine] is obtained, and so on. Now, he states the calculation for the sine of half the interval between the sine and cosine even without the operation of taking a square root: "The sine squared divided by the semi-diameter," and so forth. The square of the sine is divided by the semi-diameter.

The difference between that [radius] and the sine of the arc [obtained by subtracting the degrees from ninety] shall be the sine of the remaining [degrees]. Some half-sines here are to be calculated in this manner. For example: where there are thirty half-sines, the tenth half-sine is the radius (trijyā); its co-sine is the twentieth; the sine of fifteen degrees is the fifteenth; the sine of thirty-six degrees is the twelfth; its co-sine is the eighteenth half-sine; and the sine of eighteen degrees is the sixth.

The sine of the co-latitude (*koṭijyā*) is twenty-four (*24*). By the previously mentioned method beginning with "the square root of the sum of the squares of the [sine] and the co-sine," from the visible [sine] we obtain the fifth (*5*) and the twenty-fifth (*25*). Similarly, from the second we obtain the sixth (*6*) and the twenty-fourth (*24*); from the sixth we obtain the third (*3*) and the twenty-seventh (*27*); and from the eighteenth we obtain the ninth (*9*) and the twenty-first (*21*). These alone are established by this method, and no others. Therefore, it is said: "only some [of them] are thus here."

In the manner beginning with "the interval between the two arms" (*yaddoryayorantaram*), the fifth sine is one (*eka*) and the ninth sine is nine (*nava*). From these two, by the method beginning with "the interval between the two arms," that which is produced for the half-interval of the two arms is the second sine-half (*dvitīyaṃ jyārdham*). The cosine-sine (*koṭijyā*) is twenty-eight (*aṣṭāviṃśam*). From these two, by the method beginning with "the square root of the sum of the products of the sines in direct and reverse order," the first (*ādyā*) and the fourteenth (*caturdaśa*) sines are obtained. In this way, the other fourteen sines are established. Now, the calculation of the sines (*jyābhāvanā*).

And that is the piercing (*vedha*). There is one summary method of calculation (*samāsabhāvanā*). Regarding its internal process, he says for that purpose: "By the square root of the product of the sky, the gods, and the arrows," and so forth. In this context, it is indeed stated first regarding the case where the radius (*trijyā*) is equal to three thousand four hundred thirty-eight (*3438*) and there are ninety semi-chords (*jyārdha*): among the fundamental chords (*mūlabhūtajyā*), whichever is desired as the sine of the arc (*bhujajyā*) and its corresponding cosine (*koṭijyā*) should be set aside separately. The sine of the arc (*bhujajyā*) should be diminished by the division by six thousand five hundred sixty-nine (*6569*).

The sine of the arc (koṭijyā) multiplied by thirty-six (śaguṇā) is to be divided by five hundred and seventy-three (573). The sum of those two results is the sine of that [combined] arc; their difference shall be the previous sine. For example, when the radius (trijyā) is half [the diameter], there is a sine-arc of thirty units (30). From that, by means of the method of addition (samāsabhāvanā), there is one of thirty-one units (31); from that, one of thirty-two units, and so forth. By the method of subtraction (antarabhāvanā), however, there are [sines of] twenty-nine (29), twenty-eight (28), and so on.

Having assumed the full sine (pūrṇa-dojya) as the radius (trijyā) at the end of the quadrant, the first segment (khaṇḍa) is thus sixty (60). Now, if that same radius is twenty-four (24), he says: "multiplied by the hundredfold sine of the complement" (koṭijīvāśatābhyastā), and so forth. Here too, half the radius is the eighth sine (8); that is the sine of the arm (bhujajyā), sixteen (16). The sine of the complement (koṭijyā) is that [sixteenth] multiplied by a hundred and divided by fifteen hundred and twenty-nine (1529). As for the sine of the arm (dojya), it should be diminished by its own seven-hundred-sixty-seven (467)th part.

If their unity (aikya) is performed, then the ninth [house] becomes the half-jyā (jyādhaṃ); if it is their difference (antara), then the seventh would be [the result]. Thus, according to the method of summation (sabhavana), from the ninth comes the tenth, from the tenth the eleventh, and so forth. Likewise, according to the method of subtraction (antarabhavana), from the seventh comes the sixth, from the sixth the fifth, and so forth. In this way, the first [house] is measured by the knowledge of the reality of the seven parts (saptāṃśanatattvajña).

Alternatively, by assuming the full diameter (pūrṇī) as the sine of the arm (doṣī) and the radius (trijyā) as the sine of the adjacent side (koṭijyā), it is calculated; yet the result remains the same. Then, through the process of summation (samāsabhāvanā), all the subsequent values from the second onwards are produced. Alternatively, by assuming the radius (trijyā) as the sine of the arm (dorjyā) and the full diameter (pūrṇa) as the sine of the adjacent side (koṭijyā), it is calculated; then the twenty-third value arises, from which, by the process of subtraction (antarabhāvanā), the twenty-second is obtained, and from that, the twenty-first. In this manner, all the others are likewise accomplished.

Now, the calculation for the sines of the sum and difference of two desired arcs is stated as "of the two desired arcs," and so forth. The sines of the two desired arcs are to be placed in their respective positions on the ground. Beneath those two, the sines of their respective complements (koṭijyās) are also to be placed. Then, the first sine of the complement is to be multiplied by the second arc; thereafter, the second sine of the complement is to be multiplied by the first arc. Both of these products are to be divided by the radius (trijyā). The sum of the two results becomes the sine of the arc of the sum, and the difference becomes the sine of the arc of the difference.

This is the method of calculation (*bhāvanā*) for proving [the sine] otherwise than by means of its established [value]. For example: by the method of addition (*samāsabhāvanā*), the second [sine] is produced from the first sine added to half the sine of the arc; the third from the second, and so on up to the fourth, etc. Now, by the method of subtraction (*antarabhāvanā*): the fifth [sine] is produced from the second and third [sines] by their method of addition; the first would be produced by the method of subtraction, and so forth. Now, he states [the rule] for the purpose of knowing the sines for the sake of the desired amplitude (*vyāsa*): "Of the parts of the arc of the first sine," and so on.

The number of degrees by which one sine (jyā) is obtained are the initial sine-degrees (*ādyajyācaṣāṃśāḥ*). Regarding the method for the sine of each degree: having calculated the sine of one degree according to the previously mentioned procedure beginning with "divided by 573" (*trisa ptapañcabhir bhakte*), one should compute the sine of those degrees through successive application (*bhāvanā*) starting from that [initial sine] for two degrees, and so on. That [sine] is multiplied by the desired radius (*tri-jyā*) and divided by 3438; this shall be the first sine. By means of the same successive application as that, the second and subsequent sines are established.

Thus ends the *Jyotpātavāsanā* (the explanation of the origin of sines). Ma0ḍī0: [Objection: One might ask, "But why is this a different subject? For the determination of the mean positions of the planets that have passed through the days is required as the basis for explaining the rationale of the *spaṣṭakriyā* (true calculation), which serves as the answer to that question. To this, he says in a single sentence: "Thus ends the *Jyotpatti*. The meaning is this: since even that [mean calculation] depends upon the sine (*jyā*), because the *spaṣṭakriyā* is dependent on the sine, the *Jyotpatti* (origin of sines) was explained first as it presents itself immediately; therefore, it is not a different subject. || 1 ||

Now, by way of a relevant digression, I shall explain the origin of the *jyā* (sine) as composed by the original author, a reasoned exposition not found within other texts. (1) Therein, first of all, he announces its commencement along with its purpose in an Āryā verse, beginning with "ācāryāṇām. [Commentary on the Origin of the *Jyā* (Sine): Bhaṭṭotpala: Since, by knowing the *jyotpatti* (origin of the sine) and having correctly understood its essential nature, the mathematician attains the station—the status of equality—with the masters, such as the master Varāhamihira and others.

Because the calculation of the rising of the zodiacal signs (*jyotpatti*) is extremely difficult to master; and just as in regions such as Gauḍa, scholars attain the title of *Bhaṭṭācārya* by achieving excellence in this field, therefore Bhāskara, the author of the *Siddhāntaśiromaṇi*, speaks of—that is, describes—the rising of the signs. The statement "Bhāskara speaks" should not be considered as occurring within the body of this very text, but rather as belonging to a distinct work.

Otherwise, there would be no connection between the *Praśnadhyāya* and what follows, which would render the commencement of the *Bhāsvatī* untenable; furthermore, its commencement is logically justified immediately after the description of the calculation of the true longitude (*svarūpajyotpatti*) contained within the work itself. For this very reason, the mention of the *Bhāsvatī* is appropriate to dispel the suspicion that it might be a different work; however, that [mention] occurs after the completion of the [author's] desire for the attainment of the title of *Ācārya* through the knowledge of those [astronomical principles] gained by describing them.

Because that knowledge does not exist previously, others cannot have the expectation of reaching that state; thus, if it were not defined, it would remain hidden, and only he by whom this [knowledge] is understood through such an intellect would attain that state. Therefore, its definition would be useless. To this, he says: "vidagdha" (the clever one). This is for the satisfaction of those mathematicians who are clever by virtue of their mastery over the nature of the *golā* (celestial sphere) and so forth, and who are experts in the subtle methods of calculation regarding areas such as the *pakṣama*, *tridaśāstā*, and others.

And thus, since the derivation of planetary calculation (*graha-gaṇita*) is already clear in this very [work], and because it is impossible to describe its nature without first defining the sines (*jyā*), the entire essence of the nature of strength (*bala*)—which is nothing other than the sine (*jyā*)—must be described first. In this way, by such a description, those of dull intellect who possess knowledge of that [calculation] will experience a greater flash of intelligence regarding that subject; and since it is possible to achieve the attainment of that state through another method as well, there is a meaningful purpose for describing it in this manner. For this very reason, there is joy.

The intention is that by this very [work], the Gaṇakas call him their preceptor (ācārya). Now, one might object: "Even so, since the origin of astronomy has already been stated in the previous work, it is not appropriate to describe it again separately"; to this he replies with the word "variously" (vividham). The meaning is: "In accordance with what was previously stated in the earlier work, I have spoken of it briefly; now, by the power of my own intellect, I shall speak of it at length in many ways. || 1 ||

Now, under the guise of demonstrating the nature of the sine (jyā), he states the knowledge of the sine by means of the Upajāti and Indravajrā meters, beginning with "iṣṭe iṣṭe" and "dvitryādi. This passage is already explained as being of the nature of a commentary on the previously mentioned portion of the sine-table ending with "trijyotthavṛtte 'bhagaṇāikite ve" and so forth. || 2 || 3 ||

Now, having established the sine (*jyā*) by the aforementioned method through the understanding of craftsmanship, and considering that it might be thought [to be] otherwise, he states the previous definition of the sine and its requisite co-sine (*koṭijyā*) in an *upajāti* meter, beginning with "atha" (now). The word "atha" means: after the demonstration of the knowledge of that [sine] by way of its essential nature; or otherwise; or by a different method; or independently of the use of instruments such as the gnomon. If that were so, then its establishment would indeed fail; therefore, he says: "by calculation" (*gaṇitena*). "I shall state" (*vacmi*) means I shall explain.

Now, since it might be argued that while the subtle sine is established by calculation in the manner previously stated, the gross [sine] is established [differently], he says: "Those very same... (*tānyeva*). "Those" refers to those previously understood. By the word "very" (*eva*), the exclusion of anything different from them is intended; the meaning is that they are perfectly clear and subtle. The latter half [of the verse] has already been explained. (4) Next, he describes the method for obtaining the inverse sine (*utkramajyā*) used for its calculation, as well as its essential nature, in the *Indravajrā* meter: "The square root of the difference between the square of the radius and the square of the [given] sine... (*śeṣakoṭīti*). Herein is the context.

By the use of the restrictive particle *eva*, the exclusion of any form other than that which has been stated for the inverse sine (*utkramajyā*) is indicated. Here, in the context of spherical trigonometry (*aṃhagaṇita*) and so forth, the term "by the wise" (*sudhiyā*) contains a reason; by this it is suggested that, just as with the half-sine (*ardhajyā*), there is a half-inverse-sine (*utkramajyādhaṃ*), and thus another [method] previously explained is indicated. (Verse 5) In the chapter on the calculation of sines (*jyādhyāya*), Bhāskara says: Now, with the method of calculation for each degree, he states in an Āryā verse the means of determining the sines of single signs in a single direction, beginning with "for the sake of pleasure" (*priyārtham*). Because it was established previously, the meaning is clear. (Verse 6)

Now, the Noble Lady states the method for calculating the sine of thirty-six degrees: "The square of the square of the trijyā... and so forth. The meaning is as follows: the square of the square of the *trijyā* (the radius) is multiplied by five; its square root is subtracted from five times the square of the *trijyā*, and the result is divided by eight. The square root of that quotient shall be the sine (*ajyā*) of thirty-six degrees. Here, it should be noted that by determining the addition instead of subtraction, the sine of seventy-two degrees would be obtained.

In this case, the sine of the arc whose triple sine is *lakṣmīdaśamiśra* (the sine of one sign) is equal to the square root of one-fourth of the square of the triple sine diminished by two hundred and eight. This is because the results obtained from the dividend and divisor multiplied by the same multiplier are identical. Therein, the dividend, which consists of the product of the square of the triple sine, is brought forth by another method as twice the divisor minus the divisor; since the subtractive dividend (*viyojaka*) has the nature of being the square root of the dividend, the quotient diminished by the square root of the divisor shall be the dividend.

Likewise, the dividend (bhājya) shall be diminished by the square root of four times the square of the trijyā multiplied by the square of the trijyā; this [dividend] divided by eight is established as the result-root for the single revolution. In this manner, that koti-quantity becomes the sine of the arc, consisting of one-fourth of the product of the square of the trijyā and the square of the trijyā of twenty-nine degrees.

In this case, the square root of the dividend (bhājya-varga-mūla) multiplied by three and added to twice the divisor (bhājya) shall be the divisor; thus, this [result] divided by eight is the square of the sine of two signs (dvi-rāśi-jyā). By that, the sine of three signs (tri-jyā) is obtained from the square root of nine times the product of the square of the sine of three signs and nine, diminished by eight and divided [by the aforementioned divisor]. Thus, the sine of two signs is established. Furthermore, in the calculation of the sine of one sign and so forth, the multipliers are divided by four and nine respectively.

Then, for that interval, there is one proportionate calculation (*anupāta*) as follows: "If a five-fold difference is obtained by thirty units, then what is it for *ghaṭī*-units? By this, the multiplier of four, which was based on the calculation of the sine of one unit, is increased. For the purpose of calculating the sine of thirty degrees according to the aforementioned method, a nine-ṛṣi (ninety) degree interval—established as a five-fold [multiplier]—is applied. Since the multiplier is one unit for the purpose of calculating the sine of twelve degrees according to the aforementioned method, and because the multiplier is one unit for those degrees... [the process continues].

It should not be said that this [calculation] is untenable on the grounds that the sine (jyā) would exceed the radius (trijyā) due to the proximity of the degrees to the end of the arc where the sine is zero; for the method described consists of thirty-six parts, and by the stated procedure, the sines of the degrees situated within that interval are calculated. Otherwise, if one were to calculate the sine by multiplying by three and dividing by ten as per the stated method, it would result in the absurdity of having to state a calculation involving twenty-four and sixty-six added together.

Nor should it be argued that the calculation of the sine (jyā) by taking six or more parts of the forty-two parts [of the radius] and so forth results in an error in the calculation of the circle's circumference; for since the sines are related to geometric figures, their calculation via squares and square roots is logical. Since the rule of three (trairāśika) does not apply here, to insist upon its application is merely to accept a forced position. They say that as the number of parts increases, so too do the discrepancies in the resulting differences.

In this context, by taking the square root of one-eighth of the squares of the triple-sines (trijyā) corresponding to two and three signs respectively—adjusted according to the sine of two signs—one obtains the square roots of one-eighth of the squares of the triple-sines for thirty-seven and a half degrees; this results in the attainment of the subtle sine (sūkṣmajyā). This is because the method for calculating the sine of thirty-six degrees will be demonstrated as being subtle, and because [the other methods] would otherwise be considered gross.

However, having accepted the inverse sine (arajakramajyā) of eighteen degrees—which is one-twentieth of the radius of the trigonometric circle—as being equal to the square of the direct sine (kramajyā) of eighteen degrees according to the previously stated method, [it is calculated as follows]: the square of the direct sine of eighteen degrees is 39; from this, the odd sine (ojya) is 499, which is equal to the difference between the squares of the [resulting] values divided by half the lunar day (tithyasidalārdha). [Commentary (ma0ḍī0): It is equal to the difference between the cubes of the obtained values divided by half the lunar day.

The attainment of the difference between [the squares of] the sines of forty-five degrees and sixty degrees would occur in the manner to be described. The square of the trijyā (radius) for fifty-four degrees is 40,000, which is the square of the trijyā for thirty-six degrees: 14,079. Here, having reduced the multiplier and divisor by five thousand, we get 400 and 101. In the place of the multiplier, there is the number 2 increased by two parts less than one-eighth, namely 2; 45; 50. By this multiplier, the sine of thirty-six degrees produced is excessively gross.

Therefore, the multiplier taken is forty-two minus one-sixth, which is two and forty-five and fifty parts (2; 45 | 50). By this multiplier, combined with the desired [value], the fifth multiplier is formed according to the stated method of "in the Nidhana. Hence it is said: "from the product of the square of the trijyā and five. Here, the multiplier multiplied by the desired value must be subtracted; therein, this root of five is joined with fourteen parts plus one-sixth of the desired value.

Then, by the rule "one should multiply a square by a square," the square root of the trijyā (radius) squared multiplied by five is diminished by the square root of the product of the desired multiplier and the square of the radius. This resulting quantity, multiplied by the constant factor of sixty-four, is the dividend; it is established as being divided by eight, and the square root of the result is said to be the sine of thirty-six degrees. This is because the sine of twenty degrees is less than eighteen parts of the trijyā, due to the nature of the calculation. By this multiplier established through your stated method, [the value is] 2148; 56; 52.

48. Since there is no reason for the non-establishment of the sine of thirty-eight degrees, it does not occur through this assumed multiplier (2; 45; 50). Furthermore, there is a lack of evidence for establishing the accuracy of that sine. || 7 || Now, by means of a more concise method, he states the knowledge of the forty-fourth sine of the Savana [degrees] in an Āryā verse—beginning with "gajahaya" (elephant-horse).

The radius (trijyā) multiplied by five thousand eight hundred and seventy-eight, and divided by ten thousand, yields the sine (jyā) of thirty-six degrees according to the simplified method. Its cosine (koṭijyā) is the square root of the difference between the square of the radius and the square of the sine of thirty-six degrees; this shall be the sine of fifty-four degrees. Herein lies the proof: the square of the radius is obtained from the square root of the square of the square of the radius multiplied by five, [divided] by the fifth root.

In that context, its root is the subtle approximation with parts: 2; 45; 10. By this, the square of the radius (trijyā) multiplied by five is divided, resulting in a square of the radius: 2; 45; 3; 17. This is multiplied by five and reduced by its fifth root, then divided by eight; the square root of the result is the sine (jyā). Therein, the square root of the small square of the radius is the radius itself: 2; 45; 50. This is multiplied by the subtle approximation with parts—the root [of the previous result]—which is one unit plus thirty-nine degrees and forty-five minutes (1; 39; 45).

It is multiplied by the eighth root, which is the subtle denominator; that is, it is divided by 2 49/42. This is established. Here, because multiplication and division involving fractional parts involve excessive labor, the multiplier and divisor are simplified to 5985 and 10182 respectively for the sake of brevity. Furthermore, for the ease of division, the divisor is made into ten thousand (10,000), and its fifty-fold multiple is 505,000.

Because this [distance] is hidden by the thighs being drawn close together, its measurement is subtle and beyond the reach of the senses; thus it is appropriate [to say], "O you who have abandoned the horse," and so forth. (8) Now, although the sine of eighteen degrees is established through the calculation of the sine of half a degree, the justification for the previously mentioned sine is as follows: even though the calculation of the sines of such degrees is possible, it is not stated here because it is not necessary. The sines of sixty degrees and other values are derived from the radius (*trijyā*). In the *Golādhyāya-ṭīkā*, it is stated: "The square root of five times the square of the radius, diminished by the radius and divided by four... (144).

The result of twenty-eight parts becomes the fine sine (sūkṣmajyā). Thus, the sine of seventy-two degrees becomes its co-sine (koṭijyā). Here too, it should be understood that by subtracting this from the place of addition, the sine of fifty-four degrees would be obtained. If you ask how the calculation for the sine of thirty-six degrees is derived through the reasoning of its proof, listen.

The method for calculating the measure of the sine (jyā) of eighteen degrees is as follows: the square root of the product of the arrow (iṣu) and the diameter (trijyā), diminished by the diameter and divided by four, is *mū* 1 *tri* me. This, when subtracted from the diameter, results in *mū* e 1 *tri* 9 5, which is the form of the versed sine (utkramajyā) of seventy-two degrees. From this, by the rule "the square root of half the product of the diameter and the versed sine," as used in the calculation of the sines of thirty-six degrees, its square is established as *mū* 0 *tri* 0 1 *tri* *va* 0 5.

In this case, since a square root cannot be obtained from the product of the square of the trijyā (the radius) and five, and because taking an approximate root and subsequently multiplying it would result in a large error, it is stated from the very beginning that one should multiply the square of the vani by the square of the trijyā. Thus, the square of the trijyā multiplied by its own square-rooted value (the *pada*)—which takes the form of the product of the roots of the trijyā—is the precise [result]. Dividing that by the trijyā and subtracting the quotient from the product of the *dhu* and five, the result divided by six is the square of the sine of thirty-six degrees; the square root of that is the sine of those [degrees]. This is established as the square of the trijyā derived from the product of the trijyā and five.

"From the square root of the product of the two sides of the group, divided by eight, the square root is the sine of thirty-six degrees. The justification for calculating the sine of eighteen degrees is as follows: having divided the circumference of the circle into equal parts, one should draw east-west and north-south lines through the circle using those marks as centers.

From the ends of the north-south line, a chord reaching to the opposite mark—which divides the circle into equal parts—is a full sine (sampūrṇajyā) of thirty degrees. Then, using a radius equal to the measure of that full sine, one should draw another circle from the ends of the north-south line.

In that circle, the line between the center and the circumference is the sine of thirty-six degrees; therefore, for the sake of calculation, one should determine the measure of half the diameter of that circle by first marking the radius (trijyā) on the east-west line of the original circle's center, and then, using a compass with that mark as the center and half the radius as the span, draw a circle that touches the original circle’s center and east-west line at its true circumference—this is the circle of the sine of thirty-six degrees, which meets the original circumference.

The distance between the southern and northern marks of the half-circumference of the radius, drawn as a chord, is a full sine (sampūrṇajyā) equal to thirty-six degrees, being less than the radius by one-third. This is because, in the third small circle, the radius is the semi-diameter. In that case, the distance between the centers of the first and second circles is measured by the radius.

The distance between the centers of the first and second circles is the side (bhuja), measured as half the radius (trijyārdha); the distance between the centers of the second and third circles is the hypotenuse (karṇa). From this visualization of the figure, the square root of the sum of the squares of the half-radius and the sine is the hypotenuse, which is the radius (trijyā), the full sine of thirty-six degrees (ghanaghaṭatriṃśadaṃśa).

In that case as well, since the square of the *karṇa* (hypotenuse) is equal to one-fourth of the product of the square of the *trijyā* (radius) and five, this operation is performed for the purpose of finding the square root of the product of the *jyā* and the arrow (*iṣu*). By subtracting the *trijyā* from the square root of the product of the *trijyā* and nine, and then taking half of that, there is brevity; for this is the full half-chord (*jyārdha*) of eighteen degrees. Thus, the square root of the product of the *trijyā* and nine, diminished by the *trijyā* and divided by four, is the correct derivation.

If it is asked what the reasoning is for the conjunction of the second and third arcs, know that direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is the authority here, just as the observation of a side equal to the radius of the circle of the sine of one arc is obtained by depending on the full six-arc radius. In this regard, the proof for both cases has been explained in detail in the *Yavana* treatises, such as the *Śilpayukti*. However, that exposition has been omitted here for fear of excessive length and because of the great effort required for its transcription; this should be kept in mind.

Others, however, say: "This square of the side of a ten-sided figure, diminished by or added to the square of the radius, shall equal the square of the radius; this is certain, there is no doubt here. According to the method for finding a single unknown in this text, using the root of the equation, the measure of the radius (*ga*) is 1. Then, twice the side of a fifteen-sided figure (145 + 10 = 155) is the side of a ten-sided figure: *yā* 2. From this, by the aforementioned method, the square of the radius of the nine-sided figure is *yāva* 4 + *yā* 2.

This is equal to the square of the radius (trijyā). By subtracting the like terms from both sides, the two sides become: *grava* 4, *yātri* 2, *triva* 1. To find the square root of these, both sides are multiplied by four and increased by the square of the radius; thus, on the known side (*vyaktapakṣa*) it becomes *trijyākṛtīṣu* (the product of the square of the radius and four), and on the unknown side (*avyaktapakṣa*) it becomes *yāva* 16, *yātri* 8, *triva* 1. The square roots of these are: for the unknown side, *yā* 4, *bi* 1; and for the known side, the square root of the product of the square of the radius and four. By again subtracting like terms from these two, the value of *yāvat-tāvat* (the unknown quantity) is obtained as the square root diminished by the radius.

They say that this very [sine] of eighteen degrees is the "fourth part" (*caturbhakta*). However, Lakṣmīdāsa Miśra says: "From the square of the sine of twenty-five degrees multiplied by five, subtracting the cube of the radius (which is equal to the square of the radius multiplied by five), one obtains the square of the radius minus the fourth part [of the remainder]. Thus, since the multiplier for the square of the radius when deriving the sine of ninety degrees is *avatirguṇa*, what would be its multiplier for the derivation of the sine of eighteen degrees? By proportion, it is established that it is *pañcaguṇaka*. This is incorrect.

By the method described, through the calculation of the sine of thirty-six degrees as ten times [the sine of three degrees], it follows that where the sine of fifteen degrees is "sky-mark-ogre" (180), the sine of eighteen degrees—which is more than a quarter of the radius (trijyā)—ought to be "earth-fire-ogre" (34).

Therefore, assuming a value for *y* such that one-fourth of the sine of *y* (or the sine of eighteen degrees) would be the true measure, one should calculate the *kalās* or *asus* of this sine of eighteen degrees divided by twenty-five. By means of the mathematical method of equating it with these forms equal to the sine of eighteen degrees—namely, 1062—one obtains the multiplier as 1;14,10. This, increased by one, becomes 2;14,10.

The square root of the product of the three sines of the five [arcs] is multiplied by the sine of the sum of the three [arcs]; this result, when divided by the product of the radius (*trijyā*) and the sine of the desired multiple of the arc (which is here the radius), yields a quotient. This is because, according to the method of calculation found in the *Āryabhaṭīya*, the sine of eighteen degrees lacks precision; consequently, the multiplier established for making that value equal also lacks precision. Therefore, this particular method cannot be considered precise. || 9 ||

Now, for the purpose of knowing the other sines (*jyā*), he states two methods for calculating the sine of the ascendant (*adheśaka*) in the *Upajāti* meter: "In direct and inverse order" (*kramotkrama*). This was explained previously. (Verse 10) Next, stating that the sine of the desired degrees related to that [ascendant] should be computed according to the aforementioned method, and concluding the calculation of sines by means of this non-standard mathematical procedure, he announces his own devised method of calculating sines in the *Indravajrā* meter: "Of that" (*tasyāḥ*). The first half-verse has been explained. Thus, by this method of establishing the sine of the ascendant, the calculation of other sines is accomplished.

The calculation of the sines (jyās) related to other [angles] from all the sines of one, two, and three signs has been previously stated by Brahmagupta, Laghv-āryabhaṭṭa, and others; the meaning is that this [method] is not devised by me. Now, one might ask: "What is your excellence compared to the previously mentioned exposition on the generation of sines? To this he says: "I shall explain. That is, I shall now describe the previously mentioned method for calculating sines with greater precision. Next, he describes the promised calculation of sines using the Upajāti meter: "By the trijyā... and so forth.

The square of the radius (trijyā) multiplied by the sine of the arm (bhuja-jyā), when diminished by one in one case and increased by one in the other, yields the squares of their respective halves. In the chapter on the calculation of the *galadhya* (the difference between the elapsed and remaining portions of a sign): first, the square root of the product of the sines of the lords of the elapsed and unelapsed portions of the three signs minus the arm; and second, the sine of the lords of the three signs plus the arm. By the aforementioned method, two sines are obtained: the sine of the arm and the sine of the complement (koṭi-jyā) related to that sine of the arm. Having assumed the sine of the arm as the hypotenuse (*bhujaṅgī*), the two sines are thus derived in the manner described.

The meaning is that all desired sines (jyās) are to be produced from the ninety degrees and the degrees of the [remaining] lord, respectively, by means of the previously stated method for each sine starting from the [first] degree, even beyond the [initial] signs. For example: the sine of forty degrees is calculated from zero degrees according to the stated method; to this, twenty-two and a half degrees and sixty-seven and a half degrees are to be added. In the present case, these correspond to six, eighteen, and fifteen degrees; and to eighteen, three, and twenty-one degrees. The sine of one sign is the eighth [term].

From the eighth to the sixteenth; from the sixteenth to the fourth and the twentieth; from the fourth to the tenth and the fourteenth; from the twentieth to the second and the twenty-second; from the tenth to the seventeenth; from the fourteenth to the sixth and the nineteenth; from the second to the eleventh and the thirteenth; from the twenty-second to the first and the twenty-third. In this manner, it should be calculated elsewhere as well. Herein lies the proof.

By the rule: "The square root of half the product of the versed sine of the complement of the arc of the hypotenuse (the radius) and the versed sine of the radius is the sine of its quarter-part," the sine of the side of the triangle formed by the hypotenuse and the base is derived as follows: when the sine of the base is multiplied by the radius, the product of the sine of the base and the radius is subtracted from the square of the radius; the square root of that remainder is the sine of the complement of the base, which is the sine of the quarter-part. The square of this [sine] is half the product of the sine of the base and the radius, minus half the square of the radius. By the method of equal denominators, this is equivalent to the radius squared diminished by the square of the sine of the base.

The square root of half the sum of the square of the radius (*trijyā*) and the product of the radius and the sine of the complement of the desired arc is the sine of those complementary parts. These complementary parts—namely, ninety minus the degrees of the arc—are, according to the aforementioned method, transformed into half of ninety plus the degrees of the arc; this establishes the rule: "the radius, increased or decreased by the product of the sine of the arc," and so forth. (12) Now, he states the calculation for the sine of half the difference between two desired arcs using the *Upajāti* meter: "yaddorghayor iti" (of whichever two [arcs]...).

The square root of the sum of the squares of the differences between the two desired sine values of the arms (*bhujajyā*) and the two cosine values (*koṭijyā*) related to those arms shall be the sine of half the difference between those two arms. In this manner, by the method described and by the method of the cosine, the sine is established in many ways; the meaning is that all [these] arise through different methods. By the phrase "in many ways" (*anekadhā*), it is indicated that even those [sines] already established by this method from the mutual sines of the arms are established yet again.

For example: by means of two arms (bhujas) equal to the sine of zero and the sine of three signs respectively, according to the method described, the twelfth sine is obtained. Its square root (maṭhī) is the sine of its complement (koṭijyā), which is the eighteenth. From this, the ninth and the third [are derived]; from the sine of the complement, the fifteenth and the twenty-first; from the eighth, the sixteenth, the fourth, the twentieth, and so forth.

Is it not the case that this method is identical to the one stated by the verse: "The strength [of the sine] is the square root of the sum of the squares of the eighth sines; half of that shall be the sine of the arc"? For otherwise, how could the difference between the two sines of the arms (bhujajyā) and the difference between the two sines of the complements (koṭijyā)—corresponding respectively to the degrees of the interval between the two sets of arm-degrees—be established as the sine of half the degrees of the interval between their tenth-parts? Nor can this be accepted as a desired conclusion (iṣṭāpatti), because the sine of the complement of the radius (trijyā) is an *utkramajyā* (versed sine), and thus the difference between the sines of the arms or the difference between the sines of the complements would necessarily be an *utkramajyā*.

In this very way, there is an absence of sequential sine (kramajyā) for those two [angles]. Otherwise, it would result in a contradiction with the established rule (*jyotphailiva*). For, if that were the case, it would entail the statement that the difference between those sines is itself a sequential sine of the interval between the arm and the hypotenuse (*bhuja-śāntar-jyā*). Furthermore, when calculating the sine according to the method described by Īśāna regarding the interval between the arm and the hypotenuse, since the differences between the sines of the arms and the sines of the hypotenuses are equal, it is impossible for one of them to be a sequential sine. Nor can it be argued that this is not so because the sequential and reverse sines (*kramotkramajyā*) of the angles of their own and other [triangles] are not equal.

For the difference between the sines of the arms and the sides is not necessarily fixed, which would otherwise constitute the proof [of the rule]. Thus, if it is argued that the calculation of the sine as stated is incorrect because it is derived from the difference between the sines of the arms and the sides, we say no; for it is known that the square of the sum of those two differences is equal to the sum of the squares of the sines of those same angles taken in direct and reverse order. Otherwise, it would be impossible to observe that the square root of that sum divided by two equals the sine of half the angle. Furthermore, it is observed that the sum of the squares of two different quantities taken together is equal to the sum of the squares of their respective sines.

For example, the sum of the square of 9 (81) and the square of 4 (16) is 85; the sum of the squares of 7 and 6 is also 85. This is because the hypotenuse is indeed the same, as there is no certainty that the hypotenuse formed by the sine and cosine of one angle is different from that formed by the sine and cosine of another. The proof here is as follows: From the center of the circle, lines drawn to a desired point on the circumference constitute the sine and cosine of the arc, as previously stated. In this case, the larger sine minus the smaller sine is the difference between the sines of the arcs, which takes the form of a segment of the arc established by their difference; this difference is the sine, and the other component is the cosine.

The square root of the sum of their squares is the sine (*bhuja-jyā*) and cosine (*koṭi-jyā*). The distance between the two circumferences meeting at the tips of these sines and cosines is the full sine of the intervening degrees; half of that is the sine of half those degrees. This is the difference between the two [sines], as stated by Āryabhaṭa. Now, although the sines of the half-degrees of the difference between the cosine and sine can be established by the aforementioned method, the author provides another means for knowing them and announces this alternative method in an Upajāti verse, beginning with "koṭijyā... (the cosine-sine...).

The meaning is that the square root of the difference between the squares of the sines related to the two arms (bhuja) shall be the sine of the interval between the degrees of the two arms. One should reflect that this method of calculation alone does not establish the validity [of the result] as in the previous method; therefore, both methods have been stated here using the sines of the arms and the perpendiculars (koṭi). However, the calculation of the sine by this method is approximate (sthūla).

Since the root cannot be found everywhere because it lacks constituent parts, and since the root is subtle and difficult to perceive, he says: "I shall explain. Now, if one were to claim that the root exists because it is possible to grasp it within the previously mentioned [quantities], and if its grossness were thus asserted, then the root would have been grasped immediately; however, by the word "api" (also), he states that he will explain (*vakṣye*)—that is, he will tell—the method for finding the chord (*jyāsādhana*). Herein is the proof: having assumed the *bhujajyā* (sine of the arc) and the *tadīyajyā* (sine of the corresponding angle) as the sine of the base (*bhujajyā*), and having likewise interchanged the sines of the adjacent sides (*tatkoṭijye*) as the sines of the base.

Likewise, in the interval, they are equal to the difference between the sine (bhujajyā) and the cosine (koṭijyā). The sum of their squares is the square of the hypotenuse (karṇa), and half the square root of twice that [sum] is the sine of half the difference of the degrees of the cosine. Since it was previously stated that "square by square," for the purpose of finding the value, four is the divisor; therefore, by reducing the denominator by two, it is established that half the square root of half the square of the difference is the sine of the cosine.

The account is not untenable, as it is directly perceived through the calculation of the circumference using the difference between the previously increased *koṭijyā* (sine of the complement) and the *bhujaphalajyā* (sine of the arc of the shadow). || 14 || Now, he states the method for pouring the granthi (knot), which was promised, in the *Indravajrā* meter: "ojyākṛti" etc. The sine of the arc (*bhujajyā*) divided by three times the radius (*trijyā*)—the result, when multiplied by the radius, shall be the sine of the degrees of the difference between the arc and its complement. [Golādhyāya 1788]—But surely, the sines are unestablished according to the method just stated.

Since the sine of one sign (*ekarāśijyā*) belonging to a single direction is established by the two—namely, the sine of the arm (*bhujajyā*) and the sine of the perpendicular (*koṭijyā*)—situated in the middle of the four fundamental sines (*mūlabhūtajyācatuṣka*), according to the method already stated, [the author] says "half-sines" (*jyārdhāni*) because the knowledge of the other two—the sine of the arm and the sine of the perpendicular—is required. Here, when the generation of sines is being performed, only certain half-sines arise through the aforementioned method, not all of them; thus, out of curiosity, it is stated that from the known sine of the arm and the sine of the perpendicular, the sine of the intervening degrees is obtained. This is the meaning.

Thus, the sine of one-eighth [of the arc] is to be calculated by the rule beginning with "multiplied by the versed sine of the trijyā" and so forth. From that, its cosine is obtained; and from those two—the sine of the arc and its cosine—the sine of the difference of the angles is found by the aforementioned method. Its cosine is likewise derived. From these two, again, the sine of the difference of the angles is obtained. Where another cannot be established, there the sine of one-eighth [of the arc] is derived from the sine of the arc or the cosine of the arc by the stated method. From that, its cosine is obtained.

The meaning is that by means of those two [sines], certain half-chords (*jyārdha*) are established again and again in the manner described according to the occasion; thus, there is no lack of proof. Here, for the purpose of knowing the sine of the interval between the arm-portion (*doḥkoṭyaṃśa*) and the hypotenuse-portion (*bhagāntarjyā*), the versed sine (*utkramajyā*) of the degrees of the hypotenuse-portion of that interval must be calculated. This is because the sine of the interval between the arm-portion and the hypotenuse-portion is not produced by the versed sine. In this context, the degrees of the hypotenuse-portion are ninety minus the degrees of the arm.

These are the intermediate angles between the arms; they take the form of ninety minus twice the arm-angle, which is the angle between the arm and the perpendicular. These, when subtracted from ninety, are the perpendicular angles for those same [intermediate] points. It follows that the versine (utkramajyā) of these, which takes the form of twice the arm-angle, is to be calculated.

In this regard, by the rule "the square root of half the product of the kramajyā of the arc of the hypotenuse (trijyā) and the bhuja-jyā," it is understood that the square root of half the product of the sine (bhujajyā) and the cosine (koṭijyā) of twice the arc of the bhuja is obtained; conversely, this results in the statement that the square of the bhuja-jyā divided by twice the trijyā is established. Therein, through reduction (apavartana), it is proven that the bhuja-jyā is the square root of the product of the koṭi-jyā and the sine of half the arc.

Thus it is established that the sine of the arcual parts of the hypotenuse and the side [of the triangle] formed by that [radius] is obtained by the difference of the three sines, and so forth. Now, one might object: "The sines of two, three, and more degrees are established from the previously mentioned methods by means of the difference of three degrees; therefore, the sines of the complete degrees contained within those [intervals] follow as a consequence. To this end, he states the method for calculating the twenty-four sines accepted by Āryabhaṭa—which depend upon the calculation of the preceding sines—by means of five *anuṣṭubh* verses, beginning with the words *svagotreṣu*.

The previously taken sine of the arc (bhujajyā) should be diminished by the sines of the degrees contained within the [first] nine and six parts of the signs. This resulting sine of the remainder (koṭijyā) should be multiplied by ten and divided by one hundred and seventy-three; the sum of these two results is the *agrajīvā*. When the sine of the degrees was taken, it shall be the sine of the degrees corresponding to the number of degrees within those [first] nine and six parts. The difference between those two results is the previous correction (*pūrvasaṃskāra*).

The sine of the number of degrees corresponding to the portion previously taken from the parts related to the arc to be traversed shall be the sine of those degrees. He replies: "the first sine. Thus, having calculated the full sine of the arc and the sine of the complement (koṭijyā), the sum of the results obtained by the aforementioned method shall be the sine of the first degree. He illustrates this with: "sixty," etc.

In the case of a trijyā (radius) measured as three times eight oceans (24), since there is an absence of sine (bhuja-jyā) for the first part according to the stated method, and because the cosine (koṭi-jyā) is at its maximum, the origin of the "fruit of the cosine" (koṭiphala) alone occurs. [Verse 149, Chapter 88] It is entirely so. And the fruit of the cosine, by virtue of the stated trijyā, is exactly sixty. Then, after the first sine is established, the other sines—the second part and so forth—are derived one after another from that first sine according to the stated method.

The first sine (jyā) to be calculated is its co-sine (koṭijyā). From these two, the sine of the complement (anasiñjinī) is derived; from this, its co-sine is found. Then, by means of the sine and co-sine of that [angle], the sines for each degree—numbering ninety-nine—are obtained according to the rule beginning with "tadājyā" (the sine of that). In the same manner, having assumed the radius (trijyā) as the sine, zero as the sine, and zero as the co-sine, the previous sine is to be calculated; that is the sine of eighty-nine degrees. From this, its co-sine is found. From these two, the sine of the half-arc for eighty-eight degrees is derived; from this, its co-sine is found.

Alternatively, by means of the sine and cosine of the arm, the other [sines] such as the previous ones may be established; thus, for each degree, ninety sines are to be calculated. This has been clearly indicated: even when postulating a trijyā (radius) other than that which was stated, ninety sines per degree—exceeding sixty and so forth—are established by the method already described. By this, the calculation according to the stated method is shown to apply to the mentioned trijyā.

The claim that "the calculation for the sine greater than that [radius] should be performed by the wise using their own ingenuity with different multipliers and divisors according to the stated method, as it has been brought forth in this manner" is refuted; for it is observed that its establishment occurs everywhere within the radius (*trijyā*) through the aforementioned procedure. Otherwise, the mention of sixty in the instruction would result in being purposeless.

Now, one might object: "In this way, it is more appropriate to calculate the sine of ninety degrees due to its simplicity; however, calculating the sines of the twenty-four [arcs] as previously described is cumbersome and therefore improper. That [line] which is the difference between the two roots—the root of the sine of the smaller arm and the root of the sine of the larger arm—is the hypotenuse, as known through direct perception. Thus, by the proportionality of the triangle: "If the sine of the angle adjacent to the smaller sine of the arm is the side, then what is the side when the sine of the larger arm is the hypotenuse?"—the knowledge of the [sine of the] angle is obtained.

Up to the limit of this perpendicular line (*koṭi*), the small arm-sine (*laghubhujajyā*) is the base (*pradyu*), the perpendicular (*koṭi*) is the small arm-sine, and the hypotenuse (*karṇa*) is that interval; the previous perpendicular itself is one part of the arm. To know that [arm], if the hypotenuse is the radius (*trijyā*) and the perpendicular-sine related to the large arm-sine is the base, then by proportion: "If this is the base, what is the base for the small arm-sine? (Note: *Pradyu* here refers to the horizontal distance from the origin to the foot of the perpendicular.)

Thereupon, they say that the interval between those two hypotenuses (*koṭibhuja*), which takes the form of a portion of a single line, is equal to what is called the "difference of arcs" (*cāpāntara*)—this is established by direct perception according to the rule beginning with "the difference of two desired arcs. However, [we reply] that in that case, the construction of a hypotenuse-line equal to the sine of the larger arc is logically untenable; furthermore, because the relationships of proportionality within the figure have not been demonstrated, there is a lack of evidentiary authority for the stated proportion.

Otherwise, since the sine of the arc (bhujajyā) is the side and its cosine is the adjacent side (koṭi), or the cosine is the side and its sine is the adjacent side, then by proportion—asking "if the sine of the arc *ka* is the side, what is the adjacent side?"—the emergence of the square of the sine of the arc as being equal to the product of the sines of the side and the adjacent side would be unavoidable; such is the detailed [explanation]. Others, however, calculate here the difference between the sine of the sum and the sine of the individual arcs of the arrows (*iṣu-cāpa*). Therein the proportion is as follows: if, with a cosine equal to the radius (*trijyā*), a difference between the sine of the sum and the sine of the small arc equal to the sine of the small arc is obtained, then what [difference] is obtained with the measure of the cosine of the large arc? Thus results the difference between the sine of the sum and the sine of the large arc.

Thus, if by a co-latitude sine (*koṭijyā*) equal to the radius (*trijyā*), an interval equal to the difference between the sines of the sum and the smaller arc is obtained, then what [interval] is obtained by the co-latitude sine of the smaller arc? This results in the interval between the sines of the sum and the smaller arc. When one arc is zero and the second is the desired arc (*sveṣṭacāpa*), then the interval between the sines of the sum and the zero-arc is equal to the sine of the desired arc; this is understood even by children. Therefore, this proportion is valid.

Since the designations "small" (*bṛhat*) and "large" (*laghu*) for the arcs were used to avoid confusion between them, it was stated [in the verse] beginning with "the sines of the two small arcs" and ending with "shines like the radius" (*trijyābhāti*). Because the difference between these two results is very slight, it is said that "the sine of the sum of the two arcs" is obtained by their addition. Now, one might object: "If the previously stated reasoning is correct—that the difference between the sines of the small arcs should be added to the sine of the smaller arc, or the difference between the sines of the large arcs should be added to the sine of the larger arc—then why is it stated that the 'sine of their sum' is the sum of those two results? To this, it is replied as follows: [The text continues with the mathematical justification.]

When this is done, since the sine of the sum of the arcs is not seen to be equal to the sine of the arc resulting from the reading "the ocean of principles (254) plus the joy (9)," and because that [relationship] is equal here as well, the underlying rationale (*vāsanā*) has been set aside; thus it was stated that "the sum of the obtained sines is the sine of the sum of the arcs," and likewise, "the difference of the obtained sines is the sine of the difference of the arcs. This is the demonstration with an example: where there are twenty-four sines within three signs (*tribha*), the first sine there is equal to 254.

By means of the *vikalā-pramāṇa* (the measure of seconds), when the first and ninth sines are known, and when the sine of their limit is known, the fourteenth sine is determined through the calculation of the sine of the sum of the arcs; the fourth sine is determined through the calculation of the sine of the difference of the arcs.

The difference between the fifteenth and fourteenth sines is 156. [Golādhyāya, Bhāskara’s commentary]: These segments of the subtracted sine are not established by equal proportions. If, when the co-sine is equal to the radius (trijyā), a difference of one hundred and twenty-five is obtained, then what is it when the co-sine is equal to the nineteenth sine? This is the difference between the fifth and sixth sines. Again, there is a proportion: [Note: The calculation follows the rule of three (*trairāśika*). If a co-sine equal to the radius yields a difference of 125, then a co-sine equal to the nineteenth sine yields what? The difference between the fifth and sixth sines is again calculated through proportion.

By means of a co-latitude sine (*koṭijyā*) equal to the radius (*trijyā*), a second segment is obtained; then, by means of a co-latitude sine equal to that [second segment] diminished by one, what is obtained is the difference between the sixth and seventh sines. In this manner, seven segments are to be calculated through seven proportional operations (*anupātas*). Their sum becomes the difference between the fifth and fourteenth sines. Therefore, the co-latitude sine of the small arc equal to the nineteenth sine is the first [segment]; those nine successive differences of sines beginning with the second (*aśvi*) are thus established.

These [nine segments] are to be multiplied by nine; since it follows that "in all cases one should divide by the sine of the radius" (*trijyā*), the rule "if there is a single divisor but two different multipliers, then the sum of the multipliers is the single multiplier" is applied. Thus, the sum of the nine segments—consisting of the cosine of the arc of the [smaller] bow and so forth—is made the multiplier, which is equal to the ninth sine (*navamī-jīvā*). The divisor, however, remains the sine of the radius (*trijyā*) itself. Here, it is stated that the ninth sine itself becomes the sine of the larger arc, as expressed in the verse beginning with "of the two arcs" (*cāpayoḥ*). In this way, the difference between the sines is also established from the cosine of the larger arc.

They say that "the remainder is as before," but this is trivial. For while your statement might be established when one of the two sine-values of the arcs is zero, it is not established elsewhere. This is because, since the difference between the sines of the smaller arcs is composed of the sum of the segments of the difference between the sines of the halves of the sum of the smaller arcs and so forth, the sine of the arc resulting from the sum of the segments of the first sine and so on—which is the sine of the arc obtained through the stated proportion by means of the respective cosine-sine as the measure—is not established. Thus, your claim fails.

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that the sine of the sum of two arcs could be derived either by adding the difference established through proportion from the sines of the individual smaller arcs, or by adding the known difference between the sine of the larger arc and the sine of the sum of the two larger arcs; furthermore, there is no logical justification for the production of the sine of the sum of two arcs from the sum of the differences obtained for each.

[Objection: But surely, by assuming the sine of the arm of the large arc to be zero, the difference obtained from the first proportion is extremely gross; for when the sine of the arm of the large arc is at its maximum, the sine of the arm of the small arc is near zero, and thus the sine of the sum of the arcs is the cosine of the small arc. Consequently, while one [difference] is equal to the versed sine of the arm of the small arc—which is directly perceived—the other [difference] is not established by the previous proportion because there is no cosine related to the sine of the large arm.

For it is not logical that the difference should be zero even when the small sine of the arc exists there, just as it is when it is absent; rather, for the sake of brevity, one should perform the subtraction using the method of equal denominators with the divisor equal to twice the diameter (ataddhibyā). Thus, from the large sine of the arc, one should subtract the value obtained by the proportion: "If by this large sine of the arc the difference between the large and small sine-strings—equal to the versed sine of the small arc—is found, then what [difference] would be obtained by that same large sine? The resulting difference, thus diminished, will be the precise difference.

Since the sine of the arc [in question] is the difference between the radius (trijyā) and the versed sine (utkramajyā), the second proportional difference in that case is applied to the large sine of the arc (bṛhadbhujajyā) itself for the sake of brevity. By the method of equal subtraction, the subtraction is performed such that the product of the radius and the large sine of the arc is divided by the product of the radius and the versed sine; this is established. Furthermore, because the multiplier—the large sine of the arc—is the same in both cases, it follows that the result of subtracting the versed sine from three times the radius, when multiplied by the large sine of the arc and divided by the radius, takes the form of the sine of the complement of the small arc.

The result is the chord of the arc of the hypotenuse (*jyāpatti*), which is the sum of the chord of the hypotenuse at the given place and the gross difference obtained from the previous proportion. Thus, for the purpose of calculating the chord of the intermediate arc, since the difference between the large chord of the hypotenuse (equal to the radius) and the small sine of the adjacent side is itself the chord of the intermediate arc, it must be subtracted from the large chord of the hypotenuse by the difference derived from the small sine of the adjacent side. Consequently, according to the previously stated method, it is established that [the chord] is the product of the large chord of the hypotenuse and the sine of the adjacent side of the small arc, divided by the radius.

Since the absence of the large sine of the arc (*bṛhan-bhuja-jyā*) is established by the method already stated, it follows that the difference between the large sine of the arc and the small sine of the arc (*laghu-bhuja-jyā*)—which is being calculated—is equal to the small sine of the arc itself. Therefore, the difference between the small and large sines of the arc, obtained through the first proportion, is established as the sum of the arc and its sine. Consequently, the previously established value corresponding to the place of the large sine of the arc must be subtracted from this [sum]. If it is argued that the remaining difference should be added to the sine of the arc, that is not correct.

Because there is no connection between the two arms of the gross proportion (sthūlānupāta), it would lead to the undesirable consequence that existence and non-existence could not be established in their mutual relationship; furthermore, there is no mention of such a method of gross proportion in any treatise whatsoever. Moreover, there is no logical justification for deriving the precise sine of the sum from results obtained through gross proportions—whether by addition or subtraction—and this would result in the values becoming merely approximate.

Indeed, the difference between the first coarse sine of the arc derived from the first proportion and the fine sine of the combined arc—which is greater—is established as having a specific magnitude in the second coarse proportion; by this, according to the stated method, there is no room for doubt regarding the fine combined sine. However, in the case of the production of the sine of the intermediate arc, there is no evidence that the large difference in the sine of the arc established in the result obtained from the first proportion exists as a true arc.

Furthermore, if it is argued that some way of establishing [the result] is possible—namely, that since the sines of the sum and difference of two arcs are respectively the sum and difference of the sines of the small arc (bhujajyā) and the large arc (koṭijyā), then by means of the assumed *kajya* and *anuṣātā* derived from the method previously stated, the fine sine of the sum and difference is established through the sum and difference of the coarse sine of the sum and difference—then this argument, which seeks to establish [the result] with ease and without depending on the versed sine (*utkramajyā*), and your proposed solution, as well as my own solution, would both be based solely on the versed sine (*utkramaja*).

It should not be said that this is intended to establish brevity; for there is no evidence that the difference between the sum and the difference of the two values obtained through proportion results in the square of the difference between the sum and the difference. This is the general direction. In the same way, regarding the second production, even for those who are dull-witted, since the sum of the nine "to-be-traversed" segments (bhogyakhaṇḍa) brought down by proportion from the differences of the first, second, and third sines (jyā) takes the form of the ninth sine—whose magnitude is established by the nineteenth sine—it follows that it is not equal to the difference between the fifth and fourteenth sines.

Since this has been thoroughly considered and heard, there is no lack of formal distinction (vaiyadhikaraṇya) in the forms of those who bear the names of the Supreme Goddess’s grace-bestowed substrates; nevertheless, a distinction in cognition is indeed fully established. Otherwise, there would be a contradiction in that designation. Thus, enough of searching for such irrelevant faults. This may be so.

By means of the calculation of the chord (*jyā*) for the two desired arcs joined by the excess, the previously mentioned method for determining the initial and preceding [chords] occurs; this results in the production of the twenty-fourth chord contained within [the circle]. If you ask how this is so, given that it is indicated in that appearance, listen: since the Sun and others accept the chord of one-eighth part as being equal to a bow (*dhanus*), the chord of a single degree is all the more so; thus, the chord of one degree is established by the measure of sixty-eight thousand three hundred and thirty-three (68,333) as the radius (*trijyā*).

Thus it was stated by me, either by way of illustration or according to that method: her *koṭijyā* (sine of the complement) is 3437;28;35;52, which is the trijyā (radius) diminished by twenty-four degrees and twenty-eight parts plus one-sixty-eighth part. When the sine of one degree (158') is combined with this [value] through the process of *samāsa-bhāvanā*, the sine of the subsequent degrees is established; likewise, the sine of the preceding degrees is established through the process of *antara-bhāvanā*.
