For instance, by means of this *koṭijyā* of one degree—namely 3420;28;35—as expressed in the verse beginning "The sines of the desired degrees are obtained from the sine of the arc and the sine of its complement," etc.

52. It is meritorious. The sine of the angle (bhuja-jyā) multiplied by three and divided by the radius (trijyā) for the sake of brevity—since it is held to be equal to the radius—is then subtracted from the result of the product of the sine of the angle multiplied by thirty-one, twenty-four, and eight, and divided by the radius. This results in the sine of the co-latitude (koṭi-jyā) of one degree multiplied by the sine of the angle and divided by one hundred, as established by the division of the radius. In that case, the difference in the multipliers is the multiplier of one unit: 31; 24; 8.

By subtracting the product of three and two from the square of the hypotenuse, the resulting value at the place of the side is 569; these [values] are held to be equal due to their very small difference. Therefore, "the sine of the arc diminished by one-sixth of itself" results in the calculated sine of the arc.

Now, since it is known that the sine of the complement (koṭijyā) related to the sine of the arc (bhujajyā) is to be multiplied by one part of the sine of the arc—which is the square root of six—and divided by the radius (trijyā), the multiplier (guṇa) 60 and the divisor (hara) 3438 are reduced by six; thus the multiplier becomes ten and the divisor three hundred. Therefore, the sine of the complement multiplied by ten and divided by three hundred results in the "complement-fruit" (koṭiphala). The sum of these two [the sine of the arc and the complement-fruit] is the sine of the sum of the arcs, because the sum of their sines is the sine of the sum; thus it has been stated.

Since it has been stated that "the sine of the arc [of the hypotenuse] is equal to the interval between the two [given] sines," and since the interval has been called the *pūrvaśiṇī*, it follows by this calculation that the first sine from the radius (*trijyā*) is indeed sixty; what wonder is there in this? Thus, because the aforementioned method of calculation is established as being based on an interval of one degree, the derivation of the sine for every single degree is achieved through this very process.

The statement "the diameter is multiplied by eight and equal to four hundred and thirty-two" is intended to indicate that this calculation was conceived by me based on the knowledge of the radius (trijyā) as desired by Sūrya; otherwise, how could such a conception be consistent given the ignorance of the sine of one degree at the tip of another radius? Now, if the sine of the hypotenuse and the sine of the perpendicular were taken according to the measure of yet another radius, there would be an error in the aforementioned method; therefore, the specification of *that* particular radius is made to avoid such a discrepancy.

Because the method described remains unerring even when the sine and cosine of one degree are taken according to an arbitrary radius (iṣṭatrijyā), it is established that by means of an arbitrary radius alone, the sine and cosine of one degree—and their respective co-sines and sines—are achieved through the proportionality of the current radius; for this is accomplished simply by reducing the multiplier and divisor by the same factor, leaving them unchanged. For this very reason, the sines from sixty up to ninety degrees are obtained by assuming a radius of eight times the number of years [of the Kali era] plus forty-two.

It has been correctly refuted previously that those [sine values] are not established by assuming a trijyā other than that [standard one]. Now, an objection might be raised: "Is it not improper for the venerable Bhāskara Ācārya—who asserts that sixty *liptās* constitute the numerical value of the sine of one degree (*ekāṃśajyā*) according to the opinion of the Sun—to state such a subtle object of measurement? This is because the *jyā* and *apajyā* arise from the [geometric] construction [of the circle]. Otherwise, since errors would inevitably arise, the effort in defining the generation of *jyās* for the purpose of mathematical calculation everywhere would be rendered useless. To this, we reply: No.

Because an extremely minute portion of the circumference must necessarily be equal, it is possible for the sine of that limited arc to be equal [to its measure]; otherwise, the existence of mustard seeds within an *āmalaka* fruit and so forth would be untenable. Therefore, it was reduced to a single part, because it is more subtle than even the eighth part of a solar sign (*rāśi*), and because there would be no stability in the results and so forth below that level. Furthermore, the method for calculating the sines has not been stated by anyone else, as it would lead to an excessive prolixity. *Jyotpattivāsanā*, verse 159: *mae80*. The method for deriving those sines is extremely difficult to understand, and thus has not been mentioned by all [authorities].

In this context, it is said that having constructed a circle with a radius equal to the sine of three signs (90 degrees), whatever half-arc or half-sine is known therein, when doubled, becomes the full arc and the full sine of the base. The arc is marked at its third parts. Therein, the line between two marks is the large [full] arc; the small [full] arc, which consists of one-third of the full arc, takes the form of the full sine. These are situated in three positions as appropriate: the two arms are located on the sides, and the mouth is in the middle.

In that case, the bow whose two parts are complete is the full chord-line (*jyāsūtra*), and the second ear (*karṇa*) is equal to it. The line between the path of the ear and the ground is the perpendicular (*lamba*); these two are indeed equal. A quadrilateral with a pause (*virāma*)—that is, an equiangular and equi-perpendicular figure—is clearly evident through the method of adding the sides. Within the perpendicular, the rectangular quadrilateral formed by the perpendicular and its face is directly measurable; thus, the ground minus the face is the portion of the ground from the base up to the tip of the perpendicular, and the sum of those two [is the total].

For that purpose, the segment of ground from the perpendicular (lamba) to the limit of the adjacent land is the base (bhuja). One-third of the bow (dhanus) with its full chord (jyā) is the previous base, which serves as the hypotenuse (karṇa). The perpendicular is the side (koṭi); thus, in one part of that field, a small right-angled triangle (laghujātyayana) is directly perceived. Therefore, the square of the chord of twice the previous base—namely *bhra*¹ + *jyā*²—is diminished by the square of the previous base (*bhuva*¹), resulting in the square of the perpendicular: *bhuva*³ + *bhujyā*⁴ + *jyāva*⁴.

Now, consider a portion of the earth situated at a distance from the perpendicular (lamba), extending to the limit of the sky, where the base is one unit (bhu 1) and the chord (jyā) is two units (jyā 2). The base minus the chord is the remaining base. The perpendicular (lamba) is the side (bhuja), and the line drawn through both ends of that [perpendicular] is the previously mentioned diagonal (karṇa) of the quadrilateral; thus, it is a great right-angled triangle (mahājātyatryasra). The square of the hypotenuse (karṇavarga) is produced by adding together: the square of the base (bhuva 1), four times the product of the base and the chord (bhu 1 × jyā 4), and four times the square of the chord (jyāya 4). This results in the following expression for the square of the hypotenuse: *bhuva 1 + bhu 1 × jyā 4 + jyāya 4*. This is the square of the hypotenuse of the great right-angled triangle, which is directly perceived as having a base of three units (*bhuva 3*) and a chord of four units (*jyā 4*).

*bhuva* 4, *bhujyā* 8. This is established by dividing by the divisor. *bhuva* 1, *bhujyā* 2. Now, the square of the hypotenuse (*karṇa*) is calculated by another method. For that purpose: half the hypotenuse of a full four-sided figure (square) is the chord of an arc; the sine of that arc is the side (*bhuja*), its versed sine (*utkramajyā*) is the perpendicular (*koṭi*), and the arc is of the nature of two signs (*dvibhaga*). The sine of the junction of the full arc is the hypotenuse in the form of the previously mentioned side of the four-sided figure. Thus, this square of the side of the equilateral quadrilateral is *bhuva* 1.

The square of that [sine] is half the square of the diameter; the square of the arc-sine (koṭijyā) is the square of the diameter minus the square of the sine. Since the sum of the arc-sine and the sine is the form of the diameter, the product of the diameter and the arc-sine is divided by twice the diameter. Thus, the arc-sine is one unit, and subtracting these from three gives two units as the diameter. The arc-sine is one unit, the diameter is two units; their squares are one and four respectively. Subtracting four from four leaves zero, and adding four to four gives eight. The square of the diameter is thus equal to the square of the sine multiplied by four, which is one unit, zero, and four times the square of the diameter.

4 times the square of half the base (ardhavarga) plus three times the square of the height (trivarga) equals 4 times the square of the height plus 3 times the square of the base. Since the previously established square of the hypotenuse (karṇavarga) consists of four equal parts, it is equal to the base (bhuva) squared and the square of the sine of the angle (bhujyā) squared. By making the denominators equal through the fourth part—namely, by equating *bhuva*² and *bhujyā*²—one arrives at the removal of the denominator (*chedagama*). The arrangement is as follows: *bhuva*²/4 and *bhuva*³/4 + *bhujyā*²/0. These two terms, when reduced by the base (*bhujena*), become: *bhuva*²/0 and *bhuva*³/1 + *bhujyā*²/2.

*bhujā* 1 *bhū* 0 *trijyā* 4 *jyā* 0 *trijyā* 0. Here, when equal terms are subtracted from equal terms, there is no loss of equality: *bhujā* 0 *graha* 0 *trijyā* 1 *jyā* 0 – *trijyā* 2 *ni* 0. Thus, when the square of the product of the *bhujā* and the *trijyā* is subtracted from both sides of the equation, the two sides become: *bhujā* 1 *bhū* 0 *trijyā* 3 *jyā* 0 *trijyā* 0.

Bhava0, bhu0, tri-varga, jyā0, tri-varga, 2. Here too, there is a loss of equality in the combination of the sides; thus, when the cube of the side is added to the two sides, the resulting sides are: bhudha7, bhu0, tri-varga, jyā0, tri-varga, bhudhe 1, bhu0, tri-varga, jyā, tri-varga, 2. Because the sides are equal, it is established that three times the product of the square of the radius (trijyā) and the side, when added to the cube of the side, is equal to twice the product of the square of the radius and the sine (jyā).

In this case, regarding the second alternative, since there is no purely unknown quantity (*kevalavyakta*), the measure of the side (*bhuja*) cannot be established in any way by the method stated for the seed (*bīja*), because it depends on the unknown. Therefore, the known portion of the second side—which consists of the product of twice the square of the sine of the third power—is divided by three times the square of the sine of the third power (the remainder of the purely unknown). This results in a rough known measure of the side. This is because, due to the absence of the previously calculated side, that first portion remains unknown.

In that case, by reducing the divisor and dividend by the sine of the arc (*trijyā*), the measure of the chord for twice the arc (*dviguṇajyā*) becomes a rough approximation of the sine. Now, since even the first segment is a portion of the chord, the measure of this rough sine, when divided by three times the square of the radius (*trijyā`²`), yields the measure of the first segment as a portion of the chord. The sum of these two [segments] is the measure of the chord; yet it remains a rough approximation compared to the previous one, because the portion of the chord derived from the first segment itself arises from a rough sine.

Therefore, that product, when divided by the square of the radius (trijyā) multiplied by three—which serves as the divisor—is the result; this, when added to the square root of the approximate chord-measure (which is in the form of a third of the double-chord), yields a more accurate, yet still approximate, measure of the chord. Then again, by adding a third of the double-chord obtained from the product divided by its own divisor, the accurate measure of the chord will be reached; thus it should be done repeatedly until no further difference remains.

The subtle measure of the bowstring (jyā) is the measure of the half-chord (ardhajyā) of that half-bow, which is the measure of the full chord of the full bow increased by one-third of it. This is the basis for the calculation of the *phalita* (the result). The procedure is as follows: the sine-portion (*jyāṃśa*) multiplied by three and divided by the square of the radius (*trijyā*) is added to its own third part of the sine-portion; from that, the result produced by the cube and so forth is calculated according to the stated method. That result is again added to the sine-portion multiplied by three, and this process is repeated until the value is precise (*sphuṭa*).

The *Thapati* (the author) observed that this third-part sine (*tṛtīyāṃśajyā*) mentioned by me was not stated by the ancients. *Bhaṭṭa-dīpikā*: Thus, the first-part sine derived from the third-part sine and the first-part sine [itself] is subtle and easily understood. By this, both [objections] are refuted: namely, the objection previously stated regarding the arc of the single-part sine being too large, and the counter-argument that since equality between those two must necessarily occur at some point, the error was committed in the single-part [calculation] itself. This is because, according to the method described, the single-part sine does not possess such [an error].

In a region where there is a deficiency of *kalās*, that subtle region is accepted as equal [to the whole] because of the extreme subtlety of the hand; otherwise, it would result in equality everywhere. In reality, however, due to the distinction between the chord (*jyā*) and the arc (*cāpa*), they are not actually equal; rather, the chord is less than the arc, for otherwise there would be a contradiction. Therefore, even in the case of *kalās* and so forth, although their equality is logically untenable, it is asserted because there is no means to perceive their subtle difference.

Even there, although the attainment of that equality of modes is logically untenable because of the absence of such modes of knowledge in the subtle, it is treated as a constituent part (*aṅga*). Even there, the attainment of those modes and their equality must be postulated for the sake of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) in that which is even more subtle than a deficient limb. This is the essential point (*tattva*). By this method of calculating the sine of the third part, the sine of one sign and the radius (*trijyā*) become equal to one unit (*rūpa*).

For instance: the cube of the radius (trijyā) is 1; divided by the square of the radius, it is 1/27; added to its own square root, it is 1/4; and adding one-sixteenth, it becomes 81/81 or 31/31. Here, for the sake of establishing the square root of the radius, the radius itself is omitted and only 29791 is taken as 31.

Then, by subtracting the square of the square root of the difference of the squares from the divisor, one obtains 29791/81 = 1594323/119164. When added to this [fraction] 1, the result is 650605. From this, the calculation must be accomplished repeatedly using the method of *cancana* (addition/subtraction) starting from 1594322 and 1594323. For a skilled mathematician, a reduction (*apavarta*) is possible there; thus, both the dividend and the divisor are to be reduced. In this way, through the completion of the mathematical operation by means of successive transformations and the adoption of near approximations, this reduction is established as 1/2.

The divisor for this [value], which resides in the vessel of the meaning of firm self-knowledge, is 1; its own operation is 1; from that, it is 4. By means of reduction (apavartana), the denominator is established as 24, 24. By this, that which is established is 1.

By this, the three parts [1] were joined through uniformity; by the addition of five, the result was established as stable. He whose toenails are kissed by the garlands of rays from the crest-jewels of all sovereign kings, who has dispelled the continuous succession of the world’s own heat with the mass of his rays, whose creeper-like fame embraces the shores of the four oceans, and who has attained the totality of the scriptures of arithmetic and astronomy—[the number] 15,162 rests upon his neck.

The universal monarch of the Persian world, Maṭīṭha, who has directly realized the entire expanse of the cosmic egg (*saṃsārakhaṇḍabrahmāṇḍamaṇḍala*), explains in detail in his own work titled *Jīvana* how to calculate the twenty-four sines (*jyā*) according to the previously mentioned radius (*trijyā*). Thus, by this method of calculating sines, the first sine with its fractional parts is 224; 51; 17; 15. The twenty-third co-sine (*koṭijyā*) with its fractional parts is 3430; 38; 17; 12.

According to the previous method, the *koṭijyā* (sine of the complement) is multiplied by the first multiplier obtained in the calculation, namely 224;51,10,15, and divided by the radius (*trijyā*) of 3438. This divisor is reduced by this slightly smaller value of two and one-quarter, namely 2;14,54,42,9. Thus, the multiplier becomes 100 and the divisor becomes 1529 (the number of Nandas [9] and Aśvins [2] and lunar days [15]).

The chord of twenty-three degrees with its three fractional parts is 12. Subtracting this from the radius (trijyā), which measures 3438, we obtain the multiplier 7 11 42 458. When both the multiplier and the divisor are reduced by the common factor of the radius (3438), the multiplier becomes 1 and the divisor becomes 467. Thus, the verse beginning with "multiplied by the hundred of the co-latitude" (*koṭijīvāśatābhyastā*) is established.

By this method of bringing [the values], the four parts less than a quarter of the first sine (prathamajyā) are determined in accordance with the previously stated trijyās as being diminished by seven parts; for the other trijyās, the first sine and its successor are derived by the aforementioned procedure. The remainder has already been explained previously. Now, incidentally, the justification for the calculation of the sine of the difference between two arcs—using the method of compounding sines (jyāntarabhāvanā), the square root of the product of the diameter and the versed sine (dorghīkṛti-vyāsārdha-bhaktyādi), and so forth—is as follows: the sine of the arc and the sine of the complement (bhujakoṭijye) are the sines of the two arcs.

The sines of the complements of those two [angles] are their respective co-sines. Furthermore, by the rule "of two desired [sines]... and so forth, it is established that the squares of the sine and cosine [of an angle] are divided by the radius (trijyā). Thus, the difference between these two is the sine of the difference in degrees between the sine and cosine [components]. In that case, since the square of the co-sine minus the square of the sine is equal to the square of the radius, the difference between them is the difference between the square of twice the sine and the square of the radius, divided by the radius; hence, here too, the difference between the two quantities divided by the radius has been computed.

In that case, when the *bhuja* (sine of the arc) is multiplied by six and divided by the radius (*trijyā*), it is reduced by the same factor; thus, the square of the radius divided by half the radius results in the radius itself. The difference between those two is obtained by the subtraction of the three sides; this is established. Enough with this incidental discussion.

Now, one might object: "In this way, when calculating the preceding and succeeding sines based on a radius (*trijyā*) measured by eight hundred and eighty-three *vedaroma* (403), since a multiplier and a divisor have been produced, how is it understood that the preceding and succeeding sines corresponding to one's own radius are established through the method described—using the sine of the arc and the sine of the complement (*koṭijyā*) associated with another radius? This is because of the lack of such reasoning. To dispel this ignorance, he provides the answer: "The first sine, [measured] by the parts of the arc... etc.

Now, regarding the first [set] of parts belonging to the greater half of the bow, one part is used for the calculation of the ninety-arched [bow], while four minus a quarter (3¾) are used for the calculation of the twenty-four arches; this is the method for determining the individual chord-parts, where "prati" refers to the portion of the interval between the chords.

Within three signs (*tribhama*), however many sines (*jyā*) are assumed, by that number ninety degrees are multiplied; the calculation of the sine for the interval between them—equal to that result—is to be performed according to the method and procedure previously established for the form of the arc-sine (*bhujajyā*). By that means, whatever the measure of their sine becomes, so it is here. In the present case, for the calculation of ninety degrees, by taking the cosine-sine (*koṭijyā*) as 872 (two *liptās* less than nine hundred), the sine of the complement (*āpateisumā*) is sixty, derived from the rule "multiplied by ten" and so forth.

In the *Caturviṃśati-sādhana*, it is stated that the measure of the sine of the radius (*trijyā*) is twenty-four. By taking this *trijyā*, according to the rule beginning with "kahijīva śaṃbhyasta" (multiplied by 120 and divided by 3438), or alternatively by the rule "saptāṃśanatatsvāśvimati," one arrives at the value. Here, one should note that the reading "atibhāśajyavidheḥ" is equivalent to "vedasādharo. That is the first sine (*prathamajyā*). It is then converted to the desired radius. This first sine, multiplied by eight hundred and sixty-four (*gajarāmayuga*), becomes the desired *trijyā*; thus, its conversion is performed by means of the continued proportion (*anupātana*).

The meaning is that the first sine (prathamajyā) is obtained by means of the measure of the desired radius (iṣṭatrijyā). In this very manner, by taking the sine of the arc corresponding to the stated radius, one should proceed—either by the method beginning with "one-sixth of the [arc] in the quarters of the sky" or by the method beginning with "one's own day and night"—according to the sequence of the twenty-four sines, so that the *koṭijyā* (sine of the complement) of the first sine becomes the *ṭijyā*. Then, by the measure of the desired radius, the difference between the first sine-value and the *ṭijyā* is obtained; and by means of the two *koṭijyās*, the third sine is determined according to what was stated in the passage beginning with "the two sines of the two desired [arcs]."

By means of the successive application (*bhāvanā*) of the third and first [sines] to the fourth, the sines of the subsequent [arcs], starting from the second, become increasingly refined; that is to say, they become precise (*sphuṭāḥ*) and subtle (*sūkṣmāḥ*) when the desired sine is sought. Here, one should note that between the two readings—*evaṃ kāryaḥ* and *visargānto bhāvanābhiḥ*—the former is the more appropriate.

And thus, since even the dull-witted recognize that the method for calculating sines according to the desired radius—derived from the method produced in accordance with the radius of three (3) and constructed from the pair of eight (8) and one (1)—is logically sound, it follows that the sines produced by the previous radius are established through reduction as before. Therefore, the conclusion is that the attainment of the previous sine-values from the sine of the arm and the sine of the perpendicular according to the desired radius is established by the evidence of direct perception, just as in the previous method.

Nor should it be said that because the half-chord (*ardhajyā*) is necessary here, the complete chord (*sampūrṇajyā*)—which would be established by that method—is not mentioned as being useless for this context; for the half-chord is established by the reading *caturdhenā* (instead of *ddinidhanā*) in the verse *caturdhenā*. To this he says: "It is approximate" (*sthūlam*). This method of calculating the chord, which was stated by me, Bhāskara Ācārya, in the chapter on *pāṭīgaṇita* (arithmetic) under the rule beginning with "the circumference multiplied by the arc," etc., was not stated by me in this context of explaining the origin of chords (*jyotpatti*).

Regarding this, he states the reason: "gross" (*sthūla*). The meaning is that at the stage of the calculation of the *taraṇya* (the sine of the ascensional difference), the section on planetary mathematics was disregarded because it was considered useless due to the fear of errors in the calculation of the planets' conjunctions. For example, for the purpose of calculating the sine of half a sign, one takes 5,400 seconds; these are multiplied by the minutes of arc of the circumference (16,200), resulting first in 87,480,000, which is subsequently divided by the fourth part of the square of the radius.

The first [divisor] is 583,200,000; subtracting 87,480,000 from this, the resulting divisor is 495,720,000. In the *Līlāvatī*, in the section on the calculation of areas (*kṣetravyavahāra*), verse 210, the value is 212; 5/64. In the chapter on the sphere (*golādhyāya*), verse 79, the numerator is multiplied by 13,752 and divided by the first divisor, 190,302,497,060; the result is the sine of the semi-quadrant, established as 2,527. However, the precise sine of the semi-quadrant is known to be 2,526. This is evident from the fact that those who recite the [sine] values at the beginning state "the sine of the semi-quadrant is 2,526," and because there is a great discrepancy [otherwise].

Now, for the purpose of understanding grossness through approximation, its proof is as follows: In a circle, when the desired arc is complete, the full chord is the base (*bhuja*), the diameter passing through it is the hypotenuse (*karṇa*), and the square root of the difference between their squares is the perpendicular (*koṭi*). This is directly perceived as the distance from the tips of the base and hypotenuse to the point where they meet the circumference. Since the desired chord is unknown there, its value is determined by the square root of the difference between the squares of the perpendicular and the hypotenuse.

Even there, due to the ignorance of the corner (*koṭi*), although it is impossible [to perceive it as such], that very part which is situated within the interior by connection with the lines of the corner is conceived as a "corner" (*koṣṭhi*) because of its grossness, even though it lacks the actual form of a corner.

By means of the relationship between the hypotenuse and the *vyāsa* (diameter) line, a hypotenuse is assumed for the sake of the circumference even in the absence of its actual side; however, the square root of the difference of their squares—which takes the form of a specific addition related to the entry of the *cāpa* (arc) associated with the desired sine—is not established as the desired sine because the hypotenuse and perpendicular would then be unreal. Furthermore, since the figure is not perceived from the circumference, the perpendicular, and the hypotenuse, the measure of the desired arc is not established; otherwise, they would merely be parts of the arrow (*iṣu*) arc.

In that case, since another arc is equal to a hundred other arcs, the product of the difference of the parts of the *koṭi* (sine) and the *karṇa* (hypotenuse) should be calculated. Here, the *koṭi* is for the purpose of the arc of the complement (*cāpona-paridhi*), and the *karṇa* is for the purpose of the circumference (*paridhi*). The sum or difference of these two is the circumference; the difference is the desired arc itself. From these two, the arc subtracted from the circumference is the first term, called the "snake" (*bhujaga*). This is stated above for the purpose of finding the sine of the arc.

The chord for half the circumference (*vyāsajyā*) is then [calculated] by the proportion "what is the chord for this [half]? This is a proportion based on the desired arc; it is accepted as subtle because, even though it is approximate, there is no visible reason for the proportionality [to fail]. Here, since the arm (*bhuja*) is understood through its first designation as being of the nature of a square (*varṇarūpa*), the square of the arm—which is of the nature of half the circumference—is the *isa*. In that regard, the square of half the circumference is one-fourth of the square of the full circumference.

In this regard, the result obtained from the divisor and dividend when they are in their original state is the same as that obtained when they are multiplied by a desired factor. Thus, the divisor becomes four times the square of the *parigha*. Since the subtraction [of the square] from the divisor is necessary for the calculation of the area (*rājya*), the diameter is multiplied by the first term which has been quadrupled; hence it is said: "the first term multiplied by four and the diameter."

In this context, although the square of the result of the multiplication by Vyāsa (the circumference) is required—and even though for its calculation the square itself must necessarily be established—nevertheless, because the square root is not taken (to avoid complexity), and because the square is not explicitly stated, there is a possibility of inaccuracy in both cases. Thus, by the aforementioned reasoning, the sine of one-sixth of the circumference (*bṛhat-ṣaḍbhāga-jyā*) as stated in the method involving the value 1½ does not hold; it does not prove to be more than a ninth part. To demonstrate: this is one-sixtieth of the circumference; subtracted by this [value]...

The circumference is one-sixth of the circumference multiplied by five; when this is multiplied by another sixth part of the circumference, it becomes the thirty-sixth part of the first [circumference] multiplied by five, namely 5/36. This, when multiplied by the diameter (vyāsa) divided by four, results in the cancellation of two equal terms of the square of the circumference; thus, the diameter multiplied by four is to be multiplied by five and divided by thirty-six. Consequently, it is established that the diameter is multiplied by twenty and divided by thirty-six.

Now, regarding the *autpattivāsanā* (intrinsic derivation): here too, since the diameter (*vyāsa*) consists of twice the square root of the area, the square root of the diameter is 40 for a Brahmin and 38 for a Kṣatriya. When dividing by the multiplier, one obtains 10 and 9 after reducing by four. Thus, it is established that [the result] arises increased by its own ninth part. Therefore, for the sake of resolving doubt there, the divisor is reduced by its own part.

In that case, the portion remains unmodified; however, when the process is reversed (*viloma*), it has been stated that the remainder is as previously described. Thus, the result obtained for the sign (*pharka*) must be diminished by its own tenth part. Even there, for the sake of brevity (*lāghava*), although the result is equivalent when the tenth part is subtracted from the kingdom (*rājya*), the divisor itself is made the ninth-part base (*navāṃśādhi*) for the sake of simplicity. This is because the divisor is the reverse [of the dividend], and since a deficiency in the result is possible through an excess in the divisor. Although the sine of the sixth part (*ṣaḍbhāgajyā*) is established by the aforementioned method, the chord equal to the diameter—which is derived from the arc of half the circumference—is not established.

For instance, since the divisor here consists of the fourth part of the square of the circumference (*paridhi*), the divisor has been made nine parts greater by means of the square of the circumference. Thus, when the square of the circumference increased by its own quarter is divided by itself, the result is precisely one-fourth of the square of the circumference, namely 5.

This [value] was reduced by this first term, which is one-sixth of the circumference (paridhi), namely 5/36, through common denominators; thus the square of the circumference became four times multiplied and divided by thirty-six. Therein, the multiplier and divisor were reduced by four, resulting in the multiplier and divisor for the square of the circumference being nine and ten respectively. By that aforementioned method, it was increased by nine parts.

However, in the case of a circumference of one and a half *dhanus*, since the square of the first radius (*paridhi*) constitutes a quarter of the square of the circumference, when that is multiplied by five, it becomes equal to the square of the circumference; thus, according to the method described, the subtle sine is established from the quotient of the square of the circumference and its square root. But as for the other sines, because they lack their own respective divisors, they are merely gross, being accumulated by taking the divisor [of the first] due to the simplicity [of the calculation]. This is because there is no single uniform method applicable to each of their respective divisors.

Because it would be cumbersome to state each of those separately, the reading provided is [as follows]: the coarseness of the sine (jyā) value is indeed evident; enough with further elaboration. Now, having promised [to explain it], he concludes the derivation of the sine (jyotpatti) with a brief statement (*phakkikā*) in order to satisfy the curiosity regarding the considerations of the sine: "Thus ends the derivation of the sine. This is clear. This faultless derivation of the sine was composed by Bhāskarācārya.

This [commentary] has been elucidated by Bhūnīśvara through the grace of his preceptor Rāma. (1) Now, he states the reason for clarifying the result: "Since the center of the terrestrial circle is indeed the center of the earth, and since the celestial body revolves in that circle but its center is not at the center of the earth; and since an observer standing on the earth does not perceive the center of the terrestrial circle as being equidistant from all points, therefore the correction for the arc of the latitude (dṛkkarma) is applied here to the mean planet. (7)

This [celestial sphere] situated within the shell of the earth consists of the asterisms beginning with Aśvinī, which revolve at equal intervals on all sides around the smoke (the atmosphere). Since its center is at the center of the earth, whereas the center of the orbit in which the day revolves is not at the center of the earth—meaning it does not maintain equal intervals from the smoke on all sides—an observer standing on the earth does not see the planet in its central position within the circle of the sky; rather, he sees it elsewhere.

The difference between those two [mean] positions is the result for the planet in its true place; this is what is meant by implication. Therefore it is said: "The wise calculate the result here from the mean planet. (Verse 7) Maṇiprabhā Commentary: Now, first, the author states the *phalavasanī* (the correction for the equation of center), which is intended to establish the true motion that serves as the answer to the question beginning with "saṃsiddham āditya... (The established [longitude] of the Sun, etc.). He expresses its brevity—which indicates the connection for explaining the meaning to be stated—through the *mandākrāntā* meter, beginning with "bhūmeḥ" (From the Earth...). For that reason, "here" (iha).

Now, that which is established following the *ahargaṇa* (the accumulation of days) within the house [of the planet] should be understood by those who know the distinction between the mean and the true [motions], as stated by the ancient teachers in the chapter on True Planets (*spaṣṭādhikāra*). The results derived from the center and the arm are the slow (*manda*) and the swift (*śīghra*) equations; the meaning is that they are "performed" or "corrected" through both direct and indirect relations. He states the reason for this: "situated on the earth," and so forth.

For this reason, O dweller on earth, an observer situated within the earth would not perceive the position of the planetary orb as being equal to the planet's mean longitude—following the ecliptic (krāntivṛtta) in the manner to be described—which is equal to the mean motion of the planet, within the circle of the zodiac. This is the meaning.

On the ecliptic, starting from the position of Revatī, Aries is marked with twelve signs, degrees, minutes, and seconds. Then, by means of proportion (anupāta) using the elapsed days of the sacrifice, one calculates the longitude of the planet's node (siṅga). At that time, the planet's disk is not seen on its orbit at the point on the ecliptic that lies on the same diameter as the position of Revatī. And where the planet's disk is seen, the point on the ecliptic lying on that same diameter is the previous mark of the planet; at that point, the planet's disk is not seen on its orbit by means of that same diameter.

And where one observes the planetary disc, the corresponding point on the ecliptic lies along that same diameter to the east of the previous planetary mark. The distance between those two points is the correction (*phala*); when this is applied—either added or subtracted—to the planet's position as established by the previous calculation, it becomes the true planetary position. Its "true" nature (*spaṣṭatva*) arises from the fact that the planetary disc is seen along that diameter.

For this very reason, since the planets are not observed at the point on the meridian line that coincides with the mark of the previous [calculation], it is established by the proportion of the *ahargaṇa* (accumulated days) that the day-measure is not precise; thus, it is not established by the means of direct perception (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*). Here too, he states the cause: "of the earth" (*bhūmeḥ*). Because of which cause: in the center of the earth, that is, at the central point of the terrestrial globe, the center of the celestial sphere (*bhavalaya*)—which resides within the sphere of the stellar cage—is indeed, with certainty, the center due to its connection with that [earthly] unity.

The meaning is that the center of the spheres of the planets and asterisms—which follow their respective orbits in the sky along with the belt of the constellations (apiśaṃydanakṣatramālā) and move in non-linear revolutions—is at the center of the Earth (bhūgarbha). The planet moves in a certain sphere (vṛtta) by its eastern motion and completes the revolution of the zodiacal signs (bhagaṇabhoga); the center of this sphere would not be at the center of the Earth (bhūgolagarbha).

And likewise, because the constellations (nakṣatras) are always seen with a single form, the stellar sphere (nakṣatragola) exists at an equal distance [from the Earth]; thus the ecliptic (krāntivṛtta) also exists in that same manner. However, because the orbs of the planets (grahabimba) are not seen as having a single form, and since their appearance as small or large orbs would otherwise be inexplicable, the circle occupied by the planetary orbs is postulated—by virtue of parsimony—as being distinct from the orbital path (kakṣāvṛtta). Therefore, it does not exist at an equal distance from the terrestrial globe; rather, it is determined by a line parallel to the equator and intersecting the Aries point of the ecliptic.

Since the motion established by [the theory of] the Earth's rotation would not account for the positions of the Sun and other planets, it is stated that—given the astronomical principle that the Earth is at the center—it is logical that the observation of a planet’s true position occurs along a line passing through the central mark of the planet situated on the ecliptic-following sphere, as determined by the proportionality of the days and nights (ajhargaṇa).

When a planet's orb is observed along a line coinciding with its orbital path (kakṣā), the longitude of the sign such as Aries and so forth at that point on the orbit is the true longitude of the planet; the difference between the mean and the true positions of the planet is the equation of center (phala), which is applied as an addition or subtraction to the mean planet for the purpose of determining the true planet—this is the practical meaning. || 7 || End of the Chapter on Geometrical Construction (Chedyakādhyāya). || 167 || Now, having thus briefly explained the entire Chedyaka [instrument] by means of a single example, he speaks a little more in detail for the sake of instructing his students.

Having drawn a diagram (*chedyaka*) for the purpose of instructing the disciple, the wise one demonstrates the north-south and east-west lines; thus the disciples said, "The [celestial] signs are correctly known. To this, the Teacher said: "The [lines] extending from east to west are the signs, and so forth," for the sake of the eightfold [knowledge]. [Commentary: By this method of calculating results, the basis for deriving the results is established. This is because the true nature of the sine of the argument (bhuja) and the sine of the co-latitude (koṭi) at the elevated center is understood.

Furthermore, how is the knowledge of the result possible, and why is the knowledge of its contrary impossible? Because there is an absence of knowledge regarding the middle of a wheel whose motion is established—just as the spokes of a wheel moving through the sky are at a great distance from the observer—it is difficult for human eyes to perceive the division of its parts. Therefore, the author says "pūrvāpara" (east and west) and so forth. [This refers to] the wise mathematician who understands the essence of the calculation.

By the word *sudhīḥ* (the wise one), it is indicated that just as there is the attainment of that [result] for Siṃdhya, so too must various methods be devised for the sake of supreme knowledge. In the phrase "extending from east to west," *pūrvāparaṃ daidhyai* means length from east to west; *ayātayā* means on the northern side. This means it is situated in the north. Otherwise, it would be impossible for the northern side of the [line] existing from east to west to be occupied by the two [sides].

The *chedyaka* (diagrammatic cutting) follows the method of the ancient teachers and consists of a geometric construction (*parilekha*) for the purpose of establishing the clear proof (*spaṣṭīyopapatti*) that is about to be explained; having drawn it according to the aforementioned procedure—which is designated by the term *chedyaka*—one should demonstrate the nature of the daily [mean] motion and so forth, which is the result of the sines of the anomaly and the equation of the center, for the sake of attaining a clear understanding of the meaning of this chapter.

And likewise, although it is easy to ascertain that [the earth] is not situated in space—because of its extreme distance and because there is no perception of its divisions even by the eyes—the nature of that inference remains unestablished due to the absence of a supporting example (*dṛṣṭānta*). Thus, there is no fault. Here, the rotation of the planets around the earth is not perceived as established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); therefore, their observation is based on tradition (*smṛti*).

In that case as well, when marking the points situated in the eastern and western directions, it is stated "from east to west" for the purpose of demonstrating the observation and non-observation of the revolution of the sun from east to west. Furthermore, when marking the points situated in the southern direction on the diagram, the marking of Aries and the other signs proceeds counter-clockwise (apasavyena) for the sake of perceiving the observation of the revolution from east to west; whereas when marking those situated in the northern direction, the marking of Aries and the other signs proceeds clockwise (savyena), and thus it is stated "starting from the north."

This is because writing the syllables in the order of the right-hand sequence (savyakrama) is approved by the learned as being in parts; otherwise, it should be understood that writing the letters and so forth according to that [other] sequence would be contradicted. || 8 || Now, having realized that we are intent on deceiving them through our cleverness, the disciples questioned him again, whereupon he said: "Even though this knowledge has been brought down to the level of the ignorant by the likes of Niya and others due to their lack of capacity for its weight, it must nevertheless be revealed."

9. This [instruction] is not intended for those who delight in crookedness; it would lead to the destruction of life and merit for those wicked people who dwell in evil conduct and abandon this boundary established by the sages. (9) Ma0 Ḍī0: Now, how is the establishment of the example of the "cuttable form" (chedyakara-rūpa) to be understood as residing in space? For the nature of an object situated in space...

Since that [knowledge] is not established because it is not within the range of human vision, he provides the answer in the Śārdūlavikrīḍita meter: "Divya... (Divine...). The meaning is that what was stated as "showing" is that which is to be cut away [from doubt]. Knowledge is that which establishes the existence of objects situated in space; it is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), transcending the senses, and is not an object for the ears, eyes, speech, or mind of humans.

The meaning is as follows: since it was created by Brahmā, and because it is necessarily required for Brahmā himself to have direct perception of the existence of the great ether (mahākāśa) he created, this [astronomical treatise] was composed by him in accordance with his own direct perception, for the sake of conveying knowledge regarding the positions of the planets and the cutting lines (chedyaka), so that other people might understand them. For this very reason, it is "divine" (divya), having as its sole domain the heavenly world (svargaloka).

Because Brahmā is present there. Now, since humans do not go to the heavenly world, how is this known? To this he says: "By the sages. This means by Vasiṣṭha, Māṇḍavya, Romaśa, Śākalya, Nārada, and others—sages who, through the power of their own penance, are capable of granting grace whenever they wish—and by virtue of tradition; that is, through the connection with a succession of mutual reports as was appropriate.

The meaning here is that "the earth" (*avanīm*) refers to a specific region of the ground presided over by us and others; it has been "brought" (*nītam*), which means it has become the object of the drawing. Otherwise, since the heavenly world (*svargaloka*) is a specific region of the earth and is already situated on the earth from the very beginning, the expression "brought to the earth" (*avanīm nītam*) would be untenable. Furthermore, because Vasiṣṭha is the son of Brahmā, through him Maṇḍavya obtained knowledge of that [region]; and by extension, other sages also obtained knowledge of it—this is the sense of the remainder [of the verse]. The implication is that it has come here because it serves as the locus for traveling to all the subterranean realms (*bhūgala*).

[Objection: Even so, does this not establish its divine nature? To this he says: "It is a secret" (*rahasyam*). [This is] the commentary. And thus, precisely because of its divine nature, its concealment is established as even more [necessary]; otherwise, if it were not concealed, its divine nature would be compromised, as there would be no distinction [between it and ordinary things]. [Objection: If this is to be concealed, why was it previously stated that "one should show it for the sake of the disciple's understanding"? To this he says: "It is to be revealed" (*prakāśyam*). The meaning is that it is to be revealed only after that [period], because of its secret nature. This refers to the *chedyaka* (diagram) which is about to be described.

For those who dwell in the vicinity of wicked people of evil conduct created by fate, there is enmity; one who is an enemy of oneself, or one for whom one is oneself an enemy, or mutual enmity—this is what constitutes "devī" (enmity).

One who, even when there is no benefit received from us, thinks "the favor done [to me] has been lost," is ungrateful (*kṛtaghna*). One who lacks even that quality is wicked (*durjana*), meaning one who desires harm toward others without any specific cause. One who lacks even that is of evil conduct (*durācāra*), characterized by the practice of forbidden acts prescribed by the *Smṛtis* and the failure to perform the injunctions of the *Smṛtis*. Furthermore, one with whom those residing for only a short time in this world have a long-lasting association—this [type of person], it should be understood, is not a factor [for fear] once there is certainty regarding the absence of the previously mentioned enemies, such as the hateful (*dveṣya*) and so forth.

The meaning is that this [knowledge] should not be revealed or spoken to those who are qualified to study these [works]. Accordingly, it is said in the *Sūryasiddhānta*: "This is to be kept secret; it should be accessible here through the sacrificial session (*satra*); this is the secret of the gods and must not be given to just anyone. This supreme knowledge should be imparted to a well-tested disciple. Based on these two statements, it is logical as previously stated that one should show [this work] only by way of concealment to those other than those specified.

Chapter on Cutting (Chedyaka-adhikāra), 169. Ma0ḍī0: This [knowledge] should be given to a disciple who is devoted, long-resident [in the tradition], and endowed with virtues; and to a brother, a friend, and a son—it is very difficult to obtain from the gola-section of the Chedyaka. This is the sense, based on the statement in the Siddhāntaśekhara. Now, one might object: "What merit is there in being good toward those who have helped? He who is good toward those who do harm is called 'good' by the wise. Since it has been stated thus, [one might think] it should be given even to those who are hateful and so forth. To this, he says: "It may be... (syāt).

For a Brahmin who abandons or forsakes this aforementioned boundary—the limit beginning with "one must not cross beyond this"—there occurs a depletion of his lifespan and merit (*sukṛta*). Here, "lifespan" (*āyus*) refers to that which is conditioned by time as understood through its connection to the state of being embodied (*śarīrabhāva*). "Merit" (*sukṛta*) refers to the religious virtue acquired by oneself, whether pertaining to this life or earned in previous births; the destruction of these two occurs [by violating the rule]. Now, one might object: "The depletion of lifespan and merit may indeed result from transgressing the boundary you have described; otherwise, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of the rule. To this, he says: "Established by the Sage" (*munikṛtam*). This means it was composed by the sage Vasiṣṭha.

And thus, there is no harm. Nor should it be argued that there is a contradiction with the Śruti regarding the exhaustion of life and merit, because the Śruti states that knowledge is powerless and thus cannot say "stay" to me; for according to the rule that whoever inflicts suffering upon another desires that person's misfortune or destruction, this was stated by the seers precisely as an implication of the Śruti’s meaning.

One might argue that since the very actions that initiate the body are *prārabdha-karma* (actions whose results have already begun), and since these are destroyed only by experience (*bhoga*), the time required for the experience of all of them constitutes "the exhaustion of merit" (*sukṛtakṣaya*). Thus, the phrase "exhaustion of the merit acquired during one's lifespan" would mean nothing contradictory. However, this cannot be maintained, because [the exhaustion of merit] occurs through various causes such as: being pierced by a poisoned arrow, being struck by lightning, being killed by a tiger, being slain by an executioner, being bitten by a snake, being killed by a wicked person, or being killed by a thief.

If it is argued that this is not so because it contradicts the statement by Śrīpati: "For one who gives away the immeasurable secret of the Tantra here, there would be the destruction of a multitude of merits," we say no. For since *āyus* (life-span) is of the nature of a mental construct (*dṛṣṭarūpa*), its destruction is logically possible; indeed, that disease is accepted as occurring precisely through the contraction of time. Furthermore, although the duration of enjoyment of Indra’s station is fixed, we hear in the Purāṇas and other texts that Nahuṣa fell from Indra’s station immediately due to a curse.

For this very reason, the statement of Yājñavalkya—that "there is nothing so detrimental to longevity as consorting with another's wife"—is consistent; otherwise, the treatise on ethics (nītiśāstra) would fall into futility. This is the summary. || 9 || Now, having described the drawing [of the diagram], he states the procedure for cutting it out: "First, having drawn the circle called the 'equator' (kakṣāvṛtta) with a pair of compasses set to the measure of the oblique ascension (tribhajyakā), one should draw from its center a perfect circle for the earth with a radius equal to the number of degrees of lunar days (tithyaṃśa) occupied by the middle planet. || 10 ||

On this circle called the *kakṣāvṛtta* (orbital circle), which is marked with the zodiacal signs (*bhagaṇa*), one should place the exaltation point (*ucca*) and the planet (*kheṭa*). Then, a line should be drawn from the center of the earth (*kumadhya*) passing through the exaltation point; another line should be drawn by the wise man horizontally from the center of the earth. Having placed the sine of the other [equation of] centering (*anyaphalajyā*) with its face upward along that vertical line, one should draw from the center of the earth to its tip using the radius (*tribhajyā*) itself; this is the so-called *pratimaṇḍala* (epicycle). That same horizontal line here is the other line, the *tiryak* (transverse) line. Indeed, where the vertical line (*dhruvarekhā*) meets the exaltation point, there is the exaltation point on that epicycle as well.

Then, conversely, by the degrees of exaltation (tuṅga), the planet moves from Aries and the mountain (seven signs) in direct order; this is the anomaly of exaltation (*uccāntara*). Here, the center (*kendra*) is between the planet and its exaltation line. The sine (*bāhu*) is the distance along the horizontal line, while the cosine (*koṭi*) is the vertical distance from that horizontal line. Having drawn a northward path on the wall, one should know the circle there with a compass set to the measure of the radius (*trijyā*); that is the circle of the exaltation.

For whichever planet one intends to construct the *chedyaka* (diagram), that point on the same [prime] vertical circle which is increased by the degrees of its mean daily motion is taken as the "Earth" (*bhū*). This Earth is for the purpose of observing parallax and declination; otherwise, the point itself is assumed to be the Earth. The orbit-circle (*kakṣāvṛtta*) is to be drawn with the appropriate radius. Therein, having established Aries and the other signs starting from the position of the Earth, one should place the mean planet and its apogee from that point and mark their respective locations. Lines should be drawn passing through the Earth and the apogee.

The apse-line (separekhā). Now, another transverse line should be drawn through the center of the earth by means of the fish-figure produced from the apse-line. Then, having fixed a cord equal in length to the radius of the planet's other [auxiliary] circle upon the apse-line at the center of the earth, the circle that is traced out with a compass set to that same measure is the epicycle (pratimaṇḍala). There too, that same apse-line is the diameter; another transverse line should be drawn through its center. The epicycle should also be marked with degrees.

Now, the apogee (*ucca*) is to be conceived as being at every point of the eccentric circle (*pratimaṇḍala*) where it is led along the line of apogee (*uccarekhā*). Therefore, having counted the signs and degrees of the apogee backward from that point, Aries and so forth are established there. From that, the planet is to be added in the direct order (*anuloma*). There, the difference between the planet and the apogee is the *kendra* (argument). The line drawn perpendicularly from the line of apogee toward the planet is the sine (*dojyā*). The perpendicular line within the center of the eccentric circle is the cosine (*koṭijyā*). That [cosine] takes the form of the minutes of arc (*kalā*). ||10||11||12||13||14||

Bhaṭṭotpala’s Commentary (Bhaṭṭotpala-vivaraṇa): Now, regarding the description of the method for drawing [the diagram], he first states two verses in the Upajāti meter beginning with "tribhajyakoṭi. Having heard that the distance between the tips of the two crab-shaped rods (karkaṭaka-śalākā) is the radius (trijyā), one should first draw a circle representing the orbit (kakṣā) starting from the position of the desired point. Then, from the center of that circle, one should draw another perfect circle called the "Earth" (mahī), having a diameter equal to fifteen times the minutes of arc of the mean motion of the planet.

Since the orbit-circle is situated at a distance from the center of the earth equal to the radius of the trijyā (trijyā = 3438'), it is separated from the circle on the surface of the celestial sphere by the same distance as the semi-diameter of the earth in yojanas. Furthermore, because the yojanas of the earth's semi-diameter are approximately equal to one-fifteenth part of the planet's motion in yojanas, [the circumference of the earth] is correctly determined by one-fifteenth part of the mean motion in minutes (kalās). This is due to the association with the term "minutes" (kalā). However, if one were to calculate the semi-diameter in yojanas and draw the direction of the orbit-circle, it would not be appropriate to draw the circle of the earth using only the two semi-diameters of the earth.

It should be understood that the drawing of the *bhūvusa* (the ground-line) and the *likhana* (the marking) is for the purpose of demonstrating the underlying rationale (*apapatti*). Now, in order to explain the determination of the diameter of the circle and the arrangement of its parts for the sake of knowing the four equal divisions of the circle, the author states the following in the *Upajāti* meter, beginning with "kakṣākhye": "Next, by the wise mathematician, having drawn the circle here, and having added the square root of the product of the [two] sides brought from the section on the hypotenuse, one should subtract that from the diameter. This means: subsequently, the intelligent calculator, having inscribed the circle here, should add the square root of the product of the two sides—which was derived in the chapter on the hypotenuse—to the diameter, and then subtract that [result] from the diameter.

A line should be drawn; this [line] is the circle of the orbit situated in space between the two numerical positions. The giving of all [the degrees] in the numerical positions is useless here, and thus there is a cover for the orbit situated in space. By saying "here," the context is the chapter on the Earth. (3.71) Bhāṣya-Ṭīkā: It is stated "orbit-support" (*kakṣādhṛ*) in order to prevent the application of those [degrees] to the circle. Now, one might object that it is impossible to give the houses and signs on the circle because their positions are unknown; therefore, he says: "marked with zodiacal signs" (*bhagaṇāṅkitā*). This means marked with equal intervals by the minutes and seconds of the sixty parts of the twelve zodiacal signs.

And thus, when that circle is drawn, there is no loss of the knowledge of the positions of the signs, houses, and nodes (pāta) at the desired location. Now, one might object: "Even so, because of the restriction to a specific location on the earth's surface, it is impossible to calculate the zodiacal revolution (bhagaṇa), and therefore there would be an absence of knowledge regarding those positions. To this he says: "It is done" (kriyate). The meaning is as follows: on that circle, by counting the signs starting from Aries counter-clockwise (asavyena) from the desired location, and then counting the high house (ucca) and the planet (graha) clockwise (savyakrameṇa) starting from the position of Aries, the knowledge of their respective positions is indeed attained.

Now, as to how the circle (vṛtta) should be constructed once the point has been established, he says: *kumadhyatuṅgopari-gati*. This means: that which has its center at the center of the circle (*ku*) and which goes above the apogee (*tuṅga*). Having made a mark six signs away from the position of the highest point (*ucca*), one should draw a straight line starting from that point up to the position of the apogee; the meaning is that this line should pass through the point situated in the middle of the diameter of the circle. In such a circle whose center is at the center of the asterism-circle (*ṛkṣavṛtta*), another second line should be drawn perpendicular to the line of the apogee.

By the phrase "by the wise" (sudhibhiḥ), it is indicated that from the point of maximum altitude (uccasthāna), [the lines] should extend nine degrees in both directions to reach the corresponding points on the line. Now, one might ask: why were the four parts of the circle measured from the point of maximum altitude, while the distance from the position of the planet was not measured? To this, the author provides an answer under the guise of explaining the drawing of the counter-epicycle (pratimaṇḍala) and so forth: "Toward the face of the apogee" (ucconmukhīm). This means that from the center of the earth (ku), which is the central point of the celestial sphere (kuvṛtta) in the form of a dot, one should proceed.

Although its center is covered by that [circle], it should nevertheless be understood that it was not mentioned separately due to proximity and for the sake of brevity. "Facing the higher position" means facing the point of maximum altitude. "The other sine of the equation" (anyaphalajyā) refers to the maximum sine of the equation (paramaphalajyā), which is the sine of the arc resulting from the correction (bhujaphala) derived from the trijyā (radius) determined in the *Sphuṭādhyāya* (Chapter on True Motion). At the tip of that [sine], one should draw the epicycle (pratimaṇḍala) using the trijyā as the radius, starting from a mark representing a portion equal in measure to that other sine of the equation.

By the word "eva" (only/itself), it is indicated that one should draw the *kakṣāvṛtta* (the orbital circle) with half the diameter of the [main] circle, and the *pratimaṇḍala* (the epicycle) with half the diameter of that same measure, using names corresponding to their actual meanings. However, even though the radius-vectors (*jyā*) for the planets are equal in length to the respective diameters of their orbits, there is a distinction between the orbital circles and the epicycles due to the difference in the measurement of the degrees (*kalā*); this is what is being pointed out. Now, he states "saiva" (that very same) in order to know the four equal divisions of this circle: here, in the *pratimaṇḍala*, the vertical line is that which touches the point of the apogee (*ucca*) on the *kā-vṛtta*.

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that [the radius] extends from the periphery of the epicycle up to the point of maximum altitude (ucca), and that its value is the portion of the epicycle up to that point? To this he says: "sva" (its own). The word "tu" (but) indicates a distinction. By this, the meaning is that the *udhrasā* (radius vector) must be increased along a straight path from the point of maximum altitude up to the limit of the epicycle's portion; thus, the matter is indeed consistent. This is the intended sense.

The meaning is as follows: from the two portions of the upward line connected to the lower [line] of the secondary circle (*pratimaṇḍala*), one should draw the lines for the head and tail of the fish-marks (*matsya*) so that they are attached to the marks in the form of the center of the respective circles and extend up to the portion of the circumference of the secondary circle. By the use of the particle *eva* (only), it is meant that the horizontal line in the secondary circle does not become a vertical line situated on the circle like the vertical line [of the primary circle], because that line lacks the property of being situated at the center of the secondary circle.

And likewise, the intention is that equal fourth-parts of the epicycle were not made starting from the position of the planet due to a lack of necessity. || 12 || 144 [End of] the Chapter on Spheres (Gaulādhyāya).

Now, desiring to clarify the purpose of the eccentric circle (*pratimaṇḍala*), [the author] first explains the nature of the radius and the perpendicular from the center by means of two verses beginning with "suṅgodhrvarekhā. In this drawn eccentric circle, there is a line segment representing the portion of a line extending from the position of the apogee (*ucca*) within the circular orbit (*kaāvṛtta*). Where it touches a portion of the circumference of this eccentric circle—at that point on the circumference of the eccentric circle—[the perpendicular is established].

The word "uccam" (the apogee) must indeed be placed at the highest point; the word "api" (also/even) has the sense of conjunction, meaning that the apogee-mark should be made at the highest point on the *kakṣāvṛtta* (orbital circle), and not in one place [only]. This is because, for the purpose of knowing the position of the apogee in the *pratimaṇḍala* (eccentric circle), it is necessary to know the position of the apogee's motion on the *kakṣāvṛtta*; therefore, the meaning is that the apogee is not truly located there [on the eccentric circle]. From that, [it is measured] from the position of the apogee in the *pratimaṇḍala*.

The meaning is: by those fractional degrees which result from the calculation of the elapsed portion of the [ascendant] signs and so forth, expressed in degrees; "in reverse" (*viloma*) means in the opposite direction from the path of Aries and the other signs situated on the ecliptic, that is, in a counter-clockwise manner—this is the intended sense. By measuring the degrees situated on the ecliptic, one must certainly (*khalu*) mark the point for Aries and the others upon the counter-ecliptic (*prativṛtta*) according to the calculation at that specific location.

The meaning is as follows: since the true longitude of the apogee starting from Aries has been established through calculation, just as the mark of the apogee was made on the epicycle (kakṣāvṛtta) at a certain number of signs and degrees starting from Aries by means of the apogee's longitude, so too here, because the position of the apogee is known, the positions of Aries and the other signs are established by the reverse process from that [apogee]. From this mark of Aries and the others situated on the counter-epicycle (prativṛtta), the planet arrived at through calculation should be applied to the counter-epicycle—just as on the epicycle—in a direct manner, following the leftward path; that is, its apogee-correction (uccāntara) should be applied.

The interval between the point on the eccentric circle (prativṛtta) corresponding to the stationary planet and the point corresponding to the apogee is a portion of the circumference of that eccentric circle. Here, the center on the eccentric circle should be understood as being at a distance equal to the apogee. Therefore, even though there is a difference between the [mean] orbit (kakṣāvṛtta) and the apogee, it does not constitute the center. This indicates that the apogee and the planet are situated on their respective [circles].

The straight line forming half the chord, situated within the interval between the planet and the Moon—which both touch two points on the upper portion of the *uccarekhā* (line of apsis) at its two ends and reside on the *prativṛtta* (deferent)—is the *bhuja-jyā* (sine of the arm) within the *prativṛtta*. By the word "and" (*ca*), the meaning is that the small interval between the two planets—situated either side of a point six signs apart from the conjunction point on the *satribhāṃśa* (trine) portion of the *uccarekhā*—which takes the form of a segment of the *prativṛtta* circumference, is the arc; that is, it is the *bhuja* (arm).

The *koṭi* (perpendicular) refers to a straight line in the form of a semi-chord (*ardhajyā*) situated between the two points marking the planets located on the same portion of the *pratimaṇḍala* (counter-ecliptic), which itself lies within the intersection of the *tiryagrekhā* (horizontal diameter) and the *maṇḍala* (ecliptic). This is the meaning of "the sine of the perpendicular" (*koṭijyā*). Here, by the mention of the *koṭi*, it is stated that the *bhujajyā* (sine of the arc) and the *koṭijyā* possess the status of base (*bhuja*) and perpendicular (*koṭi*) respectively due to their relationship within a right-angled triangle; in this case, it should be understood that the *trijyā* (radius) serves as the hypotenuse (*karṇa*).

By the use of the word "ca" (and), it is observed that the distance between two planets situated on the same side of the ecliptic and located at different points on their respective epicycles is small; this [distance] is of the nature of a single segment. Its "arm" (*koṭi*) is the arc [of the epicycle]. Now, why are these names "bhuja" (arm) and "koṭi" (perpendicular) applied to the sines mentioned? Since the names could appropriately be applied even in reverse order, he says: "That" (*seti*). The sine of the half-arc is the line drawn obliquely between the tips of the planet's positions; the vertical line, however, is like the line of apogee (*tuṅgarekhā*). This is the "multiplier of the arm" (*bāhuguṇa*); that is, the sine of the arm as previously described.

The meaning is that it lies horizontally, like the sun situated in the middle of ghee. And so it is stated in the *Chedyakādhikāra* (Chapter on Geometrical Figures), verse 173: "That which is from the desired arm to another arm in the lateral direction, whether in a triangle or a quadrilateral, is celebrated as the *koṭi* (the perpendicular side). According to the definition provided in this passage, since it is accepted that all lines drawn to the earth (the base) constitute the *koṭi*, and since it is accepted that the horizontal line constitutes the *bhuja* (the base), the designation [of these sides] is correctly stated; such is the intended sense.

Since the hypotenuse is accepted as being along the line from the tip of the radius to the tip of the [hypotenuse] at the point of intersection of the arms of the angle, the square of the hypotenuse is obtained by multiplying the square of the radius by this [ratio]; therefore, the previously mentioned "radius plus that" and so forth is correct—this is the meaning. || 14 || Now, he states the derivation for the calculation of the equation of the center (*phala*) in a single step: "The two lines situated at the center are indeed those of the two circles; in the interval between them lies the equation of the center. This is the multiplier of the cosine (*koṭiguṇa*) in the case of Capricorn and so on, because it would be below that in the case of the apogee and so on. || 15 ||

Therefore, the difference between those two [distances] is here the *koṭi* (perpendicular); the distance is the *bhuja* (base), and the line resulting from the sum of their squares is the *karṇa* (hypotenuse). Indeed, the true planet is visible within the interval between the center of the earth and the planet situated on the *pratimaṇḍala* (epicycle). When the hypotenuse-line touches the circle called the *kakṣā* (orbit), the correction (*phala*) lies between the mean planet and the true planet. That correction is subtracted from the mean when the true planet is ahead [in the orbit], and added when it is behind; and from that [resulting position], [the true longitude is determined]. (16–17)

The distance between the two transverse axes situated midway between the two circles—the epicycle (*prativṛtta*) and the deferent (*kakṣāvṛtta*)—is equal everywhere to the equation of anomaly (*anyaphala*). Therefore, due to the addition of this equation of anomaly, the cosine-sine (*koṭijyā*) of the apsis-line (*pati-vṛtta*) occurs above [the center] when the apsidal anomaly is in Capricorn and so forth, while the two circles themselves are below it. Consequently, the sum or difference of the cosine-sine and the equation of anomaly is performed. When this is done, the true cosine-sine (*sphuṭa-koṭi*) results with respect to the transverse axis passing through the center of the deferent.

The square root of the sum of the squares of the *koṭi* (perpendicular) and the *taccapadhyaya* (the difference between the true and mean positions) is the *karṇa* (hypotenuse); this is the established rule. The *karṇa* is the line of distance between the center of the planet and its [true] position. The *taccapadhyaya* is where the planet is on the eccentric circle (*kakṣamaṇḍala*); there, the planet is true (*sphuṭa*). The difference between the true and the mean [positions] is the correction (*phala*). And that correction is added to the mean planet when the true planet is greater, and subtracted when it is less; thus the proof is established.

Thus, by means of the slow correction (manda-phala), the mean planet becomes the slow-apparent (manda-sphuṭa); by means of the fast correction (śīghra-phala), it becomes the true-apparent (sphuṭa). [Commentary]—Now, he describes the determination of the true planet, its correction, and its positive or negative nature through the ear (karṇa) using Upajāti verses, beginning with "madhyasthare. The two circles refer to the epicycle (kakṣā) and the eccentric circle (pratimaṇḍala). The term "madhyasthare" (locative dual) implies two transverse lines situated at the center. Within that interval, between those two lines, on the path of the junction (jūmārga), there is the sine (jyā) of the maximum correction (parama-phala). This is indeed certain.

Since the center of the *pratimaṇḍala* (epicycle) was previously determined to be at a distance from the center of the earth, that interval is established by logical proof. In the space between the two circles, the ear-line (*karṇa*) is not equal to that interval, but rather greater; for when the planet on the *pratimaṇḍala* has fallen from its apogee or is situated at the perigee, the *kendra* (equation of the center) lies within the six signs beginning with Capricorn. In that case, because the sine of the anomaly (*anyaphalajyā*) is of great magnitude, the *koṭijyā* (sine of the complement) arises above one point of the horizontal diameter of the *pratimaṇḍala*.

When the planet is situated at an interval of three or more signs, the quadrant is within the six signs beginning with Cancer; in that case, the *koṭijyā* (sine of the complement) is below the *anyaphalajyā* (sine of the correction), because it is the difference between the sum and the product [of the sines]. Between those two—the *anyaphalajyā* and the *koṭijyā*—the sum or the difference, according to the order, constitutes the quadrant beginning with Capricorn or Cancer respectively.

The clear perpendicular (*koṭi*), which takes the form of a vertical line, is the distance between the center of the circle and a point on the horizontal diameter located at a certain distance from the center; this is stated in the *Golādhyāya* (verse 374, section 95). The base (*bhuja*) is the distance between the center of the Earth and the center of the circle, measured along a vertical line passing through the root of that perpendicular. The square root of the sum of the squares of those aforementioned perpendicular and base is the distance between the observer situated at the center of the Earth and a point on the counter-circle (*pratimaṇḍala*).

The center of the *kuvaṃśa* (the circular orbit) is the point of the *bindu*. The line drawn between that point and the mark representing the planet situated on the circumcircle shall be the *karṇa* (the hypotenuse). He states its utility: "at the conjunction with the true [planet]. For, since the line drawn in the form of a radius (*śruti-sūtra*) meets at the point where the true planet is located on one part of the circumference of the orbital circle (*kakṣāvṛtta*), the *karṇa* is therefore necessary; this is the sense. Now, what indeed is this "true" nature? To this he says: "visible" (*dṛśya*).

The meaning is this: where a planet is visible from the center of the earth within the region enclosed by its orbit, the longitude (bhoga) at that point—measured from the rising of Aries—is the true planetary longitude. This is the underlying principle: because a planet does not revolve on its own orbital path (kakṣāvṛtta), its revolution occurs on the epicycle (pratīvṛtta). To those situated at the center [of the earth], the planet situated on the epicycle is seen along its own line of sight (dṛksūtra), which is a line parallel to the line passing through the point of the ecliptic (kṣāpradeśa); the longitude at that point is the true planetary longitude.

Although the longitude of a planet situated on the *pratimaṇḍala* (counter-ecliptic) is indeed established through proportionality from the *ahargaṇa*, nevertheless, because there is no marking of degrees on the *pratimaṇḍala*—as it lies at a greater distance from the ecliptic (*krāntivṛtta*)—the longitudes of the signs on that circle are merely hypothetical; thus, the longitude of a planet situated on the *pratimaṇḍala* is not useful for determining the point of true observation. However, the line of sight is precisely the hypotenuse (*karṇa*). For the purpose of calculating that, the "clear" (*spaṣṭa*) [longitude] is assumed as the perpendicular (*koṭi*).

Although there is an absence of humans on the earth's surface, nevertheless, by virtue of their connection with a line parallel to the back [of the sphere], there is no harm to their positions within its interior. He states the nature of the result—“the result” (phalam). The word “but” (ca) has the sense of "however" (tu). By that, the subsequent construction of the term "result" is easily understood. Within the interval between the mark of the mean planet and the mark of the true planet situated on the epicycle—that is, within a portion of the circumference of the epicycle—he states the nature of the positive or negative character of that result in the verse beginning with "mean" (madhya).
