In the case of a retrograde planet (*kekṣāvṛtta*), when the true longitude of the planet minus the mean longitude is situated in the eastern half of the circle along the path following the sequence of the zodiac signs, that result is subtracted from the mean longitude; when it is situated in the western half, it is added. The word "and" (*ca*) implies that the slow correction (*mandaphala*) is indeed applied according to the stated method. The meaning is that the fast correction (*śīghraphala*)—whether additive or subtractive—is established as described for the wise in the case of a center (*kendra*) beginning with Libra, as stated in the *Sphuṭīcikā*. || 17 ||

Now, having assumed the slow-mean (mandasphuṭa) as the mean (madhyama), he states the justification for that which results [from the calculation]: "For the mean [planet] indeed moves upon its own slow epicycle, while the slow-mean moves upon the [mean] eccentric orbit (drapratimaṇḍala). Because it revolves here with a flickering motion, the slow-mean planet is to be conceived as the mean planet. (Verse 18) This [verse] concerning the swift motion preceded by the slow motion is for the sake of the sixth [chapter]. Bhaṭṭotpala’s Commentary (bha0ḍī0): But surely, by the logic already stated, there is an inconsistency in the sequence of the results for Mars and the other planets. To explain:

According to the method described, because the apogees of mean and swift motion are placed upon their respective orbits, there are two positions for the true planet on the orbital circle (kakṣāvṛtta) due to the connection with the radius-lines (karṇasūtra) related to the eccentric circles (pratīvṛtta) of mean and swift motion, as determined by the sines of their respective equations. Among these, the distance between the position of the mean planet on the orbital circle—determined by its relation to the mean eccentric circle—and the position of the true planet is the equation of the mean anomaly (mandaphala).

The difference between the position of the true planet on the epicycle and that point on the epicycle which lies at the same interval from the mark of mean anomaly is the equation of center (śīghraphala). Furthermore, since the two results for Mars and the other planets arise from the mean planet, if it is asked by which result the true planetary position is to be known—by one or by the other—then that would be a contradiction of the principles of this treatise; for otherwise, the [second] rule would be rendered useless. Ma. Ṭī.—Because it would lead to the fallacy of redundancy.

Because it has not been determined by which of those two results clarity (*spaṣṭatva*) occurs, he states the answer to this objection as follows: "In the middle" (*madhya*). For (*hi*), because the planet, whose nature is the established motion following the series of days (*ahargaṇa*), revolves—that is, moves—by its own natural slow epicycle (*mandapratimaṇḍala*). The word "own" (*sve*) is used to prevent the suspicion of a connection between the respective epicycles of the planets. [Thus] the planet, having been corrected by the slow equation (*mandaphala*), is the slow-apparent (*mandasphuṭa*); it is not yet the true-apparent (*sphuṭa*).

He states the reason: "the slow and the true" (*mandasphuṭa*). This refers to the mean planet as corrected by the equation of the center (*mandaphala*). In the epicycle of apsis (*dāyapratimaṇḍala*), which has the form of the planetary image (*bimba*), it revolves when there is an absence of latitude (*śara*). The word *ca* (and) has the sense of *eva* (only/exclusive); by this, the doubt that the mean planet revolves in the epicycle of conjunction (*śīghraprativṛtta*) as corrected by the equation of conjunction (*śīghraphala*) within the epicycle of apsis is dispelled. Thus, the meaning is that because there is no revolution in the form of the planetary image within the epicycle of apsis, that which is corrected by the equation of the center is not the true [longitude].

For this reason, the meaning is that the swift (śīghra) operations are for that purpose. Here, in the orbit (kakṣā), the mean planet (madhyagraha)—consisting of specific points marked by divisions—should be assumed as the "slowly corrected" (mandasphuṭa) position; for in reality, it lacks the status of being the true mean, and because only that which is derived from the accumulated days (ahargaṇa) is accepted as the mean. [Objection: But surely the swift correction (śīghraphala) must be derived from the mean planet?

And likewise, just as when there is an equation of the center in the orbit (kakṣā), the mean planet occurs on the slow epicycle (mandaprativṛtta), so too the slow true [longitude] situated in the orbit established by that [equation] must be applied to the fast epicycle (śīghraprativṛtta) according to the stated method; for the planetary disc is not seen along a line parallel to the radius at the point of the slow true orbit.

The true planet is that which, having been derived from the true daily motion (*ahargaṇa*), occupies a specific point on its path in relation to the *karṇa* (the distance from the center), and by that same path it occupies a point in the orbit (*kakṣā*) corresponding to the observed position of the planetary disk in the epicycle (*pratimaṇḍala*). This is the justification for the sequence of results for Mars and the other planets. Since the planetary disk is a single entity, it is impossible for it to revolve simultaneously on both the slow (*manda*) and fast (*śīghra*) epicycles. Furthermore, if there were a fixed temporal constraint, it would follow that the results of both the slow and fast anomalies could be computed [simultaneously] through calculation.

Because the images of the Earth and other [planets] are observed and not observed due to the correction for parallax (*paralasaṃskāra*) in a single [calculation], the image of the Sun is treated as one; therefore, its position at the point of opposition (*pratīvṛtta*) is established. When there is an opposition (*prativṛtta*), the planet remains in the middle; that placement in the middle for the purpose of calculating the planet's conjunction is a conceptual construct (*kalpita*) and not a real entity (*vastubhūta*). In that case, the image would otherwise be different, because the result of the parallax would be untenable.

The conception of a reversed order of positions below [the celestial sphere] is refuted by the observation of the sequence in which results are produced and by the burden of assuming a method contrary to the affection for the Sun and Moon; this is the intended meaning. As for the statement: "That which is situated on the rim of the orbital circle is the mean planet; that which is in its apsis-circle is the true [planet]; and that is the clear, manifest motion"—in that case, since the mean and true [positions] are respectively declared to be on the apsis- and velocity-circles, the [notion of their] being "clear" (sphuṭa) is untenable.

18–19 || Now he speaks of the [ecliptic] node (*ucca*): "That point which is observed in its own epicycle within the circle of the [ecliptic] orbit is indeed the *sphuṭa* (apparent) [node]; for the first teachers have designated that as the *tuṅga* (apogee/node) here for the purpose of calculating results. 19–20 || "The region of the epicycle that is farthest from the earth is given the name *chatocca* (the highest point). Since that region also moves, the motion of that [node] was likewise postulated by those skilled in motion."

76. Chapter on the Bhūla [Orb]: When the mean [longitude] is separated from the apogee by six signs (180°), it is the perigee; when it is equal to its own apogee or perigee, it is the mean [longitude]. At that time, the point where the ear-line (karṇasūtra) falls above the center of the orbit is the true [longitude], which is then equal to the mean. The commencement of the motion of the *phaṭa* (the tip of the radius vector) is observed for that which has ascended gradually from the apogee; therefore, the apogee (*tuṅga*) is postulated. The rest is clear. This has been explained in detail in the *Madhyagativāsanā*. (Verses 19, 20, 21).

[Objection: It has been stated that the allotment of planets to their orbits and eccentric circles is appropriate; since it is impossible to understand their true nature without such allotment, [we agree]. However, for what purpose is the allotment of the *ucca* (apogee) there? Since the entity known as the *ucca* cannot be perceived in space and is therefore non-substantial (*avastubhūta*), [the author] provides the answer in the *vaṃśastha* meter, beginning with "bhramāt... (due to revolution).

In its own epicycle, on the slow and fast counter-orbits, that mean planet—calculated sequentially from the *ahargaṇa* and made slow-apparent—moving eastward day by day, is seen by men standing on the surface of the earth at whatever place (*pradeśa*) within the celestial sphere (*kakṣāvṛta*). The meaning is that it is seen along a line parallel to the radius of that location, via its connection to the center of the earth. There, in that region of the celestial sphere (*kakṣāpradeśa*).

For this reason, since the degrees of the slow and fast apogees (mandasphuṭa and spaṣṭagraha) are clearly established according to their respective fitness, the result (*phala*) is the interval between the mean planet and the true planet on the orbital circle (*kakṣāvṛtta*). For the sake of its justification—that is, for the purpose of producing it—here on the orbital circle, the ancient masters, beginning with Prācīnola and Tābhiga, have assigned the apogee (*tuṅga*), namely the slow and fast apogees, as is appropriate.

The meaning is that although this [eccentric circle] imagined by him in space is non-substantial because it is not perceived, it is nevertheless accepted because the resulting anomaly would otherwise be untenable. Furthermore, since the anomaly (phala) in the form of the difference between the mean and the true longitudes of a planet is observed to be of the nature of the difference between the mean and the true latitudes (bhuja), and because that [latitude] is dependent solely on the eccentricity, it is necessary to apply the eccentricity to both [the Sun and the Moon] in the manner described in order to know that [anomaly].

For this very reason, it is stated in the *Sphuṭādhikāra* (Chapter on True [Planetary Positions]) that "the sine of the [true] anomaly, multiplied by the radius and divided by the hypotenuse, is the result, or the difference between the arc and the arm. Otherwise, since the true nature of the sine of the anomaly and the sine of the co-anomaly—which serve as the basis for the result—could not be demonstrated, the result derived from them would in no way be logically consistent. This is the intended meaning. [Objection: But why has the term "apex" (*ucca*) been used here in connection with the meridian line for the sake of explaining the result?

Since the term "beginning" (*ārambha*) is used in relation to its opposite (*taditara*), they explain the validity of the conjunction in that manner with the following *upajāti* verse: "That which would be... That region of the counter-orbit (*pratimaṇḍala*) which would be far from the center of the earth (*bhūgolagarbha*)—that region's name is [not established] because of its remoteness. And likewise, because there is no central point within the interior of the earth for the counter-circle occupied by the planet, it is [designated as] "mid-heaven" (*hemadhya*).

The point of apogee (*ucca*) is elevated by one degree from the point of return (*prativṛtta*); because the base of the sine of the argument (*bhujajyā*) and other values originate from that point, the elevation of the apogee was stated by the Great Sage (the author) as being established through proportion (*anupāta*) for the purpose of knowing the longitude of the apogee and so forth. In this regard, the intention is that even though there is no physical location for the apogee on the celestial sphere (*kakṣā*), its position is nevertheless marked for the sake of determining the longitude of the apogee. Now, an objection might be raised: since the location of the apogee is singular, it is inconsistent for its daily variation—established through the proportion based on the number of elapsed days (*ahargaṇa*)—to be different from day to day.

The epicycle does not move even slightly every day by way of retrograde motion, because such movement is impossible since the region of the orbit (*kakṣā*) consists of empty space; therefore, he says, "That too. For that portion belonging to the eccentric circle (*pratimaṇḍala*) moves, and it comes to its own former position within the orbit through its own forward motion. This is the meaning of the diagrammatic illustration (*chedyakacikāra*).

74. Commentary (Bhāṣya-ṭīkā): The meaning is that on whatever day [the planet] is in line with a point of its orbit, on the following day it comes into line with the next point of that same orbital region. Furthermore, the word "also" (*api*) indicates that although the position of the retrograde point is fixed by its nature as a command from the Lord (*ājñāśarūpatva*), its movement is nevertheless postulated through the assumption of its being composed of air (*vāyvātmakatva*), since such movement would otherwise be inexplicable.

Therefore, the motion of the sun is said to be its movement following the cause; this motion is conceptualized day by day through specific, subtle objects of knowledge. By this, it is clearly stated that even though [the motion] is not a real entity, it is postulated for the purpose of establishing the occurrence of perceived results.

Furthermore, the result that was established by Brahmā and others according to the aforementioned method—based on the position of the apogee (ucca) situated on the line of intersection with the entry point into the orbit (kakṣā)—was observed to be inconsistent on the second day. This is because the actual appearance of the planetary disc is determined through the position of the true planet as calculated via its radius (karṇa). Consequently, they postulated the apogee to be at a certain distance along the orbital path from the previously assumed location of the apogee.

Therefore, according to the aforementioned method, because the agreement with the observed results is seen on the second day through the reversal of the motion in the manner described, it is postulated that there exists a distinct [motion] at every moment. And for the sake of understanding the validity of that [postulation], it is accepted that the points on that circle—which is of the nature of space and whose radius is half the difference between the trijyā and the sum of the trijyā and the final sine of the equation (antyaphalajyā) added to the earth's center—are in constant motion, since there is no determining factor to suggest that on a given day the apogee is at one point, while on the second day it must be at the next point to its left (savyena). Thus, the rapidity of those points on the circle is admitted as occurring in succession.

In that regard, since it is necessary for the point of the apogee to be attached to a specific portion of the circumference of the epicycle (*prativṛtta*), otherwise its status as the "high" point would not be established; thus, by the difference between the other [mean] fruit-sine (*phalajyā*) from the center of the earth, the center of the epicycle moves daily to the right. Consequently, it is established by this conceptualization that the epicycle itself has moved, and through that movement, the apogee moves within the orbit (*kakṣā*).

The meaning is that there is no contradiction because the assumption of a single reflected image situated in one place is easily established based on the many distinct reflections produced at every successive moment. (20) Now, an objection is raised: "How can this upward movement, which is directly experienced, be accepted? And for what reason is its extreme height postulated for the sake of accounting for the resulting effect? To answer these preliminary objections, he says "from the high [point]" (*uccāt*), employing a clever argument.

For those situated at the apogee (ucca), within their own sign-interval, the point of descent (nīca) moves in the orbit according to its proportion; just as the apogee moves, so too does the point of descent move. This is due to the rule that the distance between the two [apogee and perigee] is the difference between the signs, established by their connection to the vertical diameter. When, in a desired result, the mean or the slow-ecliptic (manda-sphuṭa) planet—calculated from the intended day-count—is equal to its own apogee or perigee, subtraction or addition is intended by its own term.

That [mean planet] of yours, whether low or high, shall at the desired time be equal to that [true planet] of mine; for the mean [planet], when corrected by the equation of center (manda-phala) or corrected by the equation of anomaly (śīghra-phala), becomes equal to the true [planet]. It shall be equal to the true [planet] derived from the accumulated days (ahargaṇa) according to the appropriate method. Why is this? He states the reason: "Above the mean [planet] situated in the orbit" (kakṣāstha). That is, above the mean planet of the aforementioned nature situated in the orbital circle (kakṣāvṛtta).

When the line drawn from the center of the earth to the zenith above is the *karṇa* (the hypotenuse), that line which follows its own corresponding path up to the *kakṣāmaṇḍala* (the celestial equator) is related to its *pāta* (node). Indeed, the point where the *karṇa*-line intersects the region of the *kapha* (the ecliptic) is clearly the position of mean sunrise (*ahasthāna*). In this context, it is established as the very position of mean sunrise; the meaning is that because the *karṇa* is established as being a portion of the diameter. Thus, when the planet at its lowest or highest point is equal [to the mean], there is an absence of the correction for difference between the mean and the true positions.

Therefore, when the true planet is behind or ahead of that [apogee] at the equinoxes (mahe), the difference between the apogee and the planet is clearly marked by the signs of the planets; from this, the result (*phala*) is produced for the two spheres (*golārdhaye*). Thus, just as the planet is separated from the apogee and perigee, so does the result arise. Consequently, it is rightly stated that the "Apogee" (*tuṅga*) was postulated for the sake of understanding the result generated by that separation, in order to establish the derivation of the result (*phalopapatti*). This is the intended meaning.

Thus, when the true planet is observed to be equal to the mean [longitude] by means of a line parallel to the point of the *yakṣā* (the first revolution), it is likewise observed to be equal to the mean by means of a line parallel to the point of the *tarkakṣavṛtta* (the second revolution circle). However, it is observed by means of a line parallel to another point; therefore, in the absence of the [calculated] result, the planet itself is the instrument (*astra*), and its motion is not at all contrary to experience according to the authority of direct perception—this is the intended meaning. || 21 ||

Now he says something else: "When a celestial body is situated at its apogee (ucca), it appears distant in the sky; when situated at its perigee (nīca), it appears near. Therefore, the orb of the planet appears small or large according to whether it is very close to or very far from the Sun. (22) This is clear! (22) Now he states another method: "I have already explained the principle of these [planets] by means of the epicycle (prativṛtta) for the sake of the listener’s lack of confusion. For the sake of further clarification, I shall now state it again differently, according to the eccentric circle (nīcocca-vṛtta). (23) This is clear! (23)

In this context, indeed, there is the method for clarification and the breaking of the eccentric circle (prativṛttabhaṅga). Now, I shall describe that very method and the breaking of the eccentric circle. Now he describes that method: "Then one should draw a circle from the center of the earth with a radius equal to the other sine (anyaphalajyā) [of the planet] when the planet is at the middle of its orbit; and one should construct a line called the apogee (nīcoccasaṃjñā) starting from the center of the earth and passing over the middle planet. At a point much further from the center of the earth, joined by a line, the apex (tuṅga) should be established. (23–24)

Likewise, one should draw a line toward the nadir at a closer distance, and another slanting between the nadir and the zenith. In this circle of the nadir and zenith marked with degrees, the mean planet moves in reverse order through its own anomaly (kendrabhāga) when in the lower half, and in direct order from its own apogee (tuṅga) when in the upper half; for this is how the mean planet travels. Therefore, the anomaly of the slow and fast epicycles (mṛdu-dhra-kendra) should be applied as stated, starting from its own apogee. From the planet, using the sine (dojya) up to the apogee-line, there arises the perpendicular (koṭiśīrṣa) upon the horizontal line (tiryastharekhā).

As before, having drawn a side-circle (kakṣāvṛtta) marked with degrees of the zodiac, one should draw another circle there at the same distance from the center as the day-circle (ahar-vṛtta), intersecting it at midday. This is known as the apogee-perigee circle (nīcocca-vṛtta). Then, a line slightly longer than the diameter should be drawn through the center of the earth; this is the "upper line" (uparekhā) here. On the apogee-perigee circle, the point where the upper line intersects at a greater distance from the earth is to be considered the apogee (ucca), and the point where it intersects closer to the earth is the perigee (nīca). The determination of the perigee and apogee is the subject of the section on cutting diagrams (chedyakādhikāra).

479. A line should be drawn through the middle of the three [points]. In that circle, starting from the position of the apogee (uccasthāna) by means of the true motion, the mean planet moves. Here, the intellect (*dhi*) proceeds in direct order (*anuloma*). For this reason, the slow anomaly (*mandakendra*) should be calculated starting from the apogee; the fast anomaly (*śīghrakendra*) follows the sequence. That is the planet. Here too, there is a fault in the interval between the planet and its movement. The co-latitude sine (*koṭijyā*) between the meridian line and the prime vertical is 242° 5' 26" 2".

[The author] says this in the Upajāti meter to address the following objection: "Surely, since the observed results cannot otherwise be accounted for, one must assume that the planet actually exists at those positions; therefore, its actual location is there. [He replies: "The planet situated at the apsis (ucca) would be in the form of a great orb very far from the terrestrial globe (bhūgola); the planet situated at the perigee (nīca) would be near the center of the earth. Beyond this, it could not be further upwards or downwards."

Therefore, due to its proximity, the solar disc appears sequentially as minute or vast, subtle or large; it diminishes for humans on earth and for non-humans [in the higher realms]. By the word "and" (ca), it is indicated that just as the distance from the zenith increases, so too does the disc expand, and just as the distance decreases, so too does it appear to shrink. By this, it is suggested that while the solar disc remains unchanging, it appears to diminish; however, it has been established that in reality, there is no actual increase or decrease.

And so, because the sun is at a great distance from the earth when it is in its highest position (*uñcasthāna*), the solar disc appears small; whereas, because it is near when it is in its lowest position (*nīcasthāna*), it appears large. This is established by direct perception. Since being in the highest or lowest positions occurs only through the passage of time, Indra’s abiding in the *prativṛtta* (the counter-revolution) is indeed according to reality.

The sense is that if it were situated on the *ṛkṣavṛtta* (the ecliptic), then because of its equal distance from all sides, there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of seeing the planetary disc as distorted; furthermore, there is no evidence for its remaining on the *taddhitavṛtta* (the deferent). Anticipating the objection that "even when situated at its *nīca* (lowest point), a planet with a subtle form is sometimes seen by the Sun," he says: A planet situated at a great distance from the Sun appears thus: due to the longitudinal difference (*pūrvāparāntara*) between them, it appears respectively small and large in size.

Likewise, just as a planet is situated near the solar disc, so too, by those whose eyes are struck by the rays of the sun, its orb is seen to be lusterless and small; thus, even when a planet is at its lowest point (*nīcastha*) and close to the sun, the perception of a small form is not contradictory. Conversely, when a planet is very far from the solar disc, by those whose eyes are not struck by the sun's rays, its great orb is seen to be radiant and large. For this very reason, there is an increase [in size] at the beginning of its setting due to the difference in degrees of its digits (*kalāṃśa*).

The meaning is this: this [error] does not arise from the proximity of the sun or from the two [types of] contraction, because that [sun] is unchanging; otherwise, it would follow that even by its observation, the calculation of the *siṃha* (the lion/ascendant) would be established. (22) Concluding the discussion on the expected [result], he states another method for demonstrating the impossibility [of the opponent's view], beginning with the words "yuktiḥ" (reasoning), as follows: "The reasoning regarding the clear determination of the body of calculation (*gaṇitakāya*) through the formalization of forms is of the nature of a direct perception of the essential reality of things; this is exceedingly vast."

By me, Bhāskara Ācārya, this has been stated through a method of reversal—that is, by means of an inverted formulation. Indeed, for the two [circles] given as the fruit of the ascensional difference (ujjvalaphala), this would be the counter-force from the center of the earth; or else, it is a circle formed by the product of the fruit and the sine of the latitude. For this other circle, which lies on its own orbital plane, is situated at the point of the fruit.

18.9 Regarding the verse beginning with *galataye maṇḍī*, etc.: since the previous teachers have already described the methods for drawing the eccentric circle (*pratidvṛtta*) and the epicycle (*nīcavṛtta*) on the deferent circle (*kakṣāvṛtta*), why was this method of drawing the eccentric circle stated separately? To this he says: "Separately" (*pṛthak*). This is for the sake of providing a clear exposition (*spaṣṭīkṛti*) for the listener; it is intended for the intellect and is meant to prevent confusion (*asaṃbhrama*).

The meaning is as follows: since it is impossible to remove completely that confusion which is contrary to the recitation of the *am* syllable, and because of the difficulty [of the subject] for the student, this is intended so that there may be no lack of understanding regarding its dense causes. The meaning is that it has been stated solely by means of the arrangement of the *prativṛtta* meter, apart from the usual low and high meters (*nīca-ucca-vṛtta*). And thus, because the three aforementioned qualities exist in the students, they understand the single *pra* here and there; such is the purpose.

The sense is this: when it was stated that "the arc from that point toward the apogee should be added," and so forth, I merely relied upon the underlying logic (*yukti*) of that statement; therefore, my explanation by way of omitting it is not contradictory. Now, one might object: "How can the knowledge obtained regarding the motion in the apogee and perigee apply to the retrograde motion? Thus, its omission is improper. To this, he says: "That" (*tām*), meaning the *vāsanā* (explanatory rationale) for the demonstration of the true [longitude]. "Again" (*punar*) means a second time. "Otherwise" (*anyathā*) means in a manner different from the previously stated method.

I, Bhāskara Ācārya, shall explain the method for the eccentric orbit immediately hereafter. Here too, the phrase "for the sake of avoiding confusion" applies; thus, the meaning is that I am stating it by constructing only the eccentric circle, omitting the concentric circles. The implication is that since knowledge of that [eccentricity] is possible, there is no deficiency. However, drawing both of those together in one place as stated by previous teachers is not appropriate, because of the resulting complexity. Rather, [simplicity] is preferable due to its brevity (*lāghava*).

And because what was said by you is improper due to its weightiness, he says: "and furthermore" (*ca bhūyaḥ*). "Furthermore" means for a third time. The word "and" (*ca*) is used in the sense of conjunction. Therefore, the meaning is: "I shall write both of these here together in a mixed composition and state their underlying intention (*vāsanā*). Thus, even that which was previously stated—namely, "the non-existent was brought forth"—was spoken by me earlier as a necessity, though it is weighty, using a different arrangement of meters and verses for the sake of producing understanding in the listeners through mere playfulness. The sense is: "Therefore, what I have said is not improper. || 23 ||

Now, desiring to state what has been promised, he first speaks the *Upajāti* verse beginning with "kasthiti" (where situated), etc., meaning: after having established the zodiacal signs marked by the asterisms at the desired place using the previously mentioned thread-measuring instrument; from the mark of the mean planet situated on the orbit—that is, the point on the orbital circle corresponding to the mean longitude starting from the position of Aries—one should draw a circle with a radius equal to half the sine of the equation of the apsis (*antyaphalajyā*).

He states its designation: "that" (*tat*). The circle thus drawn is designated as the "eccentric" (*nīcocca*) circle. In that context, starting from the center—the point situated at the middle of the earth—one should draw one vertical line upward; having touched the fixed point of the mean planet (*madhyagrahācala*), one should extend it to the opposite side of the eccentric circle. By the word "and" (*ca*), lines should also be drawn from the center of the circle to the mark of the true planet (*spaṣṭagrahacihna*). In this way, the circle becomes divided into two equal halves.

How is it that [the circle] touches the center of the earth at the intersection of the horizontal and vertical lines, yet is attached to a portion of the circumference of the orbit at a distance of one-third of the interval between the horizontal and vertical marks? [End of Chapter 18 on the Sphere. Now, as to the question: "Why is the circle produced from the other sine called 'low' (nīca) and 'high' (ucca)?"—the answer, along with the method for determining its four equal parts, is stated in the Indravajrā meter: "From the center of the earth," etc. "From the center of the earth" means from the location of the central point.

Here, on the circumference of the circle whose radius is the sine of the equation of center (*kāntyaphala*) for the planet situated at the middle of the wood-block, one should designate the apogee (*tuṅga*)—that is, that mark should be marked—at a point far removed from the other [the perigee]. By the word "designated" (*prakalpya*), it is indicated that when the planet's disk is situated there, the position of the apogee is easily known by observing the smallness of its disk; otherwise, its knowledge would be impossible, because circles in the sky cannot be perceived.

[Objection: But how can there be a conjunction in this circle with a point situated at such a great distance? To this he says: "joined by a line" (*rekhayuta*). The meaning is that the very portion of the circumference attached to the tip of the vertical line is the distant location. [The other point] is closer to the center of the earth, being extremely near. Thus, the apogee (*nīca*) should be placed at the point where the sine of the maximum equation (*antyaphalajyā*) intersects the vertical line on a portion of the circumference of the circle whose diameter is the radius.

Here too, it is indicated that because the planet situated therein is seen with a gross disc, its state of being "low" (nīca) is extreme compared to its position at the "high" point (ucca), and not otherwise. Thus, as the planet at the center of the earth revolves on both sides through that interval at points of extreme distance and proximity, the epicycles (paridhi-vṛtta) at those high and low positions and the corresponding points on the orbit (kakṣā) situated in their midst are established by means of the sine of the equation of the apsis (antyaphala-jyā); the sense is that the designation "low" and "high" (nīcocca) is applied because of the connection with both of these. Now, immediately thereafter:

"Between the nīca and ucca" means between the trees designated by those names. By the word "and" (ca), one should draw a horizontal line from the tip of the vertical line through the center of the circle, making it equidistant on both sides of the marks for *nīca* and *ucca*. By the phrase "not in the middle," the observation of the horizontal [alignment] is indicated; the line should not be drawn outside the earth [circle], but rather its ends should touch the circumference of the circle. This is what is indicated. || 25 ||

Now, desiring to explain here the nature of the *karṇa* (radius) as it is employed in the doctrine of the fruit (*phalavāsanā*), [the author] first describes its dependent nature—the configuration of the *bhujāntara*, *koṭijyā*, and *sva*—in two verses in the *Indravajra* and *Upajāti* meters, beginning with "nīcocca": "Because of which [reason]: the mean [longitude], derived from the *ahargaṇa*, is the basis for the slow motion (*mānda*) and is dependent upon the doctrine of the slow fruit (*mandaphalavāsanā*)."

In the *śīghravṛtta* (epicycle of anomaly), which serves as the basis for the calculation of the swift [mean] motion (*śīghraphalavāsanā*), the planet situated at its own apogee (*nijakendra*) is moved by the slow apogee (*manda*) according to the motion of the slow apogee; that is, it is moved by the difference between the motion of the slow apogee and the planet's mean motion within the *śīghranīcocca-vṛtta* (epicycle of anomaly). This means it is moved by the motion of the anomaly (*śīghrakendra*). It moves in the orbit (*kakṣā*) in a retrograde or counter-clockwise direction (*viloma-apasavya-mārga*) according to the sequence of the slow and swift motions; this means it follows the path of revolution (*parītamārga*).

"In direct order" (*anuloma*) means by way of the path of friendship (*sakhya-mārga*), that is, by the same path as the exertion made in the girth (*kakṣā*) [of a horse], day after day. "From its own apogee" (*svatuṅga*) means from the position of the apogee of the slow motion (*manda-ucca*) on the epicycle of the slow motion (*manda-nīcocca-vṛtta*). "The epicycle of the fast apogee" (*śīghra-nīcocca-vṛtta*) means starting from the position of the apogee of the fast motion (*śīghra-ucca*). "Beginning from that apogee" means making that apogee the prior limit. "It revolves in the highest path" means it moves day by day in sequence. "Indeed" (*hi*) signifies certainty.

Therefore, it is highly contradictory to say that when the Moon is at its lowest or highest point, it moves by a path opposite to the path of the [Sun's] apsis; for in a single planetary orb, there cannot be two simultaneous and opposing motions. Indeed, the nature of the *prahara* (the node) is not perceived in three ways, as there is no such observation. Even if a swift motion were assumed, the same fault would apply. Thus, the suspicion raised in the *Golādhyāya*—that this might be a mere mental construction (*kalpanā*)—is refuted, as it has been indicated that the refutation of this doubt will be stated later.

For this reason, when the circle is divided into twelve signs, degrees, minutes, and seconds, and this [circle] is rotated by the motion of the mantra; then, on the slow epicycle (*mandanīcoccavṛtta*), the apsis (*mandakendra*) is to be applied from the position of the slow apogee (*mandocca*) according to the sequence of right-hand revolution (*apasavyasaṃvya-krama*); and on the fast epicycle (*śīghranīcoccavṛtta*), the anomaly (*śīghrakendra*) is to be applied from the position of the fast apogee (*śīghrocca*). The meaning is that the circle must be constructed according to the calculation of the occupation of the apsis. The purpose of this observation is stated as "the movement of the planet" (*grahacāra*).

Since a portion of the circumference of the circle situated between the high apogee mark and the center constitutes the center itself, its base is the position of the apogee (the center-mark), and its tip is the position of the planet (the planet-mark). Therefore, the planet-mark must be made. Likewise, on the epicycle of the node (the *nīcoccavṛtta*), the planet must be positioned at an interval from the apogee equal to the arc of the anomaly; this is the final meaning. He states the purpose of the planet-mark: "The sine... (*dojya iti*).

From the planet's position marked by the planetary sign, up to the line of the apex (ucca-rekhā) and extending to the vertical line, a straight line in the form of a semi-chord (ardhajyā) shall be the sine of the arm (bhuja-jyā). From that same planet, up to the horizontal line passing through the point of the apogee (nīca), a line in the form of a semi-chord running upwards and downwards shall be the sine of the perpendicular (koṭi-jyā). || 26 || 27 || Now he states the result of the correction for the epicycle: "Those two results of the arm and the perpendicular calculated for the center [of the epicycle] become the sine of the arm and the sine of the perpendicular on the circle of the apogee and perigee (nīcoñca-vṛtta)."

In Capricorn and the following signs, the kotiphala (perpendicular distance) is above the center; in Aries and the following signs, it would be below. Therefore, the sum or difference of these two is the kotiphala here, which is the long line between the Earth and the planet. Then, the correction (phala), whether positive or negative, between the center of the orbit and the planet's radius is as stated here. The first half-verse is easy to understand. In the orbital circle, the radius is called the *trijyā* (three-sine).

Since the koti (perpendicular) exceeds the koti [of the mean orbit] by one crore when the apsis is in Aries and so on, whereas it is below that when the apsis is in Libra and so on, the sum or difference of those two is the true koti. In that situation, the bhujaphala (the correction for the anomaly) itself is the bāhu (arm). The distance between the Earth and the planet is the karṇa (hypotenuse). It is well known that the square root of the sum of the squares of the doḥ (bāhu) and the iṣṭa (koti) is the karṇa. Here too, as before, when the karṇa-line is projected onto the orbital circle (kakṣāvṛtta), the planet is clearly [located there]. The difference between the true and the mean positions is the phala (correction), and so forth. Thus ends the section on the geometry of the eccentric circle (nīcocavṛtta).

Now he describes the mixed configuration (*miśrabhaṅgi*): "Because it appears as if moving slowly in the opposite direction from the swift [planet] when situated in its own apogee (*nija-kendra*) in direct motion (*anuloma*) ahead of the high point (*mahocca*), yet appearing as if moving rapidly behind it in retrograde motion (*viloma*), those two motions in the epicycle of the apogee and perigee (*nīcoccavṛtta*) are thus otherwise. That single motion is perceived differently by others; for the sake of calculating results (*phala*), that distinction has been devised. If this configuration is written down in these two mixed epicycles, then the stated rule applies here. 30–31. When a planet is in direct motion (*anuloma*) at the front of its apogee (*mahocca*), being situated in its own apogee (*nijakendra*), it appears as if moving slowly because of the retrograde motion of the swift [epicycle]. Conversely, when it is behind [the apogee] in retrograde motion (*viloma*), it appears as if moving rapidly. Thus, in the epicycle of the apogee and perigee (*nīcoccavṛtta*), those two motions are otherwise. That which is a single motion appears as something else due to the perception of others; that distinction was formulated for the purpose of determining results (*phala*). If this configuration is recorded in these two mixed epicycles, then the previously stated rule holds true here.

483. When the apsis (the point of maximum velocity) and the perapsis (the point of minimum velocity) are at the lowest and highest points [of the epicycle], the planet is necessarily retrograde at that time. Just as in the case of the water-wheel (*lailikayantra*), the rotation of the wood is contrary to the rotation of the ox; so too, when another [body] approaches, its motion occurs with a counter-epicycle (*pratimaṇḍala*) and a swift revolution at the lowest point. The day-sphere rotates by means of the counter-epicycle itself. That which is the lowest and highest circle has been constructed by Bhānuka and Tāla for the sake of calculation.

In that regard, the movement toward the mandala of joy appears as if it were moving in reverse. How does the movement there appear as joy in reverse? There is an illustration for this: just as when a piece of wood is placed in the middle of an oil-pressing machine to press sesame seeds, its rotation is contrary to the rotation of the ox; for while the ox moves in a clockwise direction (dextrally), that piece of wood, even though being rotated in that manner, moves in a counter-clockwise direction (sinistrally) from its own perspective.

Thus, when the circle is rotated downwards, it appears as if inverted; this is clearly explained here. (Verses 10, 31, 32, 33). This concludes the section on mixed methods (*miśrabhaṅgi*). Commentary (Bhaṭṭotpala): Now, since the sine of the base (*bhuja*) and the sine of the perpendicular (*koṭi*) are established by means of the radius (*vyāsārdha*) as the standard for the sine-measure, their location within a circle whose diameter is the final result-sine (*antyaphalajyā*) would seem inconsistent. Therefore, in response to that, the demonstration of the result (*phalavāsanā*) is stated in the *Svendra-vajra* and *Upajāti* meters, beginning with the word "kendre" (at the center).

The results for the sine and cosine of the anomaly (*bhujakoṭiphala*)—which were clearly stated as being produced by multiplying [the respective values] by their own radius and dividing by the circumference, as described in the verse beginning with "nīcoccakheṭe bhujakoṭijye"—are those previously established in the passage beginning with "jyeṃcarekhāyadhīti. Furthermore, the sense is that it is logical for the sine and cosine of the anomaly to remain in their natural positions within that circle when they have been transformed into the dimensions of their own eccentric circles using the radius as the unit of measure. By this very reasoning, the rationale for the calculation of the sine and cosine results should be understood as clear.

Now, he establishes the nature of the *koṭi* (perpendicular) for the purpose of knowing the true nature of the *karṇa* (hypotenuse), stating: "The *trijyā-ūrdhva*" and so forth. In the case of signs beginning with Capricorn (*mṛga*), when the apogee (*kendra*) is within the six signs starting from Capricorn, the great mark (*mahacihna*) on the eccentric circle (*nīcoccavṛtta*) lies above its own transverse line. This is because it exists at a distance equal to the *trijyā* from the transverse line of the orbit (*kakṣā*) due to the verticality of the eccentric circle. Thus, the *koṭiphala* (perpendicular correction) is measured vertically from the point where the line equal to the *trijyā* intersects the vertical. In the case of signs beginning with Cancer (*karka*), when the apogee is within the six signs starting from Cancer, [the mark on] the eccentric circle lies below its own transverse line.

Then it becomes the mark of the planet (*grahacihna*). From the point below the tip of the line of the radius of the celestial sphere (*tadadhakhijyātulyakakṣurekhā*) which points upward, the result of the hypotenuse (*koṭiphala*) lies below. Because of this—since it stands there—the sum or difference of those two, namely the radius of the celestial sphere (*khijyā*) and the result of the hypotenuse (*koṭiphala*), occurs according to the sequence of the hypotenuse (*karṇa*). Here, at the center of the earth (*bhūgarbha*), the line representing the distance between the two marks of the planet situated at the low and high points (*nīcocca*) within one part of the ecliptic circle (*krāntivṛtta*) is the hypotenuse (*koṭi*). For that very purpose, it is said: "the arm and the hypotenuse" (*bhuja-maha-vor*). The result of the arm (*doḥphala*) is the distance between the base of the hypotenuse and the mark at the center of the earth, equal to the result of the arm (*bhujaphala*).

The hypotenuse (karṇa) has the form of a chord; its nature is described as "the line between the center of the earth and the point on the circumference. The line situated between the center of the earth and a point on the circumference of the circle drawn at the nadir—that line, being horizontal, is the hypotenuse (karṇa) which constitutes the locus of conjunction for those two [points]. Following this—the purpose of the hypotenuse is stated as "thereafter" (atha). Immediately after.

Here, in the *kaṅkavṛtta* (the circle of the ear-line), at the point where it is attached to the ear-line located in the middle of the armpit (*kakṣa*), and between the two armpit regions where they are attached to the ear-line, there is a portion of the circumference of the armpit. That, however, is the fruit—either *mānda* or *śaibya*. Now, since the *pratimaṇḍala* (eccentric circle) and the *nīcecca-vṛtta* (circle of apsis) do not have a single common location, how is the positive or negative nature of the fruit to be known here? To this he says: "not negative" (*na ṛṇam*).

In the aforementioned [calculation], when the planet is in the eastern half (dhanaga), that [correction] is negative from the true planet; when it is situated in the western half (ṛṇaga), it is positive. This result is to be understood according to the method of establishing debt and credit as applied to the epicycle (prativṛtta), and not by a different method. Here, the word "ca" (and) serves as the reason, meaning that the nature of this result is identical to that established previously by the method of the epicycle. || 28 || 29 ||

Now, one might object that because there is no diversity in the planet's own nature (*svarūpa*), its simultaneous presence in two places is contradictory; therefore, having first described the states of the planet’s motion on the *pratimaṇḍala* and the *uccavṛtta*, [the author] declares—by means of the *upajāti* and *kendra-vajra* meters—that in reality it resides in only one place: "In the previously mentioned *pratimaṇḍala*, the planet moves eastward by its own motion from its position on the slow apsis (*mandocca*) located on the slow epicycle (*mandaprativṛtta*)."

It appears as if it moves in a direct (anuloma) direction by way of the sequence of the apogee and the earth, through its own apsidal motion—that is, the motion of the slow apsis (mandakendra). By this, it is indicated that although the planet actually moves according to its own motion, the movement of the slow apsis is impossible [to perceive directly]; therefore, the appearance of moving directly occurs due to the motion of the apsis from the apogee. From where does this appearance of direct motion arise? To this he says: "In front" (agre).

Because the apogee and the planet move with equal speed due to the apogee's motion, the anomaly (kendram) arises precisely from the apogee; thus, the sense is that it appears to move in direct order (anuloma). From the "swift" [point], meaning from the position of the apogee situated on the epicycle of anomaly (śīghraprativṛtta), it appears as if it moves by its own anomaly motion—the motion of the anomaly of the swift [equation]—in reverse order (viloma), that is, by a path opposite to the path of the zodiacal signs situated on the orbit (kakṣā).

In this case as well, it should be understood that when a planet has turned retrograde (*śīghri-prativṛtta*), because it moves forward by its own motion, one should conceive of its appearance as moving in the opposite direction due to its [apparent] motion in a quadrant (*kendragati*). The reason for this is stated as "delayed" (*vilambita*): because of which cause it is "touched" (*viṃcumbita*)—meaning delayed—from behind during the swift retrogression; the word "eva" (only) implies that at times it is not from the front. It is thus "touched," meaning it becomes delayed, during the swift retrogression.

Because the swift apogee (śīghrocca) and the planet move eastward, and because the velocity of the swift apogee is greater [than that of the planet], the planet comes to be behind it in the latter half of the orbit; thus, it is logical that it appears to move in the opposite direction due to the motion of the epicycle (kendragati). This is the intended meaning. He describes the configuration of the apogee and perigee circle (nīcoccavṛtta) in the verse beginning with "nīcoccavṛtte. In that apogee-perigee circle established by the previous verse, during its eastward and westward motion, the planet moves from the east of the slow apogee (mandocca) and to the west of the swift apogee (śīghrocca). These refer to the apogee and perigee circle mentioned in the preceding verse.

The word "punar" (again) is used as a poetic embellishment (*vākya-alaṃkāra*). Otherwise, it means "in the opposite manner. In the case of slow motion (*manda-prativṛtta*), there is a direct movement from the apogee (*mandocca*); therein, in the slow epicycle (*manda-nīcocca-vṛtta*), the movement of the slow planet (*mandagraha*) is in the reverse direction. In the case of swift motion (*śīghra-prativṛtta*), there is a reverse movement from the apogee (*śīghrocca*); the meaning is that in the swift epicycle (*śīghra-nīcocca-vṛtta*), the movement is in the direct direction. Therefore, in this [orb] marked by the zodiacal signs (*bhagaṇāṅkita*) according to the epicycles of apogee and perigee (*nīcocca-vṛtta*)...

The statement regarding the reversal of the position of the planet's mark was made precisely because of the reversal of its retrograde motion. However, when determining the planet’s mark here in accordance with its actual retrograde position, the following results from the difference in direction: from the point of the mean planet's mark on the ecliptic, the true planet's position—which consists of the intersection of the radius-line related to the retrograde motion and the orbit—is at a certain distance and in a certain direction; whereas the true planet's position—which consists of the intersection of the radius-line related to the apogee-perigee line and the orbit—is at that same distance but in the opposite direction. Thus, there is a reversal of the nature of the result, whether it be a debt (negative) or a credit (positive).

[This is] because of the logical necessity (*arthāpatti*). Nor should it be argued that there is no authority for the *chuścaka* [instrument] when the thighs are positioned low and high, on the grounds that "the marking of the zodiac signs occurs in reverse order in the ecliptic (*kakṣāvṛtta*) from west to east. This is because the ecliptic (*kakṣāvṛtta*) follows the form of the path of the solstices (*krāntivṛtta*), and thus its dissimilarity [to the latter] is impossible. Furthermore, the assumption that the zodiac signs exist in reverse order from west to east within the ecliptic at the point of the apogee (*nīca*) is contradicted by direct observation in many ways.

And because the planet's retrograde motion is observed on the line passing through its point of greatest elongation; therefore, for the sake of achieving the conjunction of the positions in the respective eccentric circles (vṛtta), there is the "node of apsis" (nīcocca-bhū) to achieve the conjunction of the positions in the apsidal circle. The sense is that this movement toward the apsis must necessarily occur within the day.

By this, even the retrograde motion (*vāma-kriyā*) and so forth [of planets] is established; for the celestial wanderer (*divicara*), when situated in the sign of its own exaltation (*tuṅga-lavais-tad-ucan-meghāditaṃ diviṃcaraḥ*), it is considered by the masters of the *Tīkākṛt* (commentators) to be in its direct course (*ṛju-gati*), while in the opposite case it is in retrograde (*prativṛtta-vat*). Furthermore, regarding the location of the signs in the sequence of low and high [nodes], it is stated that in heaven (*svarge*) the result is the slow-mean (*manda-phuṭa*). And in the verse beginning "When the body is behind, the soft [node] has a clear aspect on the center" (*aṅge pṛṣṭhagate mṛdu-sṛṣṭa-srag-aspaṣṭa-haṃ-kendra-sa*), the positive or negative nature of the result is explained according to the reverse method (*vyasta-rītyā*). Thus, the lower and upper [nodes] are established.

Now, one might object: "In that case, since the planets laugh [at this], there is no possibility of their remaining in both positions. To this they reply: "Because of dependence on another. His motion is connected to the path of revolution belonging to the sequence of the stationary mass; it is primary because it constitutes a limb of the prior motion through his own power of *māndya* (slowness). And how could it otherwise be so in the revolution, like a direct perception? Thus they say that for the planet, these two motions—direct and retrograde—occur in every instance.

This is the state of affairs. Now, one might object: "Since the nature of the fruit [the result] is uniform throughout both the ascending and descending nodes (*nīcoccavṛtta*), how can there be a perception of it as 'I' (*ahaṃ-pratibhāsa*) within that field? Furthermore, the movement of the planet situated on the *nīcoccavṛtta* is perceived as a manifestation; yet, in reality, there is no movement of the planet from its position on the *nīcoccavṛtta*. Why? Because no movement arises from a fixed point on the *nīcoccavṛtta*."

Otherwise, how could there be such a discrepancy in the slow motion [of planets] therein? Indeed, when a planet is situated in its true position between two nodes (apoklima), why do the results calculated by the various schools of thought not accord with reality? Since the occurrence of results is established through their respective systems of knowledge, this is a firm and endless question. According to the rule *prajñādi-bhyaḥ aṇ*, one who possesses wisdom is called *prājña*; thus, the fruit previously described has been conceived as being for the purpose of focusing on the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of those results.

And it is the true nature of things (*vastusvabhāva*). That [eccentricity] arises for one who has attained the realization of the non-abiding state. It is not like the form of a circle or a square; rather, just as the result of the *maṇḍala* (orb) is intended for the sake of the practice of the path, the name "lower circle" (*nīceṣuvṛtta*) is accepted by those who know the truth of the sages. And just as for the purpose of producing a reflection, the sine of the *maṇḍala* can be calculated, so too, for the sake of lightness, this [eccentricity] has been devised by the Lord of the World (*Śvaśura*) as the bestower of the fruit of liberation.

The sense is that, although the nature of the fruit is understood according to each specific mode for the sake of accomplishing the fruit, it is not [attained] in reality through such modes; rather, it is attained through the actual state of being. (31) In this context, how could the fruit—which is described as being free from fear—possibly arise otherwise? For fearlessness is established by great regions and great minds; otherwise, it would be explained differently. (56fthāne *phreṃdrathana kaī bhavatasyavaśyamabhyai paiye taśkathaṃ saṃbhavati | prativurbhayaṃ-vad deśairmahadvairmahāmanasyānyathā pratipā)

In response to the question "How shall I eat?", the one with the pestle (Muśalika) said, "I shall eat. In the Golādhyāya, Mañjūṣābhāṣya, two diagrams (*bhaṅga*) were presented; the two arrangements of the higher and lower [orbits] as previously stated were understood and written together in a single orbital circle (*kakṣāvṛtta*) as described. Here, within the diagram (*miśrabhaṅgī*) thus written:

In both orbits, at the point where the line of sight from the observer's eye intersects the respective orbit, the planet is marked according to the method stated for each; that is the meaning of "then" (*tadānīm*). Since the conjunction of the eye and the orbit occurs at one single point, the planet must necessarily be located there by rule. Because the planet is found at the intersection of the two orbits through the aforementioned marking on a single orbit, the word "also" (*api*) serves to exclude the possibility of assigning the planet's position redundantly on the second orbit.

In the second verse, it should be understood that this is for the purpose of removing the doubt as to whether or not a mark arrives at the previous planetary mark by means of the aforementioned addition of longitude. Furthermore, since the circumference of the [ecliptic] circle meets the circumferences situated on either side of the respective circle, and because there is no difference between the other two circumferences and the sine of the result (*phalajyā*), the planetary mark on the *kṣayavṛtta* (declination circle) is not very far from the planetary mark situated on the *ativṛtta* (oblique ascension circle). Since the oblique ascension circle has the middle of the planet as its center, by adding the longitude in the direct order (*anuloma*), the intersection with that very point occurs.

The planetary motion becomes [as described]. Otherwise, how could the planets, split asunder by the fire of destruction, remain? The sense is that this is because they are situated within the interior of the earth. (32) Now, an objection: the motion of the planets in their respective eccentric circles (*prativṛtta*) is contrary to their non-depressed motion; it has been postulated based on the necessity of explaining the resulting effects (*phalavāsanā*), but this is not logical. For it is impossible for a single entity to be the locus of two contradictory actions, since such a thing does not exist in reality. Indeed, nothing of that nature is well-known, by which one might infer such a configuration from oil.

Because conceptualization (*kalpanā*) is everywhere like the breaking of a bow, he establishes this through an illustration using the *upajāti* meter, beginning with "just as" (*yathā*). Just as oil is produced by the grinding of sesame seeds within an oil-press—well known in the world as a machine for extracting oil—so too, when a heavy stone wheel (*mūrvajhaṣa*) is placed inside a mortar (*ulūkhala*) and set in motion by the pressing of sesame seeds, its own natural rotation becomes intensified by the powerful turning of the oxen.

In that context, "counter-clockwise" (aprasavya) means that it revolves in the opposite direction; even while being rotated by its own velocity, it produces a clockwise revolution. Likewise, for a planet moving along the path of the epicycle (pratimaṇḍala), its motion in the eccentric circle (nīvṛtta) is in the opposite direction to the path of the epicycle. Furthermore, by the word "also" (api), it is indicated that the eccentric circle is not the actual agent of rotation, but rather a mere appearance.

And thus, just as in the case of the planets' movement within their respective mandalas, even on the orbital path (kakṣā), because the planet moves there in accordance with its arrival at the middle of the house (the apogee), the planet's revolution there is in the opposite direction; this is the meaning established by the illustration. (33) Now, he states the reason for the true position (sphuṭatva) resulting from the two operations of slow (manda) and fast (śīghra): "Since the center of the slow-apogee circle (mandoccapada) would move upon the circle called its own orbit (svakakṣā) which is reachable by the mean [planet]..."

In its revolution, the mean planet is likewise [located] at the apogee and perigee of the slow epicycle; thus, the true planet is found in the fast epicycle. First, the manda correction was performed to determine the mean position of the fast apogee and perigee; thereafter, the śīghra correction was applied for the sake of knowing the true position. Since these two corrections depend upon one another, they were indeed calculated by means of mutual iteration. By reflecting on the structure of the slow apogee epicycle, it is understood that this [true planet] results from such a process. Thus ends the chapter on the calculation of the true planet.

187. [Objection: Even so, since the true planet is obtained by correcting the mean planet with the equations of anomaly (manda-phala) and apsis (śīghra-phala)—which arise from the displacement of the planet's position in the eccentric orbit (nīcocca-vṛtta) according to the respective slow and fast eccentric circles located at the center of the apsis-circle situated within the orbital circle (kakṣā-vṛtta)—the state of being a "true planet" results from this correction. Therefore, he says in the *Sragviṇī* meter: "By the mean motion... (*madhyagatyā*). The planet should move through its own orbital circle (kakṣā-vṛtta) by means of its mean motion.

[Objection: Surely, because the planet's position on the epicycle (kakṣāvṛtta) is not otherwise possible due to the discrepancy in the resulting [longitude], how can it be said that "it moves through the day by its mean motion" there? To this, he says: "of the slow [mean] planet situated on its apogee-epicycle. For this reason, the mean place of the slow mean planet situated on its apogee-epicycle would be the mean [place] situated on the orbit (kakṣā). And thus, even in the absence of a fixed position on the [eccentric] circle, since the place of the mean planet's longitude exists on the orbit, it is assumed that the mean planet moves through the day by its mean motion.

Otherwise, the meaning is: how could the slow apsis-epicycle (*mandanīcoccavṛtta*) be drawn for the purpose of knowing the [slow] equation? By this, it is indicated that since there is no mark of the mean planet situated on the orbit (*kakṣā*) at the center of the fast apsis-epicycle (*śīghranīcoccavṛtta*), the fast apsis-epicycle does not intersect the position of the mean planet. Now, one might ask: "In that case, why is the fast apsis-epicycle difficult to draw? To this he says: "On those two epicycles" (*tadvṛttayoḥ*). This refers to the point of intersection on the circumference of the orbital circle (*kakṣāvṛtta*) where the line of the slow radius (*mandakarṇasūtra*) meets it; that is, the position of the slow true planet (*mandasphuṭa*).

The meaning is that [the planet] is joined with its velocity due to knowing the region of its apogee and perigee within the mandocca-nīcocca-vṛtta (the epicycle of apsis), but not because the planet is situated on the circumference of the mandocca-nīcocca-vṛtta itself. The mean [position] of the planet is obtained by adding the successive corrections for the śīghra-phala (equation of center) as understood through the method of the śīghra-phala to the apogee and perigee.

The meaning is as follows: just as the center of the epicycle of apsis (śaminīcoccavṛtta) lies at the position of the mean planet within its orbit (kakṣā), in exactly the same way, the center of the epicycle of apsis lies at the position of the slow-mean planet (mandasphuṭagraha) within that very orbit; therefore, it should be marked there. When the motion of the slow-mean planet is applied to the epicycle of apsis, the true planet (sphuṭa-graha)—which is the form of the actual celestial body—resides at its proper place therein.

And thus, since there is an absence of both corrections at the mean planet, there is no room for the doubt as to by which correction the true state [of the planet] is achieved; the sense is that the true planetary motion is established through the successive application of the two corrections. || 34 ||

Now, in the *Ghanīccocca-vṛtta*, after the true position of the planet has been established through the correction of the slow anomaly (*mandaphala*), the fast anomaly (*śīghraphala*) is applied. Under the guise of explaining the resulting corrections for the anomaly, the author states further details in the *Sragviṇī* meter, beginning with "śīghranīcocca... (the fast apogee and perigee).

In order to know the position of the center—the central location of the Moon’s orbit of apogee and perigee—these two [corrections] quickly establish the orbit within the Moon’s orbit of apogee and perigee; for this purpose, first the slow correction (*mānda-karma*) is applied to the mean planet, because that [mean planet] occupies the center of the orbit where the slow true longitude resides.

Immediately thereafter, for the sake of understanding planetary motion (*kheṭabodha*), a planet situated on its orbit at the velocity of its apogee or perigee is observed in that orbital sector by means of its arc; for the purpose of knowing its true longitude (*sphuṭabhaga*) in that orbital sector, the superior operation (*śreṣṭhakarma*) is applied to the mean-slow correction (*mandasphuṭa*). Now, he states the procedure for the repeated calculation (*asakṛtsādhana*)—namely, "mutually" (*mithaḥ*). For indeed, the two results—the slow (*mānda*) and the swift (*śaighrya*)—are mutually dependent (*parasparaṃ saṃśrite*, i.e., *sāpekṣe*). For that reason, those two results are calculated one after the other repeatedly. This is the meaning.

The mean planet corrected by the slow (manda) equation in the chapter on the true planet (388, 067) becomes the true (spaṣṭa) planet. In that context, because the mean planet is coarse, the slow equation calculated from it is coarse; the true slow anomaly produced by correcting with that [equation] is coarse, and the fast (śīghra) equation calculated from that is coarse; therefore, even the true planet remains coarse.

Therefore, because the true [mean] planet is [used as the base], the slow correction (mandaphala) calculated from it is subtle; thus, by applying that correction, the slow-mean-true planet (mandaspaṣṭa) becomes subtle. The fast correction (śīghraphala) calculated from that is also subtle; hence, the three corrections (triphala) are subtle. Since the slow correction and the mean correction depend upon the true planet, the planet is established with increasing subtlety through repeated calculation starting from the initial true planet. This has been stated extensively in the commentary on the *Sphuṭādhikāra*; therefore, enough of this digression.

In the case of the mandaprativṛtta, that place which faces the location of the Saṃghātyabhogasthāna is the center; and in the case of the śīghraprativṛtta, the śīghraprativṛtta is on the circle whose diameter is twice the trijyā, with that point as its center which lies at a distance from the center of the mandaprativṛtta equal to the interval between the trijyā and the jyā of the śīghra-antyaphala.

In that [deferent], a line drawn from the center toward the point of the mean anomaly on the epicycle of the apogee intersects the deferent at the position of the apogee. Then, by the distance equal to the mean anomaly (the difference between the mean planet and the apogee), measured from Aries and so forth, the position reached by the mean planet's revolutions is the place where the planet's disk is situated at the center of the earth on the deferent; this is the mean [longitude].

The line drawn from the point where the mean planet lies at the apogee (śīghrocca) along the radius, intersecting the epicycle (śīghraprativṛtta), marks the true apogee (sphuṭa-śīghrocca). From there, the distance to the mean planet (manda-sphuṭagraha) is exactly as previously determined for the planetary disc. The straight line from the apogee to the center of the planetary disc along the epicycle is the sine of the argument (bhujajyā). The straight line from the planetary disc to the horizontal line of the orbit (kakṣāvṛtta) is the cosine of the argument (koṭijyā). The line from the center of the earth to the center of the planetary disc is the hypotenuse (trikarṇa).

In the eccentric circle (*kakṣāvṛtta*), where the line of the swift epicycle (*śīghrakarṇasūtra*) intersects, there is the true daily motion (*spaṣṭa-rāhubhoga*). The cosine-sine (*koṭijyā*) of that [angle] is the mean true planet. The anomaly (*kendrajya*) corresponding to the swift apogee (*śīghrocca*) is the reflected center (*pratiśrutkendra*). By means of the interval between that and the center of the Earth (*bhūgarbha*), the true cosine (*spaṣṭakoṭi*) is obtained—added or subtracted according to the anomaly in the signs beginning with Capricorn (*mṛga*). From that, by the previous method, the sine of the arm (*bhujajyā*) and the swift epicycle radius (*śīghrakarṇa*) and so forth are to be understood.

By means of the line of the apogee of the mandocca situated at the lower point (*nīca*), according to the stated method, the circle of the apsis of the slow motion (*manda-nīcocca-vṛtta*) is formed; where the place of the mean planet lies within that [circle], there, by means of the radius of the circle of the apsis of the fast motion (*śīghra-nīcocca-vṛtta*)—which has the sine of the maximum equation of the fast motion as its semi-diameter—the circle of the apsis of the fast motion is drawn. There, from the center of the earth, a perpendicular line is drawn toward the position of the planet on the circle of the apsis of the slow motion, touching the circumference of the circle of the apsis of the fast motion. Where it touches, that is the *śīrya* (the point of intersection). From that line, the sine and cosine values are produced neither obliquely nor vertically.

As has been stated, by means of the slow and true longitudes of the planets; then, situated on the circle of the Sun's apogee (śanikaṭastha) and located on the two nonagesimal circles (dvinavṛttastha), they exist in the form of a line drawn from the center of the Earth to the center of the great sphere (mahāvibhva). In this system, the calculation of the "slow moment" (mandakṣaṇa) at the place of the trigonometric radius (trijyāsthāna) should be understood according to the method previously described for the Earth. They say that, as heard in the tradition, "in those two circles, the [mean] apogee and the middle [longitude] are likewise [treated]," thus it is consistent with the literal text. Now, regarding the ear (karṇa) in the operation of the slow motion (mandakarmaṇi):

Anticipating the doubt, "Why is this not done here?", he says: Some say: "Why is the ear (karṇa) not applied here, since it increases its own [radius] internally? Even when the ear is applied—though divided by the trijyā—the circumference (paridhi) becomes clear (sphuṭa) here; therefore, the result (phala) becomes equal to the [original] length. For that reason, some have stated that the ear is indeed applied and there is no inclination (nati). This should not be doubted. Why is it not so in the case of the moving [circle]? Because the underlying rationale for the results (phalavāsanā) here is manifold. How is it that it is not brought about in this very manner? It is indeed correct.

That which is not obtained through the manda-karṇa operation is like another intrinsic form; for the manda-phala-svadhās (the squares of the manda-phalas) become small. And that difference is extremely slight; such is the section on Chedyaka (geometrical construction). This is the view of some. Here, Balabhadra states the reason: "The circumference divided by the trijyā and multiplied by the karṇa," and so forth. In the manda-karman, the circle that is produced with a radius equal to the manda-karṇa is the kakṣā-maṇḍala (orbit-circle); by means of that, the planet moves.

The circumference which is recited in the text has been converted into [the value for] the radius of the circle (trijyā). Therefore, it is now converted into the chord corresponding to the hypotenuse (karṇa). From this, the proportion follows: if this circumference corresponds to a circle of radius equal to the radius of the celestial sphere (trijyā), then what would it be for a circle of radius equal to the hypotenuse? Here, the multiplier for the circumference is the hypotenuse and the divisor is the radius of the celestial sphere (trijyā). Thus, the arc (dora) is multiplied by that clear circumference and divided by 360. Then, it is multiplied by the radius of the celestial sphere (trijyā) and divided by the hypotenuse.

This being the case, when the multiplier and divisor—being equal to the sine of the argument (*trijyā*) and equal to the hypotenuse (*karṇa*) respectively—are both eliminated due to their equality, the resulting quotient is exactly the same as the previous result; such is the opinion of Brahmagupta. Now, raising the objection: "If the circumference (*paridhi*) is thus made precise by the hypotenuse, then why was this not done in the calculation of the *śīghra* (mean anomaly)? Caturveda replies: "Brahmagupta stated this solely for the purpose of deceiving others. That is incorrect. One should not raise the doubt: "Why did he not do it this way in the other operation?"

Since the retrograde motions (*phaṭaghasanā*) are diverse—Venus being otherwise than its mean longitude, and Mars likewise—why should one not suspect that Mercury and the others are also so? Therefore, there is no room for doubt; hence, the statement regarding their strength (*bala*) here is appropriate. Now, he states the rationale (*vāsanā*) for the operation of parallax (*nata*): An observer situated at the center of the earth sees a planet located on the eccentric circle (*pratimaṇḍala*) within the orbital sphere (*kakṣā*) at a certain point as having no parallax; however, one standing on the surface of the earth does not see it in that same position.

At midday, however, because the person situated at the center and the back see [the object] equally, that same logic which was stated by him in the rule for calculating parallax (*lamvana*) applies here as well. (38) Now he states the position where there is an absence of the result of motion (*gati-phala*): When the planet has reached the intersection of the circle of the apsis-line with the circle of the orbit at the point of the center, it is the mean; there, the planet’s true [longitude] is at its maximum correction. (39)

At the point of intersection between the oblique line drawn across the middle of the kakṣāvṛtta (orbital circle) and the epicycle (*prativṛtta*), the motion is indeed precisely the true motion, because there is an absence of any correction for the motion (*gatiphala*). Furthermore, at that point, the planet's maximum correction (*phala*) would occur. Where the planet's maximum correction occurs, there must likewise be an absence of any correction for the motion; for the difference between the current and previous positions of the planet is the motion (*gati*), and the difference between two corrections is the correction for the motion (*gatiphala*).

When the motion of a planet is zero, that very point of aphelion (phalābhāvasthāna) is the conjunction of the apsis (aisaṃdhi). As for what was further stated—that "when the planet is situated at the junction of two circles, its mean motion itself is the true motion"—that is incorrect; for at the junction of two circles, the planet does not possess its maximum equation (paramaṃ phalam). || 31 ||

Chapter 39, Verse 8: Regarding the calculation of the slow (manda) anomaly according to the method described for the residual correction (*mandīdha-phala-vāsanā*), one might raise the objection: "Why has the proportionality of the radius (*karṇānupāta*) not been stated here for the calculation of the slow anomaly? To answer this doubt, the author speaks in two *indravaṃśā* and *upajāti* verses beginning with "svalpa": "In this treatise on planetary calculation (*grahagaṇita*), regarding the 'slow operation' (*mṛdu-karman*)—that is, the calculation of the slow anomaly—the proportionality of the radius (*karṇānupāta*) is [omitted] because the difference is very small (*svalpāntaratvāt*)."

The meaning is that because there is a small difference between the result obtained without that proportion and the result obtained from that proportion, the *manda-phala* (slow anomaly correction) itself is small. Thus, where the result is near its maximum value, there the difference is small because the hypotenuse (*karṇa*) is equal to the radius (*trijyā*); and where the hypotenuse differs greatly from the radius—whether it is greater or less than the radius—there the difference is small because the result itself is very large. For example, this is seen in the final *phalajyā* of Mars.

The sine of the argument (bhujajyā) is 118; the result for the argument (bhujaphala) is 22; 56; 40. The degrees of the slow motion correction (manduphalāṃśa) are 10; 58; 20. From the proportion based on the hypotenuse (karṇa) of 118, the result for the argument is 23; 20. The degrees of the slow motion correction are 11; 10. The difference between these two is twelve minutes (kalās), which is a small discrepancy. Therefore, it was neither performed nor mentioned. In this manner, certain calculators who understand the underlying rationale (upapatti) speak of and accept that the proportion for the slow motion hypotenuse (manda-karṇānupāta) has not been stated [in the text].

Now, since the correction for the difference in longitude due to rising at another place, the difference in amplitude (*bhuja*), the difference in time, the difference in *svara*, and so forth, would otherwise be like offering water with one's hands empty, Brahma-gupta stated the following solution to resolve that objection—intimated by the word "some" (*kecit*)—beginning with the verse: "multiplied by the radius" (*trijyoddhṛta*). How [is this]? When the proportion based on the slow epicycle (*mandakarṇa*) has been performed, the meaning is that there is a specific difference in the slow equation (*mandaphala*) produced thereby, as indicated by the word "also" (*api*).

[Objection: "But surely, since the slow-motion anomaly (manda-phala) is always of small magnitude and thus indeterminate, it cannot be equal to the radius of the celestial sphere (trijyā); therefore, the correction made by it in the anomaly is indeed appropriate.
