To this, he provides the reason, beginning with "trijyā": because in this slow-motion operation, the previously mentioned circumference (paridhi) is multiplied by the slow hypotenuse (manda-karṇa) and divided by the radius of the celestial sphere; thus, it becomes the corrected slow circumference. It is then proper to calculate the sine and cosine anomalies from such a circumference using the rule "multiplied by its own [anomaly] and so forth. For that reason:

The result derived from the previously stated inferior circumference (mandaparidhi) yields a small fruit. This is what is meant: those inferior circumferences mentioned earlier are required on the epicycle (kakṣāvṛtta) with a radius equal to the trijyā (radius of the celestial sphere), whereas here they are required with a radius equal to the hypotenuse (karṇa). This is because [the planet] is situated at the tip of the hypotenuse during an eclipse. Indeed, it is not appropriate to calculate the result using a circumference belonging to a different dimension; for if that were the case, the result derived from the superior circumference would be correct. Therefore, [the calculation must be done] with a radius equal to the hypotenuse.

The circumferences have been stated; then, by the proportion "what [is the circumference] for a diameter equal to the radius? the circumferences are determined by the measure of the true orbit, which takes the form of a circle with a radius equal to the radius-vector (*karṇa*). Here, the apsis-circle (*mandanīcoccavṛtta*) is not at the radius-vector, but rather at the radius of the celestial sphere (*trijyā*); otherwise, the calculation of the equation of the center (*phala*) according to the stated method would be untenable.

However, there is this much distinction: in a circle whose diameter is half the radius of the epicycle (*vikṣepa*), the middle mandocca-nīca circle (the eccentric circle) becomes large or small according to the value of the *manda-karṇa* (mean distance). The *bhujaphala* and *koṭiphalā* must be calculated in that circle using such a circumference. Thus, in this case, the *karṇa* must be computed repeatedly; it should be understood that this is because the previous *karṇa* is unknown. Likewise, the mean circumference should be calculated from the fixed *manda-karṇa*. From that, the *bhujaphala* and *koṭiphalā* are derived, and these two are used as the basis for the operation of the true planet's position. From those two, by means of proportion based on the *karṇa*, the two *manda* corrections (*phale mānde*) are made precise.

Therefore, for the sake of making the previously mentioned paridhi accurate, the Cheudheira school [states]: "The divisor at the end, multiplied by the trijyā, is the same as the multiplier; thus the multiplier and divisor are equal. This concludes their view: that the results derived from the paridhi brought forward—the sine of the arc (bhuja) and the desired increment (iṣṭiphala)—are established as the sine of the latitude (koṭiphala) which serves as the basis for the manda-phala and other corrections. For this reason, at the end, due to the possibility of the elimination of both the hypotenuse-proportion (karṇānupāta) and the equality [of multiplier and divisor], there is simplicity (lāghava); such is the meaning.

The reason the proportion for the slow epicycle (*mandakarṇānupāta*) was not performed in the calculation of the result is that certain authorities, such as Brahmagupta, Śrīpati, Bhaṭṭa, and others, have provided a method to avoid this proportion for the slow epicycle as follows: "The circumference multiplied by the hypotenuse (*karṇa*) and divided by the radius (*trijyā*) is the multiplier for the sine and cosine. In the case of the slow [equation], that result is repeated until it is equal to another; therefore, there is no need for the hypotenuse here. In the calculation of the slow correction, the circumference multiplied by the radius and divided by the hypotenuse becomes the multiplier for the sine and cosine, and this should be done repeatedly."

They say that in this case the result would be equal to only a small portion, and therefore the authors of the Tantras did not include it when the correction was made; such is the meaning of statements like "the correction is not soft. Furthermore, the sense is that this previous opinion is correct. Now, one might object: if it is multiplied by the true [longitude], the apogee remains based solely on the *khaṇḍakhādya*, and in that system the maximum equation does not reach its full value; moreover, it is not logically consistent. It has been stated that because the correction (*vāsanā*) is equal to the result itself, the difference is so slight that it is as good as not done.

"The radius [of the epicycle] divided by the trijyā," and so forth; this rule for the hundred circles (śatamaṇḍalaka) is intended to produce a result with only a slight error in the case of slow motion (mandakarma). However, in the case of fast motion (śīghrakarma), it would otherwise be different. Nor should it be argued that even in fast motion it may be neglected because the error is small; for in that case, due to the extreme magnitude of the circumference (paridhi), there is a large difference in degrees. Thus, it is said that [the correction] need not be performed in slow motion because the error is small.

The previously stated resolution alone is appropriate because of the statement of Caturvedācārya; therefore, he refutes [the objection] from another perspective by means of Brahmagupta and Bhāskara, saying "No. Regarding the calculation of the *śīghraphala* (equation of center) for the moving [planet]: why should there not likewise be a removal of the proportionality involving the *śīghrakarṇa* (epicycle radius), just as there was a stated removal of the proportionality involving the *mandakarṇa*? By the repetition of the word "thus" (*ittham*), one should not entertain such a doubt based on the statement of Caturvedācārya. The meaning is that such a doubt should not be raised. He states the reason for this: "Because... (*yataḥ*).

In this investigation of the rationale for clear computational procedures, the justification for the results—the derivation of the slow and fast equations of motion—is manifold; that is to say, it is not of a single uniform form.

And likewise, the epicycles and so forth are imagined through a division of mental constructs for the sake of producing results; thus it has been said: "The manda-epicycles are also imagined upon the orbit of the middle [mean] motion in the Ārṣa texts for the purpose of rotating the trijyā (sine of three signs), because they are not explicitly stated as being proportional to the [true] motion; and the śīghra-epicycles are imagined at the tip of the karṇa (hypotenuse) when the karṇa is at its maximum value of arrow-minutes, because they are seen to be stated as being proportional to the karṇa. This raises a doubt. The sense is that when there is a superimposition (āropa), one seeks the underlying cause (nimitta), but it is not the case that a superimposition exists simply because a cause exists.

Some, however, hold that this [method] contains the seed of an underlying dissatisfaction (*asvarasa*). For, since the slow circle (*mandapārighavṛtta*) is drawn by unifying the marks of the apogee located on the kakṣā-line with the center, there is a lack of evidence for postulating a circumference following the perimeter of a circle whose radius is half the distance from the center to the apsis (*karṇa*). Furthermore, there is a lack of coordination (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*). If it were based on scripture (*āgama*), one might as well simply assume it out of parsimony (*lāghava*) without explicitly stating the proportion involving the *karṇa*.

According to the Karupaka school, however, the position of the slow-mean (manda-spaṣṭa) is not at the center of the slow epicycle (manda-nīcocca-vṛtta), but rather at the point where the line from the center of the fast epicycle (śīghra-nīcocca-vṛtta)—drawn along the radius of the slow epicycle toward the mark of the planet on the slow epicycle—intersects the circumference of the slow epicycle; this is the center of the fast epicycle and the position of the slow-mean according to the Hindu system. (Note: *Mandapratibimba-sthatvāt* means "because of being situated as a reflection of the slow [mean]"; *mandaprasiddha-sakendra-sama-sūtreṇa* means "by a line from the established center of the slow [epicycle]"; *galothāye-maeīe* is a transcription of a regional term for the intersection point on the circumference.)

And thus, the difference between the mean anomaly and the true anomaly is the equation of the center (*mandaphala*); its sine is equal to the correction for the argument (*bhujaphala*), which takes the form of a line parallel to the line joining the planet to the apogee on the epicycle of the apsis (*mandanīcoccavṛtta*). Consequently, there arises the undesirable consequence that the equation of the center would be zero. They claim that when the planet is drawn toward the point of true longitude on the orbital circle (*kakṣāvṛtta*) along a line parallel to the radius vector (*śarikaṇa*), the proportion involving the radius vector applies; however, this is to be considered.

Because the true longitude of a planet is accepted at that point on the orbital path (kakṣā) where the line drawn from the center through the observed planet intersects it—since the true positions of the Sun and Moon cannot be established without the proportionality of the hypotenuse (bhakarṇa)—it cannot be argued that the true position of the Sun and Moon occurs at the point on the orbit where the line passing through the center of the slow epicycle (mandaprativṛtta) and directed toward its center intersects the orbit, rather than on the hypotenuse-line.

For the planets beginning with Mars as well, one might argue that the true longitude of a planet occurs at the point where a line drawn from the center of the epicycle (the *pratimaṇḍala*) to the planetary image located on that epicycle intersects the [deferent] circle; however, this is not accepted because there is no determining factor for such a claim, and because it would render the calculation of the *karṇa* (the hypotenuse) in the process of rapid motion (*śīghrakarma*) untenable. This is due to the aforementioned reasoning being inconsistent.

Now, if it is argued that the correction for the ear (karṇa) is omitted for the Sun and Moon because their difference is very small, then that same omission could also apply to Mars and the other planets; furthermore, there would be unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*) and a lack of authoritative evidence (*pramāṇābhāva*) in postulating different forms for the slow-mean and mean positions by means of distinct methods. (37) Furthermore, incidentally, it has been stated that a planet moving without deviation in its own epicycle (*pratimaṇḍala*) is seen by men at a certain point on the orbital path (*kakṣāvalaya*); however, this is untenable, for [the planet] is indeed seen at the point of the true position (*sphuṭa*).

In response to the doubt that there is an absence of humans within the interior of the earth (*bhūgarbha*), [the author], refuting the view of some who cite *nata-karma* as stated by Brahmagupta, declares the purpose of the circle inscribed on the *ccheya-jhali* (the wall) in the *Dūlavikrīḍita* meter, beginning with the words "āpaścāt" (and after). In the eastern hemisphere (*prākpāla*), it extends from midnight until midday; in the western hemisphere (*paścimakapāla*), it extends from midday until midnight. Here, the hemisphere in which the planets are situated during their respective halves of the day or night is to be known as the "observable hemisphere" (*jñeyabhra*).

At that time, an observer situated on the surface of the earth perceives the planet located in its respective mandala at whichever point in its orbit it views it along a line parallel to that orbital position; the meaning is "along a line parallel to that specific point of the orbit. An observer such as Āryabhaṭa, standing on the earth's surface, does not see the planet situated on the counter-circle (pratimaṇḍala), because the line from the earth's surface to that point is not parallel to the line from the center of the earth (the *karṇa* or *bhagīratha-sūtra*).

However, the line of sight from the observer on the Earth's surface to a planet situated in its orbit is a line drawn from the Earth's surface; one observes the planet along that line where it intersects the orbit. Since there is necessarily a difference between the true planet as seen from the Earth's center and the true planet as seen from the surface, the intent is this: the difference between the lines of sight from the Earth's center and the surface must be applied as a correction to the true planet at the Earth's center in order to determine the true longitude of the planet as seen from the Earth's surface.

Since the refinement [of the celestial sphere] is not mentioned in the *Ārṣa* treatises, there might arise the notion that there is no difference between the true planet and its apparent position due to the assumption that the observer is situated on the surface of the earth rather than at its center. To refute this, the word "indeed" (*khalu*) is used. By means of drawing the terrestrial circle (*bhūvṛtta*) in the diagram (*chedyaka*), it is shown that just as the line of sight (*dṛgjyasūtra*) extends from the center of the earth to the planet situated at the observer's location on the surface, so too does the line of sight extend from the center of the earth to the planet situated at the observer's location on the circumference (the surface) of the earth. Thus, the observation of the planet from the surface of the earth is established.

Since it is known that the ear is pierced directly, and since the distinction of the clearly manifest experience is established by direct perception, it is indicated that the excavation of the "earth-tree" (bhūvṛkṣa) serves a specific purpose. [This is] stated individually. 193. [Verse 80: Now, an objection is raised: "But the distance between those two is not established by calculation. To this he says: "out of fear" (*bhayāt*). This means at the midday of the planet; because of the word "but" (*tu*), it refers to the form of the *kaṣala-sandhi*. It also means at the midnight of the planet.

The two persons situated at the center and the surface of the earth—namely, one at the center of the earth and one on its surface—observe each planet situated on its respective orbit as having an identical form and experiencing an equal motion. For this reason, the calculation of parallax (*natakarma*), as stated in the *Sphuṭādhikāra* (the chapter on true motions) and composed by Brahmagupta, is indeed logical and consistent with that principle.

Furthermore, when a planet is located on the prime vertical (*yāmyottaravṛtta*) at the junction of the celestial hemisphere (*kapālasaṃdhi*), the line extending from the center of the earth meets the orbital path (*kakṣāpradeśa*) at a certain point; from that point, the line extending to the surface of the earth is further [extended].

Since the great [disk] is seen by those like us at that point where the meridian intersects the horizon, the distance between the two lines [of sight]—which is natural due to the difference between Śiva and Parā—is clearly distinct; therefore, the interval between those two lines arises from the effect of depression (nata). Thus, they state that the calculation for the end of the solar disk as intended by Brahmagupta has been explained, while for others it was observed through a different nature. He refutes this with "No."

This [calculation] is not appropriate for the purpose of establishing the *upalabdhi* (perception) of the *brahmaguptatanuta-karman* (the operation of the curved motion of the planets), because it is inconsistent. He states the reason for this: "In the rule for parallax" (*lambanavidhau*). The velocity that exists in the method of calculating parallax is the same velocity found in the calculation of the Sun’s [longitude]. The word "api" (also/even) serves to include the correction for the difference in lunar days (*tithyantara*).

If it is argued that by considering the latitude (*lambana*) as the sine of the zenith distance (*nata*), it is obtained according to the method described, [we reply: no, for *lambana* does not occur in the *nata* values such that there would be a contradiction. Nor should it be said that there is no contradiction because of the statement regarding the attainment of the *vaṅkṣaṇa* (the flank) at the *āprastha* (the limit); for in that case, the calculation of that [latitude] is established only from the three-hour arc (*tribhonalagna*) itself.

Nor should it be said that this [lagna] is merely a name for a treasure-store (*nidhāna*), or that it is simply a variety of *mata* (the ascendant). This is because, by arising according to a single method, it possesses the appearance of such a restriction. Furthermore, since the result of the *nata* (the elapsed portion) is established by the aforementioned method, there is no contradiction with the results of the *manda-phala* (the slow-motion correction). In the case of the *prakṣālaka* (cleansing), the omission of the *sīghra-grahaṇa* (swift-correction) is intended; thus, in the final calculation, the result obtained through this analogy is appropriate for the Lord who knows all, and not otherwise, as it would lead to an inconsistency with the established tradition.

This is the *Ṛndanī* [method]. For the purpose of the sixfold knowledge (*ṣaṭkoṇajñāna*), another rule (*sūtrāntara*) must be applied: Just as when the true [longitude] of a planet at the time of the desired [calculation] is established, and the gnomon (*śaṅku*) is determined, it should then be multiplied by the fifteenth part of the midday shadow and divided by the sine [of the latitude]. The result is known as the *phīsiganalaya*. This should be multiplied by the radius (*trijyā*) and divided; the remainder, expressed in minutes (*kalā*), is to be subtracted from or added to the true planet depending on whether [the time] is less than or more than the day-measure (*aharmaya*). Thus, on the surface of the earth, the true planet shall be obtained. By this—[the verse continues: "The neck [is] pierced by the three-fold mountain... [etc.]

The portion of the moon’s light that has not been eclipsed is calculated as the divisor; the remainder is multiplied by sixty and divided by the divisor. The result is the fruit of one’s own time. Then, having subtracted the blue [portion] from the house, the remainder is the shadow. By day, this is the fruit; by night, it is the reverse. This is indeed the secret known by the experts. This dance performed here was not done because of a change in form.

[The opponent says: "If [the correction] were applied on the previous day, then at this time there would be a great utility for the *lakṣmī* situated on the earth's surface. This statement made by someone—namely, that "in the chapter on the sphere (Golādhyāya), verse 780..."—is refuted, because it is devoid of logical proof and because its assertions are mutually contradictory. Therefore, this correction is necessary; otherwise, knowledge of the planets on the terrestrial surface would not be possible in any way. [The opponent continues: "Since humans do not exist on the mountain of the earth, and since what pertains to them has no utility here [on the surface], [the correction is unnecessary]. If you say this, we reply: No.

Because the celestial sphere (bhagola) is not centered upon the surface of the earth, the observation of its diurnal motion (*cara*) cannot serve as the basis for predicting planetary results; whereas, since the center of the earth is indeed its center, the observation of that diurnal motion is necessary. Therefore, the correction for it is not applied [to the moon]—this is the intention regarding the Sun and other planets. Otherwise, how could they have stated, in the case of a solar eclipse, that the correction for the *lambana* and *avalambana* consists of a subtraction from the *cara*?

By this very statement, since the necessity of knowing the distinction between the center of the earth and its surface is established through the results of planetary motion, the mention of these [other] results makes the calculation of parallax and so forth redundant; for such [parallax] would also result in the case of a lunar eclipse. Therefore, by virtue of the connection with a point on the surface of the earth that is level with one's own location, the very planet that is uncorrected at the center of the earth becomes the corrected planet at the surface of the earth.

Otherwise, because the surfaces of the earth are infinite, the occurrence of many planets at a single time would lead to an uncertainty regarding the results for specific locations due to the movement of those planets, stars, and so forth. For this very reason, the entire collection of celestial bodies is accepted as being within the interior of the earth, not upon its surface; otherwise, even the declinations, diurnal arcs, and other such parameters would vary from place to place. Furthermore, phenomena such as parallax must be calculated on the earth's surface for the sake of empirical observation; otherwise, how could there be an observation of a solar eclipse by someone like us? And so on.

By this, [the following objections] are refuted: (1) that the word *natam* is made an adjective of *cara* and is construed with *yo bhūpṛṣṭhagaḥ*, such that since the action of bending (*nata-karman*) was already mentioned previously, this verse is intended merely to explain its nature; (2) that because the meanings are mutually contradictory, this [verse] is not by the original author; and (3) that the word *natam* is redundant, or that the action of bending has not been mentioned at all. || 38 ||

Now, as an incidental discussion, he supports his own method for calculating true motion—which differs from the method for calculating true motion stated clearly in previous works—by means of a verse in the *cheyaka* meter, beginning with "kakṣāmadhyaga" (situated in the middle of the orbit). The phrase "in the middle of the orbit" (*kakṣāmadhyaga*) refers to that portion of the counter-epicycle (*pratidvaṃsapaṛidhi*) which is situated within the circular orbit (*kakṣāvṛtta*), is horizontal, and touches the point on the ground; the meaning is: at the conjunction (*saṃpāte*) of those two, namely, the portion of the counter-epicycle's circumference that is horizontal and located in the middle of the orbit. The term "of Bhaṭṭa" (*bhaṭṭasya*) refers to [the author].

The true motion of that planet is equal to its mean motion. By the use of the word "only" (*eva*), the clear implication here is the rejection of the true motion calculated by the method described in the preceding text. The meaning is that the true motion is identical to the mean motion. Since the mean motion is indeed the slow (mean) true motion, one might ask: why is the true motion equal to the mean motion there? To this he says: "maximum. At that point, on a specific portion of the epicycle, the equation of the planet's motion is at its maximum.

In that case, when [the planet] has returned to the apogee (kendrastha), because the maximum equation is heard to be three nava-rāśis (twenty-seven signs), and because the hypotenuse and the sine of the angle are equal to the maximum sines of the anomaly and the argument respectively, and because the anomaly is at the apogee, there is an absence of correction for the apsis; thus, one side of the triangle is equal to the sine of the anomaly.

Therefore, by the rule "the result of the sine of the anomaly (thātaṅajajyā) is for those two," the three results are established; since the multiplier and divisor in the calculation of the sine of the argument (bhujajyā) and the hypotenuse (karṇa) cancel each other out, the remaining result is the maximum sine of the anomaly (paramaṃ śamraphalam). Consequently, because the hypotenuse there takes the form of the sine of the perpendicular (phalakoṭijyā), the determination of the difference between the degrees of the result is achieved through the verse beginning with "drākkendrabhuktiśrutih... In the calculation of the [mean] motion, the multiplier and divisor being equal constitutes the chapter on the correction of the anomaly (caidyakādhikāra).

195. From the [mean] motion, only the *śīghra-kendra-gati* (the velocity of the equation of center) remains; therefore, the velocity of the [mean] motion itself is equal to the *manda-spaṣṭa-gati* (the true velocity corrected for the anomaly). And this is logical, because the maximum [equation of] velocity is the velocity-result (*gati-phala*) of the anomaly, just as the maximum [equation of] fruit is the fruit-result (*phala-phala*) of the anomaly. Since there is no other fruit, it is certain that there is an absence of the fruit of velocity when the maximum fruit is reached. Furthermore, in the *mānda-karma* (the process of correction for the anomaly), it is certain that there is an absence of the fruit of velocity at the maximum fruit.

The addition and subtraction of the equations of center and the equation of anomaly occur precisely at the state where the [true] motion is zero. By this, the statement of Laḍa and others—that "the true motion is the sum of the [equations of] anomaly and center"—is refuted; for according to the method you have stated, the results of the [equations of] anomaly and center do not arise there [in that context]. Otherwise, in the first and third quadrants of the epicycle, the absence of the motion-result (gatiphala) as asserted by you would lead to an inconsistency with the earlier treatises, and it would result in the motion being merely the mean motion in all cases. || 39 ||

Now, having laughed at the crookedness [of others], he speaks for the purpose of explaining how it is correctly perceived in the *chedyaka* (geometrical diagram), as if it were cool: "Having made this as described by means of marks produced from bamboo for the sake of the circles, one should indeed move the celestial body with a bowstring and show everything, including the crocodile and other figures. (40)

Having made a division by means of a counting-stick (śalākā) and having placed the true position of the planet for the first day therein, one should determine another "peak" position (kūṭahasthāna) on the second day by calculating the rising point (udhyaṃ grahaṃ), the sign beginning with Aries (meṣādi), and so forth. If it is behind the rising point of the previous day, declare that it is moving with retrograde motion (vakragati).

Bhaṭṭotpala’s Commentary (Bha0ḍī0): Now, in this context, having laughed at the impossibility of the western course following the eastern course for a pure mind that has not yet attained clarity, he dispels the doubt regarding the nature of the [planetary] courses by means of the analogy of bamboo: "By those born of the bamboo" (*vaiṃśacābhiḥ*). This is established: that which is the great circle (*brāḍbhartimaṇḍala*) is the small circle (*kṣipratimaṇḍala*) and so forth, produced from straight and smooth bamboo slips.

Having constructed the grid of the initial squares with horizontal, vertical, and diagonal lines, along with the divisions of equal and unequal kalās and the marking of digits as previously described by the stated method; having performed the daily calculation of the planets—meaning having determined their retrograde and direct motions according to their own movements—the Guru demonstrated to the disciple the entire course of the planets, that is, the eightfold motion of all the planets as previously explained.

By the word "tu" (but/then), it is indicated that there must necessarily be a determination of the actual state of things (*vastutattva*) in that case. For instance—having placed a rough-scale diagram on a wall representing the division of zodiacal signs (*rāśivibhāga*), and having set down either the slow-mean planet (*mandaspaṣṭagraha*) or the fast-apogee (*śīghrārca*) according to one's own calculation, one should take the central point as equal to the sine of the other result and draw a line marked with the divisions of the signs. There too, having determined the planet's position according to the aforementioned method, the location of the true planet (*spaṣṭagraha*) should be known upon the epicycle (*kakṣāvṛtta*).

In this manner, on the second day as well, having given the true velocity correction (*śīghrāstra*) and the correction for the equation of center (*mandaspaṣṭīkaraṇa*) to the planet on its orbital circle (*kakṣāvṛtta*), one should determine the true position of the planet by adding the correction for the anomaly (*uccāntaram*) to the mean [longitude] and projecting it forward; there, by the addition of the [anomaly] correction according to the stated method, the true planetary position on the orbital circle is to be known. That [true position] will indeed be ahead of the true position produced on the previous day; however, when near the apogee (*nīca*), it is behind. The measure of retrograde motion (*vakragati*) on the orbital circle is not actually retrograde motion [in the physical sense].

Regarding the statement, "The neutralization of the retrograde weapon by the planet is impossible," and so forth, much has been said in the commentary on the *Sphuṭādhikāra*; enough of this digression. In the *Golādhyāya* (Chapter 393), he now states the definition of the apsis (*kendra*) and the true orbit (*sphuṭakakṣā*): "The center of the circle is indeed called the apsis; therefore, the apsis is said to be the difference between the [mean] longitude and [the anomaly]. Consequently, at that same interval, the apsis is always located above the point of the apogee. [Verse 41]

Laughing, with the rustling of his armpits, he became clearly manifest as a servant; filled with the fragments of that path, he indeed falls away by the force of the wind. (42) Both verses are clear. Now, he describes the correction for the difference in longitude: "The correction for the difference in longitude shall be negative when the result is less than the degrees of the middle mandocca; since immediately thereafter it is positive, the increase or decrease arising from the sun's correction is declared in the methods. (43)

The commentary on the eighth [chapter] regarding true motion is concluded. 43 || 787. Now, having laughed, [the author], desiring to state the difference arising from the planetary results, asks: "How is the doctrine concerning that which is designated as a *kendra* (quadrant) stated? He replies: "Of the planet," and so forth. Indeed, because that which has been traversed is designated as a *kendra*, therefore the interval between the planets is called a *kendra* by the Sun and the others. But why is the middle portion of the orbit, ending in the prefix *pra*, considered a *kendra*? To this he says: "Because," and so forth.

Therefore, O calculator! At the fifteenth degree from the apogee, in the inner circle (kakṣāvṛtta) within the interior form, the correction for the apsis (mīnoccāntara) is situated at the middle point. This is the removal of the error [previously] stated by Śrīvara. Thus, it is always located at the center (kendra). Consequently, the interval between the planet and the center is called the "distance" (sphuṭāntara) because of its connection with the distance; this is the meaning. [Objection: But surely, due to the planet's retrograde motion and so forth, there would be an undesirable discrepancy in the nights and days, as a great difference would arise because the position on the eccentric circle (pratimaṇḍala) would be gross here.

He avoids [the objection] by means of a similar illustration: "In the case of a planet. The diameter of a planet in *yojanas* divided by the radius of the celestial sphere (*trijyā*) is the true [diameter] of the planet in *yojanas*. Here he states the reason: "That," etc. Because it is separated from the center of the earth by half its diameter, the planet appears as if situated at the surface of the earth due to the distance. It moves along the *pravaha* wind.

Because it revolves there, it is joined; [the text] "aśubhra" [indicates] the bright side. The meaning is that on the right-hand side (dakṣapārśvabhāge), the earth's surface (bhūbhā) revolves within the interval between the praise and the end. By the syllable *bu* in the word *mehakṣecanamnaṇa*, the upward movement caused by the Pravaha wind is indicated. This is the intended sense (*bhāva*). By this, the orbits (*kakṣabha*) are clearly defined; they do not deviate from their positions.

The statement that "the middle axis is the middle path, and the chariots go above and below, with the eyes looking downward" is refuted. For, by way of the axis-circle (*akṣavṛtta*), the planets travel along the path of the earth's portion; thus, in the case of the *bhasmavṛtta*, the movement of the planets occurs precisely at the middle axis. This [middle axis] is merely an appearance (*ābhāsamātratvāt*). 42.

Chapter on Subtractions, 194. Commentary (Maṇḍī): Since the correction for the difference in the results of the [true] longitude and the [mean] longitude is for the purpose of determining the planet’s position, he says: "Indeed, by the flowing [equation], the mean [longitude] is corrected. When death occurs, because of that cause, prior to the time of the rising of the mean sun, how [is it]? 15. Therefore, the result of addition [is applied] after the rising of the mean sun; subsequently, the true sunrise is established. This is because, for one situated in the previous state, the possibility of sunrise exists at both the previous and subsequent times due to the force of the wind.

For that reason, the sage Sūryamathakalaka stated that the result is the sum [of the corrections], the face is the interval between the arms, the destruction is one's own, and the sequence is the ear and the positive value; this is established by reasoning. The result for the Sun, multiplied by the degrees of the Sun joined with the Sun, and so forth, has been clearly stated as the *spaṣṭadhī*.

And thus, for the sake of achieving true (spaṣṭa) planetary positions, there is no correction by means of the equation of center (bhuja-antara-phala), because the mean longitude of a planet is already established as its own true position; the intent is that even the true [longitude] derived from the epicycle is merely the result of the equation of center. || 43 || Now, regarding the Chedyaka-paddhati: "O Brahman, whatever exists here in the form of atoms (paramāṇu), whether it be the earth, the sky, or the mountains..."

For others who are dull-witted and whose splendor is blunted, Indravarman shall be like one who has struck down their wings. This [work], which is the wheel of the awakening to nirvāṇa, is difficult to understand due to its hardness; therefore, for the sake of recognition by some, he speaks of the two-fold action: "He who is Iṅgin..."—those who are mine, the Darbha, the womb within the womb, the protection therein, a portion of that, the keenness of that, the sages behold it: "This is the immeasurable splendor."

In the *Siddhāntaśiromaṇi*, the section on the Chedyaka (the cutting of diagrams) regarding the eclipses of the sun and moon has been made very easy to understand through its subtle form. Those other calculators who previously found it difficult even with great effort—those who were not proficient in the calculation of the duration of the eclipse—may now attain clear understanding through this work, which is like Indra’s thunderbolt cleaving the wings of a mountain. May there be comprehension.

Regarding "Indravajrā," there is also a rule concerning the *sūtra*. This [meter] consists of ten syllables; because it is possible for even these ten syllables to be broken, it is called "broken" (*bhagna*) by the fact that they are cast down with tears. 44. Now, by this [rule], the hundred-fold repetition of the *jyotipluta* is determined; thus it is the *phalika*. 56. Thus [ends the section]. 2. "A certain woman is a slave" (*dāsī*). In the *Bhauvādhyāya*—composed by the son of Raṅganātha Gaṇaka, born of the lineage of the Lord of the Earth (Udayadivākara), which is continuously augmented by the years of the Vaiṣṇava era—this pair of chapters on the "Arising of Sines" (*Jyotpatti*), which serves as the cause for the calculation of true planetary positions, has reached its conclusion in the *Marīci* commentary upon the *Siddhāntaśiromaṇi*. Thus ends the chapter on *Cheyakā* (the cutting of the circle) in the *Uttarādhyāya* of the *Marīci*, composed by Munīśvara, whose other name is Viśvarūpa, the son of Raṅganātha Gaṇaka, the sovereign of all mathematicians.

Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter. || 26 || Now he describes the section on the construction of the celestial sphere (*golabandha*): "A mathematician of no small skill should construct the *Bhoja-gola* using very straight bamboo rods, smooth rings, and [wooden] pieces. || 1 || This is clear. Now he describes the construction of the terrestrial sphere (*bhūgolabandha*): "First, having made a straight and well-rounded axis for the pole-star (*dhruvayaṣṭi*), and then having fixed it loosely in the middle of the axis, [one should fashion] the earth, which is not large, outside [the sphere]. || 1 ||

One should fasten firm rings for the Moon, Mercury, Venus, the Sun, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn around that [axis], and two loose rings, shaped like globes, upon the tube. First, having made a frame of solid wood, one should place the earth upon it at its proper position and fix it firmly with eight cords (gocās) representing Mahendra and the other [directional deities]. It is stated generally that their [the planets'] circles should be attached to those [rings] in accordance with their respective sizes.

Ma0ḍī0—Now, in order to understand that the aforementioned sphere (golā) is contained within the celestial sphere, this "Sphere-Binding" (Golabandha)—which establishes the nature of the celestial sphere and serves as an illustration for determining the underlying principles (*vāsanā*) of the various topics of planetary calculation (*grahagaṇita*)—is commenced independently. Regarding this, since it must be established how the illustrative celestial sphere (*dṛṣṭāntagola*) representing the configuration of planetary calculation is constructed, [the author] says: "Very straight" (*susarala*), meaning not crooked (*avakra*).

Those bamboos which were intended for the purpose of forming the globular shapes (golākara), from among them, that mountain was fashioned; its back was exceedingly thick. The rings (*valaya*) made from those [bamboos] are described as being produced from the joints of the bamboo, along with their thorns and stalks. This is an illustration: they were fashioned according to fortune, by those who run [to the task], with smooth and glossy surfaces.

Otherwise, because those who are subject to that bondage would perceive it as a cause of suffering—due to the possibility of the crushing of the pestle-like parts of the atoms within the constituent particles—it would follow that it should be disregarded. *Gaṇaka* refers to one who demonstrates the underlying principles (*vāsanā*) of planetary calculation. *Maulam* means the fundamental [sphere] constructed from the divisions of space and the celestial sphere, consisting of many circles such as the equator and the meridian. *Gola-bandham* means the construction of the sphere; the meaning is that one should construct the sphere according to one's own desire by means of the method of binding the circles. The sense is that one should fashion it in whatever manner one wishes for the sake of the students.

[Objection: But surely, even in this example where the number of padmas (lotuses) is not counted, there is the determination of the number of bhīlas (wild tribes) through their binding. [Response: To the objection that "therefore, the knowledge of that number would not occur," he states the qualification of the verse: "by those together with the degrees of the circle's parts" (*saṃcakrabhāgaikaih*). This means: in the circle there are twelve signs (*rāśi*); their parts are the divisions; by the degrees (*aṃśa*) which are associated with those [divisions].

Likewise, if the twelve divisions of the zodiac (*rāśi*) in the sphere (*yūsa*) are to be made equal, then thirty parts (*bhāga*) are to be marked in each division; then six minutes (*kalā*) are to be marked in each part; and then sixty seconds (*vikalā*) are to be marked in each minute. In this way, all the circles are marked with divisions. The implication is that even the understanding of the numerical values of the various elements of planetary calculation (*grahagaṇita*) is easily accomplished on this sphere.

The construction of the sphere (golabandha) must be performed without error; otherwise, due to its contradiction with the actual state of the celestial bodies, there would arise an incorrect understanding of the planets from that constructed sphere. With this in mind, he states "by one who is skilled" as a qualification for the mathematician (gaṇaka). Regarding the "state in the sky," this refers to the craftsmanship required for its execution. The word "ca" (and) is used for conjunction. The meaning is: "one whose intellect is not small"—that is, one who possesses extreme proficiency and expertise in that field. The sense is that it is impossible for a sphere constructed by such a person to contradict the actual state of the celestial bodies.

It should be understood that because it is impossible to achieve [the desired result] without a hundredfold mastery of the craft, such mastery is indispensable. Now, regarding the description of the procedure for constructing the celestial sphere (golabandha), the author states the introduction to that topic in the Śārdūlavikrīḍita meter: "First," at the outset, [one should take] "wood from a desired tree," meaning wood produced from a tree of one's choice that possesses excellent core-wood; otherwise, its stability over a long period would not be attained. [This is done] with stones.

Having established the two celestial poles (dhruvas) at the southern and northern ends of the axis, one should draw a fine, straight meridian line between them as the interval-sine (antarāsūtra). A gnomon (śaṅku) should be made according to that proportion, with its tip perfectly straight. Otherwise, there would be no equality of the intervals between the tips of the gnomon and the two imaginary poles. This ensures the circle is well-formed; otherwise, the rotation of the celestial sphere would be impossible. Having done this immediately thereafter—

Having made the terrestrial globe separate from the staff—that is, having placed it so that it is not obstructed by the middle of the staff and remains at the central part of the staff—one should, as it were, pierce the entire terrestrial globe through the center of the axis of the poles (*dhruvasūtra*). This is achieved by means of a model. Now, one might object: "Even for Brahmā, it would be impossible to place a model equal in size to the terrestrial globe upon a staff. To this he says: "not [equal to] the earth" (*apṛthvīm*). In accordance with the dimensions of the staff, it takes the form of a smaller globe; because it is a model, otherwise it would be impossible even for those who possess a support connected to the earth.

The meaning is that both halves of the terrestrial globe should be equal portions, and thus the terrestrial globe should be placed within the middle of the axis as a substitute. Now, one might object: "If the planets revolve in space, there is no rotation of the Earth; therefore, when the planetary spheres are established to revolve around this axis, the rotation of the terrestrial globe would also necessarily follow suit. To address this contingency, he says: "Loose" (śithilam), meaning not fixed to the axis.

Therefore, even when the sphere rotates, the rotation of the earth within it is impossible; the sense is that if the rotation of the sphere is observed by any means whatsoever, the terrestrial globe must be seen as being immobile. Outside the terrestrial globe, at equal distances all around it, the Moon, Mercury, Venus, the Sun, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, and the stars are fixed in order, one above the other, being firm and capable of enduring for a long time without breaking.

[The sphere] is situated in space, bound by a frame of wood shaped according to its position; otherwise, its rotation would not be possible due to the lack of a sharp [axis]. One should bind it. The meaning is that one should construct the spheres using bamboo and other materials according to the method of binding to be described later. Here, the sphere consists of the orbits of the planets arranged one above the other in sequence, and upon that is this single sphere of all the asterisms (nakṣatras). Ma. Ṭī.: Now, there is one sphere for those [asterisms]. It is a single sphere for them.

Otherwise, it should be understood as "I am the one who destroys the host of stars. Around that [axis], at equal intervals on both sides of the stellar sphere (nakṣatragola), two tube-end sections—one *aṅgula* each—should be inserted from both sides of the stellar sphere into the tubes, fixed within the tubes so that they are not loose; this means they are attached to the tubes in such a way that they do not wobble. These are the celestial sphere (*khagola*) and the visual sphere (*dṛggola*). As will be described later, "loose" (*ślatha*) means not touching one another.

By this, the small interval between the upper and lower [halves] of those two should be made distinct; otherwise, it would be situated in the Bhagola (Sphere of Constellations). For that reason, it is said that the Khagola (Sphere of Planets) and Haragola (Sphere of the Sun) are established separately. One should construct them according to the method to be described. Because the Khagola and Vargala (Sphere of Planetary Orbits) are situated [there], their binding at the location of the Bhagola is impossible; otherwise, an undesirable consequence would follow there. Therefore, they are shown as separate for the sake of easy understanding by means of tubes; the sense is that this is not [the case] in reality. || 2 ||

Now, he says what must be done: one should draw two circles, one called the equatorial (samamaṇḍala) from east to west, and another from south to north; and two more circles at the intermediate directions. Thus, there are four circles here—two vertical and two horizontal—and their intersection at the horizon is half of that. One circle is from east to west, and the other is likewise; having thus arranged the four circles above and below, one should place the circle called the horizon (kṣitija), which is half of that, encircling it.

Here, on the meridian circle (yāmyacara-vṛtta), one polar mark (dhruva-cihna) should be made at a distance equal to the latitude (palāṃśa) from the eastern horizon; another [mark] should be made below the southern horizon. Maṭhara’s Commentary (ma0 ṭī0): Now, since the stability of the celestial sphere (khagola) was first indicated, the author describes the binding of the five circles (pañca-vṛtta) by means of the Vasantatilaka meter, beginning with the words "pūrvāparam" (east-west). Here, the first circle to be constructed upon the celestial sphere is the equatorial circle (sama-maṇḍala-saṃjña).

The first [triangle] is connected to its own position (*svasthāna*) by means of a bow (*dhanus*), and is large and auspiciously connected to the *ākavi* [position]; it is subtle and resembles a bamboo staff (*vaṃśa*). The second, which belongs to both [categories], is situated on its own and resembles a subtle needle; it is circular (*vṛtta*) by the southern [lines]. The word "and" (*ca*) is used for conjunction. Thus, there are these two types of figures (*vṛtta*). Among the four directions starting from the East, that which is connected to the intermediate directions (*vidiś*)—specifically the North-East (*īśānī*) and South-West (*nairṛtī*)—is called the "auspicious" (*vusaha*).

The letter *ca* follows the restrictive particle *eva*, which serves to exclude other possibilities; thus, it negates the possibility of increasing the number of verses by making the two [sections] belonging to Agni, Nairṛti, Īśāna, and Dhāyana into a single verse, because those two are joined together in the neck (*gale*). Likewise, "one should fashion that essence. In this way, having freed the four verses from the pair of *vṛtta*s, one should encircle the *dharma*—which has as its sphere the paths of the intermediate directions—with the upward-facing [verses], binding them by means of that dwelling.

In this context, it should be understood that the ghee (liquid) held in the southern direction must first be poured without piercing the mark situated between the tips of the *yaṣṭi* (staff); otherwise, it would be impossible for the blade of the sword (*khagala*) to imitate the throat [of the staff]. For that purpose, from the two points of intersection of the previously traversed circle, at the half-point [5], the other traversed [circle] is empty; the light produced is from a small circle following the circle situated at the junction of the invisible hemisphere of the earth, which serves as a substitute for the thin circle of the sword-blade.

One should determine the utility of the terrestrial sphere and so forth hereafter. [Verse 3] Now he describes the Unmandala (the diurnal circle): When the southern celestial pole is situated below the horizon by as many degrees as the latitude (*palalava*), and when the northern celestial pole is above the horizon by those same degrees of latitude, that circle which touches the points of intersection of the eastern and western horizons and is fixed at the two poles is called the *unmaṇḍala*. This causes the decrease and increase of day and night, and it intersects the equator and the horizon at their respective eastern and western points. [The circle] which is drawn touching those two points of intersection and the two poles is known by the name *unmaṇḍala*.

The increase and decrease of day and night occur by virtue of that [inclination]. Now, he describes the placement of the equinoctial circle: "One should mark the inclination from the eastern and western *svastikas* toward the south by the degrees of the axis (*akṣa*), and likewise toward the north below them; and here one should construct the equatorial circle (*nāḍīvalaya*) along that path. (5)

Between those very same eastern and western intersections, a circle is likewise tied on the meridian (yāmyottara-vṛtta) at an interval equal to the latitude (akṣa), starting south from the zenith-svastika and north from the nadir-svastika; that is the equinoctial circle (viṣuva-vṛtta). Now, he describes the construction of the horizon-circle (unmaṇḍala) here using the Vasantatilaka meter, beginning with "pūrvāpara": "The circle produced from the degrees [of latitude] at the two points of intersection of the eastern and western [circles] and the horizon-circle... This means at the two points of intersection of the eastern and western circles and the horizon-circle, located in the eastern and western directions.

Consciousness is bound. This means that [the observer] is situated in the southern direction from the point of intersection of the terrestrial meridian and the southern celestial equator. By "degrees of latitude" (palalavaiḥ) is meant the degrees of declination (akṣāṃśaiḥ). When the southern pole is below, the southern gnomon is at a point on the southern part of the north-south circle connected to the interior of the altitude-circle (unnatikāgarbha); its nature is that of a line coinciding with the tip of the southern gnomon—this is the meaning. It is joined at the northern intersection of the terrestrial meridian and the celestial equator—this is the meaning. "Above" means at the upper limit of the degrees of declination.

It is joined at the northern pole (*saumya-dhruva*)—a point situated on the line equidistant from the two solstices, connected to the interior of the tube passing through its tip—and consists of a portion of a secondary circle (*yāmyacaravṛtta*). The word "and" (*ca*) implies conjunction. This refers to the circle transformed into that shape which pierces the two tubes. It would be called the "horizon of the celestial equator" (*unmaṇḍala*), resembling the local horizon (*kṣitijavṛtta*) of the earth's center at the equatorial region, situated within the local meridian circle.

In a location south of the equatorial region (nirakṣadeśa), this should be understood as being the reverse of what was stated for the northern part. Now, one might object: "Only that which is related to one's own specific location should be established here, not that which pertains to the equatorial region; otherwise, an over-extension (atiprasaṅga) would follow. To this he says: "Of day and night"—meaning, caused by the decrease and increase of the day and night.

And likewise, since the deficiency or excess of the day and the excess of the night—which are observed in one's own location—need not be demonstrated again here in this treatise, the intent is that this treatise pertains specifically to one's own location. (4) Now, since the day and night consist of *ghaṭikās*, their deficiency or excess cannot be known through a celestial globe (*gola*) because of the absence of *ghaṭikā* marks; therefore, [the author] states the following in the Upajāti meter: "In the east and west... (56).

In this context, the meaning is that there is one *vaṃśaśalākavṛtta* (bamboo-stick circle) equal to the previously mentioned [circle], which is designated as the *nāḍīvṛtta* (meridian circle), located on the plane of the celestial equator. He states the method of construction: "between the eastern and western *svastika*s" (*pūrvāparasvastikayoḥ*). This means situated at the points of the eastern and western directions. Regarding the term *yadhatikau*: because of the great distance between them, the previous teachers used many conventions; thus, due to their own differing views, the mention of the word *svaritaka* was not included in the previous verse, and its acquisition is established here for these two. At the end of the *svastika*s.

The four points situated above, at the intersection [of the equator and the meridian], are fixed by their own degrees of latitude (akṣabhāga) in the southern hemisphere at the location of the meridian circle (yāmyoccavṛtta). From the intersection of those same four points situated below, they are fixed by those same degrees of latitude in the northern hemisphere at the location of the north-south circle (yāmyottaravṛtta). The word "ca" (and) is used for conjunction.

Now, one might ask: "How is this left circle (vāmāḍīvṛtta), which corresponds to the east-west line of the equatorial region, drawn so as to be equidistant from both poles? To this he says: "aghṛitam" (not held). By the sixty marks—that is, by sixty numbers—the complete circle is divided. The word "ca" (and) implies conjunction; by this, it is indicated that the marking of the zodiacal signs (*rāśibhaga*) is not intended. One *ghaṭikā* consists of six parts; thus, the entire circle is marked with sixty *ghaṭikās*.

And thus, since this circle (the *vṛtta*) imitates the rotation of the celestial equator (*pravaha*), its own rotation follows that of the equator; and because it is appropriate to call it the "pot-circle" (*ghaṭavṛtta*) due to the occurrence of day and night, the knowledge of day and night becomes possible through this [circle] at the pole. Therefore, the meaning is that it is more appropriate to fix it in one’s own location—just as it is fixed at the terrestrial equator (*kṣitija*)—rather than binding it to the east-west circle of the non-equatorial region (*nirakṣadeśa*). Furthermore, this [arrangement] is reversed in the region north of the non-equatorial point compared to the other region.

The two circles for the non-axial regions and the corners have not been included here due to a lack of necessity; it should be understood that the meridian circle (yāmyottaravṛtta) is fixed by its own axis. Now, he describes the horizon (dṛṅmaṇḍala): Having placed a loose cord within that [instrument] between a pair of pins at the upper and lower *svastika* points, and having rotated it, one should lead it wherever the observer's eye goes. 3.

On its own *svastika*, there is a killing; on the *śvastika*, a strike; the two bricks are like birds; the vessel is loose; the circle of vision (*dṛgvalaya*) should be made. In that regard, it should be made slightly less than the previous circles, so that it is straight within the celestial sphere (*khagola*). If there is only one celestial sphere for all the planets, then there is only one single circle of vision. Whichever planet is situated wherever, having rotated that very [circle] around its circumference and fixed it, the distance from the point of observation (*dṛgkhyāśaṅka*) should be shown.

Alternatively, one should construct eight distinct *iṅmaṇḍalas* (diurnal circles). Among these, the eighth belongs to the *vitribha* (trine) point; that is the *dṛkkṣepamaṇḍala* (diurnal circle of parallax). Now, he states the specific detail: "That same [circle] is to be known for all the planets; likewise, one should construct eight distinct ones. This *iṅmaṇḍala* of the *vitribha* point is called the *dṛkkṣepavṛtta* (parallax circle); so they say. This has already been explained. (7)

Now, having thus described the celestial sphere (*khagola*), he speaks of the visual sphere (*dṛggola*): "Having fixed two tubes upon the celestial sphere at the two poles, so that they remain aligned with those very poles, a wise man should fashion the visual sphere from the celestial sphere in the manner that will be described. The celestial sphere, together with the circles of the zodiac (*bhagola*) and the circles of declination (*apamaṇḍala*), is known as the visual sphere; indeed, the figure produced by these two spheres is seen as the visual sphere, and therefore they call it the *dṛggola*. (8–9)

Having fixed two pins (nelikā) at the two half-marks on that celestial sphere (khagola), one should construct the horizon (goḍaṃ) within the hollow space of the sphere, supported by its axis (aṭikā). This is the section on the construction of the sphere according to the stated measurements of the celestial sphere and the celestial latitudes (bhagola) to be described hereafter. That [sphere] which is placed upon the ecliptic (kāntivimaṇḍala) is called the visual sphere (dṛggola). As to why this is termed the "visual sphere" (dṛggola), he says: "Because it is produced from two spheres," and so forth; for the spherical triangles (akṣakṣetra) derived from the two spheres are known by the term "two-sphere" (dvigola).

The celestial sphere (khagola) and the visual sphere (dṛggola) are produced by means of the *bhagaṇa* (zodiacal circles) and the *uḍubūta* (stellar circles). Since they are perceived as being situated within the different hemispheres (*golapradeśa*), how can there be a "visual sphere"? Thus ends the section on the construction of the celestial and visual spheres. Now, for the purpose of knowing how to position the desired diurnal circle (*digvṛtta*), the author describes the positioning of the visual circles (*dṛgvṛtta*) in the *Indravajrā* meter, beginning with the word *adhbhara*. "At its end" means within the center of the constructed sphere.

It is indicated that the Bhagola, joined together with the sphere of the fixed stars (Kṣitija), should be rotated within the space between the upper and lower Svastikas, which are fixed loosely and slackly upon a central pivot; this must be adjusted from the previous wooden frames so that its internal rotation occurs properly. Having made a circular ring out of bamboo or similar material, one should move it around to each place where a planet travels and, following its own revolution, cause the eye of that circle to remain in contact [with the planet]. The word "ca" (and) is used for conjunction.

This [model] has the form of a small (laghu) sphere attached to a svastika held by hands situated in the shoulder-region (śrāmakakṣa). Precisely because of this, since the planets are stationary, it is impossible to construct circles for every single location; therefore, the wise have conceived this as a loose sphere upon which [the circles] are strung. For by its rotation, the appearance of all circular forms is seen. || 6 ||

Now, one might ask: since there is no planetary motion at the fixed point of the stellar sphere (*khagola*), how can it be said that [the celestial equator] is "there" and so forth? To this, he replies with the verse beginning with *dhṛtikayā*—it is to be known. That is: the circle of the celestial equator (*kṛttika-vṛtta*) stretched between the upper and lower points of the cross (the poles) within the stellar sphere is to be known as belonging to all the wanderers of the sky—that is, to all the constellations (*nakṣatras*) and the seven planets. The particle *eva* (only/just) serves to exclude the possibility that this circle lacks a connection to the constellations and so on, thereby precluding the notion that it cannot be considered a "constellation-circle. This is what is meant: [The celestial equator is the great circle passing through the poles of the stellar sphere and intersecting the ecliptic at right angles.]

In this context, the circle that corresponds to the latitude circle (svastika) of the celestial sphere related to the meridian is indeed the horizon-circle (dṛgvṛtta). Furthermore, since the position of a star or other object on the celestial sphere is conceived at the very point where it lies on the plane passing through the center of the earth and intersecting that sphere, the determination of the horizon-circle was previously explained as appropriate; for there is no defect due to its being an approximation (anukalpa), and because in the illustrative model (dṛṣṭāntagola) there is an absence of the physical orb of the planet and so forth.

Otherwise, since the planetary sphere (grahagola) is situated within the celestial sphere (khagola), it would be impossible to construct the sphere of the stars (bhikṣugola) as described for the purpose of observing its three-dimensional nature. It should be understood that although the star-sphere appears perfectly spherical when bound by a tube to the axis of the meridian circle (yāmyottaravṛtta), it appears in that [spherical] shape only when the sphere is constructed with a tube through its center; this is because the axis of the meridian circle prevents the stars from being seen at the poles.

Now, one might object: "For one of dull intellect, even when this has been stated thus, there may be a lack of understanding because of the absence of a connection between Vṛtra and the sphere of the planets. To resolve this, the author says "separately" (pṛthak). Or, as an alternative view (pakṣāntara), [he means] separately in their own respective spheres. "Eight likewise" refers to the eight celestial spheres (dṛṅmaṇḍala), because the number of revolving spheres is measured as eight. One should "construct," that is, create them.

And likewise, when the celestial sphere of the stars and planets is placed upon a vertical and horizontal cross (svāstika) by means of a common thread, the circle of vision (dṛgvṛtta)—which is loosely strung through the pair of Śrī-layukas at whatever point it may be—is clearly perceived in its various positions; this is well understood by them. Although on the meridian (yāmyottara-vṛtta) the shape [of the circle] does not perfectly match the form of the obstruction caused by the two poles, that same shape should be understood to exist on the circle of vision. He states the specific detail: "The circle of the earth's shadow (chāyāmaṇḍala) is the horizon (maṇḍalīka-heḍra)."

The diurnal circle (*dṛgvṛtta*) of a point situated at two or three signs from the ascendant is derived through labor; it is known as the *dṛkṣepavṛtta* (the circle of parallax). Furthermore, some say it is not the *dṛgvṛtta*. For this very reason, in the chapter on solar eclipses, the term *kṣepa* (parallax) is defined as the arc of the sine of the latitude (*viṣuvanmaṇḍala-śaṅku-jyā*). Now, he describes the construction of the armillary sphere (*dṛggola-bandhana*) by means of an *uṣṇih* meter, beginning with the word "badhvā" (having bound): In the celestial sphere (*khagola*), which consists of the arrangement of circles as previously described, having bound two tubes to the two poles (*dhruva-dvaya*),...

Having inserted a tube at each of the two marks located on the southern side—belonging to the *lālasa* and connected to the southern region—one should then direct that fuel toward the south. This is possible from the very beginning according to the method described, as it takes the form of a circumference for the tubes and the central axis of the mandala; otherwise, the ignition would be impossible. Through the opening of the tube, the water is expelled by the force of the wind, since the tubes serve as the support for those [waters] via the staff. This occurs outside and above this celestial sphere (*khagola*).

By the use of the word *eva* (only/alone), the exclusion of that [other] is intended; for it is impossible to construct it by means of the celestial sphere (*khagola*). It is situated within the tube. The "celestial sphere" refers to the observational sphere (*dṛggola*) fixed at another internal point within that tube. Thus, with circles representing degrees and so forth, just like the celestial sphere, the wise mathematician (*gaṇaka*) should fashion it—meaning he should construct it. By the term "wise," it is indicated that just as the celestial sphere does not touch the circles, so too the tube should be fastened at another internal point in such a way [that it remains free].

[Objection: But since that mode [of calculation] does not exist, how can there be a "dart" (śalya) based upon it? To this he says: "in the manner that will be explained"—this is the meaning. [Objection: But since the celestial sphere (*dṛggola*) is unreal, for what purpose is the result based upon it? To this he says: "that indeed. The meaning is that, by necessity, the operation based upon it must certainly be performed. Thus, even though it is unreal, the point is that the operation based upon it is authoritative for the purpose of demonstrating plane figures (*kṣetra*) and so forth. || 8 ||

Now, with an Upajāti verse, he states the reason for the name *dṛggola* (visible sphere) and the cause for its designation as such, beginning with "bhagolavṛttaiḥ" (by means of the circles of the stellar sphere). The celestial sphere (*khagola*), when joined with—that is, conjoined with—those circles that belong to the stellar sphere (*bhagola*), becomes known by the name *dṛggola*. Having constructed the celestial sphere according to the method described, one should then fix the circles of the stellar sphere upon it. The meaning is that the sphere thus established is designated by the term *dṛggola*.

[Objection: But how can there be a binding of those [nodes] if the circles of the stellar sphere (bhagola) are unknown? To this he says: "by means of the apoklima-circles and the others. The *aṣamaṇḍala* is the circle of declination (*krāntimaṇḍala*); the *vimaṇḍala* is the circle of anomaly (*viśeṣamaṇḍala*). [The term is used here] because a name is often taken from a part of the whole. The first group consists of the midnight circles. The meaning is that these are the circles belonging to the stellar sphere (*bhagola*). [Objection: But since this [instrument] consists of both the celestial sphere (*khagola*) and the stellar sphere (*bhagola*), it is a mixed sphere; how then can it be called a "visible sphere" (*dṛggola*)? To this he says: "born from two spheres" (*dvigolajāta*).

The area produced by the intersection of the celestial sphere (*khagola*) and the terrestrial sphere (*bhagola*) is distinct from the second axis-area (*akṣakṣetra*). For in this mixed sphere (*miśragola*), it is indeed seen without doubt. For this reason, the ancient teachers call this mixed sphere the "visible sphere" (*dṛggola*). Likewise, the *gala*-area is directly perceived in the celestial sphere, and the *bhagola*-area is directly perceived in the terrestrial sphere.

The field produced from both of those is invisible here and there; therefore, for the purpose of seeing it, this construction of a sphere (golabandha) has been devised. This is the intended meaning of what is called the "visible sphere" (dṛggola). || 9 || End of the Chapter on the Construction of the Sphere. Now he describes the construction of the stellar sphere (bhagolabandha): One should construct a pair of rings fixed on two poles, one vertical and the other horizontal, joined to the axis of the poles. A third ring, like the equator, should be placed at sixty degrees [from the horizon]; that very same ring is called the "hour-circle" (nāḍī), and it is also the equinoctial line (viṣuvat). || 19 ||

Just as on the celestial globe there are two great circles of the same form as the support—the horizon and the meridian—fixed at the poles, one should likewise fashion another third circle in the shape of the equator, marked with sixty *nāḍīs*. This is called the *nāḍīvṛtta* (the hour-circle) and the *viṣuvavṛtta* (the equinoctial circle). Now he describes the *krāntivṛtta* (the ecliptic): "The *krāntivṛtta* should be fashioned with the twelve signs (*rāśis*), wherein the Sun revolves; and the *kubhā* (the terrestrial latitude) should be measured from the Sun."

One should mark the positions of the *krāntipāta* (the node of the ecliptic) moving in the opposite direction, as well as the *kṣepapātas* (nodes of the latitudes), in their true positions. Then, having constructed another circle of the same measure and assigned Aries and the other signs there, one should mark the twelve zodiacal signs; this is called the *krāntivṛtta* (ecliptic circle). In that circle, the revolution of the sun occurs. Likewise, within the shadow of the earth (*bhūbhā*) from the sun, and likewise there, the *krāntipāta* is situated at the beginning of Aries.

Likewise, the specific nodes (viśeṣapātas) of the planets move clearly upon the Viḍoma [circle]. Therefore, the positions of the precession of the equinoxes (kāntipāta) and so forth are marked there. Maṭī0: Now, even though the circles of the stellar sphere (bhagola) are known, because there is no method for their construction, the connection with the armillary sphere (aṃgola) is also impossible. Therefore, desiring to describe the construction of the stellar sphere, he first states the construction of three circles in the Vasantatilakā meter, beginning with "yāmya": "Like the southern and northern horizons... (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available portion.)

Just as in the celestial sphere the meridian (yāmyottara-vṛtta) extends from the center of the sky to the ends of that circle, and the horizon-circle (kṣitija-vṛtta) extends down to the nadir, so too one should construct three supporting circles firmly joined to the polar axis at both ends, at a distance of one finger-breadth from the edge. Here, the phrase "like the horizon" (kṣitijavat) is correctly understood as "like the horizon of the equator" (nirakṣa-kṣitijavat), because the rotating plate has that same shape. These are positioned above and below by means of two strings (jīvā) at the points of the local horizon.

Here, it is stated that the circles of the terrestrial sphere (bhagola) are supported by the celestial sphere (khagola). In that context, since each individual circle would otherwise be loose when fixed upon the polar axis, a supporting frame is necessary so that the axis does not occasionally slip out. Here, within the pair of supporting circles, there is a third circle marked with the signs of the axis, resembling the equatorial circle (samamaṇḍala).

Just as in the celestial sphere (khagola) there is a half-circle of equal altitude (samamaṇḍala) formed by the southern and northern horizons, so too this pair of circles, when tied together at their midpoints, becomes the equinoctial circle (nāḍīvṛtta). This is because, in the rotating sphere (bhramaśāla), it takes the form of the equinoctial circle fixed within the celestial sphere. Now, since the celestial sphere (khagola) is not required for the terrestrial sphere (bhagola), for what purpose is it [included]? To this he says: "the equinoctial circle" (viṣuvavalaya). That circle which is tied with sixty marks is that [equinoctial circle].

The particle *eva* excludes any occurrence other than that specified. This is the equinoctial circle (*viṣuvadvṛtta*). Thus, on the celestial sphere (*bhagola*), because the planet revolves according to this circle at the time when day and night are equal, the meaning is that it is called the "equinoctial circle. The letter *dha* has the sense of "but" (*tu*); therefore, on the stellar sphere (*khagola*), the circle corresponding to this is named the "meridian" (*nāḍī*) because it is fixed, whereas on the celestial sphere, the circle corresponding to this is named the "equinox" (*viṣuvat*) because it is movable.

In this context, it should be understood that the marking of the *ghaṭīs* on the ecliptic (*krāntivṛtta*) is for the purpose of showing that the measure of the constellations and so forth is sixty *nakṣatra-ghaṭīs*. (10) Now, establishing the ecliptic in its true form upon the stellar sphere (*bhagola*), he says in the *Sragviṇī* meter: "Purified by peace," etc. Another circle, equal to the equator (*viṣuvavṛtta*) and made of bamboo or other materials, marked with nine digits (*guhāṅka*), should be marked with degrees and also inscribed at the desired location with the first letters of the names of the clouds, the learned, and the ten signs of the zodiac; that is the ecliptic.

Regarding which of those situated within the stellar sphere (bhagola) located in space this circle corresponds to, he says: "The shadow," and so forth. Here, on this circle, the Sun (Bhānu) revolves in its own orbit; it moves by its own eastward motion. From the Sun (Bhānu), at a distance of six signs (six zodiacal divisions), the Earth's shadow (Kubhā) revolves in its own orbit. The Sun moves with an eastward motion. The word "ca" (and) is used for conjunction. Because the Sun revolves around the Earth, the shadow of the Earth produced thereby falls upon that circle.

Thus, the meaning is that this circle is a substitute for that circle in which the Sun, having moved forward, completes the enjoyment of the twelve zodiacal signs. In this context, he mentions other elements regarding the revolution of this circle: *kāntipāta* (the node of the ecliptic), whose nature will be described later; *pratīpaṃ* (contrary), meaning opposite to the state of the Sun's motion, and thus distinct from it; the sense being that at times it moves eastward and at times westward. However, according to the view of Mūlālādi, *pratīpaṃ* means in the reverse order, namely westward.

The meaning is "by their own motion. The "latitudes and descents" (*kṣepapātāḥ*) of the Moon and other planets refer to the latitudes and the nodes (*pāta*), whose nature will be described later. "Manifest" (*prasphuṭāḥ*) means corrected by the results of the planetary periods (*grahīṣaphala*) as will be described; it does not mean the mean [positions]. "From the *cara* [equation], they move eastward and westward" means they revolve, moving according to what is appropriate. [Objection: But surely they revolve in the sky? However, since this is a description of the events occurring in the secondary aeon (*anukalpavṛtta*), such a description might seem inappropriate. To this he says: "Their locations" (*tatsthānāni*).

One should mark the initial letters of those [names]—Sūrya, Bhūchāyā, Krāntipāta, and Śarapāta—at whatever places they occur on the ecliptic (krāntivṛtta). Now he describes the placement of the ecliptic: "One should know that the point of the ecliptic (krāntipāta) is at the intersection with the equator (nāḍikāvṛtta); and six signs (rāśis) away from the node (pāta), one should mark another point. From the node, three signs to the north or south by the established degrees (siddhabhāga), and by those same degrees in the other division. A mark for the ecliptic should be made at the intersection; another mark should be made at an interval of six signs.

Those two marks [of the node] coincide with the intersection of the ecliptic; having established them within the three signs of the ecliptic from the point of the node, one should fix them such that they occur at those same degrees on the other side of the ecliptic, twenty-four degrees from the intersection of the ecliptic, and likewise to the south. Now he describes the secondary circle (vimaṇḍala): "Just as the ecliptic is situated upon the circle of hours, so too is the epicycle of anomaly situated upon the ecliptic."

One should draw a circle for the epicycle (kṣepavṛtta) marked with zodiacal signs; therein, one should indicate the points for the apogee of the epicycle (kṣepapāta). Having made a junction between the apogee of the epicycle and the point of the apogee of the epicycle of the [ecliptic] circle increased by the obliquity (krānti), one should place the true latitudinal degrees (kṣepabhāga) to the north and south at three signs (90°) ahead of and behind the apogee of the epicycle. These [true latitudinal degrees] of the planets, multiplied by the radius (tribhajyā) and divided by the swift-hypotenuse (śīghrakarṇa), shall be the true latitudinal degrees.

Know that the equations of motion for the six [planets] are distinct from their respective orbits, revolving together with the moon and the asterisms. (Verse 15) This is the complete explanation of the [preceding] verse. Just as the orbit of the mind (*mativṛtta*) has been treated separately, so too, having separated the two [other] orbits at Rāyacūṃce, one should clearly calculate the equation of motion starting from Aries and apply it hereafter in the diagram.

Then, having made the intersection of the ecliptic and the *vipaṇḍakhā* at the points of the [mean] anomaly and the node, and having made another junction six signs away from that, one should fix the *vipaṇḍakhā* by making it stable three signs ahead of the node and anomaly on the north side of the ecliptic at the true remaining degrees, and likewise three signs behind them on the south side at those same degrees. Then, those read degrees of anomaly, multiplied by the radius (*trijyā*) and divided by the swift hypotenuse (*śīghrakarṇa*), are to be applied as the true anomalies.

Here [the author] says: "If these [circles] are drawn at the ear (karṇa), then they are made at the tip of the trijyā. For in the case of the apogee of the planets, the trijyā itself is the radius (vyāsārdha). In this manner, the six orbs (maṇḍalas) of the Moon and the other planets are to be constructed; the planets move within their respective eccentric circles (vimāṇḍalas). Now, he states the construction of these circles in the *sragviṇī* meter, beginning with "kāntipāta": "This is the constructed circle of declination (krāntivṛtta).
