At the node of declination (krāntipāta)—that is, from the point marked by the node where it falls—[the circle is drawn]."

"Six intervals apart" means in a place separated by six signs. "Yaḥ" (which) indicates a conjunction. One should join the [circle] less than a nāḍī to the two previously mentioned places on the ecliptic that are separated by six signs; by the word "ca" (and), the meaning is: joined to the two places on the ecliptic occupied by the circle of the support for the [circle of] elevation. "From the node" means from the position of the *kāntipāta* (the node of the ecliptic) along the path of the precession. "In the division of three signs" means at the point on the ecliptic separated by three zodiacal signs, by the established degrees, namely twenty-four degrees.

From the point on the base-circle (*ādhāra-vṛtta*) near the northern meridian-line (*udag-yāmya-uttara-vṛtta*), one should draw a line connecting it to the point on the base-circle opposite the position of the *śānti*-fall; this is done by moving twenty-four degrees (*tribha*) along the reverse path from the mark of the day-measure (*rājyaṅka*) toward the point on the ecliptic (*krānti-vṛtta*) at the end of the third sign (*tribhānta*). From that point on the base-circle in the south, near the meridian-line, another connection should be made. The word "and" (*yaḥ*) indicates a conjunction.

The binding by means of the relationship between the base and the support is for the purpose of directly observing the twenty-fourth part; it should be understood that there is no harm even if it is bound otherwise. Its intended meaning is as follows: starting from the time when the equinoctial shadow has arrived at the eastern or western meridian line at a place on the equator, [the shadow] is observed daily by Brahmā and others in the eastern or southern portion, moving along the path situated on the eastern or western meridian, until it reaches the twenty-fourth part of the circle.

Then, because its decrease was observed there to be exactly like its increase, and because it was seen to remain unaltered even by the power of time while situated in the sun, the circle presided over by the sun was conceived by those of superior intellect. In accordance with this, the circle on the celestial sphere (bhagola) is its apogee-circle (antivṛtta). On this circle in the celestial sphere, the zodiacal signs were primarily established for the purpose of knowing the planets, since they are understood through a uniform manner following the interior of this [circle]. For "krānti" is derived from the act of "kramaṇa" (moving).

Because the Sun moves by its own power along this [ecliptic] circle (*vṛtta*), the circle of obliquity (*krāntivṛtta*) is likewise postulated in other great spheres (*mahāgola*) in accordance with that [movement]. Although the Moon and other planets do not always appear near the Sun, they occasionally occupy positions on the solar circle even without following the same longitudinal interval. However, the Moon and others cannot occupy positions on their respective circles without following the longitudinal interval of the Sun's circle. This is also because it has been stated: "The complete revolution (*bhagaṇa*) is recorded as ending at the constellation Pauṣṇa."

Since Revatī and Tārā have no connection with the lunar orbit (candravṛtta) but do have a connection with the solar orbit (sūryavṛtta), the prediction of their results follows as a consistent rule; thus, for all planets, the calculation is derived solely in accordance with the ecliptic (krāntivṛtta). Now, following the sequence, he describes the basis of the celestial sphere (bimaṇḍala) using two verses beginning with "nāḍikāmaṇḍale": "In the circle of the equator (nāḍikavṛtta)," etc. The meaning is that just as the ecliptic is situated upon the equatorial circle—toward the north in the northern hemisphere and toward the south in the southern hemisphere—from the circle of the equator.

And likewise, one should place the *vikṣepavṛtta* (the declination circle) in that same manner as the *krāntivṛtta* (ecliptic). The two points on the *krāntivṛtta* [corresponding to the nodes] should be positioned such that the northern and southern segments of the circle—formed by the interval created by the declination—are respectively situated to the north and south of the equator. [Objection: But surely, according to the method described, the *śara* (latitude/declination) of the planets is established in the same way as the *krānti* (ecliptic), because the *krāntivṛtta* is situated twenty-four degrees to the north and south of the *nāḍikavṛtta* (equator).

Since it has been stated that the equinoctial circle (krāntivṛtta) and the diurnal circle (śaravṛtta) are situated twenty-four degrees apart in the northern and southern hemispheres respectively, this cannot be accepted as a mere assumption; for even when the declinations (śara) reach their maximum, the twenty-fourth degree is not observed. Therefore, he clarifies what was stated generally: "The diurnal circle" (kṣepavṛtta). The diurnal circle is made of a rod (śalākaja); by the word "tu" (but/and), it is equal to the previous circle, marked with degrees and so forth, and marked with the first letters of the zodiac signs starting from Aries—that circle is the diurnal circle (kṣepavṛtta).

In that context, regarding the [mean] apsis and the apsidal revolutions, at the points of the true apsis, one should mark signs on the ecliptic as previously described—meaning, likewise, the signs at the points of the product of the [mean] latitude (śara). The word "and" (yaḥ) is used in the sense of conjunction. By that [conjunction], on either one of the two—the ecliptic or the latitude-circle (vikṣepavṛtta)—which is marked with the signs of the apsis; and the word "and" (ca) is again for conjunction—at the point of the apsis (kṣepapāta), together with the two positions separated by their respective signs of the house (dhaibha), which are located at the position of the true apsis.

Having performed the conjunction (*yuti*)—the word "and" (*ca*) being used for inclusion—at a distance of one sign from the position of the node (*pāta*), one should fix the ecliptic (*śavṛtta*) on the northern or southern side of the circle of declination (*krāntivṛtta*) by means of the lunar path; at a distance of three signs (*tribha*) in the reverse direction behind [the node], that is, at a place separated by three signs from the position of the node behind it—the word "and" (*ca*) being used for inclusion—one should fix the ecliptic by means of the clear, maximum latitudinal degrees (*kṣepabhāga*) which will be described later.

This [system], which takes the form of an approximation of arrows and trees devised by King Nṛpa and others who perceive with the eye of the sages, is based on the observation of the movements of the moon and other celestial bodies. Now, one might object: "Since the arrow, the tree, and the transits are understood as being one, there would be an increase in the calculation of the *golabandha* (the binding of the sphere) due to the falling of the arrows at both the beginning and the end of every eclipse."

209. Having established the general rule, one must now explain the specific procedure; therefore, with the intent indicated by the plural "in the case of the [mean] anomaly and apsis" (*kṣepapāte tu*), he clarifies the statement regarding the degrees of the true anomaly using the *sragviṇī* meter, beginning with the words "by the swift hypotenuse" (*śīghrakarṇena*). The meaning is as follows: the maximum minutes of anomaly for the planets, Mars and the others, which were stated in the chapter on planetary shadow (*pahacchāyādhikāra*), are divided by sixty. Multiplied by the radius (*trijyā*) and divided by the swift hypotenuse (*śīghrakarṇa*), the resulting quotient shall be the true maximum degrees of anomaly.

The maximum latitude (parama-śrava) of the Moon is exactly four and a half [degrees], because of the absence of its epicycle (īghikarṇa). Here is the proof: the stated maximum latitude is the hypotenuse (karṇa), while the terrestrial globe (bhūgola) has a radius equal to the sine of the maximum declination (trijyā-vyāsārdha). Therefore, for the purpose of knowing the maximum difference between the latitudes on the celestial sphere (bhagola) and the ecliptic, the proportion is valid: "If these maximum latitudes correspond to the hypotenuse, then what do they correspond to at the tip of the sine of the maximum declination? However, in the case of the Moon, it is observed on the celestial sphere and is thus fixed. These are the latitudinal circles (kṣepavṛtta).

One should construct the *śa*-circles for each of the six planets, beginning with the Moon, individually. Thus, by the rule "the [mean] planets and nodes," the *gha*-circles of the Moon and others are converted into *śa*-circles. Within these, one should sequentially place the Moon, its latitude (*śara*), and its node (*pāta*). Then, on the ecliptic (*krāntivṛtta*) at the point of the node and at a point six signs (180°) apart from it, one should fix the planet's own latitude at its respective true (*phuṭa*) degrees. At the position of the node and at a point six signs apart from that position, one should likewise fix the latitude according to its own true degrees.

There is a rule that from the ecliptic (krāntivṛtta), the planet is at a distance of three signs (90 degrees) to the north or south. Thus, when one [ecliptic] is completed, six declination circles (śaravṛtta) are formed, bent according to their respective nodes (pātacihna) and their respective true longitudes (sphuṭakarṇabhaga). Now, it might be argued that fixing the declination circles upon the ecliptic situated on the celestial sphere (bhagola) is not appropriate; for it is more appropriate to fix the declination circle upon the path of the orbit (kakṣāmarga) of the celestial sphere, which moves along with the planet. To this, he says: "upon their respective circles" (svasvavṛtte).

The planets beginning with the Moon (Indu) revolve in their respective orbits within the sphere of the asterisms (Bhagola). They move along their own eastern paths. Furthermore, although the Sun revolves in its own orbit, because there is an absence of zodiacal signs (rāśis) that manifest the asterisms therein, the motion of the Sun is conceived as being on a straight line (samasūtratayā) with the asterisms situated within the ecliptic (antivṛtta) imagined upon the Bhagola. Thus, the motion of the Sun is considered to coincide with the asterisms.

In the same way, although the Moon and other planets are situated on the half-sphere of the stellar sphere (*bhagola*), the zodiacal signs there exist along the same meridian line. For the purpose of knowing their motion, lunar mansions, and so forth, circles of declination (*ravṛtta*) are described upon the stellar sphere; thus, it is indeed logical that the binding of the *śara* (latitude) is performed upon the *bhagola*, as it is simpler and does not require reference to the planetary sphere (*prahagola*). This is the intended meaning. Now, he states the declination (*krānti*) and the latitude (*vikṣepa*): "The declination is the distance from the ecliptic circle (*teirgajapama*); the latitude (*śara*) is the distance from the circle of declination."

The obliquity (apama) is the horizontal distance between the planet and the equatorial circle (nāḍikāvṛtta). That which is held as the true position of the planet, its distance from the equatorial circle is the declination (krānti). Now, the position of the planet on the eccentric circle (vimaṇḍala), its horizontal distance from the ecliptic (krāntivṛtta) is the latitude (vikṣepa). Then, the horizontal distance from the equatorial circle to the planet situated on the eccentric circle is the true declination (sphuṭā krānti). || 16 ||

Now he states the precession of the equinoxes (*krāntipāta*): The intersection of the equinoctial line and the circle of declination is the precession of the equinoxes (*krāntipāta*). Its revolutions according to the Sauras are three times ten thousand (*30,000*) in a Kalpa. (17) That which was stated by the ancients as the "precession of the solstices" (*ayanacalana*) is indeed this very same thing. According to that school of thought, its revolutions in a Kalpa are 19,96,69. (18) Having added the resulting [longitude of] the node (*pāta*) to the [longitude of] the Sun, the declination (*apama*) is to be calculated. Then, depending on the declination, the ascensional difference (*cara*) is to be subtracted from the [ascensional] difference at sunrise. (19)

The *krāntipāta* (precession of the equinoxes) is the point of intersection for the sake of the maiden (*kanyā*). "Intersection" (*pāta*) means a point of contact. Between what two? Between the equinoctial circle (*viṣuvadvṛtta*) and the ecliptic (*krāntivṛtta*). For their point of intersection does not occur at the beginning of Aries alone; rather, that [point] also possesses motion. Those degrees well-known as the [fixed] positions of the constellations are themselves the degrees of the precessing ecliptic moving in the reverse direction. This means that the ecliptic intersects the equinoctial circle at a distance of so many degrees behind the beginning of Aries. It cannot be said that there is no such thing as the *krāntipāta*.

Because it has been perceived through direct observation (*pratyakṣa*). If it is asked, "Since they will state the means of its perception later on, why was it not mentioned by Bāla, Guha, and others who were also experts?", the answer is that it was not mentioned then because it was very slight; now, however, because it is abundant, it has been perceived by contemporary scholars. For this very reason, it should be understood that there is a movement (*gati*) for it. If this is so, then even though it is unperceived, it is one [of the planets] because it is subtracted from the circumference of the revolutions (*bhagaṇa-paridhi*) according to the authority of the *Āgama* of the Saura Siddhānta. True.

In this science of calculation (*gaṇita*), scripture (*āgama*) alone is the authority when it is accompanied by logical justification (*upapatti*). One should not ask how those [figures for] the revolutions of the apogees were stated by them solely on the basis of scriptural authority; for the points where the equation of the center (*mandaphala*) is zero are perceived through direct observation (*pratyakṣa*), and these very points are the locations of the apogees (*mandocca*). Likewise, those points where there is an absence of eccentricity (*vikṣepa*) are the locations of the nodes (*pāta*). However, it remains doubtful whether they possess motion or not.

In that regard, there exists a motion for those [nodes] derived from the apogees of the slow motion (mandocca), established by the inference that they are like the Moon’s slow apogee and node (pāta). As for how much that [motion] is, it is said: the number of revolutions (bhagaṇa) in a period of one hundred years, which are obtained through calculation, should be understood as the annual or daily motion arising from that number. Now, if those very same positions are reached by means of different numbers of revolutions, then which of the two motions is authoritative?

Therefore, this present course [of the planets] must be accepted as being based upon current observations. However, when after a long time a great discrepancy shall have arisen, then highly intelligent individuals, possessing qualities equal to those of Brahmagupta and others, will appear. They, following that future observation-based course, will compose new treatises. For this very reason, this branch of calculation (*gaṇitaskandha*), though joined with those of great intelligence, would not perish even at the end of a cycle of Manvantaras. [End of Section] 11 Vyā 96 Ṭu Ne. *Note: The concluding portion of the text appears to contain scribal or typographical markers indicating the end of a section or commentary.*

It moves; therefore, the revolutions (bhagaṇas) of this precession of the equinoxes (kāntipāta) are three times ten thousand (30,000), as stated by the Sūryasiddhānta. Likewise, Munjala has stated that the number of revolutions is the same; this very [precession] arises as 19,96,69 (one hundred ninety-nine thousand six hundred sixty-nine). Whether those revolutions be these or others, the meaning is that when they are determined precisely by the experts, then that alone is the true precession of the equinoxes.

Having added the retrograde *kāntipāta* (node of the ecliptic) to the planet, the declination (*krānti*) is to be calculated. Bhāṣyaṭīkā: Now, as an incidental matter, he describes the nature of the declination and its motion in the *sragviṇī* meter, beginning with "nāḍika. Here, on the stellar sphere (*bhagola*), the declination (*apamaḥ* or *krāntiḥ*) is the interval measured perpendicularly from the point on the equatorial circle (*nāḍikāmaṇḍala*) toward the south or north. [An objection is raised: "But since the second limit is unknown, how can the interval be known? To this he replies: "The limits being the ecliptic (*kāntivṛtta*)."

The meaning is that the interval between the point of the true planet on the ecliptic and a point on the meridian passing through the pole, situated on a circle parallel to the equator, is called declination (*krānti*). He states its nature: "from the ecliptic" (*krāntivṛttāt*). This is the north-south distance from the point on the ecliptic corresponding to the position of the true planet. Here he states the second limit: "the limit being the circle of obliquity" (*kṣepavṛttāvadhi*).

The position of the true planet on the secondary circle (śeṣavṛtta) is the point where it moves; likewise, the interval between the two positions of the true planet, consisting of north-south declination (krānti), is situated on the secondary circle passing through the poles—this is the meaning of "latitude" (śara). Now, in this context, he states the nature of the true latitude: "In this manner," etc. It is the interval between the point of entry into the northern direction of the latitude and a portion of the region of the secondary circle of time (nāḍikāvṛtta) that serves as the locus for the planetary disc. Thus, when situated on the secondary circle passing through the poles in a transverse direction, there is the true apama (latitude), which is the true declination (krānti).

Because it remains fixed in its specific motion within the great [sphere]. By this, it should be understood that the *śara* (latitude) suitable for the correction of declination (*krānti*) is also stated as being directed toward the north pole (*dhruva*). || 16 || Now, by way of an introductory connection (*upodghāta*), he describes the nature of the *krāntipāta* (the node of declination) in verse: "The equinox," etc. The "equinox" refers to the previously mentioned intersection (*saṃpāta*) of the ecliptic and the equator—the specific point on the sphere of the stars (*bhagola*) where they meet. In the expression "the intersection of the declination and the equator" (*krāntiviṣuvavṛttasaṃpāta*), the middle syllables have been elided; thus, it is called *krāntipāta*. In the *Paddhati*, because of the subtraction of half the circle from the circle's fall, [it is called] *cakra*...

It is like the case of [the] *hāni* (loss/diminution). When it is for the purpose of calculating declination (*krānti*), the *pāta* (node) is the *saṃpāta* (conjunction/node); this is because declination, which is the distance between the equator (*viṣuvadvṛtta*) and the northern or southern limit, begins precisely from the *upasaṃpāta*. [Objection: But since there is no inherent motion of this node on the celestial sphere (*bhagola*), the previously stated claim that "the *pāta* moves due to its own nature" is incorrect; for otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of having to state its revolutions (*bhagaṇa*) separately, just as one does for the planets. To this, he says: "Its revolutions... (*tadgaṇā iti*).

The revolutions of the *krāntipāta* (the node of the ecliptic) as stated by Sūrya refer to those mentioned in the *Sūryasiddhānta*. "In reverse" means moving westward, consisting of the number of revolutions required for it to traverse the twelve zodiacal signs. In a *kalpa*, which is a day of Brahmā, this number is thirty-three thousand. Furthermore, since the *saṃpāta* (node) can be read as being like a planet, otherwise there would be a contradiction with the revolutions stated therein; thus, the statement that the *krāntipāta* moves "in opposition" (westward) is consistent. This is the underlying meaning (*prabhāva*).

But surely, since the intersection of the equinoctial circle and the circle of obliquity—which consists of the *rekhās*—is fixed at a single point on the stellar sphere (*bhagola*), its movement has been refuted. Or rather, its movement occurs precisely through the movement of the stellar sphere itself. For instance, in accordance with the two *kadamba* poles, the stellar sphere sometimes moves eastward by its own power; consequently, that movement [is observed] in the model of the upper and lower spheres placed upon it. (Bhaṭṭotpala’s Commentary on the *Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa*, 312)

That equinoctial circle does not follow that [ecliptic]; therefore, by way of following it, there must necessarily be a circle of that same nature called the equinoctial circle. From this, the precession (valana) from the intersection of this circle with the equinoctial circle toward the previous intersection of the equinoctial circle and the ecliptic is directly perceived. Nor should it be argued that the node of the ecliptic (krāntipāta) moves westward due to the impossibility of the [proposed] reasoning.

The node (bhaṅga) is traditionally held to be at the end of the asterism Pauṣṇa (Revatī). This is because it would be illogical for the statement regarding yojanas to be made later, given that the revolutions of the planets calculated from the point on the ecliptic occupied by the apogee of the Moon—which serves as the locus of Revatī—would result in a retrograde motion of the sun due to the sun's declination and other factors, necessitating the subtraction of the *krāntipāta* (precession of the equinoxes). Nor is there any inconsistency in this retrograde motion.

If it is argued that the movement of the intersection of the equinoctial circle and the ecliptic—having moved from its original position—is established by the movement of the intersection [of the lunar mansions] as determined by the *Revatī* stars, and that for this very reason the calculation of the planetary revolutions and so forth is established through the presiding positions of the *Revatī* stars and others, we say no. This is because, by postulating an equinoctial circle, it is impossible for the intersection to move precisely there [at the fixed point]. It is improper to calculate the revolution of one [circle] based on the movement of another.

Because there are multiple points of intersection (*saṃpāta*) of the *kapita* circles, and because it is logically untenable to postulate [multiple] nodes (*bhaṇaka*), one should not postulate two circles for the pair of *pravaha* winds in accordance with the *viṣuva-vṛtta* (equinoctial circle) and the *cakra-anta-vṛtta* (meridian circle). In that case, the twelve signs beginning with Aries remain fixed upon the *krānti-vṛtta* (ecliptic), which is divided into twelve parts starting from those intersections.

Rising from that [equinoctial point] due to its own motion, the node (nakṣatragraha) moves westward along the path of the ecliptic; thus, by means of the line coinciding with the movement of the intersection of the equator and the ecliptic situated on the stellar sphere (bhagola), the derivation of the zodiacal signs (bhagaṇa) is established. Indeed, Aries is at the vernal equinox; the statement regarding the retrograde motion of the planets, as they appear to move westward from the position of Revatī toward the portion of the ecliptic situated on the stellar sphere along the equatorial line, is explained accordingly.

Therefore, it should not be argued that the calculation of eclipses by means of the precession of the equinoxes is established because the planets are displaced from the fixed stars by the *pravaha* wind; for since the zodiacal signs (*rāśis*) are conceived in accordance with the constellations (*nakṣatras*), it is logical to conceive of the signs as real entities existing in their own positions. Otherwise, there would be no basis for conceiving of these signs as distinct and stable entities. Furthermore, the motion of the stellar sphere (*bhagola*) constrained by the ecliptic is untenable, because the two poles—which are fixed and attached to it—would remain stationary.

Otherwise, there would be the alternative view that the earth rotates due to the revolution of the Pravaha wind. However, this cannot be so, because it would result in a discrepancy in the degrees of latitude (akṣāṃśa) and other parameters every year; furthermore, if the zodiac were to move in accordance with the equatorial circle (viṣuvadvṛtta), the completion of the zodiacal revolutions (bhagaṇa) would be untenable, since the motion of the zodiac is based upon the ecliptic (krāntivṛtta). To this, they reply: the celestial sphere (bhagola) itself is the locus of the clouds and the constellations; it is by their movement within that very sphere that all [the stars] complete their zodiacal revolutions.

In that regard, within the tube of the form of space, the nodes (*vaidhrta*) of the ecliptic and the equator, such as the *Aśleṣā* star and others, move along the path of the sun by their own power; however, on the equator, they are immovable by their own power. And thus, at the conjunction, the stars of the *Revatī* yoga-tārā and others do not exist in the eastern ecliptic; therefore, the motion (*bhoga*) of the planets and so forth is not possible there.

Now, when it has moved to another point on the ecliptic, since the sun previously resided at one point on the ecliptic and then moves from there, it is perceived as departing from the position of Revatī; thus, by this logic, the *ayanāṃśa* (precession) of the ecliptic is to the west, and therefore its movement is reversed—this is not untenable. However, that [explanation] is to be considered further.

Even if the Revatī star shifts due to the movement of the ecliptic, there is no shift for the fixed stars (dhruvaka) situated on the ecliptic because they have no connection with the Revatī star; thus, their stability is untenable, as the Revatī star would otherwise not be fixed. Nor do those [fixed stars] move accordingly, for that would involve the shifting of their positions. This is because there is no evidence for such a shift, and it would entail unnecessary complexity (gaurava). Furthermore, the fixed stars are established by the projection of the pole-star (dhruva), and since there is no proof for their movement, and because such a theory is cumbersome, they remain stable.

Furthermore, since the heart of the elemental sphere (bhūtagola) has no connection with the two poles (dhruva), its rotation following them is impossible; otherwise, the two poles would be rendered purposeless. Thus, the conception of a material sphere (mūrtagola) is proposed there, wherein the circular lines take the form of nodes (saṃpāta) moving in accordance with the ecliptic (krāntivṛtta). However, the moderns (navya), rather than postulating many material circles, maintain that for the sake of parsimony (lāghava), only a single sphere supported by the stars is to be conceived.

In this regard, although movement toward the point of conjunction (*saṃpāta*) is logically untenable, nevertheless, because all the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) possess sentience—as it were—a prior movement by their own power is possible. Therefore, the perception of a contrary motion at the point of conjunction is consistent with the fact that Revatī follows the junction of the moon. In this matter, the motion of all [the planets] is equal. By this, the doubt is dispelled as to why the lunar mansions do not move in the same way that the planets move by their own power.

They say that this is stated in the *Sūryasiddhānta* and other texts, namely: "The circle [of the asterisms] revolves around the sun. That is not correct. Because of the statement, "The revolution (bhagaṇa) is recorded as ending at the end of Pauṣṇa (Revatī)," it would follow that after the conjunction with Revatī, when there is again a conjunction with Revatī at the time of completing the full revolution (bhagaṇa), there would be a conjunction exceeding the circle; consequently, the absence of the circle's revolutions would result. In reality, however, the stellar sphere (*bhagola*) is a single material entity, fixed there by the earth at its southern and northern poles.

The solid sphere (vṛtta) is a physical representation imitating the ecliptic circle situated within the celestial globe. At every point, the ecliptic is threaded with fine, solid threads in the form of dense segments running north-south, through which the respective constellations are strung according to their own positions. Thus, the ecliptic is continuously measured by the rotation of the celestial globe. Therein, at the point where the ecliptic meets the meridian, the star Revatī is fixed upon the lower rim in its own place.

The asterisms are not indeed fixed upon the stellar sphere (*bhagola*); rather, it is the ecliptic (*krāntivṛtta*) conjoined with the asterisms that possesses the nature of a sphere because it is attached to the terrestrial globe (*bhūgola*). Nor should it be argued that such a conception of the stellar sphere is useless; for the terrestrial globe, which serves as the support for the poles, must be conceived as a substrate so that the physical ecliptic—which touches the poles—may remain in its own form. This is because, if one were to conceive the ecliptic as being fixed at the pole-points of the asterisms, it would be impossible for it to move again by its own power.

This has been stated [in the Laghu-Bhāskarīya]: "Thus, this zodiacal wheel (bhacakra), fixed to the two poles (dhruva) and impelled by the Pravaha wind, revolves; and to it are attached the orbits of the planets in their respective order. That ecliptic (krāntivṛtta) was moved from the east by its own motion through the will of the Lord. Yet, due to its extreme heaviness and the absence of a firm connection, the sphere (bha-gola) did not move along with the ecliptic; rather, it remains fixed by the power of the poles.

The truth is that there is nothing contradictory in such statements as "from the position of Revatī, the conjunction of the throat (the winter solstice) occurs exactly to the west," or "it is retrograde," and so forth. This might be argued: according to the statement in the *Sūryasiddhānta*, Chapter on Spheres (Golādhyāya), verses 80–81: "In a Yuga, the precession (*ayanāṃśa*) of the stars is obtained thirty times; it is found by dividing the accumulated days of the Yuga (*yugagaṇa*) by three hundred and sixty. From the resulting degrees, multiplied by three and divided by ten, the portions known as the precession (*ayanābhidhā*) are to be understood. Such is the meaning derived from this [text].

The ecliptic moves gradually westward on the stellar sphere (bhagola) by its own motion up to twenty-seven degrees; thereafter, by its own velocity, it returns to its original position—thus are the revolutions described. Now, one might ask: like the planets, does it not complete a full circle through the twelve signs? Such revolutions amount to thirty-two times thirty-two, or six hundred and twenty (620), in a great yuga (mahāyuga). Therefore, when these revolutions are multiplied by a thousand for a small [yuga], they are established as sixty lakhs (6,000,000).

It is not three ayutas, nor is this work [composed] twenty times; by this, it is implied that it is thirty times. Otherwise, there would be a metrical defect (*chandobhaṅga*) in the reading. Therefore, the reading there is *triṃśatkṛtvā*. It means that in a *yuga*, the ecliptic is traversed thirty times by the Sun and Moon; thus, thirty such groups [of revolutions] constitute a *yuga*. The revolution of the asterismal circle (*bhagaṇabhoga*) is also, like that of the planets, of the nature of a complete rotation of the zodiac (*cakrabhrama*), because it is fixed.

Furthermore, there is a lack of evidence for any other interpretation. Thus, it must be stated that the thirty *yuga* revolutions, multiplied by a thousand, constitute the *kalpa* revolution; in this way, three *acyutas* are produced. For if one were to claim that the zodiacal sphere lags behind by six hundred [revolutions] in a *yuga*—which would constitute a single precession—and that these six hundred occur within the *yuga*, this would result in a contradiction with both the *Somapradā-siddhānta* and the *Siddhānta*. Moreover, even in other works of the sages, thirty revolutions are not mentioned.

Indeed, by assuming a single revolution (parivarta) of the zodiacal circle (bhagaṇa) to be equal to that [of the precession], the twelve signs (rāśis) are also assumed; then, from that count, the precession (ayana) is brought to the form of a revolution according to the stated method, and by discarding the completed revolutions of the circle, the remainder—the portion of the signs—is that which has elapsed within the current revolution.

In that regard, from the very commencement of another motion—that is, from the commencement of the revolution of the asterisms (bhagaṇa)—the ecliptic (krāntivṛtta) moves westward within the zodiacal signs (rāśi), and eastward when it is not within them; even there, its forward motion occurs precisely by virtue of being within or not within the westward-moving signs. Consequently, between two points on the current ecliptic, it is twofold in nature, depending on whether one assumes the interval to be in the middle or otherwise.

Since that [precession] consists of parts included within twenty-seven actual divisions for the purpose of calculation, when the proportion "if nine degrees correspond to twenty-seven degrees, then what do the degrees of the longitudinal motion of the planets (ayanagraha-bhujāṃśa) correspond to? is set up, the multiplier and divisor are reduced by nine. Thus, the precession degrees (ayanāṃśa), being equal to the degrees of the longitudinal motion of the planets, become ten. Therefore, by the statement of Śākalya, the *krāntipāta* (the node of the ecliptic) is established as having the nature of the precession degrees. The *krāntipāta* as a precession-planet brought forth by the delighted mathematicians is not this one.

Nor should it be said that the precession of the equinoxes (*ayanāma*) is not mentioned here; for this is established by the statement in the second verse of the *Sūryasiddhānta* and is supported by that very citation. Furthermore, having considered the *Sūryasiddhānta* itself, whatever has been presented here in our own work is merely a minor point. Many scholars, such as Agraśarman, summarize [the calculation] as three times ten thousand in the form of *karūpa*. Regarding this, some hold that the term "of whom" (*kasya*) refers to the twenty-first part of a *kalpa*.

Therefore, it is established by that same measure as being equal to the planets described in the *Sūryasiddhānta*. When, in the word "ayuta," there is the reading "niyuta," then—since the word "niyuta" denotes the number one hundred thousand (lakṣa)—the western revolution [of the node] is three hundred thousand [degrees], because the *krāntipāta* (node of the ecliptic) is to the west of the point where the ecliptic moves eastward. An equal number of revolutions occurs in the eastern portion, because it remains fixed while the ecliptic moves westward.

Thus ends the section on the determination of the nodes (*galabandha*). [Verse 2.5]: "The revolutions of the asterisms (*bhagaṇa*) are mutually separated; they are not independent and scattered. This second solution is appropriate as a remedy for the deficiency in the previous solution. It is indicated by the statement, "I shall explain the calculation of the precession of the equinoxes (*ayanagraha*) and the nodes (*krāntipāta*) according to the method taught in the *Sūryasiddhānta*," that this should be done in that manner. Otherwise, the word "properly" (*sam-*) would become redundant.

They maintain that since it is impossible to accept the positive or negative nature of the degrees of the eastern and western limits, one should add them according to the method stated in the *Bīja* (such as "the sum would be..."), and thus their summation is logical; however, this is to be considered doubtful. For, according to the method stated in the *Sūryasiddhānta*, it is not established that the western revolutions (*bhagaṇa*) amount to 584,000; furthermore, since the revolutions are established through the eastward and westward motions held by the spheres, it is impossible for those [revolutions] to be designated as "western" or "eastern. In reality, those revolutions are as stated in the *Saura[siddhānta]*.

In the *Sūryasiddhānta*, [the number of years] is stated by the meaning of the verse beginning with "thirty times in a yuga" (*triṃśatkṛtvo yuge*). And by this very [method], its calculation is explained in the *Sūryasiddhānta* by the passage beginning with "divided by the terrestrial days" (*tadvarṣadinairbhakta*) and ending with "named the precession" (*ayanābhidhā*). This is indicated in the *Mīnarṣi*. However, there is no syntactic connection for the phrase "not those stated in the Saura [system]. As for the final quarter [of the verse] ending with "in three ten-thousands in a kalpa" (*vyasta ayutatraye kalpe*), that is a different opinion; it does not describe the meaning intended by the *Sūryasiddhānta*, because of the absence of agreement and the absence of evidence.

In this view of the teachers, there is a partiality even toward the *ārṣa* (Vedic) tradition, because they postulate four types of motion following the movement of the planets. Sometimes it is like the planets, and sometimes it is the opposite of the planets' motion; furthermore, there is no logical justification for its not following [the planets] up to twenty-seven degrees. Moreover, just as the nodes (*pāta*) of the planets move westward, it is simpler and more logical to assume that the node of the *krānti* (ecliptic) also moves as a node; otherwise, the nodes of the latitudes (*śara*) would also [have to be explained in a different way].

[The sun's] movements would follow the pattern of its northern and southern courses. Furthermore, there could never have been a time when the sun was situated to the south of the midpoint of Āśleṣā and to the north of the midpoint of Viśākhā—such that it was stated in the ancient scriptures [that the solstices occurred at those points]. Thus, the statement of Varāhamihira is untenable. Now, regarding these two solstitial points (karka-markarāya) which are intended as the limits, they are fixed by the wise at the final quarter of Punarvasu and the second quarter of Dhanisthā.

Because the degrees of the precession (*ayanāṃśa*) were greater during the time of Nirayana and Varāhamihira, and because of the occurrence of the preceding nakṣatras through the reduction of those [degrees], and because at the end of the Saura system that [precession] was not established due to the absence of the former *ayanāṃśas*, yet it did occur when the western *ayanāṃśas* were present; therefore, it must be said that it occurred in the past when the western *ayanāṃśas* stood at twenty-three degrees, including twenty minutes of arc, for it was possible then. Thus it is stated that it "was."

This is possible when the precession of the equinoxes (ayanagraha) amounts to eleven signs, increased by one-sixth and forty *kalās*. As for the justification of this calculation: according to the method for determining the degrees of precession (*ayanāṃśa*) explained in the chapter on the "Apparent [Sun]" (*Sphuṭādhikāra*), an increase of nine seconds (*vikalā*) per year is observed; through proportionate calculation (*anupāta*), it is established that in a *kalpa* there are twenty-four thousand such increments. Regarding this statement: "The revolutions of the nodes (*krāntipāta*) in a *kalpa* are not equal to those of the sky."

"Because the revolutions [of the apsis] are subtracted from the revolutions obtained by direct observation, such is the reality. Now, one might object: "Since the author of the *Mūla* (the *Sūryasiddhānta*) has stated in the midst of his discussion on the apsis correction that 'therefore, the revolutions of the apsis of the Sun, as stated in the *Sūryasiddhānta*, amount to thirty thousand in a Kalpa,' and since he has thus clarified his own intention through this statement, how can you say that all of this is contrary to the author's intent? If you ask this, the answer is no; for there is no contradiction with the direct observation [implied] by what is stated in the *Sūryasiddhānta*.

3.1. Furthermore, in the *Golādhyāya*, up to the end of the section on the three [parameters], this is the opinion of others (*paramata*). In the *Pharśikā*, it is studied as the root; likewise, in the *Sūryasiddhānta*, those [parameters] are first [discussed] from the perspective of the opinions of others (*paramata*), and are therefore more primary. When the number of revolutions (*bhagaṇa*) is thirty thousand (*ayutatraya*), then according to the method stated by Varāha—“*śaruvuśuśucarāya*”—twenty-four are added (*kṣipta*). "Struck" (*hata*) means, in effect, added.

One interpretation, found in both the root text and the commentary, is that "six hundred thousand" (*lakṣa-ṣaṣṭa*) revolutions are those stated in the *Sūryasiddhānta*. Regarding the term "three ten-thousands" (*ayuta-trayam*), because the letter 'va' is a conjunct consonant (*saṃyuktākṣara*), there is the perception of the number six; thus, one might think the number six applies to the first through sixth places. Therefore, the interpretation as "six hundred thousand" is weak, because there is no restrictive rule for taking the phrase "three ten-thousands" to mean six syllables, and furthermore, it results in the inconsistency of the word "reversed" (*vyasta*). || 17 ||

[Objection: "But since the equinox (*saṃpāta*) does not move even when a point on the ecliptic (*krāntivṛtta*) moves due to the precession of the equinoxes, how can these [values] be called the revolutions of the apogee of the equinox (*krāntipāta*), given that they are stated in the *Sūryasiddhānta* and other texts to be equal in number to the revolutions of the zodiac (*bhacakra*)? Furthermore, this was not mentioned by Brahmagupta. To this, he provides a justification in accordance with the views of earlier authorities and the established tradition regarding the apogee of the equinox, beginning with the words "ayanāṃśāḥ" (precession of the equinoxes). This refers to the teachings of Munjala and other ancient masters.

As the celestial sphere moves from the north toward the southern direction, and subsequently from the south toward the northern quarter, there occurs a slight deviation known as *apama* (obliquity). At the intersection of the equator and the ecliptic in the east, Aries and the other signs begin; in the west, Libra and the others. The origin of this obliquity is said to occur at an interval of three signs from these points, starting from Capricorn according to our sequence. Therein lies the maximum declination, measured in degrees and minutes; it is precisely there that the solstitial point (*ayanasaṃdhi*) is indicated, and the precession (*calana*) occurs right there.

By the word "Revatī," the precession of the equinoxes at the beginning of the Kalpa is indicated; for at the conjunction [of the solstices], Brahmā established the Manmatha (Aries) and other signs starting from Revatī. In that [circle], the thirty-fold interval beginning with Kakudī (Capricorn) and others occurs in the east and west, due to the completion of their northward and southward movements; this is the junction of the maximum declination (*paramakrānti*), which arises because one solstice is joined with the commencement of the other.

Then, after some time, because the precession of the equinoxes (ayanasaṃdhi) was observed at the very same location where the maximum declination (paramakrānti) had previously been seen, it was established that the shifting of the solstice—the junction point of the maximum northern or southern course—occurs at a different position. Therefore, this motion, which consists of the precession of the equinoxes, has been stated and accepted [by the author]. The word "eva" (only/itself) serves to exclude other possibilities.

The meaning is as follows: the precession of the equinoxes (*ayanacalana*) cannot occur without the motion of the apogee (*antipātacalana*), because the precession of the apogee is impossible [without it]. Furthermore, since the precession of the apogee and the precession of the equinoxes are considered non-different by the ancient masters, it was stated [by them] that there is a "precession of the apogee" (*ayanapāta*), not a "precession of the equinoxes" (*krantipāta*). It should be noted that Brahmagupta did not mention this at the time of his own work because he did not perceive it.

Now, even though its precession (ayanāṃśa) has been established as three hundred and sixty [degrees] as previously stated, since the movement of the new beginning (navavilāgamana) is not observed every year according to that method of calculation, how can there be three hundred and sixty? To refute this objection regarding the difference between that calculation and other systems, he states the authorities for that calculation—just like the annual movement perceived through direct observation—by saying "in that system" (tatpakṣe). In the system of Muñjāla and others, those revolutions (tadgaṇāḥ) are the revolutions of the apogee of the ecliptic (krāntipāta) subtracted from the Kalpa day of Brahmā.

Two hundred thousand three hundred and thirty-one [years] less one; that is stated according to the words: "In the era of Kaśyapa, it is measured by the [number of] houses, oceans, mountains, and moons" (i.e., 231,059). In accordance with this, its annual rate is fifty-nine kalās and five-fourths of a part thereof. That part [is further divided], and the thirty-first part thereof is also mentioned in the Golādhyāya section. [The calculation is: 247, 59, 54, 2, 31, 12. This is my direct observation. 59 || 54 || 2 || 31 || 12 ||

For this very reason, in the *Karaṇakutūhala*, Munīśvara has set down the calculation of the precession of the equinoxes (*ayanāṃśa*) as follows: at the time [of writing], he established this precession in terms of revolutions and so forth as 9|18|9|10|54|35|23|55|41|48. Since there was no further need for the revolutions and because the signs were zero, he omitted the signs and reduced the remaining degrees to elevenths. Having accepted one-sixtieth of those degrees as seconds for each year, he stated that the precession of the equinoxes is obtained by adding the resulting minutes to the [mean] longitude from the *Karaṇa* and other such works. Thus, the method for calculating the precession of the equinoxes was composed.

As for the precession degrees (*ayana-aṃśa*) in the *Sūryasiddhānta*, which have a maximum of twenty-seven degrees, Muñjāla, based on direct observation, accepted a slightly different maximum of twenty-nine degrees, thirty minutes, one second, and eighteen thirds (29° 30′ 1″ 18″). Therefore, when the longitudinal degrees of the planet at the solstice (*ayana-graha*)—calculated from the revolutions stated in the *Sūryasiddhānta*—are multiplied by these [degrees] and divided by ninety, the multiplier and divisor are reduced by dividing both by their common factor; thus, the divisor becomes 3 2/3.

And likewise, those degrees of the [precession] arc (ayanāṃśa) divided by the divisor [of the sine table] are the [required] degrees; there, for the sake of brevity, the confusion of the calculation involving the sine of the argument has been avoided. Thus, the solar [degrees] multiplied by the number of revolutions and divided by the divisor become simplified as the revolutions, which are established as 199,669 according to one's own school. This is intended here to be conceived as a slow motion (manda). That is incorrect; because by the previous method, the inclusion of the precession degrees within that [calculation] is established, whereas by your intention, that is not established.

This is because it is understood as having the same effect as other planets, such as those in the zodiac signs (*rāśi*) and so forth. Nor can it be the lord of the desired [result], for that would contradict its essential nature as established by the *bhaga* (the zodiacal circle). Laghvārthabhaṭṭa, by calculating twenty-four degrees for the precession, stated in accordance with the *sūryasiddhānta* system of revolutions that the revolutions of the precession are 57,81,59. In the opinion of Pārāśarya, it is stated that the revolutions of what is called the precession are 58,17,09. In the *Parāśarasiddhānta* as well, it is said: "The revolutions are 58,17,02; there, the precession and that of Agastya [are included]."

At that time, the precession of the equinoxes (*ayanagraha*) was taken by the teachers as the declination sine (*krāntijyā*), being positive or negative according to the face of the horse and the dog (the solstices). However, this was disregarded because it was observed that the statement "the precession is the oblique ascension" (*ayanalambhā*) was inconsistent with what had been previously stated. Furthermore, there is no evidence for its movement being like the increase or decrease of degrees in the zodiacal signs (*jhanya*). Since it applies universally to all mean planets, the calculation of the declination sine is appropriate according to the method derived from the *Sūryasiddhānta*—which arose from the tradition of the *Dāsagaṇa*—namely: "The degrees of precession multiplied by four and divided by the lunar days (*tithi*). This method of calculation is thus justified.

In the *Parāśara-siddhānta*, however, it is stated: "Then, this [precession] is to be known as the *ayanajyā* (the sine of precession), which is the product of the sine of the planet's longitude increased by nine signs (*sāyanagrahadori*) and the sine of twenty-four degrees fifteen minutes (*siddhāṃśajīvā*), divided by the sine of three signs (*tribhajyā*). Its arc constitutes the *calāṃśas* (precessional degrees). These are additive to the planet in its own sphere, whether it be the sun or the moon. When it is said that 'the correction from that [precession] is positive for the time of the end of the day,' there is a great contradiction; therefore, it is disregarded due to the difference in the *Ārya* [tradition]. [Note: The text indicates that the calculation method provided here contradicts other authorities and is thus rejected.]

In this regard, it has been stated by Varāhamihira, as a point accepted by all: "The sine of the obliquity of the ecliptic (jyā) is 1397; when multiplied by the equinoctial shadow (iṣṭa-jina) and divided by 24, the result is the tribhajyā. This is the final chord of the circle of sines (jyā-cakra), and its arc is the declination (krānti), measured in degrees. As for the claim made by some in the *Mūlamata* that the maximum obliquity of the ecliptic is twenty-four degrees, that is due to a lack of understanding of that particular school's doctrine; so, enough of this. (18)

[Objection: But surely, since the zodiacal circle (bhagaṇa) is said to end at the asterism of Puṣya, the conjunction (saṃpāta) must be reckoned from Revatī as the starting point for the calculation of planetary longitude; thus, its description [in the *Golādhyāya*] is useless, just like the description of the precession degrees (*ayanāṃśa*), which consist of retrograde motion and serve no purpose in knowing planetary longitude. For here, unlike the Yavana system, the planetary longitude is not measured from the conjunction (saṃpāta), such that one would need to subtract the precession degrees to know it relative to Revatī as the limit. Therefore, its description is superfluous. [Response: Its description is well-founded. For the reason why the zodiacal circle is stated to end at Puṣya is because the circle of asterisms (nakṣatramaṇḍala) is fixed with respect to the sphere of the stars (jyotiścakra). However, the circle of asterisms does not rotate along with the sphere of the stars; rather, it remains stationary while the sphere of the stars rotates. Consequently, the circle of asterisms appears to move in the opposite direction [to the stars]. Thus, the circle of asterisms is considered to have the same longitude as the star Revatī. Since the circle of asterisms is fixed, the calculation of the planets' longitudes is performed by adding the precession degrees to the true longitudes of the planets. Therefore, the description of the conjunction (saṃpāta) is indeed necessary. Furthermore, the circle of asterisms is established with the star Revatī as its zero-point (origin). Hence, the conjunction (saṃpāta) is determined by adding the precession degrees to the true longitudes of the planets. This is the meaning. Note: The commentary (*ma0 ḍī0*) explains that while the *Yavana* tradition calculates planetary longitude from the *saṃpāta* (the point where the ecliptic intersects the equator), the Indian system uses the *nakṣatra-maṇḍala* (fixed star sphere) as the reference. Because the *nakṣatra-maṇḍala* is fixed while the *jyotiścakra* (stellar sphere) rotates, the former appears to move westward. By taking Revatī as the zero-point, the system requires the addition of *ayanāṃśas* to the true planet positions to find their longitudes relative to the fixed stars. Thus, the *saṃpāta* is relevant for determining the relationship between the two systems.

Since the planet’s motion in signs and so forth might not exist at the time of an eclipse due to the observation of its conjunction with the star Revatī, he says "tatsaṃjātam" (that which has arisen) out of apprehension: having added—that is, having joined—to the planet that "tatsaṃjātam," which is the motion in revolutions and so forth brought forward by the daily motion from the revolutions associated with the [mean] moon, and having converted that motion from revolutions into signs and so forth by means of the revolution-period; and having added that which consists of the precession of the equinoxes (ayanacalana).

According to the Saura-mata, however, one should calculate the *krāntipāta* (precession) in the form of *ayanāṃśas* from the *ayanagṛha* (precession point) derived from the *bhagaṇas* according to the stated method; this is to be added or subtracted—positive or negative—depending on whether the *ayanagṛha* falls within the signs beginning with Libra or Aries, respectively, following the sequence of its motion. The meaning is that it should be joined to the planet in its positive form, according to the method of Ādivaja, such that "in the conjunction there shall be a sum. Thus, in the *Siddhānta-samuccaya*: "In a *yuga*, the stellar sphere indeed lags behind six hundred times; the *ghugaṇa* (day-count), divided by the terrestrial days of a youth, is the *ayanagraha* (precession point)."

"The degrees of precession (ayanāṃśa) are to be added to those [planetary longitudes] when the planet is in an odd sign starting from Leo (Meṣa), and subtracted when it is in an even sign starting from Libra (Tulā), provided the planet is in a quadrant. The declination (apama) is to be calculated. Now, although these [precessional corrections] are not directly instrumental in determining the planetary longitude itself, it has been stated that declination is measured as the oblique distance from the equatorial plane (nāḍīmaṇḍala). Therefore, for the purpose of calculating declination, it is necessary to apply the precessional correction (ayanāṃśa) to the longitude as determined by calculation, because the point of intersection (saṃpāta) is required as the zero-point of measurement. Thus, the intention is that defining this [precession] is not redundant.

In this context, he states the correction involving the addition of the precession of the equinoxes (*ayanāṃśa*) for the purpose of calculating the ascensional difference (*cara*) and the oblique ascensions (*lagna*), beginning with the words "krāntivaśāt" (due to the influence of declination). For that reason—in order to calculate the half-ascensional difference and the oblique ascensions—the precession of the equinoxes (*krāntipāta*) must first be added to the planet. Why? He states the reason: "krāntivaśāt. The ascensional difference (*cara*) and the oblique ascensions (*rāśyudaya*) arise from the sine of declination (*krāntijyā*). Furthermore, the time of the ascensional difference (*carakāla*) and the right ascensions (*rāśyudaya-sāvana*) are produced from the declination-sine.

Therefore, for the sake of calculating that [ascensional difference] in sequence, its addition to the planet is performed by means of the rule beginning with "multiplied by the sine of the amplitude" (*akṣaprabhāsaṃguṇitāpama*) and so forth, because the calculation of the ascensional difference (*cara*) does not depend on anything else. Here, the statement regarding the "addition of the half-ascensional difference" (*caradala*) in sequence is intended to indicate its dependence on the rising of the local zodiacal signs at the ascendant. By this, it is stated that this correction of the degrees of anomaly (*ayamāṃśa*) for the planet is for a specific purpose in calculation, and not for the sake of establishing the true longitude (*sphuṭatva*).

The correction for the precession of the equinoxes (*ayanāṃśa*) is not for the purpose of calculating specific astronomical objects. This is because, since the zodiacal signs beginning with Aries do not exist apart from the asterism Revatī, the planet as determined by calculation lacks that [Revatī] as its limit. This is stated in the *Laghuvasiṣṭhasiddhānta*: "The years should be divided by forty; multiplied by that [quotient], increased by ten times the precession of the equinoxes, and added to the planet. And it is also stated in the *Somasiddhānta*: "In the case of Aries and so forth, the center [of the sign] is indeed to be corrected [by the precession] when the planet is there. However, this is not for the sake of establishing a particular entity.

When the Sun is in the portion of Devabhāga (the northern part) during the months of Meṣa and Vṛṣabha, he is visible to the gods; however, during the portion beginning with Tulā, he moves through the portion of the Asuras and is visible to them. Those situated on the terrestrial plane (kṣitija), shaking their heads, behold the Sun when he is positioned there; among these, they see each other at the destruction of the left and right directions. The Sun, having passed through Aries and Taurus, travels northward through three signs at the middle of the forenoon for those residing in the north. This concludes the section on the construction of the celestial sphere (golabandhādhikāra). Similarly, as he traverses Cancer and the subsequent signs, he moves southward through the latter half of the day.

Likewise, for the enemies of the gods (the Asuras), [the solstices] occur at Libra and so forth, and Capricorn and so forth; therefore, at the end of the day, because of their mutual reversal, the measure of the day and night for the Sun is completed by the filling of a full circle (bhagaṇa). At the end of the revolution, the day and night halves of these [planets] are reversed. However, from Aries onwards, there is always an increase in the northern direction, while in the portion belonging to the gods (the Devas) there is decrease, and the opposite occurs in the portion belonging to the Asuras. In Libra and so forth, during the increase and decrease of day and night, both [increase and decrease] occur together.

When the Sun is situated in Sagittarius (Dhanus) and Gemini (Mithuna), he is not seen in the divine region (Deva-bhāga); likewise, when he is situated in Cancer (Karkata), he is not seen in the asura region (Asura-bhāga). When he is stationed in Sagittarius, Capricorn (Mṛga), Scorpio (Alī), and Aquarius (Kumbha), he is not seen during the day in the divine region; however, for the asuras, he is not seen during the day in the four signs beginning with Taurus (Vṛṣabha). On Mount Meru, the gods behold the Sun as he moves through the signs beginning with Aries (Meṣa). Both the gods and the asuras see him only once when he has risen toward Libra (Tulā). Thus, in the fifteenth part of the terrestrial orb, both in the divine and the asura regions, [the Sun is visible].

Above, the sun is situated at the summer solstice; likewise, it moves toward the south and north within those two intermediate regions. Facing Meru, it traverses the three orbits according to its own respective declinations, starting from the northern declination. One should determine the orbits of Cancer and the others in reverse order, and similarly for Capricorn and the others in the opposite direction. For Libra and the others, the commencement of the *ṣaḍaśīti* occurs in sequence.

These four [points] would thus be located within the two dual-natured zodiac signs: at the twenty-sixth degree of Sagittarius, at the twenty-second of Capricorn, at the eighteenth division of Gemini, and at the fourteenth of Virgo. These four are well-known as the two lines of the equinoctial axis and the two solstitial lines. Between these, there are two further transits; moreover, due to their continuous succession, these transits constitute the three Vishnu-pavitra [sacrifices].

The summer solstice (uttarāyaṇa) occurs when the sun is at the junction of the constellations Bharaṇī and Kṛttikā; likewise, the winter solstice (dakṣiṇāyana) occurs at the junction of Karkaṭa and Siṃha. Furthermore, the seasons beginning with Śiśira are established by the two lunar months starting from Meṣa, and the year consists of twelve such months. By reflecting on the meaning of these statements from the *Sūryasiddhānta* and other texts, it is established that the junctions (*saṃpāta*) occur precisely at the zodiacal signs beginning with Meṣa. Moreover, nowhere in the *Āryabhaṭīya* is it stated that the limit for the position of Revatī is the starting point of the [zodiacal] circle.

For this very reason, the correction for the *ayanāṃśas* (precession of the equinoxes) applied to the ascendant (*lagna*) in the *Siddhāntaśiromaṇi* is appropriately termed "dumb" (*mūka*). Nor should it be argued that there is the undesirable consequence of admitting that the *ayanāṃśas* become "correct" (*sphuṭa*) by being corrected from the position of the *krāntipāta* (node of the ecliptic), because they are instead admitted to be "correct" through the correction of their own *śarapāta* (node of the latitude). This is because a distinction exists in the *Siddhāntaśiromaṇi*, as the *krāntipāta* is not accepted [there]. Nor should it be argued that this is due to the statement: "The circle of the zodiac is remembered to end at the point where the direction of Aries and so forth [from the *krāntipāta*] is zero."

Since the twenty-seven lunar mansions, beginning with Aśvinī, are established as being at a distance from the point of intersection (saṃpāta) and so forth, it follows that the completion of the zodiacal circle (bhagaṇapūrti) occurs at the end of the division of the ecliptic in accordance with that [intersection], meaning in the form of the conjunction (saṃparka). It does not mean that the completion of the zodiacal circle occurs at the position of the junction-star (yogatārā) of Revatī; for otherwise, the word "end" (anta) would be redundant. Now, on the ecliptic, there are ten signs (rāśis) situated starting from the direction occupied by the point of intersection.

Then, as the Kemiṭṭa [pole] moves from its point of conjunction, the moon enters the eastern direction of Aries; thus, at every moment, the calculation—following the rule of three (*vairāśika*) based on the single fixed object determined by the churning—results in the attainment of the conjunction (*saṃpāta*). This is the sequence of the calculation.

If it is argued that these [corrections] are not applied to me simply because they fall within my domain—having been derived from the *Bhagola-adhyāya* (Chapter on the Celestial Sphere) as the longitudinal positions of Aries and so forth at the beginning of the Kalpa, yet now being refined by this portion for the sake of calculation by treating them as the current points of intersection (*saṃpāta*) on the ecliptic—then that is not correct, because it would be improper to assume a lunar orbit that is not consistent [with the system]. For, since the ecliptic is not admitted as distinct from the *bhagola*, the line [of intersection] must indeed proceed from the point of intersection on the *bhagola*.

This is because the twelve zodiac signs, beginning with Aries, are conceived as following the path of the ecliptic (*krāntivṛtta*); furthermore, since no additional ecliptic is admitted, this conception is simpler than yours. Moreover, the origin of the precession of the equinoxes (*ayanāṃśa*) has already been established in the modern school (*navyamatam*) through the motion toward the *nakṣatra* Revatī. By this, it should be understood that according to this view, the objection regarding a planetary longitude exceeding a full circle (*cakrādhikabhoga*) does not apply when the revolution is accepted as starting from the limit of Revatī.

Now, if the conjunction (*saṃpāta*) were the starting point for the planetary motion (*bhoga*), then the correction for the precession of the equinoxes (*ayanāṃśa*) would be useless; for the motion of a planet, which is determined by a single fixed domain within the zodiacal revolution (*bhagaṇabhoga*), would not be contradicted by the conjunction, and thus its establishment would be impossible. Nor do the planets calculated through mathematical computation ever reach the [fixed] junctions (*rekhā*). If it is argued that this is because the position of the star Revatī is not fixed, we say no; even if the conjunction were the limit, the planetary motion cannot be accounted for without the correction for the precession of the equinoxes.

Just as the true state of a planet brought forward [from tables] is established through the correction of its results, one might object: "Since the two corrections (precession and equation of center) are established through their respective methods of calculation, whereas there is no such basis for the precession degrees (*ayanāṃśas*), how is it appropriate to apply a correction to them? Furthermore, since the slow and fast equations of a planet are well-known to be equal [in magnitude at certain points], it would follow by parity that the precession degrees must likewise have an equal effect. This objection should not be raised.

Although it is possible to establish that the precession of the equinoxes (*ayanāṃśa*) is a result included within the *sphuṭa-madhyama* (corrected mean) calculation, its correction is nevertheless accepted as being included within the *madhyama-kriyā* (mean operation). The declination (*apakrama*) is [calculated] from the degrees of the sun's meridian altitude; if the directions are the same, it is as stated, otherwise it is the reverse. When the directions differ, the remainder is the declination. That [declination] is multiplied by the radius (*trijyā*) and divided by the maximum sine of declination (*paramāpakramajyā*). If the sun is in Aries and so forth, this [result] is the *proja* (ascensional difference); if in Cancer and so forth, it is subtracted from six signs (*cakradhanu*); and if in Libra and so forth, it is added to half the circle (*bhārdha*). If in Capricorn and so forth, it is subtracted from a full circle (*bhagaṇa*). At midday, the sun thus becomes *sphuṭa* (true/corrected).

"Then the Sun [produces] a fruit that is slow, dull, and devoid of luster"—thus it is stated in the *Sūryasiddhānta* regarding the mean [longitude] with precession (*sāyana*). Otherwise, if one were to calculate the mean [longitude] equal to the Sun derived from the *ahargana*, there would be the undesirable consequence of having to state a correction for the precession degrees (*ayanāṃśa*). Furthermore, since the planet brought forward by the *ahargana* is understood through the rule of three (*trairāśika*), its mean [longitude] is already pure; therefore, the application of such corrections is untenable. This is because the corrections for longitudinal difference (*deśāntara*), diurnal motion (*cara*), and the equation of the center (*bhuja*) are merely results of the irregular motion (*asama-cālana*).

For it has not been stated that arrows (prahas) occur in a particular place and at a particular time independently of results such as reaching another location; likewise, since the precession of the equinoxes (ayanāṃśas) cannot otherwise be accounted for, a specific place and time have been mentioned to postulate their variation, whereby their correction becomes appropriate.

It cannot be argued that because the *ayanāṃśas* (precession) are assumed to have a variation due to the impossibility of the planetary revolutions having equal results, the resulting *ayanaphala* (equation of the center for precession) must also vary, and therefore a correction based on that variation should be applied uniformly to all planets; for by the rule "subtracting twenty-seven degrees from the longitude of the place," the *ayanaphala* is shown to be untenable as it would fall outside the range of twenty-seven degrees. Furthermore, since the negative value is appropriate [for the correction], its being positive is untenable. This is not so.

As in the case of the seed and so forth, for all [planets], the maximum [longitude] is twenty-seven degrees over a period of ten years. This is the product of the intermediate aspect seen in sequence. From that point, by a gradual decrease of half those [degrees], there is an absence of [longitude] (annarābhāva). Then, by a gradual increase of half those [degrees], there are twenty-seven degrees as a positive value (dhana). From there, by a gradual decrease of those [degrees], there is an absence of that state (tadbhāva). Thus, from the seventy years beginning with the [current] year, the remainder is subtracted from the divisor; the result is the elapsed portion (gata) and the portion yet to be traversed (bhogya). Of these two, the smaller [is used]; this is the section on the planetary conjunction (golabandhādhikāra).

The wealth of the portion to be enjoyed (bhogya) is thirty-six hundred. That too has been traversed; the remainder of those two is thirty daṇas, which constitutes both the lightness of action and the lightness of the operation.

Furthermore, regarding this correction (*saṃskāra*) for the fixed stars (*nakṣatra*) which was stated to be equal to that of the planets (*graha*), since the conjunction of the planets with the stars is not observed, one might argue that the fixed stars should be corrected by the same result as the others; however, because the stars are stationary (*sthiratva*), such a correction is untenable. Therefore, it is said that the movement of the stars is relative to the [observer's] island-continent (*dvīpa*). Moreover, at the end of the Kṛta Yuga, all the planets do not occupy the central positions. [The verse continues: "They are devoid of... [etc.]

However, in your own system, there is no inconsistency regarding the equality [of results] for the *pāta*, *manda*, and *ucca* nodes and so forth. To explain: "These [previously mentioned quantities] are to be known as having elapsed at the end of the Kṛta age by the number of solar years; [the revolutions] of the Moon, starting from the first, are four times their own [mean motions]. Thus, for the purpose of calculating the great epoch (mahānatha) of the solar yuga-years—which amount to 17,064,000—the multiplier (*guṇa*) for the revolutions (*bhagaṇa*) is 1,809, and the divisor (*hara*) is 4.

In that regard, since the revolutions of the sun and the other [planets] have been established as whole revolutions by dividing the zero-point of the zodiacal signs by four, there is a void in the place of signs; therefore, according to my view, that is logically consistent. It must be stated that when the precession degrees (*ayanāṃśa*) are added, the day would indeed be equal to the precession degrees, because of the difference in the calculation. In that case, the precession degrees arise from the revolutions of the precession. Thus, once the true nature of the precession-corrected planets is established, it is logical that the practical applications of the *Saṃhitās*, *Jātaka*, and so forth, should proceed from those very [precession-corrected values].

It is not [derived] from those who are well-versed [in the tradition]. Thus, by such statements as "Caitra and the others are the months" and "the *paṭa* is produced from them," the practice refined by the *ayana* has been cast aside and set in motion without foundation; the *sāraṇīs* (astronomical tables) rooted therein are likewise so. This is one prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows: Since there is no inherent connection between the twenty-seven lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*)—such as Saṃpāta and the rest—and [the asterisms] beginning with Aśvinī, how can the names "Aśvinī" and so forth be appropriately applied? [The answer is: Because of the connection through the *śara* (arrow) with the lunar mansions beginning with Aśvinī, which possess the aforementioned nature and occupy twenty-seven locations starting from the position of the star Revatī, the names of the lunar mansions such as Aśvinī are appropriately assigned. Otherwise, they would result in having some arbitrary name.

This very [series], beginning with Aśvinī and ending with Revatī, is established as the sequence of the zodiacal signs (rāśis), starting from Aśvinī, which serves as the locus for the commencement of the vows (vrata) for the signs of Meṣa and Vṛṣa. If one were to accept only the stellar sphere (bhagola), then for the purpose of following the movement of the constellations through their respective positions, the celestial sphere (jyotiścakra) would have to be accepted as distinct from the stellar sphere; for accepting only the stellar sphere is untenable, as the movement of the constellations is not heard of therein.

Nor should it be argued that the movement of the asterisms (nakṣatras) is well-known from the *Sūryasiddhānta* and other texts as being "the wheel of the asterisms" (*śanaiścakram*). For it is said: "The wheel moves westward; this is a metaphorical designation (*upacāra*). Indeed, when the western wheel has not yet reached [its destination], the eastern wheel has moved forward. It is not the case that the wise do not employ such a metaphor, thinking that when the eastern wheel has not yet reached [its destination], the eastern wheel would have moved forward. This is because, according to the statements of the *Āryasiddhānta*, the term "wheel of the asterisms" (*nakṣatracakra*) is intended for the purpose of pacifying [the mind].

This is because, in comparison with the movement of all the asterisms (*nakṣatras*), the movement of even a single *ṛṣabhanajhapana* is lighter; and it is not that one considers the natural motion to belong to the wheel alone. For those who hold that the planet itself, corrected by the degrees of precession (*bhagaṇāṃśa*), is the true planet (*sphuṭagraha*), this [theory] is not accepted. Thus, according to the statement "one should move by means of corrections," since there is no connection between the asterism at the point of intersection and the following asterism in the zodiacal sign within the representation of the ecliptic circle, it is for the sake of the clarity of the day in the conjunction of the signs. This is the refutation.

"From the correction for precession (ayanāṃśa), [one obtains] the obliquity of the ecliptic, the carakhaṇḍa, and the difference [between the true and mean positions]. (Golādhyāya 3.3.1) Commentary by Bhāskarācārya: The true planet mentioned in the *Sūryasiddhānta* is already corrected for precession (*ayanāṃśa*). In that very context, the planet is used for the purpose of calculating the [true] declination (*krānti*). If this [pre-correction] were not accepted, one would have to calculate the declination and so forth using the "pseudo-precessions" (*upacārairagrayanāṃśaiḥ*), and it would not be consistent with reason.

The meaning is that on whichever day the precessed (sāyana) planet becomes equal to the non-precessed (nirayana) planet, on that very day the optional rites (*kāmya*) and so forth should be performed. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Brahmasiddhānta*: "If the sine of declination (*dojyā*), the radius (*bijyā*), and the sine of obliquity (*kāntijyā*) are multiplied by the [equinoctial] shadow and the number of elapsed days, [the result] is the northern or southern declination for the first and second halves of the zodiac. Furthermore, the correction for precession (*ayanasaṃskāra*) is mentioned in the *Laghuvasiṣṭhasomasiddhānta* in the context of calculating declination.

Regarding the statement "in Cancer and so forth," one who understands the eastward and westward motion of a planet according to such definitions—that which is designated as a "fixed planet" (phuḍhagraha) by its southward movement, situated in Cancer, Capricorn, and so forth, being a precessional (sāyana) planet—is [correct]; for that [precessional planet] is merely corrected by the degrees of precession (calāṃśa) and is not the actual [position]. Because its true motion is not accepted [as such], it is said "by way of metaphor. The meaning is that the actual position should be understood within the interval of the degrees of precession (ayanāṃśa).

Since the term "preparatory correction" (upacāra) was previously established for the precession of the equinoxes, he says: Nor should it be said that in the *Sūryasiddhānta* the correction for precession applies everywhere because of the word "beginning" (ādi); for the word "beginning" includes all the astronomical parameters up to the limit of the *saṃpāta* (the node). Otherwise, by the statement "corrected by that," the mention of "declination, shadow, half-day-arc," and so forth would be rendered redundant.

Therefore, when the question arises as to why the correction for the *ayanāṃśa* (precession of the equinoxes) must be applied here and there, the following verse provides the justification: "In the two solstices (*ayana*) and the two equinoxes (*viṣuva*), [the calculated planet] shall clearly attain equality with observation. This indicates that the *ayanāṃśa* correction applies specifically to those instances; otherwise, it would follow that the correction is unnecessary at the equinox, which is characterized by equal day and night.
