Nor should it be argued that, since the *Brahmasiddhānta* does not mention specific locations for the *ayanāṃśa* correction, one should apply it everywhere in accordance with the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) used in the *Sūryasiddhānta*.

Because of the obliquity of the ecliptic (*krānti*), the rising and setting of the zodiacal signs occurs from their own respective celestial horizons (*kṣitija*) and not otherwise; for that reason, no correction for precession (*ayana*) is desired at the time of calculation here, whether it be from the point of the obliquity of the ecliptic or from any other location. Likewise, according to Romaka, the true degrees of setting are derived from the degrees of the equinoxes and the latitude (*lambana*). Now, this [calculation] is established through direct observation alone, and not by mere verbal authority.

The [mean] longitudes of the signs starting from Aries are stated as follows: for Aries, 296; for Taurus, 531; for Gemini, 760; for Cancer, 984; for Leo, 1213; for Virgo, 1437; for Libra, 1662; for Scorpio, 1886; for Sagittarius, 2111; for Capricorn, 2335; for Aquarius, 2560; and for Pisces, 2784. These are the middle portions [of the signs], reduced by one-sixth and multiplied by sixty. This is because the *nakṣatra*-fixed points (*dhruvaka*) at the beginning of the asterisms are described in relation to the Moon's connection with the signs starting from Aries, up to the limit of the star near the end of Revatī.

For this very reason, since the word *anta* is used in the sense of "near" (*antike*)—as in the determination of the nature of servants (*bhṛtyai svarūpe niścaye*)—it follows that the completion of the circle of asterisms (*bhagaṇapūrti*) occurs at a point near the star Revatī (the *pauṣṇa* star). Thus, it is stated that "the circle of asterisms is recorded as ending at the *pauṣṇa*," but not precisely at the *pauṣṇa* itself. Nor does this refer to the section on the construction of the celestial sphere (*golabandha*). Furthermore, one should not argue that these [mean] longitudes become true (*spaṣṭa*) through the correction for the precession of the equinoxes (*ayanāṃśa*), because no such correction for the precession of the equinoxes is mentioned regarding the fixed positions (*dhruvakāḥ*).

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of having to postulate a slow-motion correction (*manda-phala*) and so forth, as in the case of the planets. Therefore, regarding the phrase "the middle portion of Aśvinī and the others," since each of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*), such as Aśvinī, consists of a configuration of multiple stars, there arises the question: "Which star among them is the fixed point (*dhruvaka*)? In response to this expectation, the meaning is that this [specified] fixed point is the *yogatārā* (junction-star) among them. For this very reason, the *yogatārā* is mentioned here.

Furthermore, even if the Madhyama-dhruvakās (mean fixed points) are accepted, the establishment of the constellations such as Nirayaṇa and Medhā remains valid; otherwise, it would lead to the undesirable conclusion that these figures—which are the sum of the degrees—would instead be the *Aśva-viṃdhu-dhruvakās*. For this very reason, Agastya is situated at the end of Gemini; and in the twentieth degree of Gemini, Mṛgaśiras is established below [it]. Bahubhuja and Brahmahṛdaya are located in Taurus at twenty-second degrees. In Taurus, at the seventeenth degree, from two degrees south [of it]...

"He [the Moon] shall break the cart of Rohiṇī when the precession (vikṣepa) is excessive. Thus, when the true longitudes of the planets—corrected by the degrees of precession as stated by Brahmagupta, Soma, Sūrya, and others—are observed, the contradiction with direct perception arises because the correction for precession was not mentioned; consequently, the observation of the breaking of the cart of Rohiṇī and so forth is consistent only when the planets are taken as uncorrected by precession, being equal to the stated figures. Nor should it be said that these constants (dhruvakas) are for the time of the occurrence of the precession degrees, for such a statement is not found in the Āryasiddhānta, and there is no evidence for such an assumption.

Otherwise, by assuming that all statements are merely conceptual, it would follow that [the calculation] falls outside the scope of the great prima facie argument (*mahāpūrvapakṣa*), and there would be no room for human opinion to enter. Furthermore, the correction for the *ayanāṃśas* (precession of the equinoxes) is established in those cases where it is omitted simply by the enumeration [of its application]; otherwise, such enumeration would be rendered useless. By this, the argument supporting the addition of *ayanāṃśas* "in the manner of the seed" (*bījarītyā*) during an eclipse is refuted, because the "manner of the seed" is not mentioned here, nor is the correction for *ayanāṃśas* stated in the *dhruvaka* (the fixed epoch).

Furthermore, while the correction for the stars and the polar stars (dhruvakaṇāḥ) may be established by means of their motion through the asterisms (*nakṣatra*), how could such a correction for the planets be established? For the planets do not move in that same manner as the asterisms, which would necessitate such a correction; there is simply no evidence for it. Nor should it be argued that it is logical to postulate such a movement for them based on the impossibility of explaining their corrections otherwise.

At the time of the *ṛṇāyanāṃśa*, there is the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the planets' own velocity would be contradictory in their eastward and westward motions. But if this is so, how is what you have stated regarding the *mīna* [sign] justified? For even there, immediately after the maximum increase, when the fruit of the seed decreases, the planets' own velocity culminates in a westward motion; for the fruit of the seed does not arise without motion. Nor should it be argued that at that time the planet's eastward motion becomes deficient or excessive.

Because a distinct difference in motion is possible through the medium of the *ayanāṃśas* (precession), it cannot be argued that [the correction] applies only to the true motion (*sphuṭagati*). For one might object: "The fruit of the motion produced from the seed (the equation of time) is not cut off because it does not arise [from the precession]. To this we reply: No, for the *ayanāṃśas* are not accepted as being produced from a seed, both because there is no scriptural statement to that effect and because there is a lack of logical justification. Furthermore, if they were so accepted, it would result in the intrusion of human (non-scriptural) doctrine. Nor can it be argued that the addition of the *ayanāṃśas* is achieved by imagining an additional motion equal to the *ayanāṃśas* themselves within the mean motion; for this contradicts the authoritative tradition (*āgama*) and involves the intrusion of human doctrine.

Since it would be redundant to state the planetary revolutions as being already joined with the revolutions of the precession (ayanāṃśa), and because it would lead to the denial of the purpose of the term "precession" when stating the revolutions of the lunar mansions (nakṣatra), it is therefore more appropriate to accept the previously mentioned motion of the movable point on the ecliptic for the sake of establishing the precession. By this [method], one should divide the remainder of the year by 1800; [the result] is the number of elapsed years in the current Yuga, and the degrees of precession are obtained by dividing [the elapsed years] by 1893. The resulting arc is in signs, and its minutes are in gold [units].

634. Commentary on the *Gaṇādhyāya* (Ma. Ṭī.)—Chapter 6. The degrees of motion (*calāṃśaka*) are the difference between the two suns as calculated through shadow-geometry (*chāyāgaṇita*). Alternatively, they are the minutes of arc derived from the shadow. In the east, there is a decrease; otherwise, it is in the west. Therefore, the planets move forward [in the east] by addition and are diminished in the west. Consequently, the time in nāḍīs and so forth for the movement of the shadow must be calculated. This is stated in the *Vṛddhavasiṣṭhasiddhānta*. By this statement, "the planets move," the demonstration that the degrees of motion are the actual velocity of the planet is refuted. Thus it is said.

In this regard, since it would otherwise result in the fallacy of stating a conclusion (*siddhānta*) without first establishing that the longitudinal degrees of precession (*ayanāṃśa*) possess the nature of planetary motion—that is, that they represent the actual movement of the planet—it follows that the planets move forward from those longitudinal degrees of precession. Consequently, the previously calculated planetary longitude and so forth refer to the point of intersection on the ecliptic (*krāntivṛtta*). For this very reason, the statement that "the [precession] is added first" and so on is logically consistent; otherwise, the portion of the calculation beginning with "from that, the shadow-mover moves... would become meaningless.

Furthermore, the calculation of that [precession] in the *Sphuṭādhikāra* is due to the context of declination (*krānti*); otherwise, it would result in the necessity of computing the true declination there without the correction for the precession degrees (*ayanāṃśa*). In the section dealing with the computation of its [the Moon's] declination, no correction for the precession degrees is mentioned. If one intends that correction to be applied without further qualification, it would follow that it should have been stated in the *Madhyamādhikāra* itself; such is the general direction [of the argument]. Moreover: "Whether the Sun and Moon are corrected by the degrees of precession (*calāṃśa*) or left uncorrected..."

"When the Sun and Moon are in the same solstice (*ekāyana*) and their declinations (*krānti*) are equal in the same direction (*maṇḍala*), there is an eclipse; when they are in opposite solstices and their declinations are equal, there is a very terrible impact (*pāta*). Thus, according to the statement of Śākalya, even in the case of the correction for the *avaruya-kāyana* portion, the alternative of omitting the precession (*nirayana*) is stated as an option. For this very reason, it is said in the *Sūryasiddhānta*: "When the Sun and Moon are in the same solstice, there is an eclipse at their conjunction if their declinations are equal. When the Moon and Sun are in opposite solstices, [the calculation involves] the minutes of arc of their declination. (Note: The term *viparītāyamagatau* refers to the two luminaries being in opposite solstitial positions.)

"Whenever there is a *yati-pāta* (the conjunction of the sun and moon at the end of a lunar mansion), that is a *bhagaṇa-dha* (a full revolution). When those two are joined, it is preceded by that non-correction. First, it was stated: "The cutting of the zodiacal circle (*bhacakra*) by the sun and moon occurs at the junctions of the signs; when their longitudinal corrections (*dṛkkarma*) and latitudinal corrections (*apama-krama*) are calculated as equal and joined, it is stated in the *Aneka* [work] that this is due to that correction, and thus there is no additive [correction]. Therefore, elsewhere, the accomplishment of the non-ecliptic position (*nirayana-siddhi*) is all the more certain. Nor should it be argued: "In this way, why is the correction for the precession of the equinoxes (*ayanāṃśa*) not applied in the calculation of the ascendant (*lagna*), as it was mentioned in the *Ārdhāmnāya*?"

"By means of the correction obtained from the motion [of the sun], the strength is established; by its power, the transit through the [signs] corrected by that [motion] is twofold, and for this one, the ascensional difference (*unnati*) is also manifest. One should calculate the solar longitude and the time-portion from the *lagna*," according to the *Somasiddhānta*. This is because the intent of the meaning is that the day is corrected by that [longitude], since the correction applied to the [longitude] subtracted by the precession (*ayanāṃśa*) is stated as being [already] adjusted. Otherwise, if the precession correction were applied to the *lagna* intended to be corrected by the precession, the statement of the precession correction would be inconsistent, due to contradiction with the principles of the celestial sphere (*golayukti*).

Thus, when the sun is corrected by its [diurnal] motion (*cara*) and the shadow is greater, [the calculation proceeds] in sequence from the prime meridian (*madhyarekhā*). According to the statement of Brahmā, "one's own country lies at that interval," it is understood that the term "sun" refers specifically to the non-precessional (*nirayana*) sun. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of not stating that the sun is corrected by its *cara* and then multiplied by the elapsed time. In the *Sūryasiddhānta* as well, in the verse beginning "when the wheel has moved forward, [the sun is] less than the one obtained from the calculation due to the shadow," only the non-precessional sun is mentioned.

For this very reason, that dull-witted person repeatedly [asserts] that the fruit is the tree; here, the precession of the equinoxes (*ayana-śeṣa*) is established for the sake of correction (*saṃskāra*). Indeed, it is not appropriate in the *Madhyamādhikāra* (the chapter on mean motion) such that its being precessional (*sāyanatva*) would be unavoidable. Others say that in the matter of the existence or non-existence of the degrees of precession, it is "immovable" (*acala*). By this alone, the correction to be subtracted is established. Furthermore, in the *Sūryasiddhānta*, there is the chapter on the construction of the celestial sphere (*golabandhādhikāra*).

In the *Samānayana* (the process of bringing together), this correction for the precession of the equinoxes (*ayanāṃśa*)—which was not mentioned in the context of the *nirdhana* and other methods—is established here. Although the means of calculation were not previously stated and there is no equality between the true Sun and the mean Sun, nevertheless, the acceptance of the essential nature [of the correction] is unavoidable, because the independent will of the author cannot be constrained. By this, the claim that the precession of the equinoxes subtracted by Bhāskarācārya himself is merely a later fabrication (*itthaṇai*) is refuted.

The oblique ascension (*akṣakālasāyana*) at sunrise is multiplied by the degrees of the Sun and divided by sixty; from this, thirty *pala*s are subtracted. Then, the remainder is multiplied by three and divided by sixty; the result is subtracted from the ascendant. This remainder is further divided by its own subtrahend (*svaśuddhi*). This method, which involves subtracting the degrees of the Sun, was taught by Śatānanda—who preceded Bhāskara Ācārya—in his work *Bhāsvatī*. If the degrees of the Sun are less than thirty, they are multiplied by six; if it is night, they are added to thirty-six. The elapsed time is calculated from the oblique ascension (*sāyanalagna*) according to the difference between the two.

By this [statement], it is said that when some portion of the Kali Yuga has elapsed, "O Brahmā, your three-fold delusion" (*trivibhrama*) arises; from that, his face is likewise described as being in a state of three-fold confusion. The degrees of precession (*ayanāṃśa*) are the minutes of arc resulting from the motion of the equinoxes. When the sun is situated in the signs beginning with Libra (the southern solstice), the degrees of precession are applied to the sun as corrected by the *ayanāṃśas*. From the body [of the planet] thus corrected by the degrees of precession, the points of the horizon (*dṛkkāṇa*) are determined.

This is because it has been stated through such expressions as "the fortune of the sun, well-refined by the solstices (ayana), was enjoyed by him," where the meaning is expressed differently; and also because Varāhamihira said: "From the middle of Ālā [Capricorn] to the end of the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana) is auspicious; indeed, at some time he sat in those eastern signs. Now, the half of Cancer is the northern course (uttarāyaṇa) of the sun, and the other half from Capricorn is the opposite. This was stated with the intention of referring to the sun without precession (nirayana), for the aforementioned proof follows from the presence or absence of degrees of precession (ayanāṃśa).

If the correction for the precession of the equinoxes (*ayanāṃśa*) were not applied, it would result in the absurdity that the commencement of the solstice (*ayanapravṛtti*) currently occurs in Cancer and Capricorn; therefore, the statement [in the *Brahmasphuṭasiddhānta*], "Strive for that field which is called the solstice in the northern and southern courses," is indeed appropriate. Nor can it be argued that the absence of precession at the end of a solar year is impossible, since their occurrence is inevitable at the time of the solstice, and as for the question of how it is stated otherwise starting from the earth's center, it is because the difference is very slight.

Otherwise, there would arise the untenable consequence that the year [would consist of] zero days, and the months would be ten times the seasons (30), as the degrees of Aries and so forth would not be consistent with the shortest and longest solstices. Therefore, the limit for the division of the zodiacal signs is precisely the point of the deity’s proximity; it is by that very portion that the revolutions of the signs are established. Thus, the planets as calculated through mathematics are determined by that measure for the purpose of practical application in horoscopy, astrology, and the interpretation of results in the *Jātaka-saṃhitā*. However, the signs beginning with Aries do not have the equinox (*saṃpāta*) as their limit, because this is evident from the observation of their true nature.

For that [precession] is not established as a manifestor (*vyañjaka*) in the sky, by which its establishment would follow from its inclusion within that category. Indeed, the *ayanāṃśas* (precessional degrees) are derived from the sun and moon themselves, corrected by the [precession], and not from the stars corrected by them. For even for the purpose of calculating the declination and so forth, no correction for the sun and moon has been stated by any author in the astronomical treatises (*sūryagrantha*), by which [correction] the stars might be affected.

The number of elapsed days from the beginning of the solar year (arkādi) multiplied by sixty, plus the *karaṇa* value, [gives] the degrees of the planet; this is divided by the sum of the [mean] motion and the [true] motion—according to the statement in the Siddhānta and other texts. Now, an objection: regarding the meritorious time (*puṇyakāla*) at the transits (*saṃkrānti*), how is it consistent with the statements of Gālava and others in the Golādhyāya, such as: "In Libra and Aries, one should extend the *Ṣaḍaśītimukha*; at the equinoxes (*viṣuva*), the Sun [is at the transit]; in the southern solstice (*dakṣiṇāyana*) and the northern course (*saumyāyana*), there is purity (*sauśya*)"? How is this reconciled?

If it is argued that the name [of the day] is appropriate because at the time of the equinox (*viṣuvat*) and the solstice (*dhruva*), during which day and night are equal, there occurs a day measuring thirty *ghaṭīs* at the transits of Aries and Libra, and the ingress of the solstices (*ayana-niṣpatti*) occurs at the transits of Cancer and Capricorn—therefore the designation is justified—we say no. For while those names are indeed appropriate when the sun is situated in those respective signs at the time of the precession (*ayanāṃśa*), they are applied metaphorically (*upacāra*) even when precession is present.

The purpose of mentioning the specific names for the *saṃkrāntis* and the times of excessive merit (*puṇyakāla*) is to avoid prolixity; furthermore, the Sage’s use of these designations would otherwise be redundant, as their meaning could be established through their etymological derivation (*yaugikatva*). Moreover, in the *Brahmasiddhānta*, within the calculation of the *pāta*, it is stated that by means of the sun and moon corrected by the degrees of the solstice (*ayanāṃśa*), the absence of declination (*kānti*) is naturally established as being concomitant with the equinox (*viṣuva*), and the presence of the degrees of the solstice is established as being concomitant with the maximum declination (*paramārcitas*).

For this very reason, it is stated in the *Brahmasiddhānta*: "Therefore, when the equinox occurs at the point of the sun's motion, it would be the equinox. This implies that the equinox occurs during the ingress [of the sun] into Aries and Libra; otherwise, since the equinox would not possess that nature, the correction for the equation of time (*calasaṃskṛti*) would be rendered meaningless. Now, one might object: "In that case, whatever transit of the sun corrected by the equation of time is the true transit."

[Objection: It is not that the field [of the sun] goes elsewhere; rather, it is preceded by the refutation of the statement "it does not go to the vicinity of its destruction. Immediately after the mention of the times of merit for the transits (saṃkrānti) such as Aries and the rest occurring at the moment of conjunction, how is it that they are stated in the *Brahmasiddhānta*? For according to your view, they lack the status of being the beginning of Aries and so forth. Indeed, there is no transit other than the entry into the commencement of a zodiac sign, because that would lead to the undesirable consequence [of multiple transits] at all times. [Reply: This is not so.

Just as, although the true positions of the apogee, perigee, and node are established through their respective [mean] longitudes, the designations of Aries, Libra, Cancer, Scorpio, and so forth are applied to the *kendra* and other [angles] in the *Sūryasiddhānta* and other texts in order to determine the positive or negative nature of the resulting equation of center (*manda-phala*) and equation of anomaly (*śīghra-phala*), as well as the increments or decrements in velocity; likewise, there is no contradiction in applying the designations of the signs beginning with Aries to the ten divisions starting from the *saṃpāta* (node) for the purpose of determining the obliquity of the ecliptic (*krānti*) and other parameters. For it is said: "The signs are proclaimed as being like the friendship of the planets," and in reality, they begin with the clouds (*megha*).

The *Brahmasiddhi* states that there is no such thing as "friendliness toward the planets" (*grahamaitryādi*) and so forth; for this very reason, the statements of the great prima facie argument (*mahāpūrvapakṣa*) are consistent. Nor should it be argued that the transits (*saṃkrānti*) of those [planets] into their respective zodiacal signs (*rāśi*) are not [the true transits], because otherwise, one would be forced to accept multiple names based on their relationship to the cardinal points (*kendrādi*). For it is said: "The transit of the sun when its longitudinal degrees have been corrected by precession (*ayanāṃśa*) is indeed the [true] solstice (*ayana*); it is superior for bathing, giving gifts, and other rites, while a transit occurring at a middle position is mediocre."

By how many degrees the Sun has moved prior to the [next] transit, by that many degrees the solstitial transit occurs before the entry into the next zodiacal sign, as previously stated; and by how many degrees the Sun will move after the transit, by that many degrees the solstitial transit occurs after the entry into the next zodiacal sign, as previously stated. This zodiacal wheel, possessing the radiance of the solar disc, revolves due to the motion of the wind.

Therefore, this might be said: "The Sun, rising during the northern transit (ayana), fills the first half of the day for the gods with the three best [nakṣatras] of the north; he fills the latter half of the day for the Yamas with the three [nakṣatras] of the southern transit; likewise, he fills the first half of the day for the Daityas with the three [nakṣatras] beginning with Libra, and the latter half with those beginning with the northern transit. This is because the transits of the signs (rāśisaṃkrānti) are accepted as being identical to the transits of the solar terms (ayanasaṃkrānti) by the statements of Sumantu, Mārkaṇḍeya, Kaśyapa, and Vasiṣṭha, and not merely as simple transits of the signs. For this very reason: "The Sun, rising during the northern transit, fills the first half of the day for the gods with the three best [nakṣatras] of the north; he fills the latter half of the day for the Yamas with the three [nakṣatras] of the southern transit; likewise, he fills the first half of the day for the Daityas with the three [nakṣatras] beginning with Libra, and the latter half with those beginning with the northern transit.
