It is logical that a day and night for the gods and demons is the reverse [of each other], as stated in the *Brahmasiddhānta*. Furthermore, this is supported by the statement of Śrīpati Bhaṭṭa in the *Golabandhādhikāra* (verse 395): "By as many degrees as there is a fall from the meridian, the conjunction of the [planetary] sphere occurs at that same time of elapsed arc; this is the secret of the days of Viṣṇu and others as taught by the sages. Nor should it be argued that this excludes the *saṃkrānti* (solar ingress).

"Indeed, according to the maxim that 'censure is not intended to disparage, but rather to praise that which is to be enjoined,' [this passage] serves to illuminate the excellence of the *calasaṃkrānti* (the transit of the sun at the equinox), as in the expression 'by bathing with the waters of the lotus-pond' and so forth. By means of rites such as bathing, giving gifts, recitation (*japa*), ancestral offerings (*śrāddha*), and fasting, a person secures imperishable merit for their good deeds. The determination of the duration of day and night is made through the *calasaṃkrānti*; therefore, because it is said that 'all rituals are meritorious on this account,' the *calasaṃkrānti* is thus described."

Now, that transit which belongs to the sun at the end of its [previous] course is the true *saṃkrānti*. The transit into a zodiacal sign (*rāśisaṃkrānti*) is said to be like the "goat's nipple" (useless). Some wise men say that the transit into a sign occurs when the sun is moving; this is not my opinion, as it would not touch upon the essential point. Let there be a rejection of the *saṃkrānti* favored by you, based on the statement of Vṛddhavasiṣṭha: "The destruction of the [previous] portion [of the day]. Furthermore, according to the statement of Lāṣava, let there be only one solstitial transit (*ayanasaṃkrānti*), for in the absence of any scriptural authority for the existence of any additional transits, such a view might hold. If you object to this, we reply: no.

This [correction] by degrees is called the primary transit (*mukhya-saṃkrānti*); the secondary transit (*amukhyā-rāśi-saṃkrānti*) is the same, for the rule regarding time is equal for both, according to the reasoning [of the *Jātakapārijāta*]. The transit of the Sun corrected by the degrees of precession (*calāṃśa*) is called the embodied (*mūrti*) transit; the unembodied (*amūrtā*) transit is the transit by zodiacal sign (*rāśi-saṃkrānti*), for the rule regarding time is equal for both, as stated in the *Romaka-siddhānta*. Furthermore, because of the reasoning [of the *Jātakapārijāta*] that "just as there is a specific time for the transits, so it is for its [the Sun's] revolution," the existence of a transit into an additional sign (*atirikta-rāśi-saṃkrānti*) is established.

Furthermore, it is all the more well-known that the commencement of the first *saṃkrānti* itself is for the purpose of refuting [the notion of] a transition; otherwise, how could a prohibition of what has not been previously established be logically consistent? Moreover, if according to the view of some there were only one *saṃkrānti*, then the statement "of the sun whose sharp rays have moved during the *saṃkrānti*" (following the mention of the merit of the *saṃkrānti*) would be untenable, because in their view the *saṃkrānti* is established solely by its very occurrence. Some, however, [say] "balasaṃ... [and so on].

The transition (*saṃkrama*) of the sun when it has completed its [precession] is that [true] *saṃkrama*; however, the meaning is that the *ayanasaṃkrama* (the solstitial point) is indeed something else. For this reason: "That [sign] which is the *sarakṣetra* (the fixed field) moves along with the circle of declination (*krāntikakṣayā*); it does not go elsewhere. This is the intended meaning: they say that a sign, having moved together with the circle of declination due to the degrees of precession (*ayanāṃśaiḥ*), does not leave its former position in the circle of declination to go elsewhere. Now, it is logical that for the sun at the solstices of Aries and Libra there is an equinox (*viṣuva*), because of its connection with the equatorial circle (*viṣuvavṛtta*).

As for the mention of the moon and other planets, [one might argue that] their commencement and cessation of solstitial motion (ayanasthāna/ayanapravṛtti) occur at the solstitial points (ayana-saṃdhi) mentioned in the section on the *golādhyāya*, and not at the solstitial points mentioned in the section on *pāta*; however, how can the general statement by Śākalya—"The planets reach the solstices in Libra and Aries, and that is the equinox"—be consistent? For, due to their being separated by their latitudes (*śara*), the planets would then lack connection with the equinoctial circle, and thus they would not possess the equinoctial nature (*viṣuvatva*). If this is raised as an objection, we reply: no.

Since the subject matter is the absence of arrows (latitude), enough with this digression into irrelevant discussion. Now, he states the nodes of deviation (kṣepapāta): "In this way, the nodes of the intersection of the ecliptic and the deferent are the nodes of deviation. For the Moon and other planets, these are reversed; however, they are to be applied in the calculation of deviation. "For a planet moves on the epicycle of slow motion (mandapratimaṇḍala), and its node is there. From the planet’s mean-sphuta position as derived by calculation, the arrow (latitude) is obtained by adding the node. || 20–21 ||

228. [Regarding] the node (pāta): having made the result of the correction (śodhya-phala) retrograde, it is then added to the true [longitude]; thus the node of the Moon's orbit (kakṣā-valaya) is the true node joined with the mean node. Likewise, the intersection of the ecliptic (krānti-vṛtta) and the eccentric circle (vimaṇḍala) is the node of the latitude (kṣepa-pāta). Having added those to the planet, the latitude (kṣepa) is to be calculated. This is what is meant: the node of the apogee (śānti-pāta) is well known.

The meaning is that just as the [mean] longitude is calculated by adding the [mean] anomaly to the planet, so too the equation of the center (*vikṣepa*) is calculated by adding the anomaly to the planet; this refers to the process when the anomaly is added to the mean-sphuta (mean-corrected) planet. Now, he states the reason why that which is added to the mean-sphuta is done so: "In the mean-sphuta," etc. Since the planet revolves in the slow epicycle (*mandarephaṇḍala*) within the fast eccentric circle (*śīghrapraviaṇḍala*), and since the apogee (*pāta*) is located in that circle, the anomaly obtained through calculation is added to the mean-sphuta to calculate the correction (*kṣepa*). The rest is clear. ||29||21||22||

Bhāṣyaṭīkā: Now, by way of an introductory connection (*upodghāta-saṃgati*), he describes the nature of the *jhaṣapāta* (fish-descents) in verse, beginning with "evam" (thus). "Evam" means in the manner previously stated; that is to say, just as there is the intersection of the equinoctial circle (*viṣuvat*) and the ecliptic (*krāntivṛtta*). The intersections of the ecliptic and the [orbital] deviation circles (*vikṣepavṛtta*) are the remaining descents (*śeṣapāta*) of the planets, such as the Moon and others. Because of the elision of the middle syllables in the compound "the intersection of the deviation circle on the ecliptic," they are called *jhaṣapāta*; or alternatively, they are called *kṣepārtha-pāta* (descents for the sake of deviation). These are "reversed" (*vyasta*), meaning they possess a westward motion.

The meaning is that [the ecliptic] moves daily by its own westward motion, which is born of the enemy of declination (krānti). He states its purpose in the words "saiṣānayane" (this very one is for calculation); it is for the sake of establishing the arrows (śaras). The particle *tu* implies the exclusion of anything else, while the particle *eva* emphasizes this. Those are the arrows of the planets. They are to be applied to the Sun and the others. Thus, the arrow (*śara*) is the north-south distance of the planets as they move along the circle of oblique ascension (*vikṣepavṛtta*) from the point on the circle of declination (*krāntivṛtta*); for it has been stated that the arrow of the circle of declination is transverse, limited by the circle of oblique ascension.

From that point of intersection with the ecliptic (the *krāntipāta*), which serves as the fixed reference for that location, one should add the signs beginning with Aries to the longitude of the planet—whether past or future—to determine the sign of the node (*pātabha*) for the purpose of calculating the true anomaly (*śara*) of the planet. This is the meaning [of verse 20]. Now, an objection may be raised: according to the method stated above, just as the calculation of the true obliquity (*krānti*) is established by correcting the true planet with the *krāntipāta*, it is likewise logically established that the calculation of the true anomaly (*śara*) should be performed from the true planet conjoined with the node (*pāta*). Why, then, in the chapter on shadow (*chāyādhikāra*), is it said: "from the true planet corrected by the *mandaphala*"?... [The text continues].

When it was stated, "conjoined with its own apogee," [the author] said "then" (*atha*) as a response to the objection that this would not be consistent; he then said, "the slow-mean motion (manda-sphuṭa). Ah, here the "slow-mean motion" is the actual entity. For the apogee (pāta) of the planet situated on the epicycle of anomaly (dratimaṇḍala) revolves there; by means of the non-existence of the [true] latitude (śara), the position of the slow-mean motion is known as the interval between days. Here, it occurs on the circle of the shadow (śīśnaprativṛtta). The word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of "only" (*eva*).

Therefore, since there is no actual revolution of the planets in the eccentric circle (*kakṣāvṛtta*), the meaning is that even the locus of the apogee (*sadātmakaśrābhāvasthāna*) does not exist apart from the asterisms (*ṛkṣa*). By this, the objection that "let the apsis (*pāta*) brought by proportion (*anupāta*) in the epicycle (*pratimaṇḍala*) also reside there" is refuted. For the slow epicycle (*mandaprativṛtta*) of Mars and the other planets is merely a conceptual construction; for no one asserts that Mars and the others actually move in that manner in the sky. This is because the fast anomaly (*śīghraphala*) would not be perceived [otherwise].

In this context, the meaning of *cetyasya* (of this) is that the intersection of the two circles—the one produced by the *jha* and the one by the *kṣāśara*—is the point of descent (*pāta*); this is what should be understood. For this reason, the mean planet is derived through the proportion of the *ahargaṇa* (day-count) as obtained from calculation; [this refers to] the chapter on the conjunction of planets (*malabandhādhikāra*). [The commentary] *Bhāṣāṭīkā* explains: the meaning is "brought forth from the revolutions (*bhagaṇa*) of the [planetary] descents."

The meaning is that, by subtracting the revolution-number (bhagaṇa) of the apogee (pāta) and adding the apogee's own revolutions, the argument for the ascensional difference (śara)—which was indicated in the second verse of the *Chāyādhikāra* by the rule "from the slow-mean planet" (*mandasphuṭāt khecarataḥ*)—has been established in a manner consistent with logical reasoning. Now, [one might ask]: "But when the planet and its apogee are in conjunction at the same degree, why is the [ascensional difference] divided by six? [The answer follows:]...

Since the true arrow (sphuṭa-sāyaka) is destroyed by subtracting the apsis (niacala) from the circle of anomaly (ayanamaṇḍala), how was the calculation of the arrow stated by Śrīpati in his *Sphuṭapraha*? To answer this, he states the specific case of the Moon in the *Upajāti* meter, beginning with the word "pāta. Therefore, because the calculation of the arrow is based on the designation of the slow-mean planet as "true" (sphuṭa) along with its apsis (sapāta) within the epicycle of anomaly (śīghraprativṛtta)—that is, by assuming a mathematical reality therein—the result for the apsis (pāte śaniphalaṃ) is related to its own [mean] light, and is not derived from the apsis itself.

If the planet is retrograde (*viloma*), the correction is negative; if it is at its apogee (*pāta*), it is positive—this is the meaning. Having performed [the calculation] and having corrected [the planet] by means of such an apogee, the latitude (*śara*) is derived from the true planet as previously stated, which has been corrected by the two results. Or else, by another method, it becomes exactly the same as before. And thus, if the equation of anomaly (*śamraphala*) is applied in reverse to the planet, the apogee (*pāta*) should be added there to the slow-mean [planet]; that is, having applied the correction for the apogee in reverse to the slow [mean] result.

From what [calculation] is the true planet derived when joined with that? Since there is no distinction between the two ways [of calculation], the mean-true [planet] is established as the sum; therefore, the latitude (śara) has been correctly stated by Aupati as being from the true node added to the true planet. For this very reason, in order to know the true node, the correction for the slow motion (mṛdūlaphala) is introduced; it is the opposite of that, like a blind man [seeking] another's alms. Thus, it is clearly stated therein: "The determination of the elevation and depression of the eclipses is achieved through the most precise nodes."

Here, in accordance with what is to be stated later, the word *pratīpam* (contrary) is to be construed with *śaighryam antyam pareṣām* (the final swiftness of others). The sense is that one should not be deluded—that the result is to be brought near—and thus it should be understood.

[Objection: If this is so, then since the Moon's apogee is on the slow epicycle (*mandaprati-vṛtta*) while its node (*pāta*) is on the fast epicycle (*drāghu-prativṛtta*), it is logical to assume that the node is situated there [on the fast epicycle]. And since the mean motion of the planet exists at that location, the calculation of the Moon's latitude (*śara*)—either by adding the node as computed by calculation to the mean Moon, or else by subtracting the node corrected for the slow epicycle from the true Moon—is indeed established. Why, then, is it stated that the calculation of the Moon's latitude is performed by adding the node as computed by calculation to the *true* (not mean) Moon?

Nor should it be argued that because the "apparent moon" (sphuṭacandra) is not explicitly mentioned there, the term "mere moon" (kevalacandra) refers only to the mean [moon]; for by the term "mere moon," only the apparent [moon] is presented. Therefore, he says: "of the moon. For (hi), since, beyond the moon, at the intersection below the circle of the equatorial radius (trijyotpanna-kaśara-vṛtta) within the circle of the equinoctial shadow (kṣāvalaya), there occurs the intersection of the circle of the equatorial shadow with the diameter of the ear (karṇa) connected to the counter-circle (prativṛtta).

For this reason, the calculation of the arrow (śara) and the determination of its strength is derived from the true Moon—obtained by adding the established lunar apogee (siddha-candra-pāta) to the mean Moon—which itself results from the addition of the apogee to the day-count (ahargaṇa) obtained from the mean planet. Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the slow epicycle (manda-karṇa). For this very reason, the hypothesis that the apogees of Mars and the other planets are determined solely through calculation within the sphere of the stars (bhagola) is also refuted. This has been explained in detail in the section on planetary shadow (graha-chāyā), specifically in the exposition of the rationale for calculating the arrow. || 22 ||

Now he states the specific distinction between Mercury (Jña) and Venus (Śukra): The nodes (pāta-bhagaṇas) that are recited here for Mercury and Venus are greater than their anomalistic quadrants (śīghrakendra-bhagaṇas); therefore, they are stated as small for the sake of convenience. Their nodes, derived from the recited revolutions, should be subtracted from the apogees (alaka). In the chapter on the Sphere (Golādhyāya), it is indeed said that [the anomaly] is to be subtracted from the mean motion (cala) for the sake of establishing the anomaly; however, when the anomaly is with the node (sapāta), the correction (icchara) should be added. From this, the wise and learned have stated that the calculation of the equation of the center (śara-siddhi) for Mercury and Venus is achieved by adding the node. 23-24. In the Golādhyāya, the anomaly is indeed to be subtracted from the mean motion (cala) for the purpose of establishing the anomaly; however, when the anomaly is with the node (sapāta), the correction (icchara) should be added. From this, the wise and learned have stated that the calculation of the equation of the center (śara-siddhi) for Mercury and Venus is achieved by adding the node. (Note: The provided text contains a slight redundancy in the Sanskrit verse regarding the subtraction and addition of corrections, which has been interpreted to reflect the standard astronomical procedure for these planets.)

The true nodes of those two [Mars and Mercury] are obtained by adding their true apogees to their [true] anomalies; on the celestial sphere (bhagola), the node is indeed true. Now, as for the specific correction brought forth for the shadow using the center (kendra) of Venus and Jupiter as the sum of their apogees and nodes—that ought to occur at the position of the apogee itself, not at the position of the planet, since the planet exists elsewhere. In this regard, it appears as if there is a contradiction.

And so it is stated in the *Jalasiddhāntabhāṣya*: "The amount of eccentricity (vikṣepa) that occurs at the positions of the nodes (pāta) of Mercury and Venus is exactly the same as that which occurs for the planet situated anywhere else along its orbit. Regarding this, the following is the underlying rationale (*vāsanā*); no other cause can be established, and thus even Caturveda Ācārya expressed uncertainty. This is true. Herein it is said: those revolutions of the nodes (*pātabhagaṇa*) for Mercury and Venus as they are recited here, when multiplied by the revolutions of the apogees (*śīghrakendra*), become their respective [corrected] revolutions.

And thus they are read in the *Siddhāntacūḍāmaṇi* by Mādhava: "Therefore, the node (pāta) arising from the [mean] revolution-number should be added to its own apogee. When the apogee is subtracted from the planet, the true longitude (śrībhalekha) remains. To that [longitude] with the node added, the planet should be added for the purpose of producing the anomaly (kṣepakendra). Therefore, when the sum of the apogee and node is subtracted from the true [longitude], only the sum of the apogee and node remains; this is established. Furthermore, the mean-sphuta [longitude] is the anomaly (carakendra) on the epicycle relative to the apogee."

That [correction] should be applied to the node (*pāta*). When this is done, the apogee of anomaly (*vikṣepakendra*) will be separated by the equation of center (*mandaphala*). In the section on planetary shadow (*grahacchāyādhikāra*), it is stated that the true nodes (*sitajhapātau*) are joined with the apogee of anomaly (*sphuṭakendra*); thus, the apogee of anomaly minus the equation of center (*mandaphala*) is the apogee of anomaly (*śīghrakendra*), and the node (*pāta*) added to that is the corrected node. Therefore, the meaning is that the equation of center (*mandaphala*) is subtracted from the node (*pāta*). This is because the other [unadjusted] anomaly is untenable. Consequently, the negative equation of center (*mandaphala*) should be applied to the node.

Since the anomaly correction (*anupāta*) is established, the longitude of the apogee (*madhyagraha*) becomes equal to the node (*maṅśīna*) at the point of the ucca. That which is the circle of declination (*krāntivṛtta*) on the celestial sphere (*bhagola*) is the eccentric circle (*kapṛtta*). Therein, the true planet (*sphuṭagraha*) is located where the ecliptic (*dimaṇḍala*) intersects it. Indeed, the sum of that [longitude] and the true node (*sphuṭapāta*) is the center of latitude (*vikṣepakendra*). Therefore, having marked the intersection at the position of the true node, one should place the maximum degrees of latitude (*paramaviśeṣāṃśa*) at an interval of three signs (*tribha*) from there, both to the north and to the south.

Thus, when the apsis is subtracted from the mean [longitude], the anomaly at the true position is equal to the true anomaly obtained through calculation; this means that in the case of the apsis, it is not otherwise. ||23||24|| Now, as an incidental topic, he states the justification for the fact that "the true nodes of Mercury and Venus are joined with their respective equations of center" using the Vasantatilakā meter, beginning with the words "ye ca": the revolutions of the nodes of Mercury and Venus.

In this work, *Madhyamābhivara*, within the chapter on revolutions (*bhagaṇādhyāya*), those revolutions which are stated and recorded as having the numerical values of 521 for Mars and 893 for Mercury—along with others from texts such as the *Sūryasiddhānta* indicated by the word "and" (*ca*)—become the revolutions of the apogees (*śīghrakendra*) for Jupiter and Venus. When these are added sequentially to the revolutions of the apogees, they become the actual revolutions of the nodes (*pāta*). This concludes the section on the binding of the revolutions.

23. Since [the revolutions] are stated in this treatise (*karaṇa*) as being from the point of departure—that is, because they are produced from revolutions that were recited [in the original texts]—the nodes (*pāta*) of those two, Mercury and Venus, must be added respectively to Jupiter and the Moon in their forms as mean, solar, and true [longitude]. This is for the sake of obtaining the actual readings [of the positions]. If one asks, "In that case, why were such revolutions not stated previously?", he says: "For the sake of ease" (*sukhārthe*), meaning for the sake of facility in calculation (*gaṇitasaukaryārtha*).

The small [corrections] are said to be in the form of segments of a portion of the asterismal circle (bhagaṇa) of Aṣṭaka. (23) But if this is so, why did Brahmagupta state the calculation of the velocity-correction (śara) for Mercury and Venus as being from the "ecliptic apogee" (*śīghrocca*) of the true mean [longitude] conjoined with their own apogees (*pāta*), saying "from the *śīghra* [apogee]"? For a velocity-correction calculated from three apogees is not possible for those two. Otherwise, one might argue that for Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn as well, the calculation of the velocity-correction from the mean Sun would follow. Therefore, he states the resolution of this in the Upajāti meter: [The verse follows: "The velocity-correction of Mercury and Venus is indeed derived from the conjunction of the *śīghrocca* and the *pāta*; it is not that the correction is produced from three apogees. Just as the velocity-correction of the other planets is established from the mean Sun, so too is it for these two; there is no fault here. Thus he spoke.

Indeed, for the sake of determining the apogee (kendra), the mean planet is to be subtracted from the apogee. When the apogee is combined with the [previously] stated revolutions and the equation of the center (apakṣepa), the true slow-moving planet (mandaspaṣṭa) is to be added. This is the conclusion. Thus, by various methods, it has been stated by wise and clever scholars that, for the sake of brevity, the correction (śara-siddhi) for the Sun and Moon is obtained by adding the apogee and the equation of the center.

The mean anomaly (madhyahya) is to be subtracted; therefore, the correction for slow motion (mandaphala), as previously calculated from the sum of the anomaly and the apogee (ucca), should be applied there. This is because the true slow-mean planet is greater than the mean planet due to the application of the slow-motion correction. However, this is not the case for Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn, whose revolutions (bhagaṇa) are recorded as non-true (avastava). Their true revolutions are actually greater by the number of revolutions of their respective fast apogees (śīghrocca). Consequently, even for these planets, the calculation of the equatorial deviation (śara) must be combined with the fast apogee and so forth. Otherwise, such a conceptualization would be impossible, as no such method of derivation has been stated.

For this very reason, in the *Sūryasiddhānta*, because the node (*pāta*) is accepted as possessing twelve signs of zodiacal longitude like a planet, the swift equation (*śīghraphala*) is applied to the node; the true [longitude] of Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn is then derived by subtracting that from the mean [longitude]. For Mercury and Venus, the slow equation (*mandaphala*) is subtracted from the node in reverse order, and the resulting swift anomaly is used for the calculation of the latitude (*śara*). The relevant verse states: "In the case of Mars, Saturn, and Rāhu, the node possesses a swift-equation result similar to that of a planet."

The third left foot [of the verse] provides the result for Mercury and Venus. One's own fall (pāta) is the affliction caused by the planets; this applies to the Moon, Venus, Mars, Saturn, and Mercury. For the Moon, the [longitude of the] node is obtained by dividing the [equation of] deflection by the sine of the maximum deflection. By this [method], the slow-motion correction (mandaphala) for the lord of the small [periods] (Venus) is to be subtracted, while that of Saturn is added. For the remaining [planets], the true nodes are derived from the mean longitudes. Regarding the explanation of the path of Brahmagupta, why do the teachers of the Caturveda school not accept the dual connection of the eighth foot?

For Mercury and Venus, it is stated [by some] that they are derived from the true fast motion reversed by the mandaphala; or else, as stated by others, they are derived from the desired [true positions] after subtracting or adding the manda-phala and the cala-uccapāta (the anomaly and apsis). Furthermore, according to the *Laghvāryabhaṭīya*, for the other planets—Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn—they are obtained by subtracting or adding their respective manda-phalas and ucca-pātas; however, for Mercury and Venus, the degrees of anomaly (*valana-bhāga*) are corrected by their own manda-phala.

Thinking that [the results] might be inconsistent, the arrangement of the true and mean results was stated as it stands, following that [system]. Otherwise, the statement by Śrīpati, "from the mean result and from the [true] apsis," would be rendered invalid.

By the verse beginning with "ye cātra patabhagaṇā," the mean node (pāta) is established in its true form for the purpose of understanding its actual mean state within the model consisting of the fast apsis (śīghrakendra) and the slow apsis (mandakendra). Furthermore, since the addition of six signs is necessary to the true planet for the calculation of the latitude (śara), and because the correction by the established slow equation is required for the sake of the latitude, the node derived from the recited revolutions of the asterisms (ṛtabhagaṇa) is stated as it is, due to its utility in solving problems concerning the latitude.

For there is no additive correction (kṣepa) for the true node (vāstavapāta) obtained for the purpose of the true apsis (svarūpakendra) at the beginning of the slow motion (mandaśīrṣa). And since that [correction] is to be added to the mean planet for the sake of calculating the latitude (śara), it is by this means that the application of the reversed slow-motion correction (vyastamandaphala-saṃskaraṇa) to the node or the apogee is justified; because otherwise, there would be no basis for such corrections. Nor can it be argued that Mercury and Venus possess a "true node" (pataspaṣṭatva) through the application of the reversed slow-motion correction, while others do so through the reversed application of the fast-motion correction (śīghraphala); for there is a lack of evidence (mānābhāvāt).

Because it is more concise and follows the logical sequence, it is appropriate and has been established that the correction for both [equations of center] should be applied by combining their individual results. Otherwise, if one were to add the corrections to the true planet from the mean planet, the two corrections would remain as they are; however, this would lead to the undesirable consequence that the corrections for the apsis and the node would also have to be applied to the planet itself, just like the correction for the equation of center.

By this, in the *Balaguptasiddhāntabhāṣya*, Caturvedācārya—the learned Śukra—having added the [mean] anomaly to the [mean] planet by means of the [mean] apsis and the [mean] anomaly, derived the equation of center (*vikṣepa*). That [equation] ought to exist only at the position of the apsis, not at the position of the planet, because the planet resides elsewhere.

In response to the doubt that this [perception] therefore appears to be merely inferential, he has stated: "The belly of the enemy is at a high place; whatever the displacement is, exactly that much occurs for one who strikes while standing anywhere else. Here, it is established that perception itself is the cause; it cannot be said that there is any other instrument [of knowledge]. Thus, [the opponent's position] is refuted.

Therefore, as it is stated in the *Bhārdha-pī(vī)cūḍā* that [the anomaly] should be added to the anomaly of the apogee (pāta) combined with the anomaly of the center, because it is intended to be applied to the anomaly of the apsis (*takhaṣa*), it does not mean that for Mercury and Venus, their respective nodes (*pātau*) are corrected by the reversed equation of centering (*vañcala-phala*). Rather, they are corrected by the equation of centering exactly as it has been derived; this is to be understood from the fact that the term "reversed" (*vyasta*) is a qualification of the "equation of centering" (*vañcala-phala*).

Thus, in the *Ācāryakṛtabhāṣya* regarding the derivation of the [mean] revolutions (*bhagaṇa*), for Mercury and Venus, at that time, the apsis (*pāta*) is corrected by the reverse application of the slow anomaly (*mandaphala*). In the passage "the apsis is subtracted from the Moon's head (the apogee)," the phrase "corrected by the reverse application of the slow anomaly" is to be construed with "pure by subtraction from the circle" and with "the fast apogee. Therefore, the meaning to be understood is that the fast apogee, after being subtracted from the circle, is corrected by the reverse application of the slow anomaly.

Upon examining and practicing the previous texts, it is stated that when addressing Nala, the center in the slow epicycle (mandaphalamaṇḍala) is diminished by the mandasphuṭa, whereas in the fast epicycle (śīghroccapratimaṇḍala), that center is applied to the [true] planet; therefore, the slow correction (mandaphala) is applied in reverse order to the [mean] planet.

Alternatively, the meaning is that the planet whose true [longitude] is corrected by the slow (manda) and fast (śīghra) equations is such that, by means of the compound *mandaramaṭa*—where the middle planet (*madhyagraha*) is subtracted—the remaining slow equation (*mandaphala*), as it was obtained, is applied to the apsis (*pāta*). Thus, the slow equation is applied to the apsis in its direct form. The statement that it is "not reversed" (*avyasta*) is intended to indicate the inconsistency of the contrary correction mentioned by Brahmagupta; otherwise, there would be a contradiction with his own [stated] position. ||24||

Now he states the specific rule for the node of a planet: "Having constructed the apsidal circle on the sphere of the day (the ecliptic) as previously described, and having fixed the orbital circle as stated [in the previous chapter], one should bind the *śīghra-prativṛtta* (the epicycle of anomaly) upon this; that is the *vimaṇḍala* (eccentric orbit). Therein, the mean node of the planets is to be applied, increased by its own *śañji* (sine) and the argument (*iṣṭa*) of the anomaly. First, the node of the planet should be conceived as being on the celestial sphere (*bhagola*) itself; here, the node is indeed the true one.

Now, if another [orb] is bound at its end, then, having constructed there the equinoctial circle (*viṣuvavṛta*) and the ecliptic (*krāntivṛta*) as previously described, one should assume that circle to be the orbital sphere (*kakṣāmaṇḍala*). Therein, according to the method of the *chedyaka*, one should mark a point on the apsis-circle (*pratimaṇḍala*)—or here, on this apsis-circle—by counting the node (*pāta*) obtained through calculation in reverse order from Aries. A mark should be made there.

Now, having heard that the circle called the *vimaṇḍala* (eccentric orbit) returns together with the trijyā and the *cyā* (versed sine) at the beginning of the signs, one should likewise place the *pāta* (node) there. It is a wonder that the *maṇḍala* (mean orbit) and the *vimaṇḍala* meet first at one point and then a second time at an interval of half a circle; or rather, currently, the *vimaṇḍala* should be placed north or south of the *pratimaṇḍala* by the maximum degrees of deviation (*parama-vikṣepāṃśa*) as recited, at three signs ahead of or behind the *pāta*.

In that regard, the planet's true position (*sphuṭagraha*) revolves within the eccentric circle (*vimaṇḍala*). Therefore, the slow equation (*manda-phuṭa*) derived from Aries and so forth must be applied to the eccentric circle. Being situated there, it is displaced by an interval from the counter-eccentric circle (*pratimaṇḍala*); this is the specific difference at that location. Since there is no displacement when the planet is at the intersection of the circles, and the maximum displacement occurs at an interval of three signs (*tribha*), the intermediate values are determined by proportion. Consequently, the distance between the intersection of the circles and the planet must be known; that distance is obtained by subtracting the [mean] planet from the [true] planet.

It is like the retrograde motion of a planet. Suppose the apogee is at the center; if the maximum eccentricity (śara) is equal to the radius (trijyā) when the anomaly is at the center, then what is it for this desired [anomaly]? The result will be the perpendicular distance between the concentric circle (pratimaṇḍala) and the eccentric circle (vimaṇḍala). The line from the center of the Earth to the planet situated on the eccentric circle is the distance to that planet. And that is the *śīghrakarṇa* (the hypotenuse of the fast anomaly). If there is such an eccentricity at the tip of the hypotenuse from the center of the Earth, then how much would it be at the tip of the radius? This is the second proportionality (*parāśika*).

In the first case, the radius of the circle (trijyā) is the divisor; in the second, it is the multiplier. These two [results] are subtracted from sixty. The remainder is multiplied by the sine of the argument and divided by the radius; the resulting quotient is the perpendicular distance between the lines of the epicycle and the deferent. That is the true latitude (sphuṭa-śara). || 25 || 26 ||

Bhaṭṭotpala’s Commentary (Bhaṭotpala): Now, since the nodes of Mercury and Venus, as derived through the calculation of light-years (*dyutagaṇita*), are situated in the same position as the *māndhya* nodes and are thus suitable for conjunction with the slow-mean planets, the nature of the true node—which is suitable for conjunction with the true planet—is established. Therefore, he demonstrates the method for finding the difference between the true and mean nodes, as well as their observation, in two verses in the *Upajāti* meter, beginning with "sphuṭa": "The nodes of those two [Mercury and Venus], which are produced from the stated revolutions, are subtracted from the true [mean] and added [to the true planet]. [This means: The nodes of those two, Mercury and Venus, are those obtained from the stated revolutions (*bhagaṇa*). They are subtracted from the true [mean] and added [to the true planet]. [The result is the true node. (Note: The text provided appears to be a fragment of a commentary explaining how to calculate the true node by adjusting the mean node using the equation of center.)

By the word "sphuṭa" (apparent), Mercury and Venus are meant as being "clear. When these two are subtracted from their respective mean apogees, they are corrected by the mandaphala (equation of center) as it has been obtained; when added to those [mean apogees] in reverse order, they become the apparent [positions]. This is because it is stated that the mean apogee—corrected by the equation of the anomaly derived from the sum of the mean apogee and the node—is made "clear" (apparent) by the correction of its sighra-phala (equation of the faster anomaly); therefore, its inclusion here is for that very reason.

For instance: when the [mean] planet is diminished by the application of the slow-motion correction (mandaphala-saṃskāra) as it was previously calculated, and then increased by the applied fast-motion correction (śīghraphala-saṃskāra), the result—accomplished through the absence of the slow-motion correction—is the true planet (sphuṭa). Here, the result obtained through calculation is the mean node (madhyama-pāta); when this is corrected by the negative fast-motion correction, the true node (sphuṭa-pāta) is established. Therefore, the fast apogee (śīghrocca) is not to be taken alone.

Because it would follow that the [mean] apogee, corrected by the two results derived from the middle [longitude], would become the true [apogee]. Furthermore, because it would follow that the anomaly (kuṭona), which is the form of the slow-mean [longitude], would be the true [anomaly] when corrected by the result of the anomaly; and because it would follow that the slow-mean apogee, when corrected by the reversed result of the anomaly, would become the true [apogee]. This contradicts the established doctrine regarding the apogee. Chapter 2, Verse 34: And the [true] apogee should be calculated as the slow-mean apogee plus the slow-result as obtained, minus the fast-result, plus the fast-apogee. For, by this, the mean planet becomes the true planet. [Otherwise,] it would involve an excessive complexity of assumptions (kalpanā-gaurava).

Furthermore, there is the fallacy that the *sphuṭa* (apparent) and *śīghrocca* (swift apogee) would possess the status of being defined by their own specific characteristics (*lakṣaṇika*). By this, the view that the slow planet (*manda-graha*) is corrected by the *yathāgata-maṇḍala* (the attained epicycle) is refuted, because there is no distinction between the mean and the apparent [positions] in that case. Now, if it is argued that by the word *sphuṭa*, the mean planet corrected solely by the equation of center (*mandaphala*) is intended, and by the word *ucca*, the [mean] apogee corrected solely by the equation of center is intended, and that through these two the performance of the required operation is accomplished—this is not so. For by the word *sphuṭa*, the mean planet corrected by the equation of center (*calīma-phala*) is not presented. This has been explained at length in the section on the desired anomaly (*iṣṭāpavartya*).

Now, he demonstrates the location of the true node (*sphuṭapāta*) on the *niruktagola* (the described sphere). On the stellar sphere (*bhagola*), the true node is at the intersection (*saṃpāta*) of the equator of the arrows (*śaravṛtta*) and the ecliptic (*krāntivṛtta*). By the use of the particle "eva" (only), it is indicated that there is no mean node (*madhyamapāta*) at that point. This is because, by marking the location of the true declination (*vikṣepa*) at that intersection, those two points [the mean and true nodes] are distinct from one another.

Just as an actual object situated in opposition [to the observer] is perceived within the field of vision at a specific location on the orbital circle, it appears distinct at that orbital point because the epicycle (śāntivṛtta) conforms to the shape of the orbit; likewise, the intersection of the equatorial sphere with the ecliptic situated in the corresponding space is known as the true node (sphuṭapāta), which is more closely associated with that orbit, due to its fixed relationship with the actual physical form of the planet in that celestial sphere.

In the absence of arrows, the observation of the great image along its corresponding meridian line is also [required]. Now, for the purpose of showing the location of the middle point of transit, he states the position of a specific circle: "In the manner described, the connection with the ecliptic and the sphere of the zodiac (bhagola) should be understood; a latitudinal circle (takṣāvalaya) should be constructed, because it follows the form of the ecliptic and approximates the orbit of the planet. It is fixed according to the method stated in the *Cheyakakta*. Having established it in accordance with the respective positions, one should fix it.

In this *śīghraprativṛtta* (epicycle of anomaly), the orbit of that planet should be bound by means of the shadow-producers (*chāyākara*)—that is, the arrow-parts (*śarāṃśa*) fallen upon it, measured in minutes of arc (*kalā*) obtained by dividing the stated arrow-parts by sixty. Here, in this *vimaṇḍala*, the conjunction of planets occurring at its intersection (*saṃpāta*) is the one arrived at through calculation. This is the intended meaning (*bhāva*).

Since there is a common perception that the motion of a planet occurs above the ecliptic (krāntivṛtta) when it is fixed upon the ecliptic on the celestial sphere (bhagola), in order to dispel that notion, the [ecliptic] should be bound according to the path of the ecliptic upon the planetary sphere (grahagola). Therein, the orbit (kakṣāvṛtta) should also be fixed in the manner previously described. The intersection of these two is the true node (sphuṭapāta).

Then, there, in accordance with the observation of the motion of the shadow of the gnomon and the revolution of the circle of the asterisms over time, the sages—possessing supersensuous vision—conceived the celestial sphere as moving, with its center situated at another point within the meridian circle, directed toward a high elevation above the earth’s surface. Therein, they joined a secondary circle (prativṛtta) equal to the orbital circle (kakṣāvṛtta), according to the aforementioned directions; likewise, they joined a secondary circle related to the declination circle (śaravṛtta). They also [joined] the points of intersection of those two.

Now, every year, two circles with radii equal to the semi-major axes of the epicycles—having forms corresponding to the interior and exterior [of the deferent] and fixed according to the positions of the planets—are to be constructed, intersecting at the center of the earth. From the center of the earth, a circle in the shape of a bow (an arc) should be drawn. The point of intersection of those two [circles] is the *madhyama-pāta* (mean node). The maximum distance between those two is equal to the declination (*śara*) as read in the tables. In that case, the north-south distance between the two planets is the *śara* on the *karṇagola* (the sphere of the hypotenuse).

Since those two nodes are connected to the points where the epicycle meets the deferent, the difference between the nodes is equal to the correction for anomaly (*grahaphala*); this has already been explained in detail. For if one were to state that the mean node occurs at the intersection of the deferent, it would lead to the undesirable consequence of the mean node being identical to the true node. Furthermore, the positions of the apogees on the epicycles of the deferents are not determined by the marking of signs (*rāśi*) on the ecliptic. [Objection: Should not the epicycle be tied to a circle equal to the epicycle itself? [Response: No, because it was not stated that the intersection should be made there.

At the point of intersection situated at the middle node (madhyapāta), it is appropriate that the correction for the middle node itself be applied first; this has been sufficiently explained. Now, one might object: "According to the method already stated, at the intersection of the epicycle of the anomaly (karṇa) and the eccentric circle (dhyāsavṛtta), Mercury and Venus attain their nodes as established by the calculation of the day-count (ahargaṇa), whereas for the other planets they do not. How then is this consistent? To this he says: "By the mean [longitude] of the Sun. For Mercury and Venus, the node obtained through calculation is indeed the true one; since it is joined with its own respective mean apogee (śīghrakendra), it becomes correct.

It should be understood as the true node (*pāta*); for it is not merely so, but because in its conjunction with other planets, one observes the actual mean motion of the Moon, Mercury, and Venus as joined with the node calculated through mathematical computation, the sense is that this [node] is indeed correct.

By this, what was stated previously—that the sphere (*gola*) is situated within the *chedyakī*—is clearly explained. In the first verse, the first, third, and fourth feet follow the *vaṃśastha* meter, while the second foot follows the *indravaṃśā*; thus, this meter is not one of common usage. However, since there is no end to the meters used by the sages (*ārṣa*), there is no fault. Alternatively, based on the reading "patapha," because it is a mixture of *vaṃśastha* and *indravaṃśā*, it may be considered an *upajātī* patha. || 26 ||

Now he describes the daily revolution (the *ahorātravṛtta*): "At a distance equal to the desired declination (*krānti*) from all sides, one should draw a circle; this is the daily revolution-circle (*ahorātravṛtta*). Having fixed it there, one should mark it with sixty divisions for the *ghaṭīs*. The radius of this [circle] is considered to be the *khujīvā* (the sine of the co-latitude). From the meridian line, whether to the north or to the south, at a distance everywhere equal to the desired declination, whatever circle is drawn—that is the daily revolution-circle. By means of that circle, the sun moves on that particular day; such is the meaning."

Of that [circle], this is the northern limit, [marked by] the point of the equinox. || 27 || Now he says something else: "Then, starting from the mark of the *krāntipāta* (the node of the ecliptic), one should determine Aries and the other signs in direct order; one should fix the diurnal circles for these signs beginning with Aries. || 28 || Starting from the mark of the *krāntipāta*, having determined the other signs beginning with Aries at intervals of thirty degrees each, one should fix the corresponding diurnal circles (*ahorātravṛtta*) in front of them. And those [circles] are three in number, situated on both sides of the meridian circle (*nāḍīvṛkṣa*).

These very [lines] for the twelve signs of the zodiac, both with and without precession (sāyana), are according to their sequence. Commentary (Bhaṭṭotpala): Now, he describes the construction of the day-and-night circle (ahorātravṛtta) using the Sragviṇī meter, beginning with the words "īpsita. From the point where the equinoctial line (iṣuvavṛtta) intersects the meridian, one should mark it toward the south or all around that circle; at a distance equal to the desired declination (krānti) in that direction, one should fix a bamboo splinter (vaṃśaśalākā) forming the day-and-night circle. Having fixed it there upon the celestial sphere (bhagola), one should mark it with sixty divisions representing the ghaṭīs.

This [point] is the intersection of the equinoctial circle (*krāntivṛtta*) with one part of the *vṛṣa* (Taurus) circle, or the entry point of the declination circle (*śaravṛtta*). The rotations occur precisely within that interval in which the two [circles] are situated. This is always observed by the attentive observer, because it is accepted that the rotation [of the spheres] occurs through the support of the two poles of the impelling wind (*pravaha-vāyu*). That rotation follows the model of the equinoctial circle. Now, since equal circles are established on the stellar sphere (*bhagola*), one might object that this is not the same as what was stated previously; to this he says: "of this"—that is, of the daily circle (*ahorātra-vṛtta*).

The segment of the *viṣkambha* (the diameter) is the sine of the arc; these are considered the "yujyas" (*yujyāmatāḥ*), as established in the *Golādhyāya* by Bhāṭṭotpala. Furthermore, the perimeters of the celestial sphere (*bhagola*) situated above and below are indeed equal. However, when one takes the perimeters of the decrease on both sides of the central equatorial circumference of the *bhagola*, their equality is not as evident as that of the terrestrial equatorial circumference. Therefore, it is as previously maintained regarding the diameter.

By this method of the circle, the previous day-and-night circle is preceded by the revolution of that region in sixty *ghaṭīs*. Therefore, this is added to the sixty *ghaṭīs*; half of that is taken as equal to the previously established chord associated with it, because there is no equality with the chord of the night. (27) Now, since the declination is joined at every entry on the celestial sphere (*bhagola*), and because it is impossible for it to exist anywhere other than in the place four degrees from the declination, this must be established by taking the declination-equivalent at each point; otherwise, in the absence of a determining factor, it would apply to every location.

Because, due to that [obscuration], the previous occurrences would be hidden within its binding, knowledge established therein would be impossible; therefore, he says "Now, how? in order to provide a solution. The meaning is: if you suspect that a binding is improper because the obscuration of the sphere (golācchādana) is possible through the occurrence of various self-possibilities as described in the *Rātravṛtta*, then [the following applies]. "In the direct order" (*anuloma*) means from the point of the intersection of the declination (*krāntipāta*)—that is, from the location where the declination intersects—in accordance with the sequence of the signs of the zodiac (*rāśicakra*). Thus ends the section.

Twelve [revolutions] are to be subtracted. Here, on the ecliptic, thirty degrees each consisting of three parts must be imagined as the positions of the nodes. By this, the signs beginning with Aries marked at the position of Revatī are indeed the true ones. For the purpose of calculating planetary motion, these are called "true" signs; thus, the opposing view is clearly refuted. To the question, "Why should these [twelve] be imagined here?", he says: "By this... (etena).

One should construct the diurnal circles according to the method described above for Aries and the other signs, whose positions are determined by the limits of the intersection points of the equator and the ecliptic, and which extend as far as the last degrees of the respective signs. However, because the actual zodiacal signs do not have fixed locations, the construction of diurnal circles based on them has been disregarded.

And likewise, since there are thirty degrees in the *kāntivṛtta* (ecliptic), it is possible that due to the sparsity of the points fixed upon that circle, one might fail to perceive the previous positions and thus lose knowledge of their configuration; for this reason, it was stated otherwise, because without the *ahorātravṛtta* (diurnal circle), it would be impossible to know the state of its revolution. Furthermore, the *śaravṛtta* (latitude circle) is not fixed; therefore, the connection with the *ahorātravṛtta* was not mentioned [for the latitude circle] because it is impossible to do so—this is the intended meaning. || 28 ||

Now he states its summary: "The three [circles] situated on both sides of the meridian-line (nāḍīvṛtta) in direct and reverse order constitute the celestial sphere (bhagola); this very same thing should be known as the terrestrial sphere (khecaragola). Here, one should fix the ecliptic (apamaṇḍala) or the equator (sūtradhāra) upon that very [sphere], and the orbits of Saturn and the other planets, resembling the web of a spider, should be attached. Having thus bound the celestial sphere (khagola) within the tube of the terrestrial sphere (khaḍgagola), and having fixed it upon the gnomon (yaṣṭi), one should rotate it; the two spheres, supported by the gnomon, remain stable. (29–31)

Just as this sphere of the fixed stars (bhagola) is bound, so too should the spheres of the planets (grahagola) be bound. However, their cross-sections (chedyakas) should not be rotated; rather, they should be displayed exactly as they exist externally. Alternatively, on the sphere of the fixed stars, the orbits (kakṣās) of the Moon and the others should be shown by means of lower threads placed below the ecliptic band (apamagalabandha). Specifically, the orbits of the Moon and the others should be displayed using lower threads fixed at the bottom.

Having made the two celestial spheres (bhagola) of one kind, with their axes aligned, and having fixed the two stars (the poles) at the ends of the two gnomons, one should demonstrate the revolution of the spheres. || 29 || 30 || 31 || Thus ends the *Mitākṣara*, the commentary on the *Golabandha*, composed by the venerable Ācārya Māskara. Herein ends the eighteenth chapter. [End of section] 181.

Furthermore, on the sphere of the ecliptic tree, the diurnal circles (ahorātravṛtta) of the twelve zodiacal signs are bound separately. To illustrate: three diurnal circles for the regions ending at the end of Gemini are bound. Beyond that, the diurnal circle ending at Cancer is not distinct from the diurnal circle ending at Aries, because it has the same shape as the diurnal circle ending at Aries. The diurnal circle ending at Leo is not distinct from the diurnal circle ending at Aries. The diurnal circle ending at Virgo is the equinoctial circle (viṣuvavṛtta).

Thus, since the signs situated on the *rakṣiṇa-gola* (the protective sphere) are also like this, he concludes the description of the *bhagola-bandha* (the construction of the celestial sphere) as stated above and says something else regarding it: "On both sides of the equator (*nāḍīvṛtta*)," and so forth. Those celestial equatorial circles (*surātravṛtta*) are three each on both sides of the equator—in the northern and southern sectors—situated in order. Thus, there are three circles in the northern sector from the equator; these are the celestial equatorial circles for Aries, Taurus, and Gemini, respectively, starting from the vicinity of the equator.

These same [circles] belong to Vyuma, Karka, Siṃha, Kanyā, and so on. Thus, on the southern side, there are three circles of day-and-night (horātra-vṛtta) for Tuṇa, Vṛścika, and Dhanu in sequence; these same [circles], when taken in reverse order, belong to Aṅka, Mithuna, and Mīna, etc. This is the nature of the day-and-night circles on the sphere (gola). The sense is that it is not at all contradictory that they are not ten distinct [circles]. Now, one might ask: "Is this constructed sphere (gola) the 'Sphere of the Stars' (bhagola), because of its connection with the zodiacal signs (bhā) and the circles of the asterisms (nakṣatra), etc.? To this he says: "This. This aforementioned sphere is the bhagola.

This is because of its connection with the movements [of the planets]. The meaning is that the great circle, the horizon, and so forth were mentioned incidentally (*prasaṅgāt*) and not as primary; therefore, they do not belong to the planetary sphere (*grahagola*). Now, one might ask: since the planetary spheres were previously indicated by the verse beginning with "one should bind the moon and Mercury" (*badhnīyācchaśisaumya*), why have the planetary spheres not been described? To this he replies: "In the planetary sphere, this very [sphere] is to be known. This means that the aforementioned stellar sphere (*bhagola*) is to be understood as the sphere of the planets. The word "only" (*eva*) has the sense of "also" (*api*).

Therefore, for him, the celestial sphere (bhagola) [is considered] due to its connection with both; otherwise, there would be a lack of a determining factor (vinigamanāviraha) because of the lack of distinction between the two. This is the intended meaning, as it conforms to that [other] form. || 29 || Now, even so, the mention here of its being situated on the celestial sphere (bhagola), or its being situated at mutual midpoints, is not contradicted by the elevation (unnati) specified by the Jaina [tradition]. To this, he says in the verse: "Here, on the apamaṇḍala" (the ecliptic). Here, on the celestial sphere fixed within the [visible] globe, on the *apamaṇḍala*—that is, on the circle of declination (*krāntivṛtta*)—and along the path in space following that.

Of that ecliptic (*krāntivṛtta*); the particle *eva* (only) serves to exclude any other circle. In the lower portion: Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, the Sun, Venus, Mercury, and the Moon—their orbits (*kakṣā*) are circles made of bamboo strips. One should fix them. Now, one might ask: how can they be perceived in the sky as having such a shape? To this he says: "The master-builders (*sūtradhāra*) should carve them. Likewise, on my ecliptic, four marks should be made at equal intervals by means of a cord (*sūtra*).

The meaning is that there, having tied a separate string for each [component], one should fasten the *kabhaṭa*, *śamyā*, and so forth to the place of the *kakṣā* (axle-box) using those strings. Furthermore, the word "or" (*vā*) implies an alternative method: it is indicated that this procedure applies only when the *golaka* (ball/weight) is fixed in clay; in that case, the aforementioned fastening to the arrangement of the *kakṣā* below need not be performed.

Now, one might object: "Since the ecliptic is so subtle, it is impossible for all the latitudinal circles (*kakṣā*) to revolve beneath it in a serial order. To this he replies: "Like the light of a spider's web" (*ūrṇanābhalabhā*). A *markaṭikā* is that which has wool (*ūrṇā*) constantly at its navel; the meaning is that its radiance is like the web-like lattice of colored threads made by such a spider, which is well known in windows and the like. Just as in that lattice of rays the upper circle is lighter than the one below it, so too, in the case of Saturn, the circle of a hundred thousand [yojanas] is even more subtle within the ecliptic.

Between the orbits of Śani (Saturn) and Vṛtra (Rāhu), the orbit of Mercury (Laghubhūta) is situated within the sphere of Jupiter (Gurukakṣā). Within that [space], the orbits of Mars and the others are arranged one above the other; the meaning is that they are not placed according to the order of their colors. Dividing each planet's own orbit by its respective radius (śara-vṛtta), the counter-orbits (pratimaṇḍala) and so forth—though unstable—should be fixed according to the method described for that purpose. Consequently, on the stellar sphere (bhagola), the declination circles (krāntivṛtta) and the right-ascension circles (dhruvavṛtta) of the planets need not be drawn. ||30||

Now, one might object: "Since the stars and planets are fixed within the celestial sphere (bhagola), their observation [from the terrestrial sphere] would be impossible. To this, he says in verse: "Having bound the celestial sphere to the axis... In the manner described above, having bound the celestial sphere—along with the planetary sphere—to the axis, that is, the polar axis; and having fixed that axis within the tube of the terrestrial sphere (khagola) for the purpose of connecting the north and south tubes of the terrestrial sphere.

Having inserted a loose axle-rod through two holes made outside the terrestrial sphere (Bhagola) consisting of clay, one should cause the maker to rotate it westward in accordance with the observed revolution of that fixed terrestrial sphere. Thus, since the rotation of the fixed sphere is possible, there is no defect; this is the intended meaning. Now, if the fixed sphere can rotate, would it not follow that the two previously fixed circles of the ecliptic and the equator would also rotate due to their connection with the axis?

Wandering [in that manner] is not appropriate because it would result in a contradiction with that [instruction]; therefore, he says, "stable. Why? He states the reason: "supported by a staff. Even though the interior of the tube is curved, the meaning is that because it is supported by a staff, it remains in the previously mentioned alignment of the tube.

In that case, just as the measurement of the sphere of the asterisms (bhagola), which serves as the support, is possible through the rotation of a loose-tipped pin situated within a tube, so too the rotation of the two [the earth and the sphere] would be impossible because no mention is made of inserting a pin with a shaft; such is the intended meaning. ||31|| Now, since the chapter commenced has been explained, he states the conclusion: "Thus ends the chapter on the construction of the sphere (golabandha). ||32||

In this work titled *Śiromaṇimarīci*, composed by the son of Gaṇaka Raṅganātha—who belongs to the lineage of the venerable Vaivasvata—this clear exposition on the composition of the *Golādhyāya* has reached its conclusion. Thus ends the chapter on the Composition of the Sphere (*Golabandhādhikāra*) in the *Marīci* commentary on the *Siddhāntaśiromaṇi*, the latter part of which was composed by Gaṇaka Munīśvara, whose other name is Viśvarūpa, the sovereign among the Gaṇakas of the Śālva country. This is the twenty-seventh chapter. 27.
